[size=3]The latest effort from the Coen brothers somehow manages to masquerade as a taut thriller, while providing a glaring examination of the pervasiveness of violence in society. By infusing humor with images of gruesome bloodshed, it causes us to question how at ease we have become with human carnage and whether we will ever return to the generation of Old Men, when senseless murder would receive more notice than the ho-hum attitude of today.

                  In the vast Texas countryside, hunter Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon $2 million and a heap of dead bodies at a drug deal gone wrong. He takes the money home only to return to the scene to help the one living person he left behind. He is spotted and pursued by a ghostly assassin, Anton Chigurh, (Javier Bardem) who piles up an extensive body count in his search of Moss and the jackpot. Worn down Sheriff Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) leads the investigation and tries to get to Moss before Chigurh. The cat and mouse game between Chigurh and Moss is never short of thrilling, but Bell is the focal point of the film, providing context to the absurdity of the chase as well as the rising sadism in todays culture.

                  As the first gunshot plants in the middle of a mans forehead, it is clear the film will not mask violence but exaggerate the bloodbath and not merely for the sake of entertainment. Each severed limb only reinforces the brutality of murder  a far stretch from the watered down version of violence in so many movies screening right now. This isnt the fantasy world of James Bond (the series has presented violence more realistically as of late). If you get shot, you dont let out a small yelp and crumple to the ground with a petite stain that resembles red finger paint. Instead, as presented here, the victim is catapulted by the shear force of impact and blood spews like a geyser. The connection between cinema and violence in real life has been argued to no end. Although the debate continues, consider the potential impact if younger people were imbedded with these grisly images. Perhaps we could have avoided a few unnecessary deaths and front page headlines.

                  This film does not evoke such optimism. Sheriff Bell is a man who has seen more than his fair share of crimes after inheriting his position from the men of his family. As the moral compass of the film, he seems far more interested in small talk than delving deep into the investigation. If you cant change the outcome, what is the point? When asked by his deputy if he wanted to reexamine the crime scene, he responded he would, only if there were a fresh body. 

      Now, I have no background in law enforcement, but I have experienced a sense of helplessness that goes along with steady bloodshed. As a news reporter in Augusta, I sat next to a police scanner all day, waiting for the inevitable gloom that would pour out from the machine. I began to lose sight of whether I was a reporter or a professional ambulance chaser. The yellow tape, the body bags and such sights I had only seen in movies became commonplace. What started as shock morphed into disillusionment and even worse, numbness. How could I rationalize three dead bodies over something as futile as a stolen scooter? And yet, I still woke up the next morning, went to the crime scene and wrote every vivid detail as if it were just another day at the office. I have since sworn that I will never return to police reporting. Much like Sheriff Bell, I reached my breaking point. I guess when death becomes monotonous you need to find a new line of work. In the film, millions of dollars were at stake, but in comparison, it is really any different from the killings over the scooter?

                  No Country is fascinating in that in provides a critique on violence and remains entertaining as hell at the same time. Javier Bardem plays an eccentric maniac, driven by an ideology that remains unclear. Perhaps there is no reason. This sentiment would echo many of the killings that occur every day. He uses a supped up air tank attached to a bolt gun, which produces a deafening thud when fired. It made me jump out of my seat at least a half dozen times during the screening. His voice was so deep it would make Shaq sound like a high-pitch teenage girl. It would be no stretch to compare Chigurh to Hannibal Lector, played by the icy Anthony Hopkins. His antics do more than just produce a larger than life character. They create a dichotomy for the audience. A gas station clerk stutters at Chigurh while his life comes down to a coin flip. Chigurh mocks the man, and the audience erupted in laughter. When Moss is retrieving the money from a motel ventilation shaft, he hears the shots that were meant for him actually kill his neighbors. He then displays the perfect, oh shit face. Once again, the viewers went crazy. Should we feel awkward that we are laughing as bodies are flying? Considering this is coming from the people who made Fargo, in which stuffing a dead body into a wood chipper was hilarious, we should not be surprised. It seems they enjoy making the audience squirm but with a sly smile. Despite the laughs, the gravity of the murder is understood, which distinguishes it from the half-assed violence plaguing Hollywood films.

                  It seems that the cinematic landscape of this era only contains only two types of film: escapist and art house. The Coen brothers have once again obliterated this mold. No Country is part thriller, part social commentary, all the while remaining self-reflexive to the genre. As with most suspense stories, there is a buildup for a showdown between protagonist and villain. But just when this definitive confrontation is expected, the Coens pull the plug, ultimately saying this film is more than just your typical thriller. Instead of a climatic shootout, we only see a quick shot of who has perished. I heard some in the lobby after the film say they were let down by the end. But here, there is no little bow that magically wraps up everything. Instead, the finale transitions to a grizzled sheriff unable to cope with the vicious nature of a world that has grown so outlandish to him. It is meaningless that these are the characters weve followed the last few hours. Through the eyes of this disillusioned man, it is just another corpse to add to the mountain. Why should it receive any special treatment? And by resisting the conventional conclusion, the Coens have crafted a film that extends beyond entertainment to one that makes a dent in the social consciousness of the astute.

No Country for Old Men is the most formally assured film of the Coen Brothers' careers.  Faithfully adapted from Cormac McCarthy's novel, the film is meticulously constructed--almost suffocatingly so, which is appropriate given the film's themes; as the film's opening shots of unpopulated landscapes suggest, the characters in No Country exist in a universe indifferent to their presence, where the same tapestry of life and death and struggle plays out generation after generation.  Those who complain that the Coens are just cynical, empty stylists who condescend to their characters as they move them through their plots like pieces on a chessboard grossly misread their work: the coens' characters, in their films in general and in No Country in particular, grapple constantly with issues of morality, they just don't find those views validated or refuted by the world around them.  They are all, like Tommy Lee Jones' Sheriff Bell, left without "God coming into their lives," and it is the mark of the Coens' oft-unnoticed humanism that they take their characters' moral struggles seriously even as they depict the greater indifference of the world around them.  Jones, Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin, and Kelly Macdonald all deliver outstanding performances, and Roger Deakins' cinematography finds beauty in the darkest corners of the Coens' world.
My faith in filmmaking has been rejuvenated.

I am fairly certain that there will not be a better movie out this year, as gripping, intelligent, and perfectly woven as No Country for Old Men.  It was not easy for me to come to that decision.  See, the movie lays itself out as a chase with the stakes being high for Bell, Chigurh, and Moss.  No Country follows that path without skipping a beat, keeping the action tense and musings from Jones interesting.  But the film eventually takes a left turn, which I don't doubt will throw audiences as it did me.  Yet I thought about it, knowing the choice was absolutely deliberate and not poor film making.  What the Coen brothers have done is left the audience cheated, which is not entirely dissimilar from what occurs with the characters in the film.  My only qualm with the picture that I can find is just a little more screen time for Bell prior to the shift, he knows that he has high personal stakes here, but I never felt it as strongly as other characters.  Besides that, this film is miles ahead of a majority of movies released this year.  The humor is sleight but intelligent, just little quirks like at the first scene of a crime, that the first thing each person notices is that the dog was even shot.  The film is also masterfully edited, ratcheting tension by never letting the audience become comfortable.  There are also some fantastic shots, early on Moss is running away from some Mexicans only for thunder to strike off in the distance, telling us this is not going to be an easy ride.  There's also another point where Anton stares at a TV, he sees himself, but when Bell later sees the same TV, he sees himself and his shadow.  Perfectly summarizing the character they are within the chase, Anton is a definite cold blood killer, no shades to him.  However Bell feels like he cannot keep up with this modern world of killers, has this made him a shadow of a sherrif or not?  Minimal music is used throughout creating unrelenting uneasiness.  It helps that the actors are firing on all cylinders, I can't single out a performance because they are each so strong.  If anything, I'm sure we'll see a lot more of Josh Brolin in the movies soon.  There's so much to be said about this movie, it is simply a brilliant picture that will entertain, mistify, and stay with you strongly after seeing it.
Cool to see the Coens going back to their darker roots. Mix that with one of the greatest living writers in Cormac McCarthy makes this a masterpiece in its own rights.

A+

This is absolutely flawless filmmaking.
ABSOLUTELY FLAWLESS.
The first three-quarters of the movie is perfect.  I say that without fear of hyperbole or any lingering doubts.
However, at a crucial point in the film, a gross misstep in the storytelling method threatens to pull this thing entirely off the rails.  It is a testament to the Coen Brothers and all involved that it survives.
I've been thinking about this a lot in the four hours since I saw the picture, and I waffle back and forth between HATING THE FILM FOR FUCKING ME OVER LIKE THAT and not really minding so much.
My four star rating is almost arbitrary at this point.  I could go as low as three stars, as high as four and seven-eighths.
I guess the best way to put it is that this was my favorite film EVER for the first hour-and-a-half, and I walked out not knowing how to feel about it.

I need to see it again before I make a real decision, which I plan on doing as early as tomorrow.

saw it at TIFF 07.  the coens rock.

The only thing better then the movie itself, was the reaction of a crowd of confused/pissed off movie patrons as they were taken off guard by the movie's ending. I couldn't help myself as I listened to their groans of disapproval.

The actin' was top-draw'r, with Javyar Bardim givin' a performance offa the ages. He created thur one of the greatest villains these old eyes have ever seen in a movin' image. And that's a bold statement I will die on my gravestone defendin'.

The Coen's again deliver an extremely interesting flick and while I thought it got a little bit too confusing in the last half-hour or so, most of No Country For Old Men is golden. the coen brothers have always been literary directors, operating in depth of motifs and foreshadowing as well as vast, beautiful imagery. no country for old men is no exception, bringing a darkness and visceral drive not seen in their films since blood simple. no country also sports performances by some not so regular cast members (but of course stephen root shows up for a short time.) bardem's performance is the heart and soul of the film. he's messy yet strangely classy and never short of horrifying. the coen brothers again manage to create a character that's quirky and borderline laughable, yet bloodthirsty and heartless. brolin succeeds in inviting us into his madness and into his arrogance. tommy lee jones also provides off-color humor with a tinge of satire and as always a mature, wizened composure.  no country for old men is cinematic perfection; a visceral scoreless cycle of hunting and being hunted. it appeals to the mind as well as the eyes. rivaling fargo as the brother's best, no country for old men is impossible to ignore.

Bardem's calm yet clearly disturbed Anton Chigurh is one of the best on screen villains in recent memory.  Topped off with the usual excellent cinematography, a refreshingly odd story with plenty of twists, deaths, killer air pressure valves, and an importance placed on coin flipping like no other movie, this film makes me smile and break free of my usual cynical views on the garbage coming out of Hollywood, and realize that perhaps there is still some worth to American cinema.

"No Country For Old Men" was one of those movies that I was dying to see from the second that I saw the trailer back in early summer. Then I read the early reviews coming out of Cannes and I was totally psyched after that, and I couldn't wait for November to come around. The movie came out last weekend, November 9th, but I managed to see it this weekend due to its still limited, but significant expansion in theaters it had this week. The movie does not disappoint, but it did catch me off guard a little, and it ended up being something a little different than I expected.

Walking out of the film I could not help but discuss it with the person that I saw it with. It's ending is entirely unconventional and fairly uncommercial to be honest, but it certainly did spark conversation and thought. Did I like it? Not necessarily, but I'll get to that more later on. For now, I'd like to say, this was probably one of the best directed film's I have seen in a long time. The Coen Brothers absolutely mastered the art of suspense in this film and the action sequences are unbelievably unsettling because of how realistic they are. I don't know if I've ever seen this many character's killed off in a crime drama in such disturbing, realistic, unsettling manners as the character's in this film. It's a very violent film, and because it contains so much violence, it was incredibly important that the violent scenes throughout were handled with care and with proper attention. The action scenes in this film absolutely received the care and attention they deserved, no question about that. I was on the edge of my seat throughout most of the first 3/4's or so of the film and had they Brothers handled the end of the film a little differently, perhaps it could've been a pretty decent sized hit at the box office. The way it currently is, I don't think it can make more than 15 or so million just because of its inaccessibility with many regular viewers. That still has more to do with the writing than the direction so I'll get to that later once again. Otherwise this film's direction was pitch perfect.

The acting was no less impressive and was probably the most perfect thing about the movie. The best performance was no doubt from Javier Bardem who played "Anton Chigurh", in other words, the psychopathic bad guy. He is scary as hell throughout the film and his performance never ever goes out of character's, although the script does take him out of character at least once, but I'll once again, get to that later. I wouldn't be surprised seeing him not only with a nomination for "Best Supporting Actor" but with the Oscar in his hand come oscar night. He has to be seen to be believed. So far his performance and Tom Wilkinson's performance in "Michael Clayton" have to be the two stand out supporting performance's to come along this year. Josh Brolin is the main good guy through the majority of the film. He does a very good job, but his character is not nearly as interesting as Bardem's character is. Still, he deserves credit for his performance as well, but I don't expect that he'll get any oscar recognition. Then there's Tommy Lee Jones who did a very good job for the parts of the film he was in, and he definitely says some of the more interesting things in the movie. He's the only character that really talks a lot. The other two main character's are fairly manly and they tend to keep their mouth's shut, avoiding any really thought provoking character development on their character's while Jones's character tends to have a wandering mind, and he says some of the more profound things in the film. Woody Harrelson has a fairly small role, but he does a good job in the film as well. There was one casting decision that caught me off guard in a good way. Stephen Root who played "Milton" in "Office Space" and the dorky old "Gordon" in "DodgeBall" had a small part in this film that was entirely serious, and his voice was a regular old raspy southern one. It was interesting to see him in a non-comedic role, speaking his lines in a normal manly way.

Now for the script... The script is my only real issue with this film. Some parts of the script are fantastic. First off all that tension that the Coen's created with their great direction started in their screenplay that they adapted from the novel of the same name. There are some very interesting encounter's and conversation's from character to character through a lot of the film and much of the film is actually quite funny in typical Coen brothers fashion, which I honestly did not expect considering the fact that it looked to be an all out action-thriller from it's trailer. That was a nice touch as well. However here are some things I had a problem with.

(MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD!) The whole movie has people tracking things down. Now the whole first half of the film the main character is being tracked with a tracking device so that made sense, but then he tosses it out, and still, Harrelson's character finds him and says he did it in three hours. The main character was checked into a hospital in Mexico and Harrelson's character had no way of knowing this, and somehow he magically found the guy? Alright, fine. Then the script decides to avoid explaining how, and when the main character starts talking about how he can get away from Bardem's character Harrelson just says "You don't understand"... Alright, what doesn't he understand? Is there some weird connections that you're organization has to track people down? What? Well it basically just makes it look like these guys have super powers and they can find people with their laser vision or something. That was kind of annoying. Then there's the fact that the whole last quarter of the film the main character is dead. He is killed off screen by some regular old guys that the boss sent out to get the money that he had. Now what bugs me about that is the fact that the main character (Brolin's character) has been outsmarting and dodging those guys through the entire movie, and then a few of them run up and they all just shoot him to death nice and easy. When you see his body, he's not like off somewhere, like he ran and tried to get away. He's on the floor at the front of his motel room. He's also been dodging one of the smartest, most threatening bad guys to be in a film in year's and he was able to dodge getting killed by him... The slow ending following this death was bothersome and it honestly started to feel extremely slow and boring before the credits went up. The thing that really makes the movie unredeeming is the fact that Bardem's super bad character lives on after all this build up towards what looked to be his imminent death.... There is actually a scene where Bardem and Jones look as though they are about to face off, but Bardem runs out the window. This is totally out of character because througout every other scene in the film Bardem shoots firsts and does things like talking or running away later.

I gave the movie a few hours of thought before I came and wrote this review and after all this thought I decided that Bardem lives because he is the worst man can ever be, and that Jones lives because hes is the best man can ever be. Bardem kills without any real cause, and Jones can't even handle the sight of dead bodies anymore, he's tired of all of the bad thing's he's seen in his life, and he uses knowledge as his number one weapon, constantly spurting out facts through out the film's entirety. Both have to live on so that they can balance each other out. Good and evil...

Overall this movie was an expertly directed, extremely well acted film that had some flaws with it's script, but honestly, it had to much great things happening with it for any of that to matter. I really loved this movie, and I think I'll probably go see it again next week so that maybe I can understand it a little better than I did this first time around...

I was able to really appreciate what the movie was the second time around, knowing the ending.  The strength of the film lies in Cormac McCarthy's original story: it is a dismal and bleak metaphor of his own existential philosophy (which I would guess to be nihilism). The Coen Brothers have returned, back from the zany hijinks in their previous features: Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers, to make one their best films, one of the best thrillers of recent years, and one of the best films of the year. Adding to all that, it is a thinker as well.

I left this film considering everything I saw, piecing the various elements together, putting back together scenarios, and I enjoyed doing it. It was the kind of movie that benefits from the thought put into it, and it still has all that Coen Brothers flare, not to mention the benefits from repeated viewings.

The twisty plot involves a simple man in Texas. Lewelyn played by Josh Brolin in another great performance of this year, stumbles across a botched drug deal, where all of the men are found dead, and $2 million dollars is his for the taking. He wishes...

Enter Anton Chigurh, one of the most despicable and psychopathic killers around. Armed with few weapons that anyone would ever want to be on the wrong side of, Anton is a force to be reckoned with.

Anton Chigurh: What business of where I'm from is yours...friendo?

After Lewelyn barely escapes others trying to get their hands on him, he must deal with Anton's own kind of principles of how to handle the problems presented to him.

Tommy Lee Jones enters the scene as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. He is a good cop, but in his time has seen too much and just doesn't understand the world anymore. Ed also becomes involved in finding out the whereabouts of those involved in this botched deal.

Finally you have Woody Harrelson as a bounty hunter who has encountered Chigurh before, and plans to solve some problems.

Man who hires Wells: Just how dangerous is he?
Carson Wells: Compared to what? The bubonic plague? 

While the setup sounds fairly straightforward, the ways things unfold is done with a lot of subtlety for the most part, leaving the audience to piece together some of the points.

Regardless, the plot leads to some of the most thrilling scenes and face-offs I've seen in a while. Not since Blood Simple have the Coens' made a film so strict to the thriller formula. That being said, this film still has the quirky character moments and great dialog that makes it a Coen Brother's film through and through.

This is a great movie with uniformly great performances, memorable characters, great dialog, and a great look to the wasteland areas of Texas that are shown, proving once again, along with other elements in this film, that less can be more.

Ever since Fargo and The Big Lebowski, the Coen brothers seem to have gone down hill. The Ladykillers and Intolerable Cruelty are very much below what these two are capable of creating. However, they're back and better than ever. No Country for Old Men isn't one of their best films, it is their best film by far.

No Country for Old Men opens with a narration from Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones). "I always knew you had to be willing to die to even do this job - not to be glorious. But I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand." Within the next five minutes, we know exactly what he means by that. The first time Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is introduced, he has been arrested and taken to the police station. While the officer is making a phone call, Chigurh quietly maneuvers to get his handcuffs from behind his back to the front of his body. After the officer finishes the call, Chigurh walks from behind and chokes the officer to death using his handcuffs. Using the deputy's car, he pulls over a motorist, kills him with a cattle gun and swaps cars.

Out in the desert, Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a Vietnam veteran and welder, hunts for antelope. After failing to kill his target, he stumbles upon the bloody aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong. Everyone is dead except for one man pleading for water. Moss finds the drugs and knows that there could be money around. He turns out to be correct. Pondering on the situation for a while, he decides to take it. Later that night, his conscience gets the better of him. He fills a jug of water and drives back to the scene of the crime. Unfortunately for Llewellyn, the man appears to be dead and two men in a pickup truck park next to his car (which he parked far away) and slash his tires. The men spot Moss and send him on a chase, even using their dog to attack. Moss escapes and tells his wife to pack so she can stay with her mother while he devises a plan to outsmart the men who are after him. One of those men is Chigurh.

Moving at a methodical pace, No Country for Old Men builds it tension to a level rarely, if ever, seen in a film. There's one scene involving Moss and Chigurh in a hotel that scared me shitless. Chigurh, using a transponder, locates the room Moss is staying in. For about a minute or two, nothing happens, as each man braces himself for the confrontation. A similar situation happens between Chigurh and another character later.

The acting is nothing short of exceptional. The main and supporting actors are on top of their game. Josh Brolin is having a breakout year, acting in In the Valley of Ellah, Grindhouse, American Gangster, and now this. Tommy Lee Jones played a similar role in his own movie, The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada, but his emotional range appears to be much greater here. Although these two actors are great here, Javier Bardem steals the show.

Anton Chigurh might be as frightening of a villain as Hannibal Lector, if not more so. His stiff posture, menacing stare, calculated word usage, emotionless expressions, unorthodox principles and remorseless killings make him appear to be not human. In some ways he is human and other ways more of an idea, like the embodiment of violence. He views his himself as a person carrying out fate and thus has a detachment from his victims. His background is a mystery because anyone who knows something about him is dead.

Artistically, the film is superb. Seeing the vast emptiness of the desert in the first few scenes recalls similar images in Sergio Leone's Spaghetti Westerns. The minimalist music score heightens the tension and allows every sound to be heard.

The film's transition from an impressive thriller into philosophical territory elevates its lasting effect. All of the complaints from people about the third act are bullshit. The supposed "plot holes" some mention are a result of their lack of attention to details. Also, people expecting non-stop nonsenical violence are going to be disappointed. There's a lot more to this than just the thriller elements.

Just as No Country for Old Men opens with a narration from Bell, he ends the film with one too. He describes a dream he has about him and his father. It may be the only optimistic scene in this very bleak film.

A misconception about NO COUNTRY is that it is an action movie.  The assumption is fair considering how the film is marketed but it's really an unfair label. The film is a lot of blood and guns, yeah, but framed within a pretty somber, low-key narrative. I think this makes it more interesting in the end, but not everyone will. The film incorporates some pretty harsh violence which is used exclusively to disturb the viewer and never to arouse or incite any cheers for the protagonist. This works effectively for the story. The violence that chases Llewellyn Moss across Texas is relentless and though he manages to evade it temporarily he selfishly places many others in its path. He is not a hero, in the romantic sense, and is therefore not treated as such by the filmmakers. He is a simple man who is not as powerful as he believes he is and not willing to face it.  
Many I think will have a problem with the way the film side steps any sort of climactic confrontation, but there's enough bloodshed in the film that it's nothing I felt I needed to see. This isn't DIE HARD, and that the film deviates from more predictable genre formulas makes it, in my opinion, all the more interesting. The cinema of the Coens is distinguished (and in some camps, derided) for its ironic detachment, broad characterizations, and impeccable formalism. McCarthy is a moralist who writes in opaque metaphors and verbose interior monologues. Their unlikely collision crackles.
After a run of absurdist comedies, the brothers thankfully haven't lost their nihilistic edge: they've fashioned a sh*t-kicker cousin to Fargo, a seemingly simple fable steeped in symbolic landscapes, regional dialects, confounding motivations, and outrageous savagery from which the extremes of human behavior spiral into equal parts humour and horror.

The latest effort from the Coen brothers somehow manages to masquerade as a taut thriller, while providing a glaring examination of the pervasiveness of violence in society. By infusing humor with images of gruesome bloodshed, it causes us to question how at ease we have become with human carnage and whether we will ever return to the generation of "Old Men", when senseless murder would receive more notice than the ho-hum attitude of today.

In the vast Texas countryside, hunter Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon $2 million and a heap of dead bodies at a drug deal gone wrong. He takes the money home only to return to the scene to help the one living person he left behind. He is spotted and pursued by a ghostly assassin, Anton Chigurh, (Javier Bardem) who piles up an extensive body count in his search of Moss and the jackpot. Worn down Sheriff Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) leads the investigation and tries to get to Moss before Chigurh. The cat and mouse game between Chigurh and Moss is never short of thrilling, but Bell is the focal point of the film, providing context to the absurdity of the chase as well as the rising sadism in today's culture.

As the first gunshot plants in the middle of a man's forehead, it is clear the film will not mask violence but exaggerate the bloodbath and not merely for the sake of entertainment. Each severed limb only reinforces the brutality of murder, a far stretch from the watered down version of violence in so many movies screening right now. This isn't the fantasy world of James Bond (the series has presented violence more realistically as of late). If you get shot, you don't let out a small yelp and crumple to the ground with a petite stain that resembles red finger paint. Instead, as presented here, the victim is catapulted by the shear force of impact and blood spews like a geyser. The connection between cinema and violence in real life has been argued to no end. Although the debate continues, consider the potential impact if younger people were imbedded with these grisly images. Perhaps we could have avoided a few unnecessary deaths and front page headlines.

This film does not evoke such optimism. Sheriff Bell is a man who has seen more than his fair share of crimes after inheriting his position from the men of his family. As the moral compass of the film, he seems far more interested in small talk than delving deep into the investigation. If you can't change the outcome, what is the point? When asked by his deputy if he wanted to reexamine the crime scene, he responded he would, only if there were a fresh body. 

Now, I have no background in law enforcement, but I have experienced a sense of helplessness that goes along with steady bloodshed. As a news reporter in Augusta, I sat next to a police scanner all day, waiting for the inevitable gloom that would pour out from the machine. I began to lose sight of whether I was a reporter or a professional ambulance chaser. The yellow tape, the body bags and such sights I had only seen in movies became commonplace. What started as shock morphed into disillusionment and even worse, numbness. How could I rationalize three dead bodies over something as futile as a stolen scooter? And yet, I still woke up the next morning, went to the crime scene and wrote every vivid detail as if it were just another day at the office. I have since sworn that I will never return to police reporting. Much like Sheriff Bell, I reached my breaking point. I guess when death becomes monotonous you need to find a new line of work. In the film, millions of dollars were at stake, but in comparison, it is really any different from the killings over the scooter?

"No Country" is fascinating in that in provides a critique on violence and remains entertaining as hell at the same time. Javier Bardem plays an eccentric maniac, driven by an ideology that remains unclear. Perhaps there is no reason. This sentiment would echo many of the killings that occur every day. He uses a supped up air tank attached to a bolt gun, which produces a deafening thud when fired. It made me jump out of my seat at least a half dozen times during the screening. His voice was so deep it would make Shaq sound like a high-pitch teenage girl. It would be no stretch to compare Chigurh to Hannibal Lector, played by the icy Anthony Hopkins. His antics do more than just produce a larger than life character. They create a dichotomy for the audience. A gas station clerk stutters at Chigurh while his life comes down to a coin flip. Chigurh mocks the man, and the audience erupted in laughter. When Moss is retrieving the money from a motel ventilation shaft, he hears the shots that were meant for him actually kill his neighbors. He then displays the perfect, 'oh shit' face. Once again, the viewers went crazy. Should we feel awkward that we are laughing as bodies are flying? Considering this is coming from the people who made "Fargo", in which stuffing a dead body into a wood chipper was hilarious, we should not be surprised. It seems they enjoy making the audience squirm but with a sly smile. Despite the laughs, the gravity of the murder is understood, which distinguishes it from the half-assed violence plaguing Hollywood films.

It seems that the cinematic landscape of this era only contains only two types of film: escapist and art house. The Coen brothers have once again obliterated this mold. "No Country" is part thriller, part social commentary, all the while remaining self-reflexive to the genre. As with most suspense stories, there is a buildup for a showdown between protagonist and villain. But just when this definitive confrontation is expected, the Coens pull the plug, ultimately saying this film is more than just your typical thriller. Instead of a climatic shootout, we only see a quick shot of who has perished. I heard some in the lobby after the film say they were let down by the end. But here, there is no little bow that magically wraps up everything. Instead, the finale transitions to a grizzled sheriff unable to cope with the vicious nature of a world that has grown so outlandish to him. It is meaningless that these are the characters we've followed the last few hours. Through the eyes of this disillusioned man, it is just another corpse to add to the mountain. Why should it receive any special treatment? And by resisting the conventional conclusion, the Coens have crafted a film that extends beyond entertainment to one that makes a dent in the social consciousness of the astute.

My initial impressions were somewhat tainted by an extreme amount of confusion. If the story had built to the predicted showdown between badasses, it would have been not only conventional, but it would have betrayed what it was about to begin with. Nobody triumphs here, no matter how "cool" or "innocent" they may be. In this universe they are all the same. The fact that "No Country" is a pitch-perfect period piece adds points to the total. If this doesn't win Best Picture tomorrrow night I will be tremendously disappointed (and possibly suicidal)

Following a second viewing of this film, I became convinced that this is a stone-cold classic.  Javier Bardem, Tommy Lee Jones, and Josh Brolin are all amazing in this film. Josh Brolin continues what has to be one of the most successful years in film appearing in Grindhouse, In the Valley of Elah, American Gangster, and No Country for Old Men.  Tommy Lee Jones may have topped his performance in In the Valley of Elah and it is hard to say at this point which he will be nominated for.  The Coen Brothers guide us through Cormac McCarthy's story whose internal logic is no logic at all, random chance.  Chigurh places the life of a storekeeper in the hands of a coin toss.  He understands that randomness governs the world we live in.  Moss stumbles upon $2 million dollars, an entirely random event.  Sometimes characters attempt to impose order on the world in futile attempts to exercise control.  Chigurh attempts to live by principles like "keeping his word" to reduce randomness but even he knows he cannot guarantee the money will end up in his hands.  Ed Tom Bell becomes a police officer to impose order but quits when he realizes that events have spiraled entirely out of his control.  While the plot is certainly interesting and engaging (even the third act), the characters are the heart of the film.  People like Chiguhr, Ed Tom, and even secondary characters like Carson Wells are incredibly well-developed and intensely memorable.

They virtually disappear into the world that Cormac McCarthy has so lovingly crafted... losing almost all of their trademark Coenisms in lieu of simple narrative gestures.

There are no obligatory actors in this film -- every single performance is done with the same quiet genius and intensity of Javier Bardem's ultimate villain role (be it the comedic Texan retread of Frances Micky D's performance in Fargo by Tommy Lee Jones or a rare bit of understatement from Woody Harrelson).  

Then again, there are no stand-out performances because the real character driving the movie are the perfectly matched Coen's visuals with McCarthy's staccato of a plot.  

Again, this is babble -- I need to see it again to understand this movie's simple, beautiful complexity.  When long passages of silence punctuate the violence of determinism, fatalism and pragmatism... and feel like seconds as opposed to hrs -- you've got to be tip-toeing through Eden with the masters.

I don't know what the f*ck that all means -- but the Coen's bring poetry to my mind every single time.  This time, they just mighta outdone themselves.

Itâs almost 4:00 in the morning, and I canât stop thinking about No Country for Old Men. Itâs been nearly two hours since the movie ended; I canât get it out of my head. There have been plenty of good movies this year, some great, some that I gave perfect scores to (Ratatouille and Knocked Up). But now Iâll have to reconsider that, because those films werenât like this. This, friends, is a true masterpiece.

The filmâs plot is pure pulp fiction: Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a roguish if basically decent man, finds $2 million in cash while on a hunting trip, the remnant of a drug deal gone wrong. He takes the money and tries to escape with it, but things like this are never that simple. Enter Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a taciturn, quietly evil killer who pursues Moss with an implacable determination. Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), a local sheriff, attempts to protect Moss and get to the bottom of things but is generally awed by the monstrosity of it all.

For the most part this is a chase film, and it is excruciatingly suspenseful. A large part of this is due to the lack of a musical score; No Country for Old Men is a film filled with silences, punctuated by the barbaric throes of death. We donât get any editing cues, any shopworn hints about whatâs going to happen, and the unpredictability of the film makes it that much more captivating. Chigurh isnât just a soulless killing machine; the people he spares are almost as important as the people he does murder, because they make it clear that thereâs no rhyme or reason to who goes down before his gun and who walks free. The coin can just as easily land on heads as tails.

Bardem embodies this with his performance, crafting one of the most terrifying villains in film history. For Chigurh, killing isnât a source of joy or sick fulfillment, itâs a way of life. Killing is a part of his nature, just as locking a car door or knowing how to tie shoes is part of ours. He is a man who could really exist. Chigurh is unstoppable, but itâs not because heâs invincible, itâs because he doesnât stop. Thereâs a kind of supernatural air about him (at one point Bell refers to him as a ghost), but he doesnât have any supernatural powers. The scenes that focus on Moss are even more suspenseful than the Chigurh scenes, because we know the killer is out there somewhere, drawing ever closer. Josh Brolinâs work is also integral to the success of the film. Weâre rooting for him to succeed, but his human quality is no match for the killing machine that is Chigurh. To watch him squirm is to have no idea how heâs going to make it out alive.

All of this is very effective, but heart-stopping suspense can only take us so far. As the cat-and-mouse games between Chigurh, Bell, and Moss continued, I began to wonder if this whole movie was just going to be a chase between these three very different men. A chase this well executed is certainly compelling, but it canât last forever. You canât keep running. As the film entered its final third, though, certain events take place that expand the scope of the film from a superbly-wrought thriller to an American tragedy. If this third act doesnât have the relentless tension of what it follows, itâs a necessary component of the film. Itâs what makes it a masterpiece. It also reveals Tommy Lee Jonesâs performance as the heart of the film. Itâs through the sheriff character, and through Jonesâs extraordinary acting, that the movie makes its most potent points about the changing nature of the world and of mankind. âI used to think I could at least some way put things right. I donât feel that way no more,â he says. No Country for Old Menâs moral vision is more bleakly terrifying than even a psychopath of Chigurhâs stature.

I may be the only person who thinks so, but in my opinion the Coen brothers suck at making comedies.  From the mildly amusing Raising Arizona to the painful to watch Intolerable Cruelty and Ladykillers, they rely on retarded slapstick for laughs.  However, their dramas are brilliant.  I have been waiting a long time for them to return to form, to make a film that matches Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing and the classic Fargo.  This is DEFINITELY it!  The film starts off with a monologue delivered by Tommy Lee Jones, much of it taken directly from the novel.  However, itâs so much more effective spoken by Jones, who delivers it almost poetically.  Its content about a murderer Jones arrested who had killed a girl immediately sets the tone for the film.  The opening shots present a very stark landscape, and the lack of music throughout the entire film mirrors this.  Instead of a score we here the sounds of the desert, such as the whistling wind and footsteps on gravel.  The film is essentially a study of evil.  However, instead of being preachy, it presents evil in the form of a villain who rivals Hannibal Lecter in ruthlessness, cunning, and coolness.  Javier Bardemâs Chigurh is the ultimate psycho.  He oozes evil, has the look of insanity.  His weapon of choice is an oxygen tank, which he uses to blow out door locks and also to shoot people.  Bardem is incredible and amazing to watch.  He creates a character that will forever be remembered in film.  I think it is the best character and best performance ever to come out of a Coen brotherâs film, and Bardem better get a Best Supporting Actor statue come awards time.  The rest of the acting is solid as well.  Josh Brolin continues his very successful year doing solid work here, and Tommy Lee Jones is equally brilliant, fitting perfectly into the film.  Thereâs not much more to say.  The movie is extremely suspenseful, featuring some of the most intense chase sequences I have ever scene.  It is also very darkly humorous, like Fargo, which works really well.  Some people will complain about the ending.  However, it comes directly from the book (in fact, the movie in general is extremely faithful to the source novel), and personally I loved it.  Cormac McCarthy is a perfect match for the Coen brothers.  His novels are already poetic, but the Coen brothers are able to make the dialogue even more pitch perfect.  Each scene is riveting, much like Fargo.  2007 has been awesome so far, but No Country for Old Men is the first truly GREAT film to come out this year.  A+.

Simplistic, yet complex, No Country For Old Men is an unforgettable mind challenging gem of a movie.

Ed Tom Bell: "I always liked to hear about the oldtimers. Never missed a chance to do so. You can't help but compare yourself gainst the oldtimers. Can't help but wonder how they would've operated these times. There was this boy I sent to the gas chamber at Huntsville here a while back. My arrest and my testimony. He killed a 14-year-old girl. Papers said it was a crime of passion but he told me there wasn't any passion to it. Told me that he'd been planning to kill somebody for about as long as he could remember. Said that if they turned him out he'd do it again. Said he knew he was going to hell. Be there in about fifteen minutes. I don't know what to make of that. I surely don't. The crime you see now, it's hard to even take its measure. It's not that I'm afraid of it. I always knew you had to be willing to die to even do this job - not to be glorious. But I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand. You can say it's my job to fight it, but I don't know what it is anymore. More than that, I don't want to know. A man would have to put his soul at hazard. He would have to say, "OK, I'll be part of this world." Although it's been a few days since I saw No Country for Old Men - the only 2008 Oscar nominee that made me resort to 'illegal' means in order to watch it before February 24 - I still don't know what exactly to make of it. It's basically the brilliant, mesmerizing masterpiece it's been hailed as, but... but it's so side-swiping that it makes you feel as if you've melted in your seat and haven't even noticed. Words can barely describe it. There are barely any words in the picture itself. As it seems, at least. It's a very tough film fueled by very tough situations coerced by very tough characters. In theory, and put simply, this is a film not everyone would like. And yet, it's been hailed as some of the greatest American cinema in history. Funny how that works. The Coen Brothers have always shown a powerful deal of talent and strong narrative in their films, with Fargo standing as their best film till 2007, but they reached a whole other level of filmmaking sublimity with this film. Whereas Cronenberg's Eastern Promises is like English literature with western influences, No Country for Old Men is more akin to American literature with early European influences - and lots of it too. No Country for Old Men plays out like a Christopher Marlowe play or other Elizabethan tragedies. Its art lies in the thriving of evil throughout the film, and the supreme torture of any character remotely resembling good. This leaves a sort of beautiful, real-life inconsistency that seems to represent an apocalyptic outcome. It begs us to question aspects of reality that many people will find disturbing. Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is a sadistic killer on the hunt for his money that has been taken by local provincial, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin). Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) gets involved in the situation and watches the events unfold days after they have happened. As Anton continues a killing spree for his money, Bell, looking at retirement, watches the case with a poetic understanding of everything gone wrong in the world. I don't know what persuaded the Coens to create such a different film, but the result is masterful and also, very hard for audiences to "get". The last 20 minutes of the film may leave people wondering, "Why did that just happen?", "Does that make any descriptive sense?". It's hard to talk about this film without spoiling it, but the way I saw it, Anton is the absolute of evil, of death. Such a force can be beaten, tricked, won against and you can even get lucky against it - kind of like in a coin toss. Yet it always, always survives to destroy something another day. The last 20 minutes of the film is a narrative of reality. The characters thought it was going to end one way, the audience thought it was going to end that same way, but it didn't. That's because the same force that Anton represents is found everywhere - and it caught Llewelyn. Tommy Lee Jones plays a character similar to Morgan Freeman's in Seven. He represents the knowledge and purity of this world - the opposite of Anton. As such, he cannot be destroyed either, even when in close contact with the opposing force, but he can, and often is, weary of the evil, the death and the battles. His monologue at the end of the film, recalling dreams he had, might be a lot for audiences to take in before the screen cuts to the end title cards. Even the most intelligent film critics and historians are baffled and continue to converse about the ending's relevance. I personally believe Bell's dream is a longing for a peaceful world he wishes to create, but he can't. He is an old man who failed to help anyone, thus there is "no country" for him. I think it's the perfect ending. It solidifies Bell's relevance to the story and it was ultimately where the entire film was going all along. While Tommy Lee Jones delivers a masterful performance, it's Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh that will creep audiences out of their skin. His ruthlessness is undeniable and his presence onscreen is more menacing than any slasher villain I can recall in recent years. His initial "coin toss" is one of the most edge of your seat, psychological freak out moments of the film. The entire idea, while sick, is perfect for the character and Bardem handles it without fault. I'm proud to be one of the few people - world population speaking - that got to predict his success years and years ago, since the first time I saw him in Almodóvar's Live Flesh. Josh Brolin kinda underwhelmed me, but I think that's because he makes me feel uncomfortable on a cosmic level - besides the fact that I think The Goonie everytime I see him. Then, there's Kelly Macdonald. She's the kind of actress that can light up a film with one single scene, and that's just what does here. Carla Jean is, up until the third act, a "barely there" character, shining like a small nugget of pure gold you can see, but not physically reach. But then it suddenly grows and you start humping it, you love it so much. While my initial reaction to the film wasn't so positive (I still say There Will Be Blood is a superior film), I've had plenty of time to think about it. (It's part of the reason why it has taken so long for me to get a review up.) Ultimately, this film does away with the common Hollywood film traits and, like many French films, mocks the classic Hollywood style with its unusual plotline. This only enhances the film's study in reality and its evils. Dark, but witty, cunning but hits you hard. This is the Coen Brothers at their best. An exquisitely crafted film that ought to be called a picture, a fantastic one.

A shocking, bloody, relentless tale from the Coen Brothers. It never lets up and will not let you down.

Since 'Fargo,' the Coens have turned in some very good films ('The Man Who Wasn't There,' 'O Brother, Where Art Thou?' 'The Big Lebowski') and a few disappointments -- which are too much fun to be duds ('Intolerable Cruelty,' 'The Ladykillers'). 'No Country for Old Men' marks the beginning of a whole new chapter in the Coen's colorful career. While I would not put it above 'Fargo,' it's safe to say that every film the brothers make from now on will have to be compared to this, as well.

In tone, it's probably more similar to 'Blood Simple' than anything else I've seen of theirs. But to say that undervalues the degree to which the Coens have reinvented their unique style of filmmaking while still managing to play into their strengths. 

Roger Deakins' photography is gorgeous, the editing of Roderick Jaynes (the pseudonym the Coens don when they edit their own films) is sharp as a knife, and the acting is spot-on.

We see a whole new company of actors that doesn't include the usual suspects like John Turturro, Steve Buscemi, John Goodman, Frances McDormand, Holly Hunter, Peter Stormare, Billy Bob Thorton, George Clooney, etc.

There is a whole new cast of actors giving marvelous performances. To single out any would be unfair, however I must say that Javier Bardem's Anton Chigurh might have surpassed Anthony Hopkins' Hanibal Lecter as the scariest villain ever.

I haven't seen enough films in 2007 to say for sure, but I'll be hard pressed to find a better film this year. I hope to see it as a strong contender when awards season rolls around.

Josh Brolin makes an excellent leading man and Tommy Lee Jones plays the worn out, tired sheriff so well.  Steven Root, who doesn't have a huge role in the movie, plays his character well (but maybe I'm impressed because it's such a far stretch from Office Space and Dodgeball).  Even the extras give excellent performances.  However, the perfomance for this film goes to Javier Bardem.  Bardem easily makes one of the scariest villains to ever appear on screen.  Calm but intense, level-headed but psychotic, Bardem hits the nail on the head.  Every time his character is on screen your gut clenches, just waiting on his next move.  It should also be noted that this had practically no soundtrack at all, but the Coens use that to their advantage.  Instead of cramming the movie full of intense music, they let the sound effects do the work.  The sound of the wind, the engine of the trucks, the creaking of the hallway as footsteps walk down it, the cocking of the shotgun just waiting for impending doom, this film plays it so well.  You won't miss the music, in fact you'll be glad it isn't there.  It creates a entirely new level of suspense that audiences have never seen.

This film is a modern day masterpiece and the Coens deserve theirs at Awards season.  Really, there is no other movie like it this year or in past years for that matter.  The only sad part is that a large amount of people won't be able to appreciate it simply because it's not your normal run-of-the-mill film.  It takes patience, and it takes thought.  This film presents themes that it doesn't make abundantly clear, and the viewer has to ruminate on them.  Audiences are so used to being spoon fed that this might go over their heads, which is a shame because this film is gold.

This is by far the best movie of the year and I can't wait to see it again.  Thank you, Joel and Ethan Coen, for giving us a film to break the mediocrity of modern cinema.  You both should be given medals.

Rarely does a film come along that combines the best qualities of directors, actors, and screenwriters. Very few films show a perception of the world as it appears today. So far this year only one film has met both these tasks: No Country for Old Men.

A brilliant piece of art, No Country for Old Men marks the return of Joel and Ethan Coen. After producing two flops (The Ladykillers and Intolerable Cruelty), the two are back at the top of their game. With No Country for Old Men, the Coens remind us why they are the most unique voices in Hollywood. It should be remembered that the Coens were the force behind such memorable films as Raising Arizona, Miller's Crossing, Barton Fink, Fargo, The Big Lebowski, and O Brother Where Art Thou?. Reminiscent of their 1984 debut Blood Simple, No Country for Old Men seethes with bloody delight.

The story centers around a hunter who stumbles upon some dead bodies, a stash of heroin and more than $2 million in cash near the Rio Grande. Here enters the Coen's best story telling element. Much like Fargo, ordinary people are thrown into extraordinary circumstances. By doing so, the film creates an other worldly effect and ends up fabricating a story that could possibly happen. Set in 1980, the film somehow transcends its time period and becomes much more a commentary on our society today. By displaying the violence of man, No Country for Old Men forces its audience to realize the increasingly violent nature of the world.

Helping to add to the moral story are a handful of stunning performances. First is Josh Brolin playing Llewelyn Moss, the man around which most of the story centers. Earlier this year, Brolin stared in American Gangster, and his work in that film as well as in No Country for Old Men provides for a great year. The conflicted ideals he helps bring to the main character is something to behold, and the overall performance is a victory. Tommy Lee Jones also, like Brolin, turns in his second award-worthy performance of the year. In In the Valley of Elah, Jones played a father trying to come to terms with the Iraq War. As Ed Tom Bell in No Country for Old Men, Jones is largely the same character, except this time trying to come to terms with the increasingly violent nature of man. The title, no doubt, refers to Jones' character. The world we live in now isn't one for those who still hold older, most distant views. Jones' narration is highly effective, and he deserves any attention he receives. The man who steals the show, though, is Javier Bardem. Bardem plays the psychopath villain Anton Chigurh. His chilling performance is the best villain since Silence of the Lambs' Hannibal Lector. Chigurh is brutal, but yet the viewer feels for him at times. He's by no means a good man, but the nature of his character is something for any moviegoer to enjoy. He's not a clichéd character, by no stretch of the imagination a cookie-cutter version of every other screen menace. While Brolin, Jones, and Bardem are the heart and soul of the film, the supporting performances are also fantastic. Kelly Macdonald is perfectly cast as Llewelyn's wife, Carla Jean. A Scottish actress, Macdonald nails the southern accent and her character serves as an anchor for some parts of the film. Woody Harrelson has a nice cameo, and although his character serves little purpose to the overall story, he is still quite enjoyable to watch.

To touch more on the Coen's direction could take some time. In short though, they have created arguably their best film. Surely their best film since the Oscar-winning Fargo in 1996, No Country for Old Men serves as a stunning testament as to what filmmakers can do. There's no fancy special effects and no distractive camera work, just pure brilliance. For years, the Coens have been allowed to make the films they want with little, or no, studio interference. With a film like No Country for Old Men it shows. Along with directing, the Coens also wrote the script, something they do for each of their films. What's unique about No Country for Old Men is that it is the Coen's first literary adaptation. The screenplay is based on the novel of the same name by Cormac McCarthy, a recent Pulitzer Prize winner. Nearly a word-for-word adaptation, the Coen?s script is extremely loyal to the original source.

The rest of the film fits together beautifully. The editing is quick and exquisitely done. That's also the doing of the Coen brothers. Using the name Roderick Jaynes, they have edited all of their films. The overall look of the film is perfect. The dusty rolling plains serve as a perfect contrast from the snowy white landscape of that in Fargo. The pacing is just perfect. Never is there a dull moment. The film allows you to catch your breath, but then builds the suspense again. All of it builds to...well the ending, an ending which will undoubtedly have lots of people up in arms. While the ending can't be spoiled here, it will be argued for some time as to the real meaning. Yet, when the screen fades to black it is evident that the ending is actually rather profound, a pitch-perfect note to end the film on.

When all is said and done, No Country for Old Men stands as a masterpiece, a stunning achievement in any year. The film is one of the best crafted suspense stories of all time. The Oscar buzz already surrounding the film is deafening. It's the first thriller to generate such talk since The Silence of the Lambs swept the awards circuit in 1991. As of now, the film is largely being considered to be in the #1 spot for Best Picture, Director, Supporting Actor, and Adapted Screenplay. The National Board of Review just awarded the film three major awards: Best Picture of the Year, Best Ensemble, and Best Adapted Screenplay. All the praise is more than deserved. Come Oscar time, the film will be one of the only true contenders, and years from now it will still be viewed as a violent and profound piece of cinematic genius.

It's interesting to me that No Country for Old Men is based on a Cormac McCarthy novel when so much of it seems like something only the Coen brothers would create. Either way, this is a fantastic movie. On a technical level, it's perfect. Cinematographer Roger Deakins captures the stark beauty and loneliness of Texas perfectly. With the exception of some background noises and the end credits, the film is almost entirely without a score, so the tension is built entirely by the actors and the Coens. This is a spectacularly entertaining and engrossing work of art.  I thought it had the potential to reach 4.5 stars after the first viewing, but I now believe my initial reaction was correct.  The performances approach perfection.  Eastwood and the Coen Brothers seem to understand that one needs a voice like Morgan Freeman or Tommy Lee Jones in order to make voice over effective.   Brolin, Jones, Bardem, and the rest of the cast are unreal.  It almost seems as if other films are being made with amateur actors in comparison.  Every performance down to the smallest characters that Bardem, Brolin, or Jones encounters over the course of the story is wonderful.  The only exception for me is Macdonald, but this is simply because I have a hard time imagining her as being anything but Scottish.  The strongest aspect of the film has to be the script though.  The Coens have somehow managed to make "Hells Bells" sound completely natural.  Every line is imbued with hidden meaning and importance. It all fits.  The film is an exercise in efficiency, which is something I constantly strive to attain.  I suppose this is meant to be a typical Hollywood genre piece, but it is anything but.  I hardly even recognize it as a crime chase noir thriller etc.  It is simply a masterpiece.  The Coens do not waste any motion, effort, or time in unnecessary camera movements or extraneous cinematic effects.  This is a bare bones film in the same sense that Ford, Hawks, and Hitchcock made bare bones films.  They simply tell the story the best way they can and invest it with the most meaning they can.  However, this is where the film eluded my comprehension to some extent after the first viewing.  I didn't quite apprehend the underlying meaning and importance of the film after one viewing.  The same cannot be said after a second viewing.  It makes far more sense now.  If I needed to use one word to describe the film, it would be subtle.  I can't think of any other major American directors working today that are so ambivalent concerning the overtness of their message.  The Coen brothers seem to have buried it fairly deep within the subtext of the film, so as to not make it easy for the viewer to discern and understand the film.  This is a good thing.  It is very refreshing.  The lack of any sort of score serves their story very well.  Minimalism can be a wonderful thing.  The Coens are a master of detail here in the same sense that Kieslowski was.  Granted, they are definitely inferior to Kieslowski and others, but they work in small details like Brolin's character picking up the cartridge, the look of the dogs, the spurting of blood, the hiding of the money, the medical treatment, and the crumpling of the wrapper.  All add incredible depth to the film.  I don't feel like I've summed up or elaborated very well on my impressions of the film, but this will have to do for now.  In summary, I enjoyed it and I probably wouldn't care to know anyone that doesn't terribly well.

The film has received almost universally positive reviews. As of November 30, 2007, the review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes recorded that 95% of 159 critics gave the film positive reviews,[31] while another review aggregator, Metacritic, records an average score of 91%, based on 36 reviews.[32] The film is widely discussed as a possible candidate for several Oscars.[33][34] Javier Bardem, in particular, has received considerable praise for his performance in the film.

Roger Ebert gave it a four star review saying that the movie was "a masterful evocation of time, place, character, moral choices, immoral certainties, human nature and fate."[35] Walter Chaw of Film Freak Central also praised the film as an effective adaptation of the source novel, declaring "...the Coens have distilled the essence of McCarthy's gash-deep nostalgia for the illusory, ephemeral past... and packaged it in the very best moments of their own well of extraordinary visions".[36] A rare dissenting voice was Jonathan Rosenbaum in the Chicago Reader, who, while admiring the film's aesthetics, questioned its moral culpability: for him, the Coens expend great energy on depicting horror, while encouraging us to "hypocritically shake our heads at the sadness of it all".[37] Associated Press film critics David Germain and Christy Lemire both called the film the best film of 2007.

And so the Cohen Brothers come full circle. It can't be easy being lauded at every turn as the voice of American Independent cinema,  especially when you churn out terrible remakes of Alec Guiness movies. But enough of that - this is back to what the Cohens do best.
Shot locationally and tonally the same way (and ironically, in the same time period) as their first film Blood Simple, NCFOM is a lyrical, choppy, impressionistic movie. Ostensibly a money-chase, this is the maguffin that draws you into a movie about nature, and change. Javier Bardem creates an instant classic "bad guy", who is really the force of nature, something all the characters try to outrun to one degree or another. 
A beautifully shot Texan wilderness (thankyou, Roger Deakins - will that be another Oscar then? very good.) is as sparse as the use of sound in the movie - this is a film that uses silence the way Tarantino uses the F-word. And another example of how all aspects of this movie complement each other. It's also shot through with the trademark Cohen humour - surreal exchanges, pitch-black comedy, and some great lines.
If you want to criticise it, there's an awkard gear change 3/4 of the way through it, and a slow down in the third act that seems confusing. But these are petty problems. This is epic American film making. A word of advice - go see it a few weeks late, away from the popcorn guzzling, phone beeping idiots - this needs to be seen in total silence.

Javier Bardems's Anton Chigurh is a remarkable character - he seems to be as much the embodiment of fate, which chance is a part of, rather than simply the latter quality, or chaos. 'They always say the same thing', he says to Moss' wife at a point later in the movie, ''You don't have to do this''. But of course, to his mind, the very doing of such deeds is what defines him - He's not a judge or executioner in his own eyes, but a determiner of fates, immune to reason, or pleading. Methodical, almost always completely calculating, but seeming to be not so much ruthless as devoid of compassion - not the homicidal lunatic he's accused of being, but more a true sociopath.

As such it's it's small quirks that get him laughs in the movie - a fastidiousness observed in the moment where he lifts his boots from the motel room floor to avoid the dark welling pool of Carson Wells' blood (a similar move later intimates that Carla Jean Moss's refusal to call the toss of the coin might have done nothing to save her from her fate), - the slight exasperation as he patiently explains the chance of the coin toss to an elderly attendant at some isolated road house. And his weapon of choice, which seems at first bizarre and even not recognised as such by the officer who first arrests him, becomes chillingly appropriate as his methods are revealed. 'You choose the right tool' he says.

Chigurh joins the likes of Charlie Meadows from 'Barton Fink' and Gaear Grimsrud from 'Fargo' as one of the scariest creatures The Coens have put on the screen.

It's 'Fargo' and 'Blood Simple' that this movie reminded me of the most, which is perhaps the highest praise I can think of to give it. Like Fargo, it eschews the stylisations and exaggerated characterisations that Coens' elsewhere revel in in favour of a stark exactitude, realised by Roger Deakins cinematography. Like 'Blood Simple' the dark irony and laconic humour of it's characters seeps into the fabric of events like a slow beeding wound.

I can only imagine, not yet having read the book, That Sheriff Tom Bell would have been more likely to quote some whimsical 'old boy' country wisdom rather than recount his own stark dreams, and been less pithy, more garrulous, had he been the Coen's own creation rather than their adaptation of McCarthy's work. The whole film hinges on his nostalgia for times past that seem simpler and more human than the crimes he finds himself confronted with now, and the legend of pioneer sheriffs and law men he mentions at the film's beginning, who perhaps seem more capable of dealing with this uniquely amoral outlaw than his own, aging self. It's this evaluation of his, evidenced in his conversations with retired fellow officers and his 'deputy' Wendell, that explains the films title most eloquently for me.

I must admit that, despite knowing what was coming from reading the book, I still couldn't help but be a bit disappointed by the last act of the film. REVISIT: Now that I've seen the film four times, I feel I can be a little more objective about it (though I do feel a slight tinge of regret at not being able to be so objective the first time....oh, the hell with it, I still think the movie's a masterpiece).

"No Country For Old Men" is difficult to describe without wandering into the world of exaggeration and hyperbole. It is, after all, the same film that won 4 Oscars this year (Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay, Supporting Actor) out of the eight for which it was nominated. It checked in at the top of nearly every critic's year end best-of lists. It won countless awards at innumerable festivals. In short, I haven't seen this much recognition, this much unanimous recognition, for a single film in a long time. What was it about "No Country" that made nearly every single critic stand up and cheer loudly?

I think it's a combination of several things. I went to see the new Scorsese/Stones documentary "Shine A Light" this evening. It was the first film I'd seen in a cinema since "Cloverfield", and that was back in the first week of January. Three and a half months went by, and not a single thing in cinemas worth seeing (in my opinion anyways - I admit, I'm very picky). I realize that this is the time of year when the major film studios unleash their crap movies on us, hoping to make a few bucks and slowly build up to summer blockbuster season. I accept this, but I don't have to like it. I like my movies to mean something, as well as be entertaining. I want them to have a point, and not just tell a rehashed version of the same stories over and over again. I suppose that's rather demanding of me, but when films like "No Country For Old Men" are being made I just have one simple question - why can't all movies be like that?

According to IMDb, "No Country" was made for $25 million, and made around $75 million at the box office. This figure is easily the highest mark that a Coen brothers film has ever achieved. Obviously there's a market out there for movies like this. I'd love to know why "No Country" wasn't put into wide release right away, preceded by a massive promotional campaign.

Then again, I kind of know why. It's because of all the reasons why this film is so good - it takes all the conventions used by bad films today and inverts them. The good guys are not heroic, in fact they are passive and even weak at times. The bad guys "triumph", and apparently get away in the end. Wait a minute, what ending? "No Country" doesn't really have an ending - the film just stops. It's one of the most unexpected (and brilliant) conclusions in years, and it certainly had a lot of people talking after they left the cinema.

I feel that "No Country" was successful for all the above reasons, but here's one more. It feels absolutely real - there's not a moment of illusion in it. It's a reflective film, like holding up a mirror to humanity. We know deep down that bad people like Anton Chigurh do exist, and that in real life there are people far worse than he. In that regard, that acknowledgement by the film is fearless. Cormac McCarthy, who wrote the novel, is one of the best living writers today because he is unflinching in looking at the dark side of humanity. The film is just as unflinching, capturing in moving pictures all the weakness and evil that we are capable of as humans. It's a moody, haunting, unforgettable film - easily the best film of 2007.

This is the best film of the year so far.  I'm sure that it will become one of the voters' favorites come award season.  All of the major production roles of the film deserve high praise - Direction, Producing, Editing (The Coen Bros as usual, going by the alias 'Roderick Jaynes;) Supporting Actor (Bardem) - and especial high praise for Roger Deakins, who has, following "Jesse James," photographed a second film this year-- both of which are bound for oscar nominations for cinematography.  For the elitists, this film is ferociously entertaining.  In addition, for those who relish the deeper and subtle meanings behind a film's message, the main idea of the film can be seen as a sad, literate meditation  of American life.  This idea, which was constantly seeded throughout the film, left the audience disquieted and frequently giggling to ease the growing discomfort that this film delivers.  Juxtaposed to the Yokels of the American 'countryside', Javier Bardem's performance as a brutal sociopath shows only what I can  imagine to be what the Coens and McCarthy are explicating: A country filled with people, endlessly searching for the easy fix and an unchallenged way through life.  The unfortunate truth that the storytellers are highlighting here is this:  Many viewers would call these bumpkins to be "innocent" characters who are living the typical and commonly plain old, 'simple life.'  This may be so, but when experiencing this on-screen masterpiece you can't help yourself from allowing the crafty subtleties to detach your thoughts from the common and socially expected way of thinking, and in turn, validating the existence of this murderous villian who haunts the screen with his skewed perception of reality and human life. After letting this effect sink inside you, you may find that this blood-hungry sociopathic dialogue makes more sense than most of the so called, "innocent" people that he kills.  The jolt of "No Country" is undeniable; it invades your emotions and then hits you hardest after the credits roll by.
