*HEAVY spoilers ahead: do not continue reading unless you've seen the film or don't give a shit*

Based on a minor (and controversially abridged by the editor) novel by the much celebrated and Pulitzer prize winning author Cormac McCarthy, "No Country for Old Men" is perhaps the year's best reviewed film, which is generally grounds for pause. The novel itself was a bit of a mess, but its one undeniable strength was in the writing. McCarthy's trademark run on sentences and dry, western prose brought the pulpy material to life, and the novel's themes, illustrated mostly via Sheriff Ed Tom Bell's monologues and the "character" of Anton Chigurth, provided it with an elegiatic air, and ultimately elevated it to the realm of parable.  It's structure, however, was messy. It jumped from place to place at curiously random intervals and seemed hellbent on shortchanging every character, situation and circumstance, particularly during the last third. How did the Coens, then, manage to adapt this flawed but intriguing work? Rather effectively.

The film opens, like the novel, with a monologue by Sheriff Bell. The one in the film is shorter, a composite of two of the many from the novel, and more effective, not least of all because of the way it is recited by Tommy Lee Jones. Weary and somewhat apprehensive, fearful even, he describes having arrested and, by his testimony, sent to the electric chair a 19 year old boy who had murdered, for no reason whatsoever, his 14 year old girlfriend. It is the lack of a reason that gets to the Sheriff more than the brutality itself. Seeing into the boy's eyes he saw nothing that he could recognize, a new kind of evil he feels he has never faced before, and (this is key) seems unwilling to. "A man would have to put his soul at hazard. He would have to say 'Ok, I'll be a part of this world'". 

The film then introduces us to Anton Chigurth (whom Moss, in a later scene, refers to as "sugar" but for some reason the Coens opted to have everyone pronounce his name as chi-GUR, not CHI-gur). Clearly ethnic, with cold eyes, clammy skin and a terrifying smile, Chigurth is more than a psychopath. He is a man who alternatingly takes pleasure in killing and absolves himself of all responsability for it. He sees himself as an emmisary from fate, the executioner's blade. It is fate who, via a coin toss, decides who lives and who dies. The choice is made for him, and he simply acts on it. Near the end of the film, when crossing a green light, the vehicle he is driving is struck, full speed, by another one who had not stopped at the red light. It comes seemingly out of the blue, both in the novel and the film, which is rather the point. Fate is reminding Chigurth that he is as susceptible to it as anyone else. Because of the way the murder just prior to the scene was handled in the film as opposed to the novel, the significance is changed slightly. In the film it seems to be punishment for defying fate, while in the book it appears to be a reminder from fate that he is not working on its behalf, but his own. 

Moss, the character who sets the film's plot in motion, is easily the least interesting. A good 'ole boy, former special forces, taciturn, intelligent. Your typical protagonist in a hard boiled crime thriller. Interestingly, and contrary to the advertising campaign, there IS such a thing as a clean getaway. Moss stumbles upon the money and takes it. No one is the wiser. What dooms him is the one thing everyone in the story except Chigurth have, on one level or another. A conscience. Moss goes back to the crime scene with a jug of water for the dying man he had so callously ignored. This act of kindness gets him spotted, and thus the chase begins.

Much has been made about the film's last 20, 25 minutes, especially for such a well received film. People have felt they're either a momentum breaker, a shift in tone or that they make no sense. Many have even felt cheated by them. The only way someone could feel that way is if they had paid little to no attention. Moss was never going to get away. This was evident from the get-go. His act of kindness doomed him in more ways than one. Beyond the fact that it got him spotted, it also exposed him. He is not willing to play by the rules of the people chasing him, and so they have power over him. His death takes place off-screen becaue it was a foregone conclusion, for one thing, and because this is Sheriff Bell's story for another. He was too late. Too slow. Too old. His monologue in the beginning ties not just into Chigurth, but directly into Moss' death. "I feel overmatched". He simply wanted to help Moss and was unable to even do that. He had no desire to confront the "new" evil (Chigurth), none whatsoever. A few scenes later, during his trip back to the motel where the first massacre took place, he makes a calculated decision. Stepping into Moss' old motel room is as close to said evil as he is willing to get. He chooses to confront his fear, knowing full well it may cost him his life, and is so relieved when he does not have to that he chooses to retire right then and there.

Bell's visit to his uncle's cabin is a terrific scene. Bell, expecting some kind of sympathy from a wounder former deputy, instead receives a sort of lecture. His uncle explains to him that his confusion, his fear, the evil he faces every day is nothing new. He tells him the story of his uncle, who was shot on his porch in front of his wife as the murderers stood there and watched him bleed out. He explains, in essence, that whatever is coming is coming, but what he's going through isn't new. The times have simply passed him by, and this not nor has it ever been any place for the old. This ties in directly to the last scene in the film, where Bell, in a fantastic monologue, describes a dream he had last night to his wife. In it his father was riding beside him, then ahead. They could hardly see eachother in the darkness but as his father rode on Bell felt that, wherever he stopped, he would light a fire to lead him there. It becomes very clear here that Bell, the one whom the film is truly about, is realizing perhaps for the first time that his death is not far off. His mortality has been reflected back at him by the events in the film and it is an idea he has not quite been able to shed. He has realized just how old he is, how much of his life has already passed, and how little of it he has left.

It has been said the film is about violence (hardly), political in nature (wishful thinking) and a social critique (it has some mild elements, like the fact everyone seems much more affected by the death of a dog than the 7 or 8 corpses surrounding it), but they're minor and perhaps unintended) but it is none of these things. It is simply a film about getting old, not realizing quite how old, and being given a very rude awakening.

There's no doubt this is an excellent film; the production values are simply impeccable, and the script is spot-on: well-paced, literate, and respectful of its source material. And yet it nonetheless rings just a little bit hollow. No Country for Old Men is a bleak novel, no doubt, but it's also a very personal one, and it works precisely because its anxiety about the declining world feels all too close to home. I think it's the diminished presence of Sheriff Bell in the film; without that sense of perspective, the whole story feels a little less resonant.

Ladies and gentlemen, I present to you "Awesome" in its purest form.  Literally, you will be in awe at what this film can do: with silence, moody scenery, lighting, and some truly dry motherfuckers.  The Coens know exactly what the fuck they're doing here, because every scene is absolutely a work of craftsmanship and a work of grace.  The film is true to the book without pussying out, and any additions/subtractions serve only to make it more vicious.  Now, let's say you wanted to make a complaint.  You could say, perhaps, that this film is something of a retread for the Coens; that it largely echoes Fargo in its desolate backdrop and its characters (the sheriff, for one thing, and in general everyone's languid lifestyle).  There are many arguments to be made against that claim, too, but it's legitimate.  And it's also worthy of a "shut the fuck up."  The only criticisms that can be made of this film rely on comparisons to other shit--other movies, by the Coens or otherwise; the book; etc.  Otherwise, it's impervious.  And that's what makes it a masterpiece, isn't it?

No Country For Old Men is somewhat hard to pin down.  It's a western set in 1980 rather than 1880, but there are touches of noir and such magnificently constructed tension that the comparison to Hitchcock's very best must be made.  It's the most ambitious piece the Coens have done since Fargo, and while it's more serious than that past work, No Country simply works in every way they intended it to.  The film doesn't offer much in the way of hope, but there isn't one scene here that loosens its grip and lets you ignore the stark bleakness of the story's and characters' nature.  The arresting cinematography consisting of mostly desolate, sunbleached west Texas landscapes further contributes to the feeling of isolation and melancholy.  The best thing the film does is build tension through masterful and subtle editing and direction, so much so that when the ending arrives so sudden and unexpected, it's almost anticlimactic.  But that's hardly a complaint, considering the Coens' past work.  I have a feeling this will frustrate most moviegoers, the casual masses who like big explosions and nicely wrapped packages.  No Country For Old Men is not for that audience, is nearly the antithesis of their preferred fare.  But for those of us who abhor trite Hollywood happing endings, and appreciate a decent helping of Hitchcockian suspense, this is the very best movie of 2007, nearly the best work of the Coens' decades-spanning career. With the high level of anticipation I had for this film, it was inevitable that there would be some degree of disappointment, and there was. On first viewing, the film, which is based on a novel by Cormac McCarthy, appears to be some kind of bastard offspring of Fargo and Blood Simple that doesn't measure up to either of it's parents. I say 'on first viewing' because I know from past experience that repeated viewings are often rewarded when it comes to the Coen Brothers' films. 'No Country' is certainly a welcome return to form following the dismal Intolerable Cruelty (2003). I haven't seen The Ladykillers (2004), so I can't comment on that, other than to say I really have no desire to see it. So we're back in familiar Coen territory, which is definitely a good place to be. Josh Brolin (Planet Terror) plays Texas good-ole-boy Llewelyn Moss, who's out hunting when he stumbles upon a passel of dead bodies and a pick-up truck full of drugs. On further investigation, he also discovers a satchel full of cash, which he decides to keep for himself. Bad idea. On the trail of the missing loot is a psychotic killer named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), whose weapon of choice is a cattle stun-gun, which also comes in handy for getting past locked doors. He's the type of fella who uses a coin toss to decide whether someone lives or dies, having the potential victim 'call it', thus determining his or her own fate. Also in the mix is Sherriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who is trying to track down Moss before he gets his damn-fool head blown off, leaving his wife Carla Jean (Kelly MacDonald) a widow. Woody Harrelson's character adds little to the film and probably could have been left on the cutting room floor. The three lead performances are all quite good, especially Bardem, who is truly frightening as the deranged and relentless Chigurh. There are several scenes of incredibly high tension while Chigurh is hunting Moss, with the Coens' trademark low camera angles on full display. The film is at it's best while the hunt is on, but at a certain point it loses steam (I won't say what that point is, but you'll know when you get there), and it kind of fizzles at the end. I've heard that the ending is very faithful to the book, and if that's the case maybe it should've been a little less so. But, for the most part I enjoyed the film, and I know I'll be seeing it again, so where it will end up in the pantheon of Coen Brothers films remains unclear. I'm fairly certain it will never overtake Fargo, Blood Simple or The Big Lebowski, but I wouldn't bet my life on it.

It is beautifully shot and paced with elegance and maturity. Javier Bardem creates a movie monster that lingers with you for days after the film ends. I am still thinking about it. The ongoings of Brolin and Bardem's characters are just a backdrop for what is really going on in terms of not only Jones' character but the name of the film as well. One of the most prevalent aspects of what makes this movie a masterpiece is that you think you are watching one story and you are but by the end you realize that there was this overall arc with Jones that you don't even realize you sat through until it is over. It is hard to explain but that's the best way I can. Kelly McDonald takes a supporting female role and turns her character into one of the more sympathetic characters in recent memory. The way this film develops and is told is very subtly and at a couple of points unsubtly unconventional. It may put others off. In fact there have been complaints about both the end and a certain major event happening not only off screen but us not even being shown any lead up to it at all. All of a sudden this thing has happened and the audience has to cope. I admit I am still trying to figure out how I feel about this. But I think I liked it. I don't recall an event this important to a movie being told in this way before. It is certaily off putting at first and both me and my sister needed a few minutes to accept what had just happened. The end just sort of happens but it solidifies the reason the movie exists and if people cannot understand why we end where we do then they are kind of missing the point of what they just saw. My last note is just another shout out to Javier Bardem. He is incredible and iconic in my eyes already. As of this date it is the best film I have seen this year.

No Country For Old Men should please fans of Cormac McCarthy's novel, but the film's strict adherence to the novel's structure doesn't translate as well on screen. Essentially, the movie is great because the novel's story and dialog are so good, but the Coen's fail to find the darkness that exudes from every page of the novel. Goddamn! The Coen Brothers are back and in full form. It seems as though 'No Country For Old Men' is the film to beat this year for the coveted Best Picture Oscar prize. Although it was a different film than I expected, it's every bit as powerful, tense, awkwardly funny and relevant as I had hoped, perhaps even more so. Based on Cormac McCarthy's critically acclaimed novel of the same name, 'No Country For Old Men' is a deeply symbolic and straight-forward story of the struggle between good and evil. The film opens with a flawlessly delivered monologue by the ever-so-great Tommy Lee Jones who portrays Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. Bell is a small-town sheriff in the state of Texas, and in his monologue he talks about how hardened and ruthless we've become as a society. "The crimes we see today...it's hard to even take it's measure. It's just all out war." mutters Bell. This monologue is the perfect setting for Llewyn Moss (Josh Brolin) who while hunting antelope in the desert stumbles upon half a dozen dead Mexicans, heroin and $2.4 Million. Being the road scholar he is, Moss figures no one will come looking for the moola if he snatches it. WRONG! Not only does the Mexican mafia and reputable bounty hunter / smart-ass Carson Welles (Woody Harrelson) pursue Moss, but also one of the most twisted, unpredictable and unreasonable villians in recent film history. His name is Anton Chirguh (Javier Bardem), and when he's not blowing innocent civilians' heads off with a cattle gun or flipping a coin to determine whether you live or die, he quietly observes everybody and everything around him. 

'No Country For Old Men' is a triumph in film-making in that the film has no real flaws. Critics might pan it as "slow-moving" but that's essential in order to correctly build the tension for the key scenes. Most of the film is actually quite fast-paced with such nerve-wracking sequences it will have you on the edge of your seat with a knot in your stomach for a majority of it's runtime. But 'No Country's' quiet and subtle scenes are every bit as powerful as it's action-packed and suspenseful ones. This is due in large part to the screenplay. Supposedly following very closely to McCormac's novel, the Coen brothers deliver their finest work EVER from a screenwriting perspective. Yes, it's even better than 'Fargo'. As for the Coen's directing and editing, it has never been smoother. The film's transitions are nothing short of breathtaking. 

From an acting stand-point 'No Country For Old Men' is also incredible. The stand-out of the film is of course Javier Bardem as the ruthless homicidal maniac Chirguh. Just his facial expressions and body language is enough to make your skin crawl, and if that's not enough, he delivers every line including his catch-phrase "friend-O" with such brooding intensity and creepiness it makes you want to sink in your seat. Bardem is a lock for a Best Supporting Actor nomination this Oscar season, but his biggest competion is the two other key performances of the film. Josh Brolin who last week impressed me with his malicious turn in 'American Gangster' as a crooked cop, is the best he's ever been here in the role of Moss. Moss is such an unlikely hero in the sense he is kind of dumb, not very nice, makes stupid decisions and yet we still root for him to escape the drudges of the Mexican mafia and even worse, the wrath of Chirguh. Tommy Lee Jones I'd say is Bardem's biggest competion. With this and 'In the Valley of Elah', Jones has proven this year with these two performances that if anything he's getting better with age. Jones' monologues are flawlessly delivered like I previously stated, including his final one which left me with goose bumps at the end of the picture. Woody Harrelson is humorous in his limited role as a sharp-witted and over-confident bounty hunter, and Scottish actress Kelly MacDonald is phenomenal in her role as Moss' butter-brain wife. The film has a numerous amount of strong small performances including Garret Dillahunt as Bell's Deputy, Tess Harper as Bell's wife and the 'Office Space' stapler guy (Stephen Root), in a well-played dramatic role as a crime boss. Roger Deakins outdoes himself yet again with some awesome cinematography, and while quiet and subtle, the film's music score is haunting. 

There is no other film this year that I can recommend as highly as 'No Country For Old Men'. There are times when it has you on the edge of your seat in suspense, there are times when it has you laughing violently at some of the darkly humorous scenes and through-out the entire 121 minutes it has you using your brain. There's a lot of symbolism and powerful metaphors in the film, but since I'm not writing a 5-page essay, I'll let you figure them out for yourself. With 'No Country For Old Men' the Coen Brothers have once again raised the bar on how outstanding and thought-provoking a simple crime-drama can be. Grade: A

Prety simple eh? Well it's a HELL of a lot more interesting than that.

For the majority of the movie we see the movie from Brolin's perspective, it's a cat and mouse sorta thing where the hitman is always just one step behind him. They meet up at one point and there is one of the most thrilling and tense shootout/hide and seek games I've seen in film, extremely well done. The other narrative (and arguably the main narrative) is about Tommy Lee Jones' charactor who is on the trail of Brolin. He is at the end of his career as Sherrif and really wants to end this one clean so he can retire feeling like he has achieved something.

The hitman who is after him is one hell of a character. He has a fucked up moral code he lives by and is quite brutal in his murders. There is one great scene where he flips a coin and asks a gas station owner to call it, the gamble is the mans life, no if ands or buts about it, he's gotta call it and if he calls wrong he gets a bullet in the head. Another cool lil' thing I liked was this dudes rather unconventional use of a canister of CO2. He uses it to bust off locks which is prety cool but not as cool as when he calmly places it against a mans head and blows a fucking hole in it with the shear pressure of it. Also one of the end scenes when he meets up with Brolin's wife is prety sinister.

Now we come to the ending... SPOILER'S GALORE HERE!!! My buddy who I saw this with said up until the last 15 minutes it was probably one of the best movies he has seen all year, but the ending made him think it was total bollocks. I wont get too much into what happens but here are my thoughts on it. When Tommy Lee Jones shows up at the hotel and sees Brolin's dead body he feels exactly what the audience fells, disapointment. The last time we saw Brolin he was about to have a couple of beers with some random chick he met by the pool, now he is laying in a pool of blood. Jones' was too late, he failed, he is disapointed and so is the audience. The whole movie up til this point is tense and action filled, now we are sitting there in the audience going "what? what the fuck happened? gah!!!" I think this was tactic was used on purpose by the director. Jones really wanted to get this one right, to close the case and have everything wrapped up nicely. He failed and he is extremely disapointed with himself. He retires and is left with that feeling that his last signment was a failure. The rest of the movie the narrative is shifted to Jones' character who feels like he didn't do what he was sent out to do. He knows he is getting to old and can't do the job any more. This is really "No Country For Old Men"

Jones has perfected the personification of the older generation from "The Fugitive" onward, and his role here is another fantastic performance in his canon.  However, the real treat is Javier Bardem.  His Anton Chigurh is one of the finest villains to grace the screen in a long time.  He is cold and detached, and he personifies the Devil in everything he does.  It's a chilling, scary performance, and it works in spades.  The cinematography is just gorgeous, excellently capturing the vast emptiness of the border.  Add to this the fact that the Coen Brothers stayed close to the book, and the full power of the message rings true: The world we live in now is a far cry from what it used to be, with people deceiving each other and only caring about themselves.  It makes the title an altruism, and no film in 2007 had the impact this one did.  A destined classic.

This is the one movie that I allowed myself to go into with ridiculously high expectations. The reason was, that the source material, Cormac McCarthy's novel of the same name, was so perfectly suited to cinematic translation, and more specifically, to a cinematic translation at the hands of the Coen brothers. The novel was packed with a great cast of characters, a deliciously dark sense of humor, and set against the backdrop of the vast desert vistas and small towns of the American south. With stuff like this, I thought there was no way the Coen brothers could possibly go wrong, and I was right. The plot follows Lewellen Moss (Josh Brolin) who, while out hunting, discovers a stash of $2 million dollars in a drug deal gone wrong. Without fully understanding the consequences of taking the money Moss, something of a cross between average blue-collar Joe and resourceful survivalist, is thrust into a world of very dangerous men who will stop at nothing to get the money back. The brutal hunt is played against small town Sheriff Ed Tom Bell's (Tommy Lee Jones)own attempts to find and help Moss before it is too late. Cormac McCarthy, who is the premier chronicler of the loss of the American west, is here telling the story of the loss of small town America through the eyes of the over-matched Sheriff Bell who has a hard time coming to terms with the boldness and brutality of this new generation of outlaws. Figures like Anton Chigurh, who draws his victims into discussions about causality before having them flip a coin to decide their fate.

It's hard to comment on the film, because it's such a direct translation of the book, but I do have some complaints about the casting decisions. Chigurh, who is such a larger-than-life, terrifying, and seductive figure in the book really needed to be played by someone with more presence (I personally think Benicio Del Toro would have been perfect). While Javier Bardem does an okay job, he plays Chigurh too much as a pure psychopath and the biggest thing about his performance is his distracting hair cut (what was up with that?). Tommy Lee Jones also seemed a bit out of place in his role. Too often a leading man, it seemed impossible for him to play a thoroughly beaten old man who knows his limitations to draw the type of sympathy the part demanded.

Quibbles aside, the movie is propelled by its plot, and it's definitely a fun ride. Anyone that knows McCarthy's work knows they aren't going to a get a conventional feel good Hollywood fairytale, because McCarthy understands only too well that the world is a hard and pitiless place, and this ain't no country for old men.

The first time I saw No Country For Old Men, at one point during it, I realized that my mouth had been wide open for a period of minutes, and I had also been holding popcorn in my fingers halfway between my mouth and the bag.  It dawned on me that I was seeing a very significant movie.

The theme/meaning of No Country For Old Men can be taken in a few ways.  We have a definite protagonist, and a definite antagonist (in the sherrif and Chigur) but we really don't know how to feel about Llewelyn.  He is in a position where the "good guy" would normally be in most movies, yet he is not really one, because he has obvious flaws, and may not be that good of a person.  Yet we are still on his side because the men pursuing him are pure evil, (especially Chigur).  Javier Bardem plays Chigur in a way that instantly lets us know he is insane.  And we get no sense of his past, where he is from (although clearly it's not from Texas), or why he is the way he is.  We just know that he is on a mission, and is going about it with a cool and mellow fasion, and essentially purely emotionless, even as he commits one horrific crime after another; a very effective way to portray a psychopath on screen, very similar to Anthony Hopkins in the Silence of the Lambs.  Consider a scene where Chigur invades a hotel room that is filled with Mexican who are also after the money Lewelyn has found.  He kills two, and finds the third one hiding in the bath tub.  He just strolls over, pulls the curtain shut, turns away, firing his gun and killing the man through the curtain.  He does this in a similar way that I would turn off a TV.  

Chigur seems almost evil beyond the slightest comprehension, and he is just so mesmerizing to watch.

One thing that the Coen Brothers do so well is channel their setting to the audience.  In Fargo, we saw what kind of people and places were in Minnesota, and the sense of the characters there was clear. The Coens had their actors use a certain way of speaking, and certain phrases that represented that small part of America.  No Country For Old Men also has this asset, only this time it is the character and essense of a small Texas town.  And as in Fargo, the criminals are the only ones that do not fit the mold of the town and people they are surrounded by, which only makes them seem more meniacle.

Josh Brolin is good enough, and, again, we don't know whether to root for him, or hope he gets caught by Chigur, after we hear how he talks to his wife, and doesn't help the last survivor of the shootout's consequence he walks in on.

All of these little things are great, but what makes No Country the masterwork that it is?  When the Coen brothers are giving a film, we know that there is more to it than meets the eye.  We wonder what lesson they are trying to teach, or what ironies they used that we missed.  One huge irony comes in the second to last scene of the movie, involving Chigur.  

I think another lesson of this is what Tommy Lee's character conveys for most of the movie, and that is even in the battle of man vs. steer, nothing is certain, as nothing is anytime in our everyday lives.  No Country shows us how money can easily corrupt, and may even suggest that America in general is money-obsessed.  When it comes down to it, most of us are driven purely by our own individual needs.  Our distorted sense of values makes us do things that we should not do.  Surely, Llewelyn's life would have been a lot easier if he had just thrown the money back at the Mexicans right off the bat, and had not tried to keep it all for himself.  But his greed is what drives the movie.

The cinematography intentionally left things out brilliantly.  We don't even see what happens a lot of the times, but the Coens find a way to tell the story anyway, in a much more interesting way with this strategy.  Each occurrance and conversation during the movie is such an important layer in developing the story, and so utterly symbolic in nature. Not a line was out of place in this; not a shot, expression, note, or character. Everything had a purpose. Nothing was thinned out, all loose ends tied up, poetically written, and a fascinating piece of cinema.

It's hard to describe how good No Country for Old Men really is. An extraordinary, amazingly accomplished film, No Country is incredibly dark, bleak and might be the best movie the Coen brothers have made since Fargo. Which is appropriate, given that No Country exists in the same moral universe as Fargo. Essentially taking the mirror of snow-drenched Minnesota from Fargo into the Texas desert, this film is Fargo's even darker twin - there's virtually no comedy in this film, the characters are essentially dead men and women walking, and the main antagonist might be one of the most menacing villains in recent screen history. The poetic resignation the characters face in No Country is gorgeously shot, immaculately drawn out with a terrific story and provides no easy answers. Perhaps the best part of this film is the surely-to-be-nominated Javier Bardem for Best Actor - his horrific, menacing portrait of an amoral psychopath is easily one of the best performances of the year. A Best Picture candidate for sure - one of the year's finest films. Don't miss it.

But whats perhaps most impressive about this film is the lack of score; this is very effective in creating great tension. An absolute masterpiece in almost every way.

The Coen Brothers have been in a slump the past couple of years with both their Intolerable Cruelty and remake of the classic Lady Killers bombing with both audiences and critics alike.  They were also unkindly criticized after Fargo for their films like The Big Lebowski because they didnt match the visceral level that the former did.  Fargo was a masterpiece because it elevated its genre beyond its normal limitations.  Now comes along No Country for Old Men, which has been one of the most hyped films of the year ever since its premiere at Cannes.  Believe the hype because No Country for Old Men is almost every bit as good as Fargo and that is certainly saying something.  At its center is a thrilling crime story, but around the edges is where the film truly shines with its commentary on the ever-changing west and how as time goes on our society becomes more and more violent.  It would be easy to say that No Country's point is that money is the root of all evil, but its really about much more than that and its final moments are uncommonly beautiful.  I've never seen a film like this end in the way that No Country does.  The performances here are spot on all the way through.  Josh Brolin makes a charismatic leading man while Tommy Lee Jones is perfectly cast as the age worn Sheriff.  But it is Javier Bardem that steals the picture from everyone else in it as the sadistic killer on the hunt for Brolin and the two million dollars on his person.  Bardem is brilliant as the films main villain (though let it be known there is a fine line between good and evil in No Country) and every scene he is in is simply electric.  He is the most memorable cold-blooded screen villain in quite sometime.  For my money the best scene in the movie is the coin toss between him and a gas station owner.  It sent shivers down my spine from its dialogue alone.  Speaking of the dialogue almost all of it is near perfection.  The Coen's have once again balanced dark humor with thrilling drama and their style matches perfectly with Cormac McCarthy's source material.  The Cinematography is also beautiful and chilling.  Roger Deakens lensed this modern western and between this and his other western pic Jesse James, the cinematographer is having one hell of a great year.  But in the end what really makes No Country for Old Men shine is the spot on direction from Joel and Ethan Coen.  I've always believed they came into cinema too late in life.  Their films belong in the cinematic golden age of exploration in the 70's.  No Country for Old Men is very much in that tradition of filmmaking and as such it left me speechless.  Certainly this is one of the very best films of the year

I watched this again.  That makes two viewings, and two readings of the book.
Back to five stars.
You know what?  Fuck the haters.  This is damn near, DAMN near perfect.  The discipline of the adaptation, the simplicity of the visual execution, the prescience of the story- all very nearly in a league of their own.  Is this a better movie than "There Will Be Blood" or "Assassination of Jesse James"?  Maybe.  Maybe not.  At a level that high it becomes a matter of personal preference, and I would still put this as the third-best film in a year of UNBELIEVABLE movies.  
My (earlier) gripe, and the biggest gripe of the movie's detractors, is the handling of Josh Brolin's death.  You know what?  Making the decision not to tell us what happened accomplishes almost the EXACT same thing as the deliberate anti-climax of a deputy telling the story over his corpse, as it was executed in the book.  I'm no longer convinced this was the Coen's only mistake- I think it may well have been McCarthy's (blasphemy, I know, and don't think I've forgotten that the man is a legitimate genius).  
What McCarthy wrote was an anticllimax.  It remains an anticlimax- just a ballsier one.  And that's the point.  Leaving us in the dark may be dissatisfying as moviegoers rooting for a hero, but it elevates this from a bloody hunter/hunted story into a piece of contemporary art.  If you're going to make that choice, why NOT go all the way?  This isn't about Josh Brolin getting the best of Chigurh.  This is about a modern Ezekiel, a prophet of destruction, and all that he is a harbinger for in the years to come.  This is about the changing nature of the world, and of human beings.  I didn't realize, the first time I watched this, how brilliantly the third act layers meaning, how subtly it progresses through theme- the Uncle Ellis scene, for example, felt out of place the first time- but now?  Watching it again, particularly the ending- "What's comin' ain't waiting on you.  That's vanity."  Which transitions IMMEDIATELY into the scene between Chigurh and Llewellyn's wife- that's the most elevated kind of storytelling, the kind that insinuates itself into your thoughts so obliquely you almost don't know you're being told a story at all.  And Chigurh's final car accident, upon further review- not the random act it seemed, but more the final flourish of a magician, the final puff of smoke before he vanishes from the stage, the last disappearing act of the world's most invisible killer. Ebert says No Country is 'a perfect film', well if it is, it's because it was based on a perfect book. True, in the less capable hands of a filmmaker without the gusto and sheer talent of the likes of the Coen brothers, it could've fallen flat, but there isn't a single scene and nary a line of dialogue in the movie that was not in the book. So while the Coen brothers are brilliant filmmakers in their way, let's not forget the original genius behind this simple yet amazing story, Cormac McCarthy. The acting is also typical of a Coen bros. film, flawless. I don't know what they do to make their actors so great, but they are. And at the highest point of acting in No Country stands Tommy Lee Jones and Javier Bardem, themselves taking the film from really good, to great. Tommy Lee, while playing a character almost identitcal and playing it in almost an identical way, as some couple of his previous works, is perfectly cast and plays sheriff Ed Tom without flaw. And Bardem. Wow. Bardem will win the academy award for outstading acting achievment in a supporting role, I guarentee it. He's probably best known for Before Night Falls, which he was nominated for in acting a few years ago. Considering this guy didn't know barely a lick of english when filming began on this flick, his performance is one of the best I've seen in a movie in a long long time. An especial standout for me was Stephen Root, playing the mysterious man in a fancy suit in a swanky office building. His small, but memorable performance really shows off his versatility as an actor once again, and hints at bigger and better things for his career. 
There are some brilliant little visual touches here and there, very memorable; the upturned bowl of cat's milk, seeing the light in the hallway go dark through crack under the door, how you know what happened to Lewelyn's wife just by the way Chugurh checks the bottom of his boots.
Now alot of people talk about the ending being confusing or inconclusive or something. I didn't find that at all, but again that could be because I read the book and knew the ending when I went in. 
You can tell watching this that it will be a movie for the ages. One of those gems that will stand the test of time and people will come to in the future to help express all that went right with filmmaking in the first decade of the new millennium. I wouldn't go so far as to call it an epic. Just a really well made film by some really good filmmakers, based on a book written by a unique and brilliant, if somewhat bleak, literary mind.

more than worty of all the hype ladled on it, the coen brothers' latest is a masterpiece existential drama. while enjoyable at the surface level of suspense thriller, with nail biting tension sustained from the opening scene, there is also a bleak insight into the violence that has pervaded american society, the mouthpiece being tommy lee jones' weary sheriff (a role he now sinks into with consummate ease), the history of his ancestors seemingly etched into his craggy features. 
   what will stay with the viewer most however, besides the great work from cinematographer roger deakins that captures the harsh texan landscape, the absence of an obvious musical score, and the terrific sound work (wind is used brilliantly to create a desolate mood of moral absence) is javier bardems astonishing performance as dead eyed assassin anton chigurh, a villain so intimidating the audience reaction to him is palpable every time he enters a scene. the only psycho to run this villain close is dennis hopper in blue velvet. 
   It's Chirgurh that is the embodiment of the violence jones' sheriff laments, pitted against whom is josh brolins (an excellent performance and a remarkable 2007 comeback) llewyn moss, who if not sympathetic enough to act as the film's central focus- one of the many narrative sleights of hand- is nonetheless compelling as an everyman struggling with his fateful decision to steal $2 million in drug money.
   With the last act giving way to an outwardly philosophical climax that jars with the thriller mechanics that have gone before some viewers will be frustrated, but it certainly leaves a lot to think about and discuss. a formidable film to open 2008 in the UK - may the good quality continue!

The direction again is exquisite from the Coens, with terrific cinematography from Roger Deakins, and the sparse atmospheric music creates a beautifully lonely feel. Without longwinded scores, the Coens use accentuated sounds which give aethestic/realistic qualities to their films.

Wow, before I start the review I just want to ask one thing: why does facebook know that I bought tickets to this on fandango? Do they have my credit card or some shit? I have to read into this, because if that's the case, then there's going to be some serious ass-whooping going down. Anyway, "No Country for Old Men". It was great. All of the actors are awesome, the shots are cool, and it generally flows perfectly for most of the movie. Josh Brolin is likeable, Tommy Lee Jones is a good middleman, and Javier Bardem is a really scary dude. The whole weird old-school 1980 Texan vibe is cool too. There is one problem, however. There's something about 20-25 minutes to the end that happens, and after that, the movie gets REALLY crazy with dialogue. It's not actually difficult dialogue like hard words to understand, but it's sort of spoken in Texan drawl, and that, combined with a random character that pops up out of nowhere, sort of made the ending bad for me. The craziness of the plot sort of died, and it became mostly about talking. However, I give the movie the benefit of the doubt for two reasons. For one, the stuff that was being said was probably REALLY smart and tied in with the theme of the plot, and I was just too slow to get it. The other reason is that the Coens were probably being nice guys and adapting the book word for word, which is cool, but sometimes doesn't translate to the screen properly. It's fun to read long passages that sum up a whole book on paper, but it's not as fun (or easy) to listen to them onscreen (in a Texan accent, nonetheless). Simplicity is key. For example, at the end of "Fargo", Frances McDormand sums up the whole movie in like two sentences, and it was beautiful and meaningful without being hard to understand. Other than that however, the movie was GREAT. Go see it. It's awesome. Hopefully, when I can watch it again on DVD (with subtitles), I'll be able to understand the deep message that it's trying to give. The main thing I learned from the movie is this: If you see a guy with a compressed air tank walking toward you, run the fuck away.

The film opens silently, with only the whisper of wind across the open fields of Texas. Then, a voice begins, Tommy Lee Jones' voice. Being a Texas lawman isn't like it was in the old days, when some sheriffs didn't even wear a gun. These days, in 1980, you never know what evil you'll find committed in your own town. And this voice, Ed Tom Bell's voice, is a voice of age and reason. If anyone should know this country, it's an old man like him.

Meanwhile, Ed Tom's deputy is making an arrest, quietly. As his prisoner sits nearby in cuffs, the deputy calls to leave a message for the sheriff Ã¢ÂÂ everything's going smoothly, other than this strange tank the man carries with him. But we can see, before the deputy does, that this will be his last phone call. This plot is going to come out of the blue for all of us, grab us by the collar and give us a good shaking.
Jones is the center of the film, providing both poetically rich voice-over and a soulfully muted performance as the Texan sheriff who has the tiredness of decades behind his eyes and voice.  Josh Brolin is the welder who just happens to stumble across the remnants of a drug deal gone bad - complete with suitcase full of money and truckload full of product. And Javier Bardem is the maniacally calculating, cold-blooded killer who's after Brolin to get his money back. Bardem's Anton Chigurh may be the finest performance of a killer ever committed to celluloid. Even his wordless breaths are magnetic.
There's a stunning morality that the story develops like a disease - and this is no tacked-on morality that tries to tie up the loose ends of a story gone every which way. The morality surfaces subtly but breathtakingly, as if it were lurking all along in the pattern of these characters' intermingling.  Chigurh is convinced he has to kill, as if he were only a victim of fate. Brolin's Llewelyn Moss drives himself to outdo Anton, as if escape would mean salvation. And Ed Tom Bell circles the center of the story, giving us a sense of normalcy and of a world gone wrong, terribly wrong.

No Country for Old Men is by far the darkest of the brother's resume of films. The story follows three people in southwest Texas in 1980. An average local, Llewelyn Moss, who after hunting deer stumbles across a blood bath of dead body's that lead him a big bag of drug money. A psychopathic killer, Anton Chigurh, begins a game of cat and mouse with Llewelyn as he shoots his way through anyone in his path in order to get his money back. His weapons are a high-pressured cattle gun and a silenced shotgun. The third is an old sheriff on the brink of retirement when he gets involved with trying to protect Llewelyn and his wife.

The beauty of the film is its shear use of the tiny of moments that either begins to frighten you or make you laugh. Javier Bardem who plays Chigurh is chilling, smart, and funny. All of the other actors shine and give Oscar worthy performances. Like many of the other Coen Brothers movies, the film leaves you in question and has you want to see the film a second time around.

What a wonderful experience! 
Never in my life have I been simultaneously enthralled and repulsed by characters in a movie... but here we have it. This is, without a doubt, one of the best films I have seen in a long, LONG time and I assure you it is the best film of 2007.
The greatest thing about this picture, besides the intensely effective acting- is the directorial execution of each and every detail. This film has, hands down, the most intense and riveting cat-and-mouse subplot I have ever seen. Javier Bardem makes for himself, a career-defining performance and what I hope is a supporting-actor Oscar while Tommy Lee Jones gives, yet another, career enriching performance. 
Starting and ending the film with personal monologues into Jones' character's psyche was the best, best, best way to encompass the rest of the film- which adds to the complexity of the story line.
Giving away a plot synopsis would do this film absolutely NO justice, in the least, and I feel they brilliantly side-stepped that in making the trailer for this.
One of my other reasons for loving this film so much is the humor- I can't say I have ever laughed more in an intense action picture... but did I here! 
The screenplay is destined to be nominated for an Oscar as well... these characters speak in such a rich and realistic way, it adds an impecible sense of reality that carries the horrifying nature of the plot right up to the pitch-perfect ending.
GO SEE THIS MOVIE!!!

Bardem plays the sociopath, and his representation is 'our' (all persons) fate; death and how it come upon us at any time, in any way. Brolin represents 'our' succombing to the craving of wants. I admit when we started watching this I was bored. I was in the mood for something fast paced, action packed, something to appeal to my sleepy mind. Once you get into the pace of this film and embrace the lingering landscapes, you may find yourself falling in love with this  'modern western'. 

This was a film for me, that the longer I thought about it afterwards the more I could see how much of a masterpiece it really is. True there is little character development, but there doesn't need to be; it's a chase plot between good and evil. Humans will inevitably side with the good character, especially when he's being shot at with a massive gun and I mean massive! So we don't really need to see his development over the course of the film. He is poor, he finds 2 million dollars, he takes the money and must pay the consequences. 

As for the character of Anton; the emotionless killer, all we know of him is that he was hired to track down the missing drug money and instead turns upon those who hired him and decides to go after the money for himself. When a character executes such an amount of random and senseless killing we need no more motive or background to feel satisfied about this character's actions, simply put he is evil. 

This film keeps you on the edge most of the time. As far as tense dramas/ thrillers go, it's one of the best I've seen in a long time. With brilliant direction and such an enigmatic character as Anton blasting people away you can't help but feel the heart begin beating a little bit faster.

Anyway, this definitely tops the list of best movies for '07. I can't wait for the DVD to hear more commentary from the Coen brothers about how they made this remarkable film. In an interview they were talking about the discussion whether or not to show the hallway when Llewelyn enters his room and how it was decided to show it so that the audience had that image in their minds for when Anton is standing on the other side of the door. Details like this fascinate me and show how the creative minds of these brothers work. Amazing film.

The basic story is about a man who stumbles upon the results of a deal gone wrong in a desolate area somewhere in Texas. He finds bodies, empty shells... and a wad of bills, which he proudly takes. Of course, badder people are out to find this money, especially one psychopath named Anton Chigurh (pronounced "Chi-gar" almost like "sugar"), played by a creepy but calm Javier Bardem who'll scare you shitless. There's a sheriff played by Tommy Lee Jones who goes on the trail to figure out what's happening and why. All throughout the course of the film is perhaps one of the most eerie, suspensful cat-and-mouse chases depicted on screen since I dunno when.

When the movie ended (and I was given a heads up about this), it seems rather abrupt. I'd say it is, but only in the sense that one didn't really pay attention to the film's message, but just watched the all-too thrilling plot unfold. Perhaps if I hadn't gotten the heads up, I might've been like, "What the hell??" so I'm giving it to youse guys. Plot doesn't necessarily serve as the backbone, but it does grip you from start to finish, everything just calls back to the film's title as the movie serves more as a lil' commentary on violence, making the whole movie message and central characters kinda tragic in a way.

Fantastic film noir/thriller from the Coen Bros,who after a two film slump,are back with a vegeance with this viciously entertaining film.The plot is pretty straightforward:an average joe stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad, steals a bag of money and is pursued by a relentless killer.That simple premise is a springboard for a compelling game of cat and mouse between the two men with a world weary sheriff watching from the sidelines.The whole cast is great:between this,Grindhouse and American Gangster,Josh Brolin is having a hell of a year,he turns in a career best performance here as Moss,the man who finds the money who is more wily then he appears.Javier Bardem radiates menace as the psychopath on the trail of the money,he's truly frightening and I would rank him up there with Hannibal Lecter in Silence of the Lambs and Frank Booth in Blue Velvet.You're honestly afraid for the other characters when he's lurking around.Tommy Lee Jones does his best work in years as the sheriff,granted he could probably do this kind of role in his sleep,but when it's this well acted and written,who can complain.And Woody Harrelson has a small but memorable role as a cocky bounty hunter.The film is very suspenseful,there's a scene with a ringing telephone that's worthy of Hitchcock.This isn't for the faint hearted as there's violence aplenty in addition to the aformentioned nerve wracking,but there are dollops of the trademark Coens black comedy.The best film of 2007.

When I saw "No Country for Old Men" today, I left the theater perplexed. I was not only perplexed, but shocked. For the next twenty minutes I thought about this film. What does it mean? Why did they do that? Why does it end that way? I then decided that this film was the most original film I had seen in ages. It was shocking, but not in the way "A Clockwork Orange" was shocking. It was stunning , but not in the way "The Godfather" or "City of God" were stunning. No, this film packs it own kind of punch. The film opens up quietly. There are just some opening credits. Then the voice of Tommy Lee Jones, a sheriff in this film, talks about how the times are a-changin' and then it cuts to Javier Bardem, playing Anton Chigurh, getting taken away by a police officer. At the station, Chigurh strangles the officer with his handcuffs. But this isn't done like the way another villain would strangle someone. No. He smiles. And yes, there have been other villains who smile at death, but you know that he just doesn't give a damn. Around the same time, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles on a complete massacre. Dead bodies everywhere. Even the dog is shot dead. He finds some money and after being chased by some strange men in his truck, Llewelyn decides to tell his wife to scram up to her mother's house, and he will get his business done. Well, Llewelyn doesn't know that Anton Chigurh is out to get that money back and what ensues is a film all about fate. Chain reactions. It's existential, but not in the sense of "The Seventh Seal. It's violent, but not in the sense of "Pulp Fiction". If you're an "American Gangster" fan, then this film is not for you. It's nobody film but it's own. But how people will react to it makes this film a classic. Everything is this film will not be forgotten. You know that you never seen a bad ass like Chigurh. In one scene when he confronts Woody Harrelson, there's this tense moment where there is nothing but a test of wills. A phone rings. Woody get startled, and Chigurh just blasts him. You know you never seen a character like Llewelyn Moss, or sheriff Ed Tom Bell. You know you will never see a gutsy un-movie like ending like this film has. It's a film all on it own. I realized that this is a film classic. Not a modern film classic, but just classic. I did not expect to be floored by this film. And I was. There's no way in hell this movie's gonna win Best Picture. But I don't care if it wins or not. All I care is that this is a masterpiece and should be remembered for ages. There were no heroes. There was no music. There was no ending. There was, however, an unforgettable film.

A great thriller/modern western with black comedy, heart-pounding suspense, and superb performances. The Coen brothers certainly did Cormac McCarthy's novel justice. The Academy might as well give Javier Bardem the statue for Best Supporting Actor right now, as he gives one of the most terrifying performances in recent memory as the cold-blooded Chigurh. Aside from some places in the film in which the dialogue drags on, this is a very well-made film.

People may rail against the Coens' decision to stick with the novel's conclusion to end the film (as the ending doesn't really translate well to the screen), but it is somewhat appropriate because the ending expresses the bleak outlook on humanity that the film  attempts to relay. So don't look for a Hollywood ending to this story, as this film, to some extent, gives a realistic take on life.

A taut, engaging modern noir, it's the best thing I've seen this year. Much has been made of the dialogue, and given the source material and the Coen brothers' reputation, it's no surprise that this picture's loaded with memorable exchanges. But many of the best scenes play out with barely a word, particularly the sequences with Brolin's character. His discovery of the drug deal gone bad, the chase sequences, etc. are delivered with sharp, lean precision.

   It's easy to admire masterful filmmaking, but few pictures get under your skin because of technique. What really stays with you is the dark and nihilistic tone - for much of the film, it's as if hired killer Anton Chigurh is evil incarnate, overwhelming everything and everyone in the story. Towards the end, when one character tells him that no one but himself is to blame for his deeds, he dismisses her argument. On the surface, his rebuttal sounds like the typical explanation a sociopath would give - shirking responsibility with a logic only he'd believe.

   But that's not the case at all. He's not evil personified, he's only a symptom of it. All of these characters are simply inhabiting an incompassionate environment, where God as some would hope to know Him either doesn't exist or doesn't care. The point's driven home minutes later in the film's most inspired moment, when Chigurh's logic is vindicated and we see that even he's not immune to the world's cruel, capricious nature.

   Plenty of people will leave the theater unsatisfied, even disdainful of the way the picture simply ends with Tommy Lee Jones; he plays Sheriff Bell, an aging officer who's supposed to change things for the better but gradually realizes he's really an ineffectual bystander, incapable of having any impact on what's unfolding two steps ahead of him. There is no resolution, no token optimism, but in this world, there can't be.

The Coens have burst out of the recent slump they've been in and proved once again that they are masters of what they do. "No Country" has the dark comedy we've come to know and expect from them, but not very much of it. This time, they've put the emphasis on "dark", and created something ferociously raw, violent, intense and unnerving. With "No Country" they elevate suspense to an art form. They use silence like a weapon, until the anticipation is literally unbearable. This thing is unsettling edge-of-your-seat viewing like nothing else that's come out this year. A lot of this is made possible thanks to Javier Bardem's chilling performance as one of the most evil psychopathic killers ever put on screen. Josh Brolin gives a fantastic performance, and Tommy Lee Jones gives another great Tommy Lee Jones-ish performance. (subtle, wise, dry humor) But man, Bardem's getting a crapload of awards this year. Time will tell--as it always does--just how powerful and important "No Country for Old Men" really is.  But at first  glance, my feeling is that this is a classic--cold, unsparing, yet sprinkled with humor--that will one day be one of 'THE' movies.  It is certainly right up there with "Fargo" as one of the--if not the absolute--best Coen Brothers films ever.

The Coens' visual sense has never been stronger.  Their propensity to infuse the material with rampant quirks has been quelled considerably, yet their unique sense of humor and ability to create classic characters is still apparent and still sharp.  And this story--about murder, money, and the nature of man to get involved in the business of both--is powerful and riveting in every sense.  Coen Brothers films have a tendency to seem like tall tales, but here is the grand-daddy of all tall tales, based on the Cormac McCarthy novel and brought to profound and stunning life by the Coens.  "No Country for Old Men" is not a tall tale about goofy people doing goofy things.  It is a tall tale about the evils of men and money, about the predictability and unpredictability of life as we know it, about how all of us listen to the ticking of the clock, waiting for the final alarm to sound.  

We all will die one day, and we will all meet again in Heaven...where perhaps the vicious cycle will start all over again.  Yikes.

After two disappointing, sub-par efforts in a row ([i]The Ladykillers[/i], [i]Intolerable Cruelty[/i], three if you count [i]The Man Who Wasnt There[/i]), Joel and Ethan Coen ([i]O Brother, Where Art Thou?[/i], [i]The Big Lebowski[/i], [i]Fargo[/i], [i]Barton Fink[/i], [i]Miller's Crossing[/i], [i]Raising Arizona[/i], [i]Blood Simple[/i]), seemed, surprisingly, at a creative loss. If the Coen Brothers latest, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], an adaptation of National Book Award and Pulitzer Prize-winning Cormac McCarthys ([i]All the Pretty Horses[/i], [i]Blood Meridian[/i]) novel, the three-year hiatus between projects has done the Coen Brothers good. Adapting McCarthys spare, taut crime drama into an equally spare, taut film, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is the perfect antidote for all thats ailed the Coen Brothers. 
 
Hunting antelope near the Rio Grande (the U.S.-Mexico border), Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a Vietnam veteran just scraping by, runs across a drug deal thats left all but one man dead. Moss finds a pickup loaded down with bricks of heroin, but decides to search for the drug money, which he finds easily. Stirred, briefly, by his conscience, Moss returns to the scene of the crime, presumably to help the dying man who kept asking for water. Moss runs smack into heavily armed Mexicans. Forced to leave his truck behind, Moss escapes and returns home, sends his wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald), to stay with her mother, and flees with the money. 
 
The drug cartel has hired a brutal, cold-blooded assassin, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), to track down the money. Alerted to the murder of a deputy in another town and an increasing body count by a mysterious killer, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) begins an investigation that leads to Moss, a personal acquaintance. Concerned about Chigurhs very visible killing spree, the cartel sends Chigurhs ex-partner, Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson), after Chigurh and the money. Chigurh, however, proves to be far more difficult to eliminate or control than Moss, Bell, or Wells expected. 
 
[i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is as bleak and as violent as they come and then some. What starts off as a pulpy crime drama involving familiar genre elements (e.g., drug money, theft, unstoppable assassins, violent men living and dying violently), albeit one told with high production values, taut direction, impressive location cinematography by longtime Coen collaborator Roger Deakins (who should have an Academy Award by now, but hasnt, at least not yet), a polished script that retains McCarthys ear for laconic dialogue, and riveting performances by a uniformly talented case, all of which makes [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] an immensely entertaining genre exercise. [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], however, tries to be more, far more than that, though, and it succeeds, often brilliantly.
 
The Coen Brothers, closely following McCarthys novel, reject narrative closure for an ambiguous, frustrating ending that offers none of the niceties (e.g., justice, retribution, moral balance, or moral equivalency) almost universally present in Hollywood films, regardless of genre. [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is both a morality play about the usual pitfalls associated with crossing over into an underworld of crime and violence and a meditation about the nature and existence of evil in a profane world. In that, the Coen Brothers succeed, perhaps too well, as [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is the type of film difficult to watch more than once and the reason can be summed up in two words: Anton Chigurh. 
 
By the final scene of end of [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], we learn little about Chigurh that we didnt already know by the end of the first or second scene: Chigurh is a sociopathic assassin with a twisted, coldly rational worldview. He has no history, no family, no friends, nothing to tie him to the world except business relationships. Chigurh is less a character than an archetype of the Angel of Death or, more accurately, the closest McCarthy comes to a god in a universe devoid of the divine, an Old Testament god of vengeance, wreaking bloody havoc while simultaneously imposing order on a chaotic universe. Combined with Bardems dark appearance, blank, almost expressionless face, deliberate line deliveries, and heavy physicality, Chigurh will go down as one of the most memorable villains on film.

No Country For Old Men has so much going for it its almost frustrating for a young filmmaker like myself looking to make a good film. They make you glue your ass to the seat and your eyes to the screen as Josh Brolin or Tommy Lee Jones go head to head with Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurhe, the best bad guy I can remember in recent years.  At the filmâs center is aging and soon-to-retire lawman Tommy Lee Jones.  His existential dilemma of not knowing where his legacy fits in his cop family lineage and the worldâs messed-up greater order becomes the filmâs ultimate statement, a profound and heartbreaking notion that is rarely found in most thrillers.  The action is top notch: the blood makes squirm, each gunshot makes you jump, and you can almost hear the blood rushing through the characters ears in moments with the maximum at stake.

The film thrives on its pitch perfect cast.  Josh Brolin plays an ex-Viet Nam vet turned welder who stumbles on a bloodbath drug deal gone wrong and walks away with $2 million in drug money.  His grit and toughness are surprising coming from Bran in The Goonies.  He really has transformed himself into a top-notch actor (also appearing in the underwhelming American Gangster this year).  Tommy Lee Jonesâs performance is a joy to watch.  His absolute disappearance into the role of the southern sheriff is amazing.  For an actor of his stature to become the character that he does is really impressive and a joy to watch.  Like I mentioned earlier, his mentally nomadic search for answers or comfort in such a violent and criminal time is heartbreaking as you see the wear and tear of the weary world right on the creases on his face.  Despite Jonesâs brilliance in the film, Javier Bardem steals the show, no doubt about it.  His turn as the quietly demonic assassin Chigurhe could be the most interesting, daring, and fun-to-watch performance Iâve seen all year.  The initial âcoin tossâ scene between him and a down-home gas station owner showcases the Coen Brothers skill for dark comedy mixed in with a little dread and tension to boot.  Overall, I walked out thoroughly entertained not only by how interesting and well-told the story was but also by how good the Coen Brothers really can be. Joel and Ethan Coen bring a touch of levity to their faithful adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's relentlessly bleak 2003 novel No Country for Old Men, though it's the type of nervous humor born from relieving immense tension. The Coens' first film since their leaden remake of The Ladykillers is an exceptional return to their Blood Simple roots, offering up a crime saga in which money is almost as irresistible as bad choices are inevitable. Their cynical streak finds its perfect complement in McCarthy's gloomy tale of Biblical-scale chaos in 1980 Texas, and yet the Coens nonetheless locate the black comedy hidden within the acclaimed author's terse, punctuation-sparse prose. Brusque exchanges and austere violence are the story's stock-in-trade, with both elements so downbeat and harsh that they occasionally veer close to absurdity, thereby providing the filmmaking siblings with opportunities to wryly alleviate the oppressive despair and viciousness that hovers over the proceedings in the same way that the enormous Western landscape and its weighty silence hang over its human inhabitants. As Tommy Lee Jones's sheriff Ed Tom Bell says in reference to a particularly grim anecdote, "I laugh sometimes. 'Bout the only thing you can do." 

Hunting out on the expansive plains, Vietnam vet Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon a gruesome scene: vehicles abandoned, heavily armed men dead (aside from a solitary survivor begging for agua), a pickup truck flatbed full of heroin, andâa little ways off, next to another stiffâa suitcase full of $2 million in cash. Moss discovers this mess by following a trail of blood spied on the dry, cracked earth, a perceptiveness that immediately marks him as a man attuned to the land's rugged ferociousness, and thus makes his subsequent decision to take the cash and run a consciously foolish one. Moss realizes hard men will soon come for what's theirs but absconds with the money anyway. Overstepping his boundaries at great risk, he's something of a noir protagonist, albeit minus the romanticism, since the Coensâdiligently following McCarthy's leadâdepict his momentous choice as the unwise but natural act of someone bred in a lunatic world. Unlike Ed Tom, whose old-school values are ill equipped to confront the mayhem of the modern era, and very much like his pursuer, the psychopathic Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem)âwho, later, will also ascertain knowledge from blood on the groundâMoss does what he does because he's the product of a fundamentally out-of-whack environment. 

This generational gap is intrinsic to No Country, which laments with confused, terrified resignation the dawn of a new, more insane ageâor, as one cop puts it, "the dismal tide." Ed Tom is the story's nominal good-guy detective, attempting to figure out the who, what, where, when, and why of Moss's disappearance and the carnage wrought by Chigurh, but he's really just a street sweeper, left to clean up the mess left in these two younger men's wakes. The Coens' concise, efficient script proficiently captures McCarthy's melancholic view of old-young disparities, whether it be Ed Tom's utilization of horses to scour the desolate desert for clues, or his bafflement at the callous disregard for the dead (and propriety) shown by a guy transporting corpses to the morgue. Meanwhile, their economical, decidedly un-flashy direction (mimicking McCarthy's writing, and aided by longtime collaborator Roger Deakins's beautifully severe cinematography) repeatedly conveys narrative undercurrents in entrancingly subtle ways, such that the plethora of animal carcasses, instances of man-versus-beast violence, and Ed Tom's yarn about a slaughterhouse mishap coalesce into a chilling portrait of anarchic interspecies warfare. 

At the center of this maelstrom is the cattle stun gun-wielding Chigurh, a madman with a Prince Valiant bowl-cut and an expression both bemused and remorseless. His methodical comportment, like that exhibited by Moss when hiding his stolen loot in a motel room air duct, makes him seem innately in harmony with his surroundings. And yet the crazed glint in his eyes simultaneously casts him as an alien, an intruder recently arrived from Hades to tender unholy blessings (as during a lethal carjacking) and confession (to a gas station owner). Bardem plays Chigurh like the calmest lunatic known to heaven or hell, and he's never more frightening than when uttering, in his bizarro bass voice, the faux term-of-endearment "friend-o" to prospective prey. Chigurh's stillness is emblematic of the Coens' use of surface tranquility to conceal latent brutality, as well as an external reflection of his fatalism. The villain's habit of granting victims a chance at amnesty via a coin flip turns out to be the sole exception to his governing belief that he's incapable of affecting ongoing events, all of which he implies are byproducts of everything that's come before. It's a pessimism shared by the film, which makes clear (spoiler alert!) the unavoidability and inconsequentiality of Llewelyn and wife Carla Jean's (Kelly Macdonald) deathsâjust two more drops of blood for the thirsty Texas earthâby keeping their murders off-screen. 

"You're not cut out for this," a drug kingpin's hired hand (Woody Harrelson) tells Llewelyn, and though that's technically true, the increasingly bullet-riddled Llewelyn remains better suited for his situation than his elders, such as a senior citizen who picks him up on the side of the road andârevealing an amusing lack of perspectiveâtells him, "Hitchhiking is dangerous." Thanks to its dour depiction of unreasonable, unstoppable evil, the film courts topical terrorism-related allegorical interpretations, even as it strives for Old Testament classicism. The Coens don't shy away from McCarthy's epically dark aspirations but their touch is a tad drier, affording their superb cast's performances room to breathe, and allowing the action's bursts of maliciousness to resound with greater impact. An even more forceful impression, however, is left by the mournful epilogue, in which Jones's weary, admittedly "outmatched" sheriff resigns in defeat to a universe he no longer comprehends. His recurring attempts to understand the modern condition through the filter of old tall tales are ultimately, pitifully futile. Yet if this failure represents an admission that the past, despite having begat the here and now, holds no keys to understanding the present, it also demands the creation of contemporary fictions to help make sense of the new world madness. With the masterful No Country, the Coens and McCarthy give us one.

After two slumps ('Intolerable Cruelty' and 'The Ladykillers'), the Coen Brothers seemed like they had dried up as storytellers. Those previous two movies exhibited none of the qualities that made their previous work such a joy to watch. Of course, as they are prone to doing, Joel and Ethan surprised everyone with their next film: an adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's haunting novel 'No Country for Old Men'. The Brothers' choice to adapt this book was inspired and the result of this perfect match of source material and filmmakers is nothing short of absolutely stunning.

'No Country for Old Men' is a violent, thrilling tale that showcases everything that has made the Coen Brothers masters of their trade. There are touches of 'Blood Simple' here and there, a bit of 'Fargo', even 'Raising Arizona' comes to mind. However, none of those films can possibly measure up to the all-encompassing power and beauty of 'No Country', the film that won the Coen Brothers their first directing Oscar and Best Picture of the year.

The acting is superb. The Coen Brothers have once again outdone themselves assembling a team of the finest actors the industry has to offer (their casting director deserves a raise). Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones are just fantastic, with Jones delivering one of his finest performances to date as a world-weary, aging sheriff. Woody Harrelson and Kelly Macdonald are here in top form as well, with Harrelson pulling off a really spectacular performance despite his short screen time. However, the real find here is, of course, Javier Bardem, as the terrifying beyond description killer Anton Chigurh. He earned an Oscar for his performance and it was more than deserved. His portrayal of this truly unsettling character is unforgettable and one of the greatest villains the screen has ever displayed.

The Coens are firing on all cylinders here as storytellers and visual artists. With every frame, they prove, once again, their mastery of the craft and it's nothing but exhilarating to behold. Roger Deakins finally gets another opportunity to demonstrate why he is one of the best cinematographers working in the business today, and it is, arguably, his best work yet. 

Thrilling, unsettling, and beautiful beyond all logic, 'No Country for Old Men' is the best movie the Coen Brothers have ever made and it deserves to go down as one of the finest films that cinema has to offer.

Javier Bardem could kick Hannibal Lecter's ass, hands down. Tommy Lee Jones is a weathered, wise everyman. For the rest of us, I recommend never taking money that doesn't belong to you, because there's a whole world of depravity out there you know nothing about.

In a nutshell: An unusuall slow burning game of cat and mouse with a philospohical twist in its tail.

A much darker and bleak film from the normally quirky Coen Brorthers, and one that isn;t easily categorised. Is it a Western? A horror? A film noir?

And it usually does, with liberal amounts of treacly blood and nasty no frills violence peppering the plot.

Using three main players rather than just one, it's more thoughtful and ponderous a film than a straight forward thriller, but all three are excellent and Javier Bardem's villain will surely go down in history as one of the most original and deeply menacing bad guys.

No Country For Old Men is on the level of Fargo and Blood Simple. No Country can best be described as a think-piece. It bears all the traits and markings of a thriller, which it most certainly is and an excellent one at that, but the ending, which is the source of extreme polarization, is one of much more substantial film. If this film had any sort of conventional ending, it would be more satifyling in a narrower way. You'd be content when the lights came up but by the time you got home you'd have forgotten about the movie. More importantly is this film ended any other way, if it were less ambiguous, it would not be a Coen Brothers film. The more suspensful scenes had me holding my breath and on the edge of my seat, literally. Javier  Bardem has one of the best performances of the year as one of the most memorable and scary characters ever on screen. Everthing about him, his always neat appearance, his blank face, and his weapon of choice (an air gun used to kill cattle), even his voice make the character incredibly creepy and menacing. I'm more afriad of Anton Chigurh than Hannibal Lecter. Tommy Lee Jones is naturally cast as the aging sheriff who struggles to keep up with the horrible and bizarre violence of the changing world. The tone, photography, and color pallete (blood is deep dark red) are all very fitting of this unique thriller which is one the year's best films, if not the best.
