   [color=DarkRed][b][size=5]"N[/size][/b][/color]o Country for Old Men" is a film of such incalculable power it deserves its own course in film schools. Students could learn that a story's efficacy stems not from plot or trickery, but from characters' behavior. The people in this film behave not according to what's written in a screenplay, but to their essential natures. It seems incidental that a camera is filming them.
   
    Like Cormac McCarthy's novel, the film cries out for detailed analysis, theory and open-ended discussion. I left the theater wanting to immediately talk about it, deconstruct it and watch it again one scene at a time. The filmmakers, Joel and Ethan Coen, provide no rationals for what happens because they know it's what each individual makes of a movie that counts. One answer won't suffice.
   
   This is another masterpiece from the Coen Brothers, whose best efforts deal with grave, serious subjects. They should know better to tell more stories like "Blood Simple" and less like "O Brother Where Art Thou." Their comedies can be funny, but they're mostly misguided because they end up trying too hard to be clever. Not since "Fargo," of which this film shares a similar air and tone, have the Coens made a film so profound, intense and deeply felt. 
   
    In a remote West Texas town, a large, brooding figure named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is arrested by a skinny deputy. At the sheriff's office, in a shot that uses depth of field to its most chilling effect, Chigurh strangles the deputy to death while displaying a look of uncompromising determination. This cannot be the first time Chigurh has murdered someone and it certainly won't be his last.
   
   In a parallel time, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) hunts antelope along the Rio Grande and comes across a band of murdered Mexicans. A heroin deal has gone terribly wrong and all but one of the Mexicans is dead as a result. He pleas to Llewelyn to bring him some water but Llewelyn follows a blood trail to another dead man and a satchel full of $2 million. 
   
   Chigurh was obviously connected to this massacre and meant to receive the money. He begins to hunt Llewelyn down by any means necessary. His weapon of choice is a captive bolt pistol, which we know will play a large role the moment we see it. 
   
   Investigating the murders is an old-time sheriff named Ed Tom Bell, played by Tommy Lee Jones, who was perhaps the only choice for such a role. The character calls to mind Jones' other ventures into law enforcement after "The Fugitive" and "The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada." Bell can be considered a continuation of those two characters, only now he's slowly realizing his purpose in this small town is fading. In fact, the look on his face suggests he's uncertain he ever had any to begin with. 
   
   The film opens with a melancholy voiceover as Bell goes on about the different sheriffs from various Texas counties. He's like a grandfather whose thoughts and memories wander with each passing word.
   
   As Bell searches for the truth, Chigurh [/color][color=Wheat]and Llewelyn [/color][color=Wheat]find themselves in a game of cat-and-mouse, chasing each other through small towns where the most exciting thing to happen is, well, two grown men battling for a bag full of cash. No one else seems to exist in these towns, and the deserted streets make for an open playground where Chigurh [/color][color=Wheat]and Llewelyn [/color][color=Wheat]can shoot each other at will. 
   
    The Coen Brothers' screenplay is simplistic and succinct in the way it reveals only what we need to know. There's nothing tricky or manipulative about it--no twists, bends or waves. It simply boils down to primal human nature. And boy, is it intense. It's violent, yes, but not pervasively so, and when it is, it is brutal, shocking and frightening. 
   
   Much of that comes from Chigurh operating with the mentality of a Terminator, and indeed there is a scene where Chigurh repairs himself like Arnold Schwarzenegger in "The Terminator." Chigurh's only mission is to recover the $2 million for a businessman (Stephen Root), who in turn hires the smart-alecky Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) to recover the money from Chigurh. 
   
   The themes running through the film--greed, vengeance, old age, endurance--collectively induce us into an experience unlike any other we're used to in mainstream movies. The film is practical and carefully measured against the audiences' intelligence, and it's with great honor the Coen brothers believe in us so much. They want to share this film's insight rather than condescend.
   
    The performances all hit the right note and although many people will be extending due praise to Jones and Bardem, I think it's Brolin who has the toughest role because he's asked to play more or less the straight guy--the everyday man whom everyone seeks out. Whereas Bardem and Jones play characters with distinct personalities that showcase wonderful moments of dialogue and acting, Brolin must respond to them without being overshadowed. He's not allowed to go over-the-top or speak solemnly like his counterparts. Notice his restraint when he tells a store owner that white socks are the only kind he wears. He's really kind of brilliant.
   
   Many will compare this film to "Fargo," and it too has the same lonely, barren locations; the same offbeat moments of bizarre humor that may make you feel guilty for even thinking about laughing; and the same naive, selfish characters. 
   
   But there's also a similarity in theme. In "Fargo" the law and sense of order was memorably embodied by Francis McDormand, whose character was expecting a baby. She signified that even in a harsh, murderous world, people who find there's more to life than money are willing to bring children into it. In "No Country for Old Men," it's another woman, Llewelyn's wife Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald), who's the voice of reason and morality. Like Francis McDormand, she has a magnificent speech at the end that proves she's not as naive as her husband thinks. [/color][color=Wheat]She continues the Coen Brothers' theme of showing strong-willed women in male-dominated societies remain the most practical creatures of them all.
  [/color] [color=Wheat]
   The men in these stories make things more complicated because they live with guarded fear, which is represented this time by the dream Bell describes to his wife (Tess Harper), who just looks at him amusingly while drinking coffee. [/color][color=Wheat]"No Country for Old Men" is about men who realize their only means for existence is destroying themselves and others. They see this as inevitable. 
  [/color] [color=Wheat]
   But I believe I've only begun to scratch the surface about what this film means and how well-made it really is. No review can give it justice because a review is from a single person's point of view. This film should have an entire panel devoted to praising it. It's a film that unites us with its intelligence and through its characters' universal needs to wanting to be remembered after leaving this world.[/color]

Eu vi "Onde os Fracos não têm Vez" há umas semanas, mas preferi esperar algum tempo para amadurecer mais o que eu tinha achado do filme.

Primeiramente, é um filme inegavelmente bem pensado e bem estruturado. É quase brilhante a forma como o roteiro frustra as expectativas de quem assiste. Não há uma coisa sequer que siga o que se espera. As matanças deixam de ser mostradas quando se tornam banalizadas, o personagem que viria para salvar o mundo dura menos de 15 minutos, o embate entre o "bem" e o mal não é sequer mostrado... A tônica do filme é escapar até dos clichês hypados da modernidade.

Outra coisa (e outro ponto muito positivo) que guia o filme é o clima de pessimismo, que é fruto da terrível sensação de impotência perante a matança sem fim feita pelo personagem do Javier Barden. A narração do velho xerife interpretado pelo Tommy Lee Jones é perfeita como fio condutor da trama.

Falando em Javier Barden, ele rouba a cena como o lunático psicopata que assassina 90% do elenco. O personagem tem um cabelinho ridículo e um visual bizarro, mas imprime um misto de terror e humor, já que a banalização das execuções e forma como elas são realizadas acabam provocando várias gargalhadas. É verdade que o riso vem com uma certa dose de culpa, mas eu confesso que passei boa parte do filme rindo da desgraça alheia.

Um detalhe que me chamou bastante atenção é que o filme, além de pessimista e violento, dá um grande destaque aos princípios do personagem do Javier Barden. Ele é, sem sombra de dúvidas, o personagem com um código de conduta mais firme e fiel a suas errrr... crenças. Os outros personagens, supostamente "do bem" - a mera comparação de qualquer um com o personagem do Bardem já bastaria para colocar a pessoa na Santa Ceia -, são ardilosos, gananciosos, covardes e traiçoeiros. O personagem do Bardem "só" é mau. Muito mau, na verdade. No fim das contas, penso que houve uma coroação da manutenção dos princípios pessoais.

Apesar dessas várias qualidades, o filme me desapontou em alguns aspectos. O maior deles foi o hype criado. Eu fui ao cinema com uma expectativa de ver um filme que mudaria minha vida para todo o sempre. E isso não aconteceu... nem de longe.

Outro fator negativo: a ofensa à máxima de que cinema é a maior diversão. O plano de frustrar quem assiste ao filme é interessante dum ponto de vista formal, mas pode quebrar vários ganchos e quebrar o ritmo do filme. Penso que o roteiro poderia fugir do óbvio sem que isso significasse necessariamente uma frustração. No fim das contas, a frustração era a minha única certeza quanto ao desfecho da trama, até porque o filme perde o ritmo de uma forma gritante em sua segunda metade.

A impressão que fiquei é de que é um filme muito inteligente e bacana na estrutura, mas que peca no conteúdo.

Não entendo muito bem o porquê de a Academia ter escolhido o filme como o melhor do ano. OK, o filme é atípico, não faz o gênero oscarizável, certamente. O problema é que já houve outros filmes nada óbvios na história recente do cinema americana que podiam ter sido coroados com o Oscar e que não foram. Só para citar alguns: "Pulp Fiction", "Magnólia" e "Brokeback Mountain". Os três são consideravelmente melhores do que "No Country for Old Men" e têm um lado underground e marginal acentuado. 

Para variar, a Academia recompensou uma idéia/um profissional na hora errada e pelos motivos errados, o que anda virando uma constante, né? Na minha singela opinião, o Oscar iria pra "Atonement" (ainda não vi "Sangue Negro", frise-se), que não é moderno e é bem oscarizável, mas me agradou bem mais.

The movie tells the story of Llewlyn Moss (James Brolin) stumbling on a drug deal gone wrong in the middle of the Texas desert. Here, he finds a briefcase full of drug money which he decides to take. However, now he becomes the target of a mysterious hitman with a Buster Brown haircut named Anton Chigurh (a brilliant Javier Bardem). I just saw this again recently and the second viewing gave me a very different perspective. Whereas I was rather blown away the first time I saw the movie, this time, I could see the flies in the ointment, and there were many. The movie is still a masterwork of suspense and dread, and Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones, and Javier Bardem turn in fine performances (Bardem is a great actor, but despite all the praise he's getting, I just don't think Chigurh is layered enough to merit an Oscar). I guess my biggest problem with the film is that it's basically a watered down version of an imperfect but compelling book by the great Cormac McCarthy. A friend of mine summed the whole thing up perfectly -  as a "run-hide-bang-shoot-oh no-shoot-hide-oh look, some depth" kind of movie. The popular argument that the movie is all about fate is pretty weak, simply because (now) fate is a pretty weak, and boring, theme to base an entire narrative on. The Coens have always had this juvenile fascination with gore and action, and it comes across here quite clearly. A conversation between Tommy Lee Jones and his wife is all fine and proper, but you can tell that they're much more invested in how the blood is going to spill (spill, not dribble) out of the poor truck driver who gets plugged in the neck by Chigurh, mid-chase. Therefore, it's decent as a suspense-action movie with some metaphorical pondering here and there. I can see why it's more appealing in general than, say, "There Will Be Blood". It's faster, it's got a lot of violence that's pretty easy to digest (read: enjoy), it's full of references and nostalgia, and it's bad-ass. I just think it's sad that even critics call this the best American film in years.

Always engaging, often edge-of-your-seat entertainment, [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is one of the best westerns we've seen in a very long time. It definitely trumps this year's [i]3:10 To Yuma[/i], which was still a very good film. I thought that Tommy Lee Jones' recent appearance in another Western film ([i]The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada[/i]) represented his apogee as an actor in the genre, but this is far and above superior.
 
The 2 hours go by unbelievably quickly. There's just no way that this film won't keep your interest. Javier Bardem's work here is flawless. We see plenty villains in movies that we dislike... but when a villain actually gives you the creeps and when you literally get chills when he appears on screen, that's when you know the actor portraying the villain has done a stellar job. As I sit alone in my room, the fear of seeing Chigurh has a far more intense effect on me than any terror that most horror movies can pull off. He is that amazing.
 
Several aspects of the film's conclusion are surprising. There are plenty of things that we are NOT shown in the film that we would ABSOLUTELY be shown in a conventional movie. However, I think that if you pay close attention to the things that are said, you'll understand why we see what we get to see and hear what we get to hear, and why we DON'T get to see and hear certain things. Nothing that is shown or not shown to us in [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is accidental.
 
This has been a great last few days for me, having seen [i]Gone Baby Gone[/i], [i]Lars and the Real Girl[/i], and now [i]No Country For Old Men[/i], all three great movies that will certainly figure among my list of favorites for this year.

[FONT=Times New Roman][SIZE=2]Recent films by the Coen Brothers just havent lived up to the earlier brilliance they demonstrated themselves to be capable of. [I]No Country for Old Men[/I]-based on the 2005 novel by Cormac McCarthy of the same name reverses the trend and puts the Coen Brothers back on the map as two of the few filmmakers that absolutely matter. Anyone who has questioned their talent or even more broadly, wondered what happened to great first-rate cinema (is there anything left to see now?) will surely find their appetites satiated. The latest by the Coen Brothers is the best film of the year (and I cant imagine anything could replace it-that would be impossible) and one of three or four films from this decade I wouldnt hesitate to describe as perfect.

[IMG]http://www.tiff07.ca/images/films2007/705291550231386.jpg[/IMG]

The year is 1980 and the plot is deceptively simple-Llewelyn Moss (played by Josh Brolin in an excellent performance that cements 2007 as his year) a welder and Vietnam veteran stumbles across a crime scene in which several men have been slain (even a dog!) in a drug deal gone terribly bust. Moss finds 2 million in cash and countless bags of heroin. Foolishly or cleverly, Moss makes off with the money (I think a lot of us would). But [I]No Country For Old Men[/I], rooted in the same morality as [I]Fargo[/I] and [I]Blood Simple[/I], is out to make the same point as Sam Raimis masterful [I]A Simple Plan[/I]: that the costs of crime always outweigh the benefits. Moss is hunted by Anton Chigurh (played by Spanish actor Javier Berdam in a performance that is certain to be legendary) a ferociously mannered incarnation of pure evil armed with a cattle gun and a haircut that was probably never in vogue. Chigurh kills with out remorse, even belaboring the process by flipping a coin and making the victim call it. When hes introduced at the beginning of the film hes just been arrested. A poor sap of a cop explains over the phone that hes got him and everythings fine. Big mistake; Chigurh uses his handcuffs to choke him to death then makes off with a police car only to kill another innocent person. 

Following both of these men is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, played by Tommy Lee Jones in a tough, controlled, and utterly riveting performance that compliments nicely his work in Haggiss [I]In the Valley of Elah[/I]. Bell has been sheriff of the town since he was 25 at the same time his father was sheriff of a neighboring town; a fact that he proudly divulges to us in the opening moments of the film. Now his love of the work has dropped off dramatically; in his eyes society has been going horribly awry (he says at one point that it all starts when people stop saying sir and maam) and he is disgusted by the pervasive violence that surrounds him. 

Berdams performance as Chigurh is a brilliant work of art. His accent hard to pin down (you expect ethnic cliches or a growling bass when you see him, but get neither) Berdam avoids going off the deep end. He could have taken a cue from Dennis Hoppers Frank Booth in [I]Blue Velvet[/I] or Daniel Day Lewiss Bill the Butcher in [I]Gangs of New York[/I] (for my money two of the scariest villains in cinema history) but his performance transcends hysterics or theatricality. Berdam gives Chigurh a stare so focused and intense that its almost as though his probing eyes were able to see half way across the world. The last shot of him gripping tightly to his cattle gun (a particularly revolting method of execution) ups the ante by letting hurt and anguish coexist with the aforementioned qualities.

[IMG]http://www.thedailyreel.com/spotlight/trailers/archive/2007/07/31/no-country-for-old-men/image[/IMG]

The real star of [I]No Country For Old Men[/I] is the Coen Brothers. This is absolutely flawless, expert direction. The build up of the story in the earliest stages is directed with a patience that would elude many younger more inexperienced filmmakers and certainly some members of the audience. When all of the pieces of the puzzle fall roughly into place they dont lose their command. Joel and Ethan Coen know what to show on the screen, what to explain, and what to edit out. The result is a seamless flowing narrative that keeps you on the edge of your seat without haste yet a firm sense of economical drive. And the first face off between Moss and Chigurh is such a thrilling, visceral explosion of gun shots and movement that is more exciting than anything in [I]The Bourne Ultimatum[/I] by a significant margin (and keep in mind I thought Greengrass's latest was hugely exciting). 

This is a masterpiece of silence, and Coen Brothers make a character, a soundtrack, and a soundscape out of silence. Few films so boldly feature less dialogue. And the dialogue that each of the three central characters (and minor characters also) speak is poignant and cuts to the bone. Sometimes like when Carla Jeans (played by the terrific Kelly McDonald) mother matter-of-factly explains to a man helping her with her bags that its rare to see a Mexican in a suit it touches on the off-kilter humor of earlier efforts. The music by Carter Burwell passes the ultimate test the soundtrack should be held up to: its completely undistracting, but totally enhancing. The cinematography by master Roger Deakins who has also shot other Coen classics like [I]Fargo[/I] and [I]The Big Lebowski[/I], and recently the gorgeous [I]Assassination of Jesse James[/I] is beyond stunning. His expertise makes each shot feel like the classic it is. I find myself now haunted by the long shots of Texas desert, skies so intensely colored it almost hurts the eye, and by an amazing shot of Chigurh being reflected off his television screen as he waits in Moss's trailer. In this shot one can see his dark frame alarmingly contrasted with the ineffably beautiful desert blue sky through the window. You wont forget it either when you see it.  

[I]No Country For Old Men[/I] is a masterpiece of the highest order right down to its assured ending (faithful to the novel). Its more than one of the Coen Brothers best films-its one of the great theatergoing experiences of my life, one that I cant wait to repeat. Its perfection, a reminder that crime doesnt pay and that violent crime is an awful domino with copious consequences that spiral out of control. And no, I cant gloss over the fact in writing this that the Coen Brothers [I]Fargo[/I] is my favorite film. That too is a masterpiece that thrills, chills, delights, and makes one contemplate. Im usually not the type to re-watch films in short periods-but Ive seen [I]Fargo[/I] five times in one month and it felt new every time. Each time was a thrilling experience. If you asked me what other film has that kind of repeat value, off the top of my head Id say [I]No Country For Old Men[/I].

Grade: [B]A+[/B][/SIZE][/FONT]

[COLOR=DarkRed][FONT=Arial]Joel and Ethan Coen are two of cinema's most talented oddballs. Together, they've created some of the most intricate, eclectic, and best movies of the last 25 years. Their last two efforts, 2003's [I]Intolerable Cruelty[/I] and 2004's remake of [I]The Ladykillers[/I], didn't feel like Coen movies; they felt like they were compromised and missed the artistically deft touch. As a result, both movies were mild failures for filmmakers that have a series of genre-spanning masterpieces to their name. [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is the first time the brothers have adapted someone else's work, in this instance Pulitzer Prize-winning author Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel. Not too shabby if I say so. Fortunately for all lovers of film, the Coens have embraced McCarthy's blood-soaked tale and crafted an exciting, honest, and intensely provocative modern Western that stands out as one of the greatest films of the year. 

In dusty West Texas, Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is out hunting the lonely plains when he discovers a blood trail. It leads him to four empty cars riddled with bullet holes, dead bodies collecting flies, and a sack containing two million dollars in cash. The signs are all there that this was a drug deal gone badly, and two million will never go unnoticed, but Moss sees this as an opportunity of a lifetime and takes the money. The men in power have hired Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) to find their drugs and money and exact retribution. Chigurh's preferred method of killing involves a high-pressured air canister that can blow out doorknobs and human brains. Chigurh chases after Moss all the while Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is following the trail of death to try and save Moss or any future innocent victims.

What a fine-tuned, nerve-wracking, and engrossing cat-and-mouse thriller this film is. The action is brief but the buildup can be nearly unbearable to endure. The tension is magnificent. Chigurh chases Moss from hideout to hideout and some of the tensest moments are just waiting. There's a moment where Moss is calling the front desk of his newest motel and we hear the phone ringing unanswered again and again from the hall, all the while Chigurh's footsteps inch closer. But it's the moments of silence that cause the most dread. When Moss is trying to recover his loot, all the while Chigurh is in the opposite motel room, it becomes a balancing act of sound and silence. [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is expertly orchestrated to involve the use of sound as a tool for high suspense. None of our main three characters inhabit a scene together. Sure Moss and Chigurh shoot at one another but even then it's short and focused on waiting for response and counter response. Moss is no dummy and he sets up some traps for his would-be dispatcher. [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is unnerving, intelligent, near flawless entertainment. 

Chigurh, as masterfully played by Bardem, is the stuff of nightmares. I was literarily afraid to go home after seeing this movie and it is because [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] fashions a villain so methodical, so cold-blooded, and so downright deadly and cunning that I felt as if he could very well be residing under my bed at night waiting. Bardem is hypnotically horrifying and the Coen brothers establish early on how ruthless their cinematic boogeyman is. The very first moment we're introduced to Chigurh he escapes from police custody and strangles the inattentive officer on duty. He drags him to the floor and chokes the life out of him, but the Coens position the camera not on the last desperate kicks of the officer but on the face of Anton Chigurh, and it is nasty. His eyes are bugged out and his intensity comes across as sadistically jubilant. He seems like a caged animal finally let loose. It's a scary yet fascinating introduction to a deadly character. 

Chigurh is a humorless and determined man, and every scene he steps into instantly changes. A gas attendant casually asks Chigurh about the weather and gets on his bad side and the stone-faced killer in the Dutch boy haircut proceeds to press the poor man with increasing agitation, yet Chigurh always speaks in such a placid tone that makes him far creepier. He's a maniac that never raises his voice. Chigurh then corrals the man into one of his signatures, having a victim decide their fate by the flip of a coin. Before the man can say anything the coin is flipped, Chigurh intones to "call it," and the man nervously repeats that he needs to know what he's at stake to win. "Everything," Chigurh responds. This scene starts off so innocuous but becomes monumentally unsettling thanks to the rising dread and Bardem's deeply committed portrayal. Bardem is alarming, ferocious, grimly efficient, mesmerizing, and deserves an Oscar win, not just a mere nomination, for what is his finest performance to date. 

There are many ways to describe Chigurh, but it seems most appropriate to speak of him as nothing short but the full-tilt vengeance of God. He's a hired killer, yes, but that doesn't stop him from killing indiscriminately. He murders several innocent victims, he murders his competition sent out to nab Moss just because it insults him, and even after the money no longer becomes a concern, Chigurh still plans to continue his wrath out of sheer moral principle. He made a promise of swooping vengeance and he will stick to it. This means that anyone could die at any moment while onscreen with Chigurh, and [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] has plenty of surprises as it toys around with our baited anticipation. When Chigurh gets the drop on his competition he doesn't shoot the man immediately; instead the scene plays out for an agonizing length even after we listen to the room phone ring several times, and then blam! Chigurh answers the phone and casually raises his boots so the pooling blood doesn't touch his feet. This is the most memorable incarnation of soulless evil I have seen in the movies since Hannibal Lector came to iconic form in 1991's [I]Silence of the Lambs[/I]. 

Brolin is having quite a career year for himself after compelling turns in [I]American Gangster[/I] (where he also shoots a dog), [I]In the Valley of Elah[/I], and Robert Rodriguez's [I]Planet Terror[/I] half of [I]Grindhouse[/I]. Brolin gives the audience a figure to root for even though he never actually displays true heroism, just survival instincts. Jones serves as a wise and guiding father figure that feels out of place in a world that is becoming increasingly, shockingly violent. It's a role that Jones has performed before but it's a role that fits the actor exceptionally well. Woody Harrelson pops up as a charming and laid back handler trying to convince Moss to give up before things get worse. Kelly Macdonald, as Moss' wife, cuts through the darkness in a refreshing performance.

The technical craftsmanship is on par with previous Coen excellence. Roger Deakin's cinematography is exquisite, Carter Burwell's score barely makes its presence felt, and the editing is tight and focused. The sound design, which I've already discussed in detail, deserves an Oscar. This being a Coen brothers' film, it wouldn't be complete without some dark humor to punctuate the bleakness. They have a perfect ear for local vernacular and Texas shorthand, so the dialogue feels sharp but realistically twangy without being condescending as some had accused [I]Fargo[/I] (I do not agree with this accusation). 

What works in the favor of [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] may perhaps be its undoing for a mainstream audience. The film works against conventions and this provides for some stellar surprises and upheavals, none of which is bigger than killing a certain character off-screen. [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] definitely seems like it's laying stage for a climactic showdown and then one key figure has been bumped off by a group of ancillary characters that have little overall bearing over the plot (I have read that the same gap happens in McCarthy's novel). If this doesn't perturb audiences then the final 10 minutes ought to do it. There's no sense of closure for the movie and this will frustrate many, but it all fits rather nicely with the movie's highly nihilistic tone. Like Chigurh's coin, the film focuses much on the randomness and cruelty of fate. By sticking to this ethic, the Coen bothers are eschewing the traditional Hollywood rulebook and playing around with our expectations for characters and plot. The outlook isn't too sunny for many involved. It works and demands an audience remain on edge for fear that anything could happen at any moment. However, don't say I didn't warn you if you walk out of [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] and say, "What was that all about?" 

[I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is exactly the kind of material the Coen brothers needed to return to form. This is a lean and stirring thriller that plays to their strengths and echoes some of their most riveting and twisty work, like [I]Blood Simple[/I] and [I]Fargo[/I]. In many ways the film feels like a Western, a high-stakes drama, and a tragedy that takes its time to unravel. It may have taken some time but the Coen brothers are back, baby, and [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is fit to stand beside their hallowed pedigree of cinematic classics.

No Country For Old Men has so much going for it its almost frustrating for a young filmmaker like myself looking to make a good film.  With a cast so perfect its spooky, Roger Deakins spot on photography, tension coming out of it ears, and so many interesting characters, the movie simply captivates, entertains, and lingers long after.  The Coen brothers are behind this thriller to the core.  Their trademark humor is on display in drier bits here but their ability to establish tension and draw out confrontation is nothing short of pure fun and pleasure.  They make you glue your ass to the seat and your eyes to the screen as Josh Brolin or Tommy Lee Jones go head to head with Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurhe, the best bad guy I can remember in recent years.  At the film?s center is aging and soon-to-retire lawman Tommy Lee Jones.  His existential dilemma of not knowing where his legacy fits in his cop family lineage and the world?s messed-up greater order becomes the film?s ultimate statement, a profound and heartbreaking notion that is rarely found in most thrillers.  The action is top notch: the blood makes squirm, each gunshot makes you jump, and you can almost hear the blood rushing through the characters ears in moments with the maximum at stake.

The film thrives on its pitch perfect cast.  Josh Brolin plays an ex-Viet Nam vet turned welder who stumbles on a bloodbath drug deal gone wrong and walks away with $2 million in drug money.  His grit and toughness are surprising coming from Bran in The Goonies.  He really has transformed himself into a top-notch actor (also appearing in the underwhelming American Gangster this year).  Tommy Lee Jones?s performance is a joy to watch.  His absolute disappearance into the role of the southern sheriff is amazing.  For an actor of his stature to become the character that he does is really impressive and a joy to watch.  Like I mentioned earlier, his mentally nomadic search for answers or comfort in such a violent and criminal time is heartbreaking as you see the wear and tear of the weary world right on the creases on his face.  Despite Jones?s brilliance in the film, Javier Bardem steals the show, no doubt about it.  His turn as the quietly demonic assassin Chigurhe could be the most interesting, daring, and fun-to-watch performance I?ve seen all year.  The initial ?coin toss? scene between him and a down-home gas station owner showcases the Coen Brothers skill for dark comedy mixed in with a little dread and tension to boot.  Overall, I walked out thoroughly entertained not only by how interesting and well-told the story was but also by how good the Coen Brothers really can be.  And I also really appreciated how tight my chest was through more than two hours of storytelling.

[indent][left][color=#000000]After several departures over the last several years, the Coen Brothers are predictably going back to the time when their movies were at their best. [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is essentially a West Texas version of [i]Fargo[/i] with dust and dirt replacing snow. The comparison is too easy to make an almost inevitable, so I decided to get it out of the way early. However, [b]this is a comparable film to [i]Fargo[/i] in every way, they are both mixed with humor, suspense, crime, and they are both very, very good. This latest is one of the best of 2007.[/b][/color]

 
[color=#000000][i]No Country for Old Men[/i] revolves around a drug deal gone wrong. Llewlyn Moss (played perfectly by Josh Brolin) stumbles upon 2 million dollars of drug money in the desert. Of course, you cant just pluck two million dollars without any consequences, and so the story kicks in. Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) and his Howdy-Doody haircut immediately starts hunting down Moss and his bag of money. Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) and his novice partner Wendell (Garrett Dillahunt) are following closely in Chigurhs tracks, at one point, so close, they notice the glass of milk is still sweating in Llewlyns trailer. [/color]

[/left]


 
 
[color=#000000]At its core, the film is essentially a chase movie, but its done effectively and smartly as to shy away from the stereotypes that follow it. In an extremely interesting move, the Coens chose not to include ANY score or music in the film whatsoever. It works, surprisingly, as strings are replaced by gushing winds and swirling sands. [/color]
 
 
[color=#000000]For the first hour and thirty minutes, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is engaging and extremely tense. In one scene, we hear a beeping that steadily increases coming towards Llewlyns hotel door. He rifles through the bag of money to realize hes being tracked. The scene is a truly remarkable exercise in surreal suspense, and it feels as if these 30 seconds are taking an eternity. [/color]
 
 
[font=Times New Roman][font=Verdana][size=2][color=#000000]The ending (or the last twenty minutes or so) follows closely to Cormac McCarthys source novel, or so Ive heard. In it, the book is mainly about how these old sheriffs and farmers are overmatched and taken aback by the ways of these crimes and they feel helpless, as things arent the way they used to be, hence the title, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i]. I know some people will dislike the ending, but I found it to be quite fitting with the tone of the movie.[/color][/size][/font][/font]

Chigurh is detached, and less sociopathic than he is methodical and successful in his tasks. After a hunter finds two million dollars in the aftermath of a desert shootout, Chigurh attempts to track him down, luring Josh Brolin's character, Moss, into a cat and mouse chase, with rules Moss has no choice but to agree with. Bardem's ghostly Grim Reaper-like appearance booms over the entire film, the hunter trying to make a better live for himself amidst poverty, and Tommy Lee Jones' sheriff, a once-wise man who realizes he's powerless to stop natural forces. The ending is as effective as it is disheartening, but it concludes the film's theme: everybody dies and you have no say in when it happens.

The best of 2007! At least the best so far. "No Country for Old Men" is without a doubt a masterpiece from the brothers, Coen. A film not exactly for the faint of heart but definitely one for an admirer of great cinema. The question then becomes what makes this picture great? And the answer is simple, almost everything!
The direction, production, and screenplay (all by Joel and Ethan) are nearly flawless. The story is simple and their telling of the story combines art and brilliance with sheer insanity. First off, the always dreaded paradox. The film essentially had no music! Aside from some mariachis, there was neither a score nor soundtrack. However, the feel of the film worked perfectly with the absence of music. I love scores in cinema and soundtracks are also very nice when done correctly. But the truth of music in films is that it essentially comes from nowhere.
With that in mind, both Joel and Ethan Coen deliver there best work since "Fargo". But not everything can solely be credited to the brothers. Unlike "Fargo" and also "The Big Lebowski", this film was adapted from the Cormac McCarthy novel. Cinematography was spot on with memorable shots and lasting impressions but nothing Oscar caliber. As for the editing, it is nothing shy of perfect.
The acting was stellar all-round as well. Javier Bardem was superb as "Anton Chigurh," a psychotic assassin whose as dangerous as 'the bubonic plague' and complex as Freud. Josh Brolin's sixth film of 07' is an excellent performance. His days from "The Young Riders" give him some added material into the cowboy life for the role of "Llewelyn Moss".
Supporting roles from Kelly Macdonald and Woody Harrelson give them picture even more assured star quality. Last but not least is Academy Award winner Tommy Lee Jones, as a character that is not too difficult for him (a Texan police officer, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell). Limiting screen time left me wanting more from his role. Perhaps the realest of the characters, Jones' presence on the film leaves a great mark on the whole production, maybe the most important one.
In conclusion, this film is the years' best and will be until something else knocks it out of first. That is, if another film will.

The brothers Joel and Ethan Coen's latest creation "No Country For Old Men", is a gripping adaptation of the acclaimed novel of the same name by Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Cormac McCarthy.

It's a modern day Western with a reflective homage to the Texas (and the world) of an earlier time, when people respected the law, their elders, and each other.

As much as I enjoyed their previous films; "O' Brother Where Art Thou?" very much so and "Intolerable Cruelty" it was their film's "Fargo" and "The Man Who Wasn't There" that spoke volumes with their darker tones. This new film takes that to a whole new level and could well be The Coen Brothers most adult picture so far and quiet possibly their best.

Tommy lee Jones is excellent as Sheriff Edward Tom Bell, the aging and disheartened lawman of West Texas, that realises the world is going to Hell in a handcart. Woody Harrelson is also superb in the supporting role of gun-for-hire Carson Wells. But a lot of the praise must go to Javier Bardem and his portrayal of psychopathic killer Anton Chigurh.

On a interesting side note. In the novel (but not in the film), Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) says of the dope-dealers, "Here a while back in San Antonio they shot and killed a federal judge." McCarthy set the story in 1980. In 1979, in San Antonio, Federal Judge John Howland Wood was shot and killed by a free-lance contract killer named Charles Harrelson. Actor Woody Harrelson is his son.

[size=3]I waited with bated breath for the NYC opening of "No Country for Old Men." I went on opening night expecting to be dazzled. It has been generating tremendous buzz on the festival circuit, and it's [/size][size=3]based on a [b]Cormac McCarthy[/b] novel. It also has the [b]Coen brothers[/b], [b]Javier Bardem[/b], and [b]Tommy Lee Jones[/b]. Cinema heaven.[/size]
 
[size=3][img]http://bigdaddyseashell.files.wordpress.com/2007/12/javierbardem-no-country-for-old-men.jpg[/img][/size]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3]But I have to say, I was not dazzled. For the first 30 minutes I was. But as the film wore on, I felt it got emptier and emptier. To me it's the classic case of a filmmaker conjuring up a fascinating world in Act I but having nothing of much consequence to say about it in Act II. Sure it's cool to watch Bardem play a demented killer[/size][size=3] with a crazy hairdo and an airgun. Th[/size][size=3]e cinematography and overall Western look are[/size][size=3] fantastic. The mise-en-scene is breathtaking, as you would expect from the Coens. [/size]
 
[size=3]But snazzy, masculine direction, great locations [/size][size=3]and scene-chewing performances aren't enough to make a film. The story has to matter. I ultimately [/size][size=3]didn't give a damn about anyone in this movie and in the end non[/size][size=3]e of them seemed like real people to me.[/size]
 
[img]http://hollywood-elsewhere.com/images/column/520/desertmen.jpg[/img]
 
[size=3]The dramatic arc was also unsatisfying. The film is built around a chase. It becomes a real nail-biter. [b]Josh Brolin[/b] plays a working-class man in the middle of the Texas desert who stumbles upon a huge amount of drug money at a crime scene before the authorities arrive. He keeps it but is chased by a hitman (Bardem) sent to recover the money. [/size]
 
[size=3]The Coens do a superb job of building tension in the sequences when Bardem catches up to Brolin. You really feel the danger that the character is in. At the end of this long chase there is a capture, actually two of them. And both appear off-screen. So the thriller elements of the film ultimately are anti-climactic. All this build-up for something that happens off-screen. The film then just stops.[/size]
 
[img]http://images.pastemagazine.com/images/articles/5697_image_1.jpg[/img]
 
[size=3]One could perhaps argue that the movie only makes use of thriller elements to bring out philosophical points -- that it wants to move to the meta-narrative level, if you will, and make commentary on the world it's depicting rather than be absorbed in it. Thus it undercuts the thriller element in the end so as to keep the focus on more serious matters. I would certainly love if this were the case. The smidgen of philosophical rumination that we get in the film ultimately doesn't add up to much either. Mostly we just have the poorly educated sheriff (Jones) muttering to himself about not understanding the world around him.[/size]
 
[size=3]I recommend this film, but as an example of a half-finished film that could have been a gigantic achievement. If both sides of it were developed more completely, the philosophical and the thriller side, we'd really have something. [/size]
 
[size=3]But I suspect that the Coens wouldn't really be able to pull off a fuller version of this film. More and more I consider them showmen, not philosophers. The kind of show they want to put on is not in the mainstream style. It's more quirky, offbeat, and less noisy. But it's a show. This literary novel needs more serious filmmakers to tackle it. Cool guns, cool hairdoes, cool black humor, and cool camera angles aren't going to cut it.[/size]

Upon leaving the theater I had the feeling that it was a simpler film than the masterpiece that many folks are calling it.  But in the time since then, I find the movie in my thoughts quite a bit. Further investigation into the original Cormac McCarthy book and reviews of the film have given me food for thought, including this person's comments from IMDB:

"So far I haven't heard anyone discuss this very important part of the story - Bell's personal struggle - which runs parallel to the rest of the story and is endemic to understanding the deeper and more fundamental theme McCarthy is attempting to put forth ... that the enormous sophistication crime has achieved is beyond our ability to deal with it. Chigurh is a symbol for the modern criminal and Bell is a symbol of traditional methods of law enforcement. Just as in 'All The Pretty Horses', 'Blood Meridian' and 'Suttree', the book ends with the strong suggestion of enormous change either being wrought as the book ends or destined to occur at some later time in the future. Change and destiny are two of McCarthy's trademarks. They are a reoccurring motif which run through all of his books. McCarthy, through the mouth of Chigurh, voices his views of destiny in the conversations Chigurh has with his victims before he kills them as well as the symbol of the coin flip. Coins also appear in 'All The Pretty Horses' and tarot cards appear as the symbol of destiny in 'Blood Meridian'. "

I think that subsequent viewings of this film may elevate its status in my mind as the years pass.  However, as it stands I've got issues with my lack of involvement in some of the characters.  I'm not yet convinced, for example, that's it my own fault that I couldn't connect with Tommy Lee Jones' character, who seems pretty integral to fully understanding the theme.  I'll read the book at some point.

Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is a grizzled old lawman in some small town in Texas near the Mexican border. Its 1980 and though hes gone most of his career without even carrying a gun, the burgeoning drug business has spawned a new nastier sort of criminal that makes him nostalgic for the good old days of cattle rustlers and horse thieves.
 
Llewelyn Moss is a regular sort of guy with iffy morals who stumbles upon the aftermath of a drug deal gone bad while out hunting what appear to be antelope. Unfazed by all of the blood and gore and dead bodies, he keeps on poking around the scene until eventually he finds a suitcase containing two million dollars. And then he takes it.
 
Unfortunately for Moss, buried within all of the cash is a transponder which emits signals which can be used to track its location with a handheld device. And the guy who has that handheld device is a psychopath with a Buster Brown haircut by the name Anton Chigurh (pronounced kind of like sugar but with the accent on the grr) who travels with this weird pressurized air gun hooked to an oxygen tank which he uses to blow holes through things like cylinder locks and peoples foreheads.
 
Most of the movie involves Chigurh pursuing Moss from town to town and Moss escaping just in the nick of time. Im a little hazy on the details, but Im pretty sure some Mexicans are also after Moss, and Woody Harrelson is after both Moss and Chigurh for reasons I couldnt even begin to explain. Meanwhile, Sheriff Bell is conducting an investigation back in Jipip, taking frequent breaks to prattle on about the downfall of society and kids these days with their baggy pants and their rap music andoh wait, thats actually Bill Cosby.
 
I kept a running tally of the deaths because I thought you all might like to know and plus it gave me something to do during the occasional slow scenes. Ready? Ten people and one pit bull killed on-screen (including one strangulation and one air gun to the forehead), at least eight people and another pit bull shot off-camera with us just privy to the bloody aftermath, and two implied murders where the scenes were mercifully cut short just before the actual act. Theres also a scene where Chigurh performs surgery on his own leg and another where one of his arm bones is sticking out of his skin.
 
I actually kind of liked this movie despite expecting to totally hate it and having had to force myself to see it instead of the Joe Strummer documentary, which was playing at a closer, cheaper theatre with better popcorn, or at least better butter which is all that really matters. Long, violent westerns just arent my thing, but after the first four or five dead bodies, I guess I kind of just got used to it.
 
After two cold-blooded murders early on, almost every scene with Chigurh is filled with tension, even those which have nothing to do with his pursuit of Moss. What should have been just a benign conversation with a friendly gas station attendant turns out to be one of the most suspenseful scenes in the whole movie. Chigurh isnt just a loose cannon; hes more like a loose nuclear missile.
 
But this film isnt just all violence and suspense. It also has a good bit of humor -- Beth Grant (who?) is a riot in a brief appearance as Moss disapproving mother-in-law. In fact, all of the acting is top-notch, especially Tommy Lee Jones excellent portrayal of a tough old coot whos just coming to the realization that hes outgrown his usefulness.
 
My biggest gripe about this film is the meandering ending which just goes on and on long after its climax. Everythings just about wrapped up and all of a sudden theres a brand new character and next thing you know Sheriff Bell is talking about his dreams and I started to feel like I do when Im in a meeting and its just about to end and someone asks if anyone has any questions and some suck-up always does and fifteen minutes later Im still sitting there. 
 
I suppose I shouldnt complain; I never know how to end my movie reviews either. Perhaps instead of trying to come up with some sort of clever conclusion I should just take my hands off the keyboard and stop typing.

this film is fascinating for the way it subverts the normal workings of the moral universe whose laws usually determine who lives and who dies in films, and why. you're never sure if the film's world is governed by immutable laws of nature or pure chance. a certain degree of chance also seems to play a role in the way the narrative unfolds around a central character, who is neither a very reliable narrator nor really all that central. but then again that might be the point. it is ultimately a tale about a moment of incomprehensible historical change--a moment uncertain about its future and therefore about its present. in such situations with nothing to organize your observations, you're never really sure which are meaningful and which meaningless. and the film really gives you this experience of not knowing what lies ahead or even how the story should be framed. in this case the meaninglessness of the story and its parts reflects the meaninglessness of the acts of an inexplicable killer, who may not even be human, a killer who no one seems to attempt to understand or venture any theories about. since uncovering motive is the usual resolution of such mysteries, and here the motive is thought to be beyond human comprehension, i think this may explain the film's mixture of both minute details and significant gaps in the narrative. in the face of the unknown, the film essentially gives up, pessimistic about our ability to know. this is brilliantly dramatized by the aging sheriff. in a way it also dramatizes our own current historical impasse. with no idea of a better possible future, the present remains incomprehensible.

Let me preface this review by saying that I wasn't familiar with the Cormac McCarthy novel so I went into the film fresh as far as the story is concerned. Thus, my thoughts on the film are also fresh, meaning that I'll judge this thing based on its value as a film, not on how well the book was adapted.

There are three things that I absolutely loved about this film: Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin and the Coen Brothers' direction. All three are top-notch, and I expect an acting nomination for SOMEBODY in this film. Bardem is intense, creepy, methodical, and about ten other adjectives I can't think of right now. I'd say he's one of the best villains, if not THE best villain, we've seen onscreen since Anthony Hopkins' Hannibal Lecter. As for Brolin, he's charismatic but in an everyman sorta way, a good ol boy with a decent heart who just gets caught up in something that we desperately want him to beat. If you read my AMERICAN GANGSTER review, you knew that I was excited to see Brolin in this film, and I wasn't disappointed. He's definitely earned his leading man stripes, and I look forward to seeing both him and Bardem do even more than what they've already accomplished.

As for the Coen Brothers, their command of the language of cinema is masterful. They weave nail-biting suspense throughout this film, and many scenes will have you on the edge of your seat. What they choose to show is just as powerful as what they choose not to show, and the camera is always in the right place to create the desired effect.

I thoroughly enjoyed this film, but was severely disappointed in its ending. The story is structured in such a way that we as an audience develop certain expectations, but in the end, these expectations are dashed, and we're left somewhat dumbfounded and unsatisfied. Now perhaps if I had read the novel, I would've known what to expect, but as a film, the story doesn't deliver the catharsis that I so desperately wanted. This lack of catharsis was palpable throughout the audience, which sat in shocked silence once the credits started to roll (it was a packed house in Times Square, had to be sold out--a 7:30pm showing). My immediate disappointment in the ending was followed by a desire to see the film again, to pay closer attention to it in order to determine its message. However, even if I were to glean something more regarding this film's message upon another viewing, the lack of catharsis would remain the same, and my opinion of the film most likely would not change. A better solution would perhaps be to read the book, where there is no doubt much greater detail and perhaps a less disappointing denouement. 

In the final analysis, this film is absolutely worth your money--you'll see modern masters both in front of and behind the camera. However, don't expect to leave the theatre satisfied. It's a great full course without the dessert and coffee.

For around three-quarters of the Coen Brothers new film, No Country for Old Men, I was completely enthralled in their flawless presentation, convinced that it was not only the best movie of the year, but one of the best movies I've seen in years. Then came the final act, which was such an abrupt change from expectations and the direction of the first three-quarters of the film that it has left my overall impression of the movie in doubt.

Which isn't to say that it's a bad ending, or one that ruins the movie by any stretch. In fact, I'm willing to admit that given another viewing, I might even agree with and prefer the ending. But I can only go with the viewing I've had with which to judge the movie, and upon that viewing I can say that there were some choices made that I don't think I agree with, with a jarring shift in the final act that left me scrambling to readjust.

Other than that, everything else in this movie is absolutely phenomenal, with the Coen's attention to detail and masterful use of suspense flooring me throughout. The movie follows Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a Vietnam war vet who stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad while hunting, coming away with a satchel containing $2 million in bills. Taking the money puts him in danger, when hired killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is brought in to recover the money, while Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) follows both to find out what happened at the crime scene and perhaps save Llewelyn's life.

I really can't state enough how powerful the suspense is throughout this movie. I'd say things like "edge of your seat" or "pulse-pounding" if they weren't such hoary movie reviewer clichÃ©s. The tension generated by Llewelyn's attempts to evade Anton's pursuit is truly remarkable, resulting in some of the most thrilling scenes of the year. Without giving anything away, I'll say that one of the scenes wtih Llewelyn and Anton is probably the most genuinely terrifying scene of the year, owing largely to the way the Coen's construct the sequence.

Bardem is chilling as Anton, a character you can expect to see pop up in "best villain", "best hitman", or "ultimate badass" lists for years to come. You should also expect to see Bardem holding a lot of hardware in the months to come for the supporting role. The entire cast is uniformly excellent, with Tommy Lee Jones showing each weary year of his character's life with each wrinkle on his face. As with most Coen Brothers movies, it takes a few minutes to adjust to the rhythms and quirks of the dialogue and dialects in the movie, but the cast handles it well, adding to the overall flavour of the film.

Going in, my expectations for this movie were sky high. Reviewers have been very high on it, and I was very excited to see the Coen's return to form with this venture into modern western noir. For most of the movie, my expectations were met or exceeded, with only a slight mis-step near the end, one that played so much with the expectations I'd developed while watching the movie that it might even be a secret success. No Country for Old Men is definitely the work of the Coen Brothers at the top of their games, a work I look forward to re-examining again in the future.

One reviewer referred to it as taking all the lovable characters from "Oh Brother, Where Art Thou?" placing them in the desert, and essentially killing all of them. Frankly, that just about sums it up for No Country For Old Men, the latest in the line of movies from the Coen brothers since the ill-received Lady Killers. Of course this film has much more of a message going for it beyond "kill this, kill that," but at the same time I'm willing to question whether or not that really is such a great thing.
Say what you want, perhaps it is my own personal taste, but let's face it, the killing really makes this movie what it is. What the Coen brothers have excelled in is building up a tremendous storyline, and then showing us what would happen if it were to simply be torn to shreds. It is tremendously entertaining to watch. Take for example one spectacular shootout on the abandoned streets of a small town (I'm not giving anything away here). There is this unbridled man vs. man conflict, only met by the equally foreboding tension proceeding it. The ensuing fight is so bracing and jarring, you can't help but get involved yourself. For many films, moments like these are necessarily built up with long, drawn out, scenes of exposition meant to define character. Here, the characters are fleshed out in ways which are engaging and often terrifying. The highlight for me is one piece of dialog between the main antagonist, a merciless hitman, and a simple hearted gas attendant, who is faced with a fifty fifty shot at life or death.
I really feel no need to point how magnificent Javier Bardem is, or how wonderful his supporting actors Tommy Lee Jones and Josh Brolin shine, because nothing needs to be said (and I'm sure every other critic will take liberties to say it). They're all great.
So here is my only gripe with No Country For Old Men, and that is my slight disappointment that the movie had to have some kind of message to it. Yeah, I get it's based off a book, and yes, messages do tend to help benefit the viewer beyond the theater. Still, I couldn't help but imagine how amazing No Country For Old Men could have been if it was made as a straight for the gut thriller. All those moments of tension and action are abruptly shifted to aid a message, which, I presume is probably about our need for tension and action. Maybe the film was to provide insight to the violence of man, and the violent nature of man's mind. Hmm, profound. But who cares? I already know the human mind wants to see violence, heck, that's one reason why most people would spend ten bucks to see a movie about a soulless killing machine. This is what we prepared ourselves for, so frankly, I would prefer to see a movie that built up to a big finale, rather than the deus ex machina we are already aware of.
What this film amounts to is a standard Shakespearian tragedy in structure, which in itself is a feat. The standard elements of a tragic hero, a villain, even one remaining character which signifies hope or wisdom. As one definition says, "a story of exceptional calamity, leading to the death of a man of high estate." In their definition of what men can consider "high estate" the Coen brothers have found a truly great film. I highly recommend watching it.

The Coens have done it again! No Country for Old Men is a well-paced crime-thriller that will leave a satisfying bitter taste in the mouth. The three lead actors perform phenomenally in this film, displaying a unique and personal touch upon their characters. 

Josh Brolin, sporting yet again a stache (check out American Gangster), stylish Texan shirts and a dusty hat, is able to grab the audience with his rational, yet adamant, demeanors. He is the guy for whom the audience might identify with; he is the guy for which you will hold to succeed. After finding a suitcase full of wealth from a drug deal gone awry, he is fiercely bound into a rival chase between himself and a hired killer. Now, this hired killer is what makes the film! 

Javier Bardem showcases such an untamed evil that you wish you never meet such a man in your lifetime, and yet, you cannot help but to be amused with his dark and disturbing behavior and perspective. From the initial sequences in the deputy's holding area, you will know what kind of creature every single character in the film will have to deal with, only to notify if they are lucky in a coin toss. 

Tommy Lee Jones, playing Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, is the third man in this violent, bloody and chaotic pursuit. With his reassuring, collected and blunt wit, he tries to understand, along with the spectator, the nature of the events following the drug deal massacre. Through my eyes, his character is with whom I identified with. Amid the insignificant and naive aid of his deputy, he follows every wounded step, every brutal clue left behind by these two characters in order to help Brolin, who has gone over his head, and to catch the killer, who has lost his head. 

The filmmakers and the keen eye of cinematographer, Roger Deakins, shelter the characters within a desolate, bare, wild, sandy and vast landscape where nothing and everything can happen. And that is what occurs in this film. Events are unfolded, people are killed and the unconcerned land plainly permits such atrocities leaving its inhabitants two options; either you survive or you keep a blind eye. 

With the film's opening confession, the viewer will see that, along with the Sheriff, sometimes the nature of things cannot be fully explained and cannot be fully prevented, leaving the conclusion fully opened.

No Country For Old Men, by Joel and Ethan Coen opens with a monologue from Tommy Lee Jones. In a solemn voice he describes a teenage killer he once sent to the electric chair. The boy had killed his 14-year-old girlfriend. The papers described it as a crime of passion, "but he tolt me there weren't nothin' passionate about it. Said he'd been fixin' to kill someone for as long as he could remember. Said if I let him out of there, he'd kill somebody again. Said he was goin' to hell. Reckoned he'd be there in about 15 minutes." Jones delivers this exchange with a reserved astonishment, as if to suggest a disillusioned man in a  world that has drastically changed around him.  The monologue is coupled with  widely framed imagery of the vast Texas landscape, a harsh landscape that seems to engulf its inhabitants, suggesting a large amount of freedom-to do wrong or to do right. West Texas is known to be harsh environment that has a long standing history of bloodshed and crime. It's an isolated region where it seems the only sound one can hear is their own voice. This isolation  seems to play with the notion of free will, and weighs heavily on moral decisions made throughout the film. 
	
	 The sheriff of this town is played by Tommy Lee Jones. Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a poor man who lives with his wife in a house trailer, and one day, while hunting, comes across a drug deal gone wrong in the desert. Everyone on the scene is dead. They even shot the dog. In the back of one pickup are neatly stacked bags of drugs. Llewelyn realizes one thing is missing: the money. He finds it in a briefcase next to a man who made it as far as a shade tree before dying. The plot involves Moss attempting to make this $2 million his own, Chigurh, (Javier Bardem) a creepy ghost like villain  trying to take it away from him and Sheriff Bell trying to interrupt Chigurh's ruthless murder trail. We will also meet Moss' childlike wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald); a cocky bounty hunter named Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson); the businessman (Stephen Root) who hires Carson to track the money after investing in the drug deal, and a series of hotel and store clerks who are unlucky enough to meet Chigurh.
	
	On the surface, No Country For Old Men is an extremely well crafted thriller. The Coens create a tense cat and mouse game between Moss and Chigurh. Moss continuously tries to hide himself and the money in small motels, and Chigurh is never far behind. Each man is extremely proficient and handy with weapons and pervasion, and it's fun to witness the extreme attention to detail within each frame. There is brilliant use of sparse dialogue, lack of score, and long unbroken takes which  all combine to build unbearable suspense. There is one scene in particular in which Moss finally locates the beacon within the briefcase that Chigurh has been using to track him. At this moment the floor creeks outside. Moss quietly picks up the phone to call down to the front desk. The sound of the phone pierces the silence within the scene. (The use of heightened sound against utter silence made me jump more than once)  There is no answer. The sound of the beeping tracking device can be heard nearing closer to Moss's room. Moss cocks his shotgun and turns off the light. He sits on the bed and waits. There is a shadow cast underneath the door. We hear a light bulb being twisted and the light outside turns to darkness. The lock on the door suddenly flies off due to Chigurh's high powered cattle gun. Moss fires a shot through the door and action ensues. The fight is eventually taken to the streets where the chase continues. This is just one example of the many meticulous, well constructed sequences in which the Coens completely absorb their audience in what seems like a never ending game of violence.  

	Because this No Country is set up like a thriller, it's possible that some may miss the layers within this film. Underneath the thrills and flare lies insightful commentary, and one such commentary  is on violence. The Coen's immediately establish an extremely bleak mood with their shocking and realistic depiction of violence. The film utilizes an array of grotesque images and unrelenting spurts of violence to truly test how unsusceptible audiences have become to bloodshed. There is a clever mix of dark humor coupled with this brutality to reinforce the ho hum attitude toward violence that seems to be so prevalent now a days. However, violence, as we soon find out, is not something that should be taken lightly. According to the film and its post modern sensibilities, we live in a harsh world where it seems even the most innocent of store clerks of lily white wives aren't even safe. No Country doesn't cater  to the mentality of the innocent being spared. It's truly a dark view of humanity . At the center of this violent spectacle is Chigurh. He is viewed as a ghost like figure, a manifestation of the overly absurd nature of senseless violence. He gives an outwardly performance, capturing a man who makes little sense but spreads his terror upon the world like the plague.  His use of the coin as a way to decide weather or not his victims die is a creepy little quirk that once again reinforces the absurdity of violent action in today's society. 

	The next layer in this film that I found to be interesting is the motif of money. The film seems to be teasing the audience, tempting us by using a constant  incorporation through imagery and dialogue. Money forwards the action, serving as the driving force behind the murders within the film. As the audience, we are forced from the very beginning to take a stance. Would you take the money or turn it in? It's such a lonely and isolated place. Nobody is around. Why not?  Moss constantly uses it to buy his way out of trouble. There is one scene where a bloody and battered Moss offers a guy 500 bucks for the shirt off his back. The guy of accepts only after he has the money in his hand. Moss also asks for the beer one of the men is holding. The man quickly replies: "How much?" This kind of disregard for humanity is tragic, and it's common practice within the film. Is 2 million dollars really worth all the human life that is lost?   There are some scenes where money is literally dripping with blood to emphasize how corrupting it can be.  There is a scene at the end in which Chigurh's arm bone is poking out after a bad car wreck. He asks a kid how much he wants for his shirt. The kid replies with a simple "Hell Mr. you can just have my shirt."  Even still, Chigurh insists on paying the kid the money. Chigurh like the other characters live in a high capitalistic, post modern society of the 1980's where money dominates all. It's almost comical to see a cold blooded killer pay a kid for his shirt, but no matter how funny it seems to be, this exchange suggests the all consuming power of the dollar over a particular generation. The fact the out villian walks off into the distance at the end, comments on the never ending nature of evil and violence in society.

	This brings me to my last and most important point. There is a clear distinction between generations within this film and Tommy Lee Jones is a clear case in point. His character is part of an older generation that is lost in a world of vanquished values. A world where murder seems to be just one of those things. "Sometimes all you can do is laugh," says Jones. But is the good old sheriff truly incorruptible? Does he too have the capacity for a cease of values in a world where it doesn't seem to matter.  You make the decision for yourself as to why the sheriff truly retiring by the end of the film. Regardless, the sheriff is truly the personification of disillusion and sorrow of an older generation, a generation who rely on stories and dreams of a better time and place to escape a world  that is unfamiliar.  Moss is ultimately nothing more than a cog in the spinning wheel of violence. Instead of a final grandstand between hero and villain, Moss is killed off screen by a group of Mexicans. To the sheriff, he's just another body. It doesn't matter. He's long past feeling. He's numb and tired of the absurd life in which he leads. He's done with the chase. The final moment of the film involves Tommy Lee Jones melded into his memories and dreams of better days. The last line: " And then I woke up," speaks volumes about the inevitability of facing the harsh realities of the world in which we live. Maybe the only way to escape is through the mind, but like Jones says, we all must in fact wake up and face life.

The Coen Brothers are the most important American existentialist filmmakers of this generation and No Country for Old Men could be their best work to date. A perfect blend of brutal violence, subtle humor and heart-pounding action, No Country for Old Men sets a new standard for post-modern filmmaking in a generation of re-hashed storylines, effects-laden blockbusters and uninspired dramas. Tommy Lee Jones gives his best performence since The Fugitive as Sheriff Bell, totally embodying a character disillusioned and overwhelmed by a world he can't control. And then there's Javier Bardem, whose chilling take on the brutal Anton Chigurh is both utterly terrifying and surprisingly charming. No matter how many atrocities he commits in the film (and believe me, there's a lot of them), you can't take your eyes of him as he moves from one kill to the next. From a cinematic standpoint, it's brilliantly shot. One sequence in particular (an intense chase between Anton and the over-confident cowboy Llewelyn Moss, played by Josh Brolin) will have you gripped to your seat as bullets seem to rip from the screen. The locations are stark and poignant, adding a great deal to the films message of hopelessness. Some people may be frustrated with the pacing of the film, but if you're patient and let yourself get lost in the story, I think you'll really enjoy it. Overall, it's one of the best films I've seen in years. If you're a Coen Brothers fan, I think you'll really appreciate it, but even if you're not, give it a chance... you may be surprised at what you take away from it.

Bardem's Anton Chigurh is one of recent cinema's most horrifying villains, a ruthless killing machine who will stop at nothing to retrieve the $2 million in drug money from a deal gone wrong. A scene in which he determines a gas station owner's fate based on a coin-toss ranks as one of the most suspenseful scenes the brothers have ever directed. Based on Cormac McCarthy's acclaimed novel, this is one of the best films of the year. One warning: this movie doesn't neatly tie up every single loose end, so those looking for closure and resolution may be disappointed by the movie's ambiguous final scenes. (For example, if you hated the way the finale of "The Sopranos" ended, you'll probably be pissed when the credits start to roll.)

 At first glance, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] just looked like your typical dramatic thriller. But at the end of seeing that first trailer, the Coen Brothers show why they have been know to make most outstanding novels or other adaptations into excellent movies.
 
 [img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_06_hires.jpg[/img]
 [i]No Country for Old Men [/i]is based off the novel of the same name from Pulitzer Prize-winning author Cormac McCarthy that is regarded by many as a staggering masterpiece. In this almost impossibly faithful adaptation, the film takes place in a small Texas border town in 1980. Sheriff Bell (a never-been-better Tommy Lee Jones) has ruled the land for years without the use of a gun, but a new brand of reckless lawlessness has taken over his town. Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is an innocent Everyman with a devoted wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald), but when he stumbles across a drug deal gone deadly and finds two million dollars, he's determined to keep it for himself. There's only one problem. He's being pursued by one of the most amoral, evil psychopaths that the big screen has ever seen. Wearing an absurd haircut and brandishing a pressurized weapon that's used to murder cattle, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) creeps forward on his mission to track Moss down and return the money to its rightful owners to save his own skin. As the tension mounts, the body count begins to rise, confirming Sheriff Bell's inability to battle this new wave of modern brutality. --© Miramax Films
 
 [img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_07_hires.jpg[/img]
 All in all, this adaptation of McCarthy's masterpiece is so well done that when the movie is over, you scream for more. The Coen Brothers have made a movie that many will regard as their finest since 1996's [i]Fargo[/i], which I still have not seen. The performances here are excellent & easily some of the best that I have seen all year long. Tommy Lee Jones as usual is cast perfectly here as Sheriff Bell. Javier Bardem puts on the performance of a life time here as the psycho Anton Chigurh with an air gun. Josh Brolin also puts on what may be the best performance that I have seen from him with his character Llewelyn Moss. The rest of the cast including Kelly Macdonald & Woody Harrelson is excellent as well. Macdonald does a fantastic job in every one of her scenes. The entire movie is so well shot, that the Coen Brothers make you feel like you are right there.
 
 [img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_09_hires.jpg[/img]
 So overall, [i]No Country for Old Men [/i]is definitely one of the best movies that I have seen all year long. The only problem with this one is that by the end of the movie, you leave wanting more. I really recommend that fans of the Coen Brothers & the Cormac McCarthy novel check this out. Also, if you haven't read the novel or haven't seen many of the Coen Brothers movies, I still recommend that you check it out. PEACE OUT!!! & GO BLUE!!! Beat those DAMN Buckeyes!!!

No Country for Old Men was on its way to being the best movie of 2007 until it fell flat on its face in the last 20 or so minutes.  The movie, which revolves around a cowboy being hunted down by one of the most twisted villains since the lieutenant in Pan's Labyrinth, is cleverly written and full of edge of your seat scenes.  Some of these scenes involve gunfire and some involve complete silence.  What worked so well in No Country was the quiet fear brought to the screen by every single move both men took.  It was almost like a all star chess game where someone, somewhere along the line was eventually going to make a fatal move.  Then your left with the questions of who, when and what will it be.  All those answers are more than sufficiently answered but it's how the movie was ultimately edited that left a sour taste in my mouth.  One of if not the biggest scene of the movie was never even shown and although many argue its artistic purpose I refuse to accept it.  I can usually look past a single flaw but for a movie like this its as though that chess game you were watching was blacked out for the final move.  Two hours go by and checkmate... but you missed it. It doesn't make sense as to why a movie with superb acting, a mesmerizing plot line, and great originality would make such a critical mistake that could have easily been avoided.  Either way 90% of this movie is brilliant and still should not be missed by anyone.  Maybe you can be a bit more forgiving than me.

The Coens' best, and most thematically complex film. Such a decision is offputting, but not unprecedented, for those who remember Barton Fink and The Man who Wasn't There. It'll annoy you, kick you out of the immersion, make you feel cheated, but please don't think it was a mistake. The Coens know quite exactly what they're doing, as evidenced by the Hitchcockian direction, as seamless and complex as a pocket watch. This is a meticulous film about meticulous men, made by meticulous men, and if they make a 'mistake,' then they damn well meant to from frame 1. I'm still thinking about this film and what it was trying to get across about life, fate, death, a week later. If the price is a little wheezing, I wish more films were this bull-headed.
