No Country For Old Men is not a masterpiece as reviewers suggest. The film reminds one of the Hitcher and follows a similar predator/prey super villain formula but masquerading as something artier and therefore pretentious. The Coen brothers are imitating themselves with a variation on Fargo/Blood Simple in a new dusty setting.  But the film is not on par with Fargo and has a more rudimentary and typical action chase plot. The main character, Llewelyn Moss, accidentally comes across money belonging to drug dealers and he decides to run off with it. This is where the movie begins. There has been no background development of Moss as a person so you feel little sympathy or connection to him when in trying to recover the money a psychopathic assassin pursues him and also intends to punish him for taking it. This lack of feeling for the main character is a major flaw. 
 The psychopath is a portrayed as a super killer with "interesting" eccentric quirks and we are supposed to be fascinated (and secretly impressed) by his weird but slightly funny ruthlessness. The fine actor Javier Bardem does his best with this limited role making awkward intentionally cryptic, less than Mamet, remarks to his victims. But there is not a clue to what makes him tick we are simply to be awed by his mysterious power. This character is not enough to make a great film. In the conflict between these men the film puts forth a macho posturing but without the necessary tongue in cheek for an action film and distracting for a thoughtful reflective movie. This attempt at combining these things is one of the story's failings compromising a strong statement in either field.
         Unusually late in the movie the Sheriff played by Tommy Lee Jones enters the scene. In imitation of the Fargo recipe he and his deputy make  contrived, provincially funny-yet clever remarks as they try to figure out what is going on. It does not come off with the style or humanity of Fargo and has now become formulaic. In these early scenes the Sheriff comes off as a slightly amusing local character. Later he turns out to be a boring and weary mumbler, nostalgic for the good old days who has no useful impact on the plot  Acting as unecessary narrator his ramblings, much longer in the book, are even more tiresome. 
        Woody Harrelson appears in the middle of the movie for the sake of a cameo and turns out to be a more dynamic than the sheriff or the pursued main character who are supposed to have primary roles but turns out to be relatively out of place.
       The movie has some exciting suspense pursuit scenes particularly at the opening of the movie but there are many half-intentional unexplained events and a very unsatisfying truncated ending (and the book shouldn't be used as an excuse for flaws- the book is Cormac McCarthy's weakest).  There is little of the humanizing dimension of Fargo. 
 There are also some similarities to the better first Coen Bros film, Blood Simple, which when going the cold blooded route, has a more satisfying realism and consistently compelling mood of darkness and threat. But here in No Country the Brothers C. have added aspects of a Hitcher related bad guy hunts down good guy chase plot with unsubstantially tiny touches of Pulp Fiction/Blue Velvet black humor. They do so with less creativity and variety.  The Sheriffs underdeveloped philosophical comments about fate and scenes left out in this movie may confuse some viewers into thinking that there is more here than meets the eye. Underneath a new set of clothes are a conventional concept and a cowardly, fatalistic, pessimistic view of humanity. This may appeal to those who are comforted by the lay back in your chair and proclaim that life stinks and then you die philosophy (while getting off on all the "neat" violence). 
        Undoubtedly you dont feel anything for the characters. The film is not as cohesive as The History of Violence, which was similarly dark but had greater character development (and even that film was overrated). The Brothers have talent and their own style but now they're imitating themselves and less bizarre bits of David Lynch thrown in. 
       However if oddball "cool" cold-blooded killers pursuing people is enough to satisfy you, you may enjoy this film. Apart from that there is no great artistry here  and little emotional dynamic, ultimately souless.  It does not sustain the tension or plot twists to the degree of a genre film such as the Hitcher (or Hitchcock for that matter) despite it's slightly artier "strangeness" around the edges and cowardly pessimistic philosophical pretensions posing as "reality".
 The film is well shot but the cinematography is nothing exceptional.
       One notes a somewhat new look in the killer, an unexpected Hispanic casting with retro 70s haircut and wielding unusual weapons but such details do not make great film. The movie breaks no barriers and stays far within the confines of stylists such as Tarantino, David Lynch or Cronenberg. Perhaps this is why so many people are raving about it. I has just enough familiarity.
      No Country for Old Men puts forth the rationalization of being a commentary on greed and chance but not developing those ideas. Rather, No Country for Old Men indulges the viewer in another villain worship of the killer badass. Ah, the many uses of compressed air. But seriously, this film was unbearably disappointing. It started out well, but went to the dogs after the first half-hour. Now, I enjoy seeing a movie that can express violence, but only to the extent that there is a reason for it. In No Country, it seemed as if the Coen brothers wanted to show as much violence as possible, then sell it with an equally Terentino style plot. Most of the characters received minimal back story and seemed to have been created only for the purpose of being part of more unnecessary violence. I wasn't expecting a thriller, and was actually glad that it wasn't, but c'mon. The movie never seemed to start. I will say that the performances, headed by Javier Bardem (to play Pablo Escobar in Killing Pablo in '09), were outstanding, along with suitably colorless cinematography. A much better film that I would recommend with a similar plot is Nick Cave's The Proposition. Just as dreary, but at least it has a resolution.

Three Oscar-worthy performances?  Check.

A taut, beguilingly minimalist screenplay stuffed with gallows humor?  Check.

Hitchcockian flair for atypical camera work and narration?  Check.

A chillingly nihilistic thrill-ride that leaves you grinning from ear-to-ear about everything except for that "country"?

9/10 I've seen the words "brilliant" and "genius" on here quite a bit and they're certainly fitting adjectives for this stunning (there's another one) film. This is the Coen Brothers at the top of their game, everything here presented in such a meticulous manner. I was completely engrossed from the very beginning and not once lost interest.
But however engrossing the film is, it's thematically and symbolically where No Country for Old Men truly stands apart. With an immense amount of layers to dig through and pick apart afterwards this has got to be one of the more weightier films of recent years. I'd explain this a bit more if I didn't think it would ruin the film. Just know that this is more a parable or morality tale than a true to life fiction story; nearly all of the characters here more representions of an ideal than actual humans. Of course Javier Bardem is fantastic here, but not to be overshadowed is Tommy Lee Jones who's character provides the only sense of rationality or normalcy in the film. His sheriff character makes quiet realizations throughout. Like us he's an outsider looking in trying to make some sense of the film's craziness. Jones' performance, though small, is understated brilliance.
This film is about the randomness of life. Bardem's insane killer Anton Chigurh chooses to kill according to the laws of chance ("What's the most you've ever lost on a coin toss") and makes it clear to take people from this world as unbiased and random as they came into it. The passage of time and the heavy toll it takes on all of us is also a clear theme. Death is quite literally at every corner. How will we chose to spend our limited amount of time? We better make the best of it quick for we live in a country not made for old men. In that sense, this is a modern version of The Seventh Seal, witty relaxed humor and all.

I don't think it was a mistake that the audience was left perplexed and hanging at the abrupt ending to this odd Coen brothers' flick. The performances were dynamic and complex. Javier Bardem pulled off the calmest, most confident sociopath I think I've ever viewed on screen. Undeniably, this was Josh Brolin's best role ever and Tommy Lee Jones fit his part perfectly as a laid back, cool & collected small-town lawman from another time (like a John Wayne that is in the wrong time in history). The interplay between Bardem and Brolin was so unique that I felt as if I was in a strange Hitchcock-like suspense, but enough violence was happening that I had to add an action category too-I'm sure that was a purposeful choice by the strange Coen brothers. My only complaint was that the side characters, along with Woody Harrelson, seemed fragmented, slightly irrelevent and thrown into the film with odd timing. Having not read the novel this film was adapted from, I didn't feel there was enough explanation as to who they were and what led up to the opening scene or the significance of the second group of Mexicans murdered at the motel or the money trail. I like Woody, but his part was overly edited in my opinion so that I didn't get a real sense of his character. Too many loose ends made the audience confused or letdown and I realize that it was for effect, especially the ending, but I think just a little more development of the storyline and the support characters would have made this film that much more powerful. I don't think it would have taken away from the cat-and-mouse dynamic going on between Brolin and Bardem. I kept thinking back to Jones in "The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada" and felt a little let down after all the hype of this newer film. I gave it a high score because of the artfully done suspense that kept me rivoted to the screen, despite it's long run time, and the complex range that Bardem and Brolin exhibited. 
 
I think matinee price is warranted for this film if you are more of a traditionalist when it comes to movies. If you are into unique films, you won't be disappointed if you pay full price. I still think "Three Burials" is a better film than this one. I highly recommend you rent it for a better Tommy Lee Jones performance and similarly odd (but more cohesive) storyline with a little more resolution.

The mess in this case is Anton Chigurh (a chilling but funny Javier Bardem) who is somehow tied to the 2 million dollars that Brolin's Llewelyn Moss stumbled upon.  A very stupid move--admittedly by Moss--leads to a turn of events that are high throttle, but really just a slow march to what we, as too Chigurh, know is the inevitable conclusion.
 
The Coen Brothers are at the top of their game here, and the story moves along with a quick tempo, and strong, but somehow undeveloped characters.  
 
What motivates a seeming psychopath--money?  It seems far too asymmetrical.  Don't psycho killers kill for sport?  Here, Chigurh seems to kill for money.  Sure, as mercenary of sorts Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) says, there is a principle to Anton's killings, but it doesn't explain the point money would serve to somebody who is crazy.

As the sole real female character in the movie, she represents fairly well.  It's just too bad that a strong woman isn't to be found in three dimensional form in the film.

  "No Country For Old Men" was one of those movies that I was dying to see from the second that I saw the trailer back in early summer. Then I read the early reviews coming out of Cannes and I was totally psyched after that, and I couldn't wait for November to come around. The movie came out last weekend, November 9th, but I managed to see it this weekend due to its still limited, but significant expansion in theaters it had this week. The movie does not disappoint, but it did catch me off guard a little, and it ended up being something a little different than I expected. 
   
  Walking out of the film I could not help but discuss it with the person that I saw it with. It's ending is entirely unconventional and fairly uncommercial to be honest, but it certainly did spark conversation and thought. Did I like it? Not necessarily, but I'll get to that more later on. For now, I'd like to say, this was probably one of the best directed film's I have seen in a long time. The Coen Brothers absolutely mastered the art of suspense in this film and the action sequences are unbelievably unsettling because of how realistic they are. I don't know if I've ever seen this many character's killed off in a crime drama in such disturbing, realistic, unsettling manners as the character's in this film. It's a very violent film, and because it contains so much violence, it was incredibly important that the violent scenes throughout were handled with care and with proper attention. The action scenes in this film absolutely received the care and attention they deserved, no question about that. I was on the edge of my seat throughout most of the first 3/4's or so of the film and had they Brothers handled the end of the film a little differently, perhaps it could've been a pretty decent sized hit at the box office. The way it currently is, I don't think it can make more than 15 or so million just because of its inaccessibility with many regular viewers. That still has more to do with the writing than the direction so I'll get to that later once again. Otherwise this film's direction was pitch perfect. 
   
  The acting was no less impressive and was probably the most perfect thing about the movie. The best performance was no doubt from Javier Bardem who played "Anton Chigurh", in other words, the psychopathic bad guy. He is scary as hell throughout the film and his performance never ever goes out of character's, although the script does take him out of character at least once, but I'll once again, get to that later. I wouldn't be surprised seeing him not only with a nomination for "Best Supporting Actor" but with the Oscar in his hand come oscar night. He has to be seen to be believed. So far his performance and Tom Wilkinson's performance in "Michael Clayton" have to be the two stand out supporting performance's to come along this year. Josh Brolin is the main good guy through the majority of the film. He does a very good job, but his character is not nearly as interesting as Bardem's character is. Still, he deserves credit for his performance as well, but I don't expect that he'll get any oscar recognition. Then there's Tommy Lee Jones who did a very good job for the parts of the film he was in, and he definitely says some of the more interesting things in the movie. He's the only character that really talks a lot. The other two main character's are fairly manly and they tend to keep their mouth's shut, avoiding any really thought provoking character development on their character's while Jones's character tends to have a wandering mind, and he says some of the more profound things in the film. Woody Harrelson has a fairly small role, but he does a good job in the film as well. There was one casting decision that caught me off guard in a good way. Stephen Root who played "Milton" in "Office Space" and the dorky old "Gordon" in "DodgeBall" had a small part in this film that was entirely serious, and his voice was a regular old raspy southern one. It was interesting to see him in a non-comedic role, speaking his lines in a normal manly way. 
   
  Now for the script... The script is my only real issue with this film. Some parts of the script are fantastic. First off all that tension that the Coen's created with their great direction started in their screenplay that they adapted from the novel of the same name. There are some very interesting encounter's and conversation's from character to character through a lot of the film and much of the film is actually quite funny in typical Coen brothers fashion, which I honestly did not expect considering the fact that it looked to be an all out action-thriller from it's trailer. That was a nice touch as well. However here are some things I had a problem with. 
   
  (MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD!) The whole movie has people tracking things down. Now the whole first half of the film the main character is being tracked with a tracking device so that made sense, but then he tosses it out, and still, Harrelson's character finds him and says he did it in three hours. The main character was checked into a hospital in Mexico and Harrelson's character had no way of knowing this, and somehow he magically found the guy? Alright, fine. Then the script decides to avoid explaining how, and when the main character starts talking about how he can get away from Bardem's character Harrelson just says "You don't understand"... Alright, what doesn't he understand? Is there some weird connections that you're organization has to track people down? What? Well it basically just makes it look like these guys have super powers and they can find people with their laser vision or something. That was kind of annoying. Then there's the fact that the whole last quarter of the film the main character is dead. He is killed off screen by some regular old guys that the boss sent out to get the money that he had. Now what bugs me about that is the fact that the main character (Brolin's character) has been outsmarting and dodging those guys through the entire movie, and then a few of them run up and they all just shoot him to death nice and easy. When you see his body, he's not like off somewhere, like he ran and tried to get away. He's on the floor at the front of his motel room. He's also been dodging one of the smartest, most threatening bad guys to be in a film in year's and he was able to dodge getting killed by him... The slow ending following this death was bothersome and it honestly started to feel extremely slow and boring before the credits went up. The thing that really makes the movie unredeeming is the fact that Bardem's super bad character lives on after all this build up towards what looked to be his imminent death.... There is actually a scene where Bardem and Jones look as though they are about to face off, but Bardem runs out the window. This is totally out of character because througout every other scene in the film Bardem shoots firsts and does things like talking or running away later. 
   
  I gave the movie a few hours of thought before I came and wrote this review and after all this thought I decided that Bardem lives because he is the worst man can ever be, and that Jones lives because hes is the best man can ever be. Bardem kills without any real cause, and Jones can't even handle the sight of dead bodies anymore, he's tired of all of the bad thing's he's seen in his life, and he uses knowledge as his number one weapon, constantly spurting out facts through out the film's entirety. Both have to live on so that they can balance each other out. Good and evil... 
   
  Overall this movie was an expertly directed, extremely well acted film that had some flaws with it's script, but honestly, it had to much great things happening with it for any of that to matter. I really loved this movie, and I think I'll probably go see it again next week so that maybe I can understand it a little better than I did this first time around...

NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN
Written and Directed by Joel & Ethan Coen

Llewelyn Moss: Cant help but compare yourself to the ol timers.  Cant help but wonder howd they do in these times.

The Coen brothers have been making movies for over 20 years now.  NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN is their twelfth feature together.  While they were once considered princely collaborators held at the highest esteem by film enthusiasts the world over, they have recently been the victims of their own identity crisis.  Caught between their signature exploration of all things quirky and abnormal found in the parts of America thought to be forgotten and the demanding pressures of delivering bankable Hollywood fare, the Coens finished by delivering sub-par work that tarnished their lustrous reputation.  The film enthusiasts thought they might have lost great talents to Hollywood while Hollywood wasnt even sure they wanted them.  What were these aging filmmakers to do?  They could have polished off another Tom Hanks picture and crossed their fingers.  They could have appealed to their fans and told another tale of the idiosyncrasies of those living in the middle of nowhere.  They could have tried appeasing both parties by attempting THE BIG LEBOWSKI 2.  Instead, they did none of these things.  No, instead, the Coen brothers crafted a film that is unlike any film they have ever made and is also perhaps the best film theyve ever made.

Translating Cormac McCarthys novel about the relationship between the hunter and the hunted to the screen may be smoothest decision these boys have made for years.  Not only does it allow for the brothers to explore the grim sides of characters consumed by money and an unnerving peace derived from killing, but NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN also leaves the door open for an interpretive commentary on the Coens career itself.  Allow me to explain by painting a picture from the film.  Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin) aims his rifle at an unsuspecting animal grazing alongside the herd.  He is right now in charge, in control, the hunter.  He fires and misses, thus beginning his steady descent into ruin.  He moves toward the spot where his prey once stood only to find the site of a drug deal massacre.  Here, he innocently stumbles upon an enormous amount of money.  He picks it up and goes without realizing the hell that is about to be brought upon him.  He inadvertently becomes the hunted.  He spends the remainder of the film calculating and executing different attempts to regain the superior position he once held.  The comparisons are subtle and come about naturally rather than existing as the initial basis for the film to grow out of, reinforcing their genuine nature.  I could explain my logic behind this analogy but that would be very un-Coen like.

Another consistency throughout the Coen Brothers careers is the elevated caliber of talent they attract to their diverse projects.  With their writing at top of its game, performances by Brolin, Javier Bardem and Tommy Lee Jones are pushed to the heights of their potential.  Moss is a quiet man, focused and constantly thinking about what his next play will be.  He has no time for ego, only function, and though most of his motivation is to avoid drawing attention to himself, Brolins interpretation cannot help but capture our notice.  For the second time this year (in conjunction with his slimy crooked cop turn in AMERICAN GANGSTER), Brolin reinvigorates his skills by inhabiting Moss fully as an instinctual and reactionary being.  While Jones is also impressive as a police officer resigned to following the action without any possibility of curbing the outcome, it is Bardems performance as Anton Chigurh that will leave audiences with a haunting chill after experiencing it.  His portrayal of a psychopathic hunter is both disturbing and riveting.  This is a man who enjoys torturing his victims mentally by asking them questions meant to expose the inconsistencies in the way they live their lives before ushering them out of this world.  He abides by some form of ethical code that only makes sense in his own mind and fully justifies his killings.  His adherence to this code is what sends him to an internal state of ecstasy as he chokes a man and stares intently at the ceiling.  The hunter is always frightening but Bardem is worse; hes unsettling.

NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN is entirely disconcerting but is somehow still a tranquil experience.  There is a normality amidst the unrest that thrives in the plain, natural manner in which the story unfolds.  The chase is constantly surprising without ever seeming forced.  Each move made makes perfect sense but is not seen coming.  On this level, even their formal execution of this film speaks to the trajectory of their career.  Who knew that leaving quirk behind for harrowing humour and a story that serves itself instead of as a platform for character would invigorate the Coens method and assert their place as two of the greatest American filmmakers operating in a country thought not to have any place for the them?  I like to think they did.  In doing so, they have also made a movie for a sharp adult audience in a country bent on catering to all things youthful and disposable.

This type of movie should have been a slow, dull and boring ride, but it wasn't. The Coen brothers are great at setting beats and creating a great pace. I think one reason it's so easy to watch is because it's so believable. I never found myself questioning the characters motives or decisions they made throughout the film. The film is smart in it's simplicity and has a lot of underlying subtleties that can either make you laugh or appreciate the good direction into making these characters have such personality. I don't want to give too much away, thus the reason I'm not talking to much in detail. In fact, there isn't even that much to give away, so telling any of the story would be unfair to you. Go out and see this movie and support film. It's one of the best films I've seen this year.

No Country for Old Men begins with Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) out hunting in the barren lands of Texas, minding his own business, coming across a drug deal wrong. Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is following the trail of dead bodies hoping to save Llewelyn Moss. 

This film is written and directed by the Coen Brothers based on the 2005 novel by Cormac McCarthy. It is rare that movies accurately capture the tone and meaning of the novel it is based on but the Coen Brothers did just that. Since I am a huge fan of them, I gave the book a read. The story is set in 1980 and it is a classic tale of greed and violence but the real meaning is about the decline of our society over the years because of various elements like drugs, liberalism, etc. 

The Coen Brothers previous two films were big budget bombs with Intolerable Cruelty and Ladykillers (I loved it though) so it is great to see them return to their low budget, independent roots. No Country for Old Men (their 12th film) is similar in tone and style to Blood Simple, Fargo and The Man Who Wasnât There, slow but gripping where you canât lose focus. The violence in this film is honest and true. Time was spent showing getting shot actually hurts. Consider for a moment how in normal films like Die Hard and Bond movies, they endure an endless supply of pain and seem to be superhuman. In No Country for Old Men, they vomit because the pain is so severe. 

This film does challenge the audience into thinking differently. The climax is very anti-climatic and takes place closer to the middle than the end. The side stories that have nothing to do with the actual chasing is what makes the movie so rich. You need to pay attention to everything Tommy Lee Jones says because that is the underline message of the movie. 

The acting is remarkable in No Country for Old. Javier Bardem has played an exiled gay Cuban poet in Before Night Falls and a paralyzed Spaniard in The Sea Inside. Well, he really shows he range by played a sociopath here. I had nightmares of his death stare. Josh Brolin (big brother in the Goonies) and Tommy Lee Jones turn in great performances. Woody Harrelson and Kelly MacDonald (Ewanâs teenager girlfriend in Trainspotting) have remarkably intense scenes that you will forget to breathe. 

I recommend this for anyone who enjoys independent films or non-traditional stories. This is not a typical Hollywood movie so if you expect that, you will be pissed with the ending. All others will love it.

Lately, its been taken for granted that the Coen's are comic film makers. It's been more than a decade since Fargo followed the bloody path of criminal caper gone awry. And there, ironic humor and satirical characters soften diabolical plot lines, such as a dismembered body being passed through a wood chipper. Since then, the brothers have given us mostly comedies of varying quality and questionable execution (O Brother Where Art Thou being the best of this period) along with the curious but ultimately droll noir mystery, The Man Who Wasn't There. In No Country for Old Men, the Coens return to the bleakly nihilistic and deeply pessimistic territory that they so aptly explored in their debut film Blood Simple. Tone is something not lost in the process, as No Country manages to make even its humorous moments uncomfortable and tense, without even a single note of cinematic score. Still, this film is not perfect. There are a few noticeable and irksome plot holes, but the characters, the dialouge, the direction, cinematography, art direction and editing combine in creation of what is arguably the best American film to be released this year. The ending will no doubt incite fury and anger from those deeply attached to linear narratives, but for any and all who appreciate films such as Children of Men, the new Coens' have made a tasty new flavor of pitch black just for you.

Lately, its been taken for granted that the Coen's are comic film makers. It's been more than a decade since [i]Fargo[/i] followed the bloody path of criminal caper gone awry. And there, ironic humor and satirical characters soften diabolical plot lines, such as a dismembered body being passed through a wood chipper. Since then, the brothers have given us mostly comedies of varying quality and questionable execution ([i]O Brother Where Art Thou[/i] being the best of this period) along with the curious but ultimately droll noir mystery, [i]The Man Who Wasn't There[/i]. In [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], the Coens return to the bleakly nihilistic and deeply pessimistic territory that they so aptly explored in their debut film [i]Blood Simple[/i]. Tone is something not lost in the process, as [i]No Country[/i] manages to make even its humorous moments uncomfortable and tense, without even a single note of cinematic score. Still, this film is not perfect. There are a few noticeable and irksome plot holes, but the characters, the dialouge, the direction, cinematography, art direction and editing combine in creation of what is arguably the best American film to be released this year.

Every character, even Tommy Lee Jones (!), was wonderfully acted and the dynamics, both between any two characters and between characters and their environments, were stunning. Despite my initial hesitation to see it, because the trailer did not do its scope any justice, I have to suck it up and admit that this is the best movie of 2007. See it. Now.

I've always adored the Coen brothers, and having just read the book in preparation, I couldn't wait to see it. It didn't disappoint, except for one thing. Two things. The Coens paint southern women (especially the hotel clerk/store clerk/grandmother) with a broad, Beverly Hillbillies brush. The men seem to come out okay. (Is it laziness, or are they injecting some levity into what's otherwise a difficult film? Still, they can do better.) The second issue is with their choice to put the two marriages (Ed Tom's and Llewellyn's) in shadow. In the book, those relationships were central to the characters, and exploring that  could have helped the movie.

Although the plot is driven by a character who is little more than a tiresome caricature -- Javier Bardem's cartoonishly quirky hitman -- everything else about the Coen Brothers' adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel is above reproach.  The deliberate pace and stark photography elegantly evoke McCarthy's spare prose, as do the taciturn protagonists, all convincingly essayed.  Grisly, bleak, and frustratingly opaque in places, it's an easy film to admire, even if it rarely deviates from predictable genre conventions.

What to say about "No Country for Old Men"?  The Coen Brothers have been in my top ten list of directors since Raising Arizona.  Their characters are never really extraordinary people. Their circumstances are real because the characters are real.   

I've only recently been turned on to the writings of Cormac McCarthy.  There never (well, in the books I've read so far) is a resolution at the end.  You finish the book never sure what really happened to these fantastic, simple people who you've come to relate to and cherish in just a few paragraphs of text.  And his books always leave me ill at ease and a bit sad for it.  The ambiguity of it all, that's life right?

The pairing of this excellent writer with these two phenomenal filmmakers would seem a match made in heaven.  Well, let me tell you, "No Country..." doesn't disappoint.  It starts out slow with a voice over from the Sheriff telling us about the country and his (and his family's) relationship to it.  A moment of intensity hits us.  Then it slowly builds up to another and another like a roller coaster keeping you nervously tittering and clutching your seat until the very end of the ride when it slows down again and the Sheriff relates to us another story.  

There's no Hollywood ending to this movie.  There's no happy ending.  The guy doesn't ride off into the sunset with the girl.  Nobody walks away from the events in this movie whole again.  Everyone lives, and dies, by the choices they made.  I'm left again with that uneasy feeling.  It's beautiful and terrible and I couldn't imagine this movie being made any differently.
Go see it now.

This film is really two films. The first two acts make up a bloody, tense, intriguing cat and mouse thriller. The last act is a dreamy lamentation on the evil nature of man and the relentless passing of time. The film starts us with an involving thriller where Josh Brolin's opportunistic and clever trailer park resident tries to outwit Javier Bardem's psychopathic hitman. Then the third act completly shifts our perspective as we follow Tommy Lee Jones' lawman as he ponders the state of man. Where the Coens fail is how jolting and clunky they make this shift in perspective. We are left without a satisfying conclusion to the Brolin/Bardem storyline, and the film cuts to the end credits so suddenly that you will probably be left asking yourself if the movie really is over. It took me a while to appreciate the uniqueness of this approach. I imagine many viewers (my little brother included) will not be so forgiving. Still, this film is very good, and deserves a second viewing, keeping in mind what you learned the first time around.

The Coen Brothers have went and outdone themselves on their latest work, a brilliant adaptation of the Cormac McCarthy novel, "No Country for Old Men".

"No Country..." takes place in Texas in 1980.  Another way of saying that is simply that it takes place in a simpler time in a simpler place. Things don't move as fast down there and back then and that much is emphasized straight from the get go in a voiceover by local Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, played by Oscar winner Tommy Lee Jones. It starts off the film nicely painting beautifully landscapes in all their peace and glory. Before they are bathed in a opera of bad decisions, greed, and bullets.

Recently surging actor Josh Brolin plays Lleweylen Moss, a poor welder who stumbles across a drug deal done bad while doing some unsuccessful hunting. Moss sees the green glow that twinkles in his eye when he sets his peepers on a case full of folding money. Two million in folding money to be exact. He takes it and thus our story sets into motion. Picking up that suitcase may have brought instant wealth but in turn it brings something much worse. That being a manaical stun gun killer by the name of Anton Chigurh, portryed to a chilling brilliance by Javier Bardem. Chirgurh is the devil incarnate, another form of death, a remorseless killing machine who dispenses of people the way we dispense of our fecal waste. He does so with no hesistaiton, no pause, other than the one he takes to breathe in what he loves to do. Kill. Period.

Moss inadvertently brings his naive wife into the mix and any poor person that gets in Anton's path on his way to the cash. Anton wants it and will do anything necessary to get it. It is what he does. And he does so with some nasty tools of the trade. A airblast cattle stun gun that fires a metal cylinder into his victims before retracting back into the machine. He also carries a spread shotgun fitted with a silencer that turns humans into confetti. Tommy Lee Jones is the sheriff investigating all the murders and mishaps, Woody Harrelson is a bounty hunter hired to retrieve the money too, and Stephen Root is the man who hires him.

The film is shot brilliantly by Roger Deakins and is written, edited, and directed to seemless perfection. The Coen Brothers have managed to craft a film of raw power that hits you like a blast from Chigurh's gun. It is an excercise of flawlessness in the film medium. It also unfolds before you with an eerie silence as there is no music in the film to go along with the action thus adding a realistic feel to the film that makes you feel uncomfortable at times because you don't feel like you're watching a movie as much as you are watching a real life horror story before your very eyes.

After watching the film I sat for a minute and thought about what I just saw. What the characters could have done. What the characters should have done. But the only thing for certain is that they did what they did and where it ended wasn't important. It was the journey that shook us so much.

All in all, "No Country for Old Men" is hands down the best film so far this year. I am so excited to go see it again knowing where the characters end up and soaking in exactly how they got there.

PS, Anton Chirgurh just may best Clint Eastwood's William Munny ("Unforgiven") as the biggest badass in film history.

Should I throw out the now familiar phrase and say best film of 2007 so far? Nah, I won't be so hasty, and I don't feel that at this point I could compare this film to anything else I've seen in a long while.
There are the obvious things in the film that make it work (or not); the performances, the cinematography, the script - those things that we all see in some way, big or little working in unison. What made the film for me though were those little moments; split seconds, though "a part of" certainly... The use of milk, the reflections and silhouettes, the boot motifs.  These weaved a tapestry, created a study an exercise in the similarities between Josh Brolin's Llewelyen Moss, Javier Bardem's Anton Chigurh and even Tommy Lee Jones' Sheriff Bell, who is observing, following, trying to figure out these two hunters, these scavengers... Or just trying to deny their presence all together.
Did it come out cold at the other end? Yes, certainly, but that was what made the film so satisfying to me; A build of up of tension, of tact, that uncoils to a disillusioned, fractured sigh.
It is a film about perspective and truth, it may be hard to take in, and like life comes with no easy answers or perhaps none at all...

I go into a Coen brothers movie expecting awesome and when I get a well-crafted build-up to something that concludes with vagueness and lazy writing, I am annoyed. Let me explain. 

Carson: What a completely useless character. They implied that he was intuitive and brilliant enough to track Llewelyn down (which wasn't shown so we're just supposed to take their word for it = lazy), but so stupid that he not only got caught, but tried to barter with Anton against his own advice. Dream interpretation: Nuff said. Hunting: Scenes earlier in the movie implied that the hunter (Llewelyn) became the hunted when immediately in danger for his life. What happened at the end there? He got distracted by pussy and then got shot by a bunch of minor Mexican characters even though he was keeping a lookout? Come on. They turned a perfectly good epic showdown into anticlimactic existentialist crap. That is the key here: existentialism is a great topic if you're a high school English student writing an essay, but wind sounds and tumbleweeds and empty landscapes are insulting to an adult because it removes the need to write cleverly and tie in details.  I think the Coen brothers are either (a) so consumed with their own sense of superiority that they think their ending is "fresh" and not a copout, or (b) having a joke at the expense of their fans. Then again, maybe they half-assed the ending as a statement of their existential angst. "Let it go, dude, I'll just whip some inconsistent ending together and people will say it's about the unpredictability and futility of life. We'll break the 'rules' of making movies just like our characters all break the 'rules' that they make for themselves in life. That's deep, dude!" If so then I salute them, but somehow I doubt it.

Every setting seems empty, almost devoid of human life.  The filmâs major characters seem to exist primarily in these empty spaces â these are the places where their dramas quietly play out.  Fantastic events occur with no fanfare, no sensationalization, no spikes in the musical score.  In fact, there is almost no music to speak of, which only contributes to the atmosphere of this bizarre vacuum-universe.

Tommy Lee Jonesâs Ed Tom Bell and Josh Brolinâs Llewelyn Moss seem like they could have been friends of my grandfatherâs. This film blew me away.  It is violent and haunting...Fargo is the closest Coen bros film, but in many ways this film even tops that. In many ways, this approach to a crazy killer picture is the absolute opposite of a Tarantino flick.  There's no cool, flashy slickness here.  The dialogue is sparse in this movie - not a word is wasted, and each one is written extremely well and with deep purpose.  In addition, there's no score to this movie at all - the silence adds to the eerie nature of the film - with some superb sound work that really adds some heft to the busting of each door and the clink of each boot.  And the performances were all fantastic - every single role was cast perfectly.  Javier Bardem...wow.  Extra points for the haircut. From its opening frames (as Tommy Lee Jonesâs monologue plays out over cinematographer Roger Deakinsâs shots of the Texas desert) until the credits roll, No Country for Old Men moves at a slow, stately pace that is completely hypnotic.  For the 122 minute running time, the viewer is sucked into a different world, one with its own rules and rhythm, and the result is one of the most engrossing film experiences Iâve had in some time.  

The filmmakers have given viewers a place that seems alien and desolate, vast and lonely, while somehow still very real.  Deakinsâs photography communicates the hugeness of the Texas desert, the empty spaces between places of interest.  Indeed, emptiness pervades the film.  Every setting seems empty, almost devoid of human life.  The filmâs major characters seem to exist primarily in these empty spaces â these are the places where their dramas quietly play out.  Fantastic events occur with no fanfare, no sensationalization, no spikes in the musical score.  In fact, there is almost no music to speak of, which only contributes to the atmosphere of this bizarre vacuum-universe.

In the midst of all this nothingness, the filmâs major players give uniformly strong, quiet performances, etching out rich characters who feel so completely real, the viewer is shocked to see them go when the credits roll.  Tommy Lee Jonesâs Ed Tom Bell and Josh Brolinâs Llewelyn Moss seem like they could have been friends of my grandfatherâs.  Kelly Macdonaldâs Carla Jean reminds me very strongly of a girl I knew in high school.  And of course, Javier Bardem.  Bardem plays the psychotic Anton Chigurh with businesslike menace as he goes from place to place, hunting his prey.  I am by no means a film historian, but this has to be one of the most unique and memorable villains ever committed to film. Thereâs nothing generic about him.  Like the film itself, he manages to be simultaneously otherworldly and shockingly real, and the result is terrifying.  Indeed, his performance is the driving force of the movie, and, combined with the Coensâ strong script and direction, creates several long sequences of almost unbearable tension.

If I had one problem with the film it was the last ten minutes.  Not to say I think theyâre bad.  I just wish I had them to watch over again, because Iâm not sure I really understood them.  I mean, I understood what was happening in the story, but I thought the story made a couple of unusual choices towards the end.  But then, this is a deep film that doesnât purport to hand out a tidy resolution or easy answers.  The ending seems that it could have meant several different things, and maybe itâs meant to.  Iâll have to think on it some more.

All in all, mark up another victory for the Coen brothers.  Itâs bizarre to think that these are the same guys who made âThe Big Lebowskiâ and âRaising Arizona,â but itâs also great.  Itâs a testament to their amazing power as storytellers that theyâre able to bring audiences such a wide variety of entertainments so successfully.

Joel and Ethan Coen created one of American cinema's landmark films in 1996--the superbly atmospheric, very bloody, and painfully hilarious 'Fargo', which cemented their elevated status in Hollywood. Since--aside from 'The Big Lebowski' and their characteristically moody noir, 'The Man Who Wasn't There'--the two have danced around their obvious forte with films like 'O Brother', 'Intolerable Cruelty', and 'The Ladykillers'. As you'll hear or read all too much about 'No Country', it's truly a reflection of their greatest works, and it's perhaps their most engrossing and dangerous one yet.

In the Coens' guileless and forthright screen version of Cormac McCarthy's 2005 acclaimed novel, Josh Brolin puts in another great performance in his second of two films released within a month of each other ('American Gangster' was released on November 2) as Llewelyn Moss, a welder and inhabitant of a small Texas town who stumbles across an apparent drug-deal gone sour--nearly a half-dozen bodies, an equal number of bullet-sprayed pick-ups, a truck bed-full of unclaimed drugs, $2 million in cash, and a near-death Mexican who begs him for aqua--while out hunting. He claims the money for himself (as anyone would) and heads back to his humdrum trailer, where he's bombarded with inquiries from his concerned wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald).

Later that night, he returns to the bloody site with a jug of water, where--in addition to learning that the only left survivor is now dead--he is shot at and chased by a vicious canine into a streaming river close by. When he staggers to safety, drenched, exhausted and wounded, unbeknownst to him he is now the subject of a plethora of pursuers, most notably Sheriff Bell (played very well by the baggy-eyed Tommy Lee Jones) and a mysterious and terrifying killer named Anton Chigurh, whose murders are provoked by anything from pre-designated assignments to random encounters to--this is great--a coin flip (in which case he asks unaware civilians to "call it" for their right to live).

Javier Bardem ('The Sea Inside') is given the part of Chigurh, an unyielding psychopath whose moral principles rival Hitler's. He is the epitome of evil--emotionless, nonnegotiable--and is absolutely horrifying to even think about. Chigurh is so ominous on his own, in fact, that the Coens don't even bother telling us his name until the last half of the film''s final act--and by then we've learned why: because any who knew it are already dead. Bardem's portrayal of the murderous villain is as dark and scrupulous as his character (it could garner an Oscar nod), and is one of the most memorable of any in Hollywood history. With the support of his accompanying cast (which also includes Woody Harrelson as Carson Wells, a smug conciliator for the drug cartel from which the payoff slips away), Bardem drives this film far past one of the best offerings of recent years and qualifies it as an all-time classic and one of the Coen brothers' best, alongside 'Blood Simple' and 'Fargo'.

I'm not saying 'No Country' is the greatest movie ever--it's not, at all--but it does to viewers what few films can: it makes them wary and fearful of the world's very darkest realities. Through the desolate presentation of the Old West (captured impeccably by veteran cinematographer Roger Deakins), and an ingeniously sparse score by Carter Burwell, viewers are given the opportunity to live in the story itself. Though, upon sight of Anton Chigurh, they quickly appreciate their existence as it is: in a movie theater, frozen still and blown away.

You`re afraid of what he`ll do but you can`t wait for him to do it. He is the ultimate villain, cold, smart, patient, brutal and totally fucking insane.

Ok, so what`s the movie about. It`s actually about this other guy, Josh Brolin, who stumbles across a drug deal gone bad. He finds 2 million dollars and decides to keep it for himself. Javier is the hitman sent to retrieve the money. What follows is a cat and mouse game that ends in the most unlikely way. There are moments in this film that are tense as hell. Some great shootouts and some amazing stalking sequences. 

Now Josh Brolin is no slouch. His character maybe a cliched redneck but he`s pretty smart. He manages to outsmart and stay just one step ahead of Javier (but just barely). This is a great role and Brolin knocks it out. To be honest, I never cared much for Brolin. But after Planet Terror and now this, I`ve really come around on him. 

The Coen brothers kick ass in this movie. Not since Fargo have they nailed such a perfect movie. Beautiful camera shots, a nice steady pace and some awesome sound design. They were able to maintain some incredible moments of suspense in complete silence. You see, I don`t think the movie has a score. I don`t once remember hearing any kind of music (unless it was coming from a car stereo or something in the background). So for long moments at a time, we`re in complete silence listening for footsteps, or looking for a shadow, watching the characters trying to stay alive and it`s riveting stuff.  

The only issue some might have is a decision the Coens make in the 3rd act. The way they handle the climax is very... odd... I don`t want to give it away, but I can see how some people might feel disconnected by it. But what follows are some great scenes with Tommy Lee Jones (oh yeah, he`s in this too) that really hammer home the theme of the movie. So if you can survive that third act switcheroo, you`ll probably get a lot out of this movie.

So overall, this is an amazing movie. One of the best of the year, and that`s saying a lot because I`ve seen some solid movies lately.

I love Coen brothers films, from Hudsucker Proxy to Barton Fink. I love edgy, experimental narratives. But this is my least favorite of their efforts. Normally, when a film changes direction, it gives the audience an anchor that represents what the film was really about. If, in this case, the main character was the sheriff, then there just wasn't enough of an arc to bring me into his character. As one reviewer put it, he occupied a role much like a Greek chorus, detached from the action; a mere observer. If the entire film hangs on his transformation, then it seems a mostly wasted exercise. If the killer is the main character, then there's no arc whatsoever, and the film is a self-indulgent exercise in nihilism (which would have been fine, if it had established itself as such). I suppose the film could have kept me engaged if it had told the story of Moss' death with as much care, and attention to detail, as it had told the story of his initial evasion from the assassin. Up until the hospital scene, the chase is meticulously plotted. Following that scene, we are left to guess how the killer is able to keep tabs on his quarry. We are left to guess how Moss is ultimately bested. If Moss had been given a final scene as powerful as his first, I might have followed along. If the sheriff had been given a more prominent arc in the narrative, I might have followed along. Instead, it was as if all the energy started to leave the storyline when the sheriff's character arrived at the Moss' motel too late.

The Coen brothers initially seem to be heading back toward their starting point, "Blood Simple," which I actually count among the scarier films I've seen, but this is deeper, more intimate, more sweeping, more philosophical, and yes, scarier. Frankly, this is one of the most interesting and visceral moviegoing experiences I can recall. As strange as Anton Chigurh seems, during the film, you never disbelieve him. Ever. It's only afterwards that you begin to wonder: what was Llewelyn Moss really up against? Who are these people? I won't spoil anything here, but I will say that you can expect to spend some time mulling over the true nature of the plot, as well as the countless good scenes and odd diversions. I've been a Coen fan for a long time, and it's rewarding to see them release a film this mature, complex, and entertaining. The cast, by the way, is uniformly excellent. The raves will be for Javier Bardem with leftovers for Josh Brolin, but Tommy Lee Jones' haunted performance becomes the heart of the film.

A quick browse of the reviews on the Rotten Tomatoes website reveal a number of critics using words like 'searing', 'acerbic', and 'masterpiece' to describe the Coen Brothers' new film, [i]No Country for Old Men.[/i] While I believe this film to be a technical triumph, and quite possibly the most cohesive and assured work of the Coen's to date, I'm not ready to go so far as to claim it an undisputed work of genius, as many are clearly prepared to do. As a formalist work, it begs to be seen by those who yearn to understand how imagery and moving pictures can express emotion in a way that no other art form can. The cinematography is breathtaking, yet sparse, the camera movements are strong enough to show you just what you need to see and nothing more, and each frame seems meticulously crafted to convey the sense of looming dread and shadowy atmosphere that surrounds each character. One particular shot, a POV of a man's feet, clad in shiny black shoes, as a small stream of blood inches ever closer on the hardwood floor of a cheap motel is simply incredible. Another example, and probably my favorite scene in the film, concerns the main character sitting alone in his hotel room...I won't give anything away, but the manner in which the Coen's fashion suspense in this scene is completely worthy of Hitchcock.  At times the production design reminded me of the other-wordly southern style you might find in a Sam Peckinpah film or [i]The Texas Chainsaw Massacre[/i]. Brilliant sound design works with the picture to showcase a magnificent caper flick about the loss of innocence in middle America.  The acting is occasionally brilliant (though the characters are underwritten) and the snappy dialogue is just as inventive as you'd find in any Tarantino picture. Unfortunately, this is where the innovativeness ends. While well-crafted, I'm at a loss to describe what any of it really means...the characters are of no praticular importance , and I have a feeling that all of this technical prowess that the Coen Brothers have been quick to display was all used in the service of making a fairly straightforward thriller. This is the kind of film that would be great to watch in an introductory filmmaking class, but would be left clawing at the door in a discussion of intellectual film theory. And while one doesn't have to have the philosophical subtext of a Tarkovsky film to be considered a great movie watching experience, I would hesitate to call [i]No country For Old Men[/i] a Best Picture contender, as it really doesn't explore many deep themes or topics of real importance. Perfectly formed, well constructed, and entertaining movie experience? Absolutely! A Masterpiece? Not quite...

As sparse as my current dating life, as lean as my abs, and as contextually excessive as it needs to be, No Country for Old Men offers a very unique cinematic experience. At its heart it is a truly amazing thriller with more intense chills and creepy tension than a modern horror film. But at the core of its soul lies an exploration of the ways of man and the gradual destruction of a way of life.

Wasting neither a moment nor a role, No Country takes viewers on a cat-and-mouse thrill ride for the bulk of its runtime, but moviegoers familiar with the book know this will not sustain. If you demand convention then prepare for a shock to the system. Love it or hate it, the Coens refuse to buckle to genre rules and have remained completely faithful to the book. That's all I'll say about that.

Like any good recipe, minor ingredients are essential to the overall quality, and it's the film's constant influx of background characters that serves to give it just a little more flavor. Whether it's the poor gas station attendant who has no idea his life hinges on the flip of a coin, or the trailer park manager who couldn't care less that she's giving lip to a cold-blooded killer, each leaves a memorable impression and a small addition to the enjoyment.

But just like grandma's favorite recipe, the major ingredients are what truly set this dish apart. Kelly McDonald is remarkably innocent and helpless as Moss' wife, Tommy Lee Jones is pitch-perfect as the sheriff, Bardem is disturbingly convincing as the cold, calculated, "principled" Chigurh - one of the best movie villains cinema has seen in a long time, but it is Josh Brolin who really steals the show. As bad and as ruthless as Chigurh is, Brolin portrays Moss in such a way that you never doubt his ability to square off with the guy and come out the victor. He's seen the terror that Chigurh has left in his wake, yet he never gives an inch nor shows an ounce of fear. It has certainly made an impression on Sheriff Bell, but Moss refuses to bat an eye.

The quiet, eerie desert landscape is also an essential character. With no music upon which to crutch, the crunching of boots and the whistling of the desert wind serve as the film's only soundtrack; the silence forcing Brolin to carry portions of the film on his swaggering body language and steely-eyed glare, something he accomplishes with natural ease.

Audiences who can handle the film's brutality and tension will absolutely love the first 3/4ths of the film. As for the ending? That will depend strictly on personal taste. Some will love it, calling it brilliantly clever, insightful, and realistic. Others will leave unsatisfied. But it's crafted to elicit both responses. Mission accomplished.

I have my own thoughts on the conclusion, so feel free to email me and we will discuss. But don't let your fear of uncertainty of how you'll view the ending be the decider on whether to see this or not. I'd place it right below 3:10 to Yuma on my "Best of 2007" list and am looking forward to multiple viewings. There's a reason this is no longer country for old men. Did you really expect it to be a pretty one?

Ever since Fargo and The Big Lebowski, the Coen brothers seem to have gone down hill.  The Ladykillers and Intolerable Cruelty are very much below what these two are capable of creating.  However, they're back and better than ever.  No Country for Old Men isn't one of their best films, it is their best film by far.
 
 No Country for Old Men opens with a narration from Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones).  "I always knew you had to be willing to die to even do this job - not to be glorious. But I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand."  Within the next five minutes, we know exactly what he means by that.  The first time Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is introduced, he has been arrested and taken to the police station.  While the officer is making a phone call, Chigurh quietly maneuvers to get his handcuffs from behind his back to the front of his body.  After the officer finishes the call, Chigurh walks from behind and chokes the officer to death using his handcuffs.  Using the deputy's car, he pulls over a motorist, kills him with a cattle gun and swaps cars.
 
 Out in the desert, Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a Vietnam veteran and welder, hunts for antelope.  After failing to kill his target, he stumbles upon the bloody aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong.  Everyone is dead except for one man pleading for water.  Moss finds the drugs and knows that there could be money around.  He turns out to be correct.  Pondering on the situation for a while, he decides to take it.  Later that night, his conscience gets the better of him.  He fills a jug of water and drives back to the scene of the crime.  Unfortunately for Llewellyn, the man appears to be dead and two men in a pickup truck park next to his car (which he parked far away) and slash his tires.  The men spot Moss and send him on a chase, even using their dog to attack.  Moss escapes and tells his wife to pack so she can stay with her mother while he devises a plan to outsmart the men who are after him.  One of those men is Chigurh.
 
 Moving at a methodical pace, No Country for Old Men builds it tension to a level rarely, if ever, seen in a film.  There's one scene involving Moss and Chigurh in a hotel that scared me shitless.  Chigurh, using a transponder, locates the room Moss is staying in.  For about a minute or two, nothing happens, as each man braces himself for the confrontation.  A similar situation happens between Chigurh and another character later.
 
 The acting is nothing short of exceptional.  The main and supporting actors are on top of their game.  Josh Brolin is having a breakout year, acting in In the Valley of Ellah, Grindhouse, American Gangster, and now this.  Tommy Lee Jones played a similar role in his own movie, The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada, but his emotional range appears to be much greater here.  Although these two actors are great here, Javier Bardem steals the show.
 
 Anton Chigurh might be as frightening of a villain as Hannibal Lector, if not more so.  His stiff posture, menacing stare, calculated word usage, emotionless expressions, unorthodox principles and remorseless killings make him appear to be not human.  In some ways he is human and other ways more of an idea, like the embodiment of violence.  He views his himself as a person carrying out fate and thus has a detachment from his victims.  His background is a mystery because anyone who knows something about him is dead.
 
 Artistically, the film is superb.  Seeing the vast emptiness of the desert in the first few scenes recalls similar images in Sergio Leone's Spaghetti Westerns.  The minimalist music score heightens the tension and allows every sound to be heard.
 
 The film's transition from an impressive thriller into philosophical territory elevates its lasting effect.  All of the complaints from people about the third act are bullshit.  The supposed "plot holes" some mention are a result of their lack of attention to details.  Also, people expecting non-stop nonsensical violence are going to be disappointed.  There's a lot more to this than just the thriller elements.
 
 Just as No Country for Old Men opens with a narration from Bell, he ends the film with one too.  He describes a dream he has about him and his father.  It may be the only optimistic scene in this very bleak film.

A film about much more than a man trying to getting away with some money.  Running subtextually throughout the film is an examination of space and time -- the nature of it and how humans percieve it.  The film seems to address two conflicting schools of thought: 1) Time is malleable and there is no such thing as "fate," and 2) Time is immutable, pre-determined and unchanging, and we all are inexcapably hurtling toward a set fate.  Most of the film's characters would seem to believe in the first school of thought, as they try, often desperately, to change things and alter fate.  Josh Brolin's character is this way.  Tommy Lee Jones' character is this way.  Most characters in the movie are this way.

But then you have Javier Bardem, the supposedly crazy Anton Chigurh, who doesn't submit to either school of thought.  Instead, Chigurh wholly dedicates himself to the completion of his task -- no matter the cost -- and submits himself to the outcomes that emerge from the coin he flips.  There's safety in those things. There's no need to worry about either school of thought.  All that matters is the task at hand and the outcomes that emerge from the coin.  In this sense, Chigurh is really the only principled character in the movie.  Whereas the others will do anything to save themselves and forstall the seemingly inevitable, Chigurh always follows his "code" and doesn't deveate from it.  He's the only character where you know exactly what you're going to get.

Aside from the first school of thought and the code by which Chigurh lives, there is one character in the film who believes in the second school of thought -- the crippled brother of Jones' character -- and it seems that the Coen Brothers ultimately try to steer the film toward that conclusion.  In his conversation with Jones' character, the brother tries to hammer home the point that "You can't stop what's coming."  Time is immutable and we are all just hurtling along toward a set fate that we cannot change or escape.  To try to do so is foolish.  Brolin's character, Moss, who tries to change things and alter his supposed fate more than anybody else in the movie, is ultimately killed and is made to submit to the fact that he was never going to escape or get away.  Things were always, inevitably, going to end the way they did.  

Even the one character in the movie who didn't percieve time or fate like any of the other characters did -- Chigurh, the character who lives by his own set of rules -- is shown not to be invincible or all-knowing.  Just as it was foolish for Moss to presume that he could change things and alter his fate, it was foolish for Chigurh to think that the only thing that mattered or had any bearing on life was his own, simple code. 

Rammed by a car that inexplicably ran a red light, there was no way Chigurh could have seen or anticipated the crash happening.  Even he is made to submit to the fact that time is immutable, and to think that we, as humans, can operate above that plane is foolish. 

Jones' character would seem to accept his brother's aforementioned viewpoint by the end of the movie.   His dream about his father communicates how he, too, is now beginning to see that one can't stop what's coming.  You can only submit yourself to that fact, live your life, and go along for the ride in blissful ignorance.  To do otherwise, to operate by any other pretense, is foolish... and it can even lead to tragedy.

While I haven't reached any ultimate conclusions on this topic myself, I think I now see what the Coen brothers were trying to communicate with this movie, and the realization of that has only made me appreciate this wonderful picture even more than I already did.

'All the Pretty Horses'- a movie I actually thought was well done- was another adaptation, so I figured it would be an interesting read at best. I was not disappointed in the story or characters, but was with McCarthy's punctuation (more like "lack of"). However, I stuck it through, and did actually enjoy the novel, lack of punctuation notwithstanding. 

As for the movie, it's almost perfect. Almost. The storyline is fairly straightforward- Guy stumbles upon a deal gone wrong, finds a suitcase of money, takes it, and goes on the run. However, it's really the characters and acting that take this over-used plot line (combined with a few Coen brother additions to the script) and elevate it to so much more. If Javier Bardem does not get a nomination for this movie, then the Oscars will certainly be recognized as the farce it has truly been over the past number of years. He's great as the villainous Chigurh- a character that captures evil in it's purest form. A villain you like watching on screen, but can't actually root for. That's because of the 'Yang' to Bardem's 'Yin': Josh Brolin as the everyman who happens to stumble upon a hefty suitcase of cash, Llewelyn Moss. Brolin's Moss attempts to stay one step ahead of Bardem's Chigurh, and the tension built in scenes where a mere door stands between them is almost unbearable to watch. Tommy Lee Jones portrays Sheriff Bell, a smart and determined yet disheartened man attempting to help Moss and catch Chigurh, all the while realizing that his type of character, the 'old men' of the title, are a dying breed. Turns by a great supporting cast: Woody Harrelson as a cocky bounty hunter, Kelly Macdonald (last seen by me in 'Gosford Park') as Moss' naive yet sweet wife, and Stephen Root as a businessman associated with the entire deal, are all very good in their respective roles. I could continue to go on about the direction, or how the lack of sound or music adds to the film's taut atmosphere, but I think many many people will moreso comment on the anti-climactic ending. I won't spoil it here, but remember something as you begin to watch the movie: Pay close attention to Jones' narration at the beginning, talking about older generations, then listen the the last character's scene while eating breakfast. It ties together quite nicely actually, but I realize many viewers will moreso anticipate an ending tying all the pieces together in a neat little package. However, it does, and this movie deserves accolades for not only it's filmmakers, but especially for the actors. Why did I begin in saying the film is almost perfect and not give it a five star rating? I always have a hard time giving a film a perfect rating, but rest assured that this is as close to perfect as a film can get in this day and age. Great great film.

The film is well crafted. great and deliberate editing that unleashes suspense, but never gives in to fast cutting to produce the illusion. 

The acting is also great. Josh Brolin is Lewellyn Moss, a Texas man doing the best he can with a seemingly simple, country life. javier bardhem is Chigurn, a coldblooded, ruthless psychopath; an unstoppable force who cares nothing for the destruction left in his wake. Tommy Lee Jones is the old County Sheriff who has seen it all and just wants to end one last case as well and cleanly as can be so he can retire without being troubled. A great cat and mouse game is espoused when Moss happens upon a drug deal gone bad and takes the two million dollars left at the scene before before Chigurn and other thugs can recover it. 

But for all the set up and suspense, the story telling is a sham. For all the  trouble the Coen brothers go through to show you what Brolin can do when pushed to the brink to survive and how relentless bardhem is in pursuit - there is no pay off. The MAIN NARRATIVE of the movie is swept aside so tommy lee Jones can soliloquize about the sad state of affairs and the disappointment he feels in failure.  The whole frickin point of a chase is to get that final confrontation between two opposing forces - no matter the outcome. 

There is absolutely no reason to comletely side step that final clash. We could still follow Bardhem moving on to another kill. We could still listen to Tommy Lee give the movie it's title. Switching the narrative focus of the story from Brolin to Jones at that crucial point is not clever. It is underwhelming and wholly unsatisfying.

What will bother people the most about "No Country For Old Men" may not be the unconventional plot unfolding, but that the movie actually has to end. "No Country" is the latest installment by Joel and Ethan Coen (Fargo, The Big Lebowski) and is based on the novel of the same name by Cormac McCarthy. The basis for the story may be the brutal cat and mouse game that ensues between Lleweyln Moss (Josh Brolin) and the ruthless seriel murderer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), but the backbone of the story is rooted in the musings of Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) who is the one constant in a wildly unpredictable landscape. The acting is particularly superb, especially Bardem and Kelly Macdonald (Moss' wife) and the filming is once again exceptional. The Coens effectively use little background music in the film, and instead add real life sounds like whirling wind currents to take you deeper into the heart of the West Texas plains. 

"No Country" is a gut-wrenching blood fest for the full 2 hours, with some usual patented Coen humor mixed in. It is not an easy movie to enjoy, but after reflecting on it for about a day I cannot find a single glaring imperfection in the film.  Overall "No Country" is going to get some serious Oscar consideration and is the best movie of the new season to date.

"As flies to wanton boys are we to the Gods, they play with us for their sport."

Gloucester's words in King Lear go right to the heart of the Coen brothers' latest and best film. But in this portrayal of our condition, the Coens offer something a good deal more uncomfortable than Gods to trouble us: they show us our own utter insignificance, in the face of the towering indifference of the universe.

An adaptation of the Cormac McCarthy novel, No Country for Old Men ostensibly follows the trail of three men, who, at different points in time, come across the scene of a drug deal gone wrong in the Texan desert.

This event unfolds into one of the most bleak, uncompromising and sophisticated stories that has ever been set to film. No Country has characters who look and act like heroes, and it has an exemplary villain, yet by sticking to the deeply humanistic stance of McCarthy's book, the Coens give the finger to cinematic convention, and transcend mere storytelling.

For this is a film far greater than the sum of its parts, and much more than the best film of 2007. Never mind that it contains some the best writing, acting, and directorial flair we've seen for a generation, these elements serve as pawns to a higher purpose: to make us truly know that we don't matter. Chaos is the principle character here. To drive this notion home, we're shown oblivion, in the form of Javier Bardem. Many film reviewers have mistaken Bardem's character for a psychopath, or Satan, but neither could be further from the truth: Bardem is simply the personification of chance. The only law that governs him is his own. Chance knows that we must die, yet sometimes our choices can postpone the inevitable. It matters not. 

To embrace this central tenet of the film sounds a pessimistic thing indeed. But one might also view it as strangely liberating: We're not even flies to wanton boys; the void doesn't know we exist. So we might just make it.

Or not.

[font=Arial][size=3][color=red]Based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is a powerful return to form for the Coen Brothers. This is an intensely unnerving and thought-provoking drama. Set in the barren deserted lands of West Texas, the film is like the polar opposite of Fargo. Tommy Lee Jones plays Ed Bell, a sheriff of a small town who tries to stop a nearly unstoppable psychopaths ceaseless bloodbath. The psychopath is Anton Chigurh, played hauntingly perfect by Javier Bardem, in one of the most compelling, fascinating portrayals of cinematic villainy since Hannibal Lecter; surely an Oscar nomination lingers on the horizon. Antons pissed (armed with a cattle gun) and in search of a stolen case containing $2 million dollars; lost when a drug deal went bad, and Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a hunter stumbles upon the scene and makes off with the cash.[/color][/size][/font]
 
[color=red][size=3][font=Arial]A bloody game of wits and bullets, and predator and prey ensues. At two hours in length, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is perhaps one of the most suspenseful films Ive seen in years; so intense, the Coen Brothers use dead silence as a lethal weaponand its sure to get your heartrate jacked and your fingers gripping the armrests. Combining dark suspense, a dark, sharp sense of humor and an unwavering, virtually unpredictable endingwhich is sure to divide audiences; the Coen Brothers have hit another homerun. [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is thrilling, at times poetic and allegorical, beautiful and haunting. This isnt a simple thriller with a simple, clichéd endingits defies convention, breaks rules and challenges your presumptions and leaves you stunned. Its one of the best films of the year, and I predict several Oscar nominations, including Best Picture. My heads still spinning. A second viewing is definitely in order.[/font][/size][/color]
