Wow. One word to explain this film. Wow. "No Country for Old Men", the new film from The Cohen Brothers, is an unquestionable return to form[i]. [/i]It is scary, funny, moving, violent, and meaningful, all in pretty much equal measure. The Coens' take on the Cormac McCarthy novel,  of the same name is a pairing as successful, as seamless, as delicious as that of chocolate and peanut butter. It is perfect.
 A personal favorite of mine, Josh Brolin, gives THE finest of his [i]four[/i] excellent performances this year as Llewelyn Moss. Moss is a struggling everyman welder who stumbles upon a circle of trucks and dead Mexicans in the desert - a heroin deal gone bad. Reallyyyy bad. The lone survivor asks Moss for some [i]"agua"[/i], and Moss ignores the request. He surveys the scene and eventually comes upon a suitcase filled with yes indeed, $2 million dollars. Moss' response upon finding the money? A simple "Yeah." Ha. It's a perfect moment in a movie packed with them. Moss takes the money and returns home to his trailer and his wife Carla Jean (superb Scottish actress Kelly McDonald of Trainspotting fame) Soon, his conscience begins to nag at him, and he decides to head back to the scene of the crime to give the dying man a drink. A compassionate decision, but not, as you can probably imagine, an intelligent one. And watch the decision ignite the wild chase that captures the rest of the film...
 Javier Bardem, plays Anton Chigurh (Sugar??) I'll leave his specific involvement in the proceedings up to you to figure out, but just know that he [i]realllllyyy[/i] wants that $2 million. Moss will come to refer to Chigurh as "the ultimate badass," and that's about right. Chigurh is a classic screen villain, the kind we haven't seen in far too long. Every time he appears on screen- somebody is going down. Much like Hannibal Lecter, the guy is a vicious, remorseless sociopath killer, but he has a strangely sensible logic and one can't help but be seduced by him. Bardem, sporting a early Beatles haircut, gives an absolute flawless performance here, one that will likely be noticed come Oscar time (along with Brolin's). He completely disappears into Chigurh. He's terrifying.
 Bardem is as unsettling, unpredictable, and strangely hilarious as the film itself. [i]No Country [/i]brings the Coen boys back to a tone they do better than almost anybody - "Laugh or Squirm." Watching the film, you're always on the edge of doing one or the other- frequently both at the same time. Much of that delightful uncertainty comes from Bardem's outstanding work.
 Tracking both Moss and Chigurh is Tommy Lee Jones as Sheriff Bell, our narrator and moral compass. The "Old Men" of the title refers to Bell and men like him. Bell can't stomach the downward spiral of society, he can't comprehend the evil that men do, and his disbelief doesn't stop there. "It starts when you begin to overlook bad manners," Bell says at one point. "Any time you quit hearin' 'sir' and 'ma'am,' the end is pretty much in sight." The film is set in 1980 -- a choice that seems random until the movie's theme becomes clear. What would Bell have to say about the sad state of the world today?
 Joining the chase/hunt is Carson Wells Woody harrelson, a bounty hunter sent out by a mysterious businessman to get that stolen cash. This thread, while entertaining, didn't seem particularly essential to me, but it helps to complicate the plot, and the Coens have always seemed much more interested in complicating matters than resolving them. Keep your eye on that $2 million, though it won't do you much good.. You know with a Cohen film, nothing is as it seems. 
 All in all, the ending, you dont see coming, the beginning takes you on a journey you never intended. How cool, to see a film like this, back in action. "No Country for Old Men" features a trio of exceptional performances, is overflowing with memorable moments, and it is easily one of the finest films of 2007- already a pretty fantastic year for cinema. Make no mistake about it - this is a fucking fantastic film, easily the best of the year so far and a strong contender for whatever Oscar gold might come its way. I love it for its explosive performances, its incredibly intense action sequences, the way the film builds its themes so subtly and effectively, and that the ending is pissing off idiots all over America. Seriously, if you're intelligent, you can wrap your brain around the ending of the movie in about thirty seconds. Apply what the characters have learned to it; the nature of entropy and the dissatisfaction of unfinished business are two of No Country's primary themes, and both of them are expressed perfectly by the ending. 

I saw this argument today. "No one in the theater's going to understand the ending, so it's a bad movie!" And that, my friends, is what's wrong with Hollywood. There's this overwhelming pressure to have an explosive, grandstanding climax, and the Coens are to be commended for avoiding that. This film acts as a mirror for real life; notice, for instance, that there is no music and the special effects are very simple. God forbid any of us run into a villain like Chigurh in our everyday lives, but as a whole, the movie succeeds completely at this goal. 

It isn't all a brainy romp, to the relief of the actioners in the audience. No Country For Old Men has some of the tensest moments I think I've ever seen on film. Part of this is aided, as I said, by the lack of music, which really makes it a lot more terrifying than it sounds. But most of it is that it's just a fucking scary movie. There are sections where I had to remind myself to breathe because I'd been holding my breath with sheer anticipation. That is some good filmmaking, folks. 

Anyway, if you've got half a brain and 9 dollars to burn, there is no reason at all to not see this movie. It is a stunning return to form for the Coens after two disappointing movies and, ostensibly, the best movie of the year. (To be chased out by There Will Be Blood? We will see, we will see.)

A Texan welder stumbles across the aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong and helps himself to the $2 million in cash no-one is left alive to claim. Unfortunately he does not count on a single minded psychopathic killer with a tracking device...This film basically distills elements of all their best work and creates a cold and cynical statement on the state of man. Javier Bardem's character is the most chilling and amoral bastard you will ever see; on more than one occasion he reminded me of a terminator with bad hair, except more cold-blooded! The pursuit of the stolen money just leads to bloodshed and tragedy for all involved, many innocents dying for just being in the wrong place at the wrong time. The underlying theme is the randomness of life; good things DO NOT happen to good people and there is no karmic "masterplan". This means that the ending may leave some feeling a little cheated because things aren't tied up nicely into a complete and satisfying package as so many stories are conventionally presented. But the journey there is as gripping as anything you are going to see; it has the tension, brooding atmosphere and cynicism of Blood Simple, the pragmatic investigation by a dismayed lawman in a similar way to Fargo and the style and brutal violence of Miller's Crossing. Meditations on the inevitability of death and the unfathomable implacability of evil. Sounds like a barrel of fun, now doesn't it? Too often in cinema, we are treated to stories that are about beating the odds- characters who overcome circumstances that are seemingly insurmountable, felling adversaries that are next to unstoppable, and who walk away with nary a scratch to live happily ever after. It's strangely gratifying to see an exception made to this storytelling tradition: a film that acknowledges that there are harsh truths in life, not the least of which is the powerlessness of the individual will in the face of impending, certain doom. It's not a movie about beating death and the evil that causes it, but rather facing up to that unfeeling, unreasoning force, and seeing how different people deal with it and react to it. As is everything the Cohens have ever done, it is a fantastic character piece, even managing to spin some honest, realistic humor out of the different people involved and how they interact with each other (which this film desperately needed, given the weight of the material) while simultaneously crafting a seriously disturbing villain whose deranged actions are belied by his calm, relaxed (if exceptionally creepy) manner. The plot is fairly conventional: trailer-park resident Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon a botched drug deal while hunting on the plains of Texas, discovering a satchel that contains two million dollars in cash. Moss takes the money and goes on the run, but is relentlessly pursued by the Mexican drug-runners who were behind the deal and a psychopathic killer who uses a pressurized air canister as a weapon. Trailing behind both of them is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, a lawman in his autumn years who's seen a lot of misery and suffering in his time, but finds himself completely unprepared for the way the world has become. As Llewelyn Moss, Josh Brolin is a tough but likable kind of guy, a country boy with just a touch of smart-ass to him. Llewelyn is a capable man, certainly- he served two tours of duty in the Vietnam War, so he knows his way around a gun and basic tactical situations- but he's also just an ordinary guy caught in the middle of a situation he doesn't fully comprehend, trying to get away with significantly more than just his own skin; Brolin's performance gets us to root for Llewelyn, even though we know that, looking at things logically, he has no reasonable hope of getting through the coming ordeal in one piece. Another, lesser film might have vindicated that non-existent hope against the sheer inevitability of his predicament, like so many other thrillers have before it, so it really gets your attention when the Cohens allow his character arc to come to the most realistic conclusion possible. Hot on Llewelyn's trail is perhaps one of the most villainously evil characters in film history: Anton Chigurh, as played by Javier Bardem. Chigurh is something of a mystery, his introduction at the beginning of the film (his arrest for a crime that is never mentioned and his subsequent, violent escape) setting the tone for the character while never explaining who he is or where he came from; his allegiances  are never really clear- if they aren't non-existent, that is (he tends to kill pretty much everyone, no matter who they're working for)- though his aims are crystal. What makes Chigurh so disturbingly evil isn't just the atrocities that he commits, but the laid back, detached air with which he commits them, and the total lack of empathy or conscience that he displays afterwards (a recurring motif is how he tries to make sure he never gets blood on his shoes, seemingly more out of concern for the shoes than anything, which is really subtly chilling). The film is really entirely hinged on this character, who (or rather what) he is and how others interact with him, and Bardem gives the character a perverse life that makes him both fascinating and terrifying to watch at the same time. Rounding out the principle cast is Tommy Lee Jones as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, a weathered country cop who's trying his best to get to Llewelyn before Chigurh does. Bell is even more of a cowboy than Llewelyn is (but then, almost every guy in the film wears a cowboy hat at least, with the notable exception of Chigurh), but he's basically from a bygone era, ill-equipped to deal with the kind of horrors that the world presents him with and ultimately ineffective against the crushing tide of darkness that he's sworn to battle. Jones gives a spectacular performance here as a man who's lost faith in his own calling, dispirited by everything that he's dealt with and forced to accept the inevitability of death- both his own and that of others. As usual, the Cohens fill out the supporting cast with a gaggle of brilliant character actors; the one who stands out most to me is Kelly Macdonald as Carla Jean Moss, Llewelyn's strangely childlike, innocently naive wife. The two of them- Llewelyn and Carla Jean- have a sassy, easygoing chemistry, and through their banter we see a truly loving relationship between the two. She has one wonderful scene right at the end of the movie that sort of sums up the film's whole theme- the collision of innocent people with incomprehensible evil- and she just pops as a nice Southern girl who's completely in the dark about what's going on. The script is tight and naturalistic, drawing you in with sudden, shocking violence and then investing you with sharp characterization and blazing dialogue (Roger Ebert and I agree that the scene in the Texaco station is absolutely masterful, and yet, ultimately, nothing actually happens in it. Can you imagine how hard it is to write something like that?); having never read the book, I can't honestly say how much of the film's impact stems from the work of the author, but I can say with certainty that the adapted script packs quite a punch. The shots are visually compelling, making use of the vast emptiness of the desert the contrast of light and dark brilliantly; the cinematography only emphasizes this, giving us a dusty yellow color palette that evokes thoughts of desolation and decay. The score- that is, what little score there is- is also naturalistic, forgoing melody in favor of simplicity and ambiance, working heavily with wooden percussion instruments and shakers. Many people claim that No Country for Old Men is the return of the Cohens to greatness. Truthfully, I couldn't say as much for myself, because I skipped out on most of their lamented recent works (though I did get an eyeful of the Ladykillers, and boy, do I wish I hadn't), but I will say that this is absolutely the Cohens in top form, reaching the brilliant heights of Fargo and then, dare I say, surpassing them easily. This is definitely the best film of 2007 (but it's not as if Spider-Man 3 was giving it a run for its money), and the best Cohen release I have ever seen (I'll always have a soft spot for Raising Arizona, though). A must-see.

The film has the feel of a McCarthy novel, full of metaphysical dread and random death. There's a chilling genius to this tale and to the telling. Marvelous.

This is a metaphysical vision of morality in decline: people are either morally bankrupt (Chigurh), trying to negotiate living in a morally bankrupt world (Moss), or too stupefied by the moral bankruptcy to feel like there's much that can be done (Bell). "No Country for Old Men" is a bleak vision, all right, but it isn't nihilistic, and it certainly isn't soulless. As a technical achievement, it's almost perfectly made---but its technical perfection is entirely in the service of its contemplation of morality, not as flashy technique for its own sake. And as a Coen  Bros. film, I think it's better than either "Fargo" or "Blood Simple"; at least they don't seem to be laughing at their characters' misfortunes this time around. Not the best film of the year, by any means, but still pretty damn good (and more convincing in its pessimism, for my money, than Cormac McCarthy's novel).

      The Coen brothers are back with 'No Country For Old Men', a tantalizing picture that amounts to one of this year's very best offerings. It's dark, disturbing, terrifying, funny. Exactly what you'd expect from these experts of storytelling, who are as sharp now as they've ever been. It's a horrifically engrossing film that will linger in your thoughts long after the screen suddenly fades to black. Sure to be a major contender come awards season, 'No Country For Old Men' is a rare film that demands to be seen more than once.
      
      'No Country For Old Men' will have you on the edge of your seat during the film's entire running time. It teases you with silence, one of the film's most effective tools to build almost unbearable anticipation. There are numerous scenes with such sheer intensity, it should come to no surprise that 'No Country' is this year's most unnerving and perplexing experiences. The absolute deft direction by the Coen brothers is like none other, their blend of elements that are polar opposites of each other is flawlessly mesmerizing, the film will have you laughing and cowering in your seat almost simultaneously. It's a draining but completely worthwhile moviegoing experience.
      
      Easily boasting one of the best and most prestigious casts of the year, 'No Country For Old Men' sees one of the year's best performances by Javier Bardem. This villain's cool calculation is haunting, electrifyingly disturbing. He's one of the scariest psychopaths in years, a character that won't soon be forgotten. Not to be outdone, Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones, and Woody Harrelson all turn in fantastic performances. 'No Country' is a thinker, and allowing it to sink into your bones is a must. The desire to see it all over once the credits roll is strong, simply solidifying it as one of this year's most accomplished works of art. The Coen's have done it again, writing and directing a masterpiece that sticks with you long after the last shots are fired. You can certainly expect it to make some noise when nominations are announced for this year's Academy Awards.
     
     With an ending so quiet, so subtle, yet so poetic, there's nothing easy about 'No Country For Old Men'. Time doesn't wait on us to change, and fate always has a way of catching up to us. The Coens don't break any new ground with this project, but the decisions they make and the paths this film travels down are truly original and memorable. It gives us the opportunity to experience the harsh realities of life in beautiful and unexpected ways.

 Of all American directors, the signature of the Coen Brothers is the easiest to spot and the most difficult to duplicate.  Their unique characters, odd-ball dialogue, and in-your-face violence often leave the audience trying to decide whether or not it is OK to laugh.  [i]No Country for Old Men [/i] is no different.  By now I am sure you have seen the 96% rating on this very website, and I'm sure you have read about the audience dismay with the lack of closure the ending provides.  There is probably not much I can tell you that you don't already know, but here is my take anyway...

The characters in the film are outstanding and unforgettable...this is perhaps the Coens greatest strength.  They have an amazing ability to make their characters unique to a time or a place.  This can be seen in [i]Fargo, Raising Arizona, [/i]and [i]O Brother Where art Thou?[/i] to name a few.  In [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] there is Sheriff Bell (his weathered face tells the story of his life), Llewellyn Moss (the protagonist who gives in to greed and temptation), and Anton Chigurh (the most damning representation of evil that I have seen on-screen in a long time).  The minor characters also add to the feel of the film.  The old gas station attendant, Sheriff Bell's deputy, and the obese trailer tenant who stands of to Chigurh (not knowing anything about his past).  

Obviously, the characters won't stick unless the acting is up to par.  In [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], the acting transends this idea.  It is nothing less than superb.  Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin, and Javier Bardem all give career highlight performances.  The minor cast provides great support, which is rich and sweet icing on an already delicious cake.  

The idea behind the story and plot is bleak and depressing.  It plays with evil, lack of hope, and the idea that the human factor cannot change the path of fate....I have to go, will write more later.

The Coen' Brothers best film since Fargo, and possibly their best film ever.  No Country for Old Men is also perhaps one of the best novel adaptations ever to hit the big screen.  Javier Bardem plays the sociopath Chigurh to perfection, and Tommy Lee Jones and Josh Brolin put up equally strong performances.  The Coen brothers' signature writing is also present, and after years and years of polish it shines like diamond.  The dark humor littered throughout this otherwise utterly bleak and violent film adds a touch of humanity, and it's a good thing it does,  because this film is authentic and heartless enough to make you question the very nature of violence.  This is DEFINITELY not one to be missed.

The acting is fantastic, with Javier Bardem's performance being an absolute standout. I'm not a big fan of Tommy Lee Jones, but I think he turns in a decent performance here. Nothing out of the norm for him, though.

My sole criticism, and the only thing holding this back from masterpiece status in my books (at least for the moment) is the lack of a stronger moral or philosophical backing. It seems primed for it, but it never really achieves the level of depth or the emotional chords that I wished it would. The black-white-gray distinction is here, but it's not quite compelling enough on an emotional level. It certainly works brilliantly in terms of suspense and in terms of the craft of cinema, though. This is, as one reviewer put it, pure cinema. The technical form of film at its finest and most enthralling.

The world is a place where death rules, and contrary to what the older generations try to tell you, it was never any less evil in their day.  They just notice it more now.
  	No Country for Old Men is a decidedly non-traditional film.  By all accounts it is a very faithful adaptation of the book on which it is based.  It begins without a beginning, and ends abruptly without a noticeable conclusion.  The rest if the time it focuses on three characters who never really meet:
	Llewelyn Moss is a man who, against his better judgment, gets involved with death, but that is not what condemns him.  The fact is, âyou never see whatâs coming,â and the viewer doesnât either.
	Javier Bardem plays Anton Chigurh, a killer who many claimed is the creepiest villain since Hannibal Lecter.  In fact, he is never creepyâhe is too inhuman to really be scary.  He is evil in the same sense that death is evil, and he is as impersonal.
	The true key to the film is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, a man who has grown up fighting evil in the world.  As he gets older, he has begun to realize that it cannot be overcome.  A key conversation towards the end has him revealing, âI always figured when I got older, God would sorta come inta my life somehow. And he didn't. I don't blame him. If I was him I would have the same opinion of me that he does.â
	That is the message in a nutshell.  The Coens present a world where death rules, and God chooses to do nothing about it.  Perhaps we are all too evil for God to care.  The scant hope offered at the end leaves most viewers empty, and it should.  Their view of the world is more or less accurate, but their idea of God is one sided.  They see the judgment but not the love.

So, I've been thinking about this movie a lot since I saw it, and I'm sorry, but I don't see what the hype was about. Javier Bardem and Josh Brolin are great- I was glued to the screen during their scenes. Stylistically, the Coens, as always, knows how to get a reaction from their audience. But this film has so many problems that I just can't ignore. First off, it's essentially a remake of Fargo in the South, with Tommy Lee Jones in the Frances McDormand  role (who I wasn't really impressed with, to be quite honest). And the pacing of the film is just screwy. Bardem's intense scenes will be interrupted by long speeches from Tommy Lee Jones about essentially nothing. If the meaning of the movie is somewhere in those speeches, it's up to the Coens to get the viewer to care about them, and they don't do that by placing them after Bardem's scenes. Stephen Root and Woody Harrelson's characters get no explanation- after reading about their roles in the book I was just baffled at how the Coens left these bits of information out that would've made their scenes a lot clearer. The scene where Bardem and Jones are in the hotel room together really confused me when I first saw it. When I read up on it later, I understood it better, but I can't forgive the film for something that should come across better. I also read a theory that the entire story is an allegory, with Tommy Lee Jones as the Father, Brolin as the Son, and Bardem as the Holy Spirit. Sorry, but I didn't get that AT ALL, and the theory required the viewer to have an almost encyclopedic knowledge of the Bible. There are so many unanswered questions in this movie that I simply can't give it higher than 3 stars. A lot of people say that the point was not everything gets tied up in a nice little package at the end, but there's a fine line between doing that and just confusing your audience. I honestly felt like I had missed a reel when I left the theatre, and the ending is one of the most awkward I've ever seen. Perhaps I need a second viewing, but other than Bardem's amazing performance, I don't see what all the fuss is about. The Coens tried a lot of different things in this movie, but I think in the end telling a clear story got lost in the shuffle. People can defend them that they were trying to be abstract or again show that not everything gets tied up nicely at the end, but to me that's a huge cop-out. A movie has to have a story in some form, or barring that, an overall message/experience strong enough for one to forgive the lapses in storytelling (a la The Fountain). This had neither.

The quirky sense of humor found in the Coens' films takes the back seat this time, making room for a much darker and brooding tone. Music is kept down to a minimum; here silence is only broken by the Coen brothers' wonderfully written dialog, or by Anton Chigurh's eerie tank of compressed air and silenced shotgun. The story is full of twists and turns and will keep you guessing all the way through. The entire experience is wonderfully paced, and packed with highly memorable scenes. This is one of the best films of the decade.

This is the best film I've seen this year. "3:10 to Yuma" was very good, as was "American Gangster", but "No Country" is virtually flawless. It has a measured, deliberate pace that is neither boring or lacking depth. The three main characters seem to represent a larger contingent than themselves. The evil killer, who isn't random. He kills when it serves a purpose for him, or when he says he will. At times his victims get a fighting chance. There is the everyman, played by Josh Brolin. A simple, poor welder who stumbles upon the chance of a lifetime....being rich. He takes money that seems to have no owner. From that point on, he is on the run. The sheriff is a representative of things past. The old way. He doesn't care for the direction society is going, even at the simplest levels. He leaves the posturing and sense of excitement to others, the man just does his job.
The three men never really meet face to face in the film, but they are all tied together by money, death, obligation and duty. This isn't a stunning, over the top Hollywood film. It's subtle and steady. The ending may leave some scratching their heads and others in contemplating silence. If you enjoy Coen films such as Millers Crossing and Fargo, you'll probably like this one as well.      Freddy

Oyunculuk Oscarini gecip filmin geneline gelirsek film ilgi cekici bir sekilde Josh Brolin'in Texas'ta colun ortasinda uyusturucu pazarligi sonucu birbirini oldurmus bir grup Meksikaliyi ve parayi bulmasi ile basliyor. Unbelievably incredible. This film has some of the most intense and gripping scenes in cinema history: try to watch the gas station scene and not squirm in your seat; I dare you. The acting is first rate (Jones should definitely win Best Supporting Actor), mainly due to the brilliant dialogue. Beautifully shot, the cinematography will make you want to trek the lonely plains of west Texas yourself (with maybe a few automatic pistols at your side). What makes this film stand out from the rest and keeps it from merely traveling the "action-thriller" genre is McCarthy's poignant insight into principles and the men who hold them. Anton and Ed Tom (notice the phonological similarity?) are men who stratify their lives according to principles they have held all their lives. The focus on existentialism in the Texas plains ("What's the most you've ever lost on a coin toss?") reveals the strange and beautiful nature of life and all its foibles and intricacies. Each man represents the "flip-side" of the coin; they are so close to one another yet so diametrically opposed. Far and away the best film of the year, and one of the best adaptations I've ever seen (read the book; it's marvelous).

Texas is a cold and cruel place in the Coen brother's melancholy No Country for Old men. The land is slowly being overrun by brutality and senseless violence, the "dismal tide" as one character puts it. It is in this oppressive setting that Lewllyn Moss (Josh Brolin, excellent) stumbles upon a massacre, several kilos of cocaine, and a briefcase full of money. He knows the consequences of taking the cash, and yet he takes it anyway. Well wouldn't you? 
With this new feature, the Coen brothers doggedly refuse to conform to well worn cliches of Hollywood thrillers. This will understandably upset some viewers especially since the ending robs them of the usual violent climax that has become such a standard of the genre. But it is the film's undeniable originality that makes it so special. Granted, No Country for Old Men is not the Coen's best work; even though it has been compared to Fargo, it lacks the emotional depth that made the latter a masterpiece. But the film's preoccupation with unstoppable evil is appropriate for the dark times we live in, fighting a war on terror that we may never win. As such, this film will linger in my consciousness for quite awhile.

[font=Verdana][size=2]The ending may be confusing, but the overall message couldn't be clearer: No Country for Old Men is an incredible film.  Sometimes, the most impressive films end up being the ones that can say the most in a more minimalistic fashion, which is what No Country for Old Men does.  The story is told in an extremely straightforward way, stripping down the events so the audience is able to interpret what happens without obnoxious prompting.  Not every film benefits from this method of filmmaking, but it works beautifully for No Country for Old Men.
  
   The Coen Brothers, so fond of Americanism in their films, portray the rural southwest in a manner that compliments the film's content.  As the killer Anton, Javier Bardem's deadpan demeanor coheses with the isolated setting of each victim, making each scene more suspensful as a result.  Various murder scenes were free of any musical accompaniment, reminiscient of the murders in Zodiac.  In fact, the audience finds out the most about Anton when there is no dialogue or music, just sound effects.  He methodically executes tasks step-by-step, as if he was a machine.
  
 [img]http://hollywood-elsewhere.com/images/column/520/desertmen.jpg[/img]
  
   Though some of Anton's weapons may not be very convienent or realistic, their presence picks up the slack of the action sequences.  Since the overall appearance is straightforward and basic, every aspect of Anton adds life to the action in order to keep the audience entertained.  There is no deafening influx of strings during a shootout, yet every emotion remains intact.  There is symmetry in Anton's methods which make him even more memorable, like an unofficial calling card for the bad guy.  As a whole, the acting is very appropriate for the story.  Some conversations and exchanges between characters are pure gold.
  
   In fact, the dialogue is where No Country for Old Men shines the most.  Every story and conversation has it's own importance.  The appearance of dialogue may be a bit modest comparatively, but it's precision when used is excellent.  Many will gripe about how the minimalist approach stifles and confuses the events of the end (it makes sense, see it again), but it is the most effective way to portray the story.  The balance of No Country for Old Men is remarkable.  The film paces itself in a fashion that may infuriate some, but leaves those who mull it over feeling very rewarded.[/size][/font]

"No Country" is definitely a movie-going experience, and one of the best this year. To appreciate No Country is to appreciate it as a master work of film technique. The Coen Brothers meticulously bring Cormac McCarthy's story to the screen, and they master everything from writing the adaptation to the direction and amazing editing. To top it off, the best performances of the year can be found in "No Country For Old Men." The wonderful Javier Bardem (Wow... quite a change from "The Sea Inside") plays the chilling Anton Chigurh, a villain with less soul than Bill the Butcher in "Gangs of New York." He will be forever remembered for this role. Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones more than act. Brolin plays an average man with little wisdom and no conviction. Tommy Lee Jones (much better here than "In the Valley of Elah") reminds me of everything I like about Clint Eastwood. And quite unexpectedly, Kelly MacDonald adds yet another amazing performance to the already stellar cast. The Coens know what they are doing, and they love to show it. In the midst of the suspense, they add their own off-beat humor to remind you that this isn't just any pretentious prestige film. It's always good to know that these filmmakers don't take themselves too seriously. I highly recommend seeing this.

An acheivement in cinematic excellence, but quite possibly the darkest movie to ever win the Academy Award for Best Picture. Past Best Picture winners have had plenty of violence (Gladiator, Unforgiven), but this film offers the viewer no hope of salvation whatsoever. Forget a happy ending. Forget even getting an ending that leaves you feeling with a sense things are getting any better. This is NOT for the squeamish. It's a dichotomy of the times. The world isn't just going to hell, it's always been there, that it's bigger than any of us, and that it's going to stay that way no matter how tirelessly we fight against it. It is there that makes this movie so powerful. Javier Bardem's Best Supporting Oscar-winning portrayal as the cold-blooded killer Anton Chigurh was not only brilliant, but downright unnerving and he lets you know that two minutes into the film. Bardem's role sets a tone of both menace and other-world creepiness, which almost makes you feel like you're watching a horror movie. Tommy Lee Jones' performance anchors the entire picture. He's the one tie to normalcy and morality and even he feels overwhelmed at the end and is left powerless to stop the "dismal tide" The point of the movie is that Jones' sherriff character, with sad weariness, has never seen so much implacable evil and does not know if it is possible to conquer it. Is Chigurh real, or a ghost? Chigurh is definitely real in the movie and he represents all the evil in the world that will not stop, will not rest. Cormac McCarthy's novel is brilliantly adapted by the Coen Brothers. They are very loyal to the novel, but also improvise well enough to actually enhance the movie, a pitfall most directors fall victim to. It's easy to see why this won Best Picture, but it's definitely not for the faint of heart, especially if you're one who likes it when the good guy wins at the end. A quote from a review I saw from someone not long ago summed up my thoughts on this masterpiece exactly... "Death comes to us all, suddenly, randomly, and blind to "fairness," no matter if we protest or try to escape it." Amen.

Saying "He felt relly bad/guilty for not helping him" is not a justified reason whatsoever; for a character to do something that risky and stupid you would have to establish that that character was a bleeding heart humanitarian which they clearly did not do. 

2. Woody Harrelson-Did he have a point in the movie? So they established that a third (or fourth?) party was after the money. Did his death mean anything? If you deleted his character, would anything have been different whatsoever? 

3. While I'm talking about Harrelson, the part where he, after not receiving from Brolin nearly enough information about where the bag was, jumps ON THE SAME LEDGE as Brolin and just happens to see the satchel lying on the ground was terrible as well. The audience's intelligence needs to be respected more than that. 

4. And while I'm talking about unnecessary characters, did Tommy Lee Jones need to be in the movie either? Off the top of my head, all he did was show up at crime scenes after everyone was gone and make one or two witty remarks to that dufus of a deputy of his. And what was the point of the conversations with that brother (I think) and his wife near the end of the movie? Please fill me in. 

5. When Harrelson tells Brolin that Anton will never stop and can never be bargained with, that made him sound like the Terminator, which was very cool. BUT THEN IN THE VERY NEXT SCENE HE TRIES TO MAKE A DEAL WITH BROLIN. LAAAAME. 
Possible flaw aversion here is that, by this point in the film, Anton was scared/respectful of Brolin that he felt this deal was prudent. However, they had built up Anton's character enough to the point where he basically was an unstoppable killing machine badass, so.... 

6. Finally, where Anton goes into that Dallas high-rise and kills Stephen Root? Puh-lease. Are you telling me that someone can just walk into an office building in a major city with a shotgun, shoot someone with it, and then walk out undetected? And the excuse "He's a ghost/professional assassin" does not cut it; THE LEAST they should have done is (all I'm asking is for a few seconds here) shown him using some intelligent way to bypass security...or something along those lines. 

Again, there was quite a few cool/good parts in the movie, but they were more than cancelled out with the aforementioned flaws. The Coen brothers have yet to make a good movie.

An extremely welcome return to form for my favourite filmmakers.

This is a return to Fargo-esque territory for the Coens, although this one's set in Texas, and is perhaps a darker film, more like Blood Simple.

Basically, Josh Brolin stumbles upon the result of a drug deal gone wrong, and foolishly elects to keep the money he finds without really considering the consequences. Inevitably, someone is despatched to recover the money, and unfortunately for Brolin this is a man who takes his job seriously (not to mention being a complete psychopath).

Tommy Lee Jones plays the sheriff ostensibly tracking down Brolin and the killer, but this is really secondary to his character, a man who is struggling to come to terms with aging, and the changes he's seen over his life. He's somewhat detached from the rest of the characters and events in the film, but I think that works, and it allows for the unusual ending, which wasn't what I expected, but worked well for me.

This is an extremely violent film, but on top of that there are a lot of very welcome touches of humour, a lot of which comes from Jones' world-weary sheriff (in many ways a male counterpart of Frances McDormand's character in Fargo).

There are some scenes of real tension that are beatifully filmed, particularly those set in the motels. This is a top notch thriller. Biggest problem I had was understanding the Texan accents, other than that I thought it was great.

I want to love this movie. I want to give it 5 stars a rank it among my favorite movies. But I simply don't get it. The movie's chilling plot, seemingly realistic and truly human characters, and the shocking moments held me on the edge of my seat till the very end when the movie instantly dropped off. I watched the movie with 4 other people and between us we didn't know what to make of it. From listening to the people around us as we left the movie theater, our feelings seemed to also be the general consensus: "that was amazing, but what does it mean?" We eventually were able to make out some basic thoughts on what it could mean, but even those weren't concrete and were mostly up to interpretation. Good movies have a basic theme that the audience can leave with, apply to their lives, and make them enjoy the movie more. Great movies have an underlying theme that not everyone gets, and thus appeal to the more intuitive crowd and truly gives the audience something. This movie I know has a meaning buried somewhere down deep in there that is just waiting to be discovered, but for the life of me I can't find it. I'm not saying this movie isn't great, nor that I want to be spoon fed everything in a movie. I'm definitely buying this one DVD and rewatching it a couple times till I pass my final judgment. If anyone has an idea to the plot, facebook friend or not, drop me a message and tell me what you think, I'd be glad to listen. Like I said, I wanna love this movie, I wanna wrap it in my arms and love it, I wanna get this and get a bunch of people together on a friday night and watch it and enjoy it, but I wanna know what it means first.

Nothing about this movie is what you expect. It rises and sets on its own set of rules. As baffling as this is, in a sense, it is also exhilirating. It is a very singular work.

Bardem is just fucking brilliant. I first saw him when he was nominated for the Oscar for "Before Night Falls," then a few years later in "The Sea Inside." Add this to the list, and I want to seek out everything he's ever done. He has range on par with Daniel Day-Lewis, and that same undefinable attribute that draws your eyes to his at every turn.

This film is (unless I'm mistaken) entirely (or almost) devoide of music or scoring. The rustling wind pervades each scene with enough dread that any score would've detracted from its resonance. It's so fucking suspenseful! Sorry, but Jesus Christ, there are scenes where, literally, nothing fucking happens, but I swear to God you could hear a pin drop in the theater as everyone waited for something. When nothing comes, most are disappointed, but I enjoyed the rush of the build (don't get me wrong, though... many times, something does happen, and it's equally exciting).

I hate saying something is "deep." It's... kinda condesending, definitely seems pretentious. But, I gotta go for it. The Coen's layer this with themes at play so subtly that I feel the need, the absolute necessity, if only out of my long held admiration for them, a second viewing. To soak. To think. To watch and less to anticipate, like we all tend to do with films like this.

In "No Country...," things happen. They happen when they happen and when they do, the Coen's have forced you to consider every assumption to have about how a story "work." Action falls more than it rises, it climaxes early on, and then again, and then continues still. It's a brilliant experiment, and a powerful success.

. . I've literally seen thousands of films at the theatre in my life and the response to this thing was something I've never seen before. It was a near revolt. I actually saw people angrily walking to get a refund. This exchange perfectly sums up this waste of film... 

The woman seated behind me turns to the people she was with and says, "Bill, that was the LAST time you pick the movie." 

He responds, "I'm soooo sorry. That was completely awful." 

I turned to my friends and apologized as well. They were there because I wanted to see it. I had to apologize all the way to the parking lot.

This has to be, without a doubt, one of the best films of 2007. The Coen Brothers have again made their talent for film-making shine through this film. From the moment it starts to it's abrupt yet defining end, No Country For Old Men is a true masterpiece of a movie that should not be missed. I can say for a start that it wasn't quite what I had expected it to be. I knew little about the plot and tried to keep an open mind while walking into the cinema, which was probably the best thing to be doing. It surprised me, but in the best possible way. From the little I knew, I thought it would be perhaps more of a drama film. Instead, it came out to me as a very well done thriller. There was also more violence than I expected, and it wasn't just it being bloody, but everything seemed very sudden. I saw these things as compliments to the movie, for I felt that without them it wouldn't have been the multi-award winning, brilliant film that it is. Tommy Lee Jones was in the film for quite a bit less than I was expecting him to. Even so, his performance while on the screen was near perfection. Javier Bardem was... well, I can say that he 100% deserved that Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. He created a terrifying and fearless character, his performance in this film is sure to be remembered. Josh Brolin was also another stand-out performance, as was all of the acting. This is a must see movie that I strongly recommend anyone and everyone to see.

[b][color="red"]Death comes for everyone.  And in this latest outing by the Coen brothers, so does Anton Chigurh, a sociopath of such magnitude he almost defies comprehension, let alone description.[/b]  [/color]

[img]http://www.cbc.ca/arts/images/arts_old-men_392.jpg[/img]

Amid the stark landscape of west Texas in 1980, Llewelyn Moss ([i]Josh Brolin[/i]), a local retired welder out shooting antelope in the desert sagebrush, stumbles onto a horrific crime scene, an apparent drug deal gone wrong, with shot-up vehicles and decomposing bodies.  [b]It's an inadvertent act of fate that has brought him there in the first place, another act of fate that puts him in possession of a briefcase filled with $2 million in drug money that didn't correctly change hands, and still another that puts him on the run for his life, hunted by the ruthless phantom menace Chigurh ([i]played intricately by Spanish actor Javier Bardem[/i]). [/b] By the time Llewelyn Moss finds the money, we've already met Chigurh, and know something of the extent of his brutality, his unorthodox weapon, and even his off-center sense of justice and inevitability.  Moss is smart enough to realize that he's a marked man, and even before knowing who'll be hunting him, returns to his wife in their mobile home, sends her out of harm's way, and begins an odyssey to preserve his life.

[b]Meanwhile, fate has conspired to bring into this not-so-pretty picture third generation local sherriff Ed Tom Bell ([i]Tommy Lee Jones[/i]), who'd rather not be tangling with bloodbath on this level.[/b]  Checking out the newly discovered crime scene in the desert with his deputy, we realize we've seen this before, with a very pregnant Marge Gunderson in [i]Fargo.[/i]   But while [i]Fargo[/i] has plenty of darkness intermingled with humor, it never fully rises to the black heart of this film.  Marge doesn't want to be chasing after ruthless killers, either, and can't make sense of someone putting his buddy through a woodchipper in the Minnesota cold for "a little bit of money."  Still, for all that, [i]Fargo[/i] retains a strong sense of irony and humor, and even some hope amid the violence.  [b]With this adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel, the Coen brothers take their filmmaking to a new and startling level. [/b] Sure, there's still plenty of slice of life conversational and situational humor, not unlike their other films, including gentle jabs at border security (Llewelyn passes easily into Mexico posing as a drunk Mexican, and manages to get out and back into the U.S. wearing only a hospital gown when the border guard realizes he's a fellow Vietnam vet).  

[img]http://atlanta.creativeloafing.com/binary/e180/flicks_review1-1_28.jpg[/img]

[b]Really, this is Josh Brolin's film in a year that might well be described as Josh Brolin's year,[/b] just coming off of a plum role in [i]American Gangster[/i] and appearances in three other films, including [i]In the Valley of Elah.[/i]  It's primarily Brolin's Llewellyn who is the hunted, Bardem's brilliantly played Chigurh who is the relentless hunter, and Jones' Sherriff Ed Tom Bell who is trying to intervene to prevent further violence and make some sense of it all. [b] While Llewellyn is fleeing from place to place, it's [i]his[/i] life and mind we're inhabiting, and it's Chigurh, that ever present shadow, that we fear.[/b]

[b]In the end, it's Tommy Lee Jones, however, who has the first and last words in the film, and it's through those words that we come to understand the simple truths of the meaning of the film's title.[/b]  When he takes us into his dreamscape at the end, saddles us up and takes us into the mountains, we might as well be climbing that inevitable stairway to heaven.

It's a series of fateful circumstances that took him to that place and took Llewelyn on a journey to preserve his own life.  [b]Death, like Chigurh, is inevitable.  No one can escape it.  Not pitbulls.  Not drug dealers.  Not even mothers in law.

And Ed Tom Bell knows it.[/b]

[img]http://blogs.guardian.co.uk/film/nocountry_leejones_460.jpg[/img]

[color="red"][b]It's a masterful piece of filmaking by Joel and Ethan Coen, with stark landscapes and accurate interiors--both human and cinematographic.[/b]  But don't go expecting the lighthearted frivolity of [i]The Big Lebowski[/i] or the madcap mayhem of [i]O, Brother, Where Art Thou.[/i]  [b]This is a dark and intricate journey into the world of a pathological killer, and ultimately, the inescapability of the inevitable.[/b][/color]

This is 1980, not 1880, and anywhere else other than suburban Mogadishu, they were taping off crime scenes and slowly crawling through them looking for minute clues. It was hilarious. But this was West Texas, where kids get married at 15, sometimes not even being brother and sister, and occasionally, if unconventionally, not even expecting their first Mary Lou or Joe Bob. 
Javier Bardem makes a real bad baddy and the events leave a trial of bodies and bloodstains as far as the Rio Grande and beyond, but an El Paso lawman is more worried about the lack of respect shown by young people with green hair. A Coen brothers' tongue-in-cheek triumph, beautifully shot and rightly recognised by numerous awards (including best picture and best director(s) Oscars). I want to go back and re-review this because while I still like the movie just the same as when I first saw it, my opinion on the ending has changed drastically now that I've seen it five times over the past two and a half years.  It's about this small time hunter/welder (Josh Brolin) who's life gets turned upside down when he stumbles across the aftermath of a drug deal gone bad, with two million dollars and a truck bed full of heroin up for grabs near the U.S./Mexican border.  He takes the money, which causes him to be tracked by one of the best villains of the last decade, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem).  This is the only Coen brothers movie that they didn't write themselves; they adapted it from a Cormac McCarthy novel.  They did something unorthodox and something that you rarely see nowadays: they made the movie almost exactly how it was written.  The very first time I watched this, I was very taken aback by the ending, sitting contemplatively with a WTF look on my face after the abrupt cut to black before the credits rolled.  It left me thinking for so long that I actually read the book (gasp), went back and caught it a second time while it was still in theaters, and I gotta say, the movie works a lot better as a whole (even though I thought it worked pretty damn well on it's own my first viewing, anyway) if you realize that it's Tommy Lee Jones as the aging sheriff Ed Tom who is the main character.  I love the work that both Bardem and Brolin put into their characters; they both did a fantastic job, but it's not about them, it's about Ed Tom; he's the old man that the title refers to and it's about him, even though he gets the least amount of screen time.  The cinematography and scenery are top notch, as is expected from the Coens.  There are a number of scenes that will just take your breath away, and a lot of nice work done with very subtle sounds and techniques.  Bardem completely deserved the best supporting actor award; every time he is on screen, you're just so nervous because he's a completely psychotic sociopathic loose cannon.  I can't quite put it above The Big Lebowski and Fargo, but in terms of quality, it's right up there with their very best.

The story then follows the cat and mouse chase between Moss and Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), the ruthless psychopath that wants his money back, and Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) the man who reluctantly caught the case because it happened in his jurisdiction.

Finishing Cormac McCarthy's source novel just days before the movie, it's unbelievable how well they go hand-in-hand.  Save for a couple encounters/scenes, the Coen brothers bring this novel to life.  Here's what really strikes me though... McCarthy's No Country For Old Men novel is not even [i]half[/i] as good as his others.  Especially, the epic Blood Meridian.  In short, it's a straight-forward thriller thriving with wisdom of an old man who's seen it all.  So, how the Coen brothers can take that material, transfer it to the screen [i]straight[/i] from each page, and come out with one of the best movies of the year is just [i]awesome[/i].
   
   One deceptive quality of the film is the dialogue.  Deceptive only that it feels straight from original Coen writing.  More than 95% of it is actually pure McCarthy stripped out of the pages.  Even the black humor.  Yet, it all feels like the Coen brothers could claim it entirely as their own based on previous writings.  McCarthy creates the scenes, the Coens perfectly relate.  This in terms, creates the ingredients for the Coens to execute with fierce timing and utter precision into a scene.  Combined with the talented acting, it's no wonder they're being praised for superior craftsmanship.  Which brings us to the next aspect of this film.  Background music, lack thereof.  During a few scenes I wondered how music would've affected it.  And, it got me to thinking about comedy sitcoms on TV (Seinfeld, etc.)  You know, the ones with recorded laughter reminding you exhibiting the action of laughter when appropriate.  Personal beef of mine:  I hate that shit.  In a way I always think it disrespects the audience (I could be wrong).  So, in terms of No Country For Old Men, I respect of the choice of no music because it shows respect for the audience.  Whether music would've enhanced or dragged the scene though is a mystery.
     
    [img]http://www.canmag.com/images/front/lap2007/oldmen1.jpg[/img]
   
   The craftsmanship, dialogue, and story already make for a good film.  What makes it damn near perfect are maybe the finest supporting performances I've seen this year.  Fucking brilliant.  Tommy Lee Jones executes McCarthy's sheriff character, who's unable to comprehend society's dramatic shift, with pure precision.  It's a wonderful thing to watch an actor who never fails to impress.  And, interesting this time around as he gives a very subtle, raw performance that clings to the character's rugged experiences.  Josh Brolin or Mr. Up-and-Coming-of-2007 gave me a sure surprise.  I was always aware of his potential, nevertheless still modestly worried how he'd shape the movie with his role.  Never failed to disappoint me once though... well, maybe twice.
   
   Anton Chigurh.  This is the man who pushes the film into unique territory.  He pulls the movie gracefully along in fully illuminating the characteristics of society that has the Sheriff's brain (and Moss's life for that matter) in quite the bind.  Javier Bardem doesn't just play this man.  He is the [i]essence [/i]of this man.  Bardem brings a quiet demeanor to the psychopath who kills with no remorse and a slightly unconventional choice of weaponry.  Everything... From the tone and timbre of his voice, overall uncasual appearance and hair style, creepy smile, clear choice of words, sleek decisions he makes, promises he keeps based a well disciplined moral standard, and even that coin he'll occasionally use to shine the brightest side of himself that's still ever so dim.  Perhaps, my mind is going blank here, but I cannot think of a more unique villain in recent memory.  Anton Chigurh is the godsend of villains.
   
   I've had extreme hype for this movie for quite awhile now.  Even so, I am without disappointment.  Of course, with the novel already read before the screening, I was more prepared for the ending than the rest of the audience around me.  Which can be bluntly put as the big "fuck you" to all/most happy endings or those who can't desire anything but.  When those credits started rolling, I've never heard more people talk in a theater.  Most were discussing how disappointing it was and they should have seen that "C" rating movie perhaps given by some EW critic.  I mean, does this show how accustomed we've all become to happy endings?  If only those people could hold themselves together for 5 minutes, and listen deeply to the last scene... instead of how unconventional of an ending it is.  What lies beneath is a theme so goddamned insightful I read it again from the novel as soon as I got home from the theater.  It's a purely realistic ending in every possible way.  I'd love to talk more about it, but I'd rather not spit clues to people who have not seen it yet. So, I'll finish simply with:  This is truly [i]as[/i] [i]good[/i] [i]as movies[/i] [i]get[/i].  Not a doubt in my mind.

This film is both inferior to and superior to Fargo, which will forever be the Coen Brothers' masterpiece.  It is inferior in the sense that it lacks the subtle, macabre humor of Fargo with its quirky characters and uproariously tainted scenes of mayhem; that peculiar Coen Brothers elan and atmosphere glimmers through occasionally, but this film is overwhelmingly oppressive and the atmosphere is morbidly opaque.  This arguable inferiority, however, bleeds into the film's alarming success.  Where Fargo was outrageously nuanced and meticulous, No Country For Old Men is subtle and brooding.  Javier Bardem's performance as Anton Chigurh is horrifying; he, much like Louise Fletcher's Nurse Ratched in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, is an unblinking and totally formidable personification of pure, unadulterated iniquity.  Tommy Lee Jones (marvelous from beginning to end, but particularly brilliant in the contemplative finale), Josh Brolin (also exceedingly gifted), Kelly Macdonald, Stephen Root, Barry Corbin, and Woody Harrelson (shockingly great in only three scenes as the slick Carson Wells) are all beyond criticism.  This is a masterpiece - definitely one of the greatest films in recent years.

With this dark, morally complex thriller, the Coen brothers have effectively re-established the credibility they squandered on the lazy, overrated-by-lit-geeks O Brother, Where Art Thou?, the jaw-droppingly awful Intolerable Cruelty and the amusing but not-much-else Ladykillers.  Yes, this rich film puts them squarely back in Fargo territory, only they've learned a lot of neat tricks since that 1996 classic, though No Country is generally a more serious film.  That's not to say it isn't without humor, and the wit that's present carries that distinct Coen flavor -- so sharp you don't even realize you've been cut by it until you're bleeding -- er, laughing.  And speaking of blood, there's plenty being spilt in the tale of Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a retired welder who happens upon $2 million in cash, contained in a stray satchel from a drug deal gone bad.  Of course, that cash comes with a caveat, and his name is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a relentless gun-for-hire on Moss' trail who doesn't even hold much respect for those who pay to acquire his services.  Chigurh is clever, driven by his own warped code of morals and, above all, chillingly efficient.  And Bardem owns the role, making the killer as terrifying as possible without ever going over the top, which may serve to make the character even scarier.  Trying to put together all the pieces that are left in the wake of the mess that Moss ultimately creates is a close-to-retirement sheriff, a simple, quiet old-timer named Ed Tom Bell and played terrifically by Tommy Lee Jones.

What makes No Country such a modern masterpiece boils down to the classic technique of the Coen brothers.  Everything is shot simply, there are no flashy jump cuts and the scenery is used as effectively as one could ever hope for.  Lingering shots of the dusty Texas outlands where the story takes place say so much, whether speaking to the isolation of certain characters or to the idea of it representing a simpler, forgotten time.  Over and over again, the sheriff is told he cannot stop what is coming, and as much of a reference as it is to his actual case, it also serves to illustrate a generalization about society, that time and change cannot be stopped, even as people age and slow down, hoping to do the same with the world around them, hence the title.

I loved this movie, much as I pretty much expected I would.  However, some of the biggest highlights for me may turn off a lot of audience members accustomed to more conventional filmmaking.  Not only does No Country operate with a hazy morality, it doesn't offer a cut-and-dry story with simple answers or an easy ending.  I very much think that everything is said and done by the time the credits role -- as much as it needs to be on both counts -- even as certain strands are left dangling, denying us the simplistic satisfaction of traditional closure.  The last little speech is perfect and says a lot about the character speaking it and also, as it turns out, about the concept of giving into the futility of stopping change from coming, accepting the cold, hard reality of the future and trying to find whatever comfort one can in it.

The Coen's are known for giving you a strange and odd experience for every flick they put out, except for "Intolerable Cruelty", but we should just go ahead and forget about that movie.

The film opens with a shot of the west Texas desert, Tommy Lee Jones is giving an impassioned narration talking about old time sheriff's. Josh Brolin, who is quickly becoming one of my favorite actors played Llewelyn Moss, a man who stumbles across a horrible scene of death and violence while out hunting. He tracks down the last man standing, only to find him in possession of 2 million dollars, and dead as a doornail.

The performances are perfect. Javier portrays the first great villain of the 21st century, and Tommy Lee Jones should be taking home his second Oscar for his role in this, and I wouldn't be surprised to see most of the cast get nominations.

This film should get the Coen Brothers they much deserved Best Director Oscar, and I say its about damn time. No Country will stay lodged in your head for hours after viewing it, and it will soon become an essential film for American cinema goers.

 [color=Black]The Coen's brothers "No Country for Old Men" is a devestating and highly suspenseful thriller, that shoots itself in the foot with its ending.  Instead of using music to create suspense, the film uses absolute silence and subtlety to build tension.  The distant footsteps, the creaking of hard wood, a brush against the wall... these and many more elements are able to take effect and create a much more painfully tense environment.  And so it goes without saying, that "No Country for Old Men" might be one of the most suspenseful films I have ever seen.  The acting is incredible, with Javier Bardem being the absolute standout... this is a performance and a character that will haunt your memories, long past the film's last reel.  It's also the Coen's direction; their painstaking eye for detail and knowledge on how to direct their actors and make the surroundings and circumstances all the more intense... that makes this an incredible movie.  The dark humour and subtle metaphors on the future and of aging youth, are nice touches that bring meaning and coherence to the movie.  Maybe it's one of the last scenes in the film, where Anton and Leilwelyn's wife face-off in a conversation of will... that truly brought this film together for me.  But, the end completely blind-sighted me... the audience expects Jones character to have some place in the story at hand, yet it never happens.  It's one of those endings that feels like the momentum of the film is still rolling along at full-speed, then runs into a brick wall that makes everything fall apart.  Now, don't get me wrong... this film is far too good to fall apart because of a lousy ending, but I just wanted more for the finale from such a masterful movie.  Still, "No Country for Old Men" is a must-see bloodbath of raw suspense and utter fascination... I predict the Oscar for Best Picture, in its midst.

First things first: I'm a fan of the Coen brothers, I enjoy unconventional endings, and I appreciate when a film stays true to the novel it's based on. In the case of 'No Country for Old Men', which I desperately wanted to love, literary faithfulness has ruined the moviegoing experience.

Without spoiling much, 'No Country' is an utterly gripping film until the 2/3 mark, when the Coens execute their most climactic scene entirely off-camera and suddenly set the viewer on a path to nowhere. In a move apparently faithful to Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel by the same name (I didn't read it), the Coens trade in resolution and great storytelling for ambiguity and tired philosophy.

I suppose it can be said that 'No Country' is automatically a great film because I'm still dwelling on it. There's no question that Javier Bardem's portrayal of psychopath Anton Chigurh is eerily chilling and maybe Oscar-worthy. The editing and cinematography are likewise masterful. Even the film's complete lack of a score, while begging the question of why Carter Burwell was credited as composer of original music, sets the tone perfectly.

Still, 'No Country for Old Men' offers countless plot holes and stubbornly stays too true to a novel unfit for film adaptation. Despite its strengths and the introduction of one of American cinema's new great villains, the film loses all steam in the end, leaving the viewer betrayed and empty -- and I'm not sure if it's McCarthy or the Coens to blame. 3/5 stars.

It's really about the interaction than about the action (which btw doesn't lack at all). It's also about how a murderous psychopath with a bad hairdo and some exotic weapons interacts with the relatively simple (though not dumb) inhabitants of the southern state. I could call it a carefully constructed character study, but that's way cliché, so I'll just stick to calling it a really nice Coen bros film - something that I've been craving considering their more recent stinkers like Ladykillers and Intolerable Cruelty (well, Intolerable Cruelty makes for a pretty good airplane movie, but then again anything competing with screaming babies and grumpy flight attendants is gonna be a good airplane movie). The best film of the year, and the most horrifying. The Coen brothers have outdone themselves with the unforgettable masterpiece of a film. Based on the book, the film tells the story of the discovery of $2 million, heroin, and a lot of dead bodies. When an outsider cowboy type dude discovers these things, his whole life is in jeopardy when an extremely dangerous mass murderer armed with a cattle retracting gun comes after him. Meanwhile, a police man gets on the trail of the killer, but doesn't take into consideration that this man is impossible to get in contact with, without dying. The film is extremely violent, with some rather sickening scenes involving people getting holes blown into them by the killer's weapon of choice. However, the film also has three perfect performances from Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin, and Javier Bardem. Tommy Lee Jones is delightful as the old timer who isn't up to the times so much as he doesn't get what is going on. He contributes a solid supporting performance. Javier Bardem is creepy as hell as the demented killer. There were parts where he was so ratty and nasty, he reminded me of Nosferatu. He gave me the chills. Josh Brolin is the main character who finds the money and the dead bodies. He contributes a character who always has to be on his toes ad who could die any second. In many ways, the Coen Brothers as filmmakers have always placed style on a pedestal well above substance.  If anything, the style of their films sometimes serves [i]as[/i] the substance; take [i]The Big Lebowski[/i], for example, a fairly straightforward yarn once you dig past the layers of zany characters and crackling dialogue.  Their latest, the modern Western [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], is not about to break this mold; the problem is that neither the style nor the substance seem up to the task of carrying a two-hour film.

The basic plot of [i]No Country[/i] follows Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), who comes across the remains of a drug deal gone bad while out hunting.  Moss makes off with a satchel containing two million dollars, but makes the mistake of returning to the scene later that night with a jug of water for a dying man.  The man is now quite dead, and Moss has alerted those looking for the money to his presence at the scene.  He soon finds himself in a grim chase, fleeing before the hired killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem).

The Coens slow pace and lack of music for most of the film make much of [i]No Country[/i] a severe drag, although these factors both contribute to ratcheting up the tension.  We, the audience, know what manner of a man is after Moss long before he realizes it himself, and we fear for him.  At the same time, the Coens implicitly ask us whether we [i]should[/i] be fearing for him  Moss, after all, is basically a thief, and while that doesnt place him as far out on the continuum of sin as the murderous Chigurh, it certainly doesnt make him the hero of the film.  Chigurh himself appears to operate using a very warped sense of morality, though certain scenes in which he apparently kills out of sheer convenience suggest otherwise.

The films true hero, assuming there can be said to be one, is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who in curiously ironic fashion is always one step behind the actual action.  The film opens with narration from Jones, discussing how many of the sheriffs he knew as a young man didnt even wear guns; this is subsequently contrasted with the violence Bell comes across throughout the film.  But if the film is Bells story  and it opens and closes on him, suggesting as much  he is an oddly passive observer for much of it.  [i]No Country[/i]s moral lessons  in particular the idea that a punishable offense is a punishable offense, even if it seems odd that someone less moral is doing the punishing  come from the Moss/Chigurh plot, though the irony is that Moss might have gotten away clean if not for the fact that his morals got the best of him.  The films ideas get a bit muddled as a result.  What, exactly, is it saying about morality if the real moral seems to be that evil triumphs and no good deed goes unpunished?

Its the character of Chigurh that provides the stickiest subject.  How he fits into the plot to begin with is frustratingly unclear, and his motivations are correspondingly hazy.  For example, after being hired to track Moss, he kills the two men who hire him.  Why, we dont know.  My guess would be that Chigurh  who rolls through the film like a force of nature more than a character  acts almost as a kind of avenging spirit, punishing everyone who is in any way guilty.  However, our first encounters with him feature him murdering a deputy who had the temerity to arrest him and then a motorist for no other reason than, I assume, that Chigurh does not want to be seen driving a police car.  These muddy the characters waters, and even if he is placed into the film as a sort of avenger, its not clear how that connects to Bells story, nor how the vaguely supernatural nature of that angle would mesh with what otherwise seems to be an attempt at a realistic portrayal of place and time on the part of the Coens.

The Coens leave us a lot to chew on, but unfortunately they dont present it in the most appealing package.  While the deliberate pace and lack of music add to the tension, they also  particularly in places where the tension is not as high, such as the opening hunting scene, which takes place long before the chase begins  create a plodding, shift-in-your-seat, check-your-watch experience that ranks up there with the most restless Ive ever felt in a theater.  I dont inherently have a problem with slow pacing, but many scenes felt like they could have been told in half the time, if not less, without sacrificing anything in meaning.  I found this to be more distracting than anything; rather than encouraging me to search for hidden themes, the slow movement simply began to drain my enthusiasm for watching the film at all.

The Coen Brothers have made good films, and theyve made great films, but with [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] Im not willing to make a case that theyve done either.  Its a morally complex work, to be sure, but it creeps along so slowly with a wisp of a plot that the depth becomes difficult to parse  and even beyond that, the Chigurh character is so slippery that he casts doubt on any argument youd care to make for the films sense of morality.  [i]No Country[/i] may be an evocative portrait of a place and time, but what kind of meaning that setting offers regarding morals and humanity is anyones guess.

You know that one review that's given for almost every film except The English Patient? It goes something like... "edge-of-your-seat!" Yeah? Well, that review is for this movie. No Country For Old Men is the definitive movie experience because it manages to get you to invest so much of yourself into its richly-conceived world, you can't just watch-- you experience, endure, and feel every minute of it. The Coen brothers, of Fargo fame, utilize every instrument of filmmaking (particularly that of noise) to craft an unforgettable story that haunts more so than it resonates. Essentially, what we have here is a chase-flick that follows one man's attempt to escape a mistake (in this case Javier Bardem, who delivers a performance so intensely chilling, the only person unlikely to run away at the sight of him is Oscar) as narrated by an old-timer (the always reliable Tommy Lee Jones) who can't fathom the evolution of evil as it progresses into his twilight years. What we get from all this, is what you might get from a fast-food joint when ordering "the works"-- everything on it. There's a unique blend of humor, drama, thriller, and tragedy here that only the best of films can pull off without tipping the balance and make no mistake, No Country For Old Men is one of those films-- the best-- of the year and maybe even the last few. Grade: A+

Stop me if you've heard this one before.  A Texan good ol' boy finds a suitcase with two million dollars from a drug deal gone wrong and then becomes the prey of a homicidal psychopath who goes on a killing spree while the curmudgeonly local sheriff tries to bring order to a situation steadily spiraling out of control.  What sounds like the main ingredients of your basic straight-to-DVD B-minus thriller become a marvel of tightly plotted storytelling in the hands of the Coen brothers, who haven't been this good since Frances McDormand caught Peter Stormare jamming Steve Buscemi's leg into a wood chipper.  The Coens have expertly mixed film noir and Western archetypes, and the synergy they have created gives each genre new life.  This film demands your attention and rewards it with some chilling set pieces (the sequence where Josh Brolin attempts to outswim a deadly pit bull makes you feel you're in the water with him) and the creepiest movie villain this reviewer has seen in many a moon (Javier Bardem will get nominated and duke it out with Hal Holbrook for the Best Supporting Actor Oscar). Most of the film plays with no music score; instead, the Coens manipulate the sound so the audience becomes sensitive to the simplest noise they hear. The filmmakers use this strategy gradually, so it's only around the halfway point that you realize how frayed your nerves are...and that there is a noose tightening around your neck.   For all its narrative prowess, however, I can't help but feel that "No Country for Old Men" arrives at its boldly anticlimatic conclusion (retained from the book) in a way that limits our emotional attachment to the characters. There is not a false note struck here, but the Coens' shifting focus from one set of characters to another keeps us at arm's length emotionally even though viscerally we are never less than captivated by their vise-like grip on us.  They might be cold-blooded control freaks, but this blood-soaked tale shows them at the top of their game.  Bastards.

When is the last time you saw a Hollywood thriller that could actually qualify as classic Hollywood cinema? My guess is you haven't seen one in quite a long time. The Coen Brothers are gifted film makers who've produced some of the most memorable motion pictures in the last two decades. You don't have to be a fan of theirs to enjoy this film, however, if you are it's nothing but icing on the cake. There are familiar elements from most of their films here: small town folks struggling to get by, quirky humor, and a lot of cash that ends up being pursued by bumbling anti-heroes. If you're afraid that the Coen Brothers are ripping themselves off and falling into rehashed territory you might want to think again. What they've done in this film is something that htey haven't quite managed to do in any of their others...although, they've come close. The brothers have MASTERED the tone. I was on edge from the opening shots of this film to the very last frame. I literally had my hands clenched together in my lap for the duration of this picture. When you couple this kind of tension with the kind of character played by Javier Bardiem, and add some very well planned cinematography you've got the results of an instant classic. No joke. Film history. Right here. The performance by Bardiem itself is enough to rival a Hannibal Lecter or a Norman Bates. The Coens architecture is so flawless that it doens't require much of a story to keep the viewer in a trance. The film would play itself out masterfully if we didn't even know these characters' names. Do yourself a favor and see this movie. If at first you're wondering how you feel about the experience when the credits start rolling, don't worry. The Coens know enough to make something that resonates with you days after the initial viewing. As if you've truly witnessed something genuinely horrifying and fascinating all at the same time. You'll need a second to make sense of it. As someone in the picture says to a bewildered Tommy Lee Jones (trying to make sense of why his career hasn't gotten easier in his older years), "This country is hard on everyone...that's vanity." Well, if you think that you're special and won't be affected by this picture yourself...that's also vanity.
