You know that one review that's given for almost every film except [i]The English Patient[/i]? It goes something like... "edge-of-your-seat!" Yeah? Well, that review is for this movie. [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is the definitive movie experience because it manages to get you to invest so much of yourself into its richly-conceived world, you can't [i]just[/i] watch-- you experience, endure, and feel every minute of it. The Coen brothers, of [i]Fargo[/i] fame, utilize every instrument of filmmaking (particularly that of noise) to craft an unforgettable story that haunts more so than it resonates. Essentially, what we have here is a chase-flick that follows one man's attempt to escape a mistake (in this case Javier Bardem, who delivers a performance so intensely chilling, the only person unlikely to run away at the sight of him is Oscar) as narrated by an old-timer (the always reliable Tommy Lee Jones) who can't fathom the evolution of evil as it progresses into his twilight years. What we get from all this, is what you might get from a fast-food joint when ordering "the works"-- everything on it. There's a unique blend of humor, drama, thriller, and tragedy here that only the best of films can pull off without tipping the balance and make no mistake, [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is one of those films-- the best-- of the year and maybe even the last few. [b]Grade: A+[/b]

I really enjoyed the intelligence of the film. No one acts like an idiot, everyone has brains and holds their own as everyone hunts and becomes hunted. The deaths, kills, and even weapons used are creative and surprising.

This might be surprising to you, but the movie is actually filled with humor. Dark humor that is, but damn is it funny. It never seems forced nor does it seem out of place. The depressing tone remains consistent.

The actors play the parts extremly well. Josh Brolin, seems to be rising high on fame latley. He plays a retired man who happens on 2 million in cash. Tommy Lee Jones plays a tired Sheriff with the weight of serivce, change and age on his back. The man who stole the show was Javier Bardem, who plays Anton Chigurh. The themes of the movie are numerous and complex. The film isn't concerned with who gets the money involved, just the people. chance, freewill and pre-destination are abundant. Like Anton's coin-toss. Even, as the title suggests, aging, passing the torch, and our place in the ever changing world. How things become so different when we become older that we loose our usefulness and ability to be apart of a poisned society.

Every so often a movie villain will come along that is so ruthless and violent that you'll have problems going to bed at night.  Javier Bardem plays one of the best villains in recent cinema history as Anton Chigurgh, this generation's Hannibal Lecter.  He is cold, malicious and batshit insane.  
The best two words that I can use to describe this film are brutal and unpredictable.  From seeing Chigurh clean out his bullet wounds and a bloody Llewelyn Moss limping around the Mexican border this film is not for those who are afraid of blood.  It is impossible to know what will happen next in this film except that the ending goes against all movie tradition.

Finally, the Coen Brothers are back to form. After Fargo, they seemed to lose that magic they had, but eleven years later they've found it again and the result is a film that rises to the level of the aforementioned Fargo. Quite an achievement, seeing as Fargo is a masterpiece that blows, oh, ninety percent of all other movies out of the water. While No Country could be reduced to a plot synopsis, its plot isn't the real central aspect of the film. The study of the psychopathic Anton Chigurh is. Here's one of the best characters ever brought to the screen: a totally remorseless and soulless monster in human skin who murders innocents for no reason. When he gets a reason to kill someone (IE to retrieve 2 million bucks in cold hard cash) he becomes even more evil and relentless. And we, the audience, sit and watch in amazement as we wonder: can such evil exist in this world? 

No Country for Old Men reminds us that the answer is yes. And isn't that terrifying. See it.

A hunter (Brolin) stumbles onto some dead bodies, heroin, and a large sum of cash.  In trying to get away from the cash he is pursued by a relentless psychopath (Bardem). 
A classic narrative with really no discernable flaws.  This is one of the Coen brothers stronger films, and marks a return to form after some missteps involving George Clooney.  
The film works on almost every level.  Snappy dialogue, cleverly executed scenes, excellent pacing, excellent performances from all (especially Bardem), solid direction, and great character development which only adds to the proceedings.  If I had to look for a flaw in this movie I would say (and this is slightly reaching) that it was missing the beauty of the slow moments.  For example, Fargo was very similar in structure and execution, but had some beautiful still moments of the winter landscape.  No Country had none of that, which left the audience less time to reflect on the impact of the preceedings.  However, that's hardly a flaw for this film, and more a comparison.
This is one of the best films this year, and I highly recommend it.

[I wrote a long review and then Flixter wasn't working for some reason, so I am trying to re-write what I had written before, but am doing it hurriedly, out of frustration mainly. Please forgive if this review isn't coherent.] I saw this movie last night. When I got home, I immediately went to the internet message-boards to see what other people thought. And that's the first big thing about No Country for Old Men, I guess: it makes you think. Now, I don't mean "think" in the oh wow, am I living my life right Inconvenient Truth sense, I mean it in the okay so what is this supposed to symbolize sense. The movie is very complex. Which is strange because at its core, it's a very simple and straight-forward killer thriller. The killer (Bardem) is chasing the victim (Brolin) while the cop (Jones) is trying to stop him. Let me digress for a moment to say that Tommy Lee Jones totally steals the show in this film, and I found myself wishing that there were more scenes centered on him. Like I was saying, though, it excels on the entertainment level, providing tense, funny, upsetting, and exciting action all at the same time. Brilliant performances by the leads, beautiful settings (the Coens have an undeniable knack for drawing the boldest colors out of the simplest scenes), and a strong story are hampered only by the movie's insistence on having some sort of underlying meaning. It's possible to see the seemingly out-of-place ending as an impenetrable secret, and to begrudge the ending for that -- for hiding the meaning somewhere where we can't find it. On the other hand, if you believe the message-board interpreters, the meaning might be so obvious that the strange ending is just over-kill. Either way, the ending doesn't work. I will admit that it's possible that I have been misled by the message-board interpreters and perhaps there is a deeper meaning that we are all missing. Perhaps, once I know this meaning, everything will come together like putting the last piece in a jigsaw puzzle. Even if this were true, I would still fault the movie for the fact that I can't tell what it is even though there's only one jigsaw piece missing. That aside, it's mesmerizing.

No Country for Old Men makes so many perfect choices and takes so few wrong steps that when you think it actually, finally does take a wrong step, you still have to question yourself - did it actually do something wrong, or do I just need to watch it again?  It's a testament to the greatness of this film that it was as flawless as it was for as long as it was.  The last twenty minutes of the film I have a problem with, and by that, I mean I think I have a problem with it.  I'm really not sure.  But I'll discuss my reservations over the ending later, after I've finished gushing about the stellar, haunting, beautiful, suspenseful, horrifying, wonderful flick that is No Country For Old Men.  I've always stated that the Coens need to focus more on their violent dramatic thrillers than their comedies, because really - who thinks Intolerable Cruetly is a better movie than Fargo or Miller's Crossing?  Here, the Coen's nearly out-do themselves, and I mean it when I say the first three quarters of the flick are even better than anything in Fargo.  Every shot, every scene, every line of dialogue rings so true, never takes a wrong step, that I nearly hugged the screen in joy.  The movie opens with a brilliant monologue from Tommy Lee Jones, who can play a weathered man beaten down by life better than anyone.  Roger Deakins, the cinematographer, shows off his beautiful compositions, and within the first two minutes of screen time we realize this film is going to be more about the consequences of death and of people's choices more than the actual events themselves.  The whole movie leads up to this realization.  After this monologue, we are introduced to Anton Chigurh, brilliantly played by Javier Bardem (who will win an Oscar for sure).  He's the most frightening man I've ever seen in a theatre (because I have never seen Hannibal Lecter in the theatre, and he's the only villian in cinema that scares me more).  He strangles a cop ruthlessly, blood pouring from the victim's neck as he stares up at the ceiling, a smile creeping around his lips, his eyes bugging out and his horrible black hair cut sprawling out over the ground.  Minutes later, he escapes, pulls over a man, and kills him with decompressed air.  It's one of the best introductions to one of the best characters I've seen in modern films.  In the cinema, I was worried.  We were sitting directly behind a group of teenagers who smelled like pot and whiskey.  The entire theatre was packed - and I mean, literally, no available seat anywhere.  I was scared they would talk throughout, be bored by a slow beginning, and ruin it for me.  This scene gripped them immediately, and just like the rest of us, the film never let go.  In fact, it's easily one of the most gripping suspense thrillers I've ever witnessed (so much hyperbole in this review, I know, but I can't help it).  More than once - nay, more than 10 times - I was gripping the edges of my seat, scared shitless, watching Anton approach his next victims with his huge shotgun or decompressed air.  In several scenes, such as the first showdown in the hotel and the second shoot-out/chase in another hotel and city streets, the Coens clearly are taking some pages from Hitchcock himself in building tension to an almost unbearable level.  Of course, the movie is more violent than any Hitchcock film, but even then, it shows restraint.  We know, for instance, that almost every time Anton leaves a character in a scene, that character is dead.  We don't always need to see the actual murder, and the Coens know this.  We'll see him washing chicken feathers out of a farmer's truck, or checking his boots for blood, or asking someone "what's the most you've ever lost in a coin toss"?  The performance, script, and direction all combine to make Anton Chigurh a character that'll haunt your nightmares for years to come.  Having said all this, the other characters in the movie are no push-overs.  Josh Broilin's "hero", as we'll call him, is excellent throughout.  He's tough as nails, but we can hear the fear in his voice slowly crawl up the more he gets to know who exactly is chasing him.  Tommy Lee Jones is cool and collected as always, and especially in the final scenes, is brilliant.  Roger Deakins manages to pull off a very neat trick, by being the cinematographer in the two best shot films of the year (this one and Assassination of Jesse James).  The music by Carter Burwell is interesting because I never heard any music at all until the final credits - and I'm usually purposefully listening for it; so either Burwell hardly composed any musical score, or the movie had me gripped so much I didn't even notice.  Considering that this is a violent chase movie, far more action packed than any other Coen  brother's film I've seen, they still manage to give us some of their very best dialogue.  In fact, this is one of the first things me and my girlfriend mentioned after the film was over, how good the dialogue was.  The Coens have a wonderful knack for writing dialogue that never sounds like anyone you've heard, but yet you always believe 100% that the character you're looking at really would say that.  It's lyrical and yet very sparse at the same time, and always with a hint of black comedy.  Many times I found myself chuckling at the dialogue and then immediately horrified by the actions soon following, and even though this is apparently very faithful to the book it's based on, I believe the majority of this credit belongs squarely to the writer/director team.  Just wait until the coin-toss scene arrives between a gas station attendant and Chigurh.  Every line, every shot, every glance from both actors is so pitch-perfect that I nearly creamed myself when it was over.  As if the actual suspense scenes aren't intense enough - the Coens managed to make simple talking-head shots unbearably tense.  Now, onto the ending, which I will try and discuss without revealing anything (still, though, if you haven't seen it you should stop reading now).  I felt a vague sense of dissatisfaction when it was all said and done.  There's a major surprise about 20 minutes before the ending, which I kinda saw coming but not in the fashion it was shown in.  The Coens love to pull the rug out from under viewers, and this is no different.  However, I feel they may have taken a small mis-step.  Not letting a major, expected payoff happening is one thing, but to deny us seeing why it didn't happen is confusing and hard to take.  A major off-screen death like this would be murder for lesser filmmakers, but even though I felt slightly disappointed, I still nodded my head sagely and understood what they were getting at.  The final scene I also had slight problems with - I felt the final shots of Chigurh should've ended the film, and then when the actual final scene ended, it's poignancy was ruined by the audience giving it a bad laugh.  And I didn't really blame them, because ending on such a note and having the credits pop up so quickly made it feel kinda like a joke, and a lot of people responded with laughter.  Still, though, these are minor quibbles (even though I have a bad feeling they're what's stopping me from giving this film 5 stars).  If you don't have a problem with open-ended conclusions, you're likely to wet yourself from how great this movie is.  I might've wanted the final 20 minutes to go a different way, but that can't stop me from seeing how brilliant and near-perfect the rest of the production is.  Go see this film immediately, and witness one of the best suspense/thrillers of the decade.

The Coen brothers have a knack for language, for letting it create the atmosphere of a specific time and place.  In this film, it is the spare use of language that contributes to its arid, chilling atmosphere.  Gone is the playful verbosity of The [i]Hudsucker Proxy[/i] or even [i]Miller's Crossing[/i].  Gone is the lushly evocative soundtrack of [i]The Big Lebowski[/i] or [i]O Brother[/i].  This movie is stripped down to its bare aural bones.  The result is a movie that is upsets all expectations of action or thriller or Oscar-worthy or Coen Brothers.  I loved it.  I don't know if I could put myself through the rigors of watching it again.  It's not that [i]No Country[/i] demonstrates how evil triumphs over good; it is morally bleak but not without a small flicker of hope.  It's that the film takes something from you in order to make itself happen.  That's the best way I can put it.  You should go.  Just be prepared to give something up.

Never before have I seen a decent film be so completely and utterly destroyed by a horrible ending. I'm not one of those types who needs a happy ending, or even one that necessarily ends, that is not at all my complaint. Most of the movie, up until the last 20 minutes, was very well made, extremely well written, and pretty exciting to watch. There was a lot of silence, which was very effective in most places, but sometimes made it drag. Josh Brolin was by all means the focal character, and a darn good one, too. Tommy Lee Jones had barely been in it at all. WARNING: SPOILERS beyond this point! For the last twenty minutes, the plot fell apart. Josh Brolin's character died. That's disappointing, yes, but would have been ok if they had done it right. Instead, it was as if his story didn't even matter anymore, and they didn't even show his death, instead it was just a side note in the new story, which never even became a story. The last twenty minutes of the movie were disjointed, pointless, completely unresolved in every aspect, and suddenly now Tommy Lee Jones is the new focal point!?!? Where was he the rest of the movie? It seemed that someone hijacked the last twenty minutes of the movie and put in something that made no sense whatsoever. It appears a lot of people will disagree, and that is their right, but in my opinion, that ruined the entire movie for me.

"I'm not gonna call it."
 
"Call it."
 
"The coin don't have no say - it's just you."
 
That exchange (which I paraphrased) takes place late in the Coen Brothers latest, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], and summarizes the biggest question the movie asks, "When is our fate determined?"
 
For Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) it's possibly the moment he decided to go hunting one particular morning. Maybe it's the moment he takes off after wounded prey. It most definitely was determined when he stumbles upon the scene of a drug deal gone terribly wrong, and takes off with two million dollars in cash.
 
This action sets off a chain reaction of violent events, mostly caused by psychotic Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) as he hunts Moss to retrieve the money. Trying to put the puzzle together is aging sherriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) who can't wrap his head around a world that seems to be getting inexorably worse. Or maybe it's just that he's getting older, and the world has always been like this.
 
The Coens take this premise and create one of the tensest movie going experiences you will see all year. Their decision to eschew a musical score creates an uneasiness that permeates throughout. As moviegoers, we're trained to listen for those musical cues to warn us of an ominous situation. Absent that, we are at the mercy of Chigurh, who's decisions as to when to strike his prey are coldly random.
 
What irritates me most in thriller movies like this are when characters do something completely stupid to allow their tormentor to find them or gain an upper hand. That is decidedly not the case here. Not veering one bit from the plot of their source, we have one smart guy being pursued relentlessly by another smart guy. The only upper hand Chigurh has is that he is ruthless and will do what it takes.
 
The script may be lifted directly from McCarthy's novel, but the brothers trimmed just enough to give this movie perfect focus, while emphasising enough darkly comic material to give it their own flavor. Roger Deakins cinematography is, as always, excellent, and there is not one bad performance. Brolin, Bardem, and Jones I'm sure will get their proper notice come awards season, but I hope voters don't overlook Kelly McDonald as Carla Jean Moss. Watch her final scene in the movie as she is be able to show fear, strength, confusion, and finally resignation.
 
Having read the book, I wasn't sure what initially intrigued the Coens to the story, but it's plainly obvious, and I'm not sure how I missed it. They revel in stories of an ordinary guy swept up in a situation that grows well beyond his control. Whether it's Jerry Lundergaard in [i]Fargo[/i], the Dude in [i]The Big Lebowski[/i], or Ed in [i]The Man Who Wasn't There, [/i]their protagonists seem to be reluctant pawns in the grand sceme of things.
 
Surely the ending will leave some heads scratching, and probably some unsatisfied. Me? Well, I think it's all summed up in the film's tagline: "There are no clean getaways."
 
I know there's five weeks left... but it's the best of the year. If something better comes along, then us moviegoers are extremely lucky.

Has there ever been a more unlikely Best Picture winner than No Country for Old Men? It's a dark, somewhat cold picture that will confound your expectations at every turn. I've probably seen it about a dozen times, and I find something different to love about it each time-from the brilliant performances and incredible framing techniques, to the gutsy choices to not score the film and end things very inconclusively. From beginning to end, it's a film full of risks, and even though I've never felt emotionally involved in it, I admire the film and the Coens' work on it immensely.

On the surface, the film's plot is pretty simple. Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is a simple man in South Texas who stumbles across a drug deal gone wrong. The good news in it all: He comes away with a suitcase full of $2 million. On the trail of the money, however, is Anton Chigurh, who's as evil as they come. Equipped with his weapon of choice-a cattle gun-Chigurh isn't afraid to dispose of anyone in pursuit of Moss and the money. The third man in the equation is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who's dogged determination to do what's right might just put him in serious danger.

What the plot lacks in originality (it's a veritable road movie, really), it makes up for in complex meaning and subtext. The ending, which I still don't fully comprehend to be honest, calls into question everything that we've seen. To that end, the film's ambiguity makes it work on many different levels-a good vs. evil story, a dark Western comedy, and a twisty, suspenseful thriller.

For this film, the Coens' have managed to assemble one of the best ensembles of any of their films. It's not so great in terms of quantity of established actors, but each and every actor is so appropriately cast. Javier Bardem is undeniably the standout. His Anton Chigurh is a villain for the ages-so downright evil it's not even funny. Josh Brolin plays a good everyman here, but he's a Coen interpretation of an everyman-very cynical and not necessarily always on the up-and-up. Tommy Lee Jones is as close to an emotional through line as the film has. We like his character much more than any other because he's a voice of goodness and morality in a morass of wickedness and bad choices. Also, he's really funny.

I love some of the Coens' stylistic choices, the boldest and bravest one being not to score the film. It's about as uncommercial a move as you can make, yet folks still responded to it. Better than just being gutsy, however, it also really adds something to the film. It allows you to respond to it in your own way, without the help of musical cues. On top of that choice, the film is also showcases Roger Deakins extensive talent. The way he plays with light is absolutely masterful. In any other year, he would have walked away with a Best Cinematography Oscar (2007 was just an amazing year in that category, and it didn't help that he was competing against his perhaps superior work in The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford).

What's most amazing about No Country for Old Men though might just be how original this film is. It's truly unlike anything else I've ever seen. And considering the directors are adapting a real masterpiece of modern literature, I think that's one impressive feat.

A wonderfully made movie by the Coen brothers, one of their best. It has their usual Southern style, yet improves on it. One thing that really impressed me with the film is that the Coen brothers get you so interested with whatever is happening on the screen, that you don't even think about the fact that you really don't know much about the bad guy, or even the situation at hand fully until after the movie is over. Great performances by the whole cast, especially Javier Bardem as the bad guy, and Josh Brolin has become a lot more popular in movies lately (Grindhouse, American Gangster, this...it's funny how far he's come since The Goonies as Sean Astin's older brother). Extremely well-written, with alot of great dialogue; I'm admittedly jealous of how well the Coen brothers can write good dialogue, as I don't think I could come up with anything as smart as what they come up with. They also do a great job with suspense, as there were many times I was expecting a "boo" moment, one of those moments that deliver a quick jump. Sometimes they do deliver them, but most of the time their timing is much more smarter than what we'd expect, which makes it that much more intriguing. While Carter Burwell is credited for the music, aside for the end credits, I really don't remember any music playing at all during the whole movie, just sounds that compliment the mood and tone of whatever is happening at the moment. This movie will most definitely get nominated for Best Picture, and as far as I can tell, has the best chance of winning at this point.

That's OK though, because this film will hook you in and won't let go.  The one element that exceeded my expectations was the performance by Javier Bardem.  He was scary in his calmness, comfortably killing for whatever reasons that make sense only in his mind.  It's to the point that if you met him, you would already be convinced that you will die.  He will get the Oscar for Supporting Actor this year, hands down.  What the film lacks is a comprehendible ending... perhaps the intention was to have an ending that may be only understood the second time around.  But then, one needn't such an excuse to see this great film again.

(Note, I saw this film a second time about 2 months after writing this review. It's difficult to start reviewing this film.  I'd like to re-watch it, or at least give the book a chance.  The Coen Brothers' attention to minutia is, as usual, impressive and astounding. The Coens, though not sweepingly popular, are just as masterful filmmakers as the likes of Jackson and Spielberg, say.  The craft of the editing, sound design, acting, writing, and cinematography is impeccable.  However, the great part is that the package doesn't call attention to itself, unlike the epic overkill of many films (see: "Beowulf").  Similarly, the contrast of the extremely evil and unsettling performance of Javier Bardem and the hapless sadness of Tommy Lee Jones's character is well-played, and essential in understanding the theme of the film.  In fact, I prefer this film to other Coen fare like "Fargo" and "Blood Simple," in that it feels more genuine and true.  There's an undue amount of parallels between this and other Coen films, and the ending could have been trimmed slightly.  Those small complaints notwithstanding, this movie (especially in an artistically weak movie year) is a must-see.

Lives up to the hype.  This is a masterful piece of cinema.  After the back-to-back successes of Fargo and The Big Lebowski, the Coens diluted their resume with almost ten years of lazy, indulgent, and subpar outings.  However, this movie signals their return to their roots (see Blood Simple) and top-drawer filmmaking.  How come?  The plot isn't new (guy finds briefcase of drug money, gets chased across Texas and over the border by killers).  But its the strong characters and attention for detail that leave an indelible impression.  Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, and Tommy Lee Jones have turned in a trio of career performances as the hunted, hunter, and weary sheriff.  Each scene is meticulously constructed for the maximum possible suspense.  Bardem's villain is established early as a remorseless, humorless, and instantly memorable killer with a methodical and insanely ingenious style of dispatching his victims.  The rest of the film involves him matching wits with Brolin's resourceful everyman.  Secondary characters have shining moments (see the coin-flipping scene in the gas station betwen the attendant and Bardem).  Jones, the moral compass of the film, worries about the state of the world as the bodycount increases.  However, the proceedings never become shrill or glamorized.  Nobody's safe in Texas, circa 1980 and that's why this film is so engrossing.  There is not a wasted moment - indeed, the end of the film occurs abruptly, so pay close attention at the two hour mark.  Best film I've seen this year.

No Country For Old Men is no movie for young girls, one of which I continue to consider myself. I've not yet read the book, and so cannot judge the film by its compliance, instead, only by the dread tedium with which it filled me as I sat in the near-empty movie-palace late late on a weeknight, expecting to be blown away, and instead wishing I could blow all the wooden characters away (they are thick enough that it would take a gunshot rather than a breath, but thick is not deep, contrary to popular misconceptions).

I would like to argue that the film is simply objectively dreadful, but I've found that a number of my male friends (and even one of my lady friends) thought it was the best movie of the year (and it wasn't just a really bad year), so I will have to accept that there is something about this movie, which is chock-full of random, non-campy violence, cold, stiff characters with no penetrable motivation, and big, empty landscapes to please my philosophically- and artistically-inclined friends. I don't know what it is, because I found the film to be irrational and aesthetically uninteresting, but these are people whose opinions I tend to value.

The plot is as as follows: somewhere in rural-ish Texas, a guy out hunting comes upon a scene: two bullet-riddled trucks, a number of dead Mexicans, a dead dog, and a truckload of narcotics. He collects all the weapons and keeps them, and trudges off to find another dead body resting in the shade of the plain's only tree, and there finds a case of money (which turns out to be $2 million). This scene is well-crafted, and the artistic mind will appreciate the way his scavenging mirrors the scavenging of the hyena that had, minutes earlier, eaten up the deer the hunter had shot and wounded. From that point on, though, I had a similar response to Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) that I had to Bigger Thompson in Native Son: he makes wrong decision after wrong decision, for the sole purpose of furthering the plot. A writer who treats his characters like pawns in the game of pushing his agendaâwhether it be philosophical or politicalâis a hack, and having read Blood Meridian, I'm hesitant to label McCarthy by that epithet, and more inclined to pin the blame on the Coens.

But back to the plot. Llewelyn decides to go back to the "scene of the crime" (mistake number one, which no man of his mettle would, in real life, do) in the middle of the night with a can of kerosene. Before he can torch the tableaux, another truck pulls up to his, slashes his tires, and starts to shoot and chase him. Llewelyn runs. He outruns the truck. This, dear readers, is ludicrous; men simply cannot outrun trucks. The truck drivers send a nasty, muscled dog after him when Llewelyn tries to escape by jumping into a river. This, dear readers, is again unlikley; a man probably cannot outrun and swim a dog of such breed. When the dog does catch up, Llewelyn shoots it dead. This moment is nicely done, although it requires a grand suspension of disbelief to get to that point.

Llewelyn knows that shit is going down, so he sends his hemmy-hawy wife to her mother's house and prepares for combat by abandoning his trailer and moving into a motel. Meanwhile, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), looking for the money, begins to hunt him, first going to his trailer, then his motel. Also on the trail is the sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones, who else?!) who is as disinterested and detached from his case as I am about this film; he goes through the motions up to a point, and then throws in the proverbial towel and wonders why he ever bothered in the first place. Before that, though, Llewelyn and Anton circle each other, predator and poisonous prey. In and out of a variety of motels and stolen vehicles, they shoot at each other and service their own wounds in the same "manly" way Mark Wahlberg's character does in Shooter (for some reason, we are supposed to take the hulking, animal-like Bardem much more seriously). Once it's too late, Llewelyn realizes that Anton has been tracking him thanks to a blinking device lodged in the suitcase of bills; rather than ditching the tracker, jumping out the window, and getting the hell out of the motel room (movie-goers, suspend your disbelief), he waits behind the door for Anton, prepared to shoot upon the beast's entrance. He eventually does leap out the window, jumping into a stolen car, but sustains wounds thanks to his delay.

Eventually, Llewelyn wises up (after a drunken, bloodied night in Mexico followed up by a conversation with bounty hunter Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) (who, not surprisingly, will also end up dead at Anton's gunpoint)) and instructs his wife to load herself and her mother into a cab to a motel in the nearest city with an international airport. While they're on their way, though, Llewelyn arrives at the motel and joins a woman lounging poolside for a beer in her room. Needless to say, when wifey arrives, close on the heels of the sheriff, it's already a crime scene; Llewelyn is shot dead (we don't see the shot or body, as if anything could be to graphic after all the killing we've witnessed along the way) and Anton is long gone with his money. Afterward, there is no need for the audience to wonder what the poor young widow will do; Anton arrives in her house and engages her in a succinct cat-and-mouse conversation before, presumably, shooting her dead. Again, one wonders why the Coens chose to add the seed of non-ambiguous ambiguity by protecting the audience from witnessing the actual shooting.

Once Llewelyn is dead, of course, the audience looses whatever vestigial interest in the film it might have had, even though the Coens go on to show the sheriff have two impenetrable "deep" conversations, one with a wheelchair-bound ex-colleague, who serves four-day-old coffee, and one with his wife over breakfast, while he tries to decide how to spend his day now that he's retired, and recounts the bad dream he had the night before. And, with this unpleasant mouth of spit-up to be swallowed, the film ends.

Reviews have had their socks knocked left and right over Bardem's "chilling" performance as either an amoral or weirdly ethical killer, but I found Anton's character to be the biggest intellectual turn-off of the whole hollow mess. The king of empty, he's so methodical that he performs most of his executions with an air gun, a kind of heavy gas-tank that he carries around that has a tube attached to the top; he uses it to blow locks out of doors and to blow holes in people's foreheads with equal perfunction. He toys with a few of his victims, threatening to use a coin toss to determine their fate (a gas-station owner doesn't understand what's happening, but Llewelyn's widow does), and this is being considered by some as ascribing to his character a philosophical bent. To me, though, Anton functions completely outside of philosophy, and in fact outside of humanity (I have wondered, after watching this film, whether there are people like him, and I have decided there are notânot that there are not serial killers, mob-men, and murderers of every kind, that kill for work or play. But Anton doesn't kill for work or for play or for revenge or for attention (those seem to be the the newest killers lighting up the front page); he's just a killing machine. He kills because that's what he does. He came into the world the age that he is, shooting; he had no childhood, no family, no lover. His character is a character that kills, and his violence is clean and dispassionate, often an afterthought (at one moment, while driving, he pauses to shoot dead a bird standing on a bridge's safety rail). This is lazy characterization, and as I said at the outset, I don't know whether to blame McCarthy or the Coens. But someone should be shot.

I love this movie. I love it. I hate everything. I hate every single piece of shit Hollywood throws on movie screens; I hate all modern approaches to filmmaking, from the opening credit sequences to the horribly histrionic acting to the rote directing to the patronizing proselytizing: It all sucks. 

I have seen, perhaps 8 movies this year I would consider to be very good, 3 approaching the level of great. Those films are THE HOST, THE ASSASSINATION OF JESSE JAMES BY THE COWARD ROBERT FORD and NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN. But the latter film is approaching great from the opposite side, as it has already surpassed great, and is traveling into the realm of the messianic. 

Let us begin with Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). His character is the main reason why this film deserves instant canonization, and Iâm enthralled by what makes him so amazingly chilling. As he strangles a deputy, his eyes light up with a glorious joy, an immense satisfaction with what he is doing. He enjoys killing people. Thoroughly enjoys it. It is his forte, his game, his self-appointed way of making a difference. He has a purpose in life, even if itâs just his own. He is a somebody; people are scarred of him and rightfully so. He wields his silenced shotgun with orgasmic grace, carries and uses his airgun with pride. There is not a single shred of artificiality to his detachment from humanity. He lives in a world completely of his own. He doesnât kill to regain his money or kill for any reason. He just kills. That is what he does. He spends all day thinking about killing. He can not see anyone around him, nor does he care to. Through his circular and empty philosophies, he has gone so far insane that there isnât a word in the English language to describe what he is. Yet, it is because of this intangibility that we almost identify with him! He is so damn good at what he does. If one is thinking in rational terms (instead of trite Hollywood ones) they will see that there is no way for Llewelyn to survive. Nor his wife. They are not up against evil or a monster or any one-dimensional term that can be thought of to regularly describe a person who commits the acts Chigurh does. It is his precision; his bottled jubilation for doing what he does that makes him, perhaps, the most veristic character that comes to memory. 

Then there is Ed Tom (Tommy Lee Jones). He is the character to which the title refers to, among others. Chigurh eludes him. For him, Chigurhâs actions are incomprehensible. But itâs beyond incomprehension, really, because he is far too wise to believe anything is unforeseeable. He canât understand Chigurh, but he can empathize. He knows (without ever actually encountering him) the pain he feels. He understands such pain. Life is such pain. Any life. Any tedious, mundane, boring fucking life is such pain. The seconds go by without mercy. Time travels on without pity. If you end it now, you die. If you wait it out, you die. You die. You die. You die. Ed Tom knows this. He does not understand the actions of Chigurh, but he is one with him. Chigurh has been able to abandon any pretense of acceptable human behavior. He can go about, doing as he pleases, feeling no remorse. No pain. Or human pain, rather. Chigurh verges on tears several times, but they are not those of pain. Nor triumph, either. They are tears for anything that is remotely conceivable as life. Tears for being burdened with being alive. There is no God here and Chigurh knows it. There is no one to stop him, no one to interfere. Ed Tom knows it too. But he hasnât accepted what Chigurh has been able to. Accepted that knowledge, life, death: theyâre all games. It is all a game, the outcome irrelevant. This is no country for old men and no country for anybody. Ed Tomâs faÃ§ade of reality has long since shattered; his ideals of what a âlifeâ should be are meaningless. He could never have imagined a superego smashing antagonist like Chigurh, but there he is. He exists. What does he make of it? It is an unanswerable question. There is nothing in Ed Tomâs universe that can justify such an aberration: not God, not the Devil, nothing.

Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) completes the holy trinity. Ed Tom is the father. Llewelyn is the son. Chigurh is the Holy Spirit. He is grounded in life much like Ed Tom, but he strays. He is foolish. His journey with his newfound money is a completely hollow one. The money means nothing to him. But when you find a satchel of money, you grab it. You go on the run for it. Because money is what itâs all about. Thatâs what life is all about. Money. At no point does Llewelyn have any sort of cognition about what he is doing. He has been drilled and trained to respond without reason to finding such a satchel, whether or not he knows so consciously. Money means nothing to any of these characters, ultimately. It is what superficially drives them; their actual propellant is an unconscious desire for unity with each other. The id is Chigurh, the superego is Ed Tom, the ego is Llewelyn. One should not exist without the others. Or so it is said.

To quote the Washington Post: One argument could be made for the movie's integrity by way of the arcane narrative theories it employs. I don't buy it, but it could be made. It sets up a classic thriller situation, a particularly vivid hunter hunting a surprisingly capable man across a deadly landscape, used hundreds, perhaps thousands of times. It pauses time and again to emphasize the horror of the killer. By narrative convention then, the movie is building toward a confrontation between these two. We know it, we expect it, the rules of the thriller mandate its necessity. It represents the completion of the bargain the storyteller has made with us. 

"No Country for Old Men" then vigorously subverts the convention. It's meant to be "ironic," with that big capital I. Instead it's unsatisfying, with a capital U. Nobody goes to the movies for the irony. They go for the satisfaction.

The Coen Brothers are, if nothing else, unapologetic. Their style, in their writing, in their direction, and, maybe most importantly, their editing, is their own and will not be unduly influenced. It has created masterpieces (Fargo), it has damaged potentially wonderful films (The Man Who Wasn't There), and it has blown up in their faces (The Ladykillers). I was skeptical that they were adapting a book, any book, and I wasn't overly impressed with McCarthy's novel. But, as occasionally happens, a story mediocre in book form is flawless as film (see: The Godfather). The Coens take the best parts of McCarthy's novel, add their own touches, and drop everything that made the book too heavy for its own good. No Country For Old Men is everything it has to be, and nothing else. It doesn't overreach, it doesn't preach, and it doesn't wrap everything up into a message (what message there is gets destroyed in one of the final conversations). It's unforgiving and unsentimental. As it moves forward it feels increasingly small and claustrophobic despite its wide vistas, and tense to the point of cracking despite its stillness. Passages go for long stretches in virtual silence (sadly, these days the Oscar for best sound design often goes to the loudest movie -- any film in which the simple sound of unscrewing a light bulb is terrifying deserves notice). Characters are allowed to exist without being justified. Javier Bardem is beautifully sociopathic without being psychopathic: there is a logic, twisted as it is, behind his wonderfully dead eyes -- not just murderous rage which so many lesser antagonist characters would display. There is not a word or frame wasted, and there is nothing left to be desired. I've heard complaints about the film's ending, I think because there is not a final bit of action to resolve everything. But if you listen to what is said, there's no possible better way to end it. For me, this is up there with Pulp Fiction, Goodfellas, and Dr. Strangelove: A flawless movie.

Javier Bardem is a killer who escpaes the authorities to go on a killing rampage (and look for the money), and his performance is magnificently scary.  He is one of the more fascinating characters to come out of movies in recent years, because he is scary, ruthless, appalling, and yet interesting.  Some of the dialogue exchanges he has with his soon to be victims is unforgettable.  Tommy Lee Jones plays a sheriff who, while trying to track him down, comes to the realization that society (with murderers like this in it who have no compassion whatsoever) is just getting out of control to the point that perhaps he should retire.  Josh Brolin plays the other fellow who discovers the money, and he is a poor former welder looking to make a better life for himself and his wife. [color=white]Alfred Hitchcock was a great manipulator, and it's been famously quoted that he liked to play his audiences like a piano. So do Joel and Ethan Coen, who are the greatest manipulators since Hitchcock, and their newest film, [i]No Country for Old Men,[/i] is not only the best movie they've made since [i]Fargo[/i] in 1996, but it's also the very best thriller I have seen since [i]Fargo.[/i] There have been some very good films released his year, but none quite like this: This movie blew me away, and it's such a rich and satisfying experience that I wanted the projectionist to start it over again the minute the credits started to roll.[/color]
 
[color=white]The story begins in southwest Texas, where a man named Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is hunting on the plains and discovers the aftermath of a botched drug deal. Near the site, he finds a satchel filled with money, with which he flees. Soon enough, a relentless and elusive killer named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is after Moss, resulting in one of the most gripping cat-and-mouse games ever captured on film. On the edges of the movie is Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), a small-town sheriff who is investigating the strange murders Chirgurh has left in his wakehe kills strangers with a cattle gun, which quickly sends a bolt through the brain and back out again.[/color]
 
[color=white]That's all you'[/color][color=white]ll hear from me regarding the plot, which plays out so unpredictably that you will be glad you walked in cold. This is one dark, violent, uncompromising picture, but there's a certain joy in watching a story as unsettling as this unfold as flawlessly and unexpectedly as it does. It's a masterpiece of pure tension, and I can't remember the last time a movie held me in such unbelievable suspenseI was enthralled, unnerved, terrified and giddy, all at the same time. Going back to Hitchcock, he once remarked that he liked to make his audiences suffer, and the Coens do that here, as well: The film has been deliberately constructed to be as uncompromisingly gripping as possible, and there were moments when I could literally hear my blood pounding in my ears.[/color]
 
[color=white]As Chigurh, who is so mysterious and deadly that nobody really knows anything about him, Javier Bardem is indescribably horrifying. Sporting a bizarre haircut, a below-baritone voice and a dead, glazed stare, he is the scariest movie villain since Hannibal Lecter. We don't know why he's involved in the drug deal, why he uses a coin toss to determine who he kills and who he spares, or how he's able to track down his victims (yes, he has a GPS transmitter, but his accuracy in finding Moss is uncanny). That makes him all [/color][color=white]the creepier: Every time he comes on the screen, our heart sinks, our pulse quickens, we get chills up and down our spine.[/color]
 
[color=white]To again reference Hitchcock (who, if you haven't guessed already, would have loved this movie), let us remember that he once said, "The more successful the villain, the more successful the picture." It also helps that the film is based (very faithfully, I'm told) on a novel by the great Cormac McCarthy, and it personifies the same lean, disparaging style of his writing. McCarthy, like Faulkner and Hemingway before him, is an economic storyteller (he rarely takes the time to punctuate his conversation with quotation marks). He's perhaps best known for his brutal portrayals of the Old West, and [i]No Country for Old Men,[/i] despite being set in 1980, is, more or less, a westernthe basic narrative wouldnt be much different had it been set a century before it actually is.[/color]
 
[color=white][color=white]Although the story is one of gritty simplicity, what makes it truly special is the strange ambiguity of certain key sequences. Having run the film[/color] over again in my head, a few plot developments still mystify me. That adds to the bewildering effect of the film, and in pure McCarthy fashion, story elements that are considered commonplace in traditional thrillers are willingly glossed over. It works to the movie'[/color][color=white]s advantage, though: There is neither extra baggage nor any unnecessary complications, and every single scene feels as though it's absolutely integral to the outcome of the story.[/color]
 
[color=white]This brings me to the film's ending, which itself is strange, ambiguous, audacious and somewhat glossed over. It has inspired serious discussion and debate and has been deemed unsatisfying in a few circles. I wouldn't dream of giving it away, except to say that it comes when we're not particularly expecting it. Now, as I was leaving the theater, I noticed vastly different audience reactionssome were silently ruminating, others wore looks of slight surprise, a man in the back voiced his distaste toward the ending quite openly. I suppose people expect the various story threads to be neatly tied up, and if that's the case, they've missed the point of the film.[/color]
 
[color=white]The Coens leave us in an unexpected place, yes, but it's at a point where we need to be shown no more. Certainly we have unanswered questions, but I think they can be inferred from the little hints that are dropped throughout the film. I found the last scene to be particularly effective and entirely essentialnot only does it embody the film's overarching theme (the poster tagline is "There are no clean getaways," although I think a better one would be "Life's a bitch, and then you die"), but it works as a perfect bookend to the opening scene. Thrillers so often deliver as mindless, cookie-cutter action fare, and it's refreshing to see one that doesn't give us easy answers, one that gets us thinking.[/color]
 
[color=white]The last great movie the Coen brothers made was [i]Fargo,[/i] which is, I believe, the only title to appear on the AFI's list of the most thrilling films as well as on its list of the funniest. [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is just as good, as strange, as exciting and as rewarding as [i]Fargo,[/i] which is no mean feat. What's so amazing about the movie is how well every little element comes together, how brilliantly the Coens utilize every single aspect of the filmmaking process, how they hit every note exactly right. So often thrillers bend over backward to involve us, but here's one that is so confident in the intensity of its story and the strength of its characters that it feels almost effortless. It's a great, great film, and it will stay with you for a long time to come.[/color]

Spoiler Alert:  I've been advised that this review reveals too much to those who have not seen the movie so, if you have not seen it, you might want to stop reading now.

Over two weeks ago I reviewed this movie and gave it 2.5 stars.  I was right then that it was too soon to review it.  Still difficult for me to review this one.

The movie occupied my thoughts during a couple of runs.  Scenes replayed themselves at other times as well, when I should have been thinking about or focusing on something else.  When a movie pulls on my mind like that, I want to figure out why.

The scene that opened my eyes to what I had first missed was the one in which Jones' character enters the hotel room where Llewelyn was killed and buries his head in his hands.  

Bardem's character, a sociopathic killer, the distillation of evil in man, the devil--who or what he is depends on the lens of the viewer--is hiding behind the open hotel room door.   Why is he hiding?  Why does he remain in hiding?  

Because he is afraid.  His expression, holding his breath, scrunched up behind the door, is one of terror.  In every other scene in this movie, this guy does not hesitate to put a hole in everyone he encounters, except for the  gas station attendant who happens to call the right side of a coin.  (A killer's whim that was, and a side of dumb luck.)

The prospect of taking on Jones' sheriff, who is as good as Bardem's villain is bad, causes the villain to cower in the corner.  Maybe he suspects he will lose this fight.  Maybe "the good" must survive in order to provide an ongoing context, a livlihood for "the bad."  Without the survival of this dichotomy, "the bad" would melt away and collapse into itself like the Wicked Witch of the West.  Lots of possibilities here.  And "the ugly" Llewelyn just gets lucky for awhile, running up his tab however and wherever he can find purchase.

The old trinity has been disbanded.  Llewelyn's luck of the ugly runs out during a shootout that takes place off-stage.  Off-stage!  This world has a trinity reserved just for bad guys, and two good guys, and Llewelyn.  Too many players for rules.  The rules, if they still exist, are as soft as overcooked spaghetti.

The desert is what men make of it, and in this case, most of them possess a gift for making it a mess.  Starting with Llewelyn's imperfect kill of a pronghorn and subsequent failure to find the animal to put it out of its misery because he is, oh so easily, sidetracked.  

The Mexican characters are portrayed as opportunistic, cardboard demons.  They are casualties of themselves.  The true demon is Javier Bardem's character, and he is, perhaps, the ambulatory distilIation of all that is not right in human nature.  The devil does not exist except when men bring him to life.  There's a reason why Bardem's character has red-rimmed eyes.  

Harrelson's good, bad guy, or bad, good guy in white does not last long.  He is quickly dispatched by the evil page boy wielding an idiotic but deadly airgun device.  Imagine if that had happened to a Clint Eastwood character?  But he did not wear white, and things were simpler then.

I don't care for unrevelatory moral relativism in art.  I prefer that if violence be a part, that it be a part that serves as a means to a greater end.  Here, violence is the beginning, the middle, and that is the first impression I had of the movie, but then, violence is not quite the end.

"You can't stop what's comin," a hermit friend advises Jones' Sheriff.  In NCOM, he's the only one who has a chance in Hell to stop what's coming.  And it is not in his nature to stop trying.  I give him three days before he gives up on retired life.

I watched "No Country for Old Men" last night and it has been in my head ever since.  The last time a movie did that was the hypnotic "Mulholland Drive". The cinematography is gorgeous and the dialogue is poetic - hallmarks of the Coen brothers' film resume.

   The abrupt ending to "No Country", in which Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) simply recounts a couple dreams he had the previous night, really bothered me at first.  I initially felt robbed - of what exactly, I wasn't sure.  I guess I wanted some sort of meaning to all of the death I just observed.  But after absorbing the movie, I realized that accepting the capriciousness of life and death as encapsulated in "No Country" is just plain difficult to do.  Now, I consider the ending to be brilliant.

   In an allegorical sense, it is obvious that the character Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a professional hitman hired to recover drug money, represents death or fate.  He kills without compunction and exposes how helpless we are when our "time" comes.  No matter how much begging is done by his victims, Chigurh dispenses death like it is a banal chore.  What he does, or more accurately what he is, has nothing to do with right or wrong.  In my opinion, he doesn't represent evil.  Instead he represents one of the cold facts or principles of life - our own mortality.  Chigurh is described by assassin Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) in the following way:

"You don't understand. You can't make a deal with him. Even if you gave him the money he'd still kill you. He's a peculiar man. You could even say that he has principles. Principles that transcend money or drugs or anything like that. He's not like you. He's not even like me."

   The film's rugged, dusty booted protagonist, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), is an average man fighting for that satchel of drug money, as well as for his very life.  You root for Moss, but deep down there is the feeling of impending doom.  Moss is confident that he can turn the tables and become the hunter and Chigurh the hunted.  But one can only run away from death for so long.  His hubris leads to his violent end, which the audience does not observe.  I believe this was done to underscore the inevitability of it all.  The chase was what was unique; his death was a given.  This notion is epitomized in the dialogue between Chigurh and the gas station porprietor, in which Chigurh flips a coin for the proprietor's life and states the following:

"It's [the coin] been traveling twenty-eight years to get here. And now it's here. And it's either heads or tails, and you have to say. Call it."

In other words, life is a winding and unexpected journey.  But the destination is always the same.

   Overall, Sheriff Bell is central to the story.  In the beginning, he narrates on what it takes to be a lawman in Texas and states:

"I always knew you had to be willing to die to even do this job - not to be glorious. But I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand."

What is arguably the most important scene in the movie is when Bell enters the motel room exhibiting Chigurh's signature "calling card" - blown locks.  We see Chigurh hiding behind one of the doors of the hotel room.  The bathroom window is clearly locked from the inside.  Bell discovers that the vent cover had been removed with a coin and realizes the money is gone.  He sits on the motel bed, deep in thought, before ultimately deciding to leave the room without further investigation.  In my opinion, Bell knows that Chigurh is hiding in the room.  But the question for Bell at this moment is whether or not he is willing to "push [his] chips forward and go out and meet something [he] doesn't understand".

   There are a number of things that can hasten one's meeting with their own "Chigurh".  The movie highlights a series of deaths all tied to ill-gotten money and drugs.  Bell had no intention of getting involved and risking his own death, despite the fact that is what is expected from a Sheriff.  He did not even return to the original crime scene in the desert when requested from other police agents.  In a way, Bell is a coward.  But in the end, despite all his efforts to avoid that meeting, he will get that coin flip.  This is nicely illustrated in Bell's dream, which he describes in some poetic prose:

"When he [Bell's father] rode past I seen he was carryin fire in a horn the way people used to do and I could see the horn from the light inside of it. About the color of the moon. And in the dream I knew that he was goin on ahead and that he was fixin to make a fire somewhere out there in all that dark and all that cold, and I knew that whenever I got there he would be there. Out there up ahead."

Bell's father and uncles died young, something that came along with being honorable Texas lawmen - hence the title "No Country for Old Men".  Bell may have avoided this particular fate, but his mortality is unavoidable and he will be with his father in "all that dark and all that cold ... out there up ahead."

'No Country for Old Men' is another dark thriller masterpiece directed by brothers Joel and Ethan Coen. In 1980, Lewellyn Moss, while hunting deer in the Texas desert, comes across what seems to be the aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong. There he finds a satchel containing two million dollars, which he takes. On his trail is Anton Chigurh, a hitman who is hired to recover the money. Following this case is the old experienced sherrif Ed Tom Bell, who tries to reach Moss and save him before Chigurh can get to him. This sets up for a great cat-and-mouse chase film. Josh Brolin gives a wonderful performance as Moss. A lot of the movie's focus is on him, and shows in great detail how he is able to avoid Chigurh and a Mexican gang who is also after the money. The direction from the Coens and the editing from Roderick Jaynes is very precise in following and showing Moss' methods of stashing the money, hiding in hotel rooms, and running/driving from his predators. Tommy Lee Jones is perfect in the role of Sherrif Bell. Who else could play the part of an ageing Sherrif who questions the world he's living in and laments the increasing violence in it. But the undisputed star in 'No Country for Old Men' is Javier Bardem's Academy Award-winning performance as Chigurh. Sporting an odd haircut throughout the film and using a cattle stun-gun as his weapon of choice, Bardem is cold and remorseless, stopping at nothing to fullfill his mission. He's like other great movie villains like Michael Myers from 'Halloween' or Arnold Schwarenegger's Terminator, only he isn't just a one note character, Chigurh has depth. Like another great villain, Two-Face of the Batman universe, Chigurh uses a coint-toss to make fateful decisions. And 'No Country for Old Men' 's underlining theme is fate. Something the Coen brothers have previously explored in 'Blood Simple' and 'Fargo'. 'No Country for Old Men' is a beautiful looking film, being set in Texas we are shown the wide open landscapes of the desert creating a feeling of eerie isolation for Moss, just like the Minnesota snow did in 'Fargo'. This is a crime thriller of the best kind and one of the best films to come out of the 2000s.

Brilliant, BRILLIANT movie.  The Coens have long been among my favorite directors (Blood Simple and Fargo are mandatory viewing as far as I am concerned) and while this is far different from any other film, it may be one of their best efforts in years. The usual Coen trademarks are there: terrific supporting cast, seamless editing, bizarre black humor, and dialogue that has a walloping punch.  However the film doesn't only adhere to their style of filmmaking, but is also faithful to its source.  This film really captures the cadence of Cormac McCarthy's twisted fables and has created a unique film that is part Western, part crime film, part thriller, and part Greek Tragedy.  The movie asks a very simple question: how do can decent man atone for their sins in a world that can create sinful men who feel no remorse for their crimes?  The film shows the actions and consequences that are associated with this theme throughout the film, and while the ending seemed esoteric to some, the final monologue is expertly expressing this entire concept.  The performances are great all around, but Javier Bardem is simply astounding as Anton Chigurt, one of the most chilling villains since Hannibal Lector.  He maintains a bizarre look (an absurd Prince Valiant haircut) that makes you feel as if it would be ridiculous to fear him, but his every move and action make him horrifying.  The fact that he himself still maintains a code that he never wavers from, no matter how sadistic that code may be, only intensifies the fascinating aspects of the character.  Josh Brolin is also terrific, and Tommy Lee Jones plays a role I can't see any other actor portraying to be honest as the laconic, old-fashioned sheriff who is trying to understand how some men can be driven to such violent indecency.  If you have not yet seen this film, you are really missing out on an incredible cinematic experience.

There are TWO types of Coen Bros. movies.  You have to know that in knowing their careers.  They do the really trippy dark crime movies like Fargo, Blood Simple, Miller's Crossing, and now No Country for Old Men.  Then they also love to do their sendups of the 30s screwball comedies like Raising Arizona, Intolerable Cruelty, The Ladykillers and Lebowski.  Never the two shall meet.  And it's odd because for awhile there they went on a stretch doing just the comedies, and even though Fargo was their mainstream breakthrough film, after the success of O Brother (screwball comedy), they seemed to have left the dark film behind.

Now they've returned to it, and many people seem to have a bitter taste in their mouth about it.

(I keep hearing about this crackpot theory that HE ended up with the money, which I don't buy at all)

Then they also love to do their sendups of the 30s screwball comedies like Raising Arizona, Intolerable Cruelty, The Ladykillers and Lebowski.  Never the two shall meet.  And it's odd because for awhile there they went on a stretch doing just the comedies, and even though Fargo was their mainstream breakthrough film, after the success of O Brother (screwball comedy), they seemed to have left the dark film behind.

Now they've returned to it, and many people seem to have a bitter taste in their mouth about it.

I do have to confess that the ending left something to be desired for me.  I never understood what the payoff was from Tommy Lee Jones character other than to verbalize the meaning of the film.  (I keep hearing about this crackpot theory that HE ended up with the money, which I don't buy at all)

When I read the book, I thought, "Here's a screenplay disguised as a novel." Having seen the film, I wish I hadn't read the book - I was right, it's better as a film, even if it's not quite satisfying (nor particularly disturbing) in either format.

The just okay: Tommy Lee Jones looks exhausted, which shouldn't win him any awards but probably will. As for the Coen brothers: they exercise great restraint in approaching this material, which lends considerable grace and dignity to the film. Unfortunately, I think that restraint explains also why they can't quite transcend the flaws in the book.

Spoilers:
Essentially, by eliding the final scenes of violence - presumably for thematic reasons - the movie attempts to make a decision for us. I'm not sure what that decision is, exactly, only that it has to do with our response to/expectation of violence. Whatever, it feels like a mistake. Perhaps the Coens just wanted to flout (as did Mr. McCarthy) our desire for resolution. Anyway, as in the book, we don't get to see Llewelyn's last stand, and, in fact, much of the later violence is merely suggested. And I am fine with that, except that Tommy Lee Jones can't quite carry the last thirty minutes of this movie by himself (opposite Bardem, that is. Kelly McDonald as Carla Jean tries to help out, and she does a fine job). Maybe it's because Tommy Lee Jones is just too folksy. Maybe it's because even if Llewelyn's was a fool's errand, he deserved a better end (this is the movies after all). Either way, I left out of there completely blown away by Mr. Bardem's performance. Upon further reflection, I found myself slightly disappointed by the fact that the Coen's didn't have the courage to make the story their own. After all, they long ago earned the right to do whatever they want with whatever they choose to do - and that includes even a book by the great Cormac McCarthy. 

They did achieve something, however: they let Javier Bardem run with it, and stayed out of his way. Smart.

No Country for Old Men is a strange and wonderful kind of film.  The movie creeps along at an unsettlingly slow pace and yet you will be glued to the screen every moment.  No Country for Old Men may be the Coen Brothers masterpiece.  Does it rival fargo?  I say it surpasses it; which might not be fair because they are totally different film, Fargo being much lighter, NCFOM being much grittier.  
Without going into the finer details, the movie begins with Llewelyn Moss, masterfully played by Josh Bolin stumbling upon what seems to be a drug deal gone bad.  After finding two million dollars in a satchel, he finds himself on the run for his life from various drug runners and Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem).  Tommy Lee Jones plays Ed Tom Bell, the local sheriff who catches on to what trouble Moss is in and attempts to help.  This is the setup for one of the most riveting, layer, and bleakly wonderful movies ever made.  
And so much of it rests on the shoulders of Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh.  NCFOM is definitely a character driven piece, all of them inspiringly complex and human.  But none are as profound as Anton Chigurh.  Javier Bardem has succeeded in created what I believe to be the most frightening character ever played on film.  I have seen more horror movies that I can count, yet I have never felt as tense as I did whenever he came on screen.  His role is positively brilliant, a true personification of pure evil.  This is a man who can make a quarter the most frightening thing you've ever seen.  Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones also give masterful and both darkly funny roles.  Seeing these characters entangled in a deadly chase for money that begins to lose it's value as all the characters begin to see how damned they truly are.  
In the end, No Country for Old Men is a staggeringly power, beautiful, and haunting film that is unrelentingly brilliant.  One aspect of the film that many will hate is that it leaves so much up to interpretation, when you leave the theatre you won't want to talk about anything but this film.  The true beauty of No Country For Old Men is that it's made up of seemingly unimportant moments that end up holding so much weight, not unlike all our lives.  The film also contains a scene with Chigurh at a gas station which is one of the greatest scenes I've ever had the pleasure of viewing.  The movie is gritty, bloody, and can't be ignored.  No Country for Old Men is a forced to be reckoned with.  Destined to go down as an American Classic.

A bleak showdown, played out in indistinguishably ratty motel rooms throughout west Texas. On one side, unalloyed good, the smalltown sheriff played by craggy and decent Tommy Lee Jones. On the other side, a terrifying and futuristic assassin, played by Almodovar star Javier Bardem. Too humorless to be sadistic, he wields a slaughterhouse implement designed to turn cattle (that is to say, us) into dead meat. In between them, running for dear life and two million bucks is Recognizable American Behavior-- a weak-willed welder, played by Josh Brolin, who is clever enough to elude these two titanic forces and keep hold of a pilfered bag of loot. For a while at least. The sheriff believes that the universe is being overtaken by what another Texas lawman calls "the dismal tide"-- in fact, when the welder first espies the massacre site where the fatal money lays, a sickening shadow passes over the desert landscape. Who will win in the end? The stakes are much higher than right versus wrong. The stakes are right versus utter amorality, with the survival of even the most innocent decided by the flip of a coin.

There are no clear moral heroes here, just three average man overshadowed by a psychopathic killer the likes of which haven't been seen on screen since Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs. The dialogue is sharp as a blade, and each frame serves the story to perfection. Forget anything else you may have seen from the Coens, especially Fargo, for all of the quirky humor and laughs are discarded for nerve-shredding tension and unbearable suspense. The cinematography, art direction and costumes are all grounded in gritty realism, and the screenplay is a marvel. The performances from Jones, Brolin, ad Harrelson are wonderful, but the villain created by Bardem is so opaque, so intense, and so terrifying that his is the character you will remember after viewing the film. One of the best of 2007, and perhaps the peak in the careers of two very gifted filmmakers.

I rarely say this about a film, but No Country truly is a masterpiece.

Javier Bardem is a relentless arbiter of these rules, and he is the essence of stone cold killer.  He is unstoppable.  Death is unstoppable.  Between Tommy Lee Jones as the town Sheriff, Josh Brolin as the hunter on the run with the killer's money, they work out the question of whether or not it is acceptable to give up in the face of it.  This may be the quietest film about a mass murder that I have ever seen.  Relentless and delicious.

Like Haneke's 'Funny Games' before it (among many others, I'm sure), the Coens have made two films for two very different audiences: a cat-and-mouse thriller revolving around the pursuit of wealth (a theme not unfamiliar to the Coens) and a dismal account of helplessness in troubling times (insert political interpretation here). As in 'Funny Games' (where a violent psychological thriller medium is used to subvert the medium of violent psychological thrillers), there is good deal of capitalizing on the first theme to draw in the first crowd and then drive home the second theme. A test of sorts -- which is going to be missed by most, going to feel contrived and insulting to some, and intelligent and resourceful to others (myself included in the latter camp). The reason I am in the latter camp is because I feel that 'No Country for Old Men' shows itself as more admirable than the Haneke film I am comparing it to (and other comparable films) in that it spends a good deal of time (its last 20 minutes) disallowing the possibility of the first reading, undermining the expectations of the typical cat-and-mouse thriller. 'Funny Games' as well as countless anti-war films allow themselves to be taken as pleasurable displays of violence to the bloodthirsty who choose to leave the theory aside. 'No Country for Old Men' makes it very difficult for those wishing to leave the second reading aside to get any enjoyment out of it (as demonstrated by the catcalls and booing heard after the screening I attended). I should also mention its captivating cinematography impressed me to no end.

No Country For Old Men is an absolutely brilliant tense, thrilling masterpiece from the Coen brothers. I was literally blown away by how good this film really was. It is one of the rare thrillers that wins the Best Picture award. It is a film that you get totally gripped with in such a suspenseful way that makes you feel that you are really there taking the journey with all of the characters and are feeling some of the things that the characters are feeling within it. The suspense isn't so much the events that happen but it was mostly the suspense is between the characters within the film. There is this sort of cat-and-mouse game that is played where one man chases and goes after another man for money. This is very hard to watch on some rare occasions because it is a very violent film which is so deadly and so unmerciful that it can make you feel a tiny bit sick. I don't really know whether to call this film a western or not because there aren't any cowboys but I suppose it is because it is set in deserts and large fields where they are sheriffs wearing cowboy hats. I find it to be a rather rare treasured film from filmmakers that have done similar sorts of films in the past.

It was more of the hard situations he ended up in because of his being a fugitive to Anton to earn the $2 million. His performance was a good contender for Best Leading Actor at the 80th Academy Awards but I think Emile Hirsch hada better chance at it. Tommy Lee Jones is absolutely awesome as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. He is a laconic, soon-to-retire small-town sheriff who is meant to try and hunt down Anton Chigurh. Javier Bardem delivers one of the most terrifying male performances of all time and one of the best film villains of all time too. Anton is cold hearted killer who is after the $2 million so he can buy more weapons. Anton Chigurh is a sociopathic assassin hired to recover the drug money.

 The Coen brothers have had their share of hits and misses since they exploded into the industry with [i]Blood Simple[/i], as of yet unseen by me. We've had some glorious comedies ([i]The Big Lebowski[/i], [i]O Brother, Where Art Thou?[/i]) and some mediocre ones ([i]The Ladykillers[/i], [i]Intolerable Cruelty[/i]) as well as some truly glorious dramas ([i]Miller's Crossing[/i], [i]Barton Fink[/i]). Their real success, however, came in 1996 when they created the spectacular experience of [i]Fargo[/i], the best film that year. As much as I adore their 1996 masterpiece, they might have outdone themselves with the Cormac McCarthy adaptation [i]No Country for Old Men[/i]. Here is a film so wondrous in its execution one wishes for it to last forever. There is an exchange between Javier Bardem's frighteningly calm sadist and a convenience store clerk that is so well written and acted as to be completely captivating and mezmerizing. I adored this film. If there comes a better film this year, I will be surprised. [b]**** (out of ****) A+[/b]

 [center][img]http://i63.photobucket.com/albums/h159/NuBz86/mist2.jpg[/img][/center]
 [center][i]Shockingly great shocker from brilliant minds of King and Darabont.[/i][/center]
  
 I wasn't expecting much from director Frank Darabont's third Stephen King adaptation, and I think my lack of expectations was the best thing that could ever have happened to me as a filmgoer. [i]Stephen King's The Mist[/i] is not only a terrifying, gory and delightfully ingenious fright flick, but it is also a truly top-notch film. I cannot recall being more emotionally involved with the characters in a monster movie, and for that I am grateful. I should not have expected anything less from the man responsible for both [i]The Shawshank Redemption[/i] and [i]The Green Mile[/i]. What makes the film different from all the other monster movies in all the annals of moviemaking is that the real monsters are the human characters. Marcia Gay Harden, whom I adore, creates such a despicably wicked villain here, and it is to her credit that I, having seen many of her previous roles (none of which make her out to be evil...or even bad), who did not think she could pull it off, was blown away and proved wrong in my assumptions once again. This is a great horror film, and a glorious feat of originality. [b]**** (out of ****) A[/b]
