Before anybody asks why this film's a star shy of perfection, let me explain.  Yes, I did sit in the dark chewing at my fingers and holding a drink cup dear to my eyesight but at the end of the film, just two hours past the tension filled unnerving chase thriller I started asking questions, questions about things that just didn't make much sense.  Still, what you get in every frame of this latest Coen noir is a film filled with nail-biting suspense, that can drive you bonkers at its intensity.  Yes cinematically it really works even holds up to some of their best films and other films of its genre.  It is shot for shot stunning to look at, even its blood infested scenes.  The principles are all at their finest with Bardem's memorable turn as a cold blooded psychopath edging just past Jones' conscientious  sheriff & Brolin's naive everyman.  Given the bleak nature of the story this is certainly a tough yet worthy time at the movies. Now here come the questions, and there are many unresolved issues at hand, how does everyone manoeuver from one place to another so quickly?  What is Jones' character doing tracking down everyone in areas out of his jurisdiction? Why does Bardem constantly turn into an incarnation of Michael Myers?  These are just for starters.  There are plenty more.  I do however applaud the Coen Brothers for choosing a very dignified way of killing off a central character by not exploiting the murder, especially considering how gruesome the  film is up until that point.

Javier Bardem plays one of the most intimidating villans and pure embodyment of evil I have ever seen, to the point where he "in a way has his own set of principles".  He brings such a cold, calculated and confident air to the character that it is only fitting his weapon of choice is an instrument that is used for mindlessly slaughtering cattle. Some of the best scenes in the movie involve his brief but physically unnerving conversations with other characters, my favorite of whcih is with the gas attendent. One thing is for sure I will never look at a coin toss the same way again.This would be a great action or neo-western in its own right, but if that is all you take away from it you have missed so much more.  What really makes this movie tick is the unbelievable performances from all three main actors ( Can anybody in Hollywood say so much without saying a word as Tommy Lee Jones?), and the perfectly paced and timed hand of the Coen brothers.  This is a romantic movie about how the old west has become corrupted and left behind the cowboy and honest lawman and replaced them with drug runners and psychopatich killers.  It is a movie about a man who once viewed himself as a proud and respected sheriff and now all he sees is destruction and a new way of life that has left him in the dust and you can see the hurt and admitted defeat in his eyes and voice of every scene Jones is in until the very last scene where he relates the idealized vision he still holds dear but realizes it has become no more than a dream.

This is one of the most fatalistic, cynical movies ever made, and while I'm sure most of that lies with Cormac McCarthy's book, it's exactly what the Coens needed to get back in tip-top form. Probably the best in their crime-noir series so far, the movie has all the same beautiful cinematography, inspired violence, and across-the-board memorable characters they always serve up, but this one is especially elevated by Javier Bardem in a performance and role so scary that he'd make Robert Mitchum cry like a little girl. His presence in the film shakes me to the core, and left me feeling as jacked up and shivery as if I had actually come face to face with his Death Tank and somehow lived to tell about it. It would be downright retarded to short-change Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones, and Woody Harrelson for their own award-winning performances, but Anton Chigurh is literally the new villain to beat, in my opinion. One of the darkest and starkest thrillers ever made, this is an instant classic for a reason, and while I might argue that it lacks a little of the distinct personality of some of their zanier projects, this pulls off some equally difficult feats by being a masterpiece as a straightforward, Western-style suspense chaser, and a masterpiece as an essay on the rapidly declining safety and sanity of Americans. This joins other twisted, depressingly murderous recent films like the Proposition to serve as an example that they don't make 'em like they used to. They make 'em just a little bit better. And seeing the Coen Brothers, who rival the Andersons as the best living filmmakers in the world, back on their A-game again is like finding out your husband is out of his coma. I mean wife. The hollow eyes of Javier Bardem ensnare us with his unoccupied    look of absence through the eerie movie posters placed throughout the theater. This is the look of pure apathetic evil. The real kind. The kind with no mercy and total disregard to penalties. 
	 In "Country" a chillingly cold-blooded killer, Chigurh (Javier Bardem), is on a manhunt for Lleweln Moss (Brolin) who unintentionally stumbled onto a briefcase of cash belonging to Chigurh. The eyes belong to Chigurh, the absolute pentacle of evil on earth, developed by screenwriters/directors Joel and Ethan Coen.
     As I write about this film, I will do my best not to allude to the ending, which is, at the least, questionable. But it is nearly impossible to review this film without brining it up.
    The Coen brothers have created a legendary character in Chigurh. Rarely have we seen a villain with such subtle eeriness and abandon for reproduction. He is much like the Terminator (if he were real). The character development is perfect in this flick. The Sheriff Bell (Jones) character plays a wonderfully contrasting roll as a similarly apathetic law enforcer. 
     This film comes out of the gate in full force. The plot is incarcerating and paralyzes the viewer in a unique way. The story unfolds on screen visually, there is very little dialog in most of the film, but what dialog there is, is vintage Coen brothers nasty wittiness. Unfortunately, the end, I feel hurts this film. 
     To me this is a great example of the differences in two medias. Story telling in books is much different than story telling in movies. A book can give you so much more than a film can visually illustrate and I believe it is shown in this adaptation, especially the end. 
     This film runs 122 minutes and is rated R for violence and language. Even with the downside, this is still a highly entertaining film full of mystery, wit, and blood. There is no doubt this film will be in the big five on Oscar night and Bardem will be nominated individual and will probably win. Fittingly, the Coen Brothers will be awarded in their own right as they have put out one of the best films of the year.

Lean, tense, uncompromising.   Damn near perfect, and hard to take.  What starts as a bloody and thrilling chase film turns out to be a haunting study of failed masculinity.  A lot of people will have trouble with the last 20 minutes, as the Coens omit a couple of key moments of violence that would be gratuitous -- by then, nothing is more menacing than Javier Bardem casually checking his boot for blood as he exits yet another crime scene.  They get major points for not pandering to the audience, although this means many will be confused by the ending -- anyone who missed what Tommy Lee Jones saw on the floor of the motel room might not understand the depths of his despair at the end, having failed to live up to the example of his father and uncle or to his responsibilities as a lawman to confront evil, even at risk to his own life.

No Country For Old Men is a stark, chilling masterpiece;
A masterpiece that is executed perfectly in tone and feel and a masterpiece with oscar-worthy performances abound -- especially from Javier Bardem as what will surely be remembered as one of the most grim and harrowing big-screen antagonists in years. 

This is a film that makes no attempt at stylizing or dressing up the characters and their situations. In fact, with no real typical movie sheen to speak of, there's plenty of room for substance, though some movie-goers will certainly find this substance hard to recognize. The film takes you on a harsh, bloody, and unapologetic journey and in the end, when the credits roll, you are left alone; drained and numb, with hardly the will to think over what you've seen. This is undoubtedly a mark of success for the film and it's film-makers, as it definitely seeks to paint the most bleak and apathetic picture possible.

When I use the word "masterpiece" to describe this film, it says a great deal about just how much I love the atmosphere and mood provided by the Coen Brothers' direction and the performances from their all-star cast because truly I think to myself that the film is flawed. I can say this and still declare it a masterpiece because, as a stand-alone piece of art in the medium, it is without any real flaw. However, having read Cormac McCarthy's novel before watching, I have to say that this is a flawed film strictly to me personally because of what was chosen to be left out from the source material. Certainly when translating a novel for the big-screen it's necessary to judge what works and what doesn't for the recipient medium, but I feel that the pieces that were chosen to be left out could've worked EXTREMELY well and, in many cases, could've given the amazing cast a chance to further flex their acting muscles. 

Still -- the focused direction and writing, the superb performances, and the beautiful cinematography all speak loudly through subtlety and together forge a triumphant return for the Coen Brothers in this gritty, all-too-realistic thriller.

With a truly evil and unsympathizing villain and plenty of terrifying encounters, No Country for Old Men transports the viewer to 1980s Texas, where a serial killer is on the loose and will stop at nothing to reacquire a briefcase full of over $2 million.  While making this film, the Coen Brothers achieved a remarkable feat: not only do we know that this takes place in the desolate Texas deserts, but we can FEEL it.  Every outdoor shot makes you feel further engrossed in the story, whether it's Brolin out hunting or Bardem stranded on the side of the road waiting for an unsuspecting villain to come along.  An incredible story with an incredible cast, No Country for Old Men is the runaway (haha, pun) hit of the year, receiving some of the strongest reviews in movie history.  Don't let the badmouthing of the ending dissuade you.  You may not get it at first, but if you think on it, you will realize exactly what it meant and why it was the perfect way to end.  Films that make you think should be praised, not denigrated.

Words cannot express the sheer brilliance of "No Country for Old Men." Ethan and Joel Coen are cinematic masterminds. Josh Brolin is fantastic as a cowboy who stumbles upon a satchel of drug money and flees for his life. And special mention should be given to Javier Bardem for playing the most fearsome, psychopathic murderer to hit cinema in recent years. The Coen Brothers' writing here is among some of their finest work. Even though the film was adapted from a novel, you'd almost swear they'd invented the story themselves. And "No Country for Old Men" turns violence into an absolute art form. This is unarguably one of the very best movies of the year (perhaps the very best). I am in awe by its greatness.

The film, adapted from the novel by Cormac McCarthy, examines the situation which follows after Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin in another excellent turn) discovers a drug deal gone bad in the deserts of Texas.  He finds the bodies, the guns, and then the money.  He takes some of the guns, all the money, and leaves the bodies behind.  He soon realizes that he is being hunted; on one hand by a gang of Mexicans who have something to do with the deal; on the other hand by a ruthless psychopath named Anton Chigurgh (played incredibly by Javier Bardem).  Both parties were hired by a rich businessman of sorts (William Root), who in turn hires a bounty hunter (Woody Harrelson) to take care of things when things get out of hand.  Also in the mix is Sherriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones in anther great performance).  He investigates the killings in the desert, and the bodies of others who were unfortunate enough to meet Chigurgh along his hunt for the stolen money.  
Jones delivers two great monologues in the film.  One at the start, off-screen, narrated to Roger Deakin?s beautiful cinematography, and the other at the very end of the film as the camera remains steady on his face.  These monologues are just two of the marvels of No Country for Old Men.  The cinematography is breathtaking; the dialogue superb.  Another marvel of delivery in the film is virtually every line of dialogue delivered by Bardem. Consider one scene in which, after being offended by the small talk of a gas station attendant, where he forces the man to call a coin toss.  The wager is ?everything,? and though it goes unspoken, the attendant quietly realizes the brevity of the situation.  The only issue I take with the film is with some of the lines given to Carson Welles, the bounty hunter played by Woody Harrelson.  Some of his lines seem out of place, but that they are delivered so well it hardly matters.  That the film makes no real false steps completely erases any other small issues.  
The film merits some serious artistic credits.  Shots, dialogue, editing all have moments of incredible beauty and meaning.  The camera work and set up of shots are incredibly well crafted.  Things move at a deliberate speed, never too fast, never too slow, and serve to heighten tension to a tee.  I was reminded of one of two films this year that blew me away.  That film was Bela Tarr?s The Man from London.  The other was No Country for Old Men.  Though the camera shots are never as long or as lingering, some of it?s fluid and slow movements reminded very much of Tarr?s style.  Whether the Cohen?s have seen his work or not however is irrelevant.  One of the most glorious moments in the film comes as one character makes his final appearance.  The framing, the dialogue, and the final slow fade amount to such a great sendoff a better one can not be imagined.   
The film takes its subject matter more seriously than Fargo did, and contains just the right mix of violence, poetry, odd humor and pathos.  Therein lies the .5 missing from Fargo.  In that film the mixture was off, not a bad thing but nevertheless after seeing No Country for Old Men I recognized that?s what had been perplexing me.  
The closing monologue by Ed Tom Bell about a dream he had of his father, is one of the most important moments in the film, delivered by its most important character.  His final words and the final cut in the film will stay with you:  '?And then I woke up?.' Cut to black.

Or, how the Coen Brothers got their groove back.  After years of toiling with appealing, if unmemorable, fluff, the masterminds behind "The Big Lebowski" and "Barton Fink" are back.  

Like the two aformentioned titles, "No Country" is a pastiche of genre films, and a great one at that.  It crossbeeds the Western, the gangster film, and the chase thriller with a masterful injection of naturalism and introspection, making the end result enthralling, exciting, thought-provoking, and terrifying all at once.

Llewellyn Moss (Brolin) stumbles across a satchel of money at the scene of a drug-deal gone wrong.  He absconds with the money, with intentions to use it in a way even he may not know.

Psychopathic killer/hitman Chigurh (a chilling Bardem) is soon in hot pursuit of Moss, leaving a trail of mostly innocent bystanders dead in his wake.

From there, "No Country" becomes an incredibly taut thriller, with one gripping set piece after another.

However, an unexpected death of a major character about 3/4 through the film changes the mood of the entire film; it's a masterful curve ball, elevating the movie from relentless chase to thoughtful meditation on the nature of man, crime, and just how much the former can take of the latter when it produces so much human suffering.

Easily the best film of 2007.  Hands-down.

Many have pissed and moaned about the ending, and many still will. But I think they're missing the big point. The movie is about Tommy Lee Jones' character. Although we spend a great deal of time with him, Josh Brolin's story is a sub-plot comment on desperation, moral choices, and the issues surrounding money (mo' money, mo' problems - as they say).

But you need to look no further than the title of the movie for what the main theme is. Quite simply, Jones' Sheriff Bell is wondering whether the world is passing him by and whether he is cut out for the job he's done so well for so long anymore. Pay close attention to his narration/monologues. From [I]The Lumberjack[/I]
When I reviewed [I]Michael Clayton[/I], I was introduced to a whole new experience as a film critic. People (only a few, but still) approached me and said, How could you recommend this movie? It was so boring (meaning slow) and talky (meaning dialogue driven). Bring on the complaints yet again, because the only movie I saw this year that trumps [I]Clayton[/I] is [I]No Country for Old Men[/I], the new film from the Coen Brothers.
[I]No Country[/I] revolves around three different individuals all intertwined in the same game. The film begins with a monologue from Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), in which he describes a teenager he sent to the electric chair for killing his 14-year old girlfriend. The words are read with the precision and contained sorrow of a tired man, and beautifully introduce the film as an analysis of the sick and twisted people in the world. Bell wonders, as the audience does, how such vile creatures can exist and roam free.
We are then immediately introduced to such an individual. His name is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), and he is a killer of principles who wanders from town to town, vehicle to vehicle, with a pressurized cow-killing tool in hand that he uses on humans. From the moment he speaks, this man is horrifying. Even Hannibal Lecter would be a little jolted by this one. Forget the monsters in [I]The Mist[/I] or Grendel in [I]Beowulf[/I]. Chigurh is the most truthful incarnation of terror at the movie theater this year.
Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is the third player, a poor hunter who stumbles across a bloodbath left behind from a desert drug deal gone awry. Moss, realizing the cash is missing among the dead men, dead dogs, bags of drugs, and empty bullet casings, uses his skills as a hunter to track down and take a satchel full of $2 million dollars.
Thus, the plot runs down like this: Chigurh tries to take the money from Moss, who wants to keep the cash for himself. Bells interest is not in the money at all, but rather to stop this killers path of death. Note that these are standout performances from Jones, Bardem and Brolin. These actors are operating on a level rarely seen in the movies, particularly Brolin, who has had an entire year of breakout success as an actor. 
The film, like many films from the Coen Brothers, has a hint of dark comedy. No Country reminds me of their Academy Award winning [I]Fargo[/I], but with a tone more to their debut piece, [I]Blood Simple[/I]. The film is an utterly pessimistic one about the nature of good and evil, and Joel and Ethan Coen have made a career out of finding humor in the strangest places. Take, for example, a scene in which Bell describes the cattle killer used by Chigurh to Llewelyns wife (Kelly Macdonald). Afterwards she asks why he would describe all this to her. Bell says, I don know. My mind wanders. There is another scene involving a Chigurh, a quarter and an old gas station attendant (Gene Jones), but I will not go into details because it is just too good to spoil.
The Coen Brothers genius stretches to of every aspect of filmmaking. However, their writing of dialogue and the actors they employ to perform their work is what always gets me excited to see their films. Like [I]Clayton[/I], if you can keep pace with the words, then good things will follow. Better things, in fact, because [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is a better movie. But good writing and smart filmmaking is not for everyone, and if you fall into this category, better to stay away from this one. Stick with the shlock that was made to eat your dollars, like [I]Hitman[/I] or the upcoming [I]Alvin and the Chipmunks[/I] movie.
[I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is a landmark masterpiece that is already #23 on Internet Movie Databases Top #250. I am flattered that my opinion is so valued, which is why I invite those interested in a good film to go out and watch this one. Based on that same flattery, I suggest those [I]Clayton[/I]-haters go see more easily digestible fare. I myself have seen this movie twice now, and will be going back for thirds, if nothing else to listen to that dialogue one more time.

While watching this movie, I kept thinking to myself "this reminds me of Traffic". In many ways, I was right. For once, this movie takes on the point of view of multiple people, though not in the more "random" sense that movies like "Crash" or "Babel" take on. All of the characters are directly related to one another, in a domino fashion. Also similar (though I know many will argue with me on this) is the cinematography. The desert landscapes and run down on horse towns in this movie remind me of the Mexican scenes in Traffic, the difference being the towns are in the US in "No Country..". 

However, if No Country for Old Men was purely a clone of "Traffic", it wouldn't be as wonderful as it was. This dialogue is spot on, every word spoken (and unspoken) serves a purpose that drives the story forward. Parts of this movie made me tense with anxiety, but not in the cheap thriller sense. No, I was genuinely interested in what happened with each of these characters. As an (ashamedly) Texas native, the draw I had into this movie was almost eerie, and I know that this movie could not have been as effective in any other setting. Though I'm hesitant to echo the words "action" near this movie (it might give the wrong impression), it is well done in the sense that it is not overdone. The acting was also great, even the minor characters. Woody Harrelson still can't jump though. 

But liking a movie is boring, I get my kicks out of nitpicking the shit out of movies. For one, this movie is slow. Make sure you have a lot of Redbull before, because at times the average instinct when someone starts talking is to just zone them out (and there is a lot of talking). Missing a line or even a word will leave you confused for a bit. Tommy Lee Jones, whose acting was really good in this film, also needs to stop playing the role of the guy whose about to retire because he's too old for this shit. I'm pretty sure he's going to make a movie about retiring from acting one day , and then come back in the sequel to save the day just one more time.

 Also, I know some people will either love or hate the ending. I hate endings like this one. Does it work for this movie? Yes. Is it a good way to end a movie? No. I don't want to get into details because I might spoil it, but suffice to say, everyone left the theater just murmuring "wtf?". I decided to try and liven up the place with a slow clap, but I think that just confused them more. Just one piece of advice, whenever Tommy Lee Jones starts talking, you better pay attention or else you might miss the whole goddamn movie. 

So go see it. Fuckers.

What is the big deal about this movie?  I'll preface this by saying I've been a huge Coen bros. fan for years (only Barton Fink and Hudsucker Proxy get thumbs down from me), but I've only experienced them on DVD thus far.  Too busy, too lazy, call it what you will.  Seeing their new movie on the big screen was an experience I was hyped up for, especially after seeing all the critical hype.  I remained basically spoiler free for the film, not wanting to tarnish the experience.
 
      People, this is not one of their finer efforts, no matter how much you want to believe otherwise.  The Coens strength lies in their ability to create zany situations and eccentric characters and totally pull the viewer into a slightly askew version of reality.  Their repeated attempts to pull off gritty realism have been among their most mediocre works, and this counts as one of them.  This movie is like Jim Carrey trying to pull off a drama.  You appreciate the effort, but then you think of how it's one less zany send up he's gonna make and you feel cheated.
 
      I personally hate movies that do a good job building up to.........nothing.  This is another one.  The Coens pretty much thumb their nose at the audience and say, "This is what happens.  Fuck you."  Well for once I'm going to do them one better and not try to think too much on the events in the latter part of the film and overanalyze and try to mistake crap for art.  I'm gonna call a spade a spade and say it was a really shitty pointless ending.  
 
 This film unjustifiably keeps drawing comparisons to Fargo.  It reminds me more of Blood Simple, which is not my favorite Coens film for a lot of the same reasons.  Good moments without a cohesive whole does not make for a great film.  You want to compare this to Fargo?  Fine let's do that.  Bardem's half college psychiatry dropout/half Terminator villain is an absurdity compared to Peter Stormare's brutish amoral thug.  Tommy Lee Jones' wizened front porch philosopher of a cop that has almost next to nothing to do with the actual plot vs.  Frances MacDormand's simple, hopeful portrayal of the same character.  Josh Brolin gets you mildly interested and is then uncerimoniously dumped (it's a cheap twist so I don't mind giving it away).  Tell me in five years which movie you'd rather watch again.  Screw what the critics are saying.  Fargo is still their Apex.
 
      In conclusion, I'd tell the Coen Bros. that whenever they look to their prior films for future inspiration, ditch Barton Fink and Blood Simple and you'll do just fine.  I know I'll take heat for the Blood Simple thing, but "No Country" is basically Blood Simple with a budget and Tommy Lee Jones and it was quite frankly one of the more boring Coen movies I've seen.  That's it I'm out.

*Big PS*  It's about 6 months later and I've seen it on DVD a few times and I've begun to appreciate it's better points a bit more.  Please allow a fledgling reviewer a revisionist history or two.  Still, it sticks out like a long boring Coen movie but damn I love the coin flip scene with the gas station attendant.  I scored it a five but I'd like to score it fresh so a six now.

[font=Arial][size=2]Nearly ten years after Fargo, Joel and Ethan Coen have yet to produce a film that manages to recapture the intensity or audacity of their Oscar-winning work of genius. In recent years, the Coen Brothers credibility has escalated down hill with some embarrassingly forgettable work like Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers. No Country for Old Men is the exceptional comeback of the Coens Ive been waiting for. This is a movie of heart-wrenching strength and poetry that utterly reminded me why I love motion pictures. The Coen Brothers have once again fashioned a great American masterpiece of the cinema. 

Like Fargo before it, this is a stimulating and graphically violent dramatic thriller of a hut for money that spirals completely out of control. The film sets itself in West Texas where a man named Llewlyn Moss, played by Josh Brolin, uncovers a suitcase filled with two million dollars in cash. Rather then contacting the legal authorities of this matter, Llewlyn decides to keep the money for himself and his wife, played by Kelly MacDonald. The money turns out to belong to a serial madman named Anton Chigurh, brilliantly portrayed by Javier Bardem, who decides to hunt Llewlyn down for whats his. Chasing both Llewlyn and Anton is none other then Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, played by Tommy Lee Jones, who resembles Marge Gunderson as one of the few genuinely good people in the movie. This is a simple yet captivating tale of mouse VS cat VS dog.

In this sensational ensemble of characters, I believe that Javier Bardem delivers the one certified Oscar-bound performance in the movie. Anton Chigurh is an invigoratingly ingenious villain who of all weapons preys on his victims with a helium pump. This is a lethal psychopath who deserves to be considered in the same league of Norman Bates and Dr. Hannibal Lector as a great American lunatic, and Im not just saying that. Bardem manages to create a real character of sophistication and intellect unlike the Jigsaw murderer from the Saw movies whose only desire is push the envelope with one ghastly death after the other. 

There is genius within every shot of No Country for Old Men. Not a moment of dull dialog goes by in this masterfully written screenplay. There are scenes in this movie in which one might not have any idea what the characters are talking about and yet theyll find themselves entranced with captivation. The silenced moments of the movie are even more enthralling, filling the audience with bone-chilling curiosity of what these characters will do next in this unpredictable extravaganza. The Conen brothers demonstrate brilliance within every minor detail of the movie from a ring stain on a wooden dresser to a diverse handful of change. 

Im confident that some will dispute over the movies conclusion, which leaves some matters unresolved. But who the hell ever declared that a movie had to wrap up every subplot I ask you? I for one prefer it when a film challenges the audience and leaves you thinking. No Country for Old Men allows you to choose its ending through symbolic details with hidden meanings. This is a bloody and even lyrical entertainment to be considered in the same league of Pulp Fiction and Fargo as a masterwork of American motion pictures.[/size][/font]

No Country For Old Men isn't just the Coen brothers' best film since Fargo, it's actually the best film of the year so far.  
The film follows a grimmer version of the same thematic formula that worked so well in Fargo.  It shows people capable of the worst deeds, but doesn't attempt to explain those deeds.  Javier Bardem is brilliantly unpredictable and creepy as he plays angel of death, executing (with a compressed air hammer no less) his own brand of twisted justice which, strangely enough, almost manages to make sense to the viewer.  
The Coens' use of lighting effects, camera angles, and intentional non-use of a score creates a noir filled with authentic tension.  There is dark humor, but unlike previous Coen films supporting characters are given to genuine fear and sympathy rather than played for laughs.  Questions are left unanswered and events are left to chance, giving to the belief that fiction should as unpredictable as reality.   Ultimately, the world that is created is regulated around its three leads, Josh Brolin, Bardem, and Tommy Lee Jones. The atmosphere is as emotionally bleak as the West Texas landscape it depicts and in a darkly poetic way draws blurred lines between past, present, and future in the sense that the  dangerous internal human condition (whether it be greed or revenge, or any other given sin) always renders society equally as unsafe.  Jones narrates the film with a sense of distance; at the beginning he remarks that his job requires "a piece of your soul" on the line, and by the end it we understand what that means.  Our mastery of ourselves is just as unsure as our mastery of the events around us, and sometimes that piece of the soul is sacrificed in the process.

The kind of rare filmmaking perfection that comes along far too sparsely, something that renews your faith in the movies as simultaneously meaningful and entertaining pieces of immortal document. Everything is perfect here- the collaborative force of Brolin, Bardem and Jones completes a trinity of ethics which claw at each other ferociously for a short two hours. There are open-ended philosophical questions abound, but also plentiful is a blissfully enlightened storytelling in a pseudo-classical spirit which is rarely breached in modern cinema; the Coens are experts in the truest sense of the word, filmmakers who know what they like and what they need. Deakins (the third Coen?) supplies the exact aesthetics needed with his beautiful Texas landscape, open and spacious- this man owned 2007, and there is no better candidate for the leader of today's cinematographers. The "ending"- though it seems arbitrary and restricting to limit the final minutes of the film to such a definite term- leaves us just the way the film presented itself to us: without boundaries, expectations or rules. The Coens' best film and one of the most striking achievements of the last several decades.

The first film I saw in theatres this weekend - [b]No Country for Old Men[/b]. Directed by the Coen brothers - one of my favorites - this is an absolutely excellent film. The film doesn't have a score, but the silence fits it perfectly, particularly in the tense scenes. You feel like you're there. The ending is good, although I'm sure it threw a lot of audience members off. I liked it, though - it added a philosophical/deeper meaning to the whole film. The Coen brothers can obviously do no wrong, but this is exceptional and definately different from what they tend to do (although they are pretty different from film to film). It has comedic moments, terrifying moments, thought-provoking moments, and plenty of wonderful cinematography. If you don't take it from me, expect to hear it from everyone else - [b]No Country for Old Men[/b] is a wonderful movie which deserves to be watched. [i]9/10[/i]

The second film was [b]Band a Parte[/b] (Band of Outsiders), a Godard film from the 60s. I wasn't as connected with this one, but I still thought it was good. The three leads did a fine job, but I can't say I was feeling the magic that I felt with [b]Contempt[/b] or [b]Breathless[/b], which are his two best films (unless [b]Weekend[/b] tops them - I'm excited to see that one). It's a playful movie in parts and philosophical in others. Don't get me wrong, it's a good movie, it just wasn't as good as most of Godard's other films from the 60s (in my humble opinion). If you're a Godard fan, I would recommend watching it though. [i]7/10[/i]

The third and final film that I have recently watched is [b]Eastern Promises[/b], a film by David Cronenberg, who is apparently a good director. The only film on his filmography that I recognized was [b]A History of Violence[/b], which I have not yet seen. However, I really liked [b]Eastern Promises[/b], a thriller set in London centering around the Russian mob. Great lead performances from Naomia Watts and Viggo Mortissen. There are some wonderfully directed scenes here and the pacing is tight. It's a great movie which should deservedly get a few Oscar noms.

No Country for Old Men is the latest picture from Oscar winning film makers the Coen brothers (Fargo, The Big Lebowski, O' Brother Where Art Thou?). This modern day western is set in Texas during the 1980s. A local welder named Lewellyn Moss, stumbles across a truck load of heroine and about 2 million dollars in large bills while he is hunting. Givin the circumstances Llewelyn decides to take the money and run (of coarse). But unfourtunately for Mr. Moss that money belongs to a cerial killer named Anton Chigurh. Anotn loves to kill and is extremely good at it, he uses very original weapons and games of chance on his victims. The man hunt begins and it does not let up. The film is a non stop thrill ride from begginnig to end. The film has one of the best casts assembled this year and maybe of the decade. Josh Brolin who is on a winning streek this year including Planet Terror and American Gangster gives another effortless preformance as the man on the run. His dialogue is given perfectly as the hard nosed war veteran. The always fun to watch Tommy Lee Jones should recieve a nomiation for best supporting actor plays Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who is following the man slaughter. He was born to play these kinds of roles, his character could've been named Tommy Lee Jones.   But this film belongs too soon to be house hold name Javier Bardem. He excells as the psychopathic killer. His lines are giving with such conviction and a slight commidic sense about them. He is chilling, he is creepy, he is haunting, he is just Anton Chigurh and no one else could've played this part. The scene where he is interigating a gas station clerk with a lucky quarter from 1958 is one of the most gripping scenes in all of cinema.  This is the best movie that you are gonna see this Fall, Winter and into the next year. The cinematography is stunning and Roger Deakins will most definitaly win an Oscar. The screenplay which was based on the Cormac Macarthy novel is excellent and is never tedious or boring. And you can never say enough good things about Joel and Ethan Coen. It is every thing you expect a Coen brothers movie to be, its nice and violent and it has that quick dry humor that you know from Fargo. So please, please hunt down this movie and see it twice (you might need to) cause its definitaly worth the price of admittance.

Old themes for the Coen's. They explore nihalistic darkness and cover it with the quirky character's, clowns (Lebowkski, Nick Cage, Clooney, Tuturro) who have to out think or out run the darkness.  In this movie our protagonist is a badass but they don't stay true to him in determining his fate.  It's kind of a rip off to have this badass go down like a clown when there is nothing to indicate he would do so.  It's inconstant to show the most careful son of a gun who ever lived (Brolin) go down over some choice as dumb as it was. When I think of the Coen brothers, two things come immediately to mind:

1. They know how to make an ensemble cast work well.

2. Humor -- be it loudly broad or quietly "dark."

No Country for Old Men -- and apparently for lots of unfortunate men and women of any age -- fits well my mental picture of a Coen brothers' project.

The cast here gives wonderful performances large and small. I'm not sure what gave them the idea to tap Javier Bardem for this one but, in a sea of good acting, he definitely stands out above the rest. He's a kind of cross between Cameron's Terminator and the character of Death in Bergman's The Seventh Seal -- with just a dash of the character of Death in Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure tossed in. A riveting and most thoughtfully executed -- no pun intended -- role fulfillment on his part. He deserves every bit of praise for an inspired job well done. Very scary.

On the humor end we're talking extremely dark and mostly subtle here. Not the exuberant comedy of my much beloved Big Lebowsky.

But you know, flixster friends, the more I think about it, the more I'm struck by similarities between this one and Lebowsky. The use of the idea and of the historical fact of Vietnam comes to mind. In fact, thinking about that, it's as if mention of Vietnam in each film is like looking at Vietnam as a coin, to borrow a great image from No Country, viewed in two distinct ways by each film. That coin, with two sides, actually works for many shared themes in both films, including mistaken identity, gun play, and "revenge." Perhaps the encompassing essence of that coin is that one side represents loudly comic treatment, while the other side is the dark humored one that goes on into deadly seriousiouness.

If you see this for nothing else, however, you must see it for Javier Bardem's inspired performance. Now there is the kind of nihilist, if you will, whom you should watch out for and beware.

The Motel sequences are gripping and when the film takes an unexpected turn, it is at first unsatisfying, but then memorably disturbing in the vision it has of violece, fate and humanity. Josh Brolin with his Nick Nolte moustache is a good choice for the anti-hero as we're never sure how we feel about him. Tommy Lee Jones is reliable as ever, but in his haunted, vulnerable performance offers something subtly different in his acting. And of course, everything you read about Javier Bardem's acting and his role are true - it is awe-inspiringly nuanced and very creepy. I've been thinking of this film days after I've seen it and have to say it's masterful.

My first time watching a Coen Brothers film (Fargo) all i could think was...What the fuck? How can they be so clever, humorous to make such a masterpiece? Well, with that being the case, When I 1st Heard of No Country For Old Men, i wasn't as surprised as i was when i read "A Film By The Coen Brothers" as the trailer kept going....As Soon as i heard that, i knew this movie would be an modern masterpiece. Guess What? I was right.

No Country starts off with fresh shots of the setting, putting up the atmosphere even better (Good Job C.B). With this being done, we're brought to what the movie is about, which is basically about this guy that finds a stash of cash and heroin in this deserted area.....As many of us would do, he took the stash with him...yup, All $2 million of it. What he doesn't know is that this is from a drug deal gone wrong that this psychotic serial killer is behind. So now we find our protagonist being chased around by this maniac. That's the basic plot of this movie.

As usual, C.B (that means Coen Brothers) try to set up their film not only with bad ass action sequences and incredible shots of them, but with terrific dialogue...yup, of Tarantinish proportions. We're often found in situations where its crucial what is being said in order to completely admire the film, which leads to the ending that not many people like and hate this movie for. 

First of, before watching the movie, Read the fucking title, NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN. It basically implies this....the world is changing, how things were done before, how our "senior" citizens acted and reacted towards actions is way different that how it was in their days, Their time is up...now its our time to rule...Now when you watch the movie and don't like the ending, think about that i just wrote. 

Javier Bardem (that would be the antagonist) is fucking AMAZING, in depth acting, total control over the shots being taken, if there's a reason why this movie needs to be seen, is because of him, Although Tommy Lee Jones and Woody Harrelson are great actors, it wouldn't have been the same without Javier, his chemistry with the world that revolves around him is top friking notch! I guess i'll never be able to stress how much i love this morning, or how graciously perfect it is....Its just one of those gems that come in a few years IF we're lucky, and yup...We definetly are lucky viewers, unless of course you chose to watch a crappy movie over this, and if that's the case, SHAME ON YOU! haha, no but seriously, Flawless acting, although i will admit no movie is perfect and this isn't really a fault, its just funny to point out. I love how The Coen Brothers apply their setting to the society, just like in fargo, No Country For Old Men strongly flows with deep accents that are difficult not to laugh at, Its not a flaw, it just adds to the humorous side of the film.

I dedicate this segment of my review to the badass shotgun used in this movie, the weapon choice was so unique, it wasn't just a maniac going on a killing spree, he had wit, morals and class in what he did.....I love how everything he stands for is in his own world, the right thing, even 10 minutes before the ending it got to me how this world has come as fucked up as it is...Amazing Storytelling.

So, to wrap it all up...Lemme say this....1970s was Clockwork Orange , 1980s was Amadeus, 1990s was Schindler's List and in 2000s is, of course....No Country For Old Men. Instant Classic, this doesn't need 25 years to turn into one...Sheer Perfection. Lets just hope the cockgobblers at the Academy Awards actually recognize this movie cuz it deserves the highest recognition of any movie in these past 7 years, except of course, City Of God.

"No Country for Old Men" is a mixed bag, frustrating in how overrated it is. The movie starts and middles strongly, with the character of Llewelyn on the run with $2m worth of drug money, and the psychotic hitman Chirgar tailing him. It is an intense, violent game of cat and mouse that builds up to what is a climax surely to savour. However, it trails off terribly following a key event to one of the characters and limps on all the way to the end credits as though mortally shot.

The third act is ruined by pointless and random events that do not add anything to the movie. It seemed as though someone had sabotaged the Coen brothers at this point and deliberately attempted to spoil everything. The hitman Chirgar seems to kill everything and anyone that looks at him funny. He is obviously established as menacing and psychotic, but his antics descend into farce.

Supposedly, the theme of "No Country for Old Men" is of obsolescence, how the world is basically going to Hell in a hand basket. Tommy Lee Jones' Sheriff bemoans how things aren't as they were in his day, or his father's day, but instead of this idea being subtly woven into the fabric of the movie, it is irkingly plated at the beginning and end in narrative, more of an afterthought than a conscious message. It is a meandering philosophy that cheapens the experience.

After a couple stumbles in screwball comedy land, the Coens are back.  No Country For Old Men harkens to their more serious works like Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing, shrugging off the typical zany Coen characters and pitch-black humor.  It's a film of incredible restraint, patience, observation, understanding, and familiarity.

The performances of every character, from the leads to the supporting roles, are as good as I've seen for a long time.  Tommy Lee Jones especially conjures up a genuine, unique character in Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who strides through the film with world-weariness and can't quite believe the atrocities that are happening around him.  He thinks about the old days when his father and grandfather were lawmen, and wonders how we got here, what's to come, and how to put any sense to it all.  His sparse dialog, dialect, expressions, and demeanor are honed to perfection by Jones... we can see the years of this man behind those sunken eyes and hear the weight of the world in his words.  On the other side of the story is Anton Chigurh, the wide-eyed, unblinking psychotic killer that has a chilling lack of respect for life.  He lives by his own moral code that somehow follows a disturbing logic and matter-of-factness in his twisted mind.  In the middle is Llewelyn Moss, a resourceful, clever trailerpark dweller gets caught when he loots a Mexican standoff over money and drugs.  In one dialog-absent scene after another, he narrowly escapes capture with remarkable wit and determination.  Chigurh is after the money and will kill anyone in his way.  Sheriff Bell is constantly one or two steps behind Chigurh, and pieces together the aftermath with the accuracy and skill of an old-school lawman that's seen more than his share of crime and human nature.  It's fascinating watching these three characters operate; we're not insulted by expository dialog, instead their actions speak for themselves.

The cinematography puts the action together deliberately, coherently, chillingly.  Here we delve into more familiar Coen territory where jarring scenes of brutal violence explode from the most placid scenes.  It's just as effective as it ever was in Fargo, capturing the bizarre, incomprehensible atrocity of cold-blooded murder as it happens.  Simultaneously we're treated to the sparse beauty of west Texas, the dust and rocks blinding in the sun and big-sky sunsets evoking that feeling of isolation.  The deliberate pacing sucks you in as the camera meanders from one setpiece scene to the next.  Once again, little explanation is offered of what you're seeing, the movie always lays everything out in plain sight for you to discover as the characters do.  It's an exhilirating and rewarding experience.

There is virtually no soundtrack or incidental music in the movie, perfectly matching the desolate and unforgiving setting.  It makes the visuals even more effective and the mood even more disturbing.. a great touch by the directors.  I love hearing the little textures of sound instead... the crunch of dust and rocks under the boots, the click-hum of someone picking up a telephone, boards creaking in the hallway as you-know-who makes his way to the room where we hide along with Llewelyn, the scraping sound of him unscrewing the lightbulb in the hallway, the faint hiss of compressed air as he opens the valve on his air gun.

It all adds up to a engrossing experience that seems to fly by.  Like all great movies, it doesn't seem long enough.  The ending isn't very neat or tidy, but I think that's part of the effect.  By the time the movie is over, we've witnessed senseless violence and there doesn't seem to be much payoff or benefit, no great realization or retribution.  It's just how things are; no explanation needed.  No ride into the sunset as the theme song reprises, no hero kissing the girl, no dry quips of the victorious.  This film is reality, in all its harshness.

The scene with Anton leaving the house, then checking his boots comes to mind. But, that also makes it seem like there's a lot of filler. Seriously, how many desert hunting scenes do we really need?

The pacing I have minor quibbles with, but I have none about the acting and the writing. Tommy Lee Jones is great at the sheriff, and I have to admit... I found his tangents amusing. Josh Brolin, fresh off his role as a mutant zombie doctor in Grindhouse, was perfect for the role of the drug money stealing Vet. And might I say, Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh... nothing short of brilliant. They could have done more with the "killer with a twisted sense of honor" motiff, but overall... everything from the CO2 tank, to the stroke of genius haircut (which the Coens chose because of prisoner photos from the time... not to mention that fact that you still see people around here with that exact style), pure awesomeness.

I do have my issues with the plot overall. The writing is great (it is based on a book by Cormac McCarthy), but what exactly was up with the ending?

Here's where I have to add the SPOILER ALERT!!!!

It's a tad anti-climatic. The Mexicans get Josh Brolin off screen, and Tommy Lee Jones realizes that he's too old to catch criminals. So... what? Is this film a commentary about the life human? Is Javier Bardem really the grim reaper with a bad haircut? Is the entire movie a morality tale on greed and cynicism? Is Josh Brolin really the living embodiment of Tommy Lee Jones' father? Or what?

Honestly, it would have been better if they had just ended it with the car wreck. That way they close by bucking western tradition and letting the villain win, but still not let him get off completely. Sort of a winking to while you turn your back on tradition type of close.

What might be a first for a major American film that is nominally about violence, is that many of the violent acts you expect would have been shown in another director's treatment - are not shown. They are suggested and hinted. The sense of the story not told lingers at the end, leaving us with what the Coen Brothers think is a sense the audience has just viewed a very finely etched ensemble character study. But does it really meet an Academy 'Best Picture' standard?

Only when I read the book did I realize what the ending's place was.

Now that I am passed the flaw of this near perfect movie, I will talk about it's many strengths, starting with of course Javier Bardem playing what in my mind goes down as one of the most realistic and scary bad guys in cinematic history, by the name of Anton Chigurh. Now through the whole film he makes this character his own, Cormac McCarthy (The Author of the book) doesn't really explain the character too much passed "He looks like he is an ethnicity" I'm paraphrasing but that is about the extent you know about him in the book, so that leaves him to 100% interpretation, And the Coens and Javier deliver on every scope.

Now lets talk about my favourite scene in the entire movie, a 10-15 minute scene in which you find Anton Chigurh in a Texaco gas station talking to it's proprietor (Played by Gene Jones, I looked it up, that is how much I loved this scene), and there is a wager of sorts made, this is the closest I have ever seen a movie come to complete perfection. The gestures, the overwhelming sense of dread, everything worked on a scale rarely seen in movies. This was almost verbatim from the book, so Cormac deserves a lot of the credit, but it really boils down to Javier Bardems excellent acting, and he hits every note. 

Also from the opening you hear the slow southern drawl of Tommy lee Jones, playing Sheriff Ed-Tom Bell, This story is about him, the movie in whole is a story about a man who the future is coming to fast for him and the past left him even before he got here. The most memorable line of his is "Back in the old days, Sheriffs didn't even carry a gun, I wonder how they would fare today" it shows the way the movie is going, and it coming from Tommy: it just sets the movie on good feet.

The rest of the cast is supurb also, Woody Harrelson, Josh Brolin, Kelly MacDonald (a relative new comer, for myself at least.) This movie; regardless of how it ended; is as close to perfect as movies come,. Also for the Coens being able to make a movie that in my mind, bests a "little known" movie; known as "Fargo", is not only surprising, it's miraculous.

I didn't realize how great [i]No Country For No Men [/i]was until roughly eight hours after I saw it.  When I left my friend's house a little while ago (it's around one in the morn), I saw the headlights of a car driving around the resevoir across the street, and I got chills, thinking of what mysterious and possibly murderous person could be behind the wheel.  The only thing that could've put me in that mindset was [i]NCFOM[/i], a movie that, for the most part, lives up to its hype.

This is my first Coen brothers film, and I admire their direction.  I was truly impressed with how the film achieved such excitement and intensity while actually being quite low-key.  As far as I can remember, there was no music (or what little there was blended so well with the movie that it wasn't noticeable, allowing the viewer to stay fully immersed in the story), and the scenes tend to be long and full of conversation, usually remaining interesting but, unfortunately, sometimes becoming a tad boring.  In fact, the last scene of the movie, I sort of zoned out during, and then the [i]Sopranos[/i] Black Screen of Death pops up and I'm like...dang, I think I missed the end.  But I digress.

But for a couple slow scenes near the end (literally only two), the movie keeps you on the edge of your seat.  While the plot really isn't anything special (a psychopath hunts down a man who found a case of money), the characters and the setting really add a lot to the story.  The sparse Texan landscape and the little towns where the action unfolds really add to the overall sense of unrest and terror, and the performances here are some of the best of the year, particularly the haunting Javier Bardem.  After seeing this movie, it's hard to imagine him as Florentino in [i]Love in the Time of Cholera[/i] (and I'm pissed I have to imagine it, because I really want to see it).  Even Tommy Lee Jones, who I tend to not care for, is really great here, although he is also responsible for my zoning out in the film's final moments.

Of course, this movie isn't for the faint of heart.  While the blood and whatnot here aren't used gratuitously, there is a lot, and I don't recommend young viewers or those with weak stomachs taking this ride.

This is sure to garner Oscar attention, which is well-deserved, and I look forward to seeing the many accolades the film is sure to accrue.

My review from Vox Magazine:

On the desolate plains of southern Texas, No Country for Old Men unfurls like a wind-blown tumbleweed. Setting off with the great force of a gale, it meets conflict like a barbed-wire fence and unhurriedly rolls into harsh and haunting terrain. 

At its ominous opening, the film finds Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) happening upon the grizzly aftermath of a botched drug-deal. When Moss takes a satchel of two million dollars found at the scene, he inauspiciously becomes prey to Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a relentless killer bent on reclaiming the money. Following in Chigurhâs bloody wake, an old hand sheriff, Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), faces the seemingly insurmountable task of ending the ordeal.

Jones has played these law-type roles countless times before with some measure of finesse, but here his execution of the world-weary sheriff is unblemished. And in a performance as exacting and ethereal as his character, Bardem becomes the embodiment of an idea â not so much a being as a pure force.

Written and directed by Joel and Ethan Coen (Fargo, The Big Lebowski) and adapted from the award-winning novel by Cormac McCarthy, the film stows dark humor in unexpected places, characteristic of the Coen brothersâ work, and daringly defies expectations. Viewers may not leave the theater with their usual dose of satisfaction, but they will almost certainly be stirred by the experience.

The film has been marketed as a clear-cut crime thriller, with television spots touting spellbinding suspense, but thereâs something much more frightening than physical violence beneath its tumultuous surface. No Country for Old Men goes beyond mere commentary on violent behavior and, like the W.B. Yeats lyrics for which itâs named, confronts questions of malevolence and mortality.

It portrays the intimate world of unusual assassins and unforgetable characters against a backdrop of a sparsely populated Texan city. 

Dialogue and Black humour
I loved the Coen brother's sense of humour in Fargo, more specifically the brilliant dialogue of the characters in ordinary settings.  If you look carefully at the characters in this film - It's not just dialogue.  There are mannerisms and pecadillos included too, there is a lot of subtle observational humour to be found and sometimes the dialogue implies a minor character has a broader understanding of human nature which actually surprises or shocks the viewer.  The film captures the same spirit of a specific region of America (much as what Fargo did).  The accents are really spooky and the grammatically incorrect voices are fascinating. 

Ugly or Beautiful?
It's very violent in places so it's not for everyone.  I get the feeling more guys than girls will rate this film highly.  However, there are loads of sweeping visual shots that are distinctive and photogenic.  It has rugged desert shots,  'drive in hotel' night time shots, simple clean lines in glorious detail.

Some people might get bored (by not much happening on screen at times), but for me the photography is so excellent, it feels like you are soaking up the scenery just before the next part of drama or dialogue unfolds!

The Psycho Killer won an Academy award!
This film won four Academy Awards and it's movies like this that make something like the Academy Awards mean something - The film is a 'must see classic' as the visual flair for imagery reveals just as much information as the dialogue. As a philosophical, "art" movie, it didn't work at all.  The three main characters were too one dimensional, the philosophy wasn't particularly interesting (basically "the world sucks nowadays" and "everybody is subject to chance"), and Tommy Lee Jones, playing the same role he always plays, rambled on for about ten minutes before the credits rolled, arbitrarily (chance intervening in the end of a movie?).

My main gripe with people defending the end of the movie is that the first argument they use centers on the end of the movie being "unconventional." Just because a movie ends unconventionally doesn't mean it's good - it's the same argument as "just because I don't understand it means it's art."  Musically, it's easy to make noise; it's hard to play well.  The second argument they use is "well that's the way the book ended."  Well - adapting a rambling, philosophically digressive book that ends poorly leads to a rambling, philosophically digressive movie that ends poorly!

Reiterating: some of the choices they used were very good (see: first hour and a half), but overall, it tried to stretch beyond its level, and thus is not the masterpiece some people claim.

   Every year, there's that movie with so much praise that it just seems too good to be true. This year, that movie everyone is running up the mountain proclaiming "best movie I've seen in years", "masterpiece" and "four stars" is the Coen Brothers' "No Country for Old Men". Having been disillusioned numerous times before, I deliberately avoided the film upon its release, knowing that I could always come back in several weeks since it would still be around. Then finally, I decided to wing it, catch a $6 early-morning show, and come in with extremely low expectations.
   
   No, I don't think the film warranted those comments, but I was definitely surprised and hooked. Not the best film in years, but definitely the Coens' best since "Fargo"- however much is to their credit for this apparently word-for-word translation of Cormac McCarthy's novel. This kind of treatment doesn't always work, especially during two-person dialogue scenes since the conversations tend to go in circles and the words sound detached from the people speaking them.
   
   Then, without overdoing it and without a note of musical score, the suspense kicks in- and I'll dare anyone to try and predict what's going to happen next, especially during an intense midpoint gunfight outside a hotel. The storyline in general runs through several unexpected twists and turns- even our serial killer (Javier Bardem) doesn't kill every man he talks to, making his character that much more unpredictable and therefore, scarier.
   
   The conclusion is also far from the one you'll be expecting, and I'm sure there are some who will find it to be ambiguous. I did, too, especially with the film's apparently abrupt ending, until I started connecting the pieces over lunch; sometimes it's not that you don't know what happened, but that it's quite clear and you just don't want to believe it.
   
   
   MPAA: R (strong graphic violence and some language)
   Runtime: 2 hours, 2 minutes (117 minutes of "real movie")

It is getting commonplace to cite this as the current best film of 2007, but it is a truly astonishing exercise in suspense, maturity, and control that it cannot be praised as anything but an bar-setting classic. This is a picture of elemental power and unnerving silence with an ending that performs a miracle of physical manipulation on the audience as it creates a drawing away/dream-like sensation which will dissapoint all of the spoon-fed American viewers used to flat emotional beats and "ironic" resolutions which feel like script tricks.  [QUOTE]Existentialism differentiates itself from the modern Western rationalist tradition of philosophers such as Descartes in rejecting the idea that the most certain and primary reality is rational consciousness. Descartes argues in his Meditations on First Philosophy that, while humans can doubt almost all aspects of reality as illusions, humans can be certain of their consciousness, which is therefore the only truth ("Cogito ergo sum").

 Existentialism decisively rejects this argument, asserting instead that as conscious beings, humans would always find themselves already in a world, a prior context and a history that is given to consciousness, and that humans cannot think away that world. It is inherent and indubitably linked to consciousness. In other words, the ultimate and unquestionable reality is not thinking consciousness but, according to Heidegger, "being in the world". Awkward and gimmicky, No Country is really disappointing.  While some scenes are chilling and effective (the look on the villain's face when he makes his first kill is frightening), and it never lags, the story and dialogue feel forced and uninspired. While most of the film is pretty tense, some one-liners are tossed in occasionally to lighten things up; some work, some don't.  In one scene, the lead character forgets that his mother is dead for the sake of a joke, while Tommy Lee Jones gets some clever lines.  Speaking of Tommy Lee Jones, his sheriff, a tired, beaten down old man who we are supposed to feel sympathy for, comes across as pathetic instead.
I never got a clean grip on who Bardem's psychotic killer is.  He's disturbingly selfish in one scene, then bizarrely detached in the next.  He's never truly scary because he doesn't feel real. Also, his use of an air-powered cattle gun seams strange given that his other weapon of choice is a huge shotgun.  It's something I would expect from a B horror film.
The twist at the end betrays the audience and thoroughly kills any momentum the film had going.  After such tight thrillers as Blood Simple and Fargo, No Country feels like a first draft script. The Coens can do so much better.
One last note: while there's not a lot of gore, this is still a very violent film with an onscreen death count in the dozens.  If you're sensitive to violence, this movie's definitely not for you.

The acting in this is amazing, especially Bardem who is very disturbing every time he comes on screen. The story keeps you thinking long after the film has ended. The cinematography is great. [font=Times New Roman][size=3]The Coen Brothers are known for quirky, provocative films.  Their latest endeavor, NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN, is no exception. [font=Times New Roman][size=3]A drug deal turns terribly wrong in a barren Texas desert badlands.  Javier Bardem is dispatched to retrieve the money for the deal.  Woody Harrelson is a professional bounty hunter on his trail, as is Tommy Lee Jones as the local sheriff.  To complicate matters, trailer park trash Llewellyn Moss, played by Josh Brolin, has wandered upon the scene and absconded with the money.  The film builds to a final reel confrontation between the principles and opts for the more realistic, but box office non-friendly ending.  Brolin does a fine job acting, while Jones and Harrelson are basically supporting and cameo roles, respectively.  Bardem is weird, but never seems quite as threatening as his shotgun silencer.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN has a different look to it.  The movie was shot on 35mm film, which, in itself, is a rarity nowadays with the technological advances of 24-frame video.  Generally movies shot on film are edited on AVID systems, however, the Coen Brothers have a unique relationship with Apple Corp., so, NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN was edited on Final Cut Pro.  FCP has been attempting to gain ground on AVID for years.  Personally, I dont think its close and viewers will be able to see a different texture in this film.  At times the color correction looks unreal and the dark sets lack vividness and crispness.  Roger Deakins serves as Director of Photography.  His work on the recent The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford is Oscar worthy.  His framing and shot composition are exceptional, leaving the films lackluster appearance squarely on the shoulders of Final Cut.  The workflow went from film to DVCPro HD tape to Quick Time files and Final Cut editing.  The rub comes in the transfer to Quick Time.  Im not a fan of QT files.  They cannot handle large screen formats without resolution loss.  While that may be more technical info than you bargained for, it does nonetheless explain the disappointing look of the movie.[/size][/font]

The Coen Brothers score again!  After a relatively "difficult" period (ie "Intolerable Cruelty" and "The Ladykillers"), the Brothers are back...with a vengeance. Let's start with the actors, who are, across the board, amazing.  Tommy Lee Jones hardly needs to be mentioned: we know how good he is.  Javier Bardem oozes an air of uncomfortable, yet facsinating, dread.  Josh Brolin, rapidly becoming one of the most interesting actors around, projecting a kind of matter-of-fact intelligence that is disarming at times.  Woody Harrelson, not having much to do in the movie, but doing it well.  And let's not overlook Kelly Macdonald, playing Brolin's wife as a confused but not dumb woman in over her head.  The Brothers tell this story with terror, violence, smarts and, most importantly, their odd sense of humor.  Another filmmaker could have made this story (and made it well) but they almost certainly would have made a deadly serious film that didn't have a laugh in it. It's all about Bardem. He plays this demonic psychopath that uses compressed air as a weapon. Chigurh is his alien-like name and no words can describe the evilness he possesses. Even upon seeing him, you won't be able to comprehend the aura of terror he seems to let explode from him. Stranger still is that he's so calm! Like some ghost or The Grim Reaper, he's simply and genuinely horrifying. His face screams death. And his voice echoes that scream. His actions speak louder than his words. His impact is so intimidating that whenever you see a corner that somebody could be hiding behind - you automatically wonder if he's lurking there... waiting to murder his next victim. Now THAT is having presence! And he doesn't stop! They say time waits for no man. Well, this man IS time itself. He's just relentless! He is the GREATEST villain ever created because he has so many of the best (or... I should say worst) qualities of all the other hall of fame villains. He's a Frankenstein mixture of Nosferatu, Hannibal Lecter, The Joker, Two-Face, The Bad AND the Ugly from TGTBATU, The Shark From Jaws, The Terminator, Agent Smith, Norman Bates, Darth Vader, Travis Bickle, Jack Torrance, Alex DeLarge, Kahn from the Wrath of Kahn and Hal 9000. Everything wrong with society, all the humanity it's been drained of, is epitomized in this soulless monster. And that's the movie's premis - facing this monster and wondering... Did/ how could humans create such a thing? And therein lies everything the movie is trying to get at. We live in a time when police forces are too afraid (or at least... told old) to do their jobs, when people think there's an easy way out of having to work for a living - that they'll 'just get lucky' and manage to escape the inevitable - and here we are praying to God to help us. There is no God. Just dumb luck, inevitable consequences, and the money that seems to rule our lives. It's a brilliant movie that's on target. The directing is about as fine as anything you'll see. There's no music - just twitchy camera angles and deadly silence that is on the edge of being bareable. My friend beside me kept saying "I can't watch. I just can't do it. This is too intense!" But, ofcourse, nothing is ever too intense - so long as it's tasteful. And this is. Until I, my friend, and the entire theatre I noticed, got totally lost as to what was happening plotwise. This might be the lone fault of the movie. There's a breif span in which, if you aren't paying very close attention, you'll blink and miss who got killed and who died of cancer and when which character died. But does the plot really matter? I still got the message, loud and clear.  And Tommy Lee Jones gives a great tragic speech to wrap things up nicely at the end. Although I came out of the theatre confused about the ending's car crash, thoughts about the human decency mankind seems to be lacking as we progress into the future are what dominated my mind. "Soon as manners go... the end is in sight." I'm not sure that's totally true...  or if things are any different now than they ever were - they might just appear differently - but whatever the case may be, it's a strong testament to what is lost when human emotions go extinct. In alotta ways... NCFOM is Fargo all over again. But more complex. I do miss Fargo's simplicity - there was nothing there that shouldn't be and you could always follow alon but this is a movie in which the style is greater than the sum of its parts. The first half is great, second half is confusing. Then seeing it again, the reverse happens... in a good way. This is an awesome film because Chigurh is such an awesome villain - the kind that knows our greatest fear... meaninglessness.

I can contemplate, graphically, serial murder. I can appreciate a 90-minute depiction of slaughter. Movies I have enjoyed: Natural 
Born Killers, Braveheart, Saving Private Ryan, Scarface, Aliens, Tarantino's, etc. I just need a ripping yarn. Or a big idea. Or a 
weird idea. Or wailing special effects and stunts. 

Well, there are no effects or stunts to speak of in this movie. There are no big or weird ideas, at least not presented in any way 
you could sink your teeth into. The official tagline is "there are no clean getaways", which I would paraphrase as "no free lunch", and hope for a commentary on "America", or greed, or laziness, or the Buddha's first noble truth. Instead, I get a video game. A guy finds money and another guy hunts him for it, killing everyone in his path. I don't know why the first guy is trying to keep the money. I don't know anything about him. No external forces bear on them. There are two other characters who appear to 
be pointless. Woody Harrelson's character appears to be intentionally pointless. Tommy Lee Jones may be intended to provide a philosophical and/or moral input, which could be good, except that it goes something like this:

-"Anytime you quit hearin 'sir' and 'ma'am' the end is pretty much in sight"

Or maybe he's intended to provide wry witticisms, which could be good, except that it goes something like this:

-"(It's a mess, ain't it.) Well if it ain't, it'll do til the mess gets here."

I haven't read the novel, but I've read that it's about causality and fate. And indeed, the film has characters say, on several 
occasions, some variation of "you can't stop what's coming". Now this could be an interesting idea, but as part of a "keep the 
psycho druglord away from his $2 million" plot, it's kind of a no-brainer.

So you watch this series of murders of innocent bystanders, wrapped in absolutely nothing but the natural suspense of hunting, 
interrupted occasionally by the confusing pointlessness of Tommy Lee Jones, and for a brief time by the confusing pointlessness of 
Woody Harrelson. 

And you say to yourself: Javier Bardem's hairdo and method of shooting people is not enough to carry this material.

A pure, trademark Coen bros flick, neither more nor less. Noirish, stylish and spellbound, packed with ironies, offbeat dialogues and quirky humor, "No Country" is a throwback to Coen's darker side, following the tradition of their other vintage film-noir classics "Blood Simple", "Miller's Crossing" and "Fargo". But here we see more brutality, more blood, more despair and a kinda chilly apathy we haven't seen since "Fargo". 

From technical viewpoint, there is nothing exceptional as well as Coen-esque standards concerned: it's elegantly constructed and well-made "seek and destroy" film with solid camera and lighting work. Apart from Roger Deakins' wonderful cinematography, there's very little artistic/visual development here that we've seen "Barton Fink" and thereafter. In terms of characterization, the film boasts one of the best in their oeuvre: from "predator" Anton Chigurh to the "prey" Llewelyn Moss, all characters are phlegmatic, solid and solitary figures who feel at their cozy home in forsaken landscapes, where death stalks the land. As their other work, the movie is seemingly indifferent to the welfare of its characters, and extravagantly aware of itself as a movie. This is Coen-way of film-making!!! 

To sum up, not everyone's cup of tea "No Country" is a much profound movie than most people are prepared for. Albeit not a significant leap forward from Coen's previous film noirs, it is the paragon of impeccable storytelling and how to let the pictures tell the story. And that doesn?t surprise me very much!!

One thing that was intriguing about No Country for Old Men was the fact that the Coen brothers pulled no punches about it. The story was entirely secondary to the underlying themes at hand. This was a very bold move in today's market of remaking every story 5 times because no one has any new ideas. The plot served instead as a catalyst for all of the different occurrences that coincided just because they coincided, according to Bardem's character. It wasn't until the end when he this philosophy is openly challenged that he becomes somewhat human, making for an interesting sort of personal climax for him. What makes the movie so affective is that we, as the audience, are constantly being reminded that things are always going to go wrong, things happen just because that's the way they are meant to be, and if something is coming, nothing is going to stop it. All the while we are hoping against all hope that it's untrue, and in the end our hopes are dashed brilliantly in every aspect involving the story. This is how tragedy is meant to look.
