My 18 year old son told me he had mixed feelings about No Country for Old Men, and in particular thought that the last 20 minutes sort of meandered without purpose and meaning.  Actually, I think purpose and meaning are the very raison d'etre for the last 20 minutes.

I suspect that my son's disappointment stemmed from his age, his masculinity, and the very tired notion that modern movie makers have bequeathed him - regarding justice obtained by the good guy beating the bad guy.  But NCFOM is not Star Wars, Rocky, or James Bond.  And the westerns that earned John Wayne his glory have much more in common with those three films than it will ever have with No Country, despite the bleak landscape and dust-laden shootouts.

No Country for Old Men has everything to do with why humans choose to engage in  - oh, hell, let's call them appropriate behaviors - when there is really very little payoff.  It is essentially made up of serial pictures of men protecting their women, trying to make something of themselves financially, or at the very least trying to fight off the destructive and evil forces in life... to essentially no good end.  We live out our lives (of quiet desperation, I think I once heard someone say) only to die (well, someday), or we fight our enemies and give our health and bodies for country or principle, or (at best it seems) retire into a bleak, bored, and all too doldrum-y day to day life.

This is not a picture about who dies in the end.  This is a picture about who lives, and why.  In the movie, Chigurgh kills we are told because of "principle."  He kills because he gave his word to kill.  Is Cormac McCarthy trying to suggest that principles are only as good as their outcomes?  That means don't justify ends?  Is he suggesting that to live by principle - when that principle is anything other than respect for the sanctity of life - is simply, evil?  Or is it really that it questions the entire definition of "principle."  Psychologically speaking, Chigurgh is not so much demonstrating "principle" as simple behavioral consistency.  It makes more sense to see it that way.  Were he really adhering to principle, the question would be, why that particular principle?  What, in his fictional history, would cause him to select that principle over, say, any of a thousand principles by which to stand... all of which are more realistic if only in their evolutionary blueprint.  Rather, he just simply behaves consistently.  Kill this.  Kill that.  Kill a bird.  We're even left at the end of the picture with the idea that he is not killing on principle at all.  He offers Carla Jean one last opportunity to "override" his principle... that of the coin toss.  Gee, how principled is it if you change your mind at the toss of a coin?

Really, the only person in the entire movie who demonstrates principle is he who literally takes his shirt off his back to help someone out, refusing to accept reward or money.  I would hardly believe it to be coincidence that this is the only child character, the only one for whom we have any reason to believe their may still be a shred of innocence. When the money is thrust into his palm, suddenly he changes.  The money is his. Not his friend's.  Not to be shared.  And he earned it, it was his shirt.

But one of the issues about Coen movies that tends to annoy and plague me afterward is that they're a little too "decide for yourself" when the entire structure of their work is almost always a fight between evil and goodness.  I know Hemmingway said "never point out your own point," but honestly, he didn't say "blindly lead your audience away from any sense of point or higher purpose."  The Coen's seem to create movies that are profoundly moral, but only for the deeply intellectualized.  To everyone else, it's a movie about just how much gore they can illustrate for you.  They behave like angry London adolescent punk fans: Now we're really going to shock you.  I guess if it gets you good reviews and a lot of money.  Critics these days.  They seem to believe that anything with violence and degradation is just grand, so long as we all get to pretend to be innured to it. It's sort of the fatal flaw in Short Bus... you know what I mean?

If I have one other (and I promise this is my last) complaint about the Coen brothers in general, it is that their antagonists are always characatures.  They are exaggerated monsters.  They almost always are referred to as ghosts.  I think what is so implausible about these creatures (and then, by extension, their movies) is the very immortal quality that they universally seem to impart.  You just can't keep these guys down.  Shoot em and they'll jump out of the way, shoot you back harder, perform surgery on themselves, walk around with bones exposed, have a pact with satan, and yada yada yada.  As such, the viewer (I suppose) is drawn into responses as if in a slightly artier form of Friday the 13th.  How scary... something so dangerous that no one will ever be able to stop.  Lame.  You know, the truth is that even the most heinous of serial murderers get caught - and they aren't half as public as Mr. Chigurgh.  Look at Dennis Rader.  I call him Dennis... I used to call him something else.  But in the real world, that person lost his grip of fear over me.  For those of you who may be lost by that statement, he was a serial killer in my native Wichita, who murdered in my youth and my neighborhood.  He used to keep me up at night.  Now, he's just "Dennis."  The truth about persons with homicidal ideation is that the very thing that breaks them and causes them to kill is almost always the same thing that leads to their IMperfection as forces of evil.  For Dennis R, it was his need to be the powerful center of attention when in reality he was a dog catcher.  Real evil, in my opinion, isn't omnipotent.  Real evil is mortal - just like the rest of us.  Mortal, and capable of creating virtually limitless responses of fear, anger, sadness, grief, and despair.  That's the real evil... emotional pain.  Chigurgh doesn't even cause pain.  Carla Jean knew what was coming and took it like a man.  Everyone else was taken by surprise.  We're all going to die; how damaging is it when it comes peacefully unaware and no one grieves?

You know, we're all aware that Bardem is outrageous in this role.  But really, he's got a wide open palette by which to get wierd.  His character is far from that which is psychologically sensible.  Brolin is amazing.  Tommy Lee Jones is his usual brilliant self.  But, beyond that, I'd like to say that this movie did have some of the most amazing acting performances I may have ever seen - in its minor cast.  It takes a lot to make me stop seeing the acting taking place and just fall into belief of the character as a real person.  From the gas station owner to the deputy, I haven't been able to suspend reality for that long with such small parts in probably 2 or 3 years.

I think I get annoyed by those who pronounce Chigurgh some sort of dead-on portrayal of evil or killing addiction... because their is virtually nothing in this portrayal which is psychological coherent.  He makes no sense.  He behaves in ways antithetical to human behavior.  That doesn't make him more real.  The truth is, people are very predictable.  Even serial killers.  I love Bardem in this role, but it isn't a movie about psychopathic killers.  He is playing a plot device, not a man.  He is powerful, but only as a stark contrast to the abstract and arbitrary world into which our two protagonists seek to find meaning and purpose... all, of course, in the last 20 minutes of the film.

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Sometimes the Coen brothers can be more concerned with evoking a certain style than telling a good story. The results are rarely boring, but ultimately they just come off as interesting experiments. Many critics are hailing [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] as the Coens best film since [i]Fargo[/i]. I contend that it is closer in spirit and tone to their first movie, [i]Blood Simple[/i]. Trust me, this is a good thing.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Heres the plot, or what little of it there is: Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is out hunting one morning when he comes across the scene of a drug deal gone bad. Everyone is dead, and there is a case filled with two million dollars. Llewelyn takes the money. Once this is discovered, a man by the name of Anton Chigurh tries to track him down. Played by Javier Bardem, Chigurh is one of the most evil villains in film history. He has no remorse, and he cannot be stopped. (Come to think of it, hes kinda like the Terminator). Following the trail of these two men, and trying to make sense of the proceedings, is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones). And thats pretty much it. The entire movie is one big game of cat and mouse. [/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Times New Roman][size=3]I suppose the movie is really a meditation on the randomness of life and death, and in that sense it achieves its goal. The acting, cinematography, and sound editing are all superb. (I noticed about halfway through the movie that there is virtually no music). I thoroughly enjoyed Bardem as the killer, although I do have one quibble: when a villain kills everyone he meets, without discrimination, dont the murders cease to have any resonance with the audience? I started to say to myself, [i]Theres one more dead person. Oh well[/i]. But again, perhaps that randomness is exactly the point. Anyway, the movie is fascinatingly bleak, and I was enjoying it right up until the last fifteen minutes. Then it went off the rails. [/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Look, heres the deal: I dont need everything wrapped up in a tidy little bow. [i]Memento[/i] had a completely ambiguous ending, and I thought that movie was brilliant. As a matter of fact, the same goes for the final episode of [i]The Sopranos[/i]. I admire when an artist decides to shake up the audiences expectations and diverge from the typical storytelling patterns. I enjoy being challenged. Also, I dont need a happy ending. The good guy didnt win at the end of [i]3:10[/i][i] to [/i][i]Yuma[/i] but I still loved it. In fact, sometimes a happy ending just isnt right for the material. Many of Steven Spielbergs recent films have suffered because he felt the need to tack on a happy ending or wrap everything up in a pat little coda. Its just not always necessary. But you know what I [i]do[/i] need? SOME ending. ANY ending. And ultimately thats what has left me feeling unfulfilled by [i]No Country[/i]. [/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Times New Roman][size=3]I havent read Cormac McCarthys book, so I dont know if the ending is true to the novel. I suspect it is, and maybe it reads better than it plays on a movie screen. Its difficult to explain without revealing key plot points, which I certainly dont want to do. Basically, throughout the movie, tension is building. The suspense is delicious. There is momentum leading us towards something. And then its over. Thats it. Now, I know many people will say that I am describing that final [i]Sopranos[/i] episode to a tee, but heres the difference: [i]The Sopranos[/i] was about the everyday lives of the characters, and the way it ended suggested that their lives simply continued on after the show was over. In No Country, certain things happen to certain characters that demand an explanation, and none is given. What is the point of everything that has happened in the movie up until the end? There is none.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Times New Roman][size=3]And let me say this: I recognize that the Coen brothers have done this on purpose. They are accomplished filmmakers who understand editing and storytelling. They certainly knew what they were doing when they made this choice. I just feel, in the case of this particular movie, that they have made the wrong choice. [/size][/font]

"No Country For Old Men" is like one of those loopy DisneyWorld rides that thrills and delights you so much, you just want to run to the back of the line and experience it all over again. It's the much-anticipated new movie adapted and directed by the Coen Brothers, and it only further solidifies their status as skilled storytellers, and crafty filmmakers.

A review of the film should not be spoiled with too much plot info, but this one is so engaging I have no choice but to make mention of some of its key points. Josh Brolin is superb as Llewellyn Moss, a former welder who stumbles across a slew of dead bodies and a briefcase full of money while out on a hunting trip. Moss makes off with the money, and soon realizes he is being pursued by the amoral Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) who wants his money back, the sheriff Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), and a cocky bounty hunter (Woody Harrelson, in a great supporting role). His wife (Kelly Macdonald) is confused when Moss sends her away by bus to stay with her mother while he tries to get away scott-free with the cash. As the cat and mouse game escalates, we begin to wonder whether Moss's real intentions are simply, as a hunter, to avoid having to be the one who is hunted.

Moss and Chigurh are smart in the way they use their environments and the film includes plenty of quirky details that make you soak the details of each new room, office, or road that pops up. The picture's cinematographer Roger Deakins is almost certain to garner an Oscar nomination not only for some sweeping panoramic shots, but for wonderful camera positioning too (probably a result of storyboarding with the Coen Brothers). In one scene, the menacing Chigurh is shown as reflected through a TV set, and the set is later used again to reflect Bell's image; we as viewers mentally connect these two men to prepare us for Bell's monologues later in the film. Or we can also connect that reflection to Moss when he spots Chigurh out of the corner of his eye in one key, suspenseful moment later in the film.

There are plenty of references you could make from the movie. The Chigurh character flips a coin to determine the fate of his victims, much like Tommy Lee Jones does as Two-Face in "Batman Forever." Jones and Harrelson both appeared in Oliver Stone's "Natural Born Killers," and the hyper-violence, blended with desert-scapes, calls to mind that film as well.

It's in the details, though, that the movie transcends the ordinary. Moss and Chigurh operate outside of the law, and respectively sport a manhood-reflective shotgun and a compressed-pressure air gun, while the doting deputy packs a shriveled piece, and hasn't the faintest idea how to use it. Extended passages of the movie are meticulously crafted and often feature no dialogue, as with the great films of Hitchcock. Like in "The Birds," some passages are devoid of musical score and rely primarily on a footstep here or a doorsqueak there.

Is it blasphemy to compare the film to the Master of Suspense? Not at all, as long as one is willing to concede there's a lot of beg, borrow, and stealing at play here. And there's nothing wrong with that. The most notable influence here is "Psycho," with several suspenseful passages taking place at motels; in particular, there's creative use of connecting and connected rooms (much like the peephole in Hitchcock's masterpiece). Like in "Psycho," there is a theft of a substantial amount of money, and once it is taken, it throws the protagonist into a world of intense suspicion and paranoia. Also, Freudian undercurrents of parental influence on the child weave their way through both films. Perhaps the most fun nod, though, is in the parallel between Chigurh and Norman Bates, generally considered to be the nastiest villain of all time alongside Hannibal Lecter (at least according to the American Film Institute). These fellows exist outside of society completely, and, in a wonderful touch, both pop candy into their mouths as if to bide time before their homicidal appetites fire up again.

Some of the most fun is the old Hitchcock rule that you create lots of suspense when the audience is aware of something but the movie's characters aren't. It's best seen when Harrelson is going up the stairs and Chigurh swoops in like a silent vulture behind him. Or when Chigurh has used a tracking device to get to the aforementioned motel, and he plots his approach on the unsuspecting Moss. Hitchcock also proved it's the anticipation leading up to a grisly act that generates the best tension, and, correspondingly, the film is at its most gripping when it builds that tension and then cuts away from a potential killing to "a few minutes later." In this way, some of the actual deaths depicted onscreen -- which are nevertheless copious -- become anti-climactic in places.

The film is based on a novel by Cormac McCarthy, but the adaptation is Coen Brothers-stamped, through and through. We have the quirky "Fargo"-style sheriff (Jones), lots of colourful smalltown characters, and dark humour interspersed throughout, to balance the dramatic intensity. Yet in some ways, "No Country For Old Men" is their most straightforward film to date; the reality of the world they create is not some parallel universe like that of "Barton Fink," it's a slice of 1980 Texas right down to the type of fonts used on the daily newspaper.

One could argue that Llewellyn and Chigurh are more alike than different, in that it doesn't take much for Llewellyn to steal two million dollars and not thinking anything of it. What's interesting is that there is no indication as to what the money really means to the two men. Certainly, Llewellyn's living conditions could use a renovation job, but is it worth the lives of so many others, some whom he knows and (presumably) loves, some whom he has only just met, some he will never meet? These are the fun kinds of questions we end up asking ourselves. It's also curious to ponder why we really find ourselves rooting for Llewellyn. Is it only because he is pitted against the grim Chigurh? One senses the story's protagonists would change rather quickly if Llewellyn and Tom were to have a showdown of their own. (Incidentally, it can be no coincidence that on several occasions in the movie, Tom's name comes out sounding like Anton. Whose stories are really being told near the end of the picture?)

The Coen Brothers choose not to answer the questions though, and the film is all the stronger for it. Rarely does the myth of the American Dream get challenged in today's movies, but "No Country For Old Men" defiantly tells the story of two younger men who will fight tooth and nail to sustain it, while the third man faces the realization that, as an older man who has just retired, his opportunity to break out from his domestic environment and pursue that same dream has passed. We end up with a vision of all that is ugly and all that is true about "the country" in one fell swoop. This is one of the best movies of the year.

The buzz around this movie is crazy.  It is winning critic's choice awards left and right and being touted as the movie to beat at the Oscars.  I don't remember a year where only one movie was getting so much buzz and I don't remember a time where the most buzzed about movie was as disappointing as this.

I have never been a fan of Cormac McCarthy's style.  I find it overly masculine and attempting to be so with its minimalism and the bareness of the reading experience itself.  However I was excited because people were claiming that this was the Coen Brothers' best film and thus I went to see it.

The plot surrounds three very different men and the circumstances that bring them together.  Josh Brolin plays Llewelyn, a simple man who stumbles into trouble while hunting in the desert.  Brolin gives the best performance of his rocky career as the gruff survivor makes a somewhat one-note role on paper human and conflicted.

Tommy Lee Jones plays the town Sheriff who is struggling with age while trying to catch a killer.  Jones is weathered and suits the cowboy role even if the role relies on a few key exposition scenes and little action.  Jones is interesting, however not captivating and thus many of those scenes drag on.

Javier Bardem plays Anton, a sociopathic killer with a Dorothy Hamil haircut.  Bardem is fascinating to watch and the highlight of the movie.  If the entire movie focused on his character it would a heart-stopping adventure through the psyche of a madman, but instead he punctuates the film allowing for terrifyingly Hitchcockian moments.

The bareness of this film takes away from what could be its genius: the complexity of the masculine experience and how that links to violence.  Instead the film drolls on and on without giving us anything to connect to and killing off characters we have connected with before we have a chance to understand them.

This is my no means the best Coen Brothers film because it lacks the sparkle of their previous works.  There are brief moments of humour and stunning cinematography, but all in all it is riddled with the taste of McCarthy's point of view.

LADYKILLERS had moments are absurd hilarity (not to mention a strong argument for Tom Hanks as Ignatius J Reilly in the  eventual adaptation of A CONFEDERACY OF DUNCES), but the overtones of fate and voyeuristic intervention became boringly over-simplified by the story itself. NO COUNTRY? I don't have much to say about this film since, even weeks later, I'm still digesting it. It's one of those ones that stick around. Lots of people have made the distinction between this and BLOOD SIMPLE, that the Coens are going back to basics, and while I agree with the former, not so sure about that latter. NO COUNTRY is miles more intriguing, baffling and surprising than BLOOD SIMPLE. It's as if the brothers had been wanting to return to their roots in order to use the lessons they've learned since then to show the copycats hows it's really done. Cormac McCarthy's story gave them that. But even that doesn't speak to the intelligence of the filmmaking and the originality of the storytelling.

Just know Javier Bardem WILL win awards for Chigurh, a killer grown out of our pop culture lexicon, but not defined by it. He's a logical psychopath with a Pontius Pilate complex, a devastating and creative weapon, and an appearance at odds with the rest of his world's environment. The coin separates his mind from his actions, justifying the unjustifiable. It'll be a tough argument to say he's completely original on the surface, but where the hundreds of "serial killer" films in the past would have stopped there, the Coen's mesh this oddity into their story so seemlessly that even his contradictory presence in the film's world IS what gives that world its complexities. Many critics marvel at the Coen's ability to make the environments in which their film's live as much a character as any person in the story; NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN speaks to how ones environment is only as stable as the ambitions of those within it.  We see these characters as an eye watching in, much like Sherriff Ed Tom Bell, witnessing the results of the their choices, but maddeningly little else. 

Who even knows if this is what the Bros were going for. I know I'm still trying to wrap my head around the experience. 

Just watch it.

The Coen Brothers stir up a Tex-Mex food chain in their latest Tour De Force.
Review by Michael Hansen

NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN (2007) (5 STARS)
Written and Directed by Ethan and Joel Coen.
Based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy.
Runtime: 123 minutes. Rated R. In theaters now. 

I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand, says Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) in the first few minutes of the film as he describes the stupor he feels towards the crimes newer generations have invented for themselves. His narration drifts across shots of rural desolation, a familiar setting for directors Joel and Ethan Coen. In No Country for Old Men the Coens work with author Cormac McCarthy to adapt his novel of the same title for the  big screen. 

The setting is 1980 in Texas, somewhere north of El Paso. The story centers on Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a welder for Robertos Mechanic Shop, who stumbles upon early retirement in the form of a drug deal-turned O.K. corral while hunting antelope in the Texas desert. 

Here the brothers Coen retrace their steps a decade back; quietly sneaking by career flops like Intolerable Cruelty and The Lady Killers, to arrive at their 1996 magnum opus Fargo. In that homespun murder story, they showed us what happens when would-be-criminals get in way over their heads. Here again in No Country they create a world where evil men have laid down a set of terrible circumstances, and an average Joe is willing to tip the first domino over. 

Where's the last guy? Ultimo hombre. Last man standing, there must've been one, Moss asks a dying man at the scene of the gunfight. With no help from him, Moss presses on, knowing that if the ultimo hombre did stop, it would be in the shade. Surely enough, under a lone tree nearby Moss finds a dead thug clutching a satchel, which just happens to be loaded with more money than hes ever seen. The only thing that could ruin this bizarre fairy tale for Moss is a man named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). 

Anton is man so intimidating that you would forget your own first name if he came up and asked you for it. He is a cold hit man for his glutton of a boss (although his actions make him seem more self-employed). As Sheriff Bell says, He has some hard bark on him. 

Moss ships his wife Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald) off to stay with her mother while he lays low for a while. Sheriff Bell, having discovered the crime scene in the desert, goes to warn Moss about the people that hes up against. But its too late, Moss is long gone and Anton is hot on his trail. 

Everyone involved gives the performance of his  or her career. Javier Bardem drains all trace of humanity from Anton, leaving behind an organism whose only function is to calculate his own best interest. Tommy Lee Jones puts on the face of someone trudging through an arctic wind, just trying to stay alive. And the character of Moss fits perfectly on Josh Brolin who dishes out recycled tough guy responses with amazing control so that we can see his trembling beneath.  

The people that inhabit No Country are men of few words. Which is appropriate because the real genius of the film is in its subtleties. Amidst the action sequences lies the theme of tension between generations of men, and the Coen brothers employ many motifs to drag humility out of all the violence. When Moss is in a Mexican hospital he is visited by Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson), another bounty hunter sent for him. Carson tries to connect with Moss, telling him that he was also in Vietnam, to which Moss asks, So what does that make me? Your buddy? With that Moss shows us a generation with no sense of camaraderie, only contempt. This is contrasted with Moss attempt to re-enter the US after his recovery, where his veteran status persuades the old man at the border to sympathize with his plight. The old man and fellow veteran gets Moss a taxi back home. Apparently camaraderie has skipped a generation. 

This sentiment is coupled with Sheriff Bells inability to keep up with Anton and Moss. I feel overmatched, he says to his Uncle Ellis (Barry Corbin, in his first noteworthy role since the demise of Northern Exposure). Bell spends the majority of the film applying conventional wisdom to cold trails. Uncle Ellis, further along in his old age, sadly tells Bell that, You can't stop what's coming. Ain't all waitin on youthats vanity.

The film cuts out after a brief monologue from Sheriff Bell, in which he recounts a dream from the night before. In the dream he and his Father are riding through a snowstorm on horseback when his Father charges ahead carrying fire. When the credits rolled, everyone in the theater under the age of twenty five collectively went, What! You call that an ending? Maybe in doing so they proved the films hypothesis, that there is a communication barrier between men of different times. Obviously they were sad to let the old cowboy have the last word, but if you pay close attention to his speech youll see that the movie is anything but a cliffhanger. 

There is a lot that washes over the viewer throughout the films two-hour runtime. Some may latch onto the movies engrossing action sequences and miss the real themes being studied, which are just as powerful as any ridiculously big firearm that Anton uses to open the door when hes feeling lazy. If youre just looking for a powerhouse of an action flick, youll certainly find it here. But if you watch closely, youll also see the Coen brothers create a world of generations pushing against each other slowly like two shifting continents. No Country tops any previous effort from the Coens, and any fan of Fargo will have no trouble calling this the best film of 07.

It's extremely difficult for me to view a movie based on a novel as two "separate" works. I admit to it willingly. I haven't read Cormac McCarthy's novel. In fact, I've never read anything by McCarthy. I have seen Coen Brother films, though. No Country is a fantastic achievement for the siblings, despite being someone else's original creation. But the dichotomy of the dialogue between the traditional and the modern is seamless, the acting is superb, the suspense is aching, and the movie encompasses the best of the Coen's without tilting one way or the other (for example, the humor here is extremely natural and subtle, unlike some of their more forceful attempts in movies like The Ladykillers). This film is one that, while only running two hours, bombards the audience with a ton of ideas to slowly digest after the credits role. It is as simplistic as it is complex, and is by far one of the best movies I've seen in theatres this year (excluding the innumerable films I've rented). Fans of the Coen's will absolutely love it.

Plot : A man out hunting one day comes across the conclusion of a shootout where he finds a huge amount of a money , meanwhile a killer with nerves of steel tracks him down - killing anyone he meets along the way. 

Story : Defintly a mixed bag of suspense and characters - though it's lack of music and extremely extended scenes do not help move the story faster. A simple man who finds a lot of money somehow knows he's being followed and makes a plan to escape with his wife - but this turns into a coincidence filled failure as this killer tracks him down time and time again. The cop investigating this (Tommy Lee Jones) never seems to help at all , he's just there as a super pointless character that never changes anything. Though the amazing use of the coin flip and fun suspense is thought provoking and fun the first time : i can't say it would be much of any fun the second time watching this movie. 

Action and Suspense : As I stated before there is no music at all to be found in this film for the most part (maybe one song plays for 20 seconds) , which really is a horrible choice for any film : but it defintly brings the suspense to a whole new level for this first viewing. Gunshots and explosions always make a big impact - with so much silence in the movie , but again - your not going to be suprised by them as much when you watch the movie a second time. 

Ending : Another film that seems to be leading up to something and ends out of nowhere. It dosen't conclude anything and just further developes the incredible out of place character : the cop. 

Visuals : Top notch cinemetography for the most part with some breathtaking scenes that will blow your mind. Though the tired and boring desert setting sure gets anoying by the end of the film : and there fail to be any "mind blowing" scenes after the half way mark.

Sypnosis : So many bad ideas combinde into some breath taking visuals and brutal action scenes. The weakest Coen brothers film I've seen - defintly didn't live up to the hype : with such a bland ending and pointless characters.

   SPOILERS
   
   I don't know, I had mixed feelings about this.  I had to be talked into going because I didn't want to see it and I didn't want to go to a late night movie in the middle of an ice storm, AND my movie choice was overruled, so I was a little biased against it to begin with.  This is also a genre that I usually don't like.  However, I found [i]No Country for Old Men [/i]suspenseful, thrilling, and smart, with terrific performances all around.  I even applaud the efforts of the Cohen Brothers, whose movies I either absolutely love or absolutely hate (more hate than love).
   
   Like most people, it was the ambiguity of the movie that bothered me, although maybe not in the same way.  I don't need all the loose ends tied up.  I don't mind filling in the blanks.  I appreciate the surprise of a sudden perspective change.  I can even take a little unclear symbollism.  But it all seemed to be in excess in this film.  
   
   I feel like the Cohen Brothers went far out of their way to confuse and play with the audience.  It seems impossible for a viewer to have caught [i]everything [/i]this movie throws at you.  Maybe you didn't catch Anton checking his boots for blood after leaving Carla Jean's house?  Or you didn't consider the image of Anton wating behind the door of the hotel room as a symbollic imagination?  Or maybe you just became completely lost after Llewelyn's unseen death suddenly shifts the film's whole perspective.  And what [i]was [/i]the point of Woody Harrelson's character anyway?  This movie was meant to confuse, and I think that it has been given a lot of credit and importance just because of all of the thought this confusion inspires.  
   
   But that's not necessarily a positive to me.  Who has never walked out of a movie alongside some pretentious asshole, loudly spouting his theories on the film's meaning as if it were fact?  Those are the kind of people who are eating this movie up.  They overanylze and create these elaborate philosophical explanations for the film and celebrate their ability to have comprehended something that no one else can.  They love the movie for this reason.  Then, on the other side, there are people who underanalyze the movie and just have no idea what it was about, but suppose that it is very clever and claim to love it because of this.  Either way, how can you really love a movie that you don't understand?  It all leads to annoyance for me.
   
   I was entertained, but I wasn't paying close enough attention, and I don't like being played with to the extent that we were in [i]No Country.[/i]  Some of it was clever, but too much of it was irritating.  I think it would take a second viewing to make my own final interpretations of this movie, and I might have to do that.

The best movie of the year, tied with American Gangster. The movie starts out with Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem, who deserves an Oscar nomination for his role) making his first of many killings. The movie then continues to the third character, Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) who throughout the movie, debates the killer instinct of man and how ruthless it gets. The Coen Brothers deserve a Best Director award for this masterpeice. The lack of music and the sounds of nature make this dark thriller chilling. Javier Bardem is thrilling to watch as he fiddles with his victims before their outcome. Tommy Lee Jones, is great even though he isnt in the movie alot, and Josh Brolin is pretty good, but his performance lacks a little bit of emotion. There are alot of concepts being told, all symbolically, and people really have to pay attention to every thing shown and spoken. The movie has twist and turns and is great as a thriller but is also amazing as a movie with a message about how dumb America's youth is, how wise and yet unwilling to change the old are, and the relentlesness and chaos of the generation between young adults and seniors is. No Country for Old Men is one of the best films of the year, a cant miss.

The search is over - and the hunt has been going on for just over eleven months; ladies and gentlemen, we have found the best film of 2007.  No Country For Old Men is a near-perfect exercise in comedy, suspense, drama and violence.  Despite wonderful performances by the ever-reliable Jones and Brolin, this is essentially Javier Bardem's movie: in Anton Chigurgh, the Coen Brothers have created an emotionless, merciless and terryfing killing machine - equal to Ben Kingsley's Don in Sexy Beast and Anthony Hopkins Hannibal Lecter.  Not a half-second is wasted and, contrary to the Hollywood mumbo jumbo we've had to put up with year in, year out, the conclusion is surprisingly well-thought out and subtle.  The cinematography is awesome, the cast is sublime; resulting in an entirely captivating movie made up of countless scenes that you never ever want to end.  Believe the critics (this time) - very finely put, this is the best film of the year and, just behind Fargo, the Coen's second best film they've made. This lack of sound adds to the tension considerably, and gives extra weight to the characters' actions.
Usually I try to avoid spoilers in my reviews, but the end is what really makes the movie. You wait for Bell to track down Moss, finding him in the nick of time from the evil Chigurh. But you are not given what nearly every film before this gives you, a happy ending. Our entire audience was quiet when the credits rolled, not out of surprise, but because they were processing what they just saw. How could you not? There is just so much to think about here. One of the few movies you want to see again as soon as you leave the theater.

The themes of this movie are strong and defined enough to give this movie a grand scale, yet do not obstruct the tale of money, greed, justice, and death.

There is so much to love and admire about this film that I hesitate to criticize it.  All the Coens' trademarks are on display: uniformly great performances; brilliant camera work (in this case lean and steady); sharp, appropriate dialog that remains clever while never wasting a word.  I have even come to reconcile my concern over the films overwhelming bleakness.  I've been placing NCfOM in comparison with Fargo...a film that ended with "goodness" prevailing despite an inability to fathom the evil confronted.  Marge apprehended without comprehending.  This film inverts that equation.  I find that deeply troubling, but I respect the Coens assertion.  I also believe that, regardless of their history as jokey ironists, they really mean this one, with all the bitterness intact.  I love how supremely tense the film is, even as it transforms a simple, cat 'n' mouse chase scene into the centerpiece of the film.  Ultimately, though, I still can't accept the characterization of Anton as this supernatural, unstoppable killing machine: the Terminator as apocalyptic angel of death.  I think other critics have focused on this aspect during the final stretch of the picture.  I see this more as a problem from start to finish.  But I can't deny that the film hit me hard.

The Coen brothers have struck again with their unmistakable style and substance. No Country For Old Men is no doubt a unique and well made film, it is slow paced and unfolds in a very tedious and uneven fashion which makes the movie hard to watch.  I enjoyed the fact that the film is not neat and calculated in the particular fashion most predictable Hollywood fare is, what you predict through common cliches to happen doesn't happen and I praise the movie for this, it takes the road less travelled in that sense. 

Its violent, intense, cold, quirky and actor Javier Bardem steals the whole movie as a serious no nonsense (so serious in fact that he has the most hilarious scenes in the whole otherwise dark film with some brilliant dialogue) hitman who uses untraditional methods to dispatch his victims to say the least.  

Critically acclaimed No Country For Old Men will no doubt disappoint a lot of viewers and have others frothing at the mouth of originality.

The best film of 2007 has finally arrived. I don't feel the need to talk of the performances because they can be summed up in one word: phenomenal. I can't say how many times I've been into a film only to have a music cue come up that just tells you what way you should be feeling. That's pompous and ridiculous. The characters don't have to say anything they don't want to say, never being tied down by having contrived words forced in their mouths. Speaking of the characters, they are classic. The psychopathic hitman, the tired sheriff, the working man that finds what he always deserved but can never have. It's all there. They never truly touch down in reality. They simply exist in a strange surrealism that restate what is so great about classic cinema: taking you out of your hectic day-to-day life and giving you a chance to enjoy yourself for 2+ hours. The ending drags out a bit, but it only helps serve the title of the film. No Country for Old Men will be here for a long time as one of the greatest movies ever made. All thanks to the Coen Brothers. Thank you.

No film in 2007 was greater than the Coen Brothers' masterpiece. No Country is a captivating thrill ride from start to finish, featuring three of the strongest performances of the year. Javier Bardem received the glory in the form of Best Supporting Actor, but all three main actors are at the top of their game. Beyond these three, the entire cast weaves the film together in a way that is rarely seen these days.  The story (adapted almost identically from Cormac McCarthy's novel) is riveting, and the direction of the film is superb. The Coen Brothers match the direction of their prior magnum opus, Fargo (these two films alone will create a huge debate over which is the better achievement), creating a sense of tension so thick it penetrates the screen and wraps itself around the audience. This tension stays, incredibly, throughout the entire film.  The film operates on two levels- the literal action occurring, which is enough to make this a great movie, but there is also an allegory beneath the surface.  It is this second layer that lifts the film into the upper echelon.  To put it in plainly: No Country is the most important film of the new millennium, and one of the best from the past 30 years.

[font=Century Gothic]Written and directed by Ethan and Joel Coen, "No Country for Old Men" is a beautiful and violent movie that is also admirably restrained. The inherent problem with all movies is that they are bound by their medium. Characters which are built up, are built up for a payoff. The camera must follow the action. Dialog must further a plot, and the plot must find a conclusion.

No Country For Old Men skillfully masters, and transcends, those boundaries. No matter the director, an observant movie goer can discern a directors style, and surprising an audience becomes harder and harder. Good movies can avoid this. The Coen brothers manage it, whilst maintaining total realism.

This film gets everything right, and still isn't satisfied. It crafts throwaway material with equal skill, and reminds you at every turn: this film will not follow the rules. Unlike many experimental films, though, and what garners it such high praise, is that it breaks these rules to the immense benefit of the storytelling itself. Yes, there is alot of "thrown away" material, and that is what garners it five-stars for me. The throwaway stuff is there to make you think about what actually mattered, and where these characters are going. It lets you imagine the story-arc as much fuller than you can cram into a couple of hours... and the abrupt ending doesn't seem nearly as biting. What else is there left to tell, really, when you think about it? It leaves you feeling like a sock puppet, yet unlike other films that do so ("Dead Man", for instance), you feel grateful for the experience.

Easily one of the top 3 films I've seen this year, No Country is a great tale of temptation set in a modern western background (El Paso). The Coens have put together a spectacular and masterful piece of work with some of the best performances and overall filmmaking you will see this year. Easily a frontrunner for Best Picture. Adapted from a Cormac McCarthy novel, what really brings this film to life is the Oscar worthy performance from Javier Bardem as a relentless, principled, coin-tossing hitman Anton Chigur. His subtle performance mixed with intense displays of cruelty and brutal violence steals every scene he is in. Tommy Lee Jones is also spectacular as an aged sheriff that throughout the course of the film must come to grips with the fact that the world is a bigger, faster, more violent place that he can no longer handle or protect the innocent from.  Without giving anything away; the final scene with him conversing with his wife is spectacular and brings the film full circle.
The Coens create scenes with such great tension between Anton and his victims (especially the coin-tosses and standoff with Carson Wells) that it is easy to see the mastery of their writing and directorial skills. The suspense created is some of the best that I have ever seen on the big screen.  Great performance by Josh Brolin as well; and the way the Coens displayed the subtle similarities between Anton, Sheriff Bell and Llewelyn despite their very different roles and backgrounds was another small but brilliant addition to this film.
While I donât necessarily like the way it ended or the way they handled the fate of Llewelyn, since it was sort of anticlimactic, it fit well with the overall message of the film regarding temptation and the inevitable violent turn of humanity.  The only reason I donât give this film a 5 star rating is that a few scenes dragged on a past the point of significance and almost into the realm of detracting from the overall plot and main themes.
Bottom Line: Some of the best acting, directing, cinematography put up on the big screen in 2007; deserves nod for Best Picture and could very well walk away with the award; Brolin, Jones and Bardem also deserve lead and supporting nods respectively.  Go out of your way to see this film.

A Texas good-ole-boy (Josh Brolin) stumbles across the aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong.  But when he finds a case of cash among the dead bodies and decides to walk off with it, he opens a pandoras box of violence he cannot close.  In particular he incurs the wrath of a serial killer-cum-force of nature called Chigur (Javier Bardem) who wants the money back at any cost.  A tired old Texas lawman (Tommy Lee Jones) tries to intervene before the mayhem reaches what appears to be an inevitably tragic conclusion.  This film, by brothers Ethan and Joel Coen (Fargo, Miller's Crossing) is similar to David Cronenberg's "A History Of Violence" in that it is a meditation on manhood, that is at times calm and yet is punctuated by stark and horrifying reminders of the evils men inflict upon one another. No Country for Old Men is really two movies in one. It starts one way and ends a completely different way. In that, it is similar to Robert Rodriguez's From Dusk 'Till Dawn, except it approaches its subject matter with more seriousness. I can't help but feel as if the source material (a novel of the same name by Cormac McCarthy) wasn't entirely suited to an adaptation. The movie's strong first hour is a textbook example of how to build suspense with little violence. Unfortunately, the Coen brothers fail to bring the story home. Characters we've followed with such intensity are taken away from us with little warning, and we are forced to deduce what happens because we do not see it.

The story and its mystery are extremely well-presented. We are introduced to the film's villain, the psychopathic Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), in a terrifying manner befitting a man who cannot be understood, merely described. The hero is a poor country man named Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), who stumbles upon the remains of a massacre, takes a chance, and steals a suitcase full of money from a dead man. We follow Llewelyn as he tries to run from the danger posed to him and his young wife Carla Jean by Chigurh, and the details slowly unravel. We discover why the massacre occurred, we briefly explore the relationship between Llewelyn and his wife, and we watch Llewelyn's deceptions and innovations as he tries to hide both himself and the money from Chigurh, who always seems to be just a step behind him, from town to town, and hotel to hotel. They finally confront one another in a tense but curiously anticlimactic gunfight on the streets of Del Rio, a town on the border of Mexico. When the fight is over, we know that nothing has changed -- the final confrontation has just been delayed another day.

We are treated to brief glimpses of Llewelyn's inner character. He is a man with guilt on his shoulders, but he is not able to simply run away from his troubles. An early scene sees him almost get killed after returning to the scene of the massacre against his better judgement to offer water to a dying man. Similarly, he refuses merely to disappear with Carla to escape from Chigurh, and instead choses to go after the killer to protect his wife. It is at this point that the movie loses its way.

The most curious inclusion in this book is the character of Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), the head of law enforcement in Llewelyn's home county. Bell is at this point a relic of the past, an old man who remembers a time when the local sheriff didn't have to carry a gun, something that we are told is no longer feasible. Bell deduces what has happened, and tries vainly to warn Llewelyn about Chigurh, but his main purpose seems to be to preach about how the world has changed to something that he doesn't really understand anymore. The last half of the film deals mainly with Llewelyn's attempt to get in contact with his wife, and Bell's attempt to save Llewelyn from his fate, but after a strange and essentially unexplained turn of events, we are left just with Bell's recollections and bleak view of the future.

The character of Chigurh is the most interesting aspect of No Country for Old Men. We have met men, who, like him, lack scruples when money is involved. The annals of film are ripe with murderous villains who are willing to do anything where money is involved. We have also seen scores of cruel, twisted men who will kill and maim and torture for the pure pleasure of it. Chigurh is different, though. He does not kill for pleasure, and he is not changed by money. He can't betray you, because he is loyal to nobody. He doesn't enjoy killing you, but he doesn't find it distasteful, either -- he simply does it. Life means nothing to him, people mean nothing to him, but he is always a man of his word. He is not emotional, and he does not punish people for their actions, but if he tells you he is going to do something, he will surely do it. The movie ends on an ambiguous note, with Chigurh never really held accountable for what he is, or without us knowing if his humanity ever found him.

Woody Harrelson has a brief and solid appearance as a bounty hunter sent to retrieve the money. His contrast as a human being to Chigurh is worthwhile, and it's a shame that the character wasn't expanded.

No Country for Old Men has been mentioned as an Oscar contender. Bardem's performance of Chigurh has given us one of the most memorable film villains, but the rest of the movie falls short. It's a shame to watch such a promising beginning fade away by the end of the film. Maybe it's a generational thing about the world changing, something that I would understand if I were my father's age, but I suspect that No Country for Old Men is just a novel that wasn't entirely suited to the silver screen.

Most overrated film of the year
This was a movie I was initially going to avoid because I had seen the trailers so many times and was less than thrilled. However, after hearing a great review from one of my best film friends, who's opinion I respect highly, I thought what the hell I'll give this a shot.

I'll admit I really enjoyed the the first half of the film up until the confrontation between Anton and Llewelyn where they first set eyes on each other. I loved the fact that no music is used, and I love that we know so little about the main characters as we go into the film, yet the acting and dialouge is done so well, although dialouge is sparce in this first half, that the characters all seem like very real people. Some of the tension in this first half is almost unbearable (in a good way). When we are at the second hotel and the tracking device starts going off and Anton walks right by the room as we hear the beeping. My god, I could barely sit still. And then the way the rest of this scene plays out as Llewelyn runs to the passing car, and the driver get's shot in the throat. Wonderful.

However, after this confrontation, what happened to the tension? I was no longer gripped to my seat as we go and clear up subplots with Woody's character, that I could care less about. Does this tension compare to that of our protagonist's? Not even close. Yet you think that all this is building up to a final confrontation between Llewelyn and Anton, especially when the two talk on the phone. But no, this never comes. The next time we see Llewelyn, he is dead on a hotel floor. Along with his death goes the energy that kept this film rolling. I'm not saying that seeing this confrontation between Llewelyn and Anton is necessary, but there still needs to be away to keep the conflict rising, which the Coen brothers I guess forgot to do here.

Instead we're left with a confrontation between Llewelyn's wife and Anton and some old food for thought from Tommy Lee Jones. Yeah, I liked the confrontation between Llewelyn's wife and Anton. But was it as good as the confrontation between her husband and Anton. Nope. I feel the Coen brothers were trying to emphasize the point of there story in this second half. Having to do with both fate and pure evil. Anton embodies both these things seeming to be a soulless monster who is on a mission that he has no control of. I've heard many praise his character saying that this is a great character study of a person who embodies pure evil. Well I have seen plenty of horror films where this character is represented as well, only Anton talks and gives a voice to this evil. And it's almost as if we know what he is going to say, that is exactly what any character of pure evil would say. And after all this we're left with Tommy Lee Jones little speech at the end. I had almost completely checked out at this point. Not because I wanted to (I guess it was fate) but because THE MOVIE no longer gripped me. I only caught bits and pieces of Lee's speech once again talking about fate, and then I was happy to leave the theatre.

Sure this movie has themes of how money can make you cold and dead to life, fate, and pure evil. But is this done in a new refreshing way? No. Does it stir my mind in a different way. Nope.

I have seen most of the Coen Brothers film, and I'm left disappointed almost every time. I think they are two of the most overrated directors that are alive today. I'm not saying they make bad movies, because they don't. It's only that I feel too many of their movies are heralded as genius when they are only in the category of good. This happens to be another one of them in the good.

It's unconventional (and I think a lot of people didn't like that), but there's also no other appropriate way it could have ended. Otherwise, it would have forsaken most (if not all) of its social and ethical implications. And the dialogue was just as fundamental to developing these themes as the edge-of-your-seat tension and graphic violence were. But it's not until these latter, nerve-stimulating elements finally subside that the viewer can recognize the basic (but subtle), underlying point of it all with a comprehensive resolution. Ok...the Coen Brothers finally get serious. Saw this at Kendall a few weeks ago. No Country For Old Men is a novel by Cormac McCarthy who is, in my opinion, one of the best American writers ever. Unfortunately there hasn't been a decent film made out of his work until now with No Country For Old Men. I haven't read this one yet but I've read about 7 books by him since 1995 and only stopped when I sensed his success had tainted his writing somewhat. This was evident to me in the somewhat disappointing third installment of his Border Trilogy entitled Fires On the Plain. The first book was his big breakthrough to the general public, All The Pretty Horses, a very excellent book though not a masterpiece like the second in the trilogy, The Crossing. Overall, his single best work is probably Blood Meridian, a violent and surreal historical epic about rogue Civil War soldiers bounty hunting the Comanches for Mexico. Cormac McCarthy is not a "western writer" though his fiction has been based in the southwest of the US for almost two decades now. His first handful of novels were set in the deep south.
The Coen Brothers really do him justice with this film. Ironically, after so many diverse films by this pair, their latest recaptures the tone of their first feature film, Blood Simple.

I won't give away the plot but Josh Brolin plays a jobless vietnam vet who lives with his not too swift wife in a trailer park. While out hunting in the desert for game he discovers the recent carnage of a dope deal gone bad with no survivors. He pries a suitcase with millions in cash from a corpse's grip and returns home to stash it under his trailer. His finding of this money sets off all the objects in motion. He's soon a fugitive and hunted down by a psychopathic hired killer, federal agents, and one Vietnam vet small-town sheriff (TL jones). 
The script is classic Cormac McCarthy. The film is paced masterfully almost like a Hitchcock movie. Just when you think you've figured out what's going to happen the Coens throw out all the formulaic b.s. and you are forced to grapple with the reality of the drama as it relates to the empty theater of the human soul. Life imitating art or vice versa, who knows but this film screws with your head. Now I have to read the book.

The Coen Brothers make their most accomplished film. There is a lot to recommend in the mis en scene and composition of the film. The technical achievements are there because Coens are able to make a violent film suggestive of even more violence. 

The Coen Brothers even come close to telling an organic story. The accents aren't heightened to make everything comedic like in Fargo. Only a few scenes play out to the Coen irreverence, but the characterization is still misguided. The film is very similar to the original novel, but the film takes the characters and interprets them as running cliches of tough pulp novels. Brolin's character in the novel is more defined by his fears and weaknesses, but in the film he is an out and out killer with the same disconnect to humanity that the psychotic killer posesses. The Coen Brothers are fascinated by genre and do everything to associate this film with noir attributes. Like other bad interpretation, the noir perspective here is just based on look and feel. The Coens could care less about a psychological subtext to noir. 

The Coens have always been interpretive with their stories to make them fit their personality, but this is the first film they did that has an original source and shows that the Coens made all the choices to reduce the original story. The themes are watered down. In the novel, Tommy Lee Jones' character is the main figure who guides the themes and perspective of the violence. In the film he is a supporting one whose scenes are cute ancedotes than anything else. The film tries to make up for it by showing Jones late in the film as he was in the novel, but it's to little too late. His scenes come off as apologies to a film that designated too much story and time to an elaborate chase subplot.

The Coen Brothers are criminal filmmakers to me. Pure stylists that relate their films to nothing more than amateur fodder. There are interesting themes within No Country for Old Men, but the Coens show their talent to take a story and allow it to play out to cliche interpretation. The noir look has been overdone. Even if people interpret this film as a Western, it's still a hollow redux of a genre that had deeper meaning.

With the mediocrity of Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers behind them, the Coen Brothers are back to their usual best with the astounding No Country For Old Men.

In 1980, while out hunting in the beautifully shot Texan desert, Llewelyn Moss, a retired welder and Vietnam vet stumbles across a Mexican drug deal gone wrong. Surrounded by a stash of heroin, bullet holes, blood and dead bodies, Llewelyn takes off with a satchel of two million dollars and returns to his trailer park home. This proves to be a very bad decision when the terrifying, psychopathic yet somehow hilarious assassin Anton Chigurh, armed with a silenced shotgun and cattle bolt gun is sent to retrieve the money and kill anyone who gets in the way. A couple of steps behind the action is Tommy Lee Jones' old man of the tale Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, who's longing for his retirement and is always on hand to deliver the odd smart-arse comment while at the same time, being the voice of the film.

What precedes is a three-way chase between cheap, grotty Texan motels to Mexican border towns, with Moss trying to stay low with his new found wealth while being hunted down by a brutal assassin with a haircut that wouldn't make him look out of place in The Beatles 1960's era. 

While everyone involved puts in the perfect performance, from Josh Brolin's battered and beaten strong heart of the story to the Scottish Kelly MacDonald's flawless Texan accent, it's Javier Bardem's remorseless hitman Chigurh that is the true highlight of the film. A detached killer with a Terminator-like presence and an obsession with the chance of a coin toss, who will stop at nothing and kill anything to retrieve the money. It comes as no surprise Bardem received Academy recognition with a Best Supporting Actor nomination for the role. 

If you can forgive the little bit of anti-climax towards the end, this violent yet blackly funny tale is a fine return to form from the true masters of the dark comedy, and will no doubt draw comparisons with their 1996 thriller Fargo. No Country For Old Men could already be one of the best films of 2008.

Having not read the source material (Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel), I can only go by what I saw on the screen. "No Country" was, for the better part of the film, a gripping, well-acted, well-shot, thinking man's Terminator-style chase movie. I can only caution viewers to leave the film around an hour and 45 minutes in to escape the heresy that was the final 15-20 minutes. If you'd rather suffer horrible disappointment on your own, don't read on, because I'm spoiling it right after this colon: the character who is hands down the driving force of the movie, the main protagonist, the good in good vs. evil, the guy you're behind completely, is killed by an inconsequential character. So inconsequential, in fact, that we have no idea who did it-- the killing happened off-screen, as if to erase any semblance of a climax that could've remained. No words could describe my shock when it happened, and inevitable anger afterward. I remained to see the conclusion only because I thought to myself, "This can't possibly be it. There was has to be something redeeming. They had to have done this for a reason." Instead, I was treated to an ending that somehow infuriated me more. The antagonist is not caught, given no satisfying conclusion. The main body of the end is dominated by Tommy Lee, who hasn't really mattered the entire more. But apparently it's all about him, as the title would suggest. While I can only assume the Coen brothers have stayed true to McCarthy's novel, the greatest pitfall of "No Country" is that it kills off the reason we're watching. It's a testament to the power of the first 3/4 of the movie that I was so furious when the protagonist is killed, but that's no saving grace. Disappointing to an extreme.

I first saw the preview for No Country For Old Men (here on in to be refered to as NCFOM) on the Death Proof DVD. I found that trailer to be more entertaining than a number of movies which I have wasted money on in my life, and so I decided to do a little research about the movie. I found out it had been an official selection for the Cannes Film Festival, and all of the reviews I read on IMDB had said it to be amazing. Since it's release, it has won numerous awards, and has been nominated for four golden globes. The only way that this film will not be getting Oscar nods is if all the members of the Academy die and are replaced by a bunch of half retarded llamas.

Needless to say, I was pretty pumped for this movie. And so I went to go see it last night, rather than study for finals. Some people may think that my time could have been better spent, but I beg to differ. I can honestly say that I feel NCFOM is the best film of the year. There are those who will disagree with me, but after thinking about it for a day (yes, this is one of those movies that makes you think), I truly believe that this is the best of film of 2007, and may end up being one of the best of the decade. The film takes place in New Mexico in the 1980's, when a redneck named Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad. He finds a ton of dead bodies, a hug amount of drugs, and almost 2 million dollars in a briefcase. He takes the money home, and it is from this point on that the story takes off. A psycopath named Anton Chigurh is hired to track Llewelyn down and get the money back. Anton is the best cinematic villian to come along in years, and this is in part because of the great acting done by Javier Bardem, who plays this character in a cold, controlled way. The other main character is Sheriff Tom Bell, played by Tommy Lee Jones, a man who feels that times are changing for the worst. There are a number of other characters, such as Llewelyn's wife and Woody Harrelson's character, but the three stated above are the most important.

There is so much about the film I love. The cinematography was beautiful. The Coens make the bleak New Mexico landscape almost into a character, it works with the film so well. The editing was beyond tight. But the two things that really sold me on this film were the tension it created and the ending. Saying this film made me a little nervous for the main characters is like say the Pacific Ocean holds a little water. I literally sat on the edge of my seat for parts of this film, nervous in a way I have never been while watching a movie before. I think that the biggest part of that played into that was the lack of music throught out the film. The Coens decided (wisely, in my opinion) to use a soundtrack with no music, and the film is better for it. Some of the scenes that come to mind are the ones in which Anton is hunting Llewelyn down. There is silence, except for the sound of the floor creaking, or a man breathing. It brings the tension to a level which I have never felt while watching a movie before, and that in and of itself makes this a very good movie. The thing that make this movie great, however, is that the Coen brothers made a film that defies the standard Hollywood mold of what a film should be, and if you ever see this film I will discuss those things with you to no end. There are some people who feel they ruined the movie by taking it in the direction they did, but after having thought about it for a while, I have come to realize what the Coens were trying to accomplish, and I love this movie for that.

I give NCFOM a ten out of ten. If you keep an open mind while watching this movie, and think about it after viewing it, you will have a movie going expiernce like none other. There are quite a few people who hate this movie, but those people are morons. This is the best film of the year, and I highly recommend seeing it in theaters.

Like most Coen Brothers movies, NCFOM leaves you feeling like it's probably about something, but what? As with LEBOWSKI'S oblique references to Saddam Hussein and BARTON FINK'S... well, just about everything in Barton Fink, the Coens' knobby finger of genius points you toward some grand theme, but the trail goes cold about three minutes after the credits roll. When I read McCarthy's novel awhile back, I remember thinking, "The Coen Brothers should make this." The book bore striking similarity to BLOOD SIMPLE -- the same god's-eye-view of disconnected characters moving about a forbidding landscape and trying to get away with something. If anything, the movie version of NCFOM distills and clarifies things a bit, while managing to follow the plot nearly paragraph by paragraph. Most of the actors give wonderful, measured performances. Tommy Lee Jones walked right off the set of IN THE VALLEY OF ELAH and into this movie, pausing only to change into a sheriff's uniform. (I'm not sure he's been out of the Texas desert in three years.) Javier Bardem's creepy killing machine gets all the attention, but Josh Brolin is doing the most sparkling work of everybody. There was one movie that I was dying to see in 2007 - No Country For Old Men. There has been a great buzz surrounding this film, critics have been hailing No Country as a masterpiece, a classic and a film to be challenged. Things only got better as it was nominated for 8 academy awards, and took home four, including best picture and best director.
I was a little apprehensive at believing all of the praise, I didn't want to set my expectations too high, but I almost couldn?t help it when I viewed the trailer and clips over the internet and on television. I have been a fan of the Coen brothers since Fargo, and by the looks of it, they were back in their element, and had directed the greatest film of their careers.
I will admit, I watched No Country on the big screen, alone. I had no one to go with and was not going to miss the opportunity to see this in the theater. Right from the get-go the movie is intense, the character Anton Chigurh played by Javier Bardem is arrested and brought into the county jail for processing. However his stay is quite short as he manages to escape by strangling the officer with his handcuffs, and stealing the police cruiser. Chigurh begins his path of destruction with the help of his trusty oxygen tank and stun gun attachment.
Meanwhile Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a middle-class welder is out hunting antelope when he stumbles upon what appears to be a drug deal gone wrong. 3 vehicles, many dead bodies, and a truck bed filled with heroin. After a few minutes of inspection, and after collecting a few guns for his collection, Moss finds one dead man farther away from the others. With that man is a black satchel. Inside that satchel is 2 million dollars, cash, in 10 thousand dollar bricks. Moss can only wonder what to do, but at that point, who would leave that money? It?s a big, life-altering decision, which it seems that Moss did not put that much thought into.
Later that night, Moss returns to help out a man who was left alive, but finds that the man had eventually succumb to his injuries. But now Llewelyn has a problem, two men driving a truck have come to the scene, and have spotted his brown ford truck. They slash the tires, and eventually spot Llewelyn running for cover. While avoiding gunshots, Moss manages to get away, but not without a few wounds. Now, fearing for his life, and his wife?s, he derives a plan. Send his wife to her mothers, and flee with the money, hoping to lose the trail of whoever is chasing him.
Anton Chigurh is now on the look out for the satchel that contains the 2 million, and is leaving a bloody mess behind him to get to it. Llewelyn soon discovers that Chigurh has found him, and has been to the hotel room he is staying at, not to mention his trailer home.
Sherriff Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is caught up in the search for mass murderer Anton Chigurh, and discovers that a man he knows, Llewelyn Moss, is the pursued. Also joining the hunt for Chigurh and Moss is Carson Wells, a Texas ranger who?s mission is to locate either one of the men, or the money.
Llewelyn Moss eventually runs into trouble as Chigurh closes in, and Moss also discovers how the mad-man has been tracking him. Now more than ever, staying one step ahead is more important than anything, as Llewelyn experiences one too many close calls. Carson Wells finally tracks down Moss at a hospital, where he warns him that Anton Chigurh is not going to stop, and that to continue running is foolish. With greed being the number one motive, Llewelyn ultimately makes the choice to keep running with the 2 million dollars. With solid performances, and some of the most intense scenes in recent movie history, No Country has, for me, been one of the most thrilling and memorable movie experiences. Bloody, gruesome and bold, this film is over the top, but balanced. I am hard-pressed to find flaws, No Country is almost a perfect movie. My expectations were fulfilled, and surpassed, my mind could not stop spinning after the credits rolled.
With an ending that seems almost abrupt, but suiting and effective, No Country For Old Men becomes the definitive film about the consequences of greed. The smallest thing can bring your world crashing down, all it takes is one misguided choice.

I love the way the Coen Brothers can take a desolate landscape like the barren border country between Texas and Mexico and fill it up with so much blood, irony and metaphoric violence that the setting itself functions like a character in the story. And, the hotels where much of the interior violence unfolds have a personality of their own. And, the drug war that weaves in and out of the story is some how besides the point. Rather, it's how people either respond or not respond to violence that seems to be the point of the story. Interestingly, we never see a women killed in this film, though we know that many are. Yet, men and dogs are blown away one after another. No Country For Old Men makes the point that by the time we hit the 1980s, the world had changed in ways that let murder and killing function as a norm for younger men in the culture. The Javier Bardem character shows no remorse for his actions, and one gets the feeling that the Coen brothers find this sort of behavior all too common in a world that has grown immune to evil. They're not providing any answers or even much intelligent commentary here. It's more about showing us what we already know about the painful state of humanity. Chilling it is.

A refreshing break from the typical happy-ending movie mold. It might take you some time after the movie to fully realize the incredible amount of symbolism and subtleties embedded within the film. At first glance, it lacks character development; but then you realize that each seemingly minor action revealed a lot about the characters. The most incredible part of the film is the antagonist - he is the ultimate indestructible bad guy; he is maniacal yet has principles that he refuses to break under any circumstances. Throughout the film, you think you know everything that's going on, but at the end, that is all destroyed and you realize that even you as the viewer are powerless to the chaos. It is like those "Choose Your Adventure" books from the old days, in that the outcome of many situations are left up to your interpretation of each of the characters and what you would have expected to happen. I loved the realism of the film which was contributed to by the lack of soundtrack, the genuine attachment you felt to the antagonists, and the destroyed feeling of omniscience - because when do things work out perfectly in real life?

- Well done Coen brothers.

Joel and Ethan Coen are special film makers.  Although Barton Fink, the Hudsucker Proxy, Intolerable Cruelty, The Ladykillers, did nothing for me, Millers Crossing and the Man Who Wasnt There are movies that only an artist can make.  Put No Country for Old Men in that category.   Although it can sometimes work, I dont care for voiceover or a silioquay to start or end a movie.  No Country did that to start and end the movie.  I tuned out the words at the beginning and the end.  I'm not sure if they were poigent or relevant, I just couldnt stay intersted on Tommy Lee's voice. The dialogue may have been right out of the book the movie is based on.  Everything in between however was what filmmaking should be all about.  There was suspense and drama created honestly with skill and artistry. The editing is a tight and taut as you can get it.    If you like the standard formulas for movies with 3 Acts and the inciting incident in minute 25 with the transition to act 3 in minute 90, with standard qualities for the hero, villain, and side kicks, you may not care for this movie because Coen brothers are interested in telling a story not in formalized structure.   They dont even tell you what year it is until near the end of the movie.   Iif you like real storytelling this movie is a must see.  I've never been to the "country" nor do I have any idea what it was like during this time period, so I have no way to authenticate the feeling I got that the movie actually transported me to that time and place.  That's what a real artist can do.  That I didnt give it 5 stars is probably more to do with me not being used to a non formula movie.  I'll have to watch this one again.
