''Whatcha got ain't nothin new. This country's hard on people, you can't stop what's coming, it ain't all waiting on you. That's vanity.'' Violence and mayhem ensue after a hunter, Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon some dead bodies, a stash of heroin and more than $2 million in cash near the Rio Grande. Nothing ever goes smoothly sometimes and before you know it he's on the run from a psychopathic cold killer. Josh Brolin: Llewelyn Moss. Javier Bardem: Anton Chigurh. Relentless in method, challenging in presentation, and unforgettable in execution; The Coen Brothers' adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's acclaimed novel borders upon pure genius in its characters and suspenseful build up, but sacrifices much of the clarity (though not the power) of its narration in the strict adherence to its source material. Boasting some of the finest performances of the year, the Coen's fantastically intricate thriller demands an astute mind and a perceptive eye to decipher the multi-layered parallels that lie in No Country for Old Men.
Having watched the two Oscar heavyweights No country for old men and There will be blood round about the same time period on the big screen, I can't help noticing the sharp contrast in audio style, while Blood came with background music so overwhelming that it threatens to take over foreground, Old men had only silence, natural sound and dialogue, with no music at all. There is no right or wrong: each style serves its particular purpose. Imagine the scene in Old men with Llewelyn Moss in the middle of the night in a sunken hollow strewn with a few abandoned vehicles and dead bodies. As the menacing headlight of an ominous looking vehicle at the top of a slope threatens to approach, any kind of music would do more harm than good to the blood-chilling atmosphere present. In their inimitable fashion, the Coen Brothers crafted this adopted story through a mesmerizing plot line that is ever elusive, giving you the slip every time you feel that you have got the hang of things. The plot line looks simple: a common young man who stumbles across two million dollars becomes the prey of a serial killer who is after the money (and his life), while a season sheriff comes after both in an almost standard cat-and-mouse story. But there are more than initially meets the eye. Moss the everyday man protagonist is not your ordinary reckless young man next door. Seasoned Vietnam veteran, he shows his stuff when chased by a ferocious killing bloodhound, hurriedly loading his pistol but never losing control, and firing it when the canine's deadly teeth is within three feet of his throat. He is undoubtedly the prey, but not one that rolls over and play dead. But this is really the hunter's show. Javier Bardem (The sea inside) whom has won every Best Supporting Actor in sight is good enough to give Daniel Day-Lewis a run for his money had he been put in the contest for Best Actor, to which he has every right. The most amazing thing is that while his physical appearance is at times even comical (mainly due to the ridiculous hair style), his mere presence is so chilling that it makes Jason Voorhees, Norman Bates and Hannibal Lector look like Disney villains. ''I always figured when I got older, God would sorta come inta my life somehow. And he didn't. I don't blame him. If I was him I would have the same opinion of me that he does.'' As the movie follows the standard cat-and-mouse crime thriller development, the audience may be so hung to the edge of their seats that they forget temporarily that this is indeed the Coen Brothers. The climatic showdown that they tricked you into expecting never presents itself. Everything seems to fall apart in the last third of the movie, or does it? For some people it may do, but these certain individuals lack sophistication in plain terms; Necessary train of thought or depth albeit an ability to see between the lines. Clearly No Country is going for it's source Novel and this Story is not a straight line but one of complication, one of poetic reflection. The ending to me was a marvel, like a newly born ray of sunshine upon ones face. The words reflecting deeper meaning and wisdom, that shamefully are wasted upon mainstream audiences. For those gracious enough to embrace the ending for what it is, will certainly come off all the better for it, not to mention inspiring and awe defining. The cat-and-mouse game ended almost as an afterthought, with none of the excitement the audience thought they had been promised. The focus has long since shifted to depiction of Bell, as one of the old men, in the title, one of disconnection and unparalleled from the main story yet ultimately part of it regardless. If you think back, most of the small roles (starting with the attendant of the now famous and memorable gas station scene at the start of the story) are old individuals. While the audience might have forgotten, the directors/screen writers have not. They haven't abandoned the concept, that this movie is trying to show why this desolate, seemingly endless horizon, Texas country is quite literally no country for old men. Added to this is the final touch, the accident; showing how karmic life and reality can be. There was so many great scenes in No Countrythat it is hard to cover it all in a single review. The tension, the sounds, the beats, the uses of silence all are definitely used to perfection. Had me jumping on numerous occasions in the cinema, and that part with Anton waiting for his pursuer after finding the transmitter was amazingly shocking. Without a doubt this film has you on the edge of your seat. The audience I saw this with didn't appreciate it. They didn't see the bigger picture, the gritty realism, the beautiful poetry of that ending, and if you see the words in that finale; allow them to sink in, then truly it will blow you away. Best film of 2007-2008 I've seen to date. The level of acting and vision is unsurpassed, and it will draw you in and stay with you. Definitely want to watch again and again, there's so much crammed in this. You will soak it up like a sponge. A masterpiece. Unrivaled entertainment; a haunting thriller and an unrivaled story adaptation. ''Yeah, I'm going to bring you something, alright. I decided to make you a special project of mine. You ain't going have to come looking for me at all.''

I don't really know how to start with this movie.  It's absolutely incredible, really for no one reason.  The story first of all, is great.  The little nuances that make it different than other simple cat-and-mouse chase movies are what make it great.  Like the unique weapon choice of Chigurh's, or the bizarre obsession everyone has with milk.  The story is also freaking scary.  I spent nearly the entire movie with my hands over my face, one eye peeking out through my fingers.  Also the way it looks, for instance the desert, or the empty rooms that Chigurh blasts open, builds the sense of isolation that Moss must feel the entire movie.  The script is incredible- oddly, but ingeniously, giving the main characters virtually no dialogue.  And, the acting.  Oh, what an amazing group of actors.  I do believe Josh Brolin and Javier Bardem were my favorites, both of which were the characters with hardly any dialogue.  Of course, Javier Bardem is the one everyone is talking about, and for good reason.  The most fascinating thing about him was that it seems like the easiest thing in the world to play the "cold-hearted, psychopathic killer" type character.  But he displayed such an odd sensibility, and realism, and without any of the cockiness that most "psychopathic killers" have.  He doesn't have to think he's the best at what he does, he just is the best at it.  My favorite line of the movie, I think is when Woody Harrelson's character is asked how dangerous Chigurh is, and he responds, "Compared to what? The beubonic plague?"  It's great.  Anyway, the thing that got me the whole time was that pretty much every scene with Chigurh, his eyes are filled with tears.  I mean, they're not just glossy, they are actually welled up and sometimes a tear or two actually fall out of them.  This is something I've been seriously trying to figure out.  He has absolutely no remorse for the way he lives his life, which is very clear.  So, what is there to be sad about?  Or is he crying for some other reason?  Perhaps he just had some irritating contacts in.  But seriously, if anyone has any thoughts, talk to me, because I can't stop thinking about those big teary eyes.  It certainly makes the whole situation even more horrifying.  Buuuuut yeah, great great great movie.  It'll be interesting to see which awards it'll win.

I love how everyone called this "the Coen Brothers' return to form", when this was actually a departure. Many trademarks of the Coen Brothers are gone: the memorable soundtracks, the witty banter, and the elaborate set designs. Most of the movie took place outdoors or in motel lots, and very few words were said. Josh Brolin, Javier Bardam, and Tommy Lee Jones do amazing jobs out of their minimalist roles. The movie almost reminded me of Fargo south of the border, as many of the character structures were the same. (William H Macy and Josh Brolin as the people who try to get away with money that isn't their's, Steve Buscemi and Javier Bardam as the killer mercenaries, and Francis McDormand and Tommy Lee Jones as the emotional centerpoint of the film) It was interesting to see Joel and Ethan go back to arguably their greatest story, in a completely different fashion. One of their best movies ever.

In either case, this is the most unsatisfying ending to a film I have ever seen.  The boys do a great job of creating a story about a psycho-pathic killer chasing an okay guy who stumbles onto $2 million that isn't his.  We've seen this plot before and the Coens do a good job at executing it.  There is a little too much variation on the theme but the story moves well for a good hour and a half.  And then there's Tommy Lee Jones as an old Texas sheriff who's doing better than most at putting the story together.  We're very sympathetic to his plight, because like him we're just trying to put it together too, and we know a lot more than he does.  But then comes that ending.  And nothing is resolved.  Nothing.  So what's going on here?  Are the Coens trying to say something about the random senseless violence, that is pervading our society?  Okay, I can buy that.   Or are they trying to tell us that everything is not always resolved, and that life doesn't get tied up in a nice bow after two hours of action and intrigue?  I can buy that too.  But I think the truth is that they just ran out of ideas.  They created a great yarn but they didn't know how to end it with something up to the quality of the story.  No pat answers like good triumphing over evil, or Mr. Everyman outfoxing the bad guys.  So they just decided to end it with nothing resolved.  And the dumb critics are falling over themselves praising it for doing something entirely new -- a movie that makes absolutely no attempt to come up with an ending.  The story is just left hanging, perhaps waiting for the moviegoers to come up with an ending that the Coens were unable to find.  How avant garde!  How chic!  How dumb!

You'll have to go see it just to be able to discuss it with your friends who are as mystified as you.  Or maybe just take your $10 and put it on a 50-1 shot at the track.  I guaranetee you that the latter will have an ending, and resolution.

Then there's the film of the title, the "older man feeling lost in the modern world" movie, which lurches back to the foreground when the other storyline ends quite abruptly. After the initial shock, you realise this is actually the main story, and the shooting and chasing business was just there to support this one.

It's not exactly a happy point it's trying to make, and it doesn't wrap it all up for easy delivery. Also, the "older man's" solution to the "modern world" dilemma was very unexpected but somehow very believable. Tommy Lee Jones will be nominated for an Oscar for this, and deservedly so, and I wouldn't be surprised if the Coen brothers are as well.

The feel and tone and style of the film is simply unmatched in 99.9% of all other films.  

There is no music in the movie.  This creates a very anti-climactic feel, but it just makes it that much better.  Maybe it seems more real this way, maybe it is because of something I can't put my finger on.  Either way, it just works.  And very very well at that.

The casting had so much care put into it that I honestly believe that there is no one on this earth who would play the antagonist better.

The cinematography is stunning yet modest.  The Coen Brothers don't slap you in the face with epic arcs and helicopter shots.  The camera movement is subtle yet perfect.  

And this all on top of a great plot and set of characters with their flaws that make them seem unrealistically real.  

Everything in the movie sets the tone perfectly.  The hotel-street scene was unbelievable and could not have been better executed with any other director(s).

The following list is one of films that were critically acclaimed to the point of absolute mayhem that I found good enough to reccomend but not just fantastic:  'The Departed', 'Sideways'.  I can now add "No Country for Old Men" to that list.

This does not mean I'm not reccomending this film or that it was poorly made.  If one thing can be said about "No Country for Old Men," it is that it is probably the most well-directed picture of the year.  But Best Picture?  Definetly not.  Maybe the most overrated film of the year, in my opinion.

I mean-95 on the tomatometer?  On Roger Ebert's best list at number TWO, him calling it "perfect"?  Nominated for Best Picture at the Golden Globes and almost a shoe-in for atleast a nomination at the Oscars?  It was good, but not that good!  I'm actually quite shocked.  

I would reccomend this picture for the suspense, directing, and performances.  It was genuinely creepy and disturbing, and it left an impression, and right after it,  for a minute there, I felt as if it was five stars, but then, as I began really processing what I watched, the only opinion that stuck out was "What the hell?"  

I'm being too tough on "No Country for Old Men."  After all, this review is a reccomendation.  But its a mild one at that.  There is barely a plot, it's very repetitive, and its two hours and two minutes feels like four hours and four minutes.  I found several places where the film could have ended and left off with a better release.  There was no "release" with this film, but perhaps thats the point.

Watch for the superior directing and go in expecting to experience the movie long after it ended, but it didn't live up to the hype for me.  Its plot and development just wasn't that fantastic.  The acting, perfect blend of drama, love, and suspense, and flawless directing and cinematography make up for it enough for me to give this a thumbs up, but not enough for me to consider the film perfect by any stretch of the word.

So, in the end, this is the worst review I've ever written, because, well, I'm reccomending the film, but not to the point that I feel obligated to.  So, its become a "see this movie" review, while, all I feel i've done is point out its flaws.  But keep in mind, I am giving this film a reccomendation, as there are scenes that are very intense and suspenseful in all the rights ways.  But the plot really never became something to really care about or feel the need to show any favoritism regarding, and that's sort-of a need for a movie, isn't it?

Joel and Ethan Coen, of "Fargo" and "Oh Brother Where Art Thou?" fame, are back with a swift and unrelenting vengeance. "No Country For Old Men" is a new film by the Coen brothers, and while it holds true to the directors' immense talents and capabilities, this film is unlike anything they have ever produced. Based on a novel of the same name, by author Cormac McCarthy, the film follows a lower class, Texan hunter named Llewelyn Moss as he finds $2 million in the desert. However, he also stumbles upon a truck-load of heroin and a slew of dead bodies in what appears to be a drug deal gone completely awry. Sheriff Ed Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is hot on the trail of those involved with this massacre, including a man that seems to be the living incarnation of evil. Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) sets out to hunt down Moss and retrieve the money, and little does Moss know that Chigurh is quite potentially the most terrifying character in the history of cinema. Chigurh leaves a long trail of violence and blood, as Moss digs himself deeper and deeper into a hell of his own making. Sheriff Bell unravels the case, but always seems to arrive just a little too late. At first glance the film might give the resonance of; "even all the money in the world has a price", and while that statement stands very clear in this movie, it delves much deeper into our psyche. The title of the film may seem unfitting, or at least confusing to some, but "No Country For Old Men" is exactly what the film is about. Javier Bardem, as the horrifying Anton Chigurh, steals the show, but the movie itself, in essence, is about Tommy Lee Jones' character, Ed Bell. In the beginning of the film, a narrative by Sheriff Bell explains how his father, too, was a law man, whom we later find out died at a very young age. He discusses the measure of crime in today's world, and how nothing he has seen can compare to the ruthless brutality left behind by Chigurh, who happens to kill with a weapon that no other man on this planet would think to use. The film is a tale of self-realization, not only on the part of Sheriff Bell, but the whole movie itself. It examines the mind of the most relentless criminal I have ever seen, and strikes us with a realization of immense proportions, that the world we live in is indeed full of violence and revenge. This message may seem exhausted to some, who would rather not experience another film about the dark side of life, but it proclaims it's message with such intense poetic justice, that one can't help but take notice to how uncompromisingly realistic it is. Despite being one of the most poetic and revelatory films I have ever seen, it is also, quite honestly, the most intense. "No Country" is an indisputable American masterpiece. The Coen brothers struck gold with "Fargo" back in 1996, the film was considered one of the greatest by critics worldwide. For them to do it again, and even out-do themselves with "No Country", well it's nothing short of a miracle. "No Country" builds unbearable suspense, and is an abslutely astounding achievement in motion pictures. I have never seen a film quite like it, and I doubt that I ever will again. Not since "The Shining" have a been so frightened by a character in a film, and not since... well, never have I seen such a perfect movie. Cinema owes a great debt to Joel and Ethan Coen. This is the best film I've seen this year.

 [left][font=Courier New]There are films that I look forward to seeing that meet all expectations I had before viewing the movie. An even rarer experience is when a film exceeds my expectations and changes my thoughts on film. There have been very few modern films that I have seen that I would say have shaped how I view and think about films, the last being Tarantino's [i]Pulp Fiction[/i]. But as I walked away from the Coen Brother's [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], I knew that I had seen something great. Far greater than I could have ever imagined, and with the ability to leave a powerful impression on me.
 
 To say that [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is expertly crafted in every way is an understatement. I honestly can't put into words just how fantastic this movie is. It takes what could easily have been a standard and predictable story, and fills it with taut, suspenseful twists and turns and never lets go. I love when a film engages all aspects of my attention, and when it is able to play with my emotions. Not many films out there today have had the ability to make me jump back and forth from liking and despising characters like the ones in [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] managed to do. And for that I loved the film even more.
 
 At it's center, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] features one of the creepiest performances I have ever seen. Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh, the unforgiving and relentless killer, is one of the best performances I have seen all year. No other film this year has had me frightened and fascinated by any character like Anton Chigurh. The character never feels forced, or cheap in anyway. And Bardem's performance never falters for a second throughout the entire film. 
 
 Josh Brolin, who is having a great resurgence in his career this year, is fantastic as Llewelyn Moss, the man who discovers a case filled with drug money and becomes the target of Chigurh. I hate to be clichÃ© with a statement like this, but I couldn't help but think of Hitchcock's films when I watched Moss and Chigurh throughout this film. 
 
 Tommy Lee Jones, who is one of my favorite actors of all time, is superb as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, the man caught in the middle of Moss and Chigurh's cat and mouse game. I couldn't help but think of Sam Peckinpah's [i]The Wild Bunch[/i] whenever Bell was on screen. [i]The Wild Bunch[/i] featured a group of outlaws in the last days of the wild west, finding it hard to adjust to the changes time has brought. And Sheriff Bell faces similar sorts of changes of the time in this film as well.
 
 [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], much like the Coen Brother's [i]Fargo[/i], is a great mix of suspense and humor. I love the Coen Brothers, and have enjoyed their career. But I have to say that [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is the first film of theirs since [i]Fargo[/i] that I honestly love completely. Not since [i]Fargo[/i] has their writing or their direction been so flawless.  And no other film this year can match this film's sheer perfection.
 
 There have been many discussions about the ending to this film. Yes, the ending isn't what I expected and I can see why many people would be let down by it. But this is the sort of film that wants its audiences to think about its ending, rather than hand it over so easily. I find that the ending to [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is one of the smartest endings put to celluloid. In fact, this movie is one of the smartest films ever put to celluloid. I highly recommend this film to people who want something more challenging than your average thriller.[/font]

The Coen Brothers have returned with real authority. No Country for Old Men is a powerfully violent showcase about the consequences of the choices we make in life. A hunter, whilst surveying the wonderfully captured Texas plains, finds $2 million and decides to go on the run with the loot. He is pursued, though, by an earnest town sheriff and a ruthless killer, who is basically the Human Terminator....a man who decided a long time ago that the taking of a life was merely a step in the right direction! Only a knowledge of either Blood Simple (1986), Miller's Crossing (1990) or Fargo (1995) (three excellent thrillers by the Coen Brothers) will prepare you for the devastation and unsettling humour in this one. A clinical social commentary with no happy endings and possibly the greatest bad guy yet to grace a Coens' film, displaying all of the devious qualities which the brothers have consistently touched upon in previous films. Based on the towering book by the legendary Cormac McCarthy, 'No Country for Old Men' is one of the finest literary adaptations of recent times. *****

I don't have a lot to write so I'll keep these short. Last week I watched No Country for Old Men. I'm not a huge Coen Brothers fan and if I like any of their films I tend to think they're good but not great. I admired Fargo more than I liked it, O Brother, Where Art Thou? was entertaining but the highest I could ever rate it was an 8/10, Intolerable Cruelty was forgettable, and The Hudsucker Proxy, well actually I've literally forgotten that movie as I watched it so long ago, and it was on tv, so that shouldn't count. One of my co-workers tells me I should watch Blood Simple or Miller's Crossing.

About No Country for Old Men, it was easily the most engrossing Coen Brothers flick I've seen. The plot left a lot unexplained and unsaid (after the movie I heard at least one person in the theater ask, "So who ended up with the money?"), and I'm guessing I would like the book a lot if I read it, but the performances were great all around and, as many critics have said, the film is great at portraying a certain setting. My biggest question about it actually was how Javier Bardem's cold-blooded killer allowed himself to be arrested at the beginning of the movie by a rural young fresh-faced cop for some unknown offense, since he showed through the rest of the movie that nothing was going to get in his way of finishing his job, whatever that was supposed to be. Tommy Lee Jones, in a supporting role as a longtime sheriff of a rural west Texas county, is as good as he's been in several years. A lot of people are calling Bardem a shoo-in for the Best Supporting Actor oscar, and he probably is, but somehow I think he was a bit overrated. Are they supposed to hand out oscars to frightening cold-blooded killers now? Tom Cruise got a lot of acclaim for playing a hitman in Collateral and Anthony Hopkins won Best Actor playing Hannibal Lecter in Silence of the Lambs, but I didn't really find Bardem's character all that interesting. Aside from knowing so little about him (aside from that he's methodical and really good at killing), it's not even clear why he's involved or who he's working for. 

I watched the National Treasure sequel on Christmas Day with a bunch of family members. The people who enjoy this movie the most will be the ones who didn't think the original one was implausible enough. This one is faster-moving but pulled off the amazing feat of casting Ed Harris as the villain and then making his character boring. I'd much sooner believe that America's founding fathers buried a fortune in ancient artifacts under Boston than I'd believe the plot of this mess. Even the film's own internal logic makes no sense. It involves a legendary city of gold that some native american tribe built and then was lost, and a plot by members of the Confederacy to find it during the Civil War. At least twice characters in the movie say lines like, "Can you imagine what would have happened if the Confederates had found this place?" Actually, no I can't imagine what would have happened, since the war was already over when they were seriously looking for it, and I don't see how finding a city of gold buried in present-day South Dakota would have helped their cause. That's still not as dumb as The Legend of Zorro (partly written by Ted Elliot and Terry Rossio, who also had a hand in writing both National Treasure movies), where the villains' evil scheme is to deliver newly-invented nitroglycerine to "the Confederate army" to de-stabilize America and make it weak, even though that movie takes place a decade before the confederacy even existed. Once Nicholas Cage and company have gone to Europe and back, kidnapped the U.S. President, and found a clue in Queen Victoria's desk, it becomes hard to care anymore when they've found what they were looking for, and even harder to not wonder how the events at the beginning of the movie could have anything to do with what follows it.

I had wanted to see Juno for quite a while and I finally watched it earlier tonight. After Waitress, Knocked Up, and Bella, this makes the fourth "I'm pregnant, what am I supposed to do now?" movie I've seen this year. I've heard of movies that were said to be too in love with themselves, but with Juno I'm tempted to say that the question has been answered about whether it's possible for a movie to be in lust with itself. A lot of the dialogue sounds like something you might hear in a PG-13 version of a Gilmore Girls episode, with a lot more cynicism thrown in. There are some good lines, to be sure, but for the first 2/3 of the movie the dialogue feels way too self-congratulatory, as if Diablo Cody (the moniker for the stripper-turned-blogger-turned-screenwriter who penned Juno) patted herself on the back for each quirky, clever new line she added as she wrote the script. When Good Will Hunting came out I heard it described as having a "show-offy script"; I think such a description fits Juno much better. 

There are some good performances in it though. Ellen Page is getting major oscar buzz for playing the title character, but she didn't really feel like a real person until the third act and as cute as she is I think she's vastly overrated in this. J.K. Simmons and Allison Janney were good as her parents, Michael Cera had some good scenes as the father of Juno's baby, and Jennifer Garner does some of her best work as the childless suburban wife to whom Juno offers to give her unborn baby for adoption. 

There are some scenes that work very well in subtle ways, but far more scenes where subtlety is thrown out the window and clever dialogue is thrown on top of yet more cute, clever, cynical, non-conformist sort of dialogue. It starts out as a quirky romp (can it be anything other than quirky when Rainn Wilson from The Office shows up in a cameo as a drug store cashier), but goes through dramatic changes in tone later on and ends just a little too tidily. So the moral of the story is that you can have irresponsible unprotected sex, get pregnant, go so far as to have the baby even though you hardly seem to care about it (which she frequently refers to as "this thing"), not face any sort of consequences for your actions beyond other kids teasing your appearance, and when it's all over you can go right back to your regular life and not have learned a thing but it will be alright as long as you have a guitar and a song to sing with that special someone.

An amazing, cathartic and redemptive piece of cinema. The Coens have bounced back from Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers to deliver what is arguably the best film of 2007, and a certain multiple Oscar nominee. The cinematography is beautiful, the direction tense and foreboding, and the soundtrack sparse and haunting. 

The dialogue is typically crisp and devious - see every other Coen film for other examples - however a debt is understandly owed to novelist Cormac McCarthy. The narrative arc is a nailbiter, with a thrilling second act of almost non-stop chase scenes. However, the masterful third act transcends the relatively simple plot and opens up a wonderful philosophical jaunt on the nature of violence.

As usual for the Coens, the lead performances are excellent. Bardem is unnervingly creepy, and his presence hovers menacingly about the film in the same vein as Anthony Hopkins as Hannibal Lecter. Josh Brolin anchors the film as the likeably gruff lead, and Tommy Lee Jones has never done world-weary better. Supports are also superb, particularly Kelly MacDonald as the innocent and confused spouse.

With the Coens' attention to detail evident in every frame, No Country is a flawless example of film form and genre; and an absolute must-see for all lovers of film.

Hell, I know there's a lot of paperwork, but there might have been a few roadblocks and maybe a description of this highly visible psychotic circulated. Given this, the lone killer shows an uncanny ability to locate people in not only the vast land of Texas, but also in Mexico. This film is not a critique of modern society but just another well-made orgy of violence, although it seems that some of our serious film critics have difficulty distinguishing the two. Finally after the inconsequential "Intolerable Cruelty" and the intolerable crime of remaking the classic "The Ladykillers", the Coen brothers are back on form. This is a perfect film, with sparse dialogue that lets the pictures tell the story. It resonates with melancholy and inevitability, the beautiful but rugged landscapes as hard and unforgiving as the times. Josh Brolin has never been better, with a truly career-defining performance and Tommy Lee Jones oddly manages to play yet another lawman and make it seem subtly different than all his others. Javier Bardem cranks up the suspense in every scene he occupies, the epitome of cold-blooded violence. The Coen's direction is, as has been said, positively Hitchcockian at times, with the landscape these characters inhabit adding measurably to the threat. The denouement is unexpected (for those that hadn't read the book) but perfectly suited. Though it is not without some wry humourous moments, usually from Tommy Lee Jones's character. Utterly haunting, intense, and the best Coen film yet.

Goddamn! The Coen Brothers are back and in full form. It seems as though 'No Country For Old Men' is the film to beat this year for the coveted Best Picture Oscar prize. Although it was a different film than I expected, it's every bit as powerful, tense, awkwardly funny and relevant as I had hoped, perhaps even more so. Based on Cormac McCarthy's critically acclaimed novel of the same name, 'No Country For Old Men' is a deeply symbolic and straight-forward story of the struggle between good and evil. The film opens with a flawlessly delivered monologue by the ever-so-great Tommy Lee Jones who portrays Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. Bell is a small-town sheriff in the state of Texas, and in his monologue he talks about how hardened and ruthless we've become as a society. "The crimes we see today...it's hard to even take it's measure. It's just all out war." mutters Bell. This monologue is the perfect setting for Llewyn Moss (Josh Brolin) who while hunting antelope in the desert stumbles upon half a dozen dead Mexicans, heroin and $2.4 Million. Being the road scholar he is, Moss figures no one will come looking for the moo-la if he snatches it. WRONG! Not only does the Mexican mafia and reputable bounty hunter / smart-ass Carson Welles (Woody Harrelson) pursue Moss, but also one of the most twisted, unpredictable and unreasonable villains in recent film history. His name is Anton Chirguh (Javier Bardem), and when he's not blowing innocent civilians' heads off with a cattle gun or flipping a coin to determine whether you live or die, he quietly observes everybody and everything around him.

'No Country For Old Men' is a triumph in film-making in that the film has no real flaws. Critics might pan it as "slow-moving" but that's essential in order to correctly build the tension for the key scenes. Most of the film is actually quite fast-paced with such nerve-wracking sequences it will have you on the edge of your seat with a knot in your stomach for a majority of it's runtime. But 'No Country's' quiet and subtle scenes are every bit as powerful as it's action-packed and suspenseful ones. This is due in large part to the screenplay. Supposedly following very closely to McCormac's novel, the Coen brothers deliver their finest work EVER from a screen writing perspective. Yes, it's even better than 'Fargo'. As for the Coen's directing and editing, it has never been smoother. The film's transitions are nothing short of breathtaking.

From an acting stand-point 'No Country For Old Men' is also incredible. The stand-out of the film is of course Javier Bardem as the ruthless homicidal maniac Chirguh. Just his facial expressions and body language is enough to make your skin crawl, and if that's not enough, he delivers every line including his catch-phrase "friend-O" with such brooding intensity and creepiness it makes you want to sink in your seat. Bardem is a lock for a Best Supporting Actor nomination this Oscar season, but his biggest competition is the two other key performances of the film. Josh Brolin who last week impressed me with his malicious turn in 'American Gangster' as a crooked cop, is the best he's ever been here in the role of Moss. Moss is such an unlikely hero in the sense he is kind of dumb, not very nice, makes stupid decisions and yet we still root for him to escape the drudges of the Mexican mafia and even worse, the wrath of Chirguh. Tommy Lee Jones I'd say is Bardem's biggest competition. With this and 'In the Valley of Elah', Jones has proved this year with these two performances that if anything he's getting better with age. Jones' monologues are flawlessly delivered like I previously stated, including his final one which left me with goose bumps at the end of the picture. Woody Harrelson is humorous in his limited role as a sharp-witted and over-confident bounty hunter, and Scottish actress Kelly MacDonald is phenomenal in her role as Moss' butter-brain wife. The film has a numerous amount of strong small performances including Garret Dillahunt as Bell's Deputy, Tess Harper as Bell's wife and the 'Office Space' stapler guy (Stephen Root), in a well-played dramatic role as a crime boss. Roger Deakins outdoes himself yet again with some awesome cinematography, and while quiet and subtle, the film's music score is haunting.

There is no other film this year that I can recommend as highly as 'No Country For Old Men'. There are times when it has you on the edge of your seat in suspense, there are times when it has you laughing violently at some of the darkly humorous scenes and through-out the entire 121 minutes it has you using your brain. There's a lot of symbolism and powerful metaphors in the film, but since I'm not writing a 5-page essay, I'll let you figure them out for yourself. With 'No Country For Old Men' the Coen Brothers have once again raised the bar on how outstanding and thought-provoking a simple crime-drama can be. Grade: A (screened at Harkins Camelview 5, Scottsdale, Arizona)

The Coen Brothers have always been filmmakers I?ve had mixed feelings about.  On one hand they?ve made a lot of movies I really love like Fargo, Blood Simple, and The Man Who Wasn?t There are all favorites of mine.  As much as I love these darker, more dramatic works, I tend to tune out whenever they make comedies like The Hudsucker Proxy, O Brother Where Art Thou, or even Raising Arizona.  Basically anytime they decide to make a glorified parody of an old film genre with John Turturro, John Goodman, and Steve Buscemi I tend to find myself underwhelmed.  The Big Lebowski is the notable exception to this; I simply find that movie a lot more funny than the above mentioned works.  Generally I find the Coen Brothers to be auteurs almost to a fault; I?d probably enjoy their work a lot more if their stamp wasn?t all over every frame of their work.  Thankfully, the new film from the Coen brothers, No Country for Old Men, manages to completely avoid each and every problem I have with this filmmaking duo?s work.  It not only stands among the darker films of their cannon that I named before, but it rises above almost all of them, it?s not just a great Coen Brothers film but a great film in general.
	The film takes place in rural Texas and centers on Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), an ordinary man who stumbles upon a drug deal gone wrong while hunting in a secluded prairie.  Amidst the carnage of the crime scene he finds a case filled with two million dollars.  Moss, takes this opportunity and grabs the money, but as the films tagline reads ?there are no clean getaways.?  Moss quickly finds himself in a cat and mouse chase with an absolutely ruthless hitman named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) who will stop at nothing to recover this money.  As Chigurh tracks Moss, a Sherriff named Ed Tom Bell (Tommey Lee Jones) is on the trail of the entire situation.
	That description makes this sound like a simple thriller, this is not entirely accurate.  The film is indeed a thriller, and a great one at that, but there?s more going on here than can really be described through mere plot summery.  The film is an adaptation of a novel by the Pulitzer Prize winning novelist Cormac McCarthy.  McCarthy?s novel seems to generally be considered a solid work, but overall a minor entry in the acclaimed author?s cannon.  I haven?t read the novel, but it comes as no surprise to me that this film comes from literary origins.  This is one of those rare films that seem to have the scope and gravitas of a full novel, but without the type of decade spanning such a description would suggest.
	The main themes of the film are violence and greed, the same themes that run through the Coen?s Fargo and Blood Simple.  This is the most refined and deep look at these themes the Coens have yet to create.  These themes are embodied by the two main components of the film?s central chase, Moss and Chigurh.  
	If nothing else, the film will be remembered for creating one of the greatest villains in cinema history, that of Anton Chigurh.  Chigurh, as expertly played by Javier Bardem, is like a hurricane of destruction.  He?s a cold, ruthless killer whose single minded pursuit of his victims makes him an almost unstoppable force.  Chigurh is like a hurricane of violence; he goes straight for his target and destroys everything in his path without so much as thinking.  Only through sheer luck can this force of nature be escaped, as he occasionally allows his victims to live if they correctly call a coin toss.  All this ruthless efficiency is placed into a singularly bizarre physical specimen of a human.  Bardem is given an off putting 70?s style haircut and speaks in a completely out of whack accent.  What the Coens seem to be doing is trying to keep this mindless violence from looking cool, by making the bringer of this carnage look like a dork.
	The mouse in this chase is Llewelyn Moss, as played by Josh Brolin.  If Chigurh represents violence in this tale, Moss represents greed.  He?s an everyman who comes across an opportunity, takes it without thinking, and finds himself in a world of trouble.  Brolin?s performance is not as showy as Bardem?s, but his work is almost as important.  This performance is like the cherry on top of a great year for Josh Brolin.  Brolin has been acting in films for more than twenty years, but is only now having a breakout year with performances in Grindhouse, In the Valey of Elah, American Gangster and of course No Country For Old Men.
	As important as Bardem and Brolin are, it is Tommy Lee Jones as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who ultimately holds the film?s success on his shoulders.  It is this Sheriff who goes through the greatest transformation in the story, he is the old man that this is no country for.  This frankly seems like the role Tommy Lee Jones was born to play, he?s the perfect actor to be playing this aging, grizzled, but also somewhat sensitive Texas sheriff.  The character is like a cross between the determined U.S. Marshal of The Fugitive and the principled modern cowboy of The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada.  He?s the main deliverer of some of the film?s profound dialogue, his monologues in the film are of great importance and it is Jone that makes them fully believable.
	No Country for Old Men is so rich in sub-text that I almost don?t feel qualified to comment on it after only one viewing.  The film delivers profound and sophisticated messages in a blue collar setting.  It?s quite likely that McCarthy?s novel is the main reason for this, from what I?ve heard this is an extremely faithful adaptation.  This faithfulness is likely also the reason this may not work for all audiences, particularly during the film?s third act.  I will not give the ending away, except to say that it is not a conventional cinematic catharsis.  This ending could be compared to the finale of ?The Sopranos,? in that it?s an ambiguous ending that will drive closed minded audiences insane.  I was initially a bit dumbfounded by this closing shot, but it has stayed with me since I saw it.  It?s a bold, interesting way to end a film; it stays focused on the film?s important themes and avoids pandering to commercial interests.  
	Though McCarthy may be the one responsible for the film?s rich sub-text, it?s the Coen Brothers who are responsible for bringing this story to the screen so wonderfully.  This is a film that manages to have its cake and eat it too, throughout.  Manages to be subtle yet over the top, profound yet exiting, and perfectly mixes moments of black comedy with moments that are dead serious.  While being a deep meditation on violence, this film is also an extremely well made movie with moments of gripping suspense.  This is the Coen Brother?s most suspenceful film since Blood Simple and is flat out one of the best thrillers to come out since Spielberg?s Munich.  	
	It should probably be noted that this is a very violent movie.  The Anton Chigurh character is a ruthless character that dispatches people through very brutal means.  Early in the film he strangles a cop with a pair of handcuffs, later he blows people?s heads off with a compressed air tank, and also wields a shot gun.  As a result this is a very bloody film with a very high body count.  Those squeamish about such material should probably avoid the film.  That said this violence is not gratuitous and serves what is over-all message about the destructive effect violence has on society.  
	The Coen Brother?s filmmaking has never been better than it is hear, this is a very technically proficient film from a pair of talented auteurs.  Roger Deakins? vivid cinematography perfectly captures both the vast Texas prairie and the run down motel rooms that reside on it.  More important than that however is the subtle editing by ?Roderick Jaynes? (a pseudonym for the Coens themselves) that allows the film to go at a relaxed pace while never feeling slow.  The film?s framing consistently feels perfect, and when the violence kicks in it feels perfectly choreographed.  
	One would generally be hard set to find anything wrong with No Country for Old Men, it may be the best film the Coen brothers have ever made.  This is a film I feel compelled to go out and see again, which is something I rarely find myself doing.  All that said, I will warn potential viewers that this is a very challenging movie and not something I would recommend to everyone without some reservations.  If what you seek is pure entertainment, there are probably other movies out now that will be more up your alley.  However, if you are looking for a nearly flawless movie that will challenge you and keep you on the edge of your seat, this is the one to see.

Pure evil exists. It transcends rationality or decency. You can't barter with it, or plead with it, or pay it off, and it's this same type of evil that you will face in this film.  Greed, deception, mayhem, and murder are rampant amongst the characters to the point that its less a linear story than it is a mess, and that's what makes it feel so real. There's a point in the film in which a woman comes face to face with the villian and begs, "You don't have to do this." With a crooked grin on his lips he muses, "They always say that," before killing her. 

Leaving the theater, I felt unsatisfied, but we are meant to by the Coen Brothers. You can't witness this type of debasement between people and possibly walk away pleased...or at least, one shouldn't.  The most poignant moment I remember was one in which Tommy Lee Jones after a lifetime's occupation of witnessing carnage says, "I always thought when I got older that God would come into my life in some way. He didn't. I don't blame him. If I was him I'd have the same opinion about me that he does." I smiled, but it was a sad smile.

First off, let's get this straight: I did NOT want to see this movie. In fact,the only reason I saw it was because my family was going, and my uncle paid, so it was free, but just so you know, while standing in line I was secretly praying that this movie would be sold out and we would go see The Water Horse instead. But no, I ended up sitting down to this movie.

And, wouldn't you know it, it was the best 2 hours I've spent at the movies this year.

The story is simple, and has been done before: a man comes across a botched deal, finds some money, takes it, and then gets hunted down by people who want it. Sound familiar? It should. But I'll be damned if the Cohen Bros. didn't dust off this old genre and turn it into one of the most riveting, suspensful, and all-beit great titles in recent memory.

Josh Brolin is our main good guy, here, who's only in this whole mess because he decided to do the right thing and try and save a guy's life. He's pretty much a badass, which is good, because the guy chasing him down for the money is also a badass. So it's kind of like Aliens v. Predator except with humans and a script.

Javier Bardem, as the pyscho, is absolutley amazing. I'm an effects guy, personally. I don't care about acting. But this guy was good. Very good. Noticeably good. He plays this psycho badass guy who goes around killing people with a smile on his face. He uses a silenced shotgun and either blows them to bits or uses a can of compressed air to blow out their brains. Yet, at the same time, he's polite, he says 'please,' he's got a decent personality, and if he likes someone, he'll give them the option whether or not they want to live or die, depending on a coin toss. In short, despite the fact that Bardem plays one of the most monstrous bad guys ever in a movie, he's also, easily, the most human. 

Tommy Lee Jones does nothing in this movie. Seriously. He takes up time and adds star power. Woody Harrelson is also superfluous, but hell, the rest of the movie is so damn good that you really don't notice, nor care.

It's intense beyond words, including a long scene in a hotel room that will keep you on the edge of your seat or holding your breath. 

There is also quite a bit of humor to tone down the action and keep the pacing methodical yet engrossing. The southern, texas dialogue is flawless, and at times, funny. The script is well-written, but no film, including this one is perfect...

There are about 3 scenes in this movie that do nothing but bog it down. One is where Tommy Lee Jones, the sheriff who does aboslutely nothing (and even ACKNWOLEDGES the fact that he does nothing) is talking to some old guy, and the old guy tells some five minute story, but we can't understand it because the speech is so slurred. This didn't need to be in the film, and while I understand it is an attempt to add depth, it also adds, uh, boringness. 

The ending, that I won't spoil, I am sad to say created boos in the crowd. It's ashame to see such a great film nearly killed by one of the most abrupt, inconclusive, unsatisfying endings ever. The credits start rolling out of nowhere, and you think "What the HELL? It's over?!" It's that kind of feeling. It feels like it should have another half hour to tie up the loose ends. But it never does. And it ultimatley ruins what would've been a flawless movie.

No Country for Old Men, despite it's horrendous ending, is  well directed, brilliantly acted, and overall just a great movie. In a year full of All-Hype-No-Payoff Movies like Spider-Man 3, Pirates 3, Shrek 3, and others, it's a sigh of relief to know that one of the best films of 2007 has come right in the knick of time.

The Coen brother's latest animal, No Country For Old Men, is a refreshing and completely satisfying foray into character study, centering around greed, violence, and change. I personally really love chase films such as North by Northwest and I thought this film captured the essence of being on the run very well with the vast, open feel of the setting which was done with the help of some beautiful camera work by Roger Deakins and the Coens. Javier Bardem is downright perfect as the no holds barred, own brand of justice killer. Bardem is greatly accompanied by Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones, the other two main players in this film.

The most rampant complaint from people who did not love the film as much as someone like me did is that they did not feel that the ending was satisfactory. To not feel robbed the viewer needs to understand that Ed Tom Bell is the film's main character, not Anton or Llewelyn, despite the fact that they are featured far more often on screen than Bell. A simple understanding of the film's title will make one realize who this is really about. The monologue by Bell at the film's conclusion is the perfect way to go out. Bell's dreams are a way of him realizing that there is no place there left for him, and possibly for other older men in the game of criminal catching.

If youre a Coen brothers fan, youre gonna be extremely delighted with [i]NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN[/i]. This is Ethan and Joel at the pinnacle of their directing careers, something that should not be missed by anyone interested in film or entertainment. Forget [i]FARGO[/i]. Push aside [i]THE BIG LEBOWSKI[/i]. Move over [i]O BROTHER WHERE ART THOU[/i]. [i]No Country[/i] is leaps and bounds beyond those. In fact, it reigns supreme as 2007's best film. 

I dont always agree with movie critics but this time they got it right. It is the first time that Associated Press reviewers David Germain and Christy Lemire have both selected the same film as their #1 pick. With more award nominations than you could shake a stick at (including four [i]Golden Globes[/i], three [i]Screen Actors Guilds[/i], probably a gaggle of [i]Oscars[/i] and many, many, many others), [i]No Country [/i]will undeniably have directors, actors and screenwriters jumping up on stage come awards ceremony time. 

Equal parts thriller, western, crime-drama, and action, [i]No Country[/i] weaves a tapestry of excellence throughout its length. 

The first note of excellence must be directed at Spanish actor Javier Bardem. Probably not very well known to most American audiences, Javier has cemented himself as the leader in portraying a psychopathic killer and (dare I say it!) has surpassed that of Anthony Hopkins in his [i]SILENCE OF THE LAMBS[/i] Hannibal Lecter role (something that I thought would never happen). Ruthless, unforgiving, sociopathic, and in desperate need of a new hair style, Anton Chigurh (Bardem) is flawless. Every time he showed up on-screen I felt a chill run through my bones (Call it). Absolutely perfect.

The next note of excellence must go to Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones. Llewelyn Moss (Brolin, [i][url="http://www.filmreviewstew.com/planet_terror.htm"][color=#800000]PLANET TERROR[/color][/url][/i]) is the lucky/unlucky soft-spoken Texas cowpoke/hunter who stumbles across a veritable fortune in drug money only to be relentlessly pursued by killer Anton. Mr. Moss gradual decline in health (mainly due to wounds inflicted on him by Anton) is painful to watch up until the very end. Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is the opposite of Anton Chigurh. He doesnt understand all of the death and destruction laid at his feet. He longs for a time when murders were easy to track and solve, not these new-fangled deaths where bullets arent used (air-guns do just fine) and there seems to be no rhyme or reason to their patterns.

The fourth (perhaps this shouldve been first) note of excellence goes to the Coen brothers for their perfect adaptation of Cormac McCarthys novel by the same name. Many lines of dialogue were lifted verbatim from the novel itself, including the ending monologue by Tommy Lee. Its noteworthy to mention here that the Coen brothers not only directed but wrote the screenplay, too.

The final note has to go Cinematographer Roger Deakins (hes worked with the Coen brothers on many occasions and also did the exemplary [i][url="http://www.filmreviewstew.com/jarhead.htm"][color=#800000]JARHEAD[/color][/url][/i] work). Every scene was so well thought-out and so convincingly filmed that viewers are carried freakishly easy through this incredible story. 

Its difficult to do justice to this film with one short review, simply because there are so many great elements to it. The casting was spectacular  with Woody Harrelson ([i][url="http://www.filmreviewstew.com/north_country.htm"][color=#800000]NORTH COUNTRY[/color][/url][/i]) and Kelly Macdonald ([i][url="http://www.filmreviewstew.com/girl_in_the_cafe.htm"][color=#800000]THE GIRL IN THE CAFÉ[/color][/url][/i]) pulling in exceptional supporting roles  as was Carter Burwells haunting original musical score and Mary Zophres impeccable costume designs.

If you missed this film at your local cineplex, you may have gypped yourself from experiencing this amazing cinematic event. Now youve gotta wait for the DVD to be released and then ...its your call.

This is not your traditional western. "No Country for Old Men" follows the story of a twisted villain, played superbly by Javier Bardem. Bardem's character is the "New West", the summation of years of moral decline. Tommy Lee Jones, the last of a dying breed of honourable men, is faced with the daunting task of stopping Bardem's killing spree. Mixed into this unorthodox chase is the presence of Josh Brolin and two million dollars of drug money. No, this is not your traditional western. The Coen brothers could have easily resorted to cliched battles or tired exposition, but instead emphasized the contrast between the main characters and their individual motivations: honour, greed, and a perverted form of pragmatism. This is not a film for everyone, but it will definitely reward those with an open mind.

At first it seemed like the new millennium was not Joel and Ethan Coen?s place. They absolutely dominated the 90?s with their classic films ranging from noirs to cynical dramas to outright comedies; sure they still managed to create O Brother, Where Art Thou? and The Man Who Wasn?t There, not their greatest works but definitely fine pictures, but after that fell into obscurity and seemed to almost ?lose their touch?. Luckily for us, now, near the end of the 2000?s, they have returned to form in more ways than one, and have created a film which is not only a masterpiece of their superb body of work, but also without a doubt one of the greatest motion pictures of the decade, maybe more. The Coens had previously reached a creative peak with Fargo, but No Country for Old Men serves as a new high for the directorial duo, and if Michelangelo can have both the Sistine Chapel and his statue of David, then surely the Coens are entitled to their two masterpieces; the classic Fargo and the modern No Country. The pieces can be further viewed as companions due to their striking similarities in terms of themes, setting and visuals; both featuring stark, horizon-reaching landscapes, regular-guy characters who get mixed up with the very wrong people, and police officers as the moral cores of the film and ultimately the central subject matter. But if Fargo delivered a more uplifting moral closure with the story of Marge Gunderson, No Country for Old Men is far more pessimistic, delivering a scathing life lesson in the depressing closure to Ed Tom Bell?s tale. As in all of their films, No Country also features that very specifically Coen brothers sense of humour, which can turn even a dark and menacing dramatic thriller into a comedy by playing off the ridiculousness of the characters and the situations they get themselves into. The film also serves as a stunning, remarkable application of cinematic craft, featuring absolutely stupefying direction, cinematography, editing, production value and everything in between. Working from an utterly brilliant screenplay from the Coens, the actors deliver unnerving, compelling, show-stealing performances, in particular Tommy Lee Jones as the scarred old timer for whom this violent country is certainly no place; Josh Brolin in a brilliant lead-role debut as the naïve average Joe who gets mixed in way over his head with unstoppable forces of nature; and Javier Bardem, as the ruthless, terrifying, primeval villain and embodiment of pure evil. It is a striking, epic, complex, many-leveled work of seething bleakness and stunning desolation, delivering an all-around depressing moral and human outcome. It is a movie that lives and breathes through its fascinating characters, its visceral settings, its striking visuals. It is the best film of the year, and an astounding, incredible cinematic achievement on all possible planes. The Coens have truly outdone themselves and have finally sealed their spot as one of if not the most important modern-day cinematic auteurs. May we see only work like this from them in the future ? a masterpiece if I?ve ever seen one.

I love that this movie does not follow any cliches.  The three male leads have hardly any scenes together.  This is not a film that relies on special effects, high-action sequences, or even dialogue to capture audience attention.  Instead, the drama comes from the Coen's perfectly paced direction and the competent subtleties of its actors.

Also, there has been much discussion about the story's conclusion, but I found the movie's last three scenes to be among its best.

This film never faulters.  Its timeless themes and compelling characters will stick with the viewer for a long time to come.

Long-awaited Coen Brothers' "No Country for Old Men", a somber contemplation of tremendous power of evil and hopelessness in overcoming it might've been an intriguing one if only the pace was as good as was in "Fargo". Since it rather has one of an elephant walking through the sunny desert - messed up mainly by weak, poorly plotted story and uninspired direction - its first hour simply lacks any rythm, forcing us to meet dullness at almost every corner, endure unconvincing plot devices, making our own way from scene to scene and feel - ultimately - dissapointed. 

The story, set along the United States-Mexico border follows hillbilly cowboy named Llewelyn Moss, mysterious merciless killer Anton Chigurh and jaded sheriff Ed Tom Bell. All three lives - one after another - will connect because of failed drug deal. Llewelyn will run with the money he's stolen, Anton will chase him to get them and Ed Tom will observe this whole bloodbath from a distance since he's old, tired and soaked in fear. Anton will do literally everything to get what he wants: he's like Devil in the flesh and will make his way as if he was an outlaw from Peckinpah's cinema - choking, killing and blowing things up and, as we see in the end, no one will stop him. His clear lack of any standard emotion - as with any sociopathic personality - is so frightening that one might imagine that no such person can walk the streets, passing us or drive next to us on a freeway and Ed Tom will acknowledge that, leaving the case as if none of it ever happend. 

We may understand the message - our indifference produce more indifference and before we know we have Wild West in our town and soon all what we're able to do is to sit down with a friend and talk about how it was in the past or turn ourselves to worry about much more safe things, like keeping our wife's horse in good shape. It's pathetic, but it's real and in the end, as we see that Ed Tom and Anton never meet each other for some sort of "final confrontation", the latter personify a revenge on Ed Tom's weakness, being unbreakable force of doom for everyone who'll stand on its way. As an idea, it's a noble, important message for sure - but because of its flaws is simply depressing since it could've been a darn powerful cinematic experience as well. Coens never been so serious as they are here and it's up for a discussion whether they went on the right track here, showing us more realistic side of the world - leaving their irony, wit and compassion behind - giving us two hours of stiffness, coldness and boredom after one want go to the bathroom and slit his throat for the hell with it.

The Coen brothers take the reigns on the bestselling novel and perform it very well, capturing every theme and every intense moment the novel has to offer, and by intense I mean it. The entire cast in fantastic, with obviously praise going to Javier Bardem, whose role as hitman Anton Chigurh will be giving me nightmares for years to come. The screenplay is sharp and believable, from the plot to the dialogue, and there is never a dull momment throughout. But once again, the Coen brothers put out a great piece of cinema, flawlessly directing a no-holds-bared story of greed, morals, and chance happenings. There are only small problems I have with it, the biggest being that the first hour was much more entertaining to me than the second one, something that I've never liked out of a movie. But even though I don't give it a perfect rating, it most definitely deserves any awards that come its way, wether this year or in years to come.

Depuis ma toute première incursion dans le merveilleux monde de l'univers cinématographique, vous m'aviez bercé avec [i]Fargo[/i], un chef-d'oeuvre classique, véritable reflet de votre mentalité et de vos violentes - mais ô combien plaisantes - moeurs. Et encore aujourd'hui, près de 11 ans plus tard, vous y voilà encore, recyclant éternellement cette même ambiance qui vous est propre et dont l'intérêt qu'on lui porte peine largement à s'épuiser.

Il est évident que [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] ne possède pas réellement de générique. Les derniers mots du shériff Bell s'enclenchent comme l'ombre du jugement dernier et les noms de ceux qui ont participés à cette folle aventure défilent. Et pourtant, pour moi, impossible de voir quoique ce soit d'autre que votre signature.

[i]No Country for Old Men[/i], c'est du Coen à l'état pur, et encore davantage. Encore en 2007, vos figures de styles métaphoriques bouleversent, elles bousculent le spectateur, l'interpellent sans relâche. En près de 120 minutes, vautré dans un sofa avec une demie-douzaine d'amis - Q20 étant absent -, les visages se sont progressivement métamorphosés au fur et à mesure que Javier Bardem donnait vie à l'essence créatrice de votre impitoyable scénario.

Stupéfaction. Effroi féminin. Élastique lubrifié. Toute la gamme d'émotion y est passé, et ç'aurait été une éruption de coeurs qui auraient défoncés collectivement nos poitrines si ce n'avait pas été de ces trente dernières minutes qui, bien que vitales, ont un peu contribués à affaiblir le rythme frénétique auparavant établi par le scénario et ses silences mortels immédiatement poursuivis par le brouhaha des balles qui sifflent. 

Votre bébé n'est en rien ascendant; c'est même plutôt le contraire. Et à mon avis, c'est ce qui le rend si spécial. Tout commence par une effusion de sang, de violence et d'inhumanité pour finalement se solver par un calme logique et transcendant. Tirer d'abord, réfléchir ensuite. Un vieux dicton américain à nouveau appliqué dans votre plus récente réalisation. 

Si j'avais toutefois quelque chose à vous reprocher, ce serait d'avoir caché quelques éléments de trop au spectateur, éléments qu'il m'a fallu éplucher sur Internet pendant plusieurs demie-heures avant de parvenir à saisir complètement. Ç'aurait pu me charmer s'il s'agissait de révélations spirituelles et symboliques, ou encore de ce genre de déclic qui vous procure une sensation incroyable quelques heures après le film parce que toutes les pièces du puzzle viennent de s'emboîter. Non, au contraire, les éléments manquants du scénario étaient vitaux à la compréhension, et cet illogisme a, malgré nous, imposé une barrière discrète entre le film et notre appréciation de ce dernier. Il ne faut pas prendre le spectateur pour un con en lui donnant l'intrigue tout cru dans le bec, dans la même mesure où il ne faut pas non plus surestimer l'auditoire. L'art d'être spectateur ne comprend pas nécessairement la fonction de devenir devin.

Sinon, images fracassantes, troublantes, mettant en relief les majestueux mais ô combien lancinants paysages du Texas et du Nouveau-Mexique. Effets spéciaux à couper le souffle soutenus par un Javier Bardem dans l'un des rôles les plus surprenants de sa carrière. ''Je ne fume pas, je déteste la violence et je déteste le sang.'' avait-il argué en refusant le rôle que vous lui aviez proposé. ''C'est justement pour ça qu'on te veut.'' avez-vous répliqué. 

Et franchement, ça mérite peut-être d'être la meilleure réplique du film.

Veuillez agréer de toute mon appréciation en tant que spectateur émerveillé.
Et, surtout, vivez pour l'éternité, jusqu'à ce que votre crâne soit défoncé.

Cordialement,
[i]Frank, respirant l'ère Coen[/i]

I mean man, just... it's like ostensibly, it's about this huge sum of money, but after a while, you realize that it ISN'T about the money, there's something more going on. I love how the character Anton Chigurh, as a character is a personification of Death, and how the movie plays with the ideas of Chance and Fate.  Brilliant. Scenes like where Chigurh shoots at a raven while crossing the bridge, showing how death is random (or was it fate?) or a scene where Llewelyn is trying to escape from his pursuers, specifically a rather large pitbull, man, that scene is just so... intense. Also, you may notice that whole movie... there's no soundtrack. So many movies have to rely on a soundtrack for emotional cues. Like, oh yes, this is the dramatic scene, cue up the dramatic soundtrack, or this is the action scene, cue up the tense action soundtrack. Nope, no soundtrack at all in this movie. It's not something most people notice, which I think says a LOT about how well written this story is.

The Coen brothers ability to write and direct great movies was never in question, but after the missed opportunity of "the Ladykillers", they return to form with remarkable aplomb. Josh Brolin plays the infinately likeable Llewllyn Moss, the man who thanks to an unfortunate series of circumstances, finds himself with a bag full of cash and a killer on his tail.  Tommy Lee Jones gives an excellent performance as the world-weary, southern-as-fried-chicken sherrif, and Woody Harrelson also pops up in a memorable cameo as a cocky hitman.  The stand out turn though is an oscar worthy performance by the unknown Javier Bardem as the psychotic Anton Chigurh.  So unsettlingly believable is his killer, you really feel uncomfortable every time he is on screen.  If there is any fault to pick, it's that the final showdown you're hoping for never happens, but the clue was always there in the title.  This is the story of three men struggling (albeit in very different ways) to continue their lives as they always have in a world that has changed and left them behind.  Unmissable.

It is difficult to know where to start with this film. So I shall put it simply: this film is a masterpiece. There is no doubt that this is a masterful piece of work from start to finish and in every department. This is gripping, poignant and superior filmmaking.

The Coens' are not afraid to take their time here, and quite rightly to, but the slow pace may not be to everyone's taste. However, this is the ultimate slow burner. It winds itself up and explodes in an absolute barrage of tension and exhilarating excitement. Their script, that uses as much silence as it does words, tells this engrossing story, whilst examining morality and mortality.

The acting is superb and realises the film expertly. Josh Brolin is sympathetic as Llewelyn Moss and just seems to melt into his role and Kelly Macdonald, playing Llewelyn's wife, is brilliant in her small but crucial role. Woody Harrelson's cameo role is accomplished and Tommy Lee Jones is wonderful as the philosophical and bewildered Sheriff Bell. However, this is Javier Bardem's film. He is psychotic, and yet rational, terrifying and yet fascinating and commands the screen whenever he appears.

The cinematography has been much lauded, and rightly so. Roger Deakins has a talent of making his photography look like it is captured rather than constructed and the images are stunning and striking. The use of sound is also impressive, as the Coens use sound, and the silence, seemingly effortlessly to build tension.

Technically, it's brilliant. The acting is superb. The writing is terrific. The film is incredible. Also, once again, it is great to see a film that is both entertaining and very intelligent. The film explores the relative and absolute moralities, fate and the place of people in time, not to mention a hefty amount of life and death. There is no doubt that this is one of the films of the year and one of the films of the decade. If you want to know what cinema can do, watch this film.

I find it interesting that the first official movie that I am reviewing is the movie No Country for Old Men.  There were many great aspects to the film that I truly did love.  But after seeing all the rave reviews, the negatives stuck with me much longer.  The acting was superb and so was the cinematography.  The script was also noteworthy.  The ending was poor, as I will explain so people do not claim that I just wanted a "hollywood" ending.

The acting was great, albeit the characters were quite easy to portray.  Because the characters were very one-dimensional, these talented actors played them brilliantly.  Tommy Lee Jones' character turned out to have no effect on the plot which was an interesting angle.  It is not like many other movies where a character that has such depth turns out to have no importance.  Perhaps that was a statement about life.  I would have to ask the Coen Brothers.  Woody Harrelson also had a short but effective role as the expert bounty hunter.  Josh Brolin played the most likable character.  He did shine in this part though his ending in the movie was a bit anticlimactic.  Again, people will say that it is the stark contrast that people expect a big climax because he was important character that makes it brilliant.  Here, I differ.  I will go into that in further detail soon.  Other performances in the movie were fine as well but the one that stuck out the most was the incredible performance by Javier Bardem.  He played quite a convincing, no-mercy, no guilt, crazed killer.  Every word he uttered left me tense and ill at ease.  His performance can arguably be one of the greatest villain performances ever put on to screen.  To say the least, his performance was oscar-worthy.

And now, to complain about the ending, or lack there of.  I do not believe movies should have to wrap up every loose end.  But I do believe that movies are different than life.  Movies should be more than life.  They should move you in a way nothing you can experience in real life can.  That makes a truly brilliant movie for me.  And there are plenty of movies that have done this without a wrapped up ending.  But movies should have an ending.  They can be a twist, a cliffhanger, a cliche, but an ending nonetheless.  No Country delivers No Ending.  Not even a notion of one.  The ending could be that nothing is solved and life goes on for all who are still alive but even that is not given to the audience.  It ends with a character who has nothing to do with the story line.  Can you imagine the disappointment after loving the entire movie until then.  Not only is the ending to the movie missing, the stories of the characters involved have gaping story holes.  The Coens were trying to say something by not showing the end of things and I think people thought they got the message.  I say that they received a message that was never put into the film.

I found the movie enjoyable but nonetheless flawed.  The acting was spot on and the cinematography was beautiful as well.  The movie left a chilling and haunting feeling that I was not easily able to shake off.  But what really stayed with me was the lack of intent or ability the Coens had to portray their message.  In other words, if I had not written a conclusion to this, it does not mean that the absence of a conclusion was my conclusion.  It was that I had cut it out entirely.  But alas, I did not.  Conclusions are important.

The actors all give very strong performances but Tommy Lee Jones and Javier Bardem stand out. Josh Brolin follows up his excellent performance in American Gangster with another one in this film. There are a number of relative unknowns in this cast but they all bring their characters to life like they were veteran actors. 

This story is what drives this film. There are no CGI special effects or extended stunt sequences. The story does not follow the typical movie formula. There are no cliches in this film. The characters are called upon to make many moral choices but the choices they make are not always rewarded with the appropriate outcome. The story is complex and a number of key points are left for the audience to interpret but this is what makes this film special.

Though the performances are strong, especially Javier Bardem, and the first two acts are just great to watch, it takes a nosedive just as Saving Private Ryan did, and just falls apart. We are left to assume everything. Did Javier kill Kelly MacDonald's character, Llewellyn's girlfriend, or didn't he? Was it just a speech or threat? Did he get the money back or not? Did he go to the border and finbd it in the bushes where Llewlleyn tossed it or didn't he? And just who did the money belong to is what I want to know, since everyone at the site was dead, except for the half-dead guy in the truck. Though it can be easy to answer these questions, and any others you are left with, I also like the fact the film makes you think, the end is thoroughly unsatisfying. Tommy Lee Jones gives another monologue that ends with an exact copy of the finale for the Sopranos and just cuts out.For "Don't Stop Believing" substitute Tommy Lee Jones' voice. Though it is enjoyable to some degree, it is definitely not the best film of the year, far from it, and it is not the instant classic that will be remembered 100 years from now as some of the critics will have you believe. This is however, my opinion, and mine only, I'm sure some people share the same view, others the complete opposite, and that is fine. This is just my thoughts on the film, and just what I think.


(P.S. After revisting the film at the request of my friend, I concede that the film is a great feat of storytelling and filmmaking. The suspense in the film is insanely nail-biting and edge of your seat. I think the first time I just felt like I had too many unanswered questions the first time, most of which got cleared up on the second view. I appreciate a movie that really makes you pay attention and think and this is certainly it. A great movie, and I still think the best performance in the movie came from Kelly MacDonald)

In truth, it's more eloquent, more profound, and more profoundly cinematic in its stretches of silence than when its central trio begin to talk again; there's a definite loss of momentum and urgency late on, with the removal of one of the key players from the board, not least as those remaining then seem unwilling to go after the other. First a disclaimer: The Coen brothers are probably some of my favorite directors. I own all of their movies on DVD.
