That being said, this movie is extremely disappointing and probably the biggest over-hyped joke of 2007...and just because of this movie's ending...or rather lack thereof. You will be let down because there is absolutely no payoff whatsoever. It would be better for you to see any movie (ANY movie) and leave fifteen minutes before it's over. If you thought the last episode of the Sopranos sucked than you get the idea of what this movie does in caring so little about its audience. Now some will argue that the movie adapts closely to the book or that the message is that evil always wins in long run but I (and you) don't need to spend $10 bucks and two hours on something we already know. It seems the Coens were reacting to their last movie, the remake of "The Ladykillers" which didn't do well with critics or audiences (although I liked it). That movie had a perfect ending that tied everything up by the credit roll. This movie will just piss you off when the screen goes to black and Ethan and Joel's names pop up on the screen. Believe when all is said and done and the Oscars are over, people will wonder what the critics saw in this movie and what all the fuss is about. (Just like "Million Dollar Baby" and "Shakespeare in Love") The Coens owe me $10.

Awesome movie,this is a must see..It is 1980. In a West Texas police station, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) uses the handcuffs around his wrists to garrote the deputy who had arrested him. Somewhere else in the desert, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles across the carnage of a drug deal gone bad. Mexican criminals and pit bulls lie dead on the ground; only a mortally wounded driver remains alive. The driver asks for water but instead Llewelyn follows the trail of one of the criminals who had gotten away. Llewelyn tracks him to a tree where the criminal died. He finds a satchel filled with two million dollars. He takes the money and returns home to his wife, Carla Jean (Kelly McDonald) who is irritated that he has been gone all day and refuses to tell her where he found the guns and money he had brought home. That night, Llewelyn feels guilty for not giving the wounded driver water and resolves to take him a jug. He arrives around dawn and discovers that the driver has been shot and killed. More gunmen appear, disable his truck and fire on him, hitting him in the shoulder. They chase him to a river bank where Llewelyn tries to swim away. The gunmen's pit bull leaps in to the water after him. Reaching a far shore, Llewelyn is barely able to shoot and kill the dog before it is upon him. Realizing he is facing some dangerous individuals, he tends his wounds then sends Carla Jean to stay with her mother in Odessa while he travels separately with the money....

Tommy Lee Jones, perfectly-cast as the sherrif, meditates throughout the film on growing old in a nation he barely recognizes, which explains to us the meaning of the film's title and the perspective with which we are meant to understand it. The landscapes of west Texas that serve as the film's backdrop are as barren and cold as the northern landscape of "Fargo" and you feel just as little desire to visit them. The three main characters around which the story builds never meet, and the entire film builds to a confrontation that never comes. Strange as those facts sound, it is also brave filmmaking and shows how much the Coens know about audience expectations and how to defy them - even if it means pissing us all off. This film is both stark and contemplative, and demands to be seen more than once.

The movie talks about a man who comes across a bag containing 2 Million Dollars by accident with all the surrounding people murdered. He makes a simple mistake of taking it and now he is being followed by several personas all after this bag of money for different reasons. Of course one of those people is a psychopathic killer who obviously kills for fun. I know, just by reading this you will be so excited about watching it as I was. Every year we get hundreds of cheap horror movies about psychotic killers and none of them manages to go as high as our standards to make us tick. All of them are desperate copies of phenomenal characters such as Dr. Hannibal Lector and Norman Bates who are THE psychotic killers but none can match up to them, nor did Anton. Although he is the kind of characters I love but I always felt there is something missing, but I won't ruin everything by talking of what I didn't like coz they are very few and after all he is a savior of psychopathic killers making them again fearful not lame and cheesy. This is probably one of the most original ways of killing to ever be put on-screen. And the way he looks with that terrible hair-do a la Willy Wonka makes the character more charismatic. Anton doesn't have a lot to say during the movie since in most of the scenes he appears in he is killing. But I guess actions do speak louder than words. But the main point is that when he does speak he says the most disturbing and chilling stuff since Hannibal himself. But why spend so much time talking while you can spend your time blowing people up with an oxygen bottle. 

The movie follows a very slow pace which wasn't so helpful during the whole runtime. I found it a bit hard sometimes to keep up with it coz I was bored with what's happening. Watching someone packing his clothes to run away so many times isn't such a fun thing to watch. And I guess they wasted too many scenes on useless stuff that could have been removed and used as deleted scenes in the DVD extra features coz I don?t think they are movie material. But the movie is saved every time our cheer character Anton appears because he was the only one capable of giving us Goosebumps. The Cohen Brothers really succeeded in the scenes including Anton coz they made them so cold and chilling you feel you are breathing the cold air that is created by the presence of this character. One scene that is really memorable and probably one of the best this year is the one where our cat and dog meet in the hotel and the duel between them. It was such a great scene. But still The Cohen Brothers did a better job writing the movie than directing it. West Texas can sleep contentedly knowing it has its place in the world. It can claim the wide landscape of wind pounded earth and smooth talking Rangers, the stoicism, the grandeur. It can claim the rights to being a place where the only things bigger than its counties are the hat...well, at least in the movies.

To the outside observer Texas is a pretty homogenous place. Most New Yorkers, for instance, would probably like to believe all the Texas cliches in the movies. I know I would. So I thought a little more about Texas and how it has been portrayed thus far (cinematically, of course) and I realized that the films set in West Texas are the most memorable for me and oh so much more interesting. Perhaps this is why I have such a consistent image of Texas, because when it comes to West Texas in the movies, it's a rough world with hard truths and not so many happy endings --and I love every bit of that!

No Country for Old Men takes the general sense perception of this West Texas atmosphere and gives it a face that looks me dead in my eye and scares the shit out of me. Shot by shot I would have to call this the Coen Brothers' most straight faced, deadpan film since Blood Simple. After first viewing this film I had no idea how to think of it and walked out of the theater a little puzzled. After a while I realized my shoulders were sitting somewhere above my ears. I tried to relax the muscled in my neck and realized how tense I had been throughout the movie and I realized --I like it!

Let's do a short recap of the film: A psycho killer with esoteric principles and standards sets out to find a local Texas man who stumbled across a suitcase full of money. The killer proceeds to kill, the man proceeds to run away. That's it. That's the whole story. Sound familiar? Well it isn't. Trust me when I say, you have never seen this story told like this and guess what's the best part...I can't even tell you how or why.

For the much larger portion of the movie, the principal characters never meet but still sense the trail left by the others and seem to know all their actions. In this way, the entire film plays out like a conversation spoken entirely through middle men, broken door locks, and corpses left behind. It is precisely this failure to meet that makes the film so intensely frightening. Without giving away too much, I would have to say that when finally we see any interaction between the characters face to face, I almost breathed a sigh of relief, probably because this was the most action packed part of the film.

Josh Brolin plays Llewelyn Moss, the man who happens upon the cash. Javier Bardem plays the killer, Anton Chigurh. Tommy Lee Jones plays Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, doing what he does best. Together, these three give respective performances so plainly honest, so theatrically frightening, and so smartly adept that I wriggle in my seat just thinking about them.

You don't see a film like No Country for what happens, you see it for how it happens and to see who's there when it does.

[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=#cc9900][font=Trebuchet MS]Joel and Ethan Coen are back with a superbly-crafted thriller based on McCarthy's Pulitzer-winning book. [i][font=Trebuchet MS]No Country For Old Men[/font][/i] is a clever blend of the work from their brilliant past. It combines a Southwestern dread of [i][font=Trebuchet MS]Blood Simple[/font][/i] with the brutal criminality of [i][font=Trebuchet MS]Miller's Crossing[/font][/i] as well as black humor of [i][font=Trebuchet MS]Fargo[/font][/i]. The Coen brothers created an incomprehensibly amazing thriller that defies imitation by breaking the rules of the genre and the flow of action. The movie benefits a great deal from the Coens distinctive style along with typically outstanding composition and framing. They fill the picture with tension and unadulterated thrills not giving their characters, or the audience any time for a break. Their writing is equally strong. As we are realizing the film is unaffected commentary on the poor condition of the world, the characters are startingly ambiguous. The acting is another undisputable virtue of the film. Josh Brolin is stunning playing a man who is smart enough to stay one step ahead of a psychopath, but too unreasonable to see the fatality of such a decision. Javier Bardem also is excellent portraying prince Anton Chigurgh who is a ruthless killer using bolt gun and tossing coin. Bardem makes such a fascinating and characteristic villain that he electrifies every moment in the film, even when he is not onscreen. All in all, [i][font=Trebuchet MS]No Country For Old Men[/font][/i] offers filmmaking at its finest being among the very best movies of the year.[/font][/color]

The Coen Brothers strike again with "No Country for Old Men," their best movie since "Blood Simple," their debut. Everyone by now should know the plot, involving a clevar Texas ne'er do-well who finds across a suitcase full of money from a drug deal gone wrong, and as a result, gets the most badass serial killer ever on his tail. The action sequences, played out like a deadly game of chess, are brilliant. No character is stupid; in fact they're probably all smarter than the average human being in this situation. And they plainly show off their smarts as they try to outwit each other across the Mexican border and towards mortality. The Coens will get an Oscar nod for it, but the real brilliance behind the film is Javier Bardem, who plays the most evil man in cinema I've ever seen. He's so evil, he's funny. There are so many reasons to see this movie; it's the best movie of the year. But if for nothing else, see it for the best seen of the year, between Bardem and a poor old Texas shopkeeper.

I suppose that might fit with the simplistic theory that you're either old and tired (read: apathetic) or young and stupid.

The two important parts of the story, the young crazies part and the old tired guys part, are not that effectively linked. As directors and storytellers, Joel and Ethan Coen are no strangers to stories about morally compromised men and their violent thirst for money, percolated through with generous (but ideally not excessive) amounts of black humour. Widely regarded as their masterpiece, and I would say rightfully so, [i]Fargo[/i] looked at an oily character and his dealings with two even lower-lifes than him which ballooned into a multiple homicide case and of course that bit with the wood-chipper. But where [i]Fargo[/i] moved from a mere witty crime thriller to an emotional character-driven triumph was in introducing the character of Marge Gunderson (Frances McDormand), walking and talking the stereotypical "Midwest" walk and talk but with decidedly un-stereotypical intelligence, observational skills, professionalism, and uncorrodable morality. It was this strong female presence that presided over a realm of bad men that lent [i]Fargo[/i] its brilliance and originality. The Coen brothers' films since that have been, for the most part, equally clever, but rarely as moving or boasting characters as empathetic and fleshed-out, although some (like the moody - and clearly memorable since I haven't seen it in ages - [i]The Man Who Wasn't There[/i]) have come closer to matching the legacy of [i]Fargo[/i] than others (pretty but shallow, irritating throwbacks to old genres and ages such as [i]Intolerable Cruelty[/i] and [i]The Ladykillers[/i]). These films may have had the brain, in other words, but they missed the heart.
 
The chilling, darkly funny yet emotionally engaging and viscerally gripping [b]No Country For Old Men[/b] reverses this trend of self-conscious cleverness and snide genre spoofing in a serious way. At the same time, it indicates new and original directions for the Coens. While the cynical masculine world of [i]Fargo[/i] was enlivened by the introduction of a strong, sensible yet highly capable female presence, [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] takes place entirely in a bleak, dry, harsh, male-dominated landscape, informed by Western genre tropes and, obviously, the writing of Cormac McCarthy, on whose novel the film is based. (The female characters like Moss' wife or the secretary or the cashier in the shop that Chigurh visits flit around the periphery of the plot.) The Coens also eschew their usual stream of ironic, witty dialogue in favour of an aura of stoic silence.
 
Probably the most notable aspect of [i]No Country For Old Men[/i]'s effect is the use of silence, broken only by the most basic, natural of sounds and, at one point, an eerily unnatural beeping. Silence pervades the proceedings, often lending them unbearable suspense and aura of danger. The quietness also brings out the sense of the moral vacuum at the core of the movie and the profound weariness and instinct of the characters (communicating with force rather than words). The silence also reinforces the hardness of the characters, their isolation from each other and the good in the world.
 
Going hand in hand with the brilliant and often intense use of silence in developing the film's theme is the wide open spaces chosen for the film's setting (the southwest US and parts of Mexico) and shot smoothly and for maximum impact by the Coens' go-to cinematographer, Roger Deakins. The action even starts off in a wide open desert, with Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a scruffy hunter out by himself stalking some prey stumbling upon a jumble of dead, bloody bodies, abandoned jeeps, and a briefcase stuffed with $2 million, pointing to a drug deal gone terribly wrong. We are then introduced to the psychopathic enforcer named Anton Chigurh, played with a shivering and yet still modest ferocity by Javier Bardem in a page boy-gone-dark haircut, whose methods involve a compressed air gun and whose targets are often decided by the mere flip of a coin, as he pulls up at a middle-of-nowhere gas station and questions the grizzled attendant. (Bardem's very pronunciation of the word "friend-o" becomes menacing.) And even when the action moves into larger towns and cities, the atmosphere of quiet and desolation continue, as when Moss is pursued in the dead of night through city streets lined with parked cars and few evident witnesses.
 
The dazzling from the Coens bring to the film serves to enhance not only the action and suspense, but the cynical theme of a masculine world starting to implode in on itself, a frightening thought especially for the men who have been immersed in it for so long that they can no longer seem to comprehend it. Especially with the introduction of Tommy Lee Jones as a veteran police officer on the case of the ill-gotten cash and the murders that start accumulating as Chigurh tracks down his briefcase. His performance, probably his most serious and focused in some time, makes the character look downright exhausted and perplexed by what he has recently seen, his professionalism starting to be chipped away by emotion and moral outrage. [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] takes place in a bleak, cynical world where money has taken precedence over human life to the point where human beings can be snuffed out with hardly a blink or a concern. The Coens do a great job in showing the quickness of these murders and the way the killer essentially gets away scot-free, further establishing the brutality and immorality of this world. And Jones, right along with them, embodies the attitude suggested by the title. This [i]is[/i] no country for old men, or anyone with a heart, a stomach, and a sense of morality. Especially in his final monologue which develops the relationship his character had with his father (followed perfectly by the sound of a clock ticking away into silence), Jones embodies the commentary the film seems to be making: that the world has gone topsy-turvy with greed and violence, and that that is a depressing, tiresome shame and an outrage.
 
The concept of men driven to violence and chaos by money is not exactly an original one - the Coens have often explored it in their own work, and many parallels can be drawn between [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] and Sam Raimi's wintery tragedy [i]A Simple Plan[/i]. The ending scene is also a bit striking - at first, it seemed to me to be quite inconclusive and abrupt, but really, it is thematically fitting, disquieting, and appropriately cynical. It is the stark formal beauty, controlled skill, and energy that the Coens bring to this story that is remarkable. Also remarkable is the marked change from their usual tongue-in-cheek attitude (more brain than heart when it comes to characterization). [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is serious, not only clever, and even moving, with the silence and the haunting landscapes and the three characters so perfectly, memorably played by Brolin, Bardem, and Jones creating untold depths of sorrow. This cinematic territory might be no country for old men, but it is exciting, dramatic territory for the audience, and for the filmmakers too, whose style has been infused with thrilling new life and poignantly empathetic tendencies by this jaunt in this arid, eerie, empty, masculine desert. The film opens with shots of desolate, wide-open country in West Texas in June 1980. In a voiceover the local sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) tells of the changing times as the region becomes increasingly violent. The antagonist Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) and his unique weapon, a captive bolt pistol, are then introduced as Chigurh strangles a sheriff's deputy, escapes custody, and steals a car by using the bolt pistol to kill the driver. Meanwhile, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), hunting pronghorn near the Rio Grande, comes across a collection of corpses and one dying Mexican: the aftermath of a drug deal gone awry. He also finds two million dollars in a satchel a short distance from the newfound massacre. Initially taking the money and leaving the Mexican to die, Moss has an attack of conscience later that night and returns with water for the dying man. This good deed sets off a cat-and-mouse game in which the hunter and hunted frequently switch roles, as a gang of Mexicans, Moss, Chigurh, and Bell chase each other and the money across the Texas and Mexico landscapes.

Chigurh, a professional hitman, has been hired to retrieve the satchel of money (which contains a hidden radio transponder to which Chigurh has the corresponding receiver). Chigurh does not hesitate to kill those in his way, including those closely associated with the drug deal, the drivers of cars he steals for transportation, and people he encounters by chance. Moss, unaware of the transponder's existence, sends his wife Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald) out of town and moves from motel to motel as he attempts to elude both the Mexicans and Chigurh. In the meantime, Bell avoids the federal authorities? investigation of the original drug-deal massacre and focuses his attention on trying to locate and protect Moss. Chigurh, with his tracking device, inexorably closes in on Moss while acting as an agent of fate and chance to the people he meets along the way.

While following the money Chigurh guns down most of the remaining Mexicans and a rival hitman, Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson). Moss, realizing Chigurh will find Carla Jean and kill her, arranges a rendezvous with her in El Paso to give her the money and send her out of harm?s way. The characters all converge in a seedy hotel in El Paso, but not simultaneously: Sheriff Bell and Carla Jean do not arrive until after Moss has been killed by the Mexicans in a shootout.

Sheriff Bell, aware that blown locks are Chigurh's method of invasion, returns that night to the now-quiet motel and finds that the lock to (the now-deceased) Moss's hotel room door has been blown out. Chigurh observes Bell through a reflection as Bell stands outside the door deciding whether to enter. Chigurh is shown hiding behind the door of the hotel room, and when Bell enters the room, Chigurh is presumably behind the door. It is unclear whether the sheriff observed Chigurh through a reflection in the blown lock or whether Bell senses his presence. Bell sees that the vent cover has been removed by someone using a dime as a screwdriver, indicating that the money has probably been removed. Despite the presence of Chigurh, Bell sits quietly on the hotel room bed, then leaves the room unharmed.

Some time later Bell visits his Uncle Ellis (Barry Corbin), an ex-lawman. Bell is planning to retire due to his weariness of the changing times, but Ellis points out that the region has always been violent, and accuses Bell of "vanity" ? in thinking that he could personally make a difference. Chigurh, in the meantime, has located the widowed Carla Jean and waits for her at her newly-deceased mother's home. Despite telling her that he "gave Llewelyn his word" that she would die should Moss not hand over the money, Chigurh reconsiders -- and offers Carla Jean the same "coin flip" opportunity that Chigurh had previously given to an innocent bystander in his path. Unlike the previous party, Carla Jean refuses to call heads or tails. Chigurh leaves the house, carefully checking the soles of his boots. As Chigurh drives away he is injured in a car accident and his left arm is badly broken; he manages, however, to leave the scene before the police arrive.

The film closes on Bell at home, reflecting on his life choices. Bell relates to his wife (Tess Harper) two dreams he had, both involving his deceased father, also a lawman. Bell reveals briefly that in the first dream, he lost "some money" that his father had given him. Bell states that in the second dream, he and his father were riding horses through a snowy mountain pass. Bell states that his father, who was carrying fire in a horn, quietly passed by Bell with his head down. Bell then relates that his father was "going on ahead, and fixin' to make a fire" in the surrounding dark and cold, and that when Bell got there, his father would be waiting. Bell closes the dream narrative, and the film, with the final words: "And then I woke up.".


No Country for Old Men received eight Academy Award nominations for the 80th Academy Awards (and tied with There Will Be Blood for the most nominations). Nominations included Best Picture, Best Director (Coen Brothers), Best Supporting Actor (Javier Bardem), Best Adapted Screenplay (Coen Brothers), Best Film Editing (Roderick Jaynes), Best Cinematography (Roger Deakins), Best Sound Editing and Best Sound Mixing.

The film was also nominated for four Golden Globe Awards and won two at the 65th Golden Globe Awards. Javier Bardem won Best Performance by an Actor in a Supporting Role in a Motion Picture and the Coen Brothers won Best Screenplay ? Motion Picture. The film was also nominated for Best Motion Picture ? Drama, and Best Director (Coen Brothers). Earlier that year it was also nominated for the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.The Screen Actors Guild gave a nomination nod to the cast for its "Outstanding Performance". Also, the film won top honors on January 26, 2008 at the Directors Guild of America Awards for Joel and Ethan Coen.

Consonant with the positive critical response, No Country for Old Men received widespread formal recognition from numerous North American critics' associations (New York Film Critics Circle, Toronto Film Critics Association, Washington D.C. Area Film Critics Association, National Board of Review, New York Film Critics Online, Chicago Film Critics Association, Boston Society of Film Critics, Austin Film Critics Association, and San Diego Film Critics Society).The American Film Institute listed it as an AFI Movie of the Year for 2007, and the Australian Film Critics Association and Houston Film Critics Society both voted it best film of 2007.

[url="http://bp3.blogger.com/_tLercVPgzNQ/R42Czhg2LoI/AAAAAAAAANU/5QNqDQYchhE/s1600-h/nocountryforoldmen_poster.jpg"][img]http://bp3.blogger.com/_tLercVPgzNQ/R42Czhg2LoI/AAAAAAAAANU/5QNqDQYchhE/s320/nocountryforoldmen_poster.jpg[/img][/url][font=courier new]When it comes right down to it, I'd have to say that the Coen Brothers are my all-time-favorite directors. They make movies exactly the way I wish I could; with a wonderful all-around sense of style, just the right amount of quirky, dark humor; beautiful camera work, the best writing and great performances from every actor, so that no matter how small the character in their films, you always remember them. [/font][i]Raising Arizona, T[/i][i]he Big Lebowski[/i][font=courier new] and [/font][i]Fargo[/i][font=courier new] are all near the top of my all time favorites list. Everything else they've done is also top-notch, with the exception of their last two films; [/font][i]The Ladykillers[/i][font=courier new] and [/font][i]Intolerable Cruelt[/i][i]y[/i][font=courier new], both were far below their standards, I was afraid they'd lost it.  But when [/font][i]No Country For Old Men[/i][font=courier new] was released to phenomenal reviews, I knew they were back.[/font]
[font=courier new]There is no question that this is one of the top films of the year. If it weren't for a slight stumble towards the end, I'd be ready to call it the year's best. The old west photography by cinematographer Roger Deakins is absolutely gorgeous. Every actor in the film is at the top of their game. A brilliant screenplay, building up the intensity with every scene, until it's almost unbearable; it's broken up occasionally with some pitch-black humor, so much so, that I was the only one laughing at some of the "jokes".

Llewelyn Moss, played perfectly by Josh Brolin, which I had no idea he had in him as an actor, is a typical no-ambitions type of guy, who's been content to float through life. Until he runs across the aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong. Instantly his military training kicks in and he tracks down the injured guy who escaped with a suitcase full of money. He knows somebody is going to come looking for it; so he sends his wife off to her mother's and goes into hiding.[/font]

[font=courier new]And he's right. The chase comes in the form of the ultimate bad-ass Anton, a bob-haired psycho, with no conscience about killing and the ultimate sense of how to get to anybody and through everybody else that stands in his way. I've seen nothing but sensitive type roles for Javier Bardem so far, but he's the most memorable bad guy of the year. (I think Anton will be remembered for a long time, we'll see folks dressed as him next Halloween.) He carries with him the most unique weapon we've ever seen for a professional killer, a cattle gun, which he uses to open doors and people's heads. I can't get over how much I loved this villain![/font]

[font=courier new]Tommy Lee Jones plays a worn-down Sheriff with old-time values; he's tracking both of them, and can't understand what the world's come too. It's for him, that the film is named. Woody Harrelson shows up in a very cool, little role, as another professional killer who's sent to reign in Anton.[/font]
[font=Courier New]It's getting near the end of the film and I'm deeply involved in the game of cat and mouse between Llewelyn and Anton, it's the most tense filmmaking I've witnessed in a long time. Llewelyn gives Anton more trouble than he's probably ever had to deal with. And just when you think that Llewelyn actually has a chance to survive, the film veers off in a weird, unsatisfying way. Suddenly we're behind on the events and seeing the film from a new perspective. One woman at my screening explained it quite simply, [/font][font=Courier New][i]"That ending was stupid!"[/i][/font]

[font=courier new]I wouldn't go that far; I understood everything that happened, and there are some very cool pieces to it, but to be thrown off the track of such a beautiful narrative was unnerving. I really need to see it again, to try understand[/font][font=courier new] what the Coen's were doing here. Next time I watch the film I'll be expecting it, and hopefully have a better grasp on why they made this choice. I'll post my thoughts again then.

For now, make sure to see this film, hopefully with some friends who you can discuss the ending with. [/font]

A modern classic and maybe the Coen's best film yet. Every aspect of the film (acting, direction, scipt) is flawless, yet the true mark of its greatness is that careful thought after viewing is deeply rewarding as its subtleties are slowly revealed.

Its good, in fact, it's very good, but it's not all the critics would have you believe.

What do you get?  A beautifully shot piece of small town America, realised with dark comedy, a fantastic script, great performances and genuine edge of the seat tension.

So what's missing.  Will this is arguable and down to preference, but I am certain a lot of people left the theatre somewhat perplexed and probably asking 'what was the point of that?'  Well, this is a Coen brothers movie so don't expect paint by numbers or any shackles to convention.  

The movie is very much in two parts and the majority of viewers will probably relate to the first part which is a tense cat and mouse chase through Texas motels.  

The second part is somewhat more literary and perhaps struggles to hold the attention as successfully as rest of the film. If it wasn't allegedly such a close adaptation of the book, you would think the Coen's were intentionally baiting their audience to the point of aggravation.

"No Country for Old Men" is easily one of the best movies to come out this year.  After a string of unsuccessful comedies ("The Ladykillers, "Intolerable Cruelty") the Coen Brothers return with a dark crime thriller that may snag them the Oscar for Best Picture that many people felt they deserved for "Fargo". 

The story, adapted from the novel by Pulitzer Prize winner Cormac McCarthy, is about a man named Llewelyn ("Lou-Ellen") Moss (Josh Brolin) who stumbles across a case full of money at a drug deal gone wrong.   His decision to take the case puts him on a collision course with  ruthless killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) who is sent to retrieve the money. Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is an old lawman trying to gain control of the situation before things get even worse.

The film is magnificent because of the great work put in by all the actors in the film.  The dialogue is sparse but everything said is very meaningful!Tommy Lee Jones is the heart of the film.  He is not playing the tough-as-nails lawman we've seen him as in "The Fugitive" but a more common, simple man. Almost like a Andy Griffith type of character. The over all theme of the movie is how does a simple man like this deal with a world  that's becoming  increasingly  violent?  How does a Sheriff who doesn't use a pistol deal with a relentless killer?  The movie paints a bleak and sorrowful view of the world but sadly it's also a very accurate one in many ways.

"What's the most you ever lost on a coin toss?"-Anton Chigurh

The story is very tense and suspenseful. The violence in the film is shocking and often startling.  A lot of this has to do with the fact the the main perpetrator of the violence is a man who is so unpredictable you never know what he is about to do next.  Anton Chigurh will definitely become one of the most famous movie villains of all time. Javier Bardem does an unbelievable job of portraying this very dark yet very principled man.  Chigurh is practically death itself personified. His presence is felt in every scene even if he isn't in them. I wouldn't be surprised if Bardem is given an Oscar for his portrayal.

The only flaw many will have with the film is that it is very anti-climatic at the end.  It's a very brave decision by the filmmakers to end the story exactly the way the novel ends.  The film steadily increases the tension and prepares you for an epic showdown between all three man characters.  You can feel it coming and it's almost unnerving because you fear how it will turn out!  Then it skips the event that you are waiting for!  The shootout and confrontation you are waiting for is never seen on screen. All you see is the aftermath. The film actually closes with one character explaining a dream he had to someone else.  Many people will feel cheated but the whole point the film is trying to make is summed up so eloquently in that speech about a dream that I couldn't imagine the movie ending any other way. 

The story doesn't at all focus on the reasons people make the choices they do. I think this is a weakness of the film.  We never  know why Llewelyn  makes his choice to take the money aside from it simply being human nature in a way.  One of my favorite films is "A Simple Plan". It's a great film that depicts a similar situation where people justify their decisions to try to keep "found" money.  In this film the only person we get to understand is the Sheriff who in many ways is a true representation of each one of us. The question we are faced with answering at the end is could we have done what he did?

No Country for Old Men
Tommy Lee Jones, Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin, Written and Directed by Joel & Ethan Coen


Watching the new Coen Brothers film, No Country for Old Men, two other films came to mind. 

The first was Sam Raimi's A Simple Plan. In that film, Bill Paxton and Billy Bob Thornton, along with one of Thornton's loser friends, come across a downed plane in the middle of the woods and a sack full of money. They conspire among themselves to keep the cash and keep quiet should anyone come around to ask questions about it. Little by little, the plan falls apart.

The other movie is The Seventh Seal, the Ingmar Berman classic starring Max Von Sydow as a knight returned from the Crusades playing chess vrs. the Angel of Death to prolong his life. Along the way, Death takes those around the knight; some righteously deserving of it, others who may not deserve it. In the end, the knight sacricices himself so that a family who hosted him can escape death's touch.

The Angel of Death in No Country is named Anton Chiguhr, played by Javier Bardem, and may be the most evil, viscious killer on film in years. There is a rational method to his sinister madness that is exhilarating. He kills because people are deserving of it, because people have not lived what anyone would consider living, because someone had a choice to save them and didnt, or simply because they lost a coin flip. 

He's after Llewelyn Moss, a trailer park living Vietnam vet who came across the remnants of a drug deal gone bad. Moss, played by Brolin, finds a satchel full of $2 million, and knows the kind of people who will come looking for it. He goes from fleabag motel to fleabag motel, one step ahead of Chiguhr. Its a typical cat and mouse thriller, with each getting jabs at the other.

Here and there Tommy Lee Jones comes in as a contrast; he's an old codgy sherriff disgusted with the world. He's seen a lot, knows a lot, and wants nothing to do with the evils of the world. 

Visually, as with any Coen Brothers' film, the movie is scenic and wonderfully lit and staged. 5 stars does not do this justice. The problem is that a scale that gives a film like this 5 stars would result in the average GOOD Hollywood blockbuster getting between 1 and 2 stars... and as films like this come along once every few years, that would make the majority of reviews a bit lacking in granularity. Actually, films this good make me wonder just what sort of films I am missing... are there films this good without the violence and the stars which never get into the consciousness of even a film buff like myself? I've seen my fair share of artsy films... but this film was so good that it's left me with a nagging feeling that I'm missing out on the best of what films can offer... 

So, to the film... well it's a revelation! I've seen other reviewers describe it as 'Perfection' and I'd agree. Basically, films have certain conventions that they use, I don't just mean plot devices, but certain ways of filming things, certain ways of providing exposition, certain ways of dressing a scene and the actors - it sort of makes a 'palette' of techniques and conventions by which to 'paint' the film. Now most of these techniques are quite formulaic - whether they are the mainstream techniques or the private techniques of great directors like David Lynch... and I've always felt they were necessary shortcuts because (a) the film has to move quick - we only get around 2 hours for a film which may be from a book that takes 20 hours to read, or (b) the limitations of the technology. Well this film blows that away - it just didn't 'move' like any film i've ever seen. It moved like a novel, scene changes were like flicking the pages of a book - a really *good* book.. there seemed to be just an *unlimited* way in which the story was told. 

(Spoilers)

For example,  Normally during a violent film the audience is building a tolerance to the violence as it goes along. So for the first couple of times you see the bad guy kill someone you get the full effect.. and towards the end they need to UP the *gore* to keep the audience from being bored... is that what they do here? Nope - the opposite. As the audience would be getting immune to the shock of the violence, they just stop showing it - they start focusing on the aftereffects of it instead. When one of the main characters is killed, they don't even show it - just the body on the ground as another character sees it. The final death in the film doesn't even show that - the bad guy walks out of the house and your wondering... did he do it? ...And then he checks his boots (one assumes looking for blood). There seemed to be an unlimited number of ways that the story was developed, shot and edited. Now thats what I mean when I say it's like a book. For those that can maintain concentration during a film it was relentless - you couldn't take your eyes of the screen for even a split second. Not one moment of the film was wasted... when action was occurring it could move very fast, jumping from moment to moment like the paragraphs of a book, almost like the way the consciousnesses of the characters perceived the events around them.

Interestingly there are three main characters - the vet (Llewellyn Moss), the sheriff (Ed Tom Bell) and the killer (Anton Chigurh) whose stories weave around each other without often resulting in them being present together. In that sense it had a realism that is only readily apparent upon reflection. At times it seemed like the main way that the three characters communicated with each other was through a telephone or a third party - like Carla Jean Moss, Llewellyns wife.

There is not one aspect of this film that was a disappointment. The acting was stunning... I never thought i'd ever be blown away by Tommy Lee Jones for chrissakes.. but I was. It was one of the best performances of that genre i've ever seen. This was a *hard* man, hard like tempered steel... who was very introspective without a trace of sentimentatlity. Javier Bardem was the most disturbing bad guy i've ever witnessed on film, dark, menacing, operating under his own set of principles and just as utterly callous as to the pain and death he brings as someone swatting flies. Woody Harrelson was fantastic.. tough, funny as hell, and ultimately undone by his overconfidence.... but everyone was stunning... every tiny little role was acted perfectly. The dialog was amazing, the cinematography was awesome - the environs were shown as hard and desolate as the men that lived in it, and even more uncaring about the suffering caused. Even the soundtrack was up to the task... the use of music was minimal in the extreme. Only a few minutes out of the whole film, and what was used was unusual (buddhist chants???). 


The moral question posed at the start of the film is that of trying to understand how society has degraded into violence for it's own sake. The movie doesn't have an answer, (any answer would be tripe) but it shows just how these strikingly amoral psychopaths move through a society that has no defense from them, how even the strong are at the mercy of the unpredictability of the violence they breath.

If "Fargo" was the successful brother who made it in the world, "No Country for Old Men" is the deadbeat brother who lives in the basement with his parents when he's thirty-five. Their polar opposites, but their stories come from the same place. "No Country for Old Men" is a grittier, darker, and edgier "Fargo". There's no salvation from the likes of Francis McDormand here, No Country sinks deeper and deeper into the dark and never crawls back. The story again centers around money, over $2 million dollars. Llewelyn, played pitch perfectly by Josh Brolin, finds the cash among a flurry of dead bodies. Unfortunately, he gets in the path of a psycho, Chigurh, played by a hauntingly brilliant Javier Bardem, who breathes so much life into the character that he takes some of ours with it. Chigurh thirsts for the hunt and pursues Llewelyn across the country. There is no film in recent memory that could surpass the brilliance and suspense of "No Country for Old Men". The film that it could possibly be compared to is "Fargo", and even then, it may even surpass it. The performances are devastating, Tommy Lee Jones, as the sheriff in the hunt after both men, gives one of his best performances of his career. Javier Bardem has to be mentioned again for his performance, his dedication to the character is something rare, and will haunt your dreams. The Coen brothers have come full circle with "No Country", it easily ranks as one of, maybe even the best of their careers. There is not a scene that does wrong, not a note that is misplaced, and not a mistake in sight. Lightning strikes twice for the Coen brothers with "No Country for Old Men".

It's all quiet on the western front until this film's protagonist (Moss) inadvertently becomes privy to a drug deal gone bad.  $2 million dollars is now up for grabs, and Moss has a choice:  Should he take the money, or should he walk away?  Needless to say, Moss takes the loot, and a cat-and-mouse game of death and destruction begins to carve its path through the American desert.  

Playing with ideas of causation, fate, free will, action, omission, and consequence, 'No Country' examines the individual paths of three characters---all of whom are starkly different---but who nevertheless find their lives intertwined because of the past choices they've made.

"You don't have to do this" may often be the final plea of hitman Chigurh's victims before he executes them with his signature air gun, but it is an introspection that rings much louder than a simple call for mercy.  Do we really have a choice in our own human matters, or does our destiny rely on much larger forces---some as unsophisticated and arbitrary  as the flip of a coin?  'No Country' never provides a satisfactory answer.

With their own brand of subtle, dry humor and their matter-of-fact sensibilities for violence, the Coen Brothers have, in my opinion, come closer to the throne of Alfred Hitchcock than any directors in recent memory with "No Country For Old Men."  This movie oozed suspense and dramatic tension, and I'm shocked to hear someone say that they were bored at any time while watching it.  I was the opposite.  I was terrified.  Slow and quiet scenes in the film made me uncomfortable.  Impending moments of doom were as shocking as I expected them to be and the unexpected moments of chaos caused me to jump, cover my eyes, and even verbally respond while watching (which isn't something I tend to do).  And then there's Javier Bardem.  Boy...for once the person winning all of the awards DESERVES it!  I didn't sleep very well the night after I saw this.  I'm haunted by him.  A performance for the ages.  As for the rest of the film, it is a master class of filmmaking in two hours.  Being the film nut that I am, I found the frame compositions and camera work to be as exciting as the story itself.  And I love the fact that this movie can play to the common viewer as a standard thriller, when in fact it's so much more than that.  I saw it as a statement on the American desire to fix problems as fast as possible.  How do you find two million dollars like that and expect to get away with keeping it?  But at the same time, why wouldn't you take that chance?  Stellar acting, stellar direction, stellar everything.  Oh, and that open-ended finish...the one that's not satisfying?  One thought: SHOULD it be?

If you need proof that the Coen brothers are two of the finest living filmmakers, than this should do it - a return to form for what is easily one of the most stressful, stunning films of this year - or, really, any year. It is for experiences like this that the word "riveting" was created. 
     The plot is best left a secret, but it's carried out to perfection. The screen shots of the vast, violent Texas (actually New Mexico, but whatever) landscape speak sentences by themselves. Which is good, because there is very little speaking in this movie, or sound of any kind. The Coen brothers make every noise count, from Tommy Lee Jones' crusty  musings, to Kelly Macdonald's shudder, to Javier Bardem's weapon of choice and, whoo boy, Javier Bardem will stick with you after this. Hundreds of stories have strived for the "remorseless killer" type, and as many have failed. But, here, you see the real thing: a killer to freeze your blood with his very presence - truly terrifying. 
      Indeed, every actor here seems to have found a culmination of their work, as if being cast for this movie was part of their grand purpose in life. You can't take your eyes off Brolin, who brings all of his wits to bear even as he is swept up in something beyond his considerable mettle. Kelly Macdonald, as Brolin's wife, is the bravest soul here, mixing a strong resolve with wide-eyed fear. 
     As with most Coen brothers movies (from "Fargo" to "Big Lebowski", the themes here are stark, disturbing, and decidedly Old Testamental: good, simple people being brought to reckon with darkness. This is one of the best movies these guys have ever made - and they made "Fargo."

Any film with the names Joel & Ethan Coen and Tommy Lee Jones above the title has got to be worth seeing - and this one doesn't disappoint.
As you'd expect from the Coen Bros, it's impecably cast, brilliantly acted and above all - that rarest of things- unpredictable. The sparse script is perfect and the cinematography stunning.  
Set in 1980, when simple acts of human kindness were being replaced by commercial transactions, this film will leave you wondering where the rule you follow will take you. Don't expect the warm-fuzzies.
If you loved Bridget Jones, you'll hate this.

For those familiar with the Coen brothers other films this might feel uncomfortable. It contains none of the genre signposting that's really the bread and butter of their previous films, one is never left with the feeling that the Coens are slightly cleverer than their source material, be it genre or novel, and none of the dialogue or characters are as willfully perverse as before. What's most affecting here is the measured pacing, the attention to every suspenseful detail, and the fascinatingly elisive, ambiguous plot. It seems at last that the Coen brothers are using the various literary and cinematic devices that they have at their disposal to serve the story and not the genre. And then, looked at again, free from gimmicks, the Coen brothers style becomes apparent again. It has much in common with Raising Arizona, Blood Simple, The Big Lebowski - it's characters work best as real people, but as ever we can read a lot into what they stand for, what they represent. Like Meadows/Mundt in Barton Fink, Anton Chigurh, the hired killer who stalks the main character is the most interesting part of the film, even though he is not the subject of the film or the protagonist (this is neither Manhunter or Leon). His role, as well as that of the pursued, emerges as an apt and potent metaphor for whatever you want to put it's name to. And then there's the final act - by three quarters of the way the inevitability of Chigurh's actions become unquestionable, we no longer need to see what he does, and, like the Sheriff, we must search elsewhere for significance. It's quite assured in not wanting to resolve things, but it's as complete, as meaningful, and as satisfying an ending as you can hope for from a couple of excellent writers - and the Coen's are this first and foremost.

So, here's my advice. Watch the movie. At about 1 hour and 50 minutes, get up and leave. Right around the time there's a thing with a car (you'll know what I mean). Finish watching that scene and then get up and leave. Will you be satisfied? Will the ending make sense, if you leave at this point? Well, not really, but it only gets worse after that. Trust me, when I say, if you stay til the very end of the movie you'll wonder why you did. That's ten minutes you'll never get back. You could use that time to hug someone you love or read a poem or eat an egg roll, or just beat the traffic leaving the theatre. Do any of those things- they'll make you a happier, wiser, more lovable person. Staying til the end of this movie won't.  I love the Coen brothers. But the end of this movie really tested that love. I think I'm ready to see other people.

My wife and I were celebrating our 1 year anniversary and decided to round the night out with a flick.  I had heard the buzz on this picture and we were torn between seeing this and Juno.  

For my wife's sake, we probably should have watched Juno.  This movie is excellent but I will endorse it with a honest "caveat emptor."  This movie really shook both of us, but her especially.  Javier Bardem's performance as psychopath Anton Chigurh is an absolute accomplishment.  The cold delivery of his lines and his bizarre methods of dispatching both foes and locks (yes, locks) creates a character and atmosphere rarely achieved in cinema.  Though my wife's initial reaction was that she hated the movie and thought it was awful and violent, she wanted to watch it again about two weeks later.  This film stays with your for a long time, leaving you to ponder the unorthodox ending and the choices made by the pseudo-protagonist Llewelyn Moss.  Josh Brolin's Moss is a smart man, probably smarter than most the audience will give him credit for.  The plot is essentially about his discovery of $2 Million in West Texas in 1980 and the people who want their money back.  Sounds simple, right?  I mean, "Kill Bill" sounds like a simple revenge tale but we all know that to be a "roaring, rampage of revenge."  The plot is definitely outshined by the performances and editing in this movie.  Literally every actor in this film delivers a solid, if not outstanding, performance.  My only main criticism would be of Tommy Lee Jones' character.  This is essentially the same sarcastic and witty law man that Jones has played in the past, but a little older and far less aggressive.  He does well, but does nothing to surprise us.

It took me about 45 minutes to realize this movie has no soundtrack.  Usually, no soundtrack leads to a boring and bland experience but the audio editing used to build suspense and intrigue is mesmerizing.  There is a scene about halfway through the movie where the audience realizes that the good guy and bad guy are about to have a showdown.  The sound effects (transponder beeping, footsteps, light bulb unscrewing, etc) leading the audience to this realization are so subtle but perfect.  The vast landscapes and people of West Texas almost compete with Bardem for supporting role.  Never before has this landscape been shown to be so eerily beautiful and majestic.  The fine character actors we encounter along the way are entirely believable.  It seriously seems like the Coens just filmed real folks without telling them.

If you enjoy a story and presentation that challenges you both mentally and morally, I can't recommend this film strongly enough.

One of the better offerings from last year's Oscar race! The film was so minimalistic, and it actually worked. Omitting the score throughout the whole film made it more intense and complex. The sounds of the environment, the chasing, and the gunshots were great! The film started out very well, and the first "murder" scene was acted and directed very well. The film gradually got more interesting, but I believe it kind of failed short after Josh Brolin's character died toward the end. The ending was a little slow and boring for my taste after the suspenseful beginning and middle. Plus, the ending was kind of sudden, as well, and Tommy Lee Jones' scene toward the end was a little confusing. The film delivered some great action sequences, though most were a little gory for my taste, it gave the audience how horrific and freaky Javier Bardem's character was. He did surely deserved his Oscar, but it was surprising that Brolin did not receive a nomination for his role, and I believe his performance in the movie was very well done. Overall, the film's story and plot was a little sketchy at times, but it was still fun deciphering it. Los hermanos Coen (sin hache) se han ganado a pulso el título de maestros del thriller de la América más profunda. En este caso, con "No Country for Old Men", han conseguido rizar el rizo. 
Su magnífica película está basada en la novela del mismo nombre de Cormac McCarthy y corresponde al género más negro de la tradición de los Coen, en la línea de "Blood Simple", "Fargo" o "Millers Crossing". 
En este caso la sobriedad está acentuada, y poco queda del humor del que hacen alarde en otras películas. "No Country for Old Men" se basa en las poderosas interpretaciones de Josh Brolin, Javier Bardém y Tommy Lee Jones. La película hace poco más que dejar que estos monstruos campen a sus anchas y nos muestren de lo que son capaces.
Josh Brolin, el hermano mayor en "The Goonies" interpreta a Llewelyn Moss, un cazador furtivo que se encuentra con un maletín lleno de pasta en medio del desierto de Texas. Tommy Lee Jones es el sheriff quemado a punto de jubilarse que tiene que resolver el asunto, y Javier Bardém es el particular caza-recompensas que persigue a Moss, llevándose por delante a todo el que le supone un leve obstáculo.

Todo el esta película sale tan fácil y espontáneo como un crimen de Chigurh. También está igual de calculado. Lo que en ella ocurre es reflejo de una América total y universal. Digo total porque no hay nada más americano que Texas, el dinero y la licencia para llevar un revolver en la guantera. Universal, porque nos habla de las partes más feas del ser humano, en América o en cualquier otra parte. Eso que hacen tan bien los Coen: retratar de forma descarnada esos crímenes que ocurren por cualquier motivo miserable y enfatizar que lo miserable de un crimen es precisamente que nunca hay un motivo lo suficientemente bueno.
En el caso del villano, ni siquiera hace falta motivo. Su extraño código le da licencia para matar a cualquiera. 
Sobre la interpretación de Bardém, me tengo que quitar el sombrero. La capucha y hasta el bisoñé. Su asesino, Anton Chigurh, herido y renqueante, ha entrado en la memoria de la Inquisición y no quiere irse. Escalofriante.

Violence and mayhem ensue after a hunter, Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon some dead bodies, a stash of heroin and more than $2 million in cash near the Rio Grande. Nothing ever goes smoothly sometimes and before you know it he's on the run from a psychopathic cold killer.

Josh Brolin: Llewelyn Moss. An interesting guy, Josh has had a flood of movies these past few months. This role is his best yet. He plays the panicked mouse in a bid to keep his prize, in this case a cool $2 million. Some of his choices for his character were stupid but ultimately that's what makes the journey so fascinating.

Javier Bardem: Anton Chigurh. I don't know who this guy is but I've never watched such an entertaining intelligent cold villain in a film. The best villain I've seen recently in a long time. Scrap the Golden Globe he deserves an oscar for playing such a nut, such a compelling character. He does everything so cleanly, he kills at the drop of a hat. Appealed to my dark humour and i frequently laughed at stuff Anton did. For example him shooting two guys in the desert made me burst out laughing, another where he throws his socks into a bathroom next to a recent victim or putting his feet up on the bed to avoid blood on his boots. Like a human colossus or Terminator on speed. This is a grand achievement to play such a man void of morals with his own weird warped take on things. That pressurized air canister thing that he has was certainly ingenious and bloody dangerous. Oh and that Silenced shotgun, that was one powerful mother of a gun. Anyone believe in Karma? Well wait till near the end and you will see.

Tommy Lee Jones: Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. Not a big role for Tom yet an important one. He's always one step behind the story yet comes so close.

Kelly Macdonald: Carla Jean Moss. Recognized her easily, didn't see anything new in her acting apart from the accent.

There was so many great scenes in this. The tension, the sounds, the beats, the uses of silence all are definately used to perfection. Had me jumping on numerous occasions and that part with Anton waiting for his pursuer after finding the transmitter was amazingly shocking.

Without a doubt this film has you on the edge of your seat. The audience i saw this with didn't appreciate it. They didn't see the bigger picture, the gritty realism, the beautiful poetry of that ending and if you see the words in that finale, allow them to sink in, then truly it will blow you away.

Chilling and suspenseful, [I]No Country for Old Men[/I] is a very well-made drama in which Javier Bardem plays his role as a stoic serial killer with incredible poise.  He delivers a magnificent performance as a man who is totally devoid of a conscience.  Definitely one of the best played villains in recent memory.  

There are two main characters on the side of good, or at least civilized society.  Josh Brolin plays the man who is trying to avoid a death delivered by this extremely efficient serial killer.  He too does a good job.  Tommy Lee Jones plays the sheriff who lends more soliloquy-like dialogue to the film than he does to the action of it.  

This film is not without a couple of minor problems though.  The fate of one of the main characters seems a little premature and could have been drawn out a bit longer.  The ending monologue, which in addition to a couple of other scenes, seems a little too self important for its own good.  Finally, the plot has many twists and makes for a great and disturbing, yet only halfway satisfying ending.  

In addition to great acting by most of the cast, the beautifully desolate sets and visuals of the desert and such go hand in hand with the tone of the film. The movie's dark tone and contemplative nature make it one of the best suspense films of the year.  However, probably not the best film of the year among all genres.

No Country for Old Men is one of the most original thrillers Ive seen come out for cinema the past couple of decades. Even though I couldnt claim it to be perfect, it nevertheless is a spectacle to behold for film fans, full of top-notch direction and performances. The problem however is that the film sometimes never goes beyond this; Sure, its a memorable ride with a lot to admire along the way, but when it reaches its final conclusion I couldnt help but wish that I had a use for the road that brought me to where I was.
 
Generally, my favourite films stay with me throughout the feature and keep me inside their world for the whole duration and perhaps days or weeks afterwards. Movies that just miss this title of favourite or perfect usually keep me entertained for the two hours or so that Im watching, but they dont necessarily leave any permanent mark. This was the case with Old Men.
 
So while I absolutely loved nearly everything about the film, it did in the end- lack any real lasting impression. Nevertheless, it is still one of the best films Ive ever seen and definitely would like to see more films along the same tone and style of this. Of course, the Cohen brothers must be congratulated on crafting such a fine piece of cinema, both on a writing and direction level, and in addition to this, the cast as a whole give nothing short of their absolute best here, which is really incredible stuff.

No Country for Old Men is a finely crafted thriller from The Cohen Brothers; two highly talented and experienced filmmakers on top form, recapturing the magic touch that made O Brother, Where Art Thou and The Big Lebowski so popular.

"The crime you see now, it's hard to even take its measure... A man would have to put his soul at hazard. He'd have to say, "Ok, I'll be part of this world.""

Tommy Lee Jones' world weary sheriff, easing into retirement, is a forlorn figure, desperately detached from an unforgiving modern society. His subdued opening narrative resonates strongly with tones of melancholy and nostalgia that are reflected in the visual style and music score. 

The languid camera ambles aimlessly across the sweeping vistas of Texas and New Mexico, the vast scope of the luscious cinematography engulfing the landscapes and lingering in full appreciation of the unadorned spectacle it is witness to. The understated music score contributes a leisurely rhythm to proceedings that helps to dictate the early pace and mood of the story. 

Jones' disillusionment is embodied by the haunting Javier Bardem; an imposing and calculating mercenary whose eerily calm demeanour masks a predatory penchant for callous violence. Bardem commands the screen with his unsettling presence, shrouded in fear and death, casting an ominous shadow over all he encounters.

The final point of a fascinating character triangle is the impressive Josh Brolin as a restless war veteran, who occupies his time with hunting, in search of action and excitement lacking since Vietnam. 

However, the hunter soon becomes the prey when Brolin steals a satchel full of money. This incident acts as a catalyst that precipitates a riveting collision between Brolin and Bardem, igniting the fuse on a furious game of cat and mouse that frays your nerves with searing tension and explodes with disarming violence.

As the dust settles on the volatile excitement, the fractured threads of story limp onwards without direction or purpose, gradually fading into obscurity, before concluding with a frustrating lack of closure. 

However, this could be a deliberate ploy from The Cohen Brothers to mirror Tommy Lee Jones' life journey heading into retirement, where much seems to fade away or extend beyond you. Also, it could be a reminder that in an increasingly cynical and immoral society, evil often prevails.

The plot is fairly straightforward. A hunter named Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon the scene of a drug deal gone really, really sour. Dead bodies, including a dog. Shot up trucks. A huge stash of drugs. And, at the end of a bloody trail, a dead man and a satchel with $2 million in cash. Now, what would you do in that situation? Youre armed, but who knows whos out there in the wilderness, looking for their lost loot? If youre Mr. Moss, you amscray the heck out of there.

Of course, someones gonna come looking for that money, and that person is a crazy bastard named Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who has a penchant for killing and absolutely no moral compass to speak of. He wants something, he kills you and takes it. Or takes it and kills you. Either way. Chigurh is single minded, but hes by no means a simple man; hes whip smart and blindingly fast with his gun and his feet. Theres something about Chigurh that separates him from every other killer who wants his money back; its intangible, and its all because Bardem is so perfect in the role. His sad eyes belie an absolutely terrifying, methodically maniacal criminal.

Completing the trifecta is a beleagured, world-weary sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones). Sheriff Ed Tom Bell is to No Country for Old Men as Marge Gunderson was to Fargo; the no-nonsense, superclever, seasoned Johnny Law who tries desperately to piece together the puzzle before every character has been murdered, a la Shakespeare. This is a role Jones was made to play, and I can safely say he turns in the finest, most nuanced and sincere performance of his long career. Jones has the countenance of a leathery cowpoke as it is, and the unique drawl to accompany it, and the beautiful, poignant script (also by the Coen brothers) allows him to really show his stuff.

Make no mistake, though, in spite of its subtleties, this is a very violent movie; many painful, gut-wrenching deaths occur. Still and all, one thing that makes the movie work is that the violence seems real, not comic-book style; its not violence without serious repercussions.

Back to the writing. At times during the film, multiple storylines are in motion, a la Pulp Fiction, and everything moves so seamlessly that its only later, in retrospect, that you recall certain aspects that tie in one characters perspective with that of another. A mediocre screenwriter would have trouble with this, and plot holes the size of the Rio Grande itself would emerge. People would laugh about the plot inaccuracies and overall inadequacies.

And then, finally, theres that ending. Some people will absolutely love the ending, but others will stare at the screen for a few minutes, wondering if theres more to the story. Simply put, not everything is explicitly resolved, so if youre the kind of person who must have everything tied up as if in a 30-minute sitcom, youre going to have an issue or two with the finale. There was a bit of silence in the theater in which I saw this movie, but I didnt get the impression it was the angry THATS IT?? kind, just the surprised kind.

***1/2

Dark, violent and nerve-jangling thriller about a small-town guy (Brolin) that makes off with $2m from a drug deal gone bad, who is chased by a psychotic hitman (Bardem) and a weary sheriff (Jones). The Coen brothers return to form with this story of chance and fate, occasionally leavened with doses of black humour. Perplexing, challenging, edge-of-the-seat stuff.

For a gritty thriller with a high body count, No Country For Old Men is as quiet a film as they come, the silence interrupted only intermittingly by the crack of gunfire. When bullets aren't flying, mood, tension - and black humour rule the roost. the Coens treat the expansive desert the same way they treated the snow in Fargo; the beautiful landscape is destroyed by the greedy humans trampling across it. Those greedy humans are on top form, too: Brolin confidently moves into leading man territory, Bardem is as lethal as he is spooky and Jones, as always, is Jones. Although Harrelson and Kelly McDonald, playing Brolin's naive wife, are limited to smaller roles, they make each their own. This is a film that needs a second viewing - not only is it worth seeing again, all is clear first time around as 'who did that? How did they know that he'd be there? Where did he get that?' questions arise but knowing the Coens, there's a reason for everything and everything will reveal itself in time.

However, Javier Bardem is quite possibly the most sinister villain in recent history -- a perfect psychopath.

Thank goodness the Coen brothers are back. Whatever madness had taken over them during the creation of "The Ladykillers" and "Intolerable Cruelty" seems now to have left them and they are once again able to bring us an exciting blend of colloquialism, earthy philosophy and...horrific violence.
'No Country...' is a true return to form and they never seem to put a foot wrong in either the script or the direction accomplishing the bringing together of the beauty and the brutality of life.
The simple message, that despite nostalgia for the 'good old days' the world has always been frightening and hostile place, in any other hands, could have sounded mawkish but the use of the setting, the cinematography and a script brimming with sharp expressions works perfectly. The Coen Brothers show the audience that there is the side of life where everything is beautiful but that it quickly gets lost beneath a sheet of violence and greed. 
The true power of the film, however, comes in its characters. Everybody seems to speak from the heart which really encourages emotional involvement from the viewer. Almost every character, despite being on screen for just a matter of minutes, earns the audience's respect and sympathy with a formula of an implied life story, a family connection and a simple vice. Ellis for example (played by Barry Corbin) is visited by Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) and the first thing we see is his filthy shack in the middle of nowhere, which is immediately followed by a joke and a lot of colloquial  received wisdom. He's around for only ten minutes of the film but in those ten minutes his character speaks with such truth, passion and humour that by the end of the film I thought he had one of the strongest roles in the story.
I did say 'almost every character'. Javier Bardem really earns his oscar with is character Chigurh,  the most frightening character cinema has seen in a very long time. Violent, uncalculating and eloquent he walks through the story leaving few survivors. Everything about him is chilling; his weapons, his diabolic voice and especially his habit of deciding a persons life or death on a coin toss. His view of what is fair and right are so skewed yet there is just enough of a hint of sanity and even mortality in there to keep him all too human.
The film is powerful and moving and possibly the Coens' finest work to date.

Yes, the last Coens' film is an intense, effective and nearly flawless thriller-western. It keeps you glued to the chair with the tension rising while it takes its unexpected twists. But it is much more than that, with its provocative, philosophical, premonitory and nearly mythical approach, encompassing some sort of critic on the American way of life, and of the present American soul. After all this is yet another film that tells in its own way, that something is wrong with America today. And that message is synthesized towards the end, when one of the characters says "You can't stop what's coming."
But is this film really such a masterpiece, one of the best of the Cohen brothers' films, as most of the critics are writing? Or a bit of a disappointment? 
Maybe it's a bit of both, I will need more time to think over it. In the meantime the excellent photography and landscapes remain, with some great acting, in particular by Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones and Javier Bardem, unforgettable in his role of a psychopath assassin. Maybe I sense something wrong with the philosophical statement especially towards the end, maybe it was just the many week points of the script with things that seem a bit forced (okay it's a film and they are following a book...) or because things happen too fast and not necessarily well at the end, when for instance one of the three most important characters just disappears like that.

The scale of the landscape is just staggering and often it is every bit as important as the characters on screen. Admittedly, the ending leaves you feeling a little flat as it transfers the emphasis away from what you percieve to be the main character (Josh Brolin's Llewellyn Moss) and fails to tie everything up with a satisfying conclusion, however that is as much the fault of the source material as it is the viewers perception of what should constitute a 'happy ending' for this. If anything, the fact it finishes inconclusively ties in with the film's over-riding theme of control vs. chance. This is definitely one of those films that makes you think hard about whether it is good or not, and in the end I don't think you can help but think of it as a fantastic piece of work. The cinematography alone is breath taking and the central performances are all excellent. Although it isn't instant in it's gratification, I think this will come to be one of the better films I see this year, once I get a chance to see it again.

Of all Hollywood's major movie makers, Joel and Ethan Coen are the envy of the industry for the creative licence they have over the final cuts of their films.  Love interests are not bestowed upon them, action scenes are not required and endings don't get tampered with in the editorial offices.  And it's precisely their insistence on remaining faithful to Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel of the same name which ironically serves up a (deliberately) deeply unsatisfying ending to this  spine-tinglingly magnificent movie.
Tension is constant and unrelenting here.  An indescribable menace haunts every scene in a manner not dissimilar to Michael Haneke's 2006 success Hidden.  
The story is that of a war veteran, a lawman and a psychopath pursuing their agendas in the wake of a gunfight outside Odessa, West Texas in 1980.
Josh Brolin is veteran Llewellen Moss, a non-threatening hunter who is the first to stumble upon the site of the carnage. We see four motorised vehicles with significant damage sustained and several dead human bodies pepperd amongst a multitude of bulletts scattered across an arid landscape.  The aggressive, stifling sunlight provoking a lucid, burgundy tone in the conspicuous splashes of blood.  One of the trucks is filled with packaged narcotics.  Moss continues on several hundred feet to find another broken down vehicle, two more bodies, plenty more blood and a suitcase containing two million dollars in cash.  The drugs are of no interest to Moss but the money is, as is obtaining water for the spectacle's sole survivor, a heavily wounded man bleeding away in one of the trucks.  It's when Moss pointlessly returns to the scene later that night with water, having stashed the money in his caravan home, that he is noticed and pursued under gunfire.  Although he escapes he is forced to abandon his own vehicle which reveals his identity to the lawman and the psychopath.
Javier Bardem is Anton Chigurh, a toothy, jowly, hairy contract killer of notoriety amongst fellow law-vandalisers.  On an explanation of the terms of his work (find Moss and recover the money) Chigurh immediately kills his gangster employers at the scene of the massacre on the discovery of a tracking device connected to a sensor hidden inside the suitcase (a very retro early eighties contraption). What follows is a bloody episode of cat and mouse towards the Mexican border via a couple of run down buildings offering the service of accomodation.  Anyone who comes into contact with Moss during these hours finds themselves considerably richer afterwards; anyone who makes the aquaintance of Chigurh, however, finds themselves dead.  After a bordertown shootout between the two in which Moss finds himself hospitalised, he resigns to meet his scared, sweet wife Carla Jane (Kelly MacDonald) and her bothersome ratbag mother in El Paso to take the money and get on a plane and flee to safety. That's the plan, anyway.  Carla Jane, meanwhile, is being counselled by a member of the police force.
Tommy Lee Jones is Ed Toms, of a distinguished lineage of lawmen.  Toms is a world weary pessimist, his scraggly face portraying a life spent observing and investigating the gravest of events.  Naturally, he is the last to arrive at the scene of the chaos where the film opens, surveying the brutality in an everyday, matter-of-fact manner and immediately reflecting on Moss's (after recognisiing his abandoned truck) great misfortune of having found his red herring of a prize.  Toms knows what happens next, he's obviously seen Fargo, the Coens 1996 study of what ordinary folks can be driven to do for money, what extraordinary badasses do to prevent them and what keepers of the law make of it all.
As a discussion of modern America No Country For Old Men implies money to be a pot of gold at the end of a very dangerous rainbow.  What won't people do if the money's right? It is the thrill of the flashing dollar sign that is the monolith of the country's culture that makes it such a vulgar, unappealing place in the eyes of many foreigners. 
Maybe they'd be a bit more likeable, however, if they really did speak with the clarity and wit prevalant in the dialogue here.  A big, grown-up piece of cinema free from the eccentric quirkyness which has characterised much of the Coens' previoius output, there's nothing in this film that doesn't need to be in it.
The themes are relevant to and prevalant in the everyday lives of everybody on the planet thanks to the Americanization of the world.  They exist to be considered as often as one chooses to do so or to be conveniently neglected as unpleasant thoughts.  If one can be bothered thinking about such matters, this film will live long in the memory;  if not, stick to blockbusters and romantic comedies.
