I've never been as high as most on the Coen Brothers, so I went into this one with lowered expectations. I came out of it pleasantly surprised.

It's a violent modern day western where a man stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad and finds a case filled with money. As a result of this he is being hunted down for it.

The main one hunting is played by Javier Bardem in a portrayal that is nothing short of chilling. This character is just plain evil and almost inhuman. His character's coin flips are a great source of suspense. What's kind of humourous about him is how he doesn't even try to hide who he is and what he does, he walks around blatantly out in the open with large weapons. He is one of the more memorable screen villains we've had in some time.

The Coens and the way they move the camera around really add a lot to this film. Especially in a tremendous scene where Josh Brolin's character is in a hotel room with the lights out waiting for Bardem to come. We see everything only from Brolin's point of view and we wait along with him as the camera focuses on the crack at the bottom door. The tension in that scene is almost unbearable. 

No Country for Old Men probably will win the Best Picture Oscar tomorrow night. While I don't think it is the best movie of the year, it certainly is a respectable choice that won't sicken me like some past winners have (eg. Chicago and Crash).

Most people i have spoken to who have seen this film did not like it. One friend told me that people left before it ended.

Ofcourse, like anything in life, its often a matter of taste whether you like a movie or a book or whatever it is you're scrutinizing in some way or other. 

People are apparently 'baffled' (to quote other reviewers on here) by it and others simply proclaim "i didnt get it". Such comments are entirley laughable as there's not really that much to follow and such reviews are only indicative of our "if it doesnt blow up to a heavy metal tune and have a car chase then its not worth it" movie going culture. (Fast And Furious culture i like to call it). 

Ofcourse, movies where things do simply and inexplicably explode with over the top effects do have their place. But so to, do great movies such as this.

The plot, as is often the case with the two brothers,  is fairly linear involving oft used Coen themes such as money, canny depictions of the U.S (both in landscape and character) and the typical amount of violence. At the same time, there is notably less irony and dark comedic moments.

The presentation of the barren desert landscape in Texas reminds me somewhat of Blood Simple and another notable similarity is the use - or nigh complete lack of - music in the film. Often these days music is too dramatic, and used too much in anticipation of an event. Here the lack of music throughout the film serves only to heighten the tension and build the suspense perfectly.

The acting is superb ranging from our disillusioned contemplative Sheriff Tommy Lee Jones, to the sterotypical Coen "man in over his head" in Josh Brolin. But certainly the best of the bunch is Javier Bardem's violent killer who is out to hunt Brolin. The character is a masterpiece and frighteningly cold and calculated in his dialogue and demeanour contrasting with his somewhat (in my opinion) clumsy look - a deliberate feature i expect. At one brilliant point in the movie he forces someone to choose their own fate through the decisive fall of a coin.

The dialogue is sparse compared to other Coen films, but important as always. I think most people, especially the kind i mentioned earlier, would not like this film because it is slow paced (though it grips you if you let it), things dont blow up every ten seconds, people reload their guns, there's actual character behind a name not just someone else to be shot at and most of all its - if anything - too real in its personification of the violence and money orientated life of this world.

This film is not a crime thriller but a stunning meditation on the battle between good and evil. And as it is Cormac McCarthy, evil wins as good retires. The Coens are intellectual film auteurs and they know a genius when they read one. They cast brilliantly and pull out all the usual stops. When your heart is supposed to pump, it pumps. 
 
Javier Bardem plays evil incarnate, Tommy Lee Jones is decency incarnate, and poor Josh Brolin gets to be everyman. Everyman cannot be saved from his temptation (drug money discovered) - he will be destroyed by evil (with his family), while decency whinges that he is overwhelmed by evil's successes. All performances are first class - with Bardem excelling. 
 
The Coens benefit from not having to write the source material, which is deeper than even Blood Simple and Fargo. Critics who deride the ending clearly do not 'get' McCarthy at all. They complain of the last act's fizzling out - and fizzle it does, as decency hangs up his spikes. 
 
There are no tricky bends in this film - it is a straightfoward masterpiece and easily the best American film of 2007.

[font=Arial Narrow][size=2]No Country for Old Men is a film that deserves its hype and its positive reviews. It was one of the best films of 2007 for several reasons, including its notorious bloodthirsty villain, Anton Chigurh. Every aspect of Anton fits the needed qualities and key elements that make a villain. He is not overdone; he is a perfect character who does not flourish his evil with threats. He isn't a character who must use scare tactics to terrify an audience like many modern day film killers. This is what is so terrifying about him; Anton Chigurh needs no aesthetics or frills to be a horrifying villain. It wasnt only his natural facial features combined with his abnormal haircut that made him this way. The Coens have written and developed this character; they have brought him to life through his startling dialogue and intelligent mind games he may play with his victims. Javier Bardem has outperformed most modern movie villains.

[img]http://files.list.co.uk/images/2008/01/17/no-country.jpg[/img]
 
All other aspects of acting were fantastic as well. The development behind the story and characters was done to a level in which many filmmakers should aspire to reach. The Coens have outdone themselves and have made a film that meets the standards of their previous. One thing I really admired about the film was how simple the plot really was. A man comes across a drug deal gone bad. He finds the money from the deal. A professional killer is hired to track him down, but turns on his recruiters to get the money for himself. Its a very basic premise and the way themes, symbols and metaphors all tie in are what make it seem so complex, but not too convoluted with material. You never become bored or frustrated with this film, because the characters are all so likable, whether they are likable for their protagonist nature, or their pure evil acts on others who deserve to fall victim. 
The thing that really makes this all work is the whole dark comedy aspect of the Coens films. I know it is intentional, but it is so subtle that at times, you cannot remember when this comedy took place after you walk out from the film. The key is that this is part of what makes this violence okay. Chigurh pulls a man over in a hijacked police cruiser, and sends a hydraulic rod sailing through the mans head after telling him to hold still. Who in the hell would hold still? It seemed comedic that Chigurh would simply test his gun on an old man, and thus was the way he acquired new transportation. Just by the brilliant facial expression of Bardem, you could tell that it was okay not to cringe at this brutal sight. He even persuaded you to smile to yourself and possibly give a quick chuckle as you enjoyed the rest of the film.[/size][/font]

This film is both meditative and intense, showing us a changing world in which severe violence intrudes upon older values. Not so much a return to form for the Coens - more of an evolution of the form which they originally designed. Like all truly great movies the film is dense with both plot and subtext and can be interpreted in a number of ways. Javier Bardem will undoubtedly gain the most attention for his complex characterisation of Anton Sigur and all credit due to him is thoroughly deserved; for his spectacularly barren interpretation of a damaged persona; a portrayal which could so easily have been just another collection of stock Psycho Cliches (Anthon Hopkins your time is up I'm afraid!). Elsewhere - Josh Brolin expertly inhabits the growly persona with a relaxed intensity seldom seen since Film Noir. As for Tommy Lee Jones - even though he's played variations of this role several times before - the vastness of melancholy inherent within this receent pursuit is more reminiscent of "The Three Burials of Melquies Estrada" than, say - "The Fugitive". Ultimately, though, the real stars of the film are the Brothers Coen who should be (and no doubt, are) extremely proud of themselves for crafting yet another modern classic punctuated with perfectly balanced moments of beauty and horror; with an ending that will split audiences with it's poetic musings on the concept of fate.

   The last act was my issue. I love open ended, post modern, ambiguous, and etc. endings like a junkie. However, the ending delivered to me at the end of this film was just that, an ending, in the most literal sense of the word.     The characters felt like cuts out, they really did not achieve that third dimension (or change for the laymen) until the end. But by then it is too late as the movie ends. 
   It was not the fact that the ending had no closure, or that Josh Brolin's character dies off screen after almost 2 hours of emotion investment, or that the assassin does not get whats coming to him, it was the fact that the characters did not achieve this third dimension until the end. 
   Sure the sheriff quits in despair and the stone cold killer is shaken at the defiance of the widow, but these changes cannot reach their full dramatic potential as the end of the film. Granted the scenes at the end with the sheriff visiting his injured uncle and the metaphoric qualities of his dreams are poignant, somehow I am still left feeling unsatisfied. For the fans of the films I promise to watch it again sometime, and then, perhaps, I will see the brilliance of this film.

The acting is top-drawer; maximum possible impact of every tiny line, nuance and mannerism is squeezed out of a pedigree cast. And the suspense is absolutely terrific - though the next turn seems predictable, you still find yourself mentally stuttering "but... maybe not!" In many ways similar but, boy, this is in a class of it's own!  Beautiful to look at, the characters have a logic, the cast are excellent and the tension ratchets right up to 11!

It's brutal, and the death count is significant, but the violence is treated as a matter of fact (which perhaps make it even more unsettling) and not as the exploitative fetish 'slasher' movies revel in.

The ending does take you by surprise but, I'm told, is explicable if you watch and listen carefully as the final scenes play out.

The Coen brothers seem to make either near-masterpieces (The Big Lebowski, Fargo, Blood Simple) or total dross (The Ladykillers, Intolerable Cruelty). When they  get it right, however, their films are compellingly and brilliantly written, interestingly shot and invariably include at least one superb acting performance. This film fits firmly in the second group and is no exception to its precidents. Ever since Cannes everyone has been going on about how good this is and the eagerness of my anticipation meant that I failed to resist reading/watching/listening to reviews and coming across a few clips. In the light of the expectations that these clips and reviews had created, there were a couple of aspects of that I found surprising when I finally saw the film. While there is no doubt that Javier Bardem's character is terrifying, it is actually (and perversely) the mundane normality of this relentless, slow, deep talking, air-cannister-gun wielding maniac that is most chilling. There is no real tension created at any point (which might seem strange for what is basically a thriller), but that is not a bad thing - in fact it's actually an incredibly clever and thought-provoking thing. There is some humour, but light moments are few and far between - it's much more in the mold of Blood Simple than Fargo. Besides Bardem, Brolin, Lee Jones, Harrelson and Macdonald all also turn in great performances which I hope are not too overshadowed by his terminator-esque hitman. I've heard the Coens rebutt the critics of the drawn out and complex ending by saying that the last twenty minutes is the film. Although I can appreciate what they are trying to communicate with that comment, in my opinion they run the risk of undoing some of their brilliant work by even suggesting that the film might separate. For me, what made this film enjoyable was the sensibilty, the aesthetic and the impact of them on the emotions that went right throughout and led the audience to the ending. I was almost happy to let the details of the philosophical elements wash over me rather than niggle at my consciousness, it was utimately about how this film made me feel rather than what it made me think - it was aesthetic as philosophy. I did leave the cinema with one question circling round and round my head - why didn't Brolin's character put the money into a different bag? It's the first thing I would have done.

Every time the Coens release a new film it's deemed as their best ever (apart from the ladykillers and intolorable cruelty, obviously) There is no doubting this films strengths, great acting, cinematography and script, yet it sill lags behind the likes of Millers Crossing, Barton Fink and even the Hudsucker Proxy, for me.

The Coen Brothers are our National Treasure(s)

The Coen brothers western noir has been called a masterpiece by critics, who compare it favorably to their last similarly great film, Fargo. (NB - interested viewers can go even further back for evidence of the Coens' prowess in this genre: early movies Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing are both studies in calculated, thrilling violence.) No Country is gripping from start to finish: the gorgeous, wide-open landscapes and sparse dialogue provide the perfect backdrop for a psychopath's chilling pursuit of a country boy and the money he stumbles upon. Javier Bardem plays the impassive, robotic killer, and Tommy Lee Jones plays the sheriff who wearily follows his trail. Jones' worn-out look reflects the overall theme of the movie; he is beaten down by the senseless, unending violence that surrounds him, both in his town and in the world at large. As his uncle murmurs sagely at the end of the film: "This is a tough country."

Not since Fargo have these two talents, Joel & Ethan Coen, approached and delivered a text with such finesse. No Country for Old Men is an amalgamation of concentrated characters, beautifully constructed metaphors and intertwined narratives that consummates in an astounding subversion of the thriller genre. The film is an insightful interrogation of manhood, or more predominantly American manhood (so often witnessed in a lot of the Coen's work). With its unconventional storytelling and unorthodox narrative No Country for Old Men is a film that requires the viewer to be sagacious and perceptive in order to heed and unravel the films intertextuality. It is arguably one of those films that will require multiple viewings to fully appreciate it.
 
The film takes place on the Texas border in 1980 and tells of man called Llewlyn Moss (Josh Brolin) who stumbles upon a heroin trade off/massacre, loots two million dollars and returns to his wife Carla (Kelly Macdonald) only to succumb to his own stupidity and return to the scene at night to help a wounded man he had previously left for dead. A drugs cartel hire a recently escaped sociopath called Anton (Javier Bardem) to retrieve the money, meanwhile Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Le Jones) and his deputy investigate the massacre. The narrative model exercised here is evident throughout the majority of the Coen's work, this model being the recognition and tackling of an obstacle between the hero and the object of his/her desires - the obstacle often being the hero's stupidity. For example the fumbling naivety of Norville Barnes in The Hudsucker Proxy (1994), the endearing fatuousness of The Dude in The Big Lebowski (1998) and the bumbling buffoonery of the convicts in O'Brother, Where Art Thou (2000) all hinder progress.

No Country for Old Men employs an unconventional story which has dismayed some critics, some even citing occurrences in the plot as examples of the films faults. One such example is the timing and choice to dismiss a centrifugal character which has been described by some critics as an illustration of directorial arrogance and contempt for their audience. In a direct response to these widely held allegations I feel that the choice to dismiss this character was a brave decision and a more truthful representation on the musings of human life and its many dispositions fitting entirely with the over arching theme of the film. Criticisms of plot and narrative devices, such as the example mentioned, tend to occur because of a belief that generally speaking a film should serve up conventions that allow for it to be understood and followed and if these conventions are ignored or dismissed then the film is not a film but a mishmash of ideas. To put it bluntly I feel that this belief has developed through conditioning. Additionally it is often perceived that if a film challenges conventions or reworks them then it is, in essence, original - which is widely read as cinematic progress.

At its heart No Country for Old Men is a thriller that delivers brilliant levels of suspense, fear and apprehension whilst simultaneously disposing of the genre's preconceived conventions. The cinematography on show unashamedly harks back to the Coens debut Blood Simple (1983) and with their regular Cinematographer at the helm, Roger A. Deakins, it is no surprise that No Country for Old Men has been nominated for an Oscar in this category. The films score is so subtle that it aids the tension by unwittingly achieving an omnipotent silence recognisable only through an assortment of wind noises which have been superbly complemented by the bleak dialogue and dark humour.  

To complement the film further it should be noted that on show here are some of the most powerful and flawless performances for some time and Tommy Lee Jones's is purely outstanding. His character embodies a demeanour of pensive sadness beautifully portrayed by the veteran actor in what is conceivably his best role to date (shocking that he has not been nominated for an Oscar, but this could be due to a lack of screen presence) it should also be noted that the final reels of the film are probably among his best ever committed to celluloid. Javier Barden's role as the relentless and ruthless psychotic killer is astounding, his on screen presence mesmerising and his mere appearance a pure treat. When it comes to playing a psychotic I would go so far to say that his performance has only ever been equaled by Anthony Hopkins portrayal of Hannibal Lector and maybe in years to come, dare I say it, better than.   

I have yet to see There Will Be Blood, but No Country for Old Men is surely an Oscar winner and perhaps it will be the Coen's first as directors or second as writers. It is cinematic excellence of the highest pedigree that is both lasting and haunting.

A Cohen brothers film?  Really?  OK, I will say that they cast was amazing and the mood was good.

On the other hand, the story had all of direction of a tumbleweed.  Further, the characters lacked the essential quirkiness found in those of prior Cohen brothers pictures.

Over the past decade, there have been a few excellent modern Westerns.  This one does not crack the pantheon.

It's easy to see why this movie has been showered with awards nominations because the performances across the board are spot-on and the story is tense and compelling. Javier Bardem just reeks of malevolence (despite a bizarre accent and monkees haircut) when he's onscreen and makes for one of cinema's greatest bad guys. 

The reason that this film falls below the brilliance of 'The Big Lebowski' and 'Fargo' for me is that ending. It works artistically and as a meditation on the relentless evils of the world, but crucially, it doesn't work emotionally (at least not for me). To have such a great set-up with two tough badasses set on a head-on collision course and then not see what happens between them at the end just feels like such an anticlimax. However, it does make the movie more unique and less of a slave to traditional movie formula so this feeling may change upon subsequent viewings, and its definitely worth watching again...and again.

It contains all the best elements of previous Coen films but perfects them. The bizarre characters, the awful, gut-wrenching tension, the ability to continually take the viewer in new directions and surprise them, and the wonderful word-play which are a staple of Coen work are all present and correct.

Ther performances are pitch-perfect, but the credit has to go to the Coens for creating a thriller which defies all the conventional rules we have come to associate with the genre. It's stylish, stark and darkly humourous. The flip-side to Fargo not just in terms of visuals, but also thematically. There is no sense of good winning the fight against evil, it's all just a matter of luck, or rather bad-luck.

Every character is richly drawn no matter how long they stay on screen. Consider the scene between the unstoppable killer Chigurh and the roadside shop proprieter. A scene which displays the humanity the Coens put into such a small part and exemplary word-play, turning a simple coin-toss into a moment of unbareable tension.

The violence is as shocking and real as it ever was and features one of the strangest, most perverse yet oddly appropriate weapons (to the Coens at least) ever seen on screen. The brutality is frightening, the humanity touching and the soundtrack undescribable.

A film whose entire back-story is told in corpses and features the wonderful dialogue of a man informing us a coin has travelled 22 years to reach this exact moment in time, and used to decide whether a man lives or dies. These are just some of the many outstanding scenes scattered throughout the film

Perfection.

No Country for Old Men seems to take a moment to get going smoothly, but once all the pieces are set the film runs like clockwork and the characters weave in and out of it in a truly suspenseful manner.  The film's soundtrack, comprised of no musical score whatsoever and entirely dialogue and effect driven, is so raw you feel like the others in the theater can hear your thoughts.  It really makes you feel l like you're being watched or followed, just like the main character.  The film then comes to a messy but satisfying conclusion, as the pursued and the pursuer have a quarrel offscreen, and then Tommy Lee Jones is left to find the prevailing party.  Jones then gives a final speech about the simplicity but also inevitability of life and death.  A definite must see, and thought I dont think it has what it takes to beat There Will Be Blood for Best Picture, it was probably my favorite film of 2007 and an excellent addition to the Coen Brothers impressive list of cinema.

This noir-ish modern-day Western is the Coen at their pitch-perfect best - at least, the serious side of the Coen's best ... though there's still space here for some dark comedy. The performances are brilliant, but it's the long stretches without dialogue that stick the longest in the mind; tension is stretched up to and way beyond what is usually considered comfortable, the silence around events perhaps the otherwise absent moral judgement on empty greed and violence. Bardem stands out, naturally; a largely silent presence who (though a very different type of character) builds up Lecter-like levels of evil dread as he goes about his terrible business. As much as it's an exquisitely tense crime story, it's also a mediation on what it's like to feel as if the world is leaving you behind; it's not what you once knew, and what's gone can't ever be recaptured now this new evil as blown into town, exposing much else in its wake. A crime story, an elegy, a modern masterpiece.

Plot:

Texas, 1980. Hunting in the desert, Llewellyn Moss (Brolin) comes across the wreckage of a drug deal gone wrong and takes the cash â without counting on the man sent after him, an implacable killer (Bardem) intent on recovering the loot at any cost.

My Review:

The Coens have been off their game, they have been off their rocker with a short number of okay flicks. This time, the genre they tackle changes format completely. The Coens have rediscovered their mojo; with added humanity and Viagra.

A from Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Cormac McCarthy's violent neo-Western, No Country For Old Men encompasses blood, guts, gun galore, sharply and tense woven plot with a lusciously written script. It's got Blood and lots of Balls, sense of death lurking in the barren dry Texan landscape that has some flamboyant cinematography. And being a knotted tale of crime innately wrapped in circumstantial regards. 

Surprisingly foremost is how the film remains both recognisably to McCarthy's allegory, all the while being soaked in oil-black humour. With the entire jazzy corollary that the Coen's use at their detriment, with witty deadpan comebacks. "If I don't come back, tell my mother I love her," Josh Brolin's anti-hero Llewellyn Moss tells his wary discerning wife Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald) before he faces hell. "Your mother's dead," she retorts. "Then I'll tell her myself," he sighs.

Sweltering corpses cook in the thirty-plus degree desert sun, even a dead dog, and a trail of blood, with the same splinter of the recent ' The Assassination of Jess James by the coward Robert Ford' indomitable likeness, splattered like ink along the parched ground, leads Moss to a case containing two million dollars. He takes to the money and runs. We consequentially start eyeing the tremulous determination of Moss, a local hunter who happens upon the remains of a drug deal gone badly wrong. The plot is triple-headed, with the narrative shifting focus whenever one of the leads seems to be taking centre stage, some more than others.

The clean-up guy is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who is totally underestimated throughout. A killer with the implacable dedication and blend of a Cylon from 'Battlestar Galactica' and Terminator; with a haircut to match, with a psychopathic sense of hypocrisy, irony and striking intelligence. Even Carter Burwell's score is defined by its candid â made up only of groans and eerie whistles. Course with that being said, the score only builds up at the roll of the credits. Bardem's is the role with a unbelievable amount of possibilities â a stone-cold killer obsessed, leaving to fate and chance to decide the lives of the ones he holds to the flip of a random toss of a quarter. He is blank force made breathtakingly plausible.

A startling chase set of events leads to shootings shot to perfect, brutal and tense graphical scenes that really make that +18 or R rating stand out in a dry soaked red. Always two steps behind is the old man of the tale, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), a lawman up for retirement, facing an evil that he can no longer decode. 

It is true to the book, even when the end is like a downplay and ambiguous laden message instead of a crescendo-ed glorified good guy v.s bad guy. 

Verdict:

The story begins when Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) finds a pickup truck surrounded by a sentry of dead men. A load of heroin and two million dollars in cash are still in the back. When Moss takes the money, he sets off a chain reaction of catastrophic violence that not even the law - in the person of aging, disillusioned Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee-Jones) - can contain. Moss tries to evade his pursuers, in particular a mysterious Hit man ( Javier Bardem) who flips coins for human lives. 

What is different from this than most of the other Coen Brothers films is the Humour - Or lack of it in this case . This is a dark , disturbing film that very rarely tries to be be funny and to be honest does not need to.

There is absolutely no music in it whatsoever , not even any backing music and that was an inspirational decision by the Coens . You hear every foot step , every heavy breath taken and and every click of a gun and it makes you feel that you are living the nightmare of everyone that has the misfortune come across the deadly Anton Chigurh .

There are brilliant displays from Tommy Lee-Jones , Josh Brolin and Kelly MacDonald but the outstanding performance must go to Javier Bardem because without that portrayal of Anton I'm not sure this would have been half the film it is.



The ending is strangely abrupt because that's the way the book ends but i feel the last scene could and should have been cut or shown earlier . 

As for the nominations for Best film at the Academy Awards next month i have only seen No Country for Old Men and Atonement of the films nominated. Although i loved this film , Atonement deserves the Oscar.

There are strong silences which marks new territory for the Coen's who often use great sound to compound their story. With NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN, the Coen Brothers have found a perfect match in Pulitzer Prize-winning author Cormac McCarthy. Their adaptation of McCarthy's praised novel is a staggering masterpiece. In this almost impossibly faithful adaptation, the film takes place in a small Texas border town in 1980. Sheriff Bell (a never-been-better Tommy Lee Jones) has ruled the land for years without the use of a gun, but a new brand of reckless lawlessness has taken over his town. Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is an innocent Everyman with a devoted wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald), but when he stumbles across a drug deal gone deadly and finds two million dollars, he's determined to keep it for himself. There's only one problem. He's being pursued by one of the most amoral, evil psychopaths that the big screen has ever seen. Wearing an absurd haircut and brandishing a pressurized weapon that's used to murder cattle, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) creeps forward on his mission to track Moss down and return the money to its rightful owners to save his own skin. As the tension mounts, the body count begins to rise, confirming Sheriff Bell's inability to battle this new wave of modern brutality. The most striking thing about the Coen Brothers' thriller is their masterly use of silence to create an almost unbearable level of tension. Cinematographer Roger Deakins is once again at the top of his game, beautifully capturing this stark and lonely world. The well-rounded cast is clearly excited to be a part of such a stellar production--particularly Bardem, whose Chigurh is a freakishly mysterious monster, and is certain to haunt viewers long after the final credit has rolled. In a career filled with striking achievements, this might very well be the Coen Brothers' finest. It is filmmaking at its best. This is easily the strongest film of the year. Javier bardem trully out did himself in this masterpeice. This film has my vote for best picture come Oscar time.

No Country For Old Men is a new sort of movie. I was about to criticize all sorts of things about it until I read that it's an incredibly faithful rendition of a book by the same name. So, the points about the movie that make in new or different also really extend to the book and ultimately, to the culture that spawned both. 

Thing is, this movie has no real conclusion. It doesn't go anywhere cohesive, because it's exploring the concepts of chance and fate. People die. Or don't. Justice isn't served. No one wins, really. You can root for the "good guy," but he's only good in comparison to the bad guy who is psychotic; he's still trying to get away with $2 million. 

By the end of the movie, nothing is resolved, and in particular the closing scene makes absolutely no sense to me, even though it's pulled verbatim from the end of the book. It's almost as if the filmmakers didn't understand it either and just put it in for that reason. 

In all other respects, the film is masterful. It's environmentally sound, the characters are well-fleshed out and capricious as humans are. If you watch it while distracted you're not going to get what little there is to get, but hey, some might call that a blessing.

The Coen brothers return to top form in this adap of Cormac McCarthy's novel. It's been billed as their best yet and if it's not, it's pretty close. Much has been said of Javier Bardem's star turn as coiffeured hitman Anton Chigurh, but the real star is Roger Deakin's stunning photography, perfectly capturing the deserts of west Texas and matching it with the films bleak outlook; the early scene showing the brooding, taciturn Llewellyn Moss (Brolin) hunting deer in the vast, endless desert before happening upon the scene of a botched drug deal is captivating. Noticeable also is the sparing use of music and dialogue, the latter seemingly never used unless philosophical (from craggy Sheriff Ed Tom (Jones)), psycho-logical (from Chirgurh) or dry truism (from Moss) - each calculated and meticously delivered. Though central to the book, Sheriff Tom's musings are sensibly abridged here, but the film still suffers just slight hiccups in pacing, simply because you want to see the chew-your-nails, cat-and-mouse chase between Chirgurh and Moss so much. Worth seeing for Coen fans, but also for those who like their thrillers sprawling, yet taut.

The more Tommy Lee Jones starts to resemble the hard, rocky Texas scenery, the more the camera loves him and his joyless musings.  There is humor to be found here if you're looking for it, but unlike most movies where the humor is designed to provide a little relief from the carnage, here every little hopeful moment exists only so that the movie can betray you and eat your soul later.  The second act is where all the crowd pleasing cat and mouse stuff happens, and it's pants-crappingly good.  But it's that stuff that happens in the brilliantly unsatisfying third act that really sticks to the ribs and keeps you pondering.  It's not conventional, but it's a fitting end to the story that leaves an itch in your brain that can only be scratched by watching the movie over and over.

This is the most highly overrated, cliche-ridden western suspense I have ever witnessed.  

The three main characters Moss (Brolin), Chighure (Bardem) and Bell (Jones) never meet on screen or interact in any interesting way.  While Chighure spends the entire movie trying to "hunt" Moss, we hear from several characters, this is simply what he does.  Even the characters admit he is your run-of-the-mill blood-hungry psychopath.  His acting is subdued (at best) and it was nothing new.  The only way Bell's character interacts with the other two is by trying weakly and inadequately to "save" Moss from this cold-blooded killer.  

Amazingly enough, Chighure's emotionally-blunted killer instincts are continually matched by the caviler way all of the other characters act towards death.  In the opening scene we see a man stumble upon a scene of mass carnage only to steal the money and callously take the weapon of the only spared survivor.  Not only are the characters motive's hard to believe, there is no set up to where they came from or why they are they way they are, excluding Jones's character whose role in the extended chase that comprises most of the action of the movie, minimal at best.

Overall, none of the characters seem to change or react in believable ways.  Rather they creep in and out of scenes like the lost ghosts of western's past.  The few attempts at comedy are outweighed and lost to the film's superior gore and depression.  

The only good thing I can say about this movie is that Roger Deakins does a wonderful job showing the haunting beauty of the Texan desert, while keeping other simple shots interesting.  The sound mixing (as there is not music) is also quite fantastic, making shots and pulsing blood sound creepily realistic.  However, if this film wins for more than photography and sound mixing, I will be severely disappointed.

[i][b]I can see why other people are so enthused about this movie, but...[/b][/i]
  
  I sat down to watch this Academy-Award nominated movie late last night with some friends. Sadly, I expected a little more than I got. That's not to say that Tommy Lee Jones, Javier Bardem and Josh Brolin weren't excellent in their contrasting, yet brilliantly cast roles. Bardem in particular is worthy of a special mention: I thought his character was awfully disturbing, which is just what he was supposed to be.
  
  Aside from the acting though, like several movies of 2007 it seems, I felt like the plot left soemthing to be desired. The last scene, while done very well, seemed like it was missing some aspect I can't exactly put my finger on. It left you hanging on the edge of your seat, waiting for more, only to be disappointed. But, as one of my close acting friends has pointed out in the past, sometimes that toying with your emotions that this movie so skillfully does is exactly what is meant to happen.
  
  My one real critique of this movie is that until about 20 minutes in it was a little hard to follow and become attached to. Once things started coming together it all made sense and from there on out you can't help but sit there and watch intently as the beautifully-filmed sequence of events and jarring [lack of] dialogue form a cohesive movie that is very artfully done. That being said, I can't say this is one of my favorites of the past year, but I wouldn't blame anyone for having it in their top five.

Eleven years on from the unforgettable 'Fargo', the Coen brothers have made what may well be their masterpiece.

After two particularly below par releases in 'Intolerable Cruelty' and 'The Ladykillers', the largely infallible duo have demonstrated just why they are two of the finest craftsmen working in modern-day cinema.

Excelling in every aspect of movie-making, you'll be hard-pressed to see a finer piece of cinema than 'No Country for Old Men'.

It really is that good. 

Only Paul Thomas Anderson's 'There Will Be Blood' - should it live up to the critical hype emanating from the US - may realistically stand between the Coens and the Best Picture award at this year's Oscars.

Set in 1980s West Texas, 'No Country for Old Men' revolves around a bag of money, and meditates on a growing fixation amongst the populous for quick fix riches - and a bloodthirsty willingness to secure them.

Though adapted from Cormac McCarthy's acclaimed novel, the plot is pure Coen brothers and reminiscent of both 'Fargo' and their debut picture, 'Blood Simple'.

Llewelyn Moss (Brolin) is a local nobody who stumbles upon $2m in cash and is dumb enough to think that he's smart enough to simply take the money and run. As the film's tagline informs us, there are no clean getaways, and sure enough Llewelyn soon finds himself pursued by Anton Chigurh (Bardem), a terrifyingly deadpan psychopath who chills the blood each time he appears on screen.

Tracking both of them across the bleak desert landscape of West Texas' border towns is Ed Tom Bell (Jones), a weary local sheriff on the verge of retirement and all too aware of the escalation in violence throughout the country and the drugs and money which propel it.

What follows is a thrilling and unpredictable cat and mouse chase.

Unlike most adaptations, the Coens faithfully follow McCarthy's novel with each scene appearing on screen in the same chronological order as it does on page. Even the ending, which will frustrate some, can be found on the final page of the novel - a testament to the Coens' restraint in not going "all Hollywood" on the material.

Yet, though much of the attention to detail that makes 'No Country for Old Men' so great appears in McCarthy's novel, it's the way in which the Coens execute the text that is testament to their genius.

Tight editing, typically superb cinematography and immense performances all underpin the brothers' fantastic adapted screenplay.

A scene, such as Bardem's encounter with a rural store clerk, may have been culled by other screenwriters but the Coens rightly spot its importance in emphasising the film's major theme - that of fate and luck.

Furthermore, though there is very little dialogue throughout the movie, each line serves real purpose. A throwaway line such as the Deputy Sheriff commenting, "they even shot the dog" delivers humour whilst also highlighting the shock at the rise in violence which underscores the film's title.

The absence of dialogue also highlights what masterful storytellers the Coens truly are, with each shot silently moving the action along.

Sound, meanwhile, has rarely been used to better effect. Though there is no music used in the movie, the sounds of Texan desert dust crunching under feet or the creek of hotel floorboards adds to the film's tension.

One scene in particular emphasises the power of such technique as the audience remain transfixed and absorbed by the suspense of silence. Here, we hear a tracking device beep and a floorboard creek followed by the appearance of a shadow covering a sliver of light outside a door. Then the sound of a light bulb being unscrewed. Though we know what will happen next, the effect is breathtaking.

While every member of the cast is immense - from Brolin and Jones' central characters to Harrelson and Macdonald's supporting roles - the real stand out is Bardem.

Here is an unforgettable screen killer, chillingly evil and whose every appearance puts the audience on edge. Armed with a trademark weapon, a wicked sense of mirth and a sociopathic look, Bardem's Chigurh is nightmarishly terrifying and a shoe-in for the Best Supporting Actor gong.

A thundering return to form for the Coen brothers, the Oscars have their gem. 'No Country for Old Men' is not only one of the best thrillers in an age, but a haunting, unnerving, frequently funny, unforgettable classic that is as perfect as cinema can get, and a rare example of an instance where a novel has been faithfully adapted to play to the strengths of its film makers.

While it is interesting to see a film that resolutely refuses to follow normal Hollywood plot progressions, I personally can do without having one of the most important characters being killed off-screen.  Without looking for deeper meaning regarding the nature of violence, I think the film hinges mostly on the wish to display life as being influenced by the random and arbitrary.  The only continuous aspect that runs through the entire film is that Bardem's character has a sort of inverse morality, which he sticks to without any deviation.  Apart from his character, we are left with a confusing group of hazily defined people, and given no clear indications as to how they could be viewed in light of their actions in the film.  You might say that this only echoes the reality we live in, with no clear lines and easy morals existing in the real world.  However, this 'realism' can only be taken so far before it becomes grating, and leaves the viewer hoping for some sort of return to linear, generally accepted film structures.  Tommy Lee Jones' character does not take a back seat to the action, rather he is not in the vehicle at all - existing on the fringes of the film, and contributing only a raised eyebrow about his anecdotes of a world gone to shit.  His character is reminiscent of that of Dwight Yoakam in 'The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada', in that he completely fails to have any real impact on the illegal avtivities he's investigating.  However, unlike Yoakam's character, who's decision to go off on holiday at least gives some laughs, Tommy Lee Jones' purpose in the film is very puzzling.  This is compounded by his presence at the end of the movie where he delivers a final speech that seems to indicate that there is some sort of deliverance from this world after death.  It brings back strong memories of the last words of Billy Bob Thornton in 'The Man Who Wasn't There'.  Another overly familiar aspect of the movie is far to much 'Blood Simple' imagery - we are even shown some plumbing from below.  Overall the film appeared to me as if it was made by someone esle, someone who wanted to make a Coen Brothers type movie with all the expected ingredients.  I believe that the Coens are capable of doing more with a movie that relying on the power of chance, so I really don't think that random car accidents and the acts of an obsessive killer should have been put forward by them as central parts of a plot.  It takes skill to work within most of the accepted elements of film-plotting, but it does not take much skill to abandon all of them in a frankly shallow effort to look deep.  However, at least it is a major departure from the cinematic nightmares of 'Intolerable Cruelty' and 'The Ladykillers'.

In addition to the so-so romantic tradegi-comedy Burn After Reading, the Coen brothers also managed to pick up several Oscar nominations last year for this rather understated though violent addition to their already illustrious canon. 

As the first Coen Brothers'film ever to be adapted from a novel, to which the Coen's apparently stayed very true, No Country for Old Men presents itself as a film light years removed from the screwball farce of Raising Arisona, the delightful coloquialisms of Fargo or the random irreverent calamity of Miller's Crossing. Instead, the film shares very much the same tone as David Cronenberg's History of Violence, with its myriad acts of brutality being recieved coldly and without any of the sudden shock factor to which Coen fans have become accustomed.

The biggest connection between the two films is that both succeed in creating significantly human monsters. Like Cronenberg succeeded in doing with Viggo Mortensen, the Coen fabricate a complex enigmatic abomination in Javier Bardom's hitman: a character who will indulge any one in non-sensical banter, will mercilously kill any one who does so much as inconvience him but at the same time mourns the loss he feels from having to spill the blood of a female.   

However; the strangest, and most undeniably Coen, of No Country for Old Men's cast is Tommy Lee Jones' aging rural Sherriff Ed Tom Bell. Like an old sheepdog, Jones ambles obliviously through the background of the story similarly to Frances McDormand in Fargo: matter of factly interviewing and asking people whilst never knowing how close he gets. Unlike Marge Guundersen, however, Ed Tom doesn't get his man.  Instead his long, often convoluted solliloquies punctate the violance and give it a sense of near Tarantino philosophy. 

Many have berated No Country for Old Men because of its general lack of soundtrack and unfulfilling ending. Indeed, this is the most artist Coen film yet. However, it is also undoubtedly one of their best, right up there with Fargo and Barton Fink.

I imagine many people found comfort in the conventional morality of "There Will Be Blood", but I find the pitiless, indifferent universe of Cormac McCarthy and the Coen Brothers' masterful interpretation of his themes to be far closer to the truth. "No Country For Old Men" is a magnificent work; each scene is a crescendo of tension, underlying the random violence of the universe as it takes no heed of moral compasses, hypocrisies, and how innocent a person's bystanding happens to be. There is every Coen Brothers archetype here, laid bare to its logical extreme. The befuddled Dude, clever and resourceful, but so in over his head that he raises stupidity to an artform. The laconic old timey sheriff, rehashed for the upteenth time by Tommy Lee Jones, but this time the White Knight Lawman is utterly ineffectual and must finally admit he's too old and tired to fight immortal chaos. Even the agent of chaos himself, the masterful Javier Bardem giving a performance of the ages, must contend with the mindless whims of chance.  I saw his ridiculous pageboy haircut as a cruel parody of Prince Valiant, a knight errant gone horribly wrong, set loose in a barbaric land. As with all Coen flicks, they don't muck around with the cinematography, and the phantasmagoria of the Southwestern landscapes blends and upholds the themes and tones. It's a gorgeous film that left me stumbling out the theater, nonplussed with what to do with the wisdom that was shot at me via a cattle killing airtank gun. 
Though it's a cold universe, my faith in humanity is restored by filmmakers that GET Cormac McCarthy, and "Country" is a welcome relief after Billy Bob Thornton's completely bungled "All The Pretty Horses".  The best Coen Brothers film so far, and that's no small feat coming from a string of masterpieces.

     After almost two months of being unable to find playing at a theater anywhere near me I finally got a chance to see it in Olney, Illinois.  So kudos to the Arcadia Theater.  I've been extremely excited to see this movie since I first heard it announced and there was no way I would be disappointed especially after seeing crap like [i]AVP:R[/i].
 
     Llewelyn Moss (Brolin) is minding his hunting in the desert near his home in Texas when he comes across the scene of a drug deal gone wrong and a case full of money.   On his tale is the creepy and unsympathetic Anton Chigurh (Bardem) who will stop a nothing to get the money he was hired to collect and kill the man who has inconvenienced him and anyone he is associated with.  And the man in the middle of all is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who is desperately trying to save Moss and his wife.
 
     [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is nothing short of excellence.  Having already read the novel a year or so ago and seeing the Coen brothers taking the helm I was anticipating the best and that's what I got.  
 
     Chigurh is absolutely the scariest character I've seen put on film.  Whoever he confronts you immediately feel sorry for them.  Maybe he's the angel of death or maybe he's a lunatic with a strict homicidal code.  He is a very complex character as are the other characters but in such a subtle way that you want to learn more about them.  Most of the characters are veterans of war, be it Vietnam or WWII, but even in a time of peace they're still fighting.
 
     Some people will think the point of the story is that "greed destroys everything" but that's not the point.  Actually the money becomes irrelevant quickly as it really doesn't matter who ends up with it.  It's more about chance and fate as Moss exhaustingly tries to change his fate, Chigurh encounters victims entirely by chance and even let's a coin decide their fate in some cases and Bell knowing that you can't stop what's coming.
 
     The first half of the film will definitely appeal to mainstream audiences as it's fast-pace, exciting, gory and very conventional.  The second half will take you in a path that you won't see coming at all.  It's very satisfying even to mainstream audiences until the very end in which it may piss some people off.  To me the ending was fantastic and very, very emotional, the film may not end conventionally but it ends logically.
 
     The movie is pretty faithful to the book other than changing some scenes (hotel shootout,) moving scenes around (mostly Bell's scenes,) and a few things cut out of it.  One change that didn't set well with me was Bell's conversation with the old man in the wheelchair.  The conversation is changed quite a bit in the book from what I remember but the conversation in the film made it come off as "the world's always been this fucked up" which goes against the title of the movie.  Nothing huge as most of the changes worked really well.
 
     This is an extremely tense and emotional ride that will jar you to the core and will make you think long after you left the theater.  Although I haven't seen many of the great films of 2007 I'd say [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is, without a doubt, the best film I've seen in 2007.

Last night I watched NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN.


Created by Ethan and Joel Cohen (The Big Lebowski, The Hudsucker Proxy, Raising Arizona) No Country tells the story of Llewelyn Moss (good Welsh name) played by Josh Brolin, a hunter who stumbles across the left overs of a drug deal gone bad.  Every last member of the deal have killed each other and so when Brolin finds several million dollars in a suitcase he has to make a quick decision.  Almost sighing at himself at the clearly doomed route he is about to take Moss chooses to take the money and run.  This decision introduces the Terminator like hitman of Anton Chigurh who is hired to track down the money and, through the bloodbath of a trail he leaves wherever he goes, the ageing Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones).

There's no question about it - No Country for Old Men is the Fargo/ Blood Simple/ Miller's Crossing side of the Coen Brothers and far away from O Brotehr Where Art Thou or The Ladykillers.  Very slowly paced with absolutely no score (a shocking fact when the end titles appear to silence) it is however a stunning piece of work.  The photography is Leone-esq in its grandeur and the direction is subtle with extremely well framed reaction shots.  The story is simply brilliant (and I'd love to discuss that further but to give away what the film is actually about is to ruin the experience) and the performances excellent (every last one of them).

Quite frankly this is a film you MUST see on the big screen.  No question about it there are films that just won't work on anything smaller than a truck and this is one of them.

Utterly recommended.

Out of the three films I've reviewed today, "No Country For Old Men" was probably the most challenging.  There are underlying themes in this film that demand a repeat viewing, which becomes very apparent after the much discussed, ambiguous ending.  Joel and Ethan Coen, capture a people like no other directors, one has just view No Country, and "Fargo" for proof of that.  Where in that film they deal with the people of suburban Minnesota, here it's southern Texas.  The Coen's also have an accute command of language that's sorely missing from most films.  There is one scene in particular where Javiar Bardem's character "Anton Chigurh" plays a word game with Gas station attendant ending in a coin toss for his life.   The scene is perfectly paced, and the dialogue creates more tension in one scene than any other film this year.   Anton Chigurh is one of the most terrifying characters we've seen in a long time.  He's a cold, calculating murderer for hire, who, as Woody Harrelsons bounty hunter says  "... has his principles".    Josh Brolin is chased by this monster for most of the film, a game of cat and mouse over a bag of money.  Tommy Lee Jones has, in his later years, found his pace as an actor.  With this, "In the Valley of Ellah", and "Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada" he's proven himself as more than just the guy from "The Fugitive".  Although he appears to be a secondary character, "No Country.."  is  his story.  His observations of how the times have changed (and how they stay the same)...  but maybe I'm wrong and need to see it again.

Loved by movie fans, tolerated by cinephiles and not-so-secretly loathed by the more 'discerning' critics, each new Coen brothers movie marks another occasion for a humourless debate about artists relationship to their characters and audience. 

I'll be the first (okay, the fifth or sixth) to admit that there is something airless and self-canceling about the Coens synthetic, vacuum sealed mastery -- their films give the impression of being gene-spliced and sequenced by the goggled, liberally latexed brothers as if they were cloning lab mice. But hell, that's what makes there best, most superficially fatalistic films -- Millers Crossing, Fargo and, supremely, Barton Fink -- so interesting, and what makes their slavish fidelity to Cormac McCarthy's heartily masculinst thriller so surprising. Indeed, what's new about No Country is the lack of alienating-but-entertaining Coenisms, and the movies lone false note is the raging caricature of Kelly Macdonalds' mother who seems to have escaped from Nick Cages Trailer in Raising Arizona.  

Unsurprisingly, McCarthy's musical, region-specific diction is preserved with a lexicographers respect by the brothers and cast, and the serpentine narrative is brought off with more elan then the  tortured curlicues of the novel. And then there's the actors -- oh the actors! Naturally, Tommy Lee Jones comes pre-packaged in cowboy boots,  experience-weathered and portent-leaden, but the Coens uninspired (but inevitable) casting is assuaged with a greater refinement of register; no actor alive could pull off the truly shocking final speech-cum-ellipsis with more solemn gravity or craggy authority. And Kelly Macdonald proves once again that she is peerless at seeming both vulnerable and strong, naive and world-weary.  

Stylistically, as always, the brothers are in top (or characteristic) form: fastidious compositions, the precise -- at times lethal -- deployment of light and shadow, editing rhythms set to the incrementally accelerating pulse of a Geiger counter and dialogue so sharp it could slice the tongues of less experienced thespians. This is not nothing, and is too easily dismissed by Coen dismissers as aptitude in place of artistry and synthetics in place of sensibility. Yet simply put, the Coens are better at everything (i.e. everything most visible in a movie: narrative and visual control, conceptual energy and imagination, dialogue) than all of there North American colleagues and if that doesn't hurtle them into the pantheon, it is at least worth an honourable mention.   

In closing, the tremblingly humanist avenue of filmmaking (Renoir, Welles, Hou, the Dardennes, whoever) is justifiably cherished, yet does that mean there is no room for alternate, less fulsome and celebratory modes of address? Does every artist have to crawl down on the mat and spoon with their reeking oh-so-human creations, suppress comic portraiture and relinquish aesthetic control, just to be nice?  The fact that the Coens don't tender their themes with more tremulous sincerity is, in best pomo style, a good thing as it forces the viewer to keep rechecking his or her responses to what's happening on screen and not fall for easy cynicism, winking snark or crushing fatalism despite one or all of these things being present in every moment of the film. And in the end, it's this uncomfortable ease and Olympian chill that turns No Country's canned misanthropy and mouldering genre mechanics into something rich, strange and disturbing -- not to mention funny.

This story can only take place in America.  It has to take place in West Texas and it has to take place in the year 1980.  This story can't be told in London in 1999 or Argentina in 2004.  It is a uniquely American story, like "The Big Lebowski" or "Miller's Crossing".

Probably the best picture of the year, and nothing short of phenomenal. The Coen brothers have effectively crafted easily one of the greatest movies of our time. First off, Jesse, you couldn't have put it any better - Javier Bardem portrays the creepiest calm character since Hannibal Lector, hands down. And what an incredible performance it was - Bardem displays a deranged killer who makes his toughest decisions with the flip of a coin, and who shows almost no mercy to those who stand in his way of anything. Probably one of the most effective performances I've witnessed, to tell you the truth. Second of all - the suspense and thrills of this movie are amazing. I'm not ashamed to admit I jumped many times during this movie. Suspense was created through acting, quiet scenes, and utter fascination of the events that occurred. The conclusion of this film was probably the most effective and exciting I've experienced. With a short symbolic story of his dreams, Tommy Lee Jones in the end has the last line, and then the movie cuts to the credits, without mention of Anton's escape or the outcome of the money situation. It keeps the viewer's mind open, spinning from the unclear character development and questionable plot loose ends. And really, it was a simply well-thought out ending. Overall, definitely the frontrunner in my eyes (so far) for Best Picture 07, and certainly one of the most incredible, suspenseful, and thrilling films I've ever seen. Two thumbs way up. A sure winner at the Oscars this month.

I could easily write 'It's great' and leave it at that, but that'd tell you nothing. And I don't really know to start, so I'll have to just ramble on for a bit.
 
And where better to start than with quite simply the best psychopath acting performance you'll probably ever see. Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh is death himself. His callousness, his calmess, his calculative mind. His presence, his posture, his pure hatred. If the Grim Reaper exists, it is him. He stalks his soon-to-be victims with seemingly little care and absolutely no urgency, and that is what makes him so scary. You know he's coming, but you don't know when. And when he does arrive, you still don't know what to expect. There's that small ounce of doubt in your mind - whether he'll let him off or not. And it just stays there for the rest of the film, and it makes him so unpredictable. The way he speaks as well is just so intimidating. Just a truly frightening character.
 
The film tells the tale of three men crossing paths, each with very different things on their mind. There's Anton, who wants to extract revenge on Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), and reclaim the money Moss stole. And there's Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who wants to arrest Chigurh. It is the ultimate cat-and-mouse film, but with that added police element which shows up really quite rarely.
 
I think another thing which makes the film so scary is that it takes place in 1980, when things were more civilised than today. A time when people were friendlier and psychopaths were rarer. I think it's a shock for some of the audience to see that such sadistic behaviour went on just under 30 years ago. The loneliness of the main characters also makes it seem like a completely different world. It's as if it's every man for himself, and in a world like that, to refer to the title, it really is No Country For Old Men.
 
While it's certainly a very good film, it lacks something in my mind for it to be considered great. I'm certainly not going to say that the people who believe it to be 2007's best film are wrong. I can well believe that for a lot of people, who understand some of the deeper moments of the film, rate this as a 9 or 10. But for me, 28 Weeks Later remains the best film of last year, although I'm still catching up on a lot of films from 2007. It'll be very interesting to see films from the Cannes Film Festival as the British cinemas begin to release them.
 
It is an extremely deep film, one I'm almost certainly going to watch again. Tommy Lee Jones has an extremely deep piece of monologue at the end which completely went over my head (damn those writers more intelligent than me) and I'd also like to see how I feel towards Chigurh, and whether I fear him less or perhaps more now that I know what happens. It's an interesting exercise, as it's one which will help me to decide whether he should win the Best Actor Oscar or not. Although to be fair, it'll take something phenomenal to beat him.

The scariest movie I have ever seen. Nothing in the world is scarier than the deserts of Texas. So open, so expansive, and so alone. A killer (brilliantly portrayed by Javier Bardem, a shoo-in for Best Actor) roams the minimally civilized state and hunts the only thing he values, in life. And while you may think that it is money, it is in fact death. He will kill until he dies, himself. The three best characters of the year, with Ellen Page's Juno falling just short to them, Tommy Lee Jones, Javier Bardem, and Josh Brolin provide three different points at which to see the world, and they all prove the thesis of this film and the Cormac McCarthy novel. Life is too arbitrary to make meaning of the events that occur. All we can do is take them on in the way that we see fit. The Coen Brothers write with their typical brilliance, creating scenes that build, build, then move, keeping the viewer in an endless pursuit of the plot. Each scene could go on and we'd still be entertained, but as they move to the next sequence, we feel more and more suspense. The writing is superb, the directing is masterful, and the acting is perfect. Now, back the point that I was so scared. The villain is just to the left of human, making all of his scenes quite chilling. He kills with a silenced shotgun and a cattle killer, which projects a rod into the skull of the victim and pulls it out, in seconds. In one scene, the fate of a man at a gas station is decided by a coin flip, but moreso by the killer's twisted logic. This film makes a powerful statement and does so in the perfect way. There are no faults to this movie, honestly. Best Picture of the Year.

Excellent direction, just excellent. A story about the power of the abundant violence in a country -well, not for old men, really. A man finds a suitcase full of money. Someone is hired to retrieve this money. That man is a murdering machine named Anton Sugar. The sheriff is out to "protect" the man without knowing of Anton's existence. The chase extends to the frontier and into Mexico, and the tension builds and builds until it implodes. Tommy Lee Jones is great as a passive, worn-out, exhausted sheriff. His character contemplates what his world is become with sadness and impotence. He questions what Javier Bardem's character, Anton, represents. Anton is the embodiment of greed and psychopathology : detachment from emotion, absence of empathy. He represents what is wrong about this new culture that the shreiff so loathes. Javier Bardem is simply outstanding. His performance is eerie. His voice, his walk are slow,his gaze is lazy but intense when he looks at other people, as if he functioned in a separate dimension isolated from human law, amotion, love, or hate, and he entered this one only to kill for a certain amount of money. He's incredibly human, but also incredibly inhuman. Bardem has also improved his accent considerably since Before Night Falls, which helps. I'm glad to see that he can continue to develop his versatility. So, all in all, a very violent movie that doesn't only involve violence, it is about violence. Whether it is criticism, description, or analysis is up to each person. The storyline is incredibly well-strucuted. Everything is well thought-out. The suspense is magnificently built. It's a real thrill of a movie, but it makes no sense without the message behind it.

Never have I been the biggest fan of the Coen Brothers but I have always appreciated their genius. Classics like O' Brother Where Art Thou, The Big Lebowski and Blood Simple are all works of comedy with the subtlety of darkness. Until I heard that their new film, No Country For Old Men was in fact a totally serious account of drug run gone wrong, I became very intrigued. Coens? Serious? I was not disappointed. This stark, powerful, poetic, beautifully shot film is their masterwork. Although I detected a slight sense of black humour here and there which works very well and had me giggling in surprising moments it doesn't veer away from the foreboding sense of a certain character. Javier Bardem who plays the desperate psychotic seeking the bag of serious cash is superb. His presence always frightening and tense. Also I noticed is the sheer lack of music in this film which increases the intensity all the way through. Every sound makes you jump out of your seat, it does what no horror film does these days. The dialogue is fantastic and every performance is wonderful. Not only is this Coens being back on form, this is how Coens should BE. A controversial statement to many.

I saw No Country For Old Men today, and my, what the hell was that ending all about. After reading several theories and opinions regarding the film's plot, themes and ending, I've been stalemated with the exact feelings I had as soon as the credits unexpectedly and abruptly graced the screen. Indeed, I was not the only one bemused. To my amusement, the whole cinema was quiet; a pin drop would have been heard with the utmost sound. I even saw heads turn to their partners, only for both to be left with bewilderment stamped on their foreheads. 

So many fundamental unanswered questions aggravates the most intelligent of viewers. Then again, I guess that was just the beauty of the film. It's absurdness seems to tie in with its natural primary theme of existentialism.

On the other end of the unexplainable continuum, I think Javier Bardem's performance is mind blowing. It is exceptional. He is so emotionless, uncaring, socially inept, mentally deprivative, yet intelligent, calm and bound by the realms of chance (the flip of a coin toss). Josh Brolin is great to watch as well. He's the protagonist we all feel for, and can relate to in some form of another. It makes the film all the more tragic for his ultimate loss. Tommy Lee Jones is also stellar, as is expected.

The suspense throughout the film also kept me on the edge of my seat. The film felt reminiscent of Hitchcock material, and him being my favourite director, I appreciated this emotional response throughout the film.

Overall though, nothing is clear cut, and there is more than meets the eye in this film. It is recommended you do a little research about the film's plot and themes if you, like most of us, failed to 'get' the ending. Then again, even after all said research, I've gone quite full circle, took the U-turn and ended up, more or less, back where I started. 

Incredible bewilderment.

[font=Arial]When I think about No Country For Old Men, the word that comes to mind is fate. And while the film is ultimately about fate, I thinking also about how the Cohen brothers have been angling towards this film from their first bloody satisfying Blood Simple. Cormac McCarthy, whose novel is being adapted, has written better works himself (The Road by far his most important), but whose sensibility makes for the creation of the ultimate film we are bestowed upon. And we have three actors who have been moving towards their unforgettable roles in a film that I will deem now to be a classic.
 
The film starts us off with Sheriff Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) discussing in a monologue about how the times are changing when he talks about a boy who killed a 14-year-old girl just for the sake of killing. We can tell that he doesnt flinch at the violence that is around him, but he isnt unaffected. While he talks, we see the barren wastes of the open ranges of West Texas. This will be the epic battleground for a war that few will ever know existed. We meet its key warriors. Theres Lewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a Vietnam veteran-turned-welder who goes hunting one day only to find a drug deal gone terribly wrong. All are dead, the last man standing only getting so far as to the shade to die with two million dollars in a case beside him. Then theres Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a killer without remorse, though does have a knack of killing people with a bottle of compressed air. Hes after the money as well and is uncanny in tracking his prey. These three men will play a game of cat and mouse in a house full of dynamite. Chigurh has the upper hand as he tracks Moss from one flea-bitten motel to the next, finally culminating in one of the greatest moments of suspense ever filmed with Moss trapped in on one side of a door with Chigurh on the other end (though we dont see him). As the game continues, we meet others involved in the game such as a band of Mexican goons after the money for themselves, a fellow hunter like Chigurh (Woody Harrelson) who is hired to hunt the killer, and Moss wife (Kelly MacDonald).
 
The film works as a first-rate thriller for most of the film, and then takes a sharp turn into something much more satisfying, deeper, and meditative about the nature of good and evil, the delicate balance between the innocent and the murderers. And overall, this is a character study of all of these characters and a few others not mentioned. This film takes the Cohens most accomplished work, Fargo, and makes it look like a first draft. Gone are the quirky and mildly exaggerated accents, replaced by hard linguists who say little if anything at all. The film is interested in decisions, choices, and actions made by characters. We watch Bell as he reluctantly gets drawn into this dance between Moss and Chigurh. The killer is responsible for the senseless murder of one of his deputies in one of the most brutal on-screen murders Ive seen, but Bell isnt a fool. It might be luck if he ever meets the killer again. We are intrigued by Moss actions, including his first decisions in the film. Whether hes being chased through a creek by a dog (I think its the reincarnated spirit of the dog Brolin shot in American Gangster) or hes choosing a second motel room in the same motel where his hunters are laying in wait, we wonder what he has in mind. But the character we find ourselves most curious about is Chigurh. Thats a testament to Bardems deadpan performance, McCarthys infamous character, and the Cohens eye for detail in their script and direction. Take the scene where he is staring down a gas station owner who was unlucky enough to be friendly. To anybody in the audience, we know Chigurh means to kill this man. Even the man knows this even though its never even indirectly mentioned. Or the confrontation between the killer and the closest thing to a friend he has. We know hes pure evil, and yet he has a method to his madness. Not since Hannibal Lecter have we a more disturbing psychopath, and Chigurh would rip the old man into pieces and feed it to himself. 
 
This brings up an interesting element in the film, the most horrific violence in the film is seen off-screen. In fact, there are two major gun battles that occur in the film, but all we ever get to see is the aftermath. The Cohens arent interested in glorifying violence, in fact theres never a moment of murder that could be considered fun. Other interesting things about the film to contemplate when watching is the lack of Carter Burwells score for the entirety of the film but in small unnoticeable places. Also note that there is never a shot that has two of the three leads in the same frame. The lack of score is meant to keep the severity of the events in the foreground by taking away the most distinguishable element of a film. Keeping from putting characters in the same frame always reminds us that these men, no matter what they think, are hurting each other, using every resource in their possession. 
 
If you are a fan of McCarthy, I can say that it is faithful to the spirit of the novels ideas, core characters, and pessimism about the future. When the film gets to the end, we realize that the film isnt interested in conclusion, but in meditation, as the novelist himself is. Take the scene with Barry Corbin at the end, which is one of my favorites in the film. When he says, You cant stop whats coming, you understand what the film has spent every shot, every character, every storytelling device to get to. The Coens, who have never out-right adapt a film, had to realize the instant they finished the first chapter that they needed to make this film. They needed their actors, their brilliant crew headed by cinematographer Roger Deakins (who does Oscar-Worthy work here. West Texas has never looked more beautiful, or more dangerous), and their amazing control over the material (also Oscar-Worthy).
 
Acting-wise, I have nothing but admiration for every member of the cast, including those who played Chigurhs victims. But the pairing of Jones, Bardem, and Brolin is brilliant. Jones, like John Wayne before him, plays one note so well that it doesnt need to change it. And yet he allows us to really look into this disillusioned lawman who cannot understand what he sees to be a more violent world evolving away from his ideas of civility. If I could, I would nominate both Brolin and Bardem for Best Actor. Bardem would easily win since his character has more to play with, more charisma, and more interest. But I loved how Brolin allowed his character to come off as fully dimensional without saying much. Special mention must be made to Garrett Delahunt who plays the thankless part of Jones deputy. Hes partially comic relief, but not at the expense of the character as so many deputies in films. 
 
All in all, No Country For Old Men is a film that doesnt ask for a second screening, but demands it. It will be the next classic film from directors whose work has been spotty from time to time. But when theyve focused their material, theyre unstoppable. Just watch Fargo, The Big Lebowski, Blood Simple, or Millers Crossing. Here theyve made their best film so far, one that will stand alongside the tales of Margie Gunderson and Jeffrey Lebowski. What can I say, the Chugh abides.[/font]

[color=#000000][/color] 
[color=#000000]The film is very evocative even from the opening shots of the bleak Texas desert accompanied with some wise words from Sheriff Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) of how times are a-changin' - this is the central theme of the film, inevitability and it is deal with cleverly and subtly. [color=#000000][/color]

This is a great film, which has polarised viewers and reviewers alike - which says something. If the last two soliloquies leave you bemused, then the main themes of the film may have passed you by, by my reckoning. The ineradicable nature of violence - represented by the Chigurh character, who can only be contained but never eliminated - and the inevitable ageing of man, and his fight, against his own inner nature. For me, these two main themes are summed up in these last two stretches of dialogue, which are perhaps the longest in the film. Their interaction is the central theme: violence has part of us for millenia; "No Country for Old Men" says that it's not the country and its nature that have changed, it's that we age beyond the capacity to keep up the fight. As the Sherriff Bell character notes - "I feel overmatched". Brilliant. In the end, a much more insightful and hopeful film than Fargo, with an ultimately less cloying finale.
