No Country For old Men is half a great film. For about 90 minutes we have a master class in suspense - not usually the Cohen brothers forte. Of course their debut - Blood Simple - was an exception and in many ways this film resembles that particularly fine film-noir. So much about this flic is really great: I really liked Josh Brolin's performance - laconic and earthy. Flawed but very likeable. Javier Bardem's performance was a dry one - he doesn't really do a lot of talking to begin with but the little dialogue he utters seems to come from some great bottomless pit - it's such a bass growl. His scenes are terrifying, (despite being slightly undermined by a rather comic mop of hair) particularly his exchange with an understandably nervous gas-station attendant. Which is one of the film's highlights 
It's a story of coincidence and chance as Brolin stumbles onto the bloody aftermath of drugs deal that seems to have gone wrong. Obviously their was some kind of fight and there are dead and dying lying around. Instead of doing the decent thing - this being a film-noir thriller - Brolin takes the loot and runs. Leaving at least one victim, he could have saved, to die. He's then pursued by Bardem's psychopath.
What follows is a terrific tale of cat and mouse. A suspenseful thriller that comes to a head about half-way through when Bardem has finally caught up with Brolin hiding out in a hotel room. These scenes, in part, hark back to Blood Simple as the tension is piled on so densely and cleverly - little dialogue and great use of darkness and light - that I wanted to cry out in joy at the sheer thrill of it. Fantastic!
But then things started to go wrong. Without wishing to give spoilers, one of the main characters is killed off in the most clumsy way possible. I was confused. Was it a twist? Did I blink and miss something? What the hell happened there?? Then it got worse! 
Characters rambled on and on not making any sense in scene after scene of self indulgence and in the case of  Tommy Lee Jones I couldn't even understand what he was saying! Never have I seen an actor so indulged at the expense of the entire film. His character should have been cut completely along with Poor Kelly MacDonald's wife (despite a very convincing Southern drawl by the way). Her's was a totally pointless and thankless character who's sole purpose for being there was so Bardem had something to threaten Brolin with. And what was the mother in-law for?? She wandered in to the film rather late and without any discernible reason. Her twittering and silly wig made her feel like something from one of the Cohen brother's more broader comedies. 
For about 90 minutes I loved No Country For Old Men - I was deeply moved and very excited. But the last 20-30 minutes ruined it for me. None of this part of the film made any sense or had any relevance to what had gone before. Worse than this, it was lazy, self indulgent film-making. The ending, by the way, was horrible! Another character clumsily dispatched, Jones listening to his dad mumbling and a redundant scene, involving a car-crash, thrown in to confuse things even more. Watch Blood Simple instead!!

I have not read the Cormac McCarthy novel, but then I believe in judging a film--even an adaptation--on its own merits and not on its faithfulness to said adaptation.  A adaptation is, after all, a translation from one medium to another, and an interpretation channelled through the director's personal vision.  Most of my friends saw this film before I did and the impression I received from them was that this is a sort of Fargo-for-Texas.  The two films--Fargo and No Country--have this much in common: both were written, directed, and produced by the Coen Brothers, both have that same Coen Brothers brand of humor in the midst of intense atrocities.  But there the similarities end.  If there seem to be elements in this film that remind some of the other, that just confirms these brothers' continuity in writing and directing.  This film is so good; this film is so, so good.  I may go so far as to call it the Coens brothers' Citizen Kane.  Every detail and nuance is carefully planned from beginning to end, no shot wasted, no line of dialogue thrown away.  It achieves a stark realism almost completely absent in your local multiplex.  It is thrilling, intriguing.  The Coens have made something so subtle, so deceptively simple, that many people might be tempted to write off the ending.  When the screen cut (not faded) to black and the credits appeared, I could hear audible noises of confusion around me.  If I may be allowed recourse to an old cliche, this film is more about the journey than the destination.  Yet, all the same, the destination is perhaps the greatest single moment of any Coen Brothers film and is as chilling as anything they have made.

Misguided souls will tell you that No Country for Old Men is out for blood, focused on vengeance and unconcerned with the larger world outside a standard-issue suspense plot. Those people, of course, are deaf, dumb and blind to anything that isn't spelled out between commercials. Set in 1980 in Texas, where the chase is on for stolen drug money, McCarthy reveals a soulless America that is no country for anyone, never mind old men. 
The so-called codger representing besieged law and order is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, played by Tommy Lee Jones with the kind of wit and assurance that reveals a master actor at the top of his game. Here's the sheriff on how crime has gotten so out of hand: "It starts when you begin to overlook bad manners. Anytime you quit hearin' 'sir' and 'ma'am,' the end is pretty much in sight." 
That unpretty end takes the form of Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), an assassin who rivals Hannibal Lecter for dispatching his victims without breaking a sweat. 
Bardem, with pale skin and the world's worst haircut, is stupendous in the role, a monster for the ages. Beneath his dark eyes lies something darker, evil topped with the cherry of perverse humour. It's Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin) who comes down hard on Chigurh's bad side. Moss is a cowboy, one day, when he's out hunting antelope in the desert; he comes across a half-dozen dead bodies drawing flies. One man, barely alive, sits in a truck and begs for water. It's a massacre. There's also a stash of heroin and $2 million in cash. Moss takes the cash and runs. Wouldn't you? That question sets up the film's moral dilemma and puts us in Moss' boots.  Brolin rips into the role like a man possessed, giving Moss the human touch the part needs. Moss even returns to the scene that night with water for the dying man. Huge mistake. Shots ring out, and Moss, after packing his wife off to her folks, goes on the run with Chigurh on his tail and the sheriff tracking both of them.  The kick comes in watching all the gears mesh with thrilling precision. There has been some carping about the ending, which stays tone-faithful to McCarthy instead of going for Hollywood pow.  Bardem and Brolin all give award-calibre performances.

Having already heard the generous praise of this movie from all corners, I spent its entire two hours looking for something to like about it. Sadly, I was unsuccessful. This film has no strong themes, no real character development, almost no music, and no resolution. Not to say that it wasn't well made, that it didn't effectively establish suspense and that it wasn't at least somewhat engrossing, but does that matter? Are those qualities supposed to be enough? In this film, the characters are their actions, nothing more. Like just about everyone else, I'm a big fan of the Coen brothers' Fargo. This is not that film. It lacks the moral center, the subtle interactions between people, the conflict of ideals, and dozens of other things that made Fargo so good. Though the Tommy Lee Jones characters shares some traits with Frances McDormand's, he isn't really a full fledged character, so much as a mouthpiece for an unrealistically bleak worldview. Likewise, Bardem's character is merely an embodiment of this. The fact that he runs around flipping a coin doesn't make him an "agent of fate" as has so often been stated, it merely means that he thinks of himself as one. Though Bardem's performance is good (at what little he's given to do), the character isn't original, just another manifestation of the brainless Hollywood villain who runs around blasting everything in sight. It's as if they thought that by letting him stand unopposed they were creating a new and ingeniously original character. Having considered what the movie has to offer, I see no reason to move from my initial judgement coming out of the theater. No Country For Old Men is one of the worst movies I've ever seen.

No Country For Old Men
2007, 122mins, 15
Director (s): Joel and Ethan Coen
Cast includes: Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, Kelly Macdonald, Woody Harrelson
 
After 2004's frightfully dissapointing remake of [i]The Ladykiller's [/i]it seemed that the Coen brothers who at the time where fresh of another dubious product [i]Intolerable Cruelty [/i]had finally lost their punch. The pair that had brought 90's milestones [i]Fargo [/i]and [i]Barton Fink [/i]finally looked flushed of ideas, and their long absence suggested they to had assumed as much. Still never doubt what once was great, as the siblings now helm this a gripping adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's visceral novel [i]No Country For Old Men, [/i]and with it they've made one of their finest movies yet.
We are introduced to three main characters within the script, a placid sheriff with unknown terrors thrust upon him (Tommy Lee Jones) a country man who found a bag of cash, yet got caught in the process (Josh Brolin) and the merciless killer who wants his money back (Javier Bardem). All three have their stories interwoven as Jones goes after the manic Bardem who slaughtered one of his deputies, and obviously Bardem himself is intetested only in getting what was once his back....and he's willing to utilise any means necessary in which to do so.
The film plays out largely like a thriller and a superior one at that, with three blistering performances at it's centre. One could argue Tommy Lee Jones plays the same old cop he does in every other movie, but given this script and the hefty messages pushed by the picture it would be hard to argue that he doesn't do it well. Brolin pretty much are central character for the films first two thirds gives a turn filled with conviction and humanity, I've never been overly impresses with him before yet here he does the sort of acting that makes a career, and trust me you'll hear his name come Oscar night. However both men are completely left rooted by Javier Bardem, probably 2007's best screen villian, the spaniard with his monotone voice and distinctive face pushes up the tension whenever he gets any screentime. His determination and in genius methods of solving problms and dispatching enemies makes for compelling viewing and the actor who was pretty bland in [i]Goya's Ghosts [/i]scores a performance that captures your imagination totally, and explores slightly the mind of such a terrifying man.
The film is well paced and whilst it stays a little past it's welcome it conveys it's feelings and messages well. The main point of the film is within the title (or is it?) but such a complex and possibly artsey-fartsey moral is well placed within the well written and frequently highly exciting things going on around it.
The cinematography and music are also notable, both are within themselves Oscar calibre as is much of the picture, Carter Burwell brings plenty of melodic class and the shots utilsed of the desert like setting are barren yet inherently beautiful.
I found nearly nothing wrong with the film, it's exciting features some stirring performances and carries a message that everyone should at least understand, if probably not relate to. The editor might have been a bit more selective concerning what featured within the final 15 minutes but other than that this is easily one of the most satisfying outings that 2007 offered. The Coens are back....and you best not forget it.

This film displays the true extent of the Coen talent for filmmaking. The plot bears closest resemblance to Miller's Crossing, but even that comparison is a stretch. No Country embraces new genre for Joel and Ethan, yet bears their unmistakable seal. Featuring a close scenic resemblance to There Will Be Blood, the film begins in a desolate landscape from which it rarely strays, if for only short forays into small towns that remind the viewer of 19th century Dodge City or Tombstone.

No Country eschews the orthodox protagonist narrative, instead presenting a story that is hard to classify thematically. The characters run the gambit from single-minded to multi-faceted, each convincing in their own way. All of the attention has been lavished upon Javier Bardem as the murderously apathetic Anton, and not without cause. Bardem embodies the most frightening of human conditions: complete amorality. A walking statement of Determinism, his rigid adherence to the whims of fate makes him both despicable and honor-bound. Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones bring the best performances of their respectable careers to the table, each seeming comfortable and dedicated in their guises.

What could have been a mediocre action/suspense flick in the hands of the unskilled becomes an exegesis of the true American condition, and perhaps of Postmodernism as a whole. Are the standards of Good and Evil eroding into nothing? Is it in our blood to think this, no matter the circumstances? Are those standards merely constructs anyway? Are we teetering on the knife edge of barbarism? Can we carry the flame of our collective wisdom long enough to illuminate the pathway for those who will follow us? These questions and more will linger upon the mind long after the abrupt and potent finale. As philosophical as it is beautiful, No Country For Old Men is deeply stirring and my choice for best film of the year.

In the Coen brothers' latest feature, there was a scene that encapsulated the movie completely.  It was almost perfect in execution, acting, directing; Tommy Lee Jones' weary and worn sheriff is explaining to a former colleague and old friend why he is retiring and his exasperation with his job and the world.  His friend who was injured in the line of duty, carefully but unforgettably explains back his problem simply but effectively: "It ain't up to you, what's comin'... That's vanity."

That said, this movie is about running up against the inevitable, and understanding that the world and it's inhabitants don't like to wait on your terms.  Retired vet and welder Lewellyn Moss manages to come across the aftermath of a violent shootout while out hunting.  What ensues is a game of staying one step ahead of those after him, the original owners of the stash of money Lewellyn carried off with, and a emotionless, psychotic sociopath named Anton Chigurh (a phenomenal Javier Bardem) who will not stop at anything to meet his goal.
Caught in the mess is Tommy Lee Jones' wisened sheriff who is anxious to retire from the job.  The world seems to have gotten crazier and crazier and this latest case has proven beyond his understanding.  Moss thinks he can get away with the money in hopes of starting a new life with his wife, but due to his own stubborn nature he doesn't see the storm coming despite the reservations of those around him.
The Coen brothers never cease to amaze me.  I've been a fan of their work since Fargo and have went back further in the career to see how broad their pallette of work is.  Dark thrillers are not new territory for these filmmakers.  Modern classics like Fargo, Miller's Crossing, and Blood Simple show that the Coen brother's know how to craft a compelling and suspenseful storyline. The brothers also add they're trademark verbal humor in some of the film's quieter moments, letting the viewer know for sure that this has the Coen trademark all over it.
The performances are nothing short of impressive.   Josh Brolin is at a career best here as the doomed Lewellyn.  Brolin shows Moss as a man who is self assured and so confident that he can take what is coming, he is oblivious to the magnitude of the mess he's in.
Tommy Lee Jones proves reliable as ever as the sheriff   trying to save the ignorant Moss.  With a heaviness and tired exasperation in his voice from trying to figure out what is with the world he's in, Jones is the film's moral compass.

The film belongs to Javier Bardem's Chigurh.  Not since Anthony Hopkins' Hannibal Lecter in Silence of the Lambs has there been a screen villiam so terrifying and unsettling.  His pale skin, long floppy dark hair, and vacant eyes, along with a deep grating voice and calm demeanor as he executes his victims is frightening.  Bardem has created a villian for the ages.  Come Oscar time he will be on every list for best supporting actor.

There is a scene in "No Country for Old Men" where Sheriff Bell is relating to Carla Jean Moss the story of one Charlie Walser, a man who works at the local slaughterhouse. Charlie, you see, has a cow all trussed up, ready to be killed, when the cow suddenly comes to and starts thrashing about. Charlie grabs his gun to try and kill the beast and shoots, only to have the bullet glance off its target, ricochet around, and end up in Charlie's shoulder. "You go see Charlie," the sheriff says, "he still can't reach up with his right hand for his hatâ¦point bein', even in the contest between man and cow, the issue is not certain." This lesson resonates throughout "No Country for Old Men" in the fates of each of the main characters, the idea that, no matter how good you think you are, how confident you are in the outcome of your actions, there is always that uncertainty that could end up ruining your plans.

And, for the majority of the characters in this film, those plans involve the retrieval of a satchel full of money. Sheriff Bell, on the other hand, has different plans, plans that involve hunting down one of the men looking for this satchel, a cold-blooded murderer by the name of Anton Chigurh, played brilliantly by Javier Bardem. As good as Tommy Lee Jones is in the film, as good as Josh Brolin is, Javier Bardem's performance as Chigurh just steals the show. Chigurh is easily one of the most memorable and downright frightening villains I've come across in a movie. Nigh emotionless, Chigurh is a man of few words, a highly intelligent sociopath who has no qualms about killing a man based solely on the results of a coin toss. He almost seems to be more like a force of nature than a human being, a force of nature driven towards one single purpose, mowing down anything and anyone that gets in his way. Even his choice of weaponry is fascinating, be it a cattle gun (a device generally used to stun cattle by firing a pointed bolt using pressurized air) or a shotgun with a massive silencer (which is really fucking cool, by the way). All in all, he is such a great character that the film is worth seeing just for him alone.

"No Country for Old Men" moves along at a deliberate pace, which allows some breathing room for the characters to develop and become more familiar to the viewer, but I never once found the film boring. The intriguing characters, sharp dialogue, and unpredictability of the storyline kept me interested throughout. There is also a fairly consistent level of tension from beginning to end, kicked off by one of the very first scenes in the film involving Chigurh's arrest and subsequent, unnervingly easy, escape from the police. There's a plot hole or two along the way (Just how did Wells know where exactly to look for the discarded briefcase left by Moss?), but they are but minor distractions and barely worth noting, especially when there is so much other great stuff packed into the film.

One last thing I'd like to bring up is the ending where one character relates a dream in which the character's deceased father makes an appearance, an ending which has left some viewers scratching their heads. It is very low key and rather cryptic, and, admittedly, it seems an odd way to the end the filmâ¦on the surface. But, as I thought about it after the film was over, I began to like it more and more. It's an important bit of character development, underscoring the lesson of overconfidence that I brought up in the beginning of my review and revealing that, after the whirlwind of madness and violence all of these characters have gone through during the film, at least one man has learned to recognize his own limitations, take a step back, and not treat life as a race towards death. "And, in the dream, I knew that he was goin' on ahead and that he was fixin' to make a fire somewhere out there in all that dark and all that cold, and I knew that, whenever I got there, he would be there. Out there up ahead."

The wild barren border country is a harsh place indeed and it's rarely been shot as accurately. Tom Lee is amazing, as per, though quite where he is in the large chunk of the film known as the bit between the beginning and the end is anyone's guess. (I guess his ineffectiveness due to age makes for the film's title and explains his decision to retire.)

That said, he's got all the best lines where he does show up, with my fave being: "This sure is a mess." "If it ain't, it'll sure do till the mess shows up" which had me laughing out loud - but no one else.

I've not read any reviews of the film, but today's Metro does use the word "masterful", which they probably saw in the Guardian. Yes, I guess it is - it's a slow-burn kinda film, and it looks amazing: the shots (backs of car lights in the corner of shots, empty towns at night, tired diners and very Americanana-looking yokels etc all look real but also very cool; the actors too are great, and the feel is that of the Coen Bros on top form...Yes, it's all great, but I still felt cheated. Cheated, I tells ya.

**Spoiler alert**
Not because Death (sorry, weird Frenchie pyscho) acts with total randomness and ambivalence, and sees off Lew Ellen (as they pronounce it) Moss, thus preaching the message that Life (or our Fates) are as random as they are unchangeable despite our best efforts. And not just because we've always been fed movies in which the good guys win. No, we're cheated because poor Mr Moss wasn't given the respect to have his demise shown in the film. We're with him the whole way while Tommy Lee reads the paper and then we turn up with Tommy Lee to discover he's been killed moments before. Nice one lads. Unusual sure, inspired even if you consider that the audience has been cheated out of the climax just as Moss has been cheated out of life, but it also means the Coen bros are taking the p out of us, who got worked up and became anxious for the fate of their cowboy on the run.

Who cares that he had a weird penchant for air con ducts, the logic of which I wasn't 100 per cent gone on (why not just dump the briefcase and thus find the transponder?). But then, thinking like that throws up all sorts of silly questions like, how did Death find the motel given the relatively low reach of the transponder, or why did Woody Harrelson waste his considerable talents on 3 scenes in which he wasn't used properly - but ours is not to ponder such trivialities because the Coen Teachers, sorry Brothers, want us to consider larger issues.

Is it great filmmaking or just annoying? Um, maybe it's both. Maybe I'm angry with the unfairness of life! Whatever. I got two for one on Orange Wednesday though so life is sometimes not that unfair. Perhaps life does come down to tough choices - Moss should have saved his wife's life when he had the chance, and his wife is right when she says that it's not the coin's decision but solely that of the individual (though she is mistaken - she sees Death as just another man, as opposed to what he represents - the decision not to have her killed was that of her husband's to make). Thus she is arguing the belief that as mortals it is our decisions and actions that determine our fates. And it would seem the Coen Bros support this. After all, it's Moss' original decision to take the money that drew him into Death's sights.

Cohen Bros. have one of the best adaptations of book to screen I have seen.  It truly honors the spirit, plot points, tone, and ending of a dark, searching, poetic text.  I will add that "The Shining" was the worst adaptation- not movie, but adaptation.

Though there is some levity to lighten the dark journey, missing is the signature Cohen brothers wacked out humor included in characterization, dialogue, and spirit.  They so honor the book that it had to be so.  The directors' attention to detail was as common as past flicks and really immerses you in this world.   The wind is practically a character in the movie.  A creepy, hollow, dessert air haunts the sheriff's opening monologue while vast, barren landscapes fade in and out to start the movie.  That sound is still with me.

Bardem's take on the psycho-killer is hypnotic.  The character is difficult- a man who kills by code, but not too make a point (unlike Spacey in Seven).  A scene in a podunk store (gas station?) with a solitary prorprietor near the beginning of the movie illustrates how random, yet obvious to Bardem's character, the need to extirpate another's breath for being an infidel to his sensibility.  The mounting tension that clutches your throat during this scene is striking.  It begins simply with an observation of the store keeper that Bardem's plates are from Dallas and his simple, lonely, western need to make a connection with him is the beginning of a torturous conversation sure to have you squirm.  

The movie will surely cause a buzz with its finale (again, same as book) but for me was cause to return to the journey to mine it for reason.  The conclusion forces you to return to who these characters are and wonder at the state of their world.  

I did have a problem with the casting of Carla Jean and her "momma".  The momma in particular.  It constantly seemed as I was watching a younger woman try and play and older woman.  It was jarring.  Truly.  For Carla Jean, the movie format made the Cohen's cut a pretty impressive and tender part of her conversation with the Sheriff which included her sense of destiny and take on love (esp. her hubby, Moss, the protagonist) Without this her character is a little void and she acts as a necessary part of the plot more than a living being.

The Coen brothers have always inspired a critical mistrust from both the media and hollywood. Much of it has to do with a confusion of motives. In "Fargo" are they mocking or celebrating the goofy mid-western twang of the locals, principally the pregnant female sherrif? (Played by the great Frances Mcdormand, who hits it shrewd rather than coy). "The Big Lebowski", a MANGY dog story, was all attitude, even the jokes seemed ashamed of the effort, as if slacking in America had finally reached nirvana. Even funny is hopeless the movie seemed to suggest.

The Coen's didn't help themselves in interviews either, coming off like spoiled frat boys too smart for their own good. What they needed, it seemed, was a kick in the ass from daddy. A lecture from a wise and slightly mad old-timer. 

And Cormac Mcarthy was just the man to do it. One of the best writers in the US, a deadly serious one at that, Mcarthy is very much old-school, from a time when writers, painters, film-makers actually lived a life before assuming they had something to add, (as opposed to now, when it's only necessary to BE alive to have earned your two-cents). Mcarthy made the Coen brothers straighten up and fly right.

Unlike their debut film, "blood simple", (made when their were twelve I think), and which treated violence as an amusement, "No country for old men" uses the the very threat of violence as anything but playful. The story has a mythic feel, set against an American landscape that overpowers the people, inhabits THEM, making them feel small, almost cornering them into grand, foolhardy gestures. Mcarthy is a man rooted in the land and it's impossible for the Coens to shrug off his bullheaded drive, his need to settle things. The material forces the Coens to think past merely clever, to arrive somewhere they've never been. In the process the old man has re-invented them.

"No country for old men" is a great film, fearless and even, yes, "mature". It presents the Coens with the strongest material they've had in years and they rise to it with purpose, with an acknowledgement to what might be at stake...

Like grown-ups.

When small town Sherrif Tommy Lee Jones reminisces about the old days, when it wasn't necessary to carry a gun to maintain law and order, you'd be forgiven for thinking this movie is another trite essay on how times have changed.

But as the movie progresses, the brothers Coen reveal a very different story: that of a man nearing the end of his life, and becoming increasingly aware of his own mortality.

Beautifully photographed and deliberately paced, the movie is rich with incredible performances. Tommy Lee Jones is particularly impressive, in a subtle and moving portrayal as the aging lawman.

He laments not a changed country, but a change in himself. He didn't carry a gun not because his country wasn't dangerous, but rather because his youth made him unafraid of it.

By the end, he comes to realise that the greed and senseless violence he's witnessed is nothing new: his country is built upon it.

Best Coen Brothers film since Blood Simple?  Or since Miller's Crossing?  Or Fargo?  Whichever.  This one is definitely up there. Bardem and Brolin (who knew?) are both note perfect, but the supporting cast are faultless too and it is not intended as a slight to any of the actors to single out Kelly MacDonald's sweet, trusting   wife, or Tommy Lee Jones' Sheriff with haunted eyes that  may simply have seen too much.  To talk about the plot at all is to veer dangerously close to spoilers, so it's perhaps best to leave it there, pausing only to say that this is one of the few films I've seen recently that has grown stronger in both my memory and esteem in the hours that followed seeing it.

The cast is simply wonderful, Josh Brolin gives a perfect acting as Llewelyn Moss, Javier Bardem's flawless performance earned him a Oscar nomination, totally worthy in my opinion. Tommy Lee Jones excellent as always and Woody Harrelson with a brief but very convincing role. Definitely this is one of the best movies of the year and with the Academy awards right around the corner, it has very big chances to become the great winner of the night.

While it seems slightly basic on the outside, this film has layers that provide for interesting social and philosophical discussion.  Fatalism versus free will struck me as the main theme, and it is excellently portrayed in a film that has some remarkable performances, notably from its three leading men.  Javier Bardem commands every scene he is in, with a deep and reverberating baritone that makes most horror movie villains seem like caricatures.  The Coens' fascination with smalltown conflicts and bizarre crimes continues here, as it features some truly original action sequences and ideas, as well as some skillful cinematography that helps to elevate the mood of desolation and fear.  While it may be slightly graphic and a little slow moving for some, those who stick around and give it some thought should enjoy this creepy, psychotic, and ponderous film.  I found it to be tense and hypnotic from start to finish.

When the nominations for Best Picture was announced recently for the Academy Awards I was fairly sad that 1) Sweeny Todd wasn't nominated and 2) I hadn't seen a single film that was nominated. It didn't look like I'd get a chance to see any of them either. So what did I do? I read the spoilers off of Wikipedia. For shame I know. Then surprise of Surprises.. Out of the Blue two of the movies appeared at our local movie theatre! We made a bee line right for No Country For Old Men and didn't look back!
 
And thank goodness we did! This is an excellent film! This movie was so good, the story so gripping, so suspenseful, that even though I had read the spoilers I was so caught up in what was going on I wanted to yell out and warn characters to be careful and scared for their lives, everyone in the movie theatre's lives, and our own lives! I forgot the spoilers completely until after the film was over. It had me so firmly in it's grips! 
 
Javier Bardem deserves all the awards he's winning and/or is nominated for and he should win all of them. He is beyond excellent in this film. Tommy Lee Jones is also excellent in this film and I'm surprised he didn't get a nomination for his role here. Everyone is really good in this film. 
 
Something I thought was really effective was how early on they showed a few killings fairly explicitly so then later they could show less of the actual killing and you would just know what happened. That struck me as really good film making and effective in having the audience participate in a way. The amount of killing in itself was fairly effective because it made you think anyone could and would die. It added alot of suspense to the film and made us cringe and worry in so many scenes. Dark rooms will now always hold terror! 
 
When the movie ends it's a little unsettling. I think 1) That there is no release. The film has so much tension and suspense and there really is no release of it at the end. And then 2) we didn't want it to end! It was so good we wanted more! But I've been thinking about this over and over all night and I have to say, there is no other ending they could do in this film. None. This film has the only ending it can have. Watch the movie, go through the story, go through it in your head, there is no other ending. 
 
I can't recommend this film enough! I'm pulling for this film come Oscar time. Excellent excellent film! All go see it!

In No Country for Old Men Coen brothers managed to create one of the most scary villains of the decade - Anton Chigurh (brilliantly portrayed by Javier Bardem). He's a complete cypher, the unknown, a question mark. You are tempted to define this man and his violent acts, and the more you search the less you find. It's as if he's invisible to the real world. You only have to look into his vacant eyes to realise that he has no soul (check out the opening scene where Anton strangles the cop...it's not the actual strangling that's disturbing. It's that vacant look in his eyes...at least for me). 
Some things just can't be explained. Why is Anton the way he is? Who knows...who cares? He is what he is and the reasons behind his cruelty are irrelevant. 
People crave for answers, but they're not gonna find any. No Country for Old Men, like most masterpieces in my opinion, only raises questions.

For about an hour and 50 minutes this is the most disciplined, satisfyingly movie the Coens have made. Its brutal, engrossing and occasionally very funny but if there's a weakness, its the filmmakers admiration for the simple, folksy innocence that made you reach for your own gun in Fargo and here resurfaces in the form of Tommy Lee Jone's weary, shakes his head, seen it all county sheriff. He's the lament on the land's social ills personified by a horribly malevolent Javier Bardem. But having been a peripheral figure for much of the running time he pops up the end to deliver an unwelcome epilogue in place of a satisfying conclusion for Josh Brolin's character, with whom we've spent two hours on the edge of our seats. Ultimately then you feel a little cheated but there's real intelligence at work here, its just a shame that it has to be articulated through endearing simpletons - far better to let the audience draw its own conclusions.

[center][font=Trebuchet MS][size=1]The Coen brothers are back, but were they ever fully gone in the first place?. Many think the Coens haven't made a great film for years and years, this is probably true having said that I'm one of the few people who throughly enjoyed the screwball romantic comedy Intolerabe Cruelty. But trust me when I say No Country for Old Men is the return to form they need, this is quite simply one of the finest films of 2007 if not the finest. Twisted, complex and darkly humourous this is vintage film-making at its absolute finest. There are those moments in cinema where you witness something truly special, No Country for Old men is probably one of the greatest films in my lifetime. [/size][/font][/center]
[font=Trebuchet MS] [/font]
[center][font=Trebuchet MS][size=1]The films is based on Cormac McCarthy's novel No Country for old Men which sees a local guy named Lleywn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumble across several dead bodies, a van full of drugs and $2 million whilst out hunting. Moss realises its a drug deal gone wrong and takes the money. He soon wishes he hadn't because a heartless psychopath named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem-exceptional) is on the warpath. A man who carries around a weapon which looks like an oxygen tank, sports a strange hairstyle, and is pretty much Terminator like in his execution of people, unless of course they are lucky enough to win the coin toss. Local Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is on the case trying to catch the hunter and the hunted but seems to always be two steps behind.[/size][/font][/center]
[font=Trebuchet MS] [/font]
[center][font=Trebuchet MS][size=1]Wow what a mindblowing, stunning and thrilling film experience No Country for Old Men is. Its written meticulously, full of sharp black humour, contains tons of twists and downright heart thumping shocks, even when it slows down in pace, which is a rareity, it seems remains a compulsive and exhilarating film to view. Quite simply I had no idea what was going to happen in the film, it suprised me every 10 minutes, and thats what I want films to do, excite and thrill me. No Country for Old men crosses several genres thriller, western, drama, comedy but its not firmly any of them. It's best compared to the Coen's Fargo, but to call it Fargo in a dessert would be unfairly sold, No Country for Old Men is far darker in tone and overall is a far more exhilarating experience.[/size][/font][/center]
[font=Trebuchet MS] [/font]
[center][font=Trebuchet MS][size=1]The acting on show is Oscar-worthy this much we do know with the nominations already revealed. If there's any justice in the film business (and there has to be) Javier Bardem will have to walk away with Best Supporting Actor, his psychotic turn is absolutely mesmorising. His cold dead stares, his coin flipping, him brandishing his enormous gun all these moments capture the heartlessness of the character, he has no remorse and quite frankly he terrified me, no other villian has done that since Anthony Hopkins devishlish turns as Hannibal Lector. Bardem puts many actors to shame, he's so cold and calculating he makes it look so easy. Tommy Lee Jones gives his usual gruff gravitas to the role of Ed Bell, Josh Brolin who had some year in 2007 delivers another masterful performances, and there's superb support from Woody Harrelson and Kelly McDonald.[/size][/font][/center]

We're faced with three characters, literally good, bad and ugly and the reality that people can be all of these at once. I'm not all that familiar with the Coen brothers. Based on my enjoyment of 'No Country...' I want to see more.
 
 It's a film that grips you as tightly as any typical big-budget Hollywood picture might (if done right, like recent release Cloverfield) while thrilling you in new ways. Admittedly, it isn't to everyone's tastes. 
 
 Music is hardly used to enhance the experience of the movie. Usually the soundtrack to a film can, for me, make it something special. I barely noticed the lack of one here. It gives the film a more realistic feel, building tension through the apparent realism rather than the climax the music creates.
 
 The character of Chigurh is fantastic. Credit for that should probably be given to Cormac McCarthy rather than the Coens but their portrayal of this violent sociopath is fantastic. It becomes the good, the bad and the lucky (or unlucky). The sheriff, the bad guy and the average Joe riding his luck. There's a tragic romance to it all, even in the heat of the 1980's deep south.
 
 I'm trying hard not to give anything away. I enjoyed this film very much. I love the ambiguities in film and there are many here. The Coens break stereotypes about how the climax should work, how things should begin and end. with 'No Country...' they question what an ending really is and what role it plays in storytelling. When the screen went black and the credits began to roll there were audible laughs and sighs of confusion. I couldn't see it ending any other way while retaining credibility and I'm sure it left many people scratching their heads on their way home. In fact the thing that ultimately convinced me to go see the movie was my parents watching it and asking me to go see it and explain the end. They thought they'd missed something when in fact they were just asking questions that didn't need to be asked.
 
 I haven't read the novel. I'm not sure that I want to, as usually it leads to me hating either the book or the movie (usually the latter, ala I Am Legend...) but I'm told that the film is very faithful to the novel, a kind of respect that seems to be unpopular right now (damn you Will Smith!).
 
 If you want an excellent film and you are willing to approach it with an open mind then definitely go see this film. It might disappoint you. You may love it, like me. I hope you do.

It's fair to say that i'm not the biggest fan of the Coen brothers. I've just never really got into them before, and no, i didn't even think Fargo was anything special (mainly because of that annoying woman). But this...wow. It's fantastic. They've taken the Western and flipped it on its head, filling it with elements of other genres to create a scarily good film. I suppose it's not really a film for the inexperienced cinema fan, but the fact that it has managed to gain so much critical acclaim despite this is a sign of just how good it is. The symbolism and parallels between characters that jump off the screen with virtually every scene is astounding, with the visuals in general being absolutely gorgeous (the desert presenting a sort of flip-side to Fargo's snow-covered world). The plot moves at a steady pace, but refuses to reveal all of its intricacies to us in the obvious ways. Every time you expect to see a big, cowboy-style showdown, the Coen brothers invert the traditional shootout scene into a scrappier, more chaotic aftermath for us to ponder what has just happened off-screen. It may seem like a Western, but if it is, it's not what you'd expect. It's easy to leave the cinema with nothing but questions, but really, any questions you might have (like "was Chigurh actually in the room?") will almost certainly do the film a disservice. If Javier Bardem doesn't win some kind of award for his mesmorising performance as the unstoppable juggernaut whose presence defines the film, it will be a miscarriage of justice.

From The Bible to this morning's headlines, this film deals with every problem that is slowly destroying our world: greed, hatred, lack of responsibility, non-chalance for fellow human beings, a need to prove ourselves, and about a thousand other things. A masterpiece, and the wonderful Javier Bardem proves once again why he's one of the best actors working today, as he makes one of cinema's creepiest villain icons, along with Hannibal Lecter and Norman Bates. Everything about this movie is brilliant, but the main point here is that this is a new genre of film: the Anti-Western, which, ironically, is just being referred to as a Western by most people. However, it's not a Western at all. Instead of, like in most Westerns, the hero shooting and killing the Mexican or the Indian or whatever in a big shoot-out, and then riding off with his fair lady on horseback into the sunset, this film gives us exactly what we DON'T want, and we love every second of it. The hero (who actually isn't a hero, but a thief on the run) dies, the county sheriff is left depressed and wanting to die, the villain gets away, the hero's lover dies, the movie takes place in a city instead of the Wild West, the villain doesn't use an actual gun, the ending is not happy, etc., etc., etc. So if you are looking for a good old-fashioned Western like they used to make, look someplace else, because this film is, shall we say, "No Country for Old Men."

[left]I originally saw this movie way back in November. I don't know why, but I never got around to writing about it. I re-watched it recently and now have decided to give it the full review that it deserves (Not that it needs anymore praise or anything... :D).[/left]
 
 
[left][i]No Country For Old Men[/i] features three characters: Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), and Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin). Bell is who the title refers to. He is jaded and his hope is rapidly fading. He is disgusted and saddened by the fact that the world is such a violent place and appears to be turning into an even more violent one. Towards the beginning of the film, Bell is witty and optimistic. He thinks that everything will turn out okay and even declines the offer to check out a crime scene. This changes while he is tracking the other two characters.[/left]
 
[left]Anton Chirgurh is described in the film as a ghost, the ultimate badass, and a man with no sense of humor. You could also say that he's a man with morals (although his morals are probably different than yours). All of these descriptions are accurate. He walks around with a ridiculous haircut, a menacing smile, and a cattle stun gun attached to an oxygen tank. Chigurh will kill someone for simply inconveniencing him. Needless to say, Chrigurh is dangerous (even when handcuffed). [/left]
 
[left]The character that sets the events of the story in motion is Llewelyn Moss. One day, while out hunting, Moss stumbles upon the scene of a crime. It appears to be a drug deal gone wrong. There are bodies caked with dried blood attracting swarms of flies. Guns are scattered throughout the area. Moss finds one person barely holding onto life. This man has one simple request. He asks for water. Moss says that he doesn't have any water, walks away, and finds a satchel filled with money. He gets the money home safely, but is tormented with thoughts of the dying man. That night, he returns to the crime scene with a jug of water. This is a huge mistake.[/left]
 
[left]What follows is a game of cat and mouse. Chigurh chases after Moss and the money while Bell desperately tries to track down both of them. He wants to get Moss to a safe place. Chigurh is virtually Moss's evil shadow. He's always one step behind Moss and comes close to getting him quite a few times.[/left]
 
[left][i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is easily one of the most intense films I have ever seen. The pacing is flawlessly relentless and the complete lack of music further heightens the tension. A prime example of this tension is an early scene in which Chigurh goes to a gas station. He and the attendant get into a long talk. They seem to be conversing about trivial things such as what time the attendant goes to bed and whether or not he married into his business, but the discussion is much more than it seems. When Chigurh flips a coin and asks the man to call it, you can tell exactly what is at stake: the attendant's life.[/left]
 
[left]The Coen brothers are perfectionists. All of there films are shot flawlessly and this one is no exception. Every shot is perfect and there is not a single frame out of place. Their writing is wonderful and they have made as close to a page-for-page adaptation of a novel that I have ever seen.[/left]
 
[left]Another thing about the Coens is that their movies are cast to perfection. Here, every character, no matter how unimportant, shines. Javier Bardem does manage to steal the show with his portrayal of one of the most compelling and magnetic villians of the past decade. He plays Anton Chigurh to creepy perfection. In the book, there is virtually no description of the character, but as soon as Bardem hits the screen, you know exactly who he's supposed to be. Tommy Lee Jones and Josh Brolin are also standouts. You can almost feel Bell's spirits sink lower and lower as Jones says his lines. Other notables include Kelly MacDonald as Llewelyn's wife and Woody Harrelson as a bounty hunter. [/left]
 
[left]Much has been said about the violent nature of this film. Yes, at first there is a lot of blood spilled, but the movie gets progressively less violent. By the end, you only need a small hint (such as Chigurh checking his boots or washing the bed of a truck) to know that someone has been killed. So, while this film is not for the super squeamish, be assured that the violence [i]does[/i] let up a bit.[/left]
 
[left][i]No Country For Old Men[/i] made me think... possibly more than any other film has. Some will loathe the ending, but if you let it sink in and process it, instead of immediately judging it, you will find that the film could not have ended any other way. It made me think about fate and hope and the violent tendencies of humans. Above all else, it made me think of, well, itself, and what the film (and novel) meant. [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is intense, meditative, and filled with pitch-black humor. I loved every minute of it.[/left]

Of course the score (and lack of, in many parts) was perpetually proper and perfectly positioned. We've all read those things. But the writing... oh the writing! The lack of humanity written into both the protagonist and antagonist was brilliance. Despite this stoicism and aloof insouciance, this movie still delivers an extremely, unforgettably passionate presence as a film experience and delivers on every level in terms of watchability, suspense, and especially drama in its finest form. Also on the case is aging lawman Ed Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) trying to keep up with both men.

Perhaps the most surprising thing about No Country For Old Men is the identity of the most important character. It's not Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) or Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), but sherrif Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who is absent for the middle part of the film. It's his story line that shows the point that the film makes. The final scene, which is really subdued and open compared to what came before, shows a man not knowing how to keep up with the changing times, and it also tells the audience that no matter what you do or who you are - cop, criminal or just a redneck from a Texas backwater - there is no way you can tell what's going to happen. Confident killer Chigurh, who succeeds in all he plans out, gets injured in a car crashw hich is not his fault. No way he could've told it was coming. Moss is killed in a common robbery, nothing at all to do with the killer who hunts him. No way he could've told it was coming. And Bell is left with a smany questions as he started out with, and the conclusions that he can no longer tell how it's supposed to go. The times have overtaken him.
This is far more serious fare than earlier Coen productions. There are moments of comedy, mostly in dialogue, but it's filled with people just trying to lead their lives in a hard land. And that hard land is almost a character itself - bleak, windblown and unforgiving, it seems to dictate the action.
No Country For Old Men is certainly worth the hype. There is indeed very little that I find wrong with it. I f anything I'd mention the very small dip the film takes after Bell arrives at the site where Moss was killed. But that's evry minor indeed.
Highly recommended.

Nominations for movie of the year are both a blessing and a burden for films. On one hand, everyone that took part in a nominated film feels quite proud of their achievement while on the other hand those that decide to view the film after the nomination has been given out, have very high expectations for it and then see the movie for what it is, may feel as though they deserved more for their money. Simply put, this seems to be the case for "No Country For Old Men." Don't get me wrong, the acting was amazing and Javier Bardem clearly deserves every award he's nominated for his supporting actor role as the killer in this film, but the acting can only push a film's overall rating so far. The story was great at first, even if something most of us have seen before. Unfortunately, it lost steam after a bit, rather resembling the killer-hunting of "The Zodiac." In fact, in this case, the story slowed to the point of a complete stop towards the end, leaving the audience with a lot of confusion as to what was going on and how could it be qualified as a good ending to any sort of film. Although stunningly interesting at first, the film mediocrity throughout most of its runtime dramatically ruins what I thought it would be. Guess that's what a nomination does to you sometimes...

Joel and Ethan Coen pull off their best work since Fargo, and maybe The Man who Wasn't There, and like in Fargo, they come up with a tour De force of writing, directing, acting and cinematography.

No Country for Old Men is albeit a complex movie, it's certainly not a movie you can fully digest in one sitting, this review is boldly written after just two sittings, yet, that doesn't necessarily mean that it's an over the top art house movie for twelve people. The movie, being a classic Coen brothers movie, it's very entertaining from beginning to end. The story is a grabber from the start, and their narrative, so rich in the small details that make you buy into the action even more.

The performances are all great, there's no main character or anything, I don't think we could really call Tommy Lee Jones the protagonist, this is more of an ensemble piece, and as en ensemble, it's fantastic, there's not a single weak link, all of the actors were extremely effective. Tommy Lee Jones gives a great, subtle, and poignant performance as a Keystone Texas Sheriff, Josh Brolin is great as the laconic Texas loner, Kelly MacDonald is extremely convincing and honest as the Texan trailer housewife, I immediately forgot her original thick Scottish accent and completely bought her uncanny Texan accent, she was an inspired piece of casting. Woody Harrelson was quite effective as usual. 

I've been saving however, the best for last, Javier Bardem's chilling performance is the one that shines and stands out the most, his portrayal of Anton Chigurh is one of the most chilling performances since probably Anthony Hopkins in Silence of the Lambs. I know the world chilling is tossed rather lightly these days, but trust me, Bardem's really earns the adjective, his cold hearted, yet human and realistic portrayal of Chigurh is memorable, he has created, along with the Coen brothers, a memorable an assassin as The Terminator or Hannibal Lecter.

The film has an impressive look, kudos to the always amazing Roger Deakins for a strong looking cinematography, imposing long shots of the Texan country side, as impressive as North Dakota's white desert looks of Fargo, as well as an extensive use of shadows, very good stuff.

[color=dimgray][i][b]No Country For Old Men[/b][/i] is a critically acclaimed, award winning 2007 film adaptation of the novel of the same name by Cormac McCarthy. Written and directed by Joel and Ethan Coen (aka, "the Coen brothers"), the film stars Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin, and Javier Bardem. Faithfully adapted from the well-received novel, [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] draws heavily on McCarthy's themes of chance and fate. It tells the story of a drug deal gone very wrong and the ensuing cat-and-mouse drama as three men crisscross each other's paths in the desert landscape of 1980 West Texas.[/color]
 
[color=#696969][i]No Country [/i]is mainly about Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin). A welder and Vietnam veteran who occasionaly hunts. While hunting pronghorn near the Rio Grande, he stumples across a collection of corpses and trashed out vehicles: the aftermath of a drug deal gone very wrong. He also finds $2 million in a satchel a short distance from the newfound massacre. Initially, Moss flees with the $2 million in drug money but is unaware of the consiquences. A professional assassin named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is hired to recover the drug money (which contains a hidden radio transponder to which Chigurh has the corresponding receiver). Chigurh does not hesitate to kill those in his way, including those closely associated with the drug deal, the drivers of cars he steals for transportation, and people he encounters by chance. Moss, unaware of the transponder's existence, sends his wife Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald) out of town as he moves from motel -to- motel to elude both the Mexicans and Chigurh. In the meantime, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) avoids the federal authorities investigation of the original drug-related massacre and focuses his attention on trying to locate and protect Moss. Chigurh, with his tracking device, quickly closes in on Moss while acting as an agent of fate and chance to the people he meets along the way. What ensues is a tense chase as a gang of Mexicans, the desperate Moss, the almost unstoppable Chigurh, and SheriffBell chase each other and the money across the Texas and Mexico landscapes. [/color]

[color=dimgray][i]No Country[/i] has it's fair amount of tense scenes and action. With very realistic shoot outs and some very "on the edge of your seat" moments. Anton Chigurh played by Javier Bardem, is as Moss states - [i]"the ultimate bad ass".[/i] Bardem plays the role of a Terminator-like character who has no-remorse and shows no feeling. He is the movie's "bad guy", and honestly gives you the creeps everytime he steps into a room. A killing machine if you will, that sends a chill down your spine when having one of his eerie conversations with any of the innocent civillians he comes across. To be in the same room with this guy, is something I would NOT want to experience. Equipped with a pneumatic air gun and a silenced (custom-made) automatic gun, Chigurh has what it takes to make a silent and effective kill. Which happen to make some terrific scenes in the movie, if you like effective and realistic violence. Some times, Chigurh's attacks are so sudden and briefly unexpected that they would just scare the shit outta ya. One particular scene had this amazing build up with almost total silence as Moss has his first confrontation with Chigurh, resulting in a very sudden "blink and you'll miss it"/"shit your pants" moment. This scene was my favourite as it was done so well and was viewed from Moss' perspective, which added to the fear. [/color]

[color=#696969]Overall, [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] is a movie I would watch again and is a dramatic change from all of the usual tripe that comes out these days. It's a very serious and no bullshit film with a highly serious subject matter. However, [i]No Country[/i] does have a massive and brutally dissapointing downfall: the ending. The last quarter of the movie kinda swerves away from the rest of the film, the pace slows down to come to an unexpected and sudden stop. Which leaves the viewer dangling a little bit. The movie feels incomplete and the ending rushed. For such a great film it has a very bad ending that I found very dissapointing and would have liked it to end with a bang. Apart from the tragic ending, [i]No Country[/i] is undeniably a great movie and one of the best movies that I've seen in a long time. Tense, atmospheric, exciting, thrilling, engaging and totally emersive. If it were not for the ending, I would have given [i]No Country For Old Men[/i] 9/10. So I give it an[color=dimgray] 8/10[/color].[/color]

It seems like Westerns have had a renaissance of late; films like 'The Proposition', 'The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada' and the recent 'There Will Be Blood' have breathed new life into the genre.

'No Country For Old Men' is a return to form for the Coens. Although they have made some very good movies in the past ('The Big Lebowski' springs to mind), they've had a few misses more recently. However, they haven't made a movie like this since 'Miller's Crossing', their last masterpiece.

Josh Brolin plays Llewelyn Moss, a hunter who stumbles across $2m after a drugs deal goes bad. However, his gamble leads him into the path of Anton Chicurh, a maniacal psychopath who makes life-or-death decisions on the flip of a coin. Tommy Lee Jones plays a veteran cop who tries to track them both down...

'No Country For Old Men' has a number of memorable characters, but if you want one reason to watch this film, there isn't a better one than Javier Bardem's nutcase killer, one of modern cinema's greatest villains. Although the pacing may not be for some tastes, the soundtrack and the cinematography are masterful.

The ending may frustrate some, but I would recommend you to approach this film with an open mind; it may leave some questions unanswered, but the best films usually do.

This is my review: 
Well, Its about time. 



Written and Directed by: Joel and Ethan Coen.
Based on the book by: Cormac McArthy. 
Starring: Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones.


Well its about time right here to get blown away. Please welcome Ethan and Joel Coen. They are carrying a metal cylinder filled to the top with a gas, under high pressure. They are going to aim the pressure hose on your forehead and put a hole about two inches deep. You fall on the floor and thats the story of you. 


No Country for Old Men is a western set in the 1980's. While hunting for deers Llewlyn Moss (Josh Brolin) comes across a case full of hard cash amongst dead bodies. As aware as he is to face a shower of bullets, hardly he is aware of facing Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). Anton is someone who would kill even after getting the money just for the inconvenience he had suffered, as Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) mentions to Llewlyn who is under a medical observation in an hospital for the wounds he suffered from ..............well, Anton. So what happened, and what would happen? Even if you guess you are not going to believe what happens in this country. 


If you appreciated the cold-blooded wood-chipper body disposal in Fargo (1996) or fearless furious bullet shooting by Albert Finney in Miller's Crossing (1990) then you would know how fantastically Coen Brothers directed those crime thrillers. No doubt they have tight screenplays but also they sure do take their time to make a point and numb you. The visuals are gritty, bloody and absolutely extraordinary. There are sounds, there are shadows, there are quiet walks and there are blow ups of cars. And then there are punch lines like "How much you have ever bet on a coin toss?" Coes brothers come back after almost a decade with never before energy and a sharp edged knife. I smell Academy nominations for adapted screenplay and direction. This is a marvellous creation. 
One face is unforgettable on this desert and that is Javier Bardem's outlaw. He is innocently quiet and stays that way while terrorizing every one who crosses his path. His self sufficient operation of bullet ridden wounds lets you know that help is the last thing he needs. He has all the tools and if there is something missing, he has the brain and guts to get it. He has no sympathy but just a determination and will cross boundaries to follow that determination. This is perhaps the baddest character after Tony Montana and his "little friend". Absolutely Unforgettable. 


Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones as the sheriff are also entertaining and believeable. Woody Harrelson makes a short appearance with the same mystic smile from Natural Born Killers. But in the end its the desert of Texas and the deep philosophical roots that perhaps are dying with the old cowboys since the new outlaws make you forget the "ethical" Clint Eastwood from Dollar Trilogy. 


Please go and watch this intense heart-stopping drama that would keep you on the edge of the seat. 
My rating: 10/10.

Tommy Lee Jones gives a subdued but outstanding performance as a lawman in his twilight years, Josh Brolin dove into the role of the desperado cowboy who stumbles upon a load of drugs and a bag full of money-- but it's Javier Bardem, whose clever portrayal of a menacing killer who could give classic movie killers the chills, that utterly scintillates the screen.

If your ideal film experience involves a predictable plot, familiar iconography and stereotypical heroes and villains â the Coen brothers latest film will leave you feeling like youâve been mugged. Such is their disdain for the familiar; No Country For Old Men works against all the Hollywood conventions of narrative, which are routinely served up in mainstream cinema every week. Our generation is well educated in normative models of plot and can usually anticipate scenes before they happen - through a films transparency and the neat unfolding of events towards the resolution. If you fall into this trap watching No Countryâ¦you will be horrified when the final credits abruptly creep onto the screen unannounced, confirming that the film is one long, frustrating enigma; such is life. 
Events revolve around a serial killer of less-than-sound mentality, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who is on a lone mission; we never discover his intentions or any of his subjective thoughts other than his willingness to brutally kill anyone who stands in his way. He is erratic and his victims are arbitrarily chosen; this is analogous to the films random structure, which omits several key scenes that the audience will feel they deserved to see. But this âdivine rightâ of the audience should not be so, for our arrival at the aftermath of these scenes feels like authentic cinema. The reaction of shock and despair will be felt by all when Ed (Tommy Lee Jones) arrives too late to prevent Antonâs latest massacre; he was outwitted, and so were we. This is all part of the Coen brothers teasing methods throughout; they seek to de-familiarise, confuse and repeatedly unsettle the audience, as each of our expectations are dashed one by one. 
The beauty of the film is in its intense, dark atmosphere which remains constant from start to finish; never once are we treated to a comfortable moment where we can indulge in respite. Despite some slow-moving scenes where little occurs, there is always the omnipresence of a hell-bent psycho who may appear at any time; this makes it all the more compelling. There is a helplessness about the films supposed heroes; the initially likeable character of sheriff Ed Tom Jones becomes progressively morbid, and Llewellen (Josh Brolin) â who seems to possess all the heroic credentials, is fatally flawed by his machismo â his belief that he is a hero.  
Javier Bardem gives a virtuoso performance as Anton, whose personality is shallow yet he bubbles with complexity and inner conflicts that are never revealed to us. He appears to be pursuing a suitcase full of money, yet this has no real value to him and is more than likely a mere inspiration for his bloodthirsty mission. All we can see in his blank countenance is an unwillingness, or incapacity to act with reason. His frightening disregard for human life is accompanied by an air of nonchalance; so unsettling, yet this is truly a creation to be admired. His preoccupation with deciding a victims fate with the toss of a coin is a genius method of suspense in the film.  
A deafening silence suffuses each scene in No Countryâ¦ and is the essence of the films gripping tension. Music is normally a device used to let you know where you stand in a film, perhaps to warn you of a characters impending doom; the Coen brothers invert this convention so that your emotions are suspended throughout. Each event in the film is delivered without any warning and generally without any precursor. Thus the audience are vulnerable and unsuspecting; this, again, is surely authentic cinema.  The constant dissembling of our expectations is an uncomfortable, but masterful effect which should be praised in its transgression of the norm. 
The playful contempt of conventional cinema, which may offend some viewers, seems to be a genuine attempt from the Coen brothers to move away from the packaged production, enticing wider audiences to be more accepting of alternative forms. Innovative cinema like this should be celebrated. This film will be too dark for some; the silence â repeatedly punctured by the thud of the Antonâs weapon â will be too unsettling. But there is something significant in what the Coen brothers are trying to achieve; they are subverting an establishment which seeks to dumb down film production and innovation; contemporary, mainstream cinema â for better or worse - is littered with clones. No Country For Old Men will be alienated by some for its non-conformist approach, but deserves recognition for daring to be different.

[img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_09.jpg[/img]
 
 The Coen Brothers are back. After a couple of missteps with the uneven, oftentimes flat remake of [b]The Ladykillers[/b], and the under-appreciated romantic satire [b]Intolerable Cruelty[/b], Joel and Ethan Coen offer up a bleak, unforgiving contemporary American western with [b]No Country for Old Men[/b], which is based on a Cormac McCarthy novel.
 
 This is the Coen Brothers at their best, and their most bone-dry film yet. Similar in tone to the Minnesota Gothic of [b]Fargo[/b], and just as violent (or maybe more) than their 1920s gangster drama [b]Miller's Crossing[/b], with philosophical insight similar to [b]Barton Fink[/b], the slapstick escapades of such films as [b]Raising Arizona[/b] and [b]O Brother, Where Art Thou?[/b] have been replaced by reveries on the great American old west.
 
 Tommy Lee Jones stars as a taciturn, weary sheriff, a proud wearer of the badge from a long line of lawmen. But in 1980 west Texas, times have changed. Things have become too brutal. His eyes can barely stand the sight of a drug deal gone bad, out in the desert, where a dozen or so bodies are spread out among some shot-up trucks.
 
 At the scene, his dumb deputy exclaims: "It's a mess, ain't it, sheriff?"
 
 "If it ain't, it'll do until the mess gets here," says the sad-eyed Sheriff Ed Tom.
 
 Before the sheriff and his deputy rode up on the scene, it had been visited by Llwellen Moss, a local good-ol-boy who had been out hunting for deer. While following the blood trail of a buck he'd shot, he finds another blood trail, thicker, deeper red, which leads to the crime scene, and, eventually, a satchel containing $2 million.
 
 [img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_06.jpg[/img]
 
 Moss is played by Josh Brolin, who with his magnificent moustache, gives a riveting performance as the laconic Vietnam veteran who knows that keeping money is almost the dumbest thing he'll ever do in his life. But going back to the crime scene, ostensibly to offer a survivor some water, is the dumbest.
 
 On Moss's trail is the biggest, most bad-ass villain ever committed to film. Forget about Darth Vader. Forget about the Wicked Witch of the West. Forget about the shark from [b]Jaws[/b], the Alien, the Terminator or any of the laughable Bond arch-enemies. There is a new bad guy in town and his name is Chigurh. Anton Chigurh. With a crazy helmet of hair, he is played with delightful glee by Javier Bardem. For killing, he favors a compressed-air bolt that is used for dispatching cattle in the slaughterhouse. No need to waste a bullet, or leave any evidence behind. Quick and clean. But if anything, he's polite. "You, hold still," he asks the driver of a car he's about to steal.
 
 Chigurh is wickedly determined to get the money back. He lives by a code, however messed up it may be. No one can ever see him. And when he says he is going to kill someone, well, that's just what he does. Though he does have his good days, like in one hilarious scene where he asks one of the Coens' patented hayseed gas station attendants to "call it" on a coin flip. The right guess means the man can live.
 
 Woody Harrelson has a small, but memorable role as another man trying to retrieve the money. He's all too familiar with Chiguhr.
 
 Asks the man who hires Woody (played by Coens' regular Stephen Root): "Just how dangerous is he?"
 
 "Compared to what? The bubonic plague?"
 
 Kelly MacDonald trades in her Glaswegian brogue for Texas twang as Llewellan Moss's helpless wife, and gives spark to her character, who's struggling to come to grips with what her husband's done.
 
 Despite all the blood, No Country for Old Men is beautiful and profound, an ode to the old American west, and an exasperated look at the senseless greed and violence that has gripped our world.

There is so much that is superb in this film. The cinematography is magnificent, making excellent use of the dry and dusty Tex-Mex border locations.  The film tells a gripping tale in which the tension is sustained superbly. There is yet another outstanding performance by Tommy Lee Jones to enjoy, this time as the weary veteran lawman Ed Tom Bell, trying to contain the bloodshed caused by missing drug-generated millions. There are some lovely touches of wry humour in the very well-crafted script.  

For me, though, No Country For Old Men isn't quite the towering masterpiece that some reviewers have suggested. Javier Bardem's performance as the utterly ruthless  assassin Anton Chigurgh  is effectively chilling, but he's a two-dimensional character, as implausibly inhuman as a Bond villain. I certainly didn't see the depth and profundity that some have claimed for this movie; it seems to say little except that there are some very  bad  people out there who will do anything for money, and I think I already knew that. 

Still, if movies full of bullets, blood and taciturn men are your thrill, then here is a  stylish and entertaining example of the genre  that you'll probably enjoy a great deal. Personally, I admired it but couldn't love it.

 The Coen brothers are a force of nature. A pair of original and overlooked knights that live under the Hollywood round table. Consistency would also be a fitting word to use at this point, with 23 years' worth of solid filmmaking under their belts - using freshly written scripts and a range of varied character actors. So it was with some public surprise that last year the brothers Coen attempted their first fully-fledged adaptation. Tranferring the acclaimed Cormac McCarthy novel; '[b]No Country for Old Men[/b]' to the screen. A dusty ride of a script set in America's Southern states, the film follows Llewelyn Moss (played by Josh Brolin) and his coincidental discovery of a drug deal gone wrong. He retrieves that money from this broken deal and claims it for his own, sparking a chain of events that will have him running for his life by evening. His chief pursuer is the violent and psychopathic Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) - a bounty hunter who becomes fixated upon the fleeing figure of Moss. A face-off that is almost cat-and-mouse-like on reflection.
  
[img]http://i261.photobucket.com/albums/ii80/jedimoonshyne6/10-4.jpg[/img]

 This central struggle is offset by the pensieve form of aging Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), whose thoughts and worries permeate the film - just as they do the novel. His recollections and reflections hold up a mirror to today's society - wondering if it truly was better in his Father's day. '[b]No Country for Old Men[/b]' is an extremely deep piece of writing, and the Coens do their best to portray most of McCarthy's idle musings - primarily through the Bell character. With the film however, a lot more emphasis is put on the haunting Chigurh character and his hunt. Something that allows the directors to implement their usual stylish techniques for creating suspense, ones we've seen since 1984's '[b]Blood Simple[/b]' (which incidentally enough draws many similarities). And thus the film becomes more of a pacy and somewhat stripped-down thriller than anything else, an aspect that can be derived from McCarthy's piece but not too enthusiastically. Yes, I'm aware it's thrilling. Yes, I'm very aware that the Midas touch that the Coen brothers seem to have has been laid upon this movie. It's destined for some kind of greatness, and who I am to argue with that. I mean, I can't fault it none. The dialogue is meticulous and tantalizingly nondescript. The lack of a soundtrack or extra sound puts you in a void as deep as the characters themselves. A lot of art and even more time went into this film. And yet, I feel like I must say that this movie ain't all there. This movie conjures up an image of a lazy eye that casts its glance on nothing in particular; the movie is sometimes agonizingly nonlinear, and that's the point. The old days of guns and badges, of chivalry and common sense, of regularity, when violence made sense and good men made sense of it, are no where to be found in this movie. Tommy Lee Jones' character finds no answers. I didn't either. I don't know whether I'm frustrated or not. I guess I don't feel anything, and I'm right at home.
