After what seems to be a lifetime in film, the Coen Brothers are back.
Dabbling in comedy seems to have taken its toll in the brothers' impressive career. They have now wandered into a different kind of genre altogether with their latest feature  the not-so-western Western thriller, where cowboys are war veterans and Indians are badass Mexicans.
The plot seems to echo the Steve McQueen film The Getaway, as we have our wannabe anti-hero Moss, a lot of dirty money and some mad mejicanos on his tail.
It is very interesting to see the good guy realise the situation and the risk he is getting himself into, without all the 'Holy Shit!' clichés that seem to appear so often.
Josh Brolin takes his role seriously, slowly taking in the situation as it develops, climbing up to the climatic scene where his fate is decided, yet unshown.
Surely a role that will propel him into the mainstream limelight, Javier Bardem's performance as the cold-hearted assassin Chigurh has drawn many-a comparison to the Terminator  to me, he seems like a more chilling version of Jules Winnifield from Pulp Fiction: memorable hairdo, the same bulging eyes and the ability to keep you at the edge of your seat.
In between them is Tommy Lee Jones as Sherrif Bell, whose inability to decipher the whole situation seems to be overshadowed by his occasionally confusing stories found in local papers. Perhaps it is his way of dealing with the enormity of having a psychopathic killer on the loose in his state, or the fact that he has to deal with it at this day and age. 
The script itself is clean-cut, without the Coen-isms found in O Brother, Where are thou and The Big Lebowski. Instead, the Coens have made the use of very little music, emphasising the scenes of violence like a cannon in a library - the bolt pistol used by Chigurh, for instance, is innovative and yet effective in making you jump out of your skin.
Making the most of Cormac McCarthy's original prose, without taking away its focus with poignant music and screwball cameos reinforce the fact that this ain't no Ladykillers or Fargo  No Country for Old Men is something else entirely. 
Cold, violent yet elegantly made, it is no surprise why they have become a major player in the Awards season.

If this doesn't end my year in the top two films of the year then we are in for one hell of an awesome year of movies.

The new film from two of the best filmmakers working today No Country For Old Men shows the talents of the Coen Brothers on top form. After a couple of disappointments (Intolerable Cruelty had flashes of Coen genius but felt more of a Coen imitation than the real thing; Ladykillers had the odd funny moment but was the blandest film the brothers ever made, and there's just no excusing Marlon Wayans!) they knock this violent western drama out of the park.

More in the vein of their superb early mostly-serious efforts Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing (my personal favourite of the Coen back catalogue) No Country For Old Men is a slow-moving, character-driven masterpiece about uncompromising and uncompromised characters. It is very violent and bloody and not always for the squeamish.

Shot through with moments of humour these come, as in life, from real situations and observations so don't be fooled into thinking this will be the serious film with goofy-characters Coens of Fargo. No Country For Old Men is a tough, gritty story.

The unrelenting pace may take its time but you are gripped every moment. This is a thriller that genuinely thrills.

Javier Bardem gives the best performance of his career. And, yes, I have seen The Sea Inside and he in superb in that but here he is simply extraordinary. It is a portrayal of unrelenting evil, of true derangement, of a human being with no shreds of humanity that ranks at the very top of studied film psychopaths. And I say film not movie because this is not a clichéd character. This is not a character whose lunacy you enjoy over popcorn. This is one of the most frightening performances ever committed to celluloid. I felt truly nervous of what was going to happen every time he walked on screen.

Josh Brolin essentially carries the bulk of the movie and he is excellent in a role that challenges him. I have never seen him perform to this level and if Bardem didn't steal the film you'd be talking about Brolin all the way home. As it is this gives him a showcase for his talents that should see him get a lot more attention.

Tommy Lee Jones is used sparingly but to great effect. Sounding more like Michael Parks than ever before his scenes pepper the movie with a wearied view on a world he doesn't really like or understand to great effect.

I did find Stephen Root a little distracting as i have never seen him in a serious role before and he just looks amusing but he is in very little.

Roger Deakins' cinematography is breathtaking as usual and the Coens' script is superbly crafted. There are moments, almost asides from the main plot, that would be superfluous in most scripts and excised in most studio films but which work perfectly in the overall context of the movie as only the Coens can achieve. One scene featuring Bardem in a gas station is up there with the best scenes i have ever seen on film.

I have not gone into the plot here because I saw this film having not read Cormac McCarthy novel and knowing little other than the basic log-line - a man out hunting comes upon a scene of dead bodies, guns, drugs and money on the Mexican border and comes to the attention of both those behind the scene and a local world-wearied sheriff - and i think that's the way to see this film.

Go in knowing as little as you can but knowing at least this: this is a serious, violent, slow-paced character piece from the Coens. This is not a Fargo. If you are squeamish don't see it. If you have a short-attention span don't see it. If you only love the Coens for their fantastic comedies like O Brother and Big Lebowski and the comedy/thriller Fargo don't see it. But if you want to see an intelligent, superbly acted, powerful, beautiful cinematic treat that will remind you of the true power of cinema see it, see it, see it. It's a masterpiece. Bravo Ethan and Joel.

Llewelyn Moss (an under rated great performance by Josh Brolin) is a former Vietnam combatant who stumbles upon a cargo of drugs and a suitcase full of money, product of a deal gone sour. After a series of disappointing movies the Coen brothers have finally returned to form with "No Country For Old Men". Recent years had "demoted" the Coen brothers back to the art house under the category interesting directors. Problem was of course that you can start your career that way, but once you established your name it is kind of awkward. "The Man Who Wasn't There" was still an amusing film, but "The Lady Killers" was simply embarrassing for men with the talents of the Coen brothers. After that I might have missed a film or two. But the buzz around their adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's book I decided to pay the theater a visit to see if the flick was worth all the hype. I've never really seen what the fuss about Cormac's books is. His last novel "The Road" struck me as filled with one dimensional characters, addressing themes that hadn't been urgent since the Cold War. Granted "No Country For Old Men" was a bit better but McCarthy's books are inhibited by characters of who's motivations remain unclear. His novels always seem a bit too close to black and white notions of good and evil to me. I enjoy the sparsity of McCarthy's writing and his ability to set the seen in as little as possible words, but I always found his characters to be lacking a certain amount of depth. McCarthy never was the writer John Fante and Charles Bukowski were, who were able to combine bare bone writing with a strong sense of what moved the characters that inhibited their novels. McCarthy's works are of a different genre than those two of course, but I feel he could pick up a thing or two from those two authors.
 
 But as the Coen brother's recent flick testifies, McCarthy's novels might prove to be excellent movie scripts. Movies work very different from novels. In movies the director has the non-verbal expression he can work with to give the viewer more of a sense of what moves the character. A movie director doesn't need to use words, he can let the images do the talking. Voice overs in films are often very unnecessary things that are best used very sparsely. The Coen brothers do just that. Although the movie opens with a voice over from sheriff Tommy Lee Jones reflecting on the times his father and grand father held office, simpler times when they didn't need to carry guns. Neither does Jones for the major part of the movie, that is until he ventures into the city. Tommy Lee Jones resorting to his gun seems a key moment in the film. The whole movie seems to radiate a world in which innocence and simplicity is lost. Something that seems to be a main theme in McCarthy's book. His view on the world strikes me as very bleak, a sense masterfully translated to the big screen by the Coens. McCarthy's books generally seem to want to see that the world is coming to an end, that we've lost our moral, their apocalyptic even if the scenery isn't. McCarthy seems to rehash this theme very novel, which basically isn't more than a cynical form of nostalgia. The Coen brother use their trademark dark humor to take the edge of that message. Throwing you of balance all the while. There is something very uncomfortable about finding yourself bursting out in laughter during scenes of extreme violence, you almost feel like an accomplice. 
 
 For a thriller "No Country" follows a slow and dragging pace in which the outbursts of extreme violence achieve maximum impact. Other than most high action thrillers that Hollywood churns out these days, "No Country" excels in restraint. You won't find fast action car chases or major shoot outs in this movie. Yet the film keeps you on the edge of your seat. "No County" is filled with unexpected twists in plot. Those changes are often so brutal that the film manages to evoke a level of suspense I haven't seen in movies for a long time. The plot seems a cliché at first. A Vietnam veteran (Josh Brolin) finds 2 million dollars in drugs money in the desert and tries to get away with it. Of course the hardened drugs criminals won't let him and chase him, leaving a trail of blood. Nothing new here. Yet where in McCarthy's novels the one dimensionality of his characters seem to work against him, they become the films major strength. Javier Bardem plays the sociopath chasing Brolin. He manages to radiate such an evil and threat that he becomes uneasy to watch, exactly the kind of feeling you want from a thriller. The scene in which Bardem forces a gas station manager to call heads or tails for his life should not have worked, as it seems something from a cheap B movie. But the casting, acting and cinematography work together so well that you find yourself wanting to look away. The looming evil is so thick and present through out the movie that the almost idyllic closing scene comes as the biggest shock of all.

"No Country for Old Men" is a film about injustice. The question is, "Is justice even possible in a world so overrun with evil?" Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) wonders about this. Bell comes from a family of lawmen, men who dedicated their lives to hunting down and prosecuting criminals, but Bell is becoming weary of the job that seems to be getting harder with each passing generation. He's been chasing guys like Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), who stole stolen money, and guys like Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who hunt and murder guys like Moss, for a long time, and they don't stop coming. But it's not just that; Bell wonders when God is going to intervene, if He's there at all. If justice is a reality, why doesn't God just smite all evildoers or at least let the police arrest them? Such are the questions in a country where few old men care to live anymore. Old men who have given up the hope of peace that they fought for.

As suspenseful and intense as this movie is, and as good as these questions about justice, morality, and God are, the film is quite lacking of answers. Legitimate and honest questions are all well and good for films, but why not explore the multiple-choice options this world has to offer? "No Country for Old Men" is not likely to inspire anybody, and audiences will probably enjoy the cat-and-mouse gunfighting more than pondering the rather ambiguous themes, because the honest-to-goodness truth is that as frightening as Chigurh is, we like it. We enjoyed being scared by him, and as long as we enjoy it, we will never feel the way we should about real murderers, which makes the injustice and God themes numb. Quality filmmaking for sure, but it's time for cinema to move people to change. Every year we are asked excellent and relevant questions, but films like "No Country for Old Men" must be followed up by something that takes a shot at answers.

The irony of a relativist culture is that the questions are never relative, only the answers; we all seem to agree on what the right questions are, so now we must explore truth.

"No Country for Old Men" has a few Oscar nominations: Best Sound Mixing, Best Sound Editing, Best Cinematography, Best Supporting Actor (Javier Bardem), Best Film Editing, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Directing, and Best Picture. The film has a strong chance of earning the sound Oscars, mostly because of how much certain sounds add to the intensity of the plot. When there's no music, beeps, squeaks, and clops will scare you just as much. The cinematography is rather simplistic, if you ask me, so one of the others like to win this. It's a tight race this year for supporting actors, and Javier Bardem is probably not going to be on top of the nominees, but his portrayal of the cruel Chigurh is nonetheless disturbing. The adapted screenplay, I hear, is very true to the novel by Cormac McCarthy, and it is compelling, but this one may succumb to "There Will Be Blood." The Coen Brothers as directors certainly provided much guidance to the making of the film, but its likely that they may lose the Oscar to more ingenious filmmakers, at least this year, but the Coen Brothers are very talented. "No Country for Old Men" is probably only second to "There Will Be Blood" when it comes to Best Picture. As the two strongest nominees in the category, as far as the Academy may be concerned, it will be interesting to see which film they prefer. (I'm still praying that "Juno" will win.)

One of the most suspenseful movies I've seen in recent years. A chilling, somewhat Hitchcockian cat-and-mouse tale of a serial killer pursuing a man carrying a suitcase full of drug-related cash. Javier Bardem plays the most frightening psychopath since Anthony Hopkins in "Silence of the Lambs". The photography and editing are wonderful, appropriately giving off the bleak, small-town Texas atmosphere. As a Best Picture winner, it is one of the more dubious choices; clearly it isn't for everyone, given it's subject matter. As a film, it's a work of art when you consider the parts as a whole of magnificence. And lastly, in true Coen brothers fashion, the payoff in the end goes for the untraditional, this time by being anticlimactic. Understandably, this may have ticked some viewers off, but for me, it worked and made the film stronger in it's own thematic element.

Donât let the title throw you off. This movie has nothing to do with countries and/or old men. Tommy Lee Jones is really the only old guy, but it is surprising how little he has to do with the main characters or the primary story line. The reason I say that is because the movie actually follows two separate story lines that just happen to intersect at interesting moments. This film covers the action filled events that follow as a small town man happens upon the scene of a drug deal gone wrong massacre. He finds money, other people want the money, even more people want the money back, but he feels that he should keep the money at all costs. In many good ways this film keeps your attention and never really slows down. It is defiantly a movie for a more intelligent viewer, but still caters to the mob with lots of blood and bullets every few minutes.

Something to remember while watching No Country for Old Men, is that the movie takes place in the 1980âs. There are more than a few occasions where you may be watching and thinking, âHey, there is no way a hotel room costs that much!â or âThat tracking device is HUGE!â In which case you need to remember that tracking devices in the 80âs were the size of todayâs cell phones. Other than that, the time frame doesnât come into play too much. Except for of course the funny haircuts. There is also one novelty weapon that the assassin uses in the film to great extent: an compressed air-hammer. Itâs is an odd and ungainly weapon, but it seems to come in super handy for unlocking doors in a comical fashion.

Everyone, every single actor, in No Country for Old Men is excellent. I donât know if it was just the Cohen brothers genius for picking talent, or just dumb luck. I favor the former as being the truth. Tommy Lee is very solid playing a small town sheriff who is now wondering why he is where he is in life. Josh Brolin does great work as the films main character. Even though we know pretty much everything about his life, he still remains a fairly entertaining and mysterious character. Woody Harrelson is only in the movie for a short time, but actually does some good dramatic work in such a short period. The big surprise is that the movieâs villain, played by the virtually unknown Javier Bardem, steals the show. He has a terribly low voice, and a fantastic ability to hold a scene on his shoulders. Other characters in the movie do little more than just react to him and his lines. His portrayal is absolutely believable and defiantly Oscar worthyâ¦and after checking I see that he did in fact win for Best Supporting Actor.

**Final Note**
An interesting thing about this film are the endings. The first is a description of a dream, as told by one of the main characters. Itâs extremely vague and takes from the movies secondary story line. I think most people will miss the meaning. The same is true for the end of the main story line, even though I felt it was more obvious. I donât want to give away anything about the end of the film, but I will say that it isnât what you would expect. That being said, you still wont see it coming. Itâs not a Hollywood âtwistâ or anythingâ¦just an odd change of pace. Comparing this to other Best Picture nominees that I have seen, itâs leaps and bounds ahead of the other choices. A masterful piece of American cinema. The Coen brothers have given us a film worthy of the title of greatest of 2007 with this dark, powerful, and deep movie. The film feels quiet because everything is subtle - key story elements are told sometimes in only single shots. Jones' character is the glue that holds the story of cat-and-mouse together with his age and experience, and if it were not for the slow pacing and the stories that Tommy Jones told, none of the movie would have made any sense. The acting in general, especially Javier Bardem as the dark, icy assassin, is a wonder to behold. Even the beginning speech by Jones is spoken with such vocal precision that it leaves the perfect mark. In summary, the movie taps deep into the human spirit and shows the colder side of Texas in the 80's. The movie has a lot of unexpected movie devices that are very rarely seen, and the ending is very abrupt, but after meditiating on the film, I realized that these were the right choices to make. The message of the movie, if there even is one, is the lesson learned through the experience of age. Ending the movie any other way would have missed the point entirely.

Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, and Tommy Lee Jones star in this awesome tour de force of a movie and real return to form for the Coen Brothers.

Brolin stars as Llewellyn Moss, a man whose moral fortitude is tested when he stumbles on a failed drug handoff and steals $2m.  Later on he returns to the scene to remove the drugs for his own gain and sparks off an unforeseen turn of events.  By tipping off the Mexican drug cartel he attracts the attention of Anton Chigurh - wonderfully played by Bardem portraying a particularly cold and homicidal killer with a penchant for existential analysis and a strange morality.  The remaining 90 minutes follows Chigurh endlessly stalking the money and Moss eliminating any obstacles in his path and anyone able to link his identity to the case.

Brolin plays the ultimate badass in this film.  Bardem - as stated - takes a role that could easily have sidelined a lesser actor and truly makes it a memorable performance worthy of the skin crawls an audience will feel; and sporting the kind of haircut last seen on early 80's panel shows.  But it's Jones who plays, for me, the best role of the piece.  The aging Texan Sheriff is laid back and shares wisdom with a somewhat idiotic deputy completely inept at detecting sarcasm.  His humour is dark and often dry and injects the Coen's trademark humour throughout the movie.

The audience - as no doubt is happening throughout - were speechless at the end of the film, evidently not aware of the book's quite sudden stop, but it truly is in keeping with the whole tone of the movie.  The story is not about the relationship with Chigurh and Moss, but with Jones and his place in the world.

I was stunned by Deakins cinematography and the sheer desolation of the colours of the Texan wastelands and sheer lonliness of the shots, but also in the almost complete lack of soundtrack.  It truly is an inspired piece of work and almost a must for any serious fan of cinema, and not the often confused attempts that Hollywood makes when trying to interpret stories for art.  This truly is the Coen's making art.  I loved it.  Moving and disturbing, thought provoking and makes you question your own moral compass.  Not quite a masterpiece, but damn close.

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]No Country For Old Men - The Coen Brothers (2008)[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]A brutal eclipse of modern-day crime-thrillers, Ethan and Joel Coens 'No Country For Old Men' paints a disturbingly violent and beautiful image of the developing slippery slope in which society is slowly falling down.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]Starting with visually stunning shots of the baron landscape which becomes a staple of the whole film, the Coen's quickly and vividly materialize 'No Country For Old Men' into one of the most tense and suspenseful films of the last ten years. It quickly advances into a vicious chase across Texas as the deviously psychotic hired-hand in Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) attempts to track down Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a back-ward country boy who happened to stumble upon a Mexican drug deal gone bad and help himself to the $2.4million left in the dying hands of the last hombre standing, which sets into motion a series of unstoppable and deadly events of which gives ageing Sherriff Tom Ed Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) a chance to reflect upon what he's doing and who in today's modern world, he's facing.[/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]From the moment Tommy Lee Jones mutters "I've been a Sherriff of this town for twenty-five years" to his final profound epilogue at the end of the film, the acting throughout is sustained at a very high rate. Javier Bardem in particular, is fantastic as the psychotic, no-nonsense, pure incarnation of evil; hired-hitman Anton Chigurh (however he does have principles in a very funny sort of way...). Every time Bardem is on-screen, his presence radiates throughout the whole film as you know that death is just around corner, while Brolin plays his counter-part to-a-tee, a fearless redneck living out in the desert sands of Texan outback, who is willing to fight Chigurh and the Mexicans to the last-strands of death for the drug money, and is willing to put his wife, the delectable Kelly MacDonald, in the firing line of those around him too.  [/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Roger Deakins beautiful cinematography, of the baron wasteland which all the events of the film are laid out, supports Cormac McCarthy's adapted novel brilliantly. The Coen's decision to adapt the novel, with little-to-no tinkering allowed the full beauty of such a deep and thought-fuelled novel to come to life in only the way in which Ethan and Joel Coen could. In an age of CGI and 'green scenes', it's nice to see such an articulated film that ticks every single box for the basic fundamentals of film-making and in such a thought-provoking way too. 'No Country' throws you in at the moral and ethical deep-end and with no back-story, asks you to make a decision, and its the Coens finest film to date.[/size][/font]

A philosophical criminal film with a style of great horror! The atmosphere created by Coen Brothers is super, and makes me have a great frightening, dark and anxious feeling. It is an unusual criminal film, which you cannot get any wanted endings or story modes as those films of Matt Damon/ Tom Cruise/ George Clooney or any film produced by popular directors such as Martin Scorsese. You have to pay double attention to every shot and detail told in the film, otherwise you cannot get all of the plots, or even you need not ask the directors why the story is happened or ended like this, because it is somehow an artistic plus philosophical criminal film, which needs you to sit down and think about it after coming out from the cinema, instead of getting any excitement or entertainment.

What I would demerit the most must be those film critics and the Chinese translated name! Those bloody murdering scenes or the riddle-like storyline applauded by the critics is not the main themes either. The most appreciable points are those philosophical meanings behind the scenes and the way how Coen Brothers create such tensed atmosphere and anxiety. The Chinese translated names no matter in Taiwan/ Mainland/ HK are so bad that they can only mislead the audiences before they enter cinemas. I think those simple 5 English words are actually the most appropriate description for the Coen spirit in the film.

The Coen philosophy of existentialism is expressed thoroughly in the film, and I think it is the only reason why the film can take over 80 awards all over the world. Though I think it would be a bit over-praised (due to such great number of awards), it is still one of the best films in recent years. Undoubtedly, Coen Brothers did a great task in rethinking about the Nietzsche's Superman ideas through the role of Javier Bardem, and at the same time they keep asking how and whether men can decide their own fates. Lastly, Coen Brothers keep leading us to helpless exclamations for all uncontrolled stuffs happened in life. When Tommy L. Jones is talking about his comments and philosophy, I have no wonder why I would go back to an old Chinese idiom: Men will change; Moon will turn full... as Tommy L. Jones wondered why teens would dye their heads into green ones, he in fact cannot understand, and you? Coen may ask: Can you catch up the pace of the change of our world? I believe that is why the film is called NO COUNTRY for old men.

 But beyond this - all the praise for being some "deep commentary on social issues" and whatnot I find a bit forced. There is nothing mainstream about Oscar Best Picture winner No Country for Old Men, so donât expect a crowd-pleaser.  

Unorthodox in its pacing, derisive humor, thought-provoking sequences and uh, weaponry, directors Ethan and Joel Coen leave a lot for the audienceâs interpretation (reportedly more illuminated in the book by Cormac Macarthy) but throws in a number of memorable scenes.  

Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin)	is a hunter that stumbles upon a case of cash from a drug-deal gone wrong. He makes the mistake of returning to the scene of the crime and the hunter becomes the hunted: by Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), the police led by Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) and the Mexican mafia.

Bardem deserves his Best Supporting Actor Oscar. You will think twice about laughing at a guy with a bowl cut again, nor someone that seems to innocently be holding a gas tank with a hose. He will also come to mind the next time you encounter a coin toss. In fact, his character steals so much from the rest of the movie that his face is all this movieâs poster has to fill. 

Not that the rest of the cast donât deliver. Itâs just that it unravels so slowly, itâs only in scenes where he appears that you sit up and really watch. Jones surprisingly plays a weak character here, and Harrelson has a small part, too (but apparently a personal one). Kelly Macdonald is a revelation as Llewelynâs wife, Carla Jean, who stands her own against Anton in their fateful meeting.

even with the coen brothers' sweep of the oscars last night, I can't seem to get myself on the "no country for old men" bandwagon.  I thought the acting was superb, the direction stellar, but the story was disjointed and predictably unpredictable.  lemme explain, the coen's are known for their offbeat characters and anti-heroes (case in point, frances mcdormand as the pregnant sheriff in fargo), but I couldn't get past their treatment of woody harrelson's character and ultimate treatment of josh brolin's.  in being unpredictable, it became predictable to me.

motherfuckin' woody just walked up the stairs nonchalantly in the hotel lobby, and that was his undoing.  what the fuck does that do to the story?  they build up his shit like he's the next kit carson, and then dude gets blasted for walking up the stairs without looking behind him.  maybe I'm not sophisticated enough to appreciate the reality of the situation, as if most mistakes made by real folks are a simple twist of fate.  I'm not buying it.  I just don't think it added to the story.  something else that didn't add much to the story was tommy lee's soliloquy at the end.  I mean wtf was that shit all about?  granted, I was half asleep from working the night before watching the flick and not getting any sleep, but that kind of cryptic, overdrawn dialogue draws my ire.  some people blow it off as eh, it's the coen brothers, some accept it and attribute some kind of artistic sensibility to it, but I thought it was unnecessary and anti-climactic.

I'm usually someone who digs the anti-hero, but in this case, javier bardem's air-gun wielding character scared the shit outta me so much that I couldn't latch on to him.  I did dig josh brolin's character, from going back to give the obviously dying guy in the truck water, to his killer scene on the pay phone with javier's character, where he banged the shit outta that phone (how many of us have done that shit with a pay phone?  I know I have, most likely because I was forced to use a pay phone, and subject my earlobes to that soupy bacteria that belies all pay phone earpieces).  which is why I hated the anti-climactic nature of killing off his character without the classic western confrontation with the bad guy (although that scene with javier waiting in his motel room, with the look of someone who had just been ass-raped by the devil himself, was raw as a motherfuck).

call me old-fashioned, but I want my story to be wrapped up in a nice little package with a big red bow.  this story came in a fucked up, half-opened box, strewn haphazardly with duct tape, and pissed on by a three-legged dog.  anyways, here's what I did love about it:  javier bardem's sit-down scenes were fucking awesome, and had you at the edge of your own seat.  the "call it friend-o" scene was amazing, and the gas station clerk should have gotten a best supporting actor nod for that alone.

Wow. As I had expected, superb. Exquisitely paced, drawing you in and hooking you with the toned-down reveal of the plot's core, and captivating introduction of Javier Bardem's startlingly cold yet rounded and entirely genuine psychopathic antagonist, then relentlessly pounding onward to the climax, (much like said psychopath) only to ebb tantalisingly away - delicately open enough to maintain the sense of the story world's ongoing reality, and perhaps tease the viewer slightly, whilst tying up all the loose ends in the process.

Gloriously, and unlike just about every other film I've seen - no one feels safe. In almost every scene, there's a genuine tension that one of the major players could be knocked off. The benefit, I suppose, of having so many strong characters to jump between. I also loved the way the mexicans weaved their way through the story, popping to the fore intermittently to make their presence known. And Tommy Lee Jones is frequently hilarious, in fact, the dialogue as a whole is fantastic. Perhaps the best I can say is simply that even though there really was no call to make the film any longer, (and, indeed, it shouldn't have been...) I would absolutely love to see considerably more of all the characters. Shame it wasn't a longer TV drama, then they could have really let us get our teeth into the characters they've created and the world they inhabit. Still, I can hardly mark them down for that.

There is only one thing I can really hold against the film - and that's the water. It softens the blow slightly that Brolin's character actually states he knows how stupid he's being, and of course, people do plenty of stupid things - but would anyone really do anything quite that stupid...? Not enough of a stumbling block to even knock half a star off, though, and of course, it wouldn't be much of a film otherwise.

"No Country for Old Men" is a masterpiece.  Based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy and adapted for the big screen by the Coen brothers (I'm sure their mother called them Joel and Ethan),  it is a tense, suspenseful thriller with three superb lead performances from Josh Brolin, Javier Barden and Tommy Lee Jones. The pacing of this film is perfect - downright Hitchockian, and while it centers around a large sum of money, "No Country" is ultimately a character study that explores moral choices in a world full of moral uncertainty.  Javier Barden is absolutely chilling as a ruthless killer so inexplicably evil that he leaves the other characters (and the audience) dumbfounded.  "No Country for Old Men" is as stark as it's West Texas setting, and very violent to boot, but it's a movie that people will be studying and discussing for years to come.  A great piece of American cinema.

Combine the "humor and joy of murder" with the "maddeningly slow sensibility of tension" then throw in the Coen Brothers "unbelievably wonderful filmmaker's sense to completely remove the film's climax" and you have this year's "best picture". I'm going to guess that the majority of the good ratings are rating the performance of Javier Bardem and not necessarily the movie he's in. Javier Bardem portrayed an unstoppable psycho killer. He was the bogeyman, a horror movie villain as James Bond gimmick weapon assassin. This should not suggest that he did not completely embody this sociopath in a way that deserves recognition but I have several issues with the film as a whole. I've never read the novel but I imagine that it is extremely poignant and shows incredible patience. This film is built on a simple idea... Llewellyn goes back with the water jug... no one is some kind of super tracker in this film... it's just full of men that won't stop. If Josh Brolin takes that bag of money grabs his wife, gets her mother and buys three cash tickets anywhere they would be gone. If he'd given his wife the money on the bus and just kept enough to find out who's following them at least she'd have gotten away. Who doesn't look in the bag? Who doesn't flip through to see how much cash it is? Even if you're just checking to see if its booby trapped money? Now I've been told that the missing gun battle when Llewellyn dies and the psycho finds the money is missing in the novel as well. So I've seen at least one review where the person was angry at the Coens for skipping the film's climax. I don't have issue with that, I just think that in a novel you can skip a basic story element but in a limited time frame visual story like a film you can't. That suggests a poor choice of novel to adapt not an issue with the novel itself. Then throw in the fact that the Coens are very capable at constructing a sense of dramatic tension but then throw in cartoonish death and ridiculously unfunny humor. This is another in a long line of movies the Coens should not have been associated with. It's not funny, its not a good story for film and it's just boring to watch the Terminator in this film.  Amp up the craziness and turn it into a grindhouse style camp modern western and I'd have found the humor acceptable. Tone down the farcical nature of the killing and give the death scenes a moderate sense of dignity and I'd be fine. Otherwise you have movie with no release of the tension and no humor to the comedy. I am also tired of these movies and their use of horror movie elements as false excellent direction. I am tired of "boo" cuts, silent to loud sound sharps and forced audience point of view in these "great works of art" when horror films are doing exactly the same thing. Hopefully this will be the last time I ever let someone convince me that this is the Coen Brothers movie I'll actually like and that I should watch it. Anyway all said: You like Fargo, O Brother Where Art Thou?, or Blood Simple and you'll likely enjoy this film. If you're like me and dislike the Coens this won't be like Match Point was for the anti-Woody Allen set; where it is something different that you may enjoy despite his past films. This is more of the same from the Coens... enjoy.

The 80 film to win Best Picture at the Academy Awards, [b]No Country for Old Men[/b], brought to us by the Coen brothers, better known for [b]Fargo[/b], is a film definitely worth seeing for many reasons.
 
[img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_06.jpg[/img]
 
Even do my favorite film to win at the Oscars was [b]Juno[/b], there's no denying [b]No Country [/b]has enough potential to get the praise. This is the Coen's best picture since [b]Fargo[/b], and there's plenty to admire from it. First of all, the Coen's direction is brilliant, apparently they work as one, and there's not a single flaw to seek for in the film, this thanks also to its amazing screenplay. 
 
[b]No Country[/b] is also a beauty to look at. Outstanding cinematography. And there's also the fact that it's, for most of the time, a silent film. No music, and some long parts without even a sound other than the wind. Such interesting features make [b]No Country [/b]a different experience to enjoy, not to mention the plot is clever and appealing enough to have our full attention on the screen. There are many suspenseful and tense segments in the film that had me on the edge of my seat, something I really appreciated, since those parts were my favorites, highlighting the hotel scene.
 
[img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1183459/photo_04.jpg[/img]
 
Last, but not least, this year's best acting performance of the year, Javier Bardem, who doesn't only scares the hell out of me during the film, but also leaves in me a permanent feeling of paranoia. The guy really becomes Anton, probably one of the best villains in cinema history. I was speechless by Bardem's job. An incredible cast backs him up as well, including Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones, Kelly Macdonald, and Woody Harrelson, in a small, yet cool role.
 
What keeps me from giving this film a perfect rating, is the fact that, I don't know why, but there were parts during the whole experience where I got really bored, specially the ones with Tommy Lee Jones talking. And, I definitely wasn't a fan of the ending.
 
[b]No Country for Old Men [/b]is one of the biggest acheivements in modern cinema history. Obviously a must-see.

What can I possibly say about this modern classic that hasn't already been said? Well, for starters, i'll simply say- I LOVE this film!! I've always thought the Coen brothers a bit over-rated, especially after having seen "O Brother, Where Art Thou?" and "Fargo". Bad films those two aren't, but I just never saw the big fuss; and while you can obviously see the thought and talent put into the works, I just never cared much for either. Well, my view may not be 100% changed now, but the brilliance and sheer genius of this film cannot be praised enough! Many of the scenes are so flawlessly constructed, you simply want them to go on. With nimble character work, tight editing, picturesque cinematography and a towering performance from Bardem, the nightmarish quality of the thing is etched in your mind from the first shot. You'll find yourself squirming several times, especially when the demonic Anton Chigurh is on screen. Having previously read McCarthy, it can be said that he's a difficult writer to adapt. But the Coen's nail it, and you can see and feel McCarthy's Biblical cadences and bleakness bursting through. Stomach-churning, uber-violent, well-paced, nail-biting and highly entertaining, this film is the embodiment of where we are as a society and how dehumanized we have become. Having the power to disturb the mind and frighten the soul, it is a perfect model of pitch, modulation and craft.

The plot of No Country For Old Men is easily summarized.  A Texas workingman stumbles on the aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong, and walks away with two million dollars in cash.  A psychopathic hitman will do anything to regain possession of the money.

For those familiar with the Coen Brothers' work, I found it reminded me a little of Fargo. However, I found it far more austere and more poetic.  Josh Brolin plays the role of the 'lucky' man who walks away with the money, while  Javier Bardem is excellent and chilling as the man hunting the cash.  Tommy Lee Jones is in his element as the local Sheriff who is weary of the never-ending stream of ugliness that he sees in his job.

The title is taken from William Butler Yeats' poem Sailing To Byzantium and is not explained explicitly, but the movie deals clearly and subtlely with themes of mortality, fate, and greed.  As in Fargo, No Country is populated by characters - particularly Jones and Brolin's - that are flawed and human, who try to deal with their lives and the situations that begin to spiral out of control as Bardem's maniacal assassin moves among them.

In reading the trivia section on IMDB, I was pleased to see that the movie was very faithful to Cormac McCarthy's novel.  This movie proves that talented filmmakers can successfully adapt a book without ruining it.

A word on the ending.  I had heard reviews (and indeed read some below) that criticize the ending.  Like Seven, the whole point of the movie is that life is fragile, there are bad people and good people, and no one escapes death in the end.  Some people challenge fate head-on, and some give up in the face of overwhelming despair.  Jones' monologue at the end is an allegory.  Against the starkness of Bardem's angel of death, it's pretty clear what the movie was about.

I actually neglected to write this review until now, even though I saw this movie when it was in theatres several months ago. However, I'm going to pretend like I wrote it then, so that I don't look like some douchebag riding the oscar wave, because this has been one of my favorite movies since I saw it in the theatre. The interesting thing is that it didn't feel that way right away. I went back to my room, and thought about this movie for at least a couple hours. Then, the next morning when I woke up, all I could think was how awesome it was. It is truly a unique movie experience. There is literally no music throughout the duration of the film, not even for ambience, and it has an extremely unnerving effect that is incomparable to other movies that I have seen. Also, the fact that the events are so much like "what if this movie was shot in real life?" make it that much more watchable, not like it's some supervillian chasing some superhero, who's running just so he can win in the end anyway. This movie keeps you guessing the whole way along, and you can truly never guess what's next, even when you think it's over, and also when you think it isn't. Like I've said before, if you want a movie-going experience like nothing you've ever seen before, go see this film.

Nominated for eight Academy Awards, No Country For Old Men is one of the two front runners for this year's Oscars along with Paul Thomas Anderson's There Will Be Blood. Head-to-head, the latter emerges the victor. However, No Country For Old Men is by no means a pushover, giving Anderson's film a genuine run for its money. Directed and written for the screen by the immensely gifted Oscar-winning filmmakers The Coen Brothers (Fargo, The Big Lebowski) and based on the Cormac McCarthy novel of the same name, this motion picture is made to win awards in mind.

For their latest masterpiece, The Coen Brothers make the decision to stay with their tried-and-tested route, using conservative storytelling and filming techniques that serve the plot well although it lacks the scope and inventiveness of Anderson's direction in There Will Be Blood. The thing I love about the Coen Brothers is their ability to crank up the suspense to immensely unbearable levels with absolutely minimal use of sound or music. The material here presents them with many opportunities to perfect their blend of silent suspense.

There are three main characters played by Josh Brolin, Spanish actor Javier Bardem, and the evergreen Tommy Lee Jones. All give sterling performances with the standout being Bardem whose character, Anton Chigurh, is perhaps the most frightening ever, since Anthony Hopkins' cannibalistic Hannibal Lecter in Silence Of The Lambs. Armed with a high-pressure gas canister as a murderous weapon and wearing a mop-like hairstyle, Chigurh is a villain who does not know the meaning of mercy. You wouldn't want to run into him in a crowded shopping mall, let alone in a dark alley at night.

No Country For Old Men can be said to be a modern Western, an update for the next generation of movie-goers. The unexpected ending may be a sore point for some, but it will be highly appreciated by discerning viewers who demand something more though-provoking than what current movies can offer. The Coen Brothers' comeback film will be likely to dominate during Oscar night. There's no doubt that No Country For Old Men is one of the top ten films of 2007.

SCORE: 8.5/10

I believe it to be the greatest film of the modern era outside my three favourite movie sagas. (Star Wars, Bond and Lord of the Rings).
The lack of a real musical score added to the atmosphere and tension on multiple occassions. The action sequences are thankfully held back with a seeming philosophy of "less is more" and the portrayal of Chigurh was eerie, menacing, intimidating and creepy all at the same time; you never knew what he was going to do next.
Tommy Lee Jones added some lightening humour here and there yet made his character sympathetic and involved at the same time.
On a critical note, the plot is never really explained and the main protagonist seemed to lack empathy somehow; probably because at the end of the day he was the thief.
But the film is pulled off so stylistically strong that these pitfalls somehow seem irrevelant in the scheme of things; guy a is being chased by guy b cos he's got some money that aint his. Simple premise leading to an extremely well put together film.
*Semi-spoiler, read at your own risk!*
Some would criticise the greatly ambiguous ending as being unfulfilling, but it seemed to fit in with the general...not dark, but shadey tone the film had. The ending monologue is a great turn from Jones who has always been a favourite actor of mine anyways and while it doesn't elaborate or conclude the plot we'd been hooked on for the previous two hours, it did put a smile on my face. I can see though why some would criticise it and I believe it to be a bit like marmite; you're gonna love it or hate it.
As I said, outside of my fave movie sagas I would certainly promote this movie as the greatest film of the modern era through and through. It was that good.

(for the time being, I am not going to give this movie a numbered rating. I'm going to let it sink in before I come to a decision).

I want to start off this review by paraphrasing Albert Einstein: 
If I can't explain it in my review, then I probably didn't understand it to begin with.
If you've seen the movie and you've read my review, you will get why I wanted to mention that.

This is a Coen Brother's movie. If you have seen any of their other movies, then you might have a slight clue as to what you're getting yourself into. When it comes to directing a movie, they are just something else. Something I can't quite put my finger on. This might seem like an odd thing to say in a review, but when you go to watch a Coen Brother's movie, you have to adjust to a different state of mind. I don't want to say that you should think outside the box, but you have to be prepared for things not to make sense.

The first time I saw this movie was when it was released in 2007. If I'm not mistaken, this was the first Coen Brother's movie I had seen. I watched Burn After Reading in 2008 when it was released, and I'm pretty sure I watched Fargo and The Big Lebowski after that. I can say with certainty that I liked this movie more the first time I saw it. That's not to say that I don't like it now, but I guess my thoughts on it have faded as the years have passed. 

I would not call this movie brilliant. But this movie deserves praise because I think this movie is the perfect example of a slow-paced movie that keeps you on your toes. It's not a full-out action movie with loud bangs and screeching tires. It's slow, dark, and serious. There were parts that I got really sucked into. It left me with a lump in my throat and me holding my breathe. The movie did that very well.

Javiar Bardem (as Anton Chigurh), Tommy Lee Jones (as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell), and Josh Brolin (as Llewelyn Moss) all did a fantastic job. Going into this movie I'd have to say that I thought TLJ would by my favourite, but coming out, I can't say I liked any of the characters. Usually a movie has distinct characters with regards to being good or bad. When you think about it, you don't really know who the 'good guy' is. Yes, TLJ's is a sheriff, but aside from being a law enforcement representative, he doesn't really do a whole lot of good in this movie. The viewer doesn't get any explanation as to why Anton Chigurh is after the money, and we also don't know anything about Llewelyn Moss. I didn't know who, if anybody, I was supposed to root for. And I think this is adds to the confusion of the overall movie and why people have said they don't understand it.

Usually when you watch a movie you can figure out the moral of the story by the time you leave the theatre. The weird thing about this movie is that even when you sleep on it, and give it some more thought, it's still hard to figure out. I wasn't entirely sure what the point was. When I did think about it a bit more, I came to the conclusion that the moral is very ambiguous. It's up to each individual person who sees this movie to take away whatever they see fit. This is a movie that's hard to wrap your head around. And I'm not the only one that thinks that. I read a few reviews on IMDB that said they didn't understand it either. I don't want to say I didn't understand it because I believe I did. I understood it in a way that my brain allowed me to understand it. Again, my interpretation of it, is that every viewer will understand this movie in different ways. 

Like I said earlier, trying to explain a Coen Brother's film is not an easy task. This movie isn't for everyone and I'd be very selective about who I'd recommend it to.

When you sit back and really think of how many films come out each year you will probably loose count, there are a lot.
So when it comes time for something like the academy awards how do you determain which of all these films is worthy of the award title "Best Picture"?
Well watch No Country For Old Men and find out.

Thats right, the award for best picture of the year 2007 went to the Coen Brothers directed No Country For Old Men.
The story follows welder and hunter Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) who discovers two million dollars at the scene of a drug runners exchange gone violently wrong.
Taking the money Moss  is then hunted by psychopathic killer, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who dispassionately murders nearly every rival, bystander and even employer in his pursuit of his quarry and the money. Meanwhile Sherrif Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) oversees the investigation as he tries to understand the changing world and struggles to face the sheer enormity of the crimes he is attempting to thwart.

The Cinematography in this movie is brilliant. It is so good you could take a picture of almost every scene and put it in an art gallery.
Some highly suspensful scenes aided with interesting camera angles and sounds.
Great acting all round with Javier Bardem almost stealing every scene he is in. He plays the character perfectly. Perhaps one of the most memorable scenes is the coin toss scene. It is this moment we really see what makes this character tick or rather how crazy he is and just how intimidating the character can be.

Flip a coin, and no matter where it comes up, go see No Country For Old Men.

After a few average and even some bad movies the Cohen Brothers return to greatness with their new movie "No Country For Old Men" which is their best movie since "Fargo" and their second best movie ever after "Fargo".  "No Country For Old Men" Is about Llewelyn Moss(Josh Brolin), a welder and a hunter from Texas who one day, while hunting, discovers the remains of several drug runners who have all killed each other in an exchange gone violently wrong. Rather than report the discovery to the police, Moss decides to simply take the two million dollars for himself. This puts Anton Chigurh(Javier Bardem), a maniac killer, after him.
 Anton Chigurh, I will say, represent the evil in this movie, Chigurh is a maniac who loves to kill people (with a cattle gun, by the way), he pulls the trigger very easily, probably just for the fun of it and whenever he gets bored by just killing them he spices it up by flipping a coin and making the victim to "call it" and if like he isn't scary enough he has this haircut which I believe that in many years from now will be the most memorable thing from this movie.
  
 And the world is full with people like him, if not exactly maniacs like Chigurh, people like the Mexicans drags dealers. even our protagonist is not completely good. And the good have no choice but to fight the evil and he can give a hell of a fight. And this is the greatest thing in "No Country For Old Men", the Cohen Brothers are not like Sheriff Ed Tom Bell(Tommy Lee Jones) and his friend (another sheriff) that whine about the world and say things like "Anytime you quit hearing "sir" and "ma'am", the end is pretty much in sight.",The Cohen Brothers know the evil have always been in this world. it's in the Babel, it existed in the Wild West and it exists today, and the movie ,in my opinion, is quite optimistic in his believe that the good can win. But I talk of good and evil in such a contradictive way, when the movie doesn't talk about it in this way at all. The Cohen Brothers know things are not so different; this is real life over here not the Power Rangers!
  
  
 [img]http://www.ugo.com/images/galleries/nocountryforoldmen_filmtv/no-country-for-old-men-1.jpg[/img]
  
  
 The direction is absolutely flawless; the Cohen Brothers succeed to keep the movie so thrilling without almost any kind of music, the silence in this film is captivating. And the cinematography by Roger Deakins is magnificent, the movie contain some of the greatest most hypnotizing shots I have seen in a lot of time.
 The acting is fantastic by all the members of the cast, but especially by Javier Bardem who has created the most vicious, chilling, and evil villain since Anthony Hopkins Hannibal Lecter.
  
 I still don't know if I want to call "No Country For old Men" a masterpiece", I dont like to use this word so easily and I believe you need to watch a movie at least twice before you decide such a thing. But it's absolutely the best movie of the year and one of the best movies in years. Intelligent, brilliant, insightful and most important the Cohen Brothers are back!

Best Picture? Best Direction? Give me a break. This is by no means a bad film, but it's got the Coens slapped all over it. From the dry, desolate feeling that somehow lacks dread, to the seminal-screwball humour of the film. There's no doubt about the performances however, and Javier Bardem no doubt deserved his many accolades for this, already one of the most iconic "angel of death" characters in moden cinema. But to begrudge a certain film starring Daniel Day-Lewis of the top award? I mean, seriously. No Country For Old Men was a political set up. To win what it did was merely an act of rewarding the legendary Coens for their career. Now, it could just be the fact that I don't like the Coen Brothers. Am I the only one on the planet who thought Fargo was over-rated and bordering on garbage? I just dislike the dryness of all their films (sans Big Lebowski, by far their best movie), and this is the epitomé of that. Now, there was a lot to keep you glued to the screen throughout. The pacing is fine. The shocks are sharply handled. The violence is impactful. But there's just some kind of soul missing from it. Tommy Lee Jones attempts to give it the soul, and to an end achieves it, but beyond the many interpretations of the film itself, the execution feels somewhat disjointed. But then again, that's vintage Coens for you. An interesting film, but by no means a There Will Be Blood. Doesn't even rate as a top film for 2007 for me.

Right up until the debut of [b]No Country For Old Men[/b], writing-directing wunderkind brothers Ethan and Joel Coen had been having a rough time of it - their last couple of films, released over three years ago, had been savaged critically. Savagely funny remake [url="http://www.rottentomatoes.com/vine/journal_view.php?journalid=110893&entryid=118827&view=public"][i]The Ladykillers[/i][/url] and quirky take on a conventional rom-com [i]Intolerable Cruelty[/i] had been deemed disappointments and commercial sellouts - neither of which is a point of view I necessarily agree with - especially compared to the quirky genius of their earlier works. The genre-defying [b]NCFOM[/b] couldn't have come at a better time then - part Western, part crime thriller, part character study, and infused with the Coens' trademark brand of wry, subversive humour, this film has garnered the kind of critical reception most film-makers can only dream of... not to mention a Best Picture Oscar just a week ago.
 
 War vet Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon the bloody scene of a shootout - surrounded by gunned-down Mexicans and dogs, he finds one last man, still breathing and begging for [i]agua [/i](water) and also a suitcase full of money. He brings the cash home, which he shares with his bewildered wife Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald), but doesn't yet realise that he has on his trail Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a cold-blooded psychopath with a taste for death and a pneumatic air-gun to bring that about. The cat-and-mouse game that ensues, as Llewelyn evades the relentless Anton as best as an ordinary man can, is traced by aging sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), whose wistful voiceover - remembering the sheriffs that came before him and the duty they're all pledged to carry out - provides the film a narrative thread that goes beyond the pure thrill of the chase. Which man will be left standing, bloodied and broken, at the end of this bruising showdown?
 
 The bulk of [b]NCFOM[/b] is devoted to Chigurh's hunt for Llewelyn, and what a hunt it is - weighed down by a tracking device he doesn't at first realise is hidden among the bills, Llewelyn sends Carla Jean off but goes on the run anyway. Ducking through motels and crossing the American border doesn't get him away from killing machine Chigurh, however: but what a thrilling escape it is. Having never really devoted much attention to the action thriller genre, the Coens go all out here to recreate moments of utterly heart-in-moment tension: though Llewelyn and Chigurh hardly ever share the screen, the scenes when they go head to head with each other are nailbitingly suspenseful. Whether it's Chigurh bursting into Llewelyn's motel room and gunning down everyone in his way, or Llewelyn ducking down behind a car to hide from a rain of pneumatic gunfire before putting his own gun to work - and actually nicking some of Chigurh's flesh. There is nothing more terrifying than to sit in the dark alongside Llewelyn, heart in your mouth as you hear Chigurh stump up the stairs and his shadow flits across the light streaming through under the door. Chigurh's choice of weapon, one of the most innovative and devastatingly quiet in film assassin history, adds only to the frisson of horror that slides up and down your spine every time he heads toward a hapless victim, nozzle in hand and death on the mind.
  
 In fact, the film is at its best when it focuses on Llewelyn and Chigurh - on the one hand, you're painted a picture of the most stubborn, innovative ordinary man alive, pitted against a sociopath who has never failed in tracking down his prey and collecting all kinds of cannon fodder along the way. Llewelyn will not rest until he wins or tragedy catches up with him, a fact made abundantly clear to his beleaguered wife... to the extent that his dogged success at eluding Chigurh impresses even the mysterious vigilante-for-hire Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson), who is hired to bring Chigurh to heel when it becomes clear that the latter's bloodthirstiness is spiralling out of control, and is one of the few men who have survived actually coming face to face with Chigurh. Brolin, who's been in an impressive run of good films recently (e.g., [url="http://www.rottentomatoes.com/vine/journal_view.php?journalid=110893&entryid=431600&view=public"][i]Death Proof[/i][/url]), has turned in another superlative performance, mixing Llewelyn's determination with the few brief moments demonstrating his humanity - he is, after all, damned because his guilt for not providing a dying man with water leads him back to a crime scene that gives Chigurh the first clue to tracking him down. 
 
 Powerful presence though Brolin may be, the film undoubtedly belongs to Bardem, resplendently evil with a haircut reminiscent of a demented friar. When I said [b]NCFOM[/b] is a character study, I meant that it was really an examination of Chigurh - which is something rather fascinating and unusual, since who else but the noir-minded Coens would devote so much attention to the study of a psychopathic serial murderer? Well, at least we get a really artful portrait here, all guts and gore and bloody-mindedness: the camera delights in focusing on Bardem's creepily emotionless face as Chigurh offers life and death in a coin toss to the owner of a gas station who's rubbed him the wrong way, a poor innocent old man who has no idea what kind of choice he's being given. When he is finally confronted on the way he has always lived and hunted, with an utter disdain for the value of human life, Chigurh's inability to articulate his guiding principles echoes the sense of tortured destiny (yes, even for a character who is essentially a serial murderer) that underpins the entire film. This, of course, is brought into stark relief by the fate Chigurh meets at the end - for what could bring him to his knees but the careless, blind hand of Providence? Bardem is fabulous as Chigurh, possibly the scariest and most chilling film presence I've seen outside of a horror movie - whenever he arrives onscreen, whether limping from the wound inflicted by Llewelyn which he painfully (memorably!) patched up by himself, or stalking with purpose, air-gun in hand, he is black as pitch and just as mysterious. Without a doubt, one of the most deserving Oscar acting wins in recent years.
 
 Jones' segment of the film is a little more difficult to appreciate, and probably the only part of the film that can be said to be somewhat flawed. I enjoyed it, don't get me wrong - Sheriff Ed's folksy, spot-on humour is on occasion a welcome ray of light as he traces the dusty paths beaten down by Llewelyn and Chigurh: whether he's admonishing his charmingly naive deputy Wendell (Garret Dillahunt) on how criminals commit crimes or commenting on the state of the world these days after reading a particularly distressing article in the paper. He forms the counterpoint to the other characters in the film - the righteous lawman who's still trying to live his life by a moral code long lost to people like Chigurh, Llewelyn and Carson. It's the character of Ed that makes the film a Western as well, as he joins in the chase but never quite manages to catch up to the bad guys - unfortunately, the air of wistfulness he adds to the film, although a crucial point thematically, is rather jarring in the context of the heartstopping confrontations that pepper the rest of the film. Except when he comes breathtakingly close to Chigurh in one scene, most of his appearances, especially in the later part of the film, have an almost elegaic feel that you'll either enjoy or feel frustrated by. That it's Ed's story that ends the movie means you're going to either love it, hate it, or be completely confuzzled by it.
 
 But, as a whole, [b]NCFOM[/b] is unbelievably involving - you get quickly lost in the shadows and darkness of this not-quite-noir world the Coens have conjured up with the help of Cormac McCarthy's source novel. Here it's a look at the darker side of Americana, a Wild West chase set not in the rural wilderness but nevertheless featuring gunfights and showdowns in the nameless streets of a nameless American town. Boasting the Coens' usual acerbic wit, grittier and smarter than the dialogue that graces most Hollywood films these days, this is a thoroughly deserving winner of the Best Picture Oscar - arguably not something that can be said of every film that's won the same award in the past decade...

First of all, I do not think that this Oscar-loaded film is the best Coen Brothers film ever.... It is more like a return to their roots, with blood, guns and more blood. The end of this film is the best no-way-to-end-a-film ever.  But is that bad?  Every so often, it is good to be reminded that in the battle of good against evil, there doesn't have to be a winner.  Roger Deakins' camera brings the  landscape to the fore.  My mouth felt dry from the heat and the sand, just as I got pretty cold watching Fargo. Texas plays a leading role, the Coen Brothers take it back to the wild wild west, a place where law and order can do little but pick up the bodies and seal the crime scene after the shoot'em up.  Tommy Lee Jones is on very good form, strutting his tired old dog routine around and Javier Bardem is so insanely evil that one expects to see his forked tail everytime he turns his back.  Most of all this film certainly redefines the term collateral damage.  Heads or tail? You call it.

Some films demonstrate the power of narrative.

Some films illustrate the artistry of technical precision.

Some films evoke emotions through characters brought to life by gifted performers.

Then, there are those rare gems which we recognise as masterpieces.

These movies bring an audience face to face with something so primal and powerful...that words prove insufficient in articulating their message. The art of moving pictures was invented for movies like No Country for Old Men. 

Based on a novel, the themes and issues raised take on a life of their own as each beautifully framed shot is painstakingly strung into a visual experience unlike any other in recent memory.

Some criticisms have included the lack of a coherent plot. Others have attacked it's run of the mill premise of cash, drugs and being on the run. All these criticisms miss the point. NCFOM is not about drugs and cash. And if it is about running...it isn't about Moss' (Brolin) plight. 

The film studies the human condition. It is an examination of a species running away from realities bleak and difficult to comprehend. Bardem's Oscar winning turn functions as a powerful plot and thematic device, demonstrating ordered chaos...a 'principled' force. It strips away conceptions of right and wrong and forces the viewer to confront reality as it might actually be.

The viewer sees the tightrope act between order and chaos just as Jones' sheriff sees it. A balancing act which has been going on since the dawn of time. And just like Jones...we will wake from this dream and find ourselves with an unnerving sense of unease and dread.

The Coens had a 17 year winning streak, from 1984's Blood Simple to 2001's The Man Who Wasn't There, before Intolerable Cruelty (a film i personally loved) and The Ladykillers (a film no one loved) derailed them. However, now they are back with a bang (and an Academy award!) with No Country for Old Men, an adaptation of the Cormac McCarthy novel of the same name. The film. to put it simply, is a masterpiece, even by the Coen Brothers impeccably high standards. A perfectly paced, tense thriller, with a blackly-comic streak through it's center, and 3 stunning performances from its leading men. The Coens have always delighted in the abstract and the bizarre, but this film is more in tone with there sparse debut Blood Simple. Dark and violent, the film is very naturalistic, and is virtually music-free throughout, making stunning use of silence and sound effects; the howling wind, a ringing phone, each noise is cranked up in volume to constantly unsettle the viewer. The three leading men are all superb, Tommy Lee Jone's craggy old face is perfect for the role of the town sheriff, Josh Brolin gives a career-best performance, but it is Javier Bardem who stole the plaudits (and an academy award for best supporting actor). His portrayal of Anton Chigurgh is creepy, unsettling and downright terrifying. His robotic walk, metallic voice, cold eyes and bizarre haircut give him an otherworldly quality, and his performance deserves all the acclaim it has received. Grimy, dark and violent, No Country for Old Men is a stunning film, totally deserving of the Best Picture Oscar, and a clear indication the brothers Coen are back to their best. Excellent

Man, I don't know where to start with this one. No Country For Old Men is like a film geek's wet dream. This film is brutal in portraying its characters, sparse in its direction, and it refuses to pull any punches. Thankfully, the Coen Brothers have pulled themselves up after their unsuccessful foray into mainstream comedy with Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers (I liked Intolerable Cruelty, but, whatever). This film has some very dark humorous moments, especially in the conversation exchanges between Tommy Lee Jones's cynical old sheriff and his none-too-bright deputy, but the whole thing is played straight, sans the quirky asides that the Coens usually revert to.

In the film, Josh Brolin plays Llewellyn Moss, a retired welder living in a trailer park who comes across a drug deal gone bad. At the scene, Moss finds both the drugs and $2 million. He takes the money and leaves, not knowing what he's bargaining. Javier Bardem plays Anton Chigurh, an embodiment of pure evil, who is chasing down Moss for the money.

Bardem plays Chigurh as a person completely out of touch with the world. I guess his awful haircut is a result of this disconnect. Chigurh (who the fuck can pronounce that, anyways?) carries with him a pressurized air gun that he uses to kill and to knock out the locks on doors. He is completely determined and without a hint of remorse. He knows the effects of violence and what to do to get what he wants. He does this all while following his own warped sense of righteousness. At one point, he kills a man out of principle despite giving up the money in the process.

Chigurh is the type of evil that we don't see very often. Most directors try to humanize their villains. no attempt is made to soften Chigurh. He is a bad man, he is intelligent, and very little can stop him. This is the sort of evil being that Kubrick used to do so well, whether it was a computer like HAL 9000 in 2001 or a human possessed in The Shining. At one point, Chigurh sits with a glass of milk staring straight ahead; a fashion-deprived version of Alex from A Clockwork Orange.

Both Moss and Chigurh are portrayed as men that are intelligent and driven, both by their selfish desires. However, Moss's desires are purely human, while Chigurh is a psychopath who hunts out of principle, not just for the money. One wonders where Chigurh learned to set up a drug deal of this sort, but that is beside the point. The drug deal is a MacGuffin, used to set in motion an uneven game of cat and mouse between evil and humanity.

Tommy Lee Jones also puts in his usually solid work as the disillusioned Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (beauty redneck name, eh?) as the officer assigned to the mess of a drug deal. His story may be the least interesting portion of the film (I imagine it played better in Cormac McCarthy's novel), but he still serves as a moral standpoint for which the rest of the characters act around.

As for the ending, much has been made about its ambiguousness, I would have preferred it if it had ended a few scenes earlier. The focus on the storyline involving Tommy Lee Jones only serves to demonstrate that the real interest in this film is between Moss and Chigurh.

UPDATE: I assumed that Chigurh set up the drug deal, but a friend of mine thought that he was just a retriever. It doesn't effect my opinion, as I said, the drug money is just a MacGuffin anyways.

The Coen Brother's "No Country for Old Men" is a good serial killer film. Eighty percent of it is so tightly constructed, that it is easy to scream "Masterwork!" The Coen Brothers have marvelously masterful strokes in this film. They create images (the rubber shoe marks on the floor after the strangling) and feelings (epic fright, obviously) powerfully. 

Spaniard Javier Bardem is an interesting actor. His work in "The Sea Inside" where he played a paralyzed man seeking euthanasia was shattering, bewildering, and altogether heartbreaking; he played a a complex character of daring intent. Here, in "No Country," Bardem's killing-machine character couldnÃ¢ÂÂt be more varied. His is a one-sided character---gloriously explored, but one-sided nevertheless. Bardem, a talented actor, is in a similar situation as Daniel Day Lewis, of this year's ÂÂ"There Will Be Blood": he expertly presents a character with precision, yet his character shows little or no development, remaining a one-dimensional creature. 

Much has been made about the nihilism found in this film. The Coens, and Cormac McCarthy, the author, do appear to be presenting a world where man is left without God: left to their own sin, and their own exploration of evil. These are intriguing ideas that are no so much as explored and expanded up as they are presented. 

"No Country" loses its steam in the last fifteen minutes. The film slows, picks up again, and then slows down again. The filmÃ¢ÂÂs title finally comes into play, in a very philosophical, meandering way that is fascinating; but this is ultimately a misstep that lacks much connection to the rest of the film. 

Again, "No Country for Old Men" is a very, very good serial killer film, nearly one of the best films of the year. For one of the finest serial-killer films ever made, that happened to be released the same year as "No Country," see David Fincher's "Zodiac."

Coen brothers  I loved Fargo, and became their ardent fan. Surely, I have not seen all movies directed by them, but know that they put good effort in making study-worthy movies. When I heard that they are in contention of the Oscars nominations, I was too eager and itching to see this release.

Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) finds a bag full of money - $ 2 million  among dead bodies from a place in remote outskirt desert of a Texas town, where a shootout has taken place. He gets the bag home without realizing that a maniac killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who will do anything to track Llewelyn down - would follow him. The local police Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) also track the leads. The cat and mouse game start. After enough of surprises - twists and turns we come to the end of the movie.

The movie is based on the novel (by the same name) by Cormac McCarthy. Though filmed exactly in sequence from the book, the ending is a little dampening in the sense that it is not what we expected. However, this should not to take away the fantastic movie experience one gets out of watching this movie. The script and screenplay are tight and very well adapted to its core. Coen brothers again do wonders together. For a formative student who is learning movie making, watching the movie a couple of times would greatly help. 

Among actors  Javier Bardem steals the show as a mean maniac killer. He is a delight to watch with his weirdness, especially when he is simply talking with someone. 

The music is minimal  as usual of Coen style and the editing by Coen brothers under pseudo name Roderick Jaynes is good.
