I've been looking forward to this film for some time now, though maybe not as much as some. Whilst I'm certainly an admirer of the Coen's work, I wouldn't say I was an obsessive fan, or someone who was able to quote "Blood Simple" or "Fargo" in my sleep. I admit that the buzz surrounding this probably drew me in more than the filmmakers, along with the fact that I dig Tommy Lee Jones to no end. 

To begin with... Wow. This beautifully executed piece of cinema is a joy to behold, from the moment the first Southern drawl melts out of the surround sound speakers, through to the ultimately gorgeous ending. Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin and, of course, Javier Bardem really radiate their characters through this, and I love watching a film where you forget about the actor behind the character, and just focus on the character themselves. 

It's beautiful to look at, and one can only marvel that in a film like this, every single shot has it's place. I'm sure it'd be a satisfactory effort without some of the "show boating" behind the camera, but it's to the Coen's credit that the shots work so well within the film, so much so that it's only now, an hour after the movie's ended, that I really even begin to remember stuff like that. 

Brolin refers to Bardem in this as "the ultimate bad-ass", and never has a truer word been spoken. I wouldn't wanna come across this guy in a dark alley! I personally think that a lot of the real emotion (or lack thereof, depending on how you want to look at it) is displayed through his eyes, and I'm pretty sure that if we're being fair, his eyeballs should get the Golden Globe/Oscar/whatever before the rest of him does! I'm not sure whether you want that you play the perfect pyschopath on your resume, but his sure delivers an A+ performance doing just that.

Just as a starting point, I thought this movie was "okay." Well, I'd even bump that up to "pretty good." It was just... very misleading. Theres the "story" it was supposed to have, the story you watched, and then the message that has close to nothing to do with either story. The first is a drug deal gone awry and by the norms you would expect Josh Brolin to at least survive, but guess again. He's just discovered dead in a motel doorway. Nothing spectacular or exciting, sad though it was. You just come to accept him as the protagonist at that point, and then it ends. You'd be wrong obviously because of his demise, but then you start following Tommy Lee Jones' character, who doesn't die but doesn't accomplish a whole lot. Javier Bardem gets away after a mysterious car crash that seemed intentional but never acclimated to anything important, and Tommy Lee Jones retires. He's talking to his wife over breakfast about dreams he had the previous night about his dad, and its obvious this is the revelation of the implicit meaning this film was supposed to tell, but didn't really. It would seem he's depressed about this world that makes no sense to him as a law official, and even as a human being. He explains more or less his wishes that he could have lived a simpler time with his father and they would be gallant and honored instead of, basically, life's little failures. There are also some scattered points that make hints about everyone being another one of life's little failures. Just simple nobodies, but their stories aren't explored very deeply. 

This might sound like a lot of blowhard criticism but there were a lot of things I liked about this film. The acting for one was top notch and I really think the best actor/actress awards should have been awarded to Tommy and Javier, and there should have been something awarded to the cinematographer, Roger Deakins. What I liked best about this movie was the almost Bond-esque use of creative super weapons. The fact that it was basically just bursts of compressed air, and acording to Jones' Character had a basis in livestock butchering, made Bardem's character so much more sinister, and heartless, and believable of a killer because he wasn't firing randomly in front of him. He was so much more calculating and cold than any maniac could have been. That was realy what made this movie for me.

So, final line, do I really think this film should have gotten Film of the Year -- no, not really. I do however think that It is definitely worth something for the great acting and art design that went into it. Javier, you're one of my new favorite actors!

Hunting antelope somewhere on the desolate plains of Texas, Josh Brolin happens on the remains of a drug deal gone bad. Bodies of Texans and Mexicans (and one unfortunate dog) lie riddled with bullets in a circle of pickup trucks. One truck contains a load of heroin. Another holds the sole survivor, a dying man asking for "agua." Brolin then follows a trail to another body, lying near a case containing $2 million, which Brolin nabs. The grim scene, and the fact that death follows the cash around, don't seem to bother Brolin. But later that night, his conscience and the memory of that thirsty man do. He returns to the scene with a jug of water.

That's a mistake, but not his first. Adapted from a novel by Cormac McCarthy (author of All The Pretty Horses and last year's Pulitzer-and-Oprah-approved The Road), No Country For Old Men takes place in the same harsh world as McCarthy's novels. Life can end quickly, senselessly, and grotesquely, leaving survivors shocked but wiser. But it's a world with a moral force, however mysterious and unsparing of innocence. 

Brolin has found blood money, and blood attracts blood. Soon, he's hunted by hired killer Javier Bardem, whose delicate Prince Valiant bob is more than counterbalanced by his handiness with a pneumatic slaughterhouse tool. Their chase invites the attention of one character after another (including Tommy Lee Jones' laconic, soon-to-retire small-town sheriff) as it moves them from one awkward situation to the next. 

No Country For Old Men bears McCarthy's unmistakable stamp, and the equally unmistakable mark of filmmakers Joel and Ethan Coen, making a strong return after a few years off. Their latest works as a continuation of their modern noirs Blood Simple and Fargo, but also as a shaggy-dog tale in the mold of The Big Lebowski.

Only this time, there's a trail of blood that grows darker and wider as the film winds toward a revelation about the overwhelming realness of evil, and its persistence in the modern world: Its essence changes, but not its form. As Jones prepares for retirement, he slips into talk about the way the world used to be, as opposed to the harder shape it's begun to take. (Both film and book are set, not accidentally, as the '70s give way to the '80s, and the drugs-and-money cycle of violence began to escalate.) But the ultimate vision here is of a hard world in which civilization is the aberration, and the things we fear are always waiting for an excuse to make life normal again.

MOVIE REVIEW: No Country For Old Men
Notably Starring: Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin, Woody Harrelson, and of course, Javier Bardem
Unnotably Starring: uhhhh...nobody?

Summary: Wouldn't have expected anything less from the Coen brothers, just would've asked for a better explained ending.

WOW. I mean, it's a slow-mover, yes. There's no music, there's no major action sequences, just huge wide open spaces of Texas, a drug deal gone wrong, $2 Million, and a murderous demonic serial killer named Anton Chigurh (Bardem) going keeeerazy across the desert. So yeah, my eyes kind of hurt after watching it, because I really didn't glance away from the TV....ever.

The story basically goes as follows, without giving too much away: 

The story opens with a cop (Harrelson) hauling Chigurh to jail. He plops him in his cop car, and sits a curious thing in the front seat...an oxygen tank with a long hose and a compressor at the end. Chigurh sits in the county jail, awaiting his processing, and curiously wiggiling himself out of his handcuffs. Needless to say, he escapes...

Meanwhile...

Llewellen (Brolin) is pretty much a low-life blue collar worker who's out hunting one day. He spots a circle of cars in the middle of the desert and decides to go and investigate. What he finds is a drug deal gone horribly wrong, a truck full of Mexican dope, and $2 million in a satchel. He heads home to his wife and tells her to pack up and go to her mother's. 

"What ya gonna do?"
"I reckon I'll do something stupid, but hell, I'll do it anyway."

"Tell my mother I said hello."
"Your mother's dead."
"Well...I guess I'll tell her myself then."

Chigurh wreaks some anonymous havoc, attempting to find the said cash, Llewellen finds himself on the run, and all the while, Sherrif Bell (Jones) is trying to find Llewellen to protect him from these rather shady figures, and has an undying need just to retire and be done with it all. 

That's what you all get for the plot...the rest is up to you. If you've ever seen "Fargo" or "O Brother Where Art Thou?" you know that the plot cannot be given away entirely, or else certain spoilers will leak through. 

Javier Bardem, The Coen Brothers, the movie itself, they all deserved the credit they got. Personally? I think Josh Brolin is always overlooked by the Academy. He gave a fantastic performance in both this film, and as a dirty cop in American Gangster. 

The Coen brothers never cease to amaze. I just wish something more was done with the ending...

MOVIE REVIEW: Outlaw
Notably Starring: Sean Bean, Danny Dyer, Sean Harris, Lennie James, Bob Hoskins
Unnotably Starring: Rupert Friend...just absolutely no emotion.

Summary: Will undoubtedly be a cult underground hit, but with a majorly B-movie feel

This movie flew under the radar. Based on the title, one might think it's a Western, especially when starring Sean Bean (he has that ruddy kind dirt-caked look). Think of it more as a cross between "Boondock Saints" and "V for Vendetta". In my opinion, there's definitely bad low-budget films that look student, and feel student, and there's good low-budget films that were done RIGHT. This went more to the low-budget done right...

The setting is a dirty, gritty, almost post-apocalyptic feeling London in which crime has run amuck. The only difference is, it's not post-apocalyptic, it's taking place in the current day and age, with the same political problems causing the same issues all across the world. A series of characters begin to feel the pain of this world, and decide to come together to stir things back in the right direction. 

First, there's Gene Dekker (Dyer). He's getting ready to marry his sweetheart. As they're driving to the church, a strange car pulls up beside them at the light. He finds himself beaten, bloodied, and bruised after a brutal and un-called-for attack. 

Then, a plane lands at a local airport, dropping off Danny Bryant (Bean). He's a recently court-marshalled soldier just home from Iraq. He comes home, and finds his key no longer works in his door, walks around the back yard, and finds his wife in the arms of another man.

The central story surrounds the court case of a notorious criminal named Terrence Manning (who has no real substance in the film...he's just there to look evil). Two of the investigators on the case are Munroe (James) and Lewis (Hoskins). While the hearings continue, Munroe gets very real threats from some of Manning's hired guns. These threats only become more and more real, and Munroe feels that he's bitten off far more than he could chew. 

So, homeless and pissed off, Danny goes to stay at a sleazy motel, managed by security guard Simon Hillier (Harris). Together, they realize that the world has gone to shit, and it's time to do something about it. Hillier becomes a liason, if you will, for Danny, and through Hillier, Munroe and Gene, along with another assault victim, Sandy (played emotionlessly by Rupert Friend), decide to join together and form a vigilante group to stop Manning. What results is a media backlash (because other than Danny, none of them really know at all what they're doing), and suddenly, they become hero/criminals...the cops want them hauled off to jail (or just preferably dead), and the citizens praise their efforts to end the corruption. 

"Fucking coward."
"I shit myself!"
"So did I, but I still stood."

Films with, what could only be, a handheld camera this film was...amateur, but had all the right parts going for it that made it really a very good film. The acting was fantastic by all (again, except for little Sandy...for a character that's supposed to have been so brutally assautled that his face has huge disfiguring scars, Rupert friend showed more indifference than anything), and frankly, I thought the direction the film took was genious. The development of Gene into what he turns into at the end was nothing short of brilliant. Sean Bean as well put forth a stunning performance as Danny, the soldier that came back from Iraq just a little bit "off".

WELL worth a watch.

MOVIE REVIEW: Dan in Real Life 
Notably Starring: Steve Carrell, Dane Cook, Juliette Binoche, Dianne Wiest, John Mahoney
Unnotably Starring: Jessica Hecht (She's the same character no matter what she's in), the chick with the long nose who's name I have no idea...

Summary: A sweet and endearing little family flick that shows normally over-acting eccentric comics being more realistic and even touching on the drama-side of life. 

Steve Carrell stars as Dan Burns; father of three daughters, popular columnist, and widower. His daughters are growing up before he's ready for them to be, boyfriends, travelling, and even his youngest is coming up with her own philosophical sayings as they embark on their annual trip to his parent's house in the country. Oh yeah...and they all HATE HIM. 

They arrive at the happy home of "Nana and Poppy" Burns (Wiest and Mahoney...no shock there), and are greeted warmly, yet artificially by the rest of his family; notably his brother Mitch (Cook), who appears to have a lady-friend coming, which puts Dan in the "special bedroom"...aka a cot in the laundry room. Told by Nana and Poppy to get the hell out of the house for a while, Dan embarks on a journey into town, being pulled over by a cop for running the same stop sign he always runs, and decides to shop at a local book shop. Here, he runs into Marie (Binoche). Thinking he's rather sly, he assumes the role of an employee to help her find books on awkward situations. (Notably, he picks up "Everybody Poops") She plays into his hands, and buys every book he recommends, saying "make sure he gets the commission." To which Dan's cover is then blown...but they bonded, so it's off for coffee and a mammoth muffin, and Dan spilling his entire life story to the poor girl. Marie gets a phone call, and suddenly has to run off, leaving Dan confused and disoriented...obviously his first encounter with a woman since his wife died. 

He goes home, and everyone seems especially happy to see him. That's when Mitch introduces his girlfriend Annie...or should we say, AnneMarie?! uh huh...pretty sly there. 

I kid I kid. 

Mitch and Annie are very happy together, and Dan is once again, left in the dust. The whole family is drawn to Annie's...Marie's...whatever's...stories of travelling all around the world; that, and her fine knowledge of crossword puzzles. Dan can't cope with the fact that he can't keep mourning the loss of his wife, while managing to let his three daughters grow up, and allow the rest of his family to be happy in the process. It's all about growing up, and learning from past mistakes. 

Not overly funny, nor is it a sad or depressing film either. Instead, it's a film about family, and that was pretty neat, all things considered...

MOVIE REVIEW: Hitman
Notably Starring: Timothy Olyphant, Dougray Scott
Unnotably Starring: only due to character development...the rest of the supporting cast

Summary: As far as the video game-turned-movie franchise goes, this was a top pick. 

Nobody was as surprised as I was that this movie was any good to begin with. The opening credits is very "Dark Angel" reminiscent, with the kid growing up in a military-esque environment, trained in all forms of combat, then gets a mind of his own and escapes, but then the video game takes over. We see Agent Whittier of Interpol, (Scott) getting out of his car and heading home for the night. He turns on the lights, and there's Agent 47, played by Timothy Olyphant, and brilliantly at that (again, nobody's as surprised as I am). He asks Whittier a question: 

"How does a good man decide when to kill?"

...or something like that...

The film takes us two months previous. Agent 47 is preparing his next hit in St. Petersburg, Russia. This time, it's the Russian President and his brother, a known arms dealer. Something goes horribly wrong with the assassination, and as any fan of the video game knows, Agent 47 doesn't miss his target. That, and there was an apparent witness, a whore/presidential girlfriend named Nikia (played mildly well by Olga Kurylenko...kind of a nympho...but whatever). However, when 47 tries to interact with Nikia, he realizes that she's never seen him before. Suddenly, the conspiracy turns away from the Russian President, and now, 47 appears to be the target. It's up to him to figure out why, and all the while, he has to keep Nikia alive, thanks to the fact that she knows a lot more than she lets on. 

Not perfect by any means, but neither was Mortal Kombat (the original...don't get me started on Annihlation), Hitman is more of a guilty pleasure film than anything. Just fun action sequences, Timothy Olyphant is extremely good looking bald as Agent 47, and lots and LOTS of guns. Hey, we all need mindless action flicks now and again...

As I continued to watch the movie I kept expecting something great, and by the end I was still left waiting. This movie is pretty much pointless. How Javier Bardem could win an oscar for delivering every line and action completely deadpan is beyond me. I could have had a text to speech program say his lines and get better acting. It would have been more audible than his that deep gravel voice he put on. Tommy Lee Jones' character was close to useless. His interaction with the main characters is limited and he accomplishes nothing. At no point does he do anything productive in developing the story, his character, or others. The most he does is throw out a couple of decent one liners and be old. Maybe I'm old fashioned, but I like stories that have a point. It makes it so much more interesting  for the audience. We get to step into these characters lives and get to watch most of them die, and the ones who don't seem unaffected by the events that transpire, and so it wasn't really worth telling the story. It's like if I made a movie about my week of going to work and taking a nap later in the day then eating. I could even edit it like this movie where you have to watch me walk around my apartment for ten minutes cooking a meal and then cut as soon as I get the food on the table. I could probably continue writing about the things I didn't care for in this movie or I could compare it to other movies and activities I find equally enjoyable, such as 2001: A Space Odyssey or organizing my socks, but I'm going to refrain. I'll avoid that temptation and just say that I wish was a joke. I want this to be a comedy that's so subtle I'm just not getting it and there's a few people that made the movie who are cracking up, and that some day I'll think back and say "Man that movie was great! Hoje assistirei Onde os Fracos Não Tem Vez, o vencedor de 4 Oscars(incluindo Melhor Filme) e considerado por muitos como a obra-prima dos Irmãos Coen. 
  Seria ele melhor que Tropa de Elite?
  
  Critica de Tropa de Elite: Faz tempo que Tropa de Elite foi o filme mais comentado no Brasil, o Filme mais pirateado e o Filme de maior sucesso nos cinemas do ano de 2007. A trilha sonora do filme ficou entre as mais vendidas e os videos no You Tube de Tropa de Elite são os mais vistos. Varios bordões, que eram imortalizados pelas telenovelas, ficaram sendo eternizadas pelo Capitão Nascimento. De onde vem esse sucesso? Da pirataria? Do bom gosto? Essas perguntas não interessam! O fato é que foi o melhor filme nacional do ano. "Tropa de Elite" é um filme que conta a historia de 3 personagens-chave:
  
  Nascimento - Capitão do Bope que está cansado da guerra civil nas favelas do Rio de Janeiro, e quer mais do que nunca achar um substituto.
  Neto - Um policial honesto e que gosta de ação. Ele tem um coração verdadeiramente policial, mas falta a ele cabeça. Qualidade que seu melhor amigo tem de sobra.
  Matias - Um policial honesto e melhor amigo de Neto. Ele é inteligentissimo e se candidata junto com seu amigo para o Bope. Ele tem inteligencia, mas falta a ele um coração policial. Ele faz faculdade de Advocacia, e conhece seus colegas, nesse ponto é que a trama se desenvolve muito bem.
  
  Do que se trata a trama? Todo o Brasil sabe: Sobre um capitão da Tropa de Elite da Policia Militar, que quer um substituto, por estar cansado do seu trabalho. O filme é impressionantemente realista, parecemos estar de frente para personagens reais(ponto para o elenco excelente do filme) e tratamos de casos realmente proximos demais dos nossos jornais(ponto para o roteiro). O filme trata de 3 temas importantes: Corrupção, Hipocrisia e Vingança. O filme é um tapa na cara de todos os brasileiros: Desde o playboy maconheiro até o policial corrupto. O filme é uma real reflexão de varios pontos duvidosos na vida real: Deve-se legalizar a maconha? A culpa da corrupção vem do governo, e se vem, deve-se aumentar o salario dos policiais? Uma policia violenta e, ás vezes cruel, é a solução dos nossos problemas? A resposta cabe a mente de cada pessoa. O filme é inspiradissimo e nunca deixa o ritmo frenetico de ação cair. Os tiroteios são muito reais, não parecem aquelas trocas de tiro fantasiosas de blockbusters de ação, é algo que prende pelo realismo impressionante. Desde já, para as pessoas que não gostaram do filme, o "saco" é merecido. [b]Nota : 9,0[/b]
  
  Seria melhor que "Onde os Fracos Não Tem Vez"? É uma duvida cruel.

My immediate reaction after watching this film was confusion, wondering whether I actually enjoyed it or not.
After thinking about it none stop afterwards, I came to the conclusion that I did enjoy and admire it very much, my initial confusion was due to the ending which can be perceived as unsatisfactory, but thinking back other Coen Brother films have similar endings for instance The Big Lebowski. 
That being said this film is not really like anything else I've seen the Coen brothers do, the film is wonderfully mature and self assured, the usual humour is downplayed, they concentrate on mood and atmosphere, the menace and fear portrayed by various characters is almost palatable.
No scene or piece of dialogue in this film is wasted, which is a refreshing change to the usual bloated rubbish, overflowing with pointless exchanges and intrusive music.

What I most appreciate about this film is the complete disregard for typical filmic conventions, the rules are regularly broken creating a sense of confusion and disorientation for the viewer, perhaps similar to what Josh Brolins character felt?
I pretty much felt like I knew roughly how this film was going to end having seen similar tales 100 times before, but the rug was abruptly pulled from under my feet near the end.
After personally bleating about wanting this kind of disregard to the 'by-the-numbers' film making of modern cinema, it kinda knocked me on my ass when it finally happened.
I'm referring to the sudden death of one of the main characters in a really understated way that leaves you confused and shocked for several minutes.
I also liked the breaking down of the pretty tired 'Winston-Wolfe-type' demigod character (played by Woody Harrelson) who cruises through the dangerous film world with complete confidence and conviction using his intellect to become untouchable, when he is killed by Javier Bardem's character it nails home just how deadly and cold Chigurh is.

Although the moral of the film is probably "C'est La Vie" or "shit happens," which is usually a pretty wanky theme, explored multiple times in films like Magnolia and even other Coen Bros films, I feel it works here due to its understated subtle nature.
Even if you don't like the message buckle up and enjoy the fantastic game of cat and mouse played by the main characters, that doesn't let up until near the end, it could be argued that the ending provides an unsatisfactory film experience, but after a little thought I disagree - and its a fantastic change for people bored of 'join-the-dots' film making employed by 95% of modern cinema.

The Academy of Motion Picture Artists has had an annoying tendency to award "Best Picture" to films that absolutely DO NOT deserve that honor (I'm looking at you  Forrest Gump, The Departed, Shakespeare in Love, and Rocky!) while leaving truly remarkable films forgotten in the dust (I feel for you, Saving Private Ryan, Star Wars, Little Miss Sunshine, and Citizen Kane). Thankfully, that didn't happen this year. While "American Gangster" remains my personal favorite of '07, and while "Michael Clayton" was almost as good as "No Country," the Coen brothers have created a really really good movie that 100% deserved to be named Best Picture of the Year.

The story follows Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) as a rough-neck Texas hunter who comes across a drug-dealing shoot-out and bag full of $2 million in cash. Unfortunately for him, the bag has a transponder that attracts Mexican druglords, crooks, and (most dangerous of all) Javier Barden's psychopathic masterpiece, Anton Chigurh. Moss quickly becomes aware of the danger he's in, and sends his wife to live with her parents as he attempts to lose his pursuers and make off with bloodied money. From the film's start, the audience is acquainted with Anton's pure insanity and lust for killing and bloodshed. He strangles a deputy with a manic smile across his face, kills a random senior citizen for his car with a cattle killer, and mows down adversaries with his signature silenced-Uzi and shotgun with ease. Brolin also plays his role excellently, making the crowd root for his survival with baited breath in literally every scene. Tommy Lee Jones makes his presence felt as well as an average Texas sheriff in over his head as dead bodies pile all around him.

The film is ripe with awesome, intense, and suspenseful shootouts, w/ blood and gore aplenty. Furthermore, the writing and dialogue are excellent, as characters are witty, realistic, and, most importantly, likeable. All of the humorous lines are placed perfectly, and add comic relief to this very creepy film. "No Country" is not perfect, though, and does  show some small, easily-ignored errors. The ending, while probably the most realistic choice, is ant-climatic at best and a downright buzz-kill at worst. Furthermore, Tommy Lee Jones's character fails to complete any real accomplishments in the movie or move the plot along at all. It seems as if the sheriff is meant more as everyday "law-enforcement reference" for the audience to attach to...the one "morally-sound" person in the story. In spite of this, the Coen brothers' "No Country for Old Men" is a must-see for any viewer, and more than deserving of its critical fame.

This movie should have been called, "One small example of how the world is going to hell in a hand basket."

What I liked:
1) The symmetry.  This movie started off with a commentary by one of the main characters as we see a sunrise about how when he was young a sheriff didn't need to wear a gun and how now things have changed so much for the worse that a peace officer puts his soul on the line every day.  
2) The characters were vivid and iconic.  The bewildered and tired law man, the psychotic and relentless bad guy (an embodiment of evil who is not as shallow as he seems), the everyman who makes a tragic decision to follow his greed instead of doing what is right, the innocent, naive, wife, and a host of others people who I could have sworn I knew by their southern accents and mannerisms.
3) The story-telling.  This movie relentlessly tells us the story of the deterioration of our culture as we sink into greed, dishonesty, and mayhem.  Most of us look on from the fringes wondering, "What on earth is going on?"   Each character portrays a bit of this story in microcosm.  I was drawn in from the first minute and was captive until pretty near the end.

What I didn't lik:
1) This movie portrays very little hope and no meaning.  Life is lived, we do the best we can, and bad things happen.  I turned off the TV afterward intrigued but disturbed.  I am glad there is more to life than the Coen brothers depict.
2) It was abrupt in places where smoother transition was needed.  I won't spoil the movie, so you you'll just have to watch it and try to spot the scenes I am talking about.

From Roger Ebert's review ... 
"No Country for Old Men" is as good a film as the Coen brothers, Joel and Ethan, have ever made, and they made "Fargo." It involves elements of the thriller and the chase but is essentially a character study, an examination of how its people meet and deal with a man so bad, cruel and unfeeling that there is simply no comprehending him. Chigurh is so evil, he is almost funny sometimes. "He has his principles," says the bounty hunter, who has knowledge of him.

Consider another scene in which the dialogue is as good as any you will hear this year. Chigurh enters a rundown gas station in the middle of wilderness and begins to play a word game with the old man (Gene Jones) behind the cash register, who becomes very nervous. It is clear they are talking about whether Chigurh will kill him. Chigurh has by no means made up his mind. Without explaining why, he asks the man to call the flip of a coin. Listen to what they say, how they say it, how they imply the stakes. Listen to their timing. You want to applaud the writing, which comes from the Coen brothers, out of McCarthy.

This movie is a masterful evocation of time, place, character, moral choices, immoral certainties, human nature and fate. It is also, in the photography by Roger Deakins, the editing by the Coens and the music by Carter Burwell, startlingly beautiful, stark and lonely. As McCarthy does with the Judge, the hairless exterminator in his "Blood Meridian" (Ridley Scott's next film), and as in his "Suttree," especially in the scene where the riverbank caves in, the movie demonstrates how pitiful ordinary human feelings are in the face of implacable injustice. The movie also loves some of its characters, and pities them, and has an ear for dialog not as it is spoken but as it is dreamed.

Many of the scenes in "No Country for Old Men" are so flawlessly constructed that you want them to simply continue, and yet they create an emotional suction drawing you to the next scene. Another movie that made me feel that way was "Fargo." To make one such film is a miracle. Here is another.

No Country For Old Men achieves everything I'd ever want it to achieve.

It takes un-expected twists and turns. the beginning scenes with Chigurh basically killing the people who are unlucky to be the ones who stand in the way prove that the movie can go anywhere and do anything no matter how unconventional it may seem.

The film has only one score, this score can be heard only at the end credits, which is a good score too, which gives every scene a sense of dread as most conventional movies would play suspense tracks while No Country keeps it quiet, this makes for some really unknown and unfamiliar sequences.  When the film is quite, it's quiet some of the time there might be no sound on the film whatso-ever (even all background noise).  So when the jumps arrive, they really arrive!  And with alot of power too thanks to the fantastic villian Chigurh played wonderfully by Javier Bardem.
Chigurh is the typical silent hitman/stalker type with a very unconventional look of a member of the monkeys who's seen things no man should and has been hiding in a cave for years.  He's basically the 'evil' in the film, he has no reademing qualities and is completely unsympathetic like the Terminator but the fact that he is human makes him all the more terrifying.

Josh Brolin plays Llewellyn Moss, Josh Brolin has a great subtelty and never overstates anything in a good way.  He plays it in such a way and the direction shows that we are not being forced to like him, but if we have to be for him or chigurh then it'd have to be him.

The most underated performance has to be Tommy Lee Jones.  Tommy Lee Jones plays the typical retiring officer who'd seen far too many troubling things in his time.  He acts as the sort of moral and heart to the story, his monologues are done with great subtlety and emotion that you'd never find the overstated Gary Oldman type of role do.  He's really great.

The movie has an ending which alot of people find 'too unconventional for its own good'.  My opinion is that there is no other way the movie could end.  If they had gone for the traditional movie ending then the whole film would have just seemed pointless.  I also loved the ending, especially the car bit involving Chigurh.

The abrupt ending has a lot to do with what Jones has been saying since the beggining of the movie. When I first saw the movie "Pulp Fiction", I did not know what to make of it.  Unlike many other movies of its type, it did not follow the normal conventions of its cinematic genre.  Granted, there was a lot of violence and a lot of pointless pop culture banter, but the way it was presented deeply perplexed me.  I can't say that I found it to be as engaging as the "films" of Michael Bay and Jerry Bruckheimer at the time (whatever you may think, "The Rock" is still  an awesome action flick).  But, it kept my attention for the two and a half hours of its running time without me having felt that any moment on screen was being wasted.  Almost every film out there has a few pointless shots here and there.  Even the rest of Tarintino's resume is almost composed entirely of pointless shots, but in the best possible pointless of shots for geeks such as I.  Until I saw "No Country", I never believed that I would see a genre film that has absolutly no dead spots.  Along with this, I never thought I'd hate to see a film end as much as I did "Pulp Fiction".  After having had many years to stew over "Pulp Fiction", I understand why it had to end where it did.  At first, I was dissapointed, but I learned later that it was the most perfect ending to a film I had ever seen.
"No Country" is a Coen brother's film (just in case that hasn't been hammered into your heads enough at this year's Academy Awards).  I have personally prefered their comedy to their dramas, but both I have found to be quite enjoyable.  "Fargo" was great, and "Raising Arizona" is simply a classic.  When you view this movie, you won't exactly be able to place it with their other films.  To say it's a different breed of film would be an understatement.  Every moment is used to its fullest and there is almost no way to guess what will happen next.  What should be another pointless chase movie ends up being something much more.  The ending to the film, as noted by anyone with the balls to express how they really feel about a movie that critics are calling the best of the year, is a bit...awkward, for lack of a better term.  But, so is the rest of the film.  While I was not as impacted as greatly through the first viewing as I was "Gone Baby Gone", I will say that I will probably be viewing this one again sooner.  It's one of those films that, no matter how much you dispise the ending after first viewing it, you still want to see it again.  To sum it up, yes, this is as good as the critics are saying.  How you will react to it is probably questionable at best.  At the very least, this is worth a rental or ten.  It's one of the most original movies in reacent times released by a major studio (even if it is under its independent logo) and should not be missed.

When Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon a drug deal gone wrong and leaves with $2 million in cash, he is relentlessly pursued by several interested parties, including cunningly vicious psychopathic killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), cocky hit-man Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson), and Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) . While Llewelyn struggles to stay alive and protect those he loves, the inevitable confrontation with his pursuers steadily closes in on him, as does unflinching fate and its inescapable finality. Josh Brolin as Llewelyn Moss pulls the audience in to his desperate situation and though his motives aren't noble by any means, never is there a doubt who you should be rooting for. A victim of greed, obstinance, and unfortunate circumstances, Llewelyn provides an antihero whose pressing journey never ebbs in intensity or moral conflict, and ultimately never ceases to intrigue. Javier Bardem's monumental portrayal of ruthless killer Anton Chigurh reinvents the notion of an unstoppable juggernaut and also realizes one of the most imaginative instruments of murder ever given its wielder. Violently dispatching his victims with a fateful coin toss and an incomprehensible code of honor, Chigurh blends the best of stone-faced serial killers from the finest slashers with the cold and calculating demeanor of the most intelligent of his kind. Rarely does such a deviously twisted character create such a mesmerizing presence. While Tommy Lee Jones provides much of the sarcastic, witty dialogue inherent to the Coen Brothers' films, he also represents a narrator of sorts and offers the audience an untainted view of the horrific events unfolding. The supporting cast all turn in admirable performances as well, most notably Woody Harrelson as the egotistic Carson Wells, and Kelly Macdonald as Llewelyn's innocently naïve wife. No Country for Old Men is one of the best pictures of the year, even if it is flawed. Its brilliance and lasting impact with leave you haunted.

"No Country for old men" starts out with hunter who is tracking down pray that he shot, then stumbles upon a gruesome scene. A scene of bullet riddled vehicles, Dead bodies, and dead dogs. If Alfred Hitchcock was still alive he would have made No Country For Old Men. The classic story of a man that, in the midst of the daily grind, ends up walking into a situation beyond what he thought he would experience that morning. Then he has to face the consequences of all of it. In No Country For Old Men Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles on the remains of a shootout while hunting. As curiosity gets the better of him and he begins to examine the scene he discovers a briefcase full of money. Being the human being that he is, he takes the money and a pistol home and causes the dominoes to fall as he begins to be stalked by the psychotic Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), the epitomy of unstoppable hit men who kills his way to Llewelyn and the money. Throw into this Tommy Lee Jones as the sheriff that's trying to piece it all together and save Llewelyn's skin and you get a cat and mouse game between a guy that was just out hunting and a vengeful drug cartel.

Adapted from the novel by Cormac McCarthy and dircted by Joel and Ethan Coen, No Country For Old Men is a great thriller that follows that classic Hitchcock formula ala North By Northwest- the guy that stumbles into trouble and has to get out of it while running from the bad guys. Llewelyn thinks he knows how to get out of this mess, but is really just drowning in the situation he's gotten into. Brolin plays him as totally optimistic, even when bleeding and hiding in a Mexican hospital. Bardem is the philosophical killing machine, debating the significance on whether a coin is heads or tails while on his killing spree to get back his money. He's like the Terminator- he will not stop until his goal, and his own sense of duty, are fulfilled.

The Coen's have filled the film with suspense. Most thrillers such as this run around in circles, but they have kept this film on a linear path that doesn't repeat itself over and over again. Between the game between Moss and Chiguhr, Tommy Lee Jones' character tries to sort everything out and save Llewelyn's ass. The problem that all of the characters have to face is the Killer's Morality- he is described as being on a higher standard than most and satisfies everything he promises, right up until the end.

As I said, No Country For Old Men is a Hitchcock film for the new millennium. A film filled with a thrilling plot that delivers a great ride for the audience. A real classic.

There are so many problems with the movie it is ridiculous.


Why would an arresting officer turn his back on the criminal?

If you just took 2-million dollars from a drug deal gone awry, (which is never explained), Why would you go back? And if you did go back to take the poor drug dealer (who is mexican, cliche) some water, why wouldn't you take a more than a hand-gun?


 Remember the two connections Chigurh and the Mexicans have to Moss is; his vehicle is left at the scene when he goes back and the tracking device.


How smart do you have to be to take the money out of the briefcase, because there might be a tracking device in it? Moss saw the radio device earlier, if he is in fact as smart as the movie wants him to be, why wouldn't he have known what it was?


We are left with so many things unexplained.


Who orchestrated the drug deal and Why did the drug deal go bad?


Wells, (played by Harrelson), seems to be a very intuitive guy; so why does he leave the money and how does he allow himself to be ambushed by Chigurh??? How did Chigurh track him (Wells). Why weren't we, the audience, privy to that info?


At least give some kind of information on why Woody Harrelson and Stephen Root (man that hires Wells, that is the well thought out character name for him folks) were in the movie? Character developement is essential for any movie. Those two characters were not developed what-so-ever.


The movie  begs for a confrontation between Moss and Chigurh and it never happens. Why were 2 of the main characters (Moss and his wife) killed off screen?


I thought that Chigurh's character was supposed to resemble an Amalek (sp?). Why did he kill innocents then, (strangling the cop at the beginning, killing the civilian to take his car and Moss' wife).


Where did Chigurh go when he was in the motel room at the end? Why didn't he kill Bell? or Why couldn't Bell kill him? Why was there no confrontation between the 2 of them at all?


Now for the ending: 
The movie ends with Tommy Lee speaking of dreams. I couldn't help but be reminded of myself waking up from a weird dream. In my half asleep mind set; the fact that a dog is playing Mozart on the piano, while sipping on scotch and explaining why hot dogs come in packs of 8; while buns come in packs of 10, somehow relates to my entire life plan and future goals.


It made/ makes no sense whatsoever.


But Well done Coen's. You know on some level they are laughing all the way to the bank.

It was not very long before I watched 'No Country for Old Men' that I watched the other remarkable film of 2007, 'There Will Be Blood.' Back then I thought that Paul Thomas Anderson has delivered the Best Picture of the year with his oil epic, but after watching the Coen brothers chilling and violent adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel, I knew right away that here was a film destined to be even a greater film than any I've seen this past year.

It's not easy to watch 'No Country for Old Men.' The first time I saw it, I found myself dazed enough to not be able to stand-up immediately even after the whole end credits have finished. And yet, mixed with the feeling of shock is the profound sense of wonder and awe with what I have just witnessed on the screen. It took me another viewing to fully appreciate the meaning and intention of the film, and while the experience from watching the film is not one everybody will enjoy and understand, it certainly is one of the most moving and thought-provoking movies I have ever watched. This is the kind of movie that will make you think, the kind that stays with you even after a long time has passed since you've last watched it. On the literal level, it is a simple cat-and-mouse chase thriller movie, but from within its roots lie a very profound philosophical and penetrating analysis not only of the characters and the situations involved in the story, but also of the kind of world we are living in today and the more monstrous sides of it we often choose to ignore.

The story revolves around the chase between a guy named Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin,) who stumbles upon a stash of money in a drug deal gone wrong in the middle of the desert and a psychopathic but surprisingly "principled" assassin named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). The third party and the moral center of the story is the guy trying to find both the hunter and the hunted, Ed Tom Bell, the old sheriff of a peaceful, but increasingly becoming violent locality in West Texas. 

The movie features the perfect mix thrill and excitement that would be expected out of a movie in this genre. The Coen brothers' direction of the particularly intense chase scenes between Chigurh and Moss are masterful, evoking emotions of suspense to the highest level and pushing the audience to the very edge of their seats. This is achieved by very careful editing and sound direction that perfectly recreates the tense atmosphere whenever a particular scene is being played out. Also remarkable is the photography (done by Roger Deakins) of vast scenes in the desert where even what the ordinary moviegoer would consider as "empty scenes", where no action is played out, tells a story in a visual manner, where even when there is no dialogue or action on screen, the sweeping images speak out for themselves.

'No Country for Old Men' is rich in such bravura kind of film-making. The particular camera move, position and choice of background and other trivial details such as time of day, cloud cover or positioning of the props and point-of-view perspective offer the best experience for the audience, and the most effective means of story-telling for the Coen brothers. Just watch the scenes of Tommy Lee Jones as the tormented old sheriff being burdened by the challenge of something that is greater a force than himself, something that he "does not understand," and you will realize what I mean. The environment and tone created by the filmmakers perfectly accentuates the performance of Jones and more importantly, the core messages of the film. This style is present throughout the film and one of the particular points that makes it more than just a chase movie.

I must say that I can't help but agree to most people when they say the Javier Bardem's Anton Chigurh is the most disturbing character (and yet mesmerizing) to grace the screen since Anthony Hopkins introduced us to Hannibal Lecter in 'Silence of the Lambs.' Chigurh effectively radiates evil and embodies violence in a very intelligent and forceful manner that touches the fear in all of us. Like Lecter, he personifies evil not in the conventional and simple sense, but in way that somehow presents to us the whole magnitude and complexity of its nature. In the dialogue he speaks, a kind of thinking revealed is one that is calculating and deeply philosophical but essentially ruthless and sinister.

The film's monumental achievement is in its ability to remarkably transport us into a world where the places, emotions, fears, anxieties, choices, morals and realities of life are strikingly brought to life and presented to us in a manner where we, after the whole experience, can reflect upon and look back with careful consideration. In the end, the moviegoer is left to marvel at the beauty (and madness) of it all. Here the theme of innocence lost as it is corrupted by evil and violence is explored in the most cinematic fashion, delivered perfectly with richness of emotion and the greatest impact possible. The violence and bleakness of it all is not there to simply evoke reaction or engage the audience, it is there to tell a story and impart an experience of great magnitude and intention, to which the Coen brothers have brilliantly succeeded. All at the same time the movie is a character study on the effects of evil and innocence lost, an exploration on the themes of fate and chance, an analysis of the freedom to choose and its consequences, a reflection on evil and good as forces of society and the investigation of basic human emotions such as hope, fear, love, violence and aspiration in the face of a variety of situations

The killer is a representation of evil and chaos that is always lurking but is given the freedom and focus to really let loose when LLewellan  gets greedy.
 
The cops, sitting around and complaining not quite caring or doing enough in their apathy are the public that allow all this to go on. 
 
Woody Harrilsons character is a metaphor for the UN. 
 
The kids near the border that give LLewellen the means to cover up the evidence of his crime are the media and advertising duality. They allowed themselves to be bought or co-opted into not fully reporting on the human rights abuses and tremendous cost in lives and freedoms that come from the war on terror. The sleeping mexican border guard is the public to disinfranchised to care to look at what is happening.
 
The wife is the only character who still has integrity to stand up and say that we all have the ability to choose and evil isn't just a random outcome. Of course she pays for it being the only one to stand up.
 
That's my take!

No Country For Old Men is by far one of the best films I have ever seen. Based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy, this accurate envisioning, directed by none other than the Coen Brothers, fills in the gap that many mainstream movies fail to fulfill:  A sense of realism, great and unpredictable story, and amazing acting and contextual themes.

The film starts off with Llewelyn Moss, the main protagonist (although that is debatable), stumbling upon cash and heroin while hunting for game. His poor judgement for taking the money turns against him as a ruthless, sociopathic bounty hunter named Anton Chigurh hunts him down to retrieve the money. This eventually turns into a blood riot and horrible chain of events, all for the love of money.

The Coen Brothers succeed in many more ways than one in this film. While we rarely ever get big budgeted films like these nowadays, oddly enough, they hit an extreme level of satisfaction with an extreme level of distaste at the same time. You are completely engrossed with the characters' identities and personalities and this impacts the way you see the film.

The cinematography is just beautiful, as it uses the trademark use of the Coens' moving shots, moreso on dollies and steadycams in order to achieve more of a realistic and dynamic approach of visualizing the story.

The story itself is just extremely well done, with great dialogue and great adaptation of the screenplay, you almost wonder if McCarthy himself wrote the book simply for the movie. The movie is full of unpredictability and creates numerous uncomfortable levels of suspense. The story itself is also extremely existential and bends toward nihilism, as the somberness and the ultimate consequence of things to come become the victor of the film.

I recommend this film to anyone who appreciates good story, good cinematography, and good dialogue. However, I don't recommend this film to anyone under 14 as there is excessive violence and gore and language.

Supported by some amazing performances and great cinematography, this modern western was engrossing to watch on the big screen. The open ending and its refusal to fulfill any expectations of a climactic good vs evil battle helped the movie linger in my head long after I had left the theater. While I really liked this film, the fact that it was so successful at both exceeding and denying my expectations makes it a little hard to pin down exactly how much I liked it. In some ways, I'm still digesting it.

Initially it's moral ambiguity reminded me of Clint Eastwood's Mystic River, but I didn't have the same abhorrent reaction to No Country as I did Mystic. Ultimately I think that's because what I initially took as moral ambiguity wasn't ambiguous at all. It all comes down to the closing dialog by Tommy Lee Jones (in basically one of my favorite roles for him) and his reflection on how the world has changed so much in even 2 or 3 generations, and how old values and expectations no longer seem to apply or more to the point, how those definitions and perceptions of the world we exist  in are enormously flawed in light of what actually takes place in the world. What I realized was this movie is a lament, not for days gone by or anything so nostalgic as that, but a lament for what we've lost in our journey through the last century and how out of touch we seem to be with where we are now. In the process, the movie doesn't deliver any recrimination on what the world is like, in that respect, it is what it is (ie kinda screwed up and not what you'd expect) but for anyone who (like T.L. Jones' character) has lived through the transformation of yesterday to today, the distance between what you knew or thought you knew about the world and the reality that impinges itself upon you can sometimes seem like the grand canyon. Or, in the particular case of Tommy Lee Jones' character, it's like a completely different country than the one he thought he knew. Tho I hate to say it, in a very direct way, the events of this film are his character's 9/11, and no matter how he'd like to he can't look at the world the same when it's all over.

Very well done, but not the Best Picture of the year. Don't get me wrong it was superbly acted (Javier Bardem deserved all his praise for that role!), written, and directed, but I can think of several films I thought were more thought-provoking,  and all around better from 2007. This probably is more of a reflection on my measure of "Best Picture" - not this film. That being said, the movie itself can stand up as another great Coen Brothers flick, full of excellent storytelling. It has a bit of an artsy feel to it by the long cut scenes, sweeping panoramas of the Texas prairie, and Tommy Lee Jones voice-over bookends, but that doesn't take away - it only adds. The genius of the Coen Brothers is that they can mix this artistic, almost-foreign-indie-film feel into a truly terrifying chase movie. This movie just feels different, encompassing both of those dynamics at just the right times. There were a few moments when I was left wondering what was going on (i.e. the Tommy Lee Jones motel room investigation with the cut to a hiding Bardem - what happened there? Was he there? Or was this a flashback? Who knows? Does it matter for later?), but for most of the movie I had eerie sensations of both pleasure and fear, often at the same time. It takes a great movie to do that, and the Coen Brothers latest is definitely one of those.

Even if No Country for Old Men didn't have gorgeous cinematography, excellent pacing, a near perfect script, and an absolutely perfect cast, I still would have loved it for its tone. It's the most similar movie to Fargo that the Coens have done, and the similar theme of implacable and unfathomable violence in a rural American area (once again initiated by money) is one of the main reasons why I love the Coens so much.

The breathtaking, empty setting of south Texas is a seamless compliment to the measured pace of the movie. No Country has suspense coming out of its ears, as each scene seems to somehow surpass the previous ones in measured tension. The overall quiet of the film only serves to magnify the eventual scenes of violence when they come, and the fact that you don't see everything happen on-screen keeps the viewer fully invested in the story. There's no constant quick cuts and hyper-kinetic camera work to be seen; only long-smoldering sequences that pushes your anticipation to the brink of breaking, and then pushes it some more.

In a cast this good, two people stand out even beyond the others. Tommy Lee Jones as the world-weary sheriff who's the heart of the story, and Javier Bardem as the relentless, inscrutable, main antagonist of the story. Jones was perfect, there's no other way for me to say it. And Bardem gives life to the best and most interesting villain since The Operative in Serenity. Both performances were among the best that I've seen in my life.

No County for Old Men is the kind of movie that improves with every viewing. Ten years from now, I'll still be watching it and loving it.  It's film-making at its finest. When you take an amazing story and marry it to directors with immeasurable talent and a cast that couldn't have been better chosen, you get a masterpiece.

Listen to his conversation with the convenience store clerk. "Bout' now is not a time; what time do you close?",  he says. He then proceeds to decide the fate of the man based on a coin toss - a random, yes or no, booleanesque method of deciding.  He does not feel hate, love, sadness or compassion even when the viewer screams for it. In his world, what is, is simply what is. There is no middle ground, only the joy of turning every kill into an artform. And make no mistake when death does arrive at his hand it is with awe inspiring precision and absolutely mind blowing calmness, whether it's the drug dealing buisinessmen or the sympathetic characters like Carla Jean. In short without spoiling the story, I was awed by this movie....I will be watching it again to fully digest what I have just witnessed.

Based on the American Novel by Cormac McCarthy, Josh Brolin stumbles upon a mexican drug deal gone bad (remind readers it looks like remnants of the gunfight at the O. K. We are left to believe that everyone killed everybody else prompting Brolin to ask where is the "Last Man Standing." 

Then, Javier Bardem shows up out of nowhere, from who knows where, representing who knows who, and chases Brolin.

Finally, Tommy Lee Jones somehow decides to leave his devil-may-care dead Sheriff's job in an even more dead town. Amazingly, there seems to be a total lack of people in every town in which the characters find themselves uless those people directly affect the characters. Hence, tons of cars on the streets but no people. Maybe this is suppose to be some type of statement that this film really takes place only in the minds of the characters (more on that later) and they are really all in a ghost town.

But wait, there's more! Woddie Harrelson shows up hired by another man (who knows who this dude is or what he represents although we are led to believe is some type of big shot due to he lives in a high rise office tower that has no 13th floor (as Woodie lets us know before he leaves the office), to hunt down both Brolin as well as Bardem.

So everybody is hunting everybody else except that it seems Tommy Lee has some doubts as to whether or not it is all worth it. I mean, no one respects the law anymore, do they? Everyone is coloring their hair purple and wearin "bones" in their noses, right?

Let me just say first that the Coen Brothers really know how to make a suspenseful film and they do villains excellently. This seems to be the year of the Western and we've had a couple great ones (with 3:10 to Yuma) Javier Bardem steals the show in this one as an unreasonable killer with a sort of controlled psychopathic-ness about him. He's terrifying in this movie and you're literally on the edge of your seat every time he's in the scene - The Coen's really did a number with him!

Tommy Lee Jones plays the battle hardened Sheriff who just can't cope with how crime has escalated since the old days. There are now crimes that he just doesn't understand and that frightens him. 

Finally Josh Brolin plays a weathered tough-guy vietnam veteran who runs into a failed drug deal, a half-dozen dead bodies, and $2 million bucks. 

Much of the movie is a chess match between Bardem tracking down his money and Brolin trying to outrun him. But, its more than that, as the movie takes a few unexpected turns that make you scratch your head at first but you end up realizing its better that way. The ending especially, does this - and it makes the film unique. I won't spoil it. 

Anyway, I didn't quite think this was the best film of the year. I actually think I liked 3:10 to Yuma a little better, but that doesn't keep this from being an excellent film in all aspects.

The level of ass this movie kicked really boggles the mind. I struggled on Oscar night with accepting that NCFOM was considered a "better" movie than PT Anderson's latest masterpiece. After a few more viewings, I came to grips with their decision.

It's hard to compare both films on a technical level, because the Coens and Anderson created films that were doing completely different things. The script for this film is absolutely fantastic, easily their sharpest work since Miller's Crossing. The general consensus is that Javier Bardem stole the show, and I'll have to agree 100%. His portrayal of a completely lunatic who's accepted fate and the character's inability to escape it as the overarching. Brolin' & Jones's characters are the stark contrasts, which make the tension explode exponentially. 

From a technical aspect, this film excels on all levels. The shots are well crafted and make the landscape of the film feel gigantic, even the hotel scenes that make you want to jump out a window to escape the tension. The dialogue and sound are extremely important in this film, done so back the lack of a soundtrack. The Coens make you work and reach for understanding, which is why I think a lot of people disliked the ending: they didn't want to have to search for clues that began popping up around the sixty minute mark and continued to the final scene. You have to combine both what the camera is presenting, and what the characters were saying. Continuing with dialogue, it was the most culturally-accurate, sharply constructed speech in any Coen film, blowing Fargo completely away.

No Country for Old Men is a well-rounded masterpiece, combining all elements of successful filmmaking into an experience that nobody should overlook. This is a dangerous film that takes a bunch of risks, and succeeds every single time.

Of course the real hit of the film, which I feel speaks volumes to the uncompromising casting that Joel and Ethan exhibit in every one of their films, is Javier Bardem.  Add him to the list of "made the film" casting roles in the Coen's repertoire...  Nicolas Cage/Holly Hunter in Raising Arizona, Francis McDormond in Fargo, John Goodman in Barton Fink, Jeff Bridges in The Big Lebowski, the list goes on.  His strikingly animated features and hair style reminiscent of a Scooby Doo villian lent massive emotion to the film, without which, I doubt the praise for No Country would be as plentiful.  I almost expected him to pull of a rubber mask at the end of the film to reveal he was actually Tommy Lee Jones.  Perhaps they could make that alternate ending for the MTV Movie Awards ;)  Superb casting, again, is all I can say.  While I would rate it toward the bottom of my Coen top 10, it certainly is no slouch although I can't help thinking that 2007 as proved to have a dirth of magnificent memorable films, instead dominated by dark and cynical films.  The landscape of films lately reminds me of the provocative dominant media of the seventies where films like A Clockwork Orange, One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest, The Last Picture Show, Taxi Driver, and others. I'm no great fan of the Coen brothers; they've done some stuff I really [i]love[/i], a lot I really [i][u]hate[/u][/i], and....hm....no, I don't think anything in between. So, given that, and the fact that this was touted as 'ultra-violent' with a weird WTF ending, I reluctantly watched it dreading getting slammed for writing my negative review. The fact that it won Best Picture when I adore both Sweeney Todd and Juno so much and that The Orphanage and I Am Legend were completely ignored come Oscar time really didn't help. Any way (this seems to be happening a LOT lately, darn it!), I was proven completely wrong.
 
No Country [u]is[/u] terribly violent but never what I hate, which is gratuitously so, or not directly in keeping with the telling of the story from the point of view of the characters. Shot all in the same color palette, it had an interesting use of lighting, camera techniques and pans and 'matter of fact' presentation that allowed you to feel you were just somehow walking around behind these people watching each of them as the story unfolds and yet retain an intensity that almost keeps you on the edge of your seat. That it unapologetically never gives any "over-explanation" or backstory for what's happening adds to that interesting appeal.
 
The cast is, as widely recognized, astounding. I hate that Philip Seymour Hoffman OR Tom Wilkinson lost an Oscar this year to [i]ANY[/i]one, but I certainly can't argue that Javier Bardem deserved to be up on that stage. His sociopathic genius of a murderer living in his own world might have been unfeeling in any 'normal' sense of the word but, far from playing it all emotionless and deadpan, it's easy to see the complexity of layers beneath his face and body language; I actually wish we could've had even more of him. 
Tommy Lee Jones is a joy to watch, as always, if for nothing else just to hear him speak. But his world-weary, dry-witted, brilliant country sheriff is one of his best performances to date and, like Bardem, I just kept wanting more of him on the screen - but, like for each of them, it really was NO individual's story. 
Widely overlooked is Josh Brolin, whose clever, fearless, 'innocent' man not knowing what he'd stumbled into wound up being a character I really not only liked, but respected as well and gave you someone (unfortunately) for whom to really root in the whole mess. This was no idiot thinking he'd lucked into a goldmine (a la A Simple Plan); he was smart, calculating, determined and focused to win at all costs.
Woody Harrelson and Kelly MacDonald are both given very little to do, but do it excellently, heading up a rather small but completely flawless cast of supporting actors.
 
The only things I knew going into this movie were: Javier Bardem is insane and kills people [i][u]and[/u][/i] the ending was SUCH a "shocker", it not only left people shaking their heads, but actually ruined the whole movie, from a lot of reviews I'd read. So about 3/4 of the way through, I thought I was ready; thinking, "OK, this is it: here come the end credits. No, it must end here and you don't know what happened to so-and-so.", etc. I almost laughed to find out they [i][u]still [/u][/i]managed to stun me when the screen went black but, FAR from a lot of the peoples' opinions I've read here, it didn't even come close to "ruining" the film for me, or [u]even[/u] leave me scratching my head. I really think the end, and the point of view at the end, not only is the [i]title[/i] of the movie, but the entire [i]POINT [/i]of the thing as well. If you think of it as a whole, you can see it coupled with Jones' opening narration and understand the 'in between' was just the two thoughts coming together full circle. It left me contemplative and appreciative for a good while after we were done watching it and those are marks of a well-made film.
 
As far as Best Picture of the [i]year[/i]?? I dunno.....to be honest, only two others of my top ten for the year were even [u]nominated[/u] so I obviously disagree with the Academy on their choices put in that category, but even from the nominees, I think Michael Clayton should have had a slight nod over No Country; it had an even better ensemble cast and a tighter screenplay and narrative. As much as I really adore Juno, it simply wasn't "best picture" material - the way the voters see it any way - I'm surprised it even got nominted. I think, apart from the acting (not the characters themselves, the [i]acting[/i] of them), this was truly a directors' film and [u]should[/u] have won Best Director, but I'm not feeling it for the best picture of the year. 
That being said, this is the second time in a week I've had to bump my dumb, beloved Transformers to make way for something I might not "love" as much, but HAVE to admit is better so.....it's certainly deserving of some accolades, to be sure. I'm sorry I didn't see it in the theater; I'm sure it would've been even more powerful; but, regardless, a great late 'find' for 2007!

Very few movies come along that challenge everything you thought was normal. This is one of the few. On the surface it seems to be just a chase film. But if you dig deeper, you find a film that touches on themes right out of the morning newspaper. A film that is caught between old testament law and and new age rules. Throught the whole movie, the line is blurred between who you can trust and who is really on the wrong side of the law.
   It all starts with a hunting trip. Simple enough. But the hunter happens to stumble upon a drug deal gone horribly wrong. At the scene he finds a truck load of herion and a case with 2 million dollars inside. Now put yourself in his position: alone in the middle of nowhere with a cool 2 mill all to yourself. What would you do?
   Of course, things are never that easy. One live soul at the scene of the crime begs our hero for water. And what would the human in all of us do? Bring him some water of course. But in doing this he brings upon the wrath of one of the most horrible screen villians in the history of film. Anton Chigurh is heartless and shows almost no emotion besides a sly smile or a look of insanity as he strangles the life out of one of his victims. It's a stirring, riviting performance.
   It's also stirring that the film features almost no music. It lets the sound of footsteps and gunfire build the tension.
   And build it does. I'm not going to ruin anything for anyone. Just be sure to listen to everything. Follow every detail and the next time someone flips a coin and says call it, you had damn well better call it, friendo.

If you are not typically a fan of the Coen Brothers work, or like your movies to actually resolve in a manner that leaves you feeling like you didn't just waste your two hours in the theatre, or dislike gratuitous violence in movies, let me give a great piece of advice:  ingore the critics, ignore the hype, and avoid seeing this movie at all costs!  After all the buzz surrounding this movie, I went to see it with my dad, and we both enjoyed the film most of the way through.  It was suspenseful, thrilling, and I was really getting into the movie.  Then all of a sudden, about 15 minutes from it's conclusion, it jumps the shark, and goes downhill in a hurry.  See, apparently, the movie has a lot deeper meaning than is initially evident, and is really more of an allegory about how dreary life is now, and how it's no country for old men, or people longing for the good old days.  Unfortunately for the film, unless you buy into the negatively pessimistic and fatalistic viewpoint it espouses, it just comes off as a downer, and frankly, a complete waste of what was for the most part an interesting movie.

Now film snobs will tell you that if you don't like it you're just not intelligent enough to, and you should stick to mindless action flicks.  Nothing could be further from the truth, as the whole concept of the movie defies reality, and if it were made by less trendy directors than the Coen brothers, it would have been lambasted instead of lauded.  Believe me, I've spent countless hours hearing the other perspective out, and poring over their reasoning for why it's a great movie.  In the end though, it just doesn't wash, and all boils down to what your worldview is, an whether you actually by the dark assertions the movie tries to make.  Also, over 20 people get coldly, and brutally murdered in this film, so if that kind of thing bothers you, definitely stay away.  This is a frustrating movie, in that it had such promise, but squandered it in pursuit of a more artsy, and pseudo-intelligent ending.  It's based off a book, so I guess we really have the author to blame.  But don't be decieved by the hype this movie's received:  this is No Best Picture for Smart Men....

A solid thriller from the Coen Brothers that is really good for the first hour and a half, then that awful ending rears it's ugly head. Set in 1980 Texas, a man named Llewelyn Moss (a strong performance by Josh Brolin) stumbles across a drug deal gone bad and finds $2 million in cash. He takes the money and sets off a chain of events that culminates in violence and bloodshed. A psychopathic killer named Anton (played by Javier Bardem) is hot on his tail and will kill anyone that gets in his way. Tommy Lee Jones plays veteran Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who becomes involved in the proceedings. Very well done film with highly graphic action scenes and some well timed humor. The entire cast is good throughout especially Kelly MacDonald as Brolin's wife. Don't let the ending put you off. The same thing happened with The Departed, when it unraveled in the last twenty minutes or so. No Country is clearly the best film of all the ones that were nominated for an Oscar, and deserved to take home the gold. But it's doesn't quite reach that greatness level. Still, it's a must see film.

No Country for Old Men was recently awarded Best Movie of the Year at the 2008 Oscars. Personally, I don't really think it should have won that distinction. The story begins when a hunter discovers a stash a money from a drug deal gone wrong and follows his journey to escape the man coming after him to kill him and reclaim the money and the sheriff trying to keep the hunter alive. It's a pretty standard story but the movie is not that simple. Let's get the good parts out of the way first. The acting in this movie is incredible. It's certainly some of the best I've ever seen. The one actor that truly shines is Javier Barden and he deserves the Oscar win. His portrayal of the villain was well done and it certainly does send chills down your spine. There is a confrontation between him and Brolin's character that was excellent and full of tension. However, the movie never really offers any resolution. The sheriff (played by Jones) never catches the villain and it ends with him retiring and explaining a dream he had with his wife. Of course the entire point and theme of the movie was in that little segment but if you don't think long and hard about it, it's going to frustrate you. Honestly, I still haven't figured out the overall theme of the movie and probably may never will, but if the Coen Brothers' intent was to make us think, then they have succeeded. No Country for Old Men may not have deserved its Oscar win due to a lack of a good resolution that leaves a bitter taste, but the acting here is as good as it gets, and for that, this movie is highly recommended.

Wow! The Coens do it again (love those guys). This movie is not for the squeamish. The movie is amazingly suspenseful, due primarily to the dark, psychotic menace of Bardem's very cold blooded killing. I truly felt apprehension, so much so, I contemplated turning off the movie. Every scene with Bardem radiates peril, but not in the usual way.  There are not histrionics in his characterization, which makes it all the more chilling. His character is cold and unpredictable. In this film suspense flows naturally through character and not through artificial plot twists (so standard in the genre). Whenever we see Bardem it is like seeing a pistol with the hammer back--we wondering if he is going to go off.
WARNING SPOILERS BELOW:  The movie, based on a Cormac McCarthy novel, I understand, thumps all the conventions. First Javier Bardem is fantastic as a truly soulless psychopath. The movie is a meditation on random acts of cruelty and malice and it doesn't offer any of the stock plot permutations of the genre. Our hero (Josh Brolin), a greedy man-of-few-words,  who also has some morality (his trouble begins when he is caught bringing water to a dying man) doesn't survive. Our world weary sheriff, Tommy Lee Jones, does not get his man. The villain, Javier Bardem, doesn't get his comeuppance. Rather random events overtake the villain too and he merely fades into the shadows.

The acting, what little was required for the movie, was also high end, though I am not sure I see any true Oscar caliber performances here.

The movie sells itself, to a large extent on the main villain, portrayed by Bardem. A good performance, but I am not sure Oscar level. Perhaps that is because I did not think he represented the new, unexpected take on the movie killer that everyone says that he is. Quirky? Most on film are. Intellectual? We had that with Hannibal Lector a generation ago. Cold, and unflinching? Malkovich gave us that in more than one movie. Somewhat sly and sarcastic? Nicholsons Joker.

And on and on.

As for the point of the movie, I suppose on a meta level I do get it. But I have said this a million times...simply doing what most other movies would not do doesn't make you a profound movie. In the case of No Country, it makes you a rather self important attempt at a masterpiece, which ultimately falls short of greatness by the very fact that it is TRYING to be ironic, and deny expectations.

The title of the movie is the point of the piece. Itmay even be totally true, in real life. But while movies should sometimes embrace realism, I just never bought into the notion that depriving a movie of an arc, merely for the sake of being unique or ironic, makes for a good film. After all, it is supposed to be, a film. 

I'm all for breaking the rules of the game. But, if like the Coen brothers, you just flat out play a different game entirely, and yet at the same time try to sell your product as the ultimate achievement in that game, it doesn't work.

Thus is my dissenting opinion on this year's Best picture Winner.
