G. and I had to discuss this movie at length after I watched it on vacation (he'd already seen it).   Although we were both left with a lot of questions, we enjoyed it.  G. declared that American Gangster was a more enjoyable film.  I liked that one, too.  But I think No Country for Old Men is deeper.  American Gangster is easier.  I know why Denzel's character does what he does.  I understand him, I sympathize with him.  I don't think the same can be said for NCFOM.

NCFOM raises an interesting question: What happens when the only men of principle have no moral compass?  We see several characters in the movie--each a man of principle in some way.  Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is our traditional man of principle--the lawman who is trying to save lives and do right...but in the end, he cannot succeed because this is "no country for old men," and he can't get a grasp on this new world in which we live, on these new men who rule it.  We have Moss who is a thief--yet seeks to protect his loved ones and is troubled by his conscience at least once in the film.  And we have Chigurh who, well, is the exact opposite of what we'd consider a principled man.  And yet he has principles--keeping his word.  In a post-modern world where it seems a man's word is no longer sufficient as a promise, Chigurh proves himself to be as good as his word--no handshake necessary.  And so we have the question: What happens not when men no longer have principles, but rather, what happens when they are men of honor, but that honor is misplaced?  What happens when the moral compass goes haywire and we're left in a world where the qualities of good men have been usurped by the bad guys?  What happens when all the good guys have given up, sacrificing their good qualities to these "new" men?  Of course, there's also always the question of God...where is God?  Because in this movie he seems remarkably absent--in fact, Chigurh seems to play God...but in a really creepy and simultaneously playful way--turning over people's lives to fate: "What's the most you ever lost on a coin toss?" ~~shiver~~ And Chigurh, or fate actually, or God even, seems indifferent at best--it is not a pretty picture McCarthy or the Coen brothers paint for us...not a pretty picture at all.  But that the movie makes us think about these things is what makes it great.

[u]No Country for Old Men[/u]
           
         
           This is a little unfair but before I watched No Country for Old Men everybody and their mothers told me their opinions of this movie and that I had to watch it. I didn't want it spoiled though. All I knew was that it was great but the ending was supposedly horrible. I didn't so much as even watch a trailer.
           
           Here's what I think though, now that I have seen it, and maybe this is only because I was somewhat prepared for it, nonetheless I don't think the ending was bad. Most people's problem is that they became too attached to Llewellyn, and forgot about Tommy Lee Jones. This perhaps is the fault of the Coen brothers in the way they structured the movie. But if someone watching pays attention to the dialogue between Tommy Lee Jones and his partner, and then his friend with the cats, and again at the end where he is talking about his dreams, you will see that a clear explanation is all layed out there for you and I think you'd begin to understand that the $2,000,000 was not what this movie was about at all. 
           
           Think about the title: No Country for Old Men.
           
           The old sheriff is realizing that this is not an old man's world. He can't keep up with the times. The power of money and drugs (but mostly money) are stronger than morals and it's become more than he can handle. 
           
           Woody Harrilson's character says that Anton has morals that supercede money, and that he isn't like most people because of that.
 
           In the end I think the point was that nothing was going to stop this sociopath. Tommy Lee Jones said that God never intervened in his life to make it easier; that wisdom doesn't just come to a person because they get old. That sort of thing takes time yes, but time that was used on dedicated work toward something. His dream, the finale of the movie, was about his own death. "Life in this country is hard."
           
           Anyway, he knows that there is no way he can catch Anton, and that he is going to die soon so he just retires. That's the ending of the movie. Anton would have just killed more people, kept stitching up his own wounds, finding new cars and moving on. Even in the beginning when they had caught him, he managed to escape. Times are changing, and criminals are getting worse. 
           
           The worst part for most people is that Llewellyn's death was off screen. Was it the gang of Mexicans from the drug deal? Was it Anton? Was it a good fight? I guess it doesn't really matter though. But I agree that it'd have been nice to have seen that.
           
           Now that I've attempted to defend the bad half of the movie, allow me to explain the good half. The suspense is amazing. The entire movie gives the feeling of walking across a tightrope and accidently looking down. The acting is also amazing. Anton is a great psychopath. The atmosphere really really emerces you in it. Everything is great, there isn't much to say. Even if you hate the end, I think it's unanymous that the beginning (...first 95% of the movie), the action and the tension is just amazing. 
          
   While I see the problem with this ending I don't think its that bad. The thing is, I was expecting a bad ending so i was prepared a little better. People were pissed when Llewellyn died abruptly, and they were also pissed that the movie ended on such a slow paced boring note. I also think, it's not that the writers were lazy or stupid, but that it's appropriate that the police just gave up looking for Anton. I think it was a wild goose chase because he was just too good. He always gets away. They cant follow his car because he always switches it. He's always moving, they had no leads. He left no witnesses alive. 
      
     As for the "after building up all that tension, they dropped the ball on delivering a good ending" argument, it depends on what you were looking for. I mean, maybe this wasn't the best way they could have set it up but the point of the movie "No Country for Old Men" is that this is no country for old men. The cop is old and is retiring because he cant keep up with the times. Criminals are getting worse and they get away and that's just the way life is.
   
 In all honesty Tommy Lee Jones probably didn't really get enough screen time but those scenes in which he is featured all allude to that message. They are few and far between, misplaced, and relatively boring parts though, and I'm sure a lot of brains tune out at those points but because I knew there was something wrong with the ending I really payed extra attention. 
 
 They emphasized the awesome parts too much. I think in writing this story they started out with the ending and the message they wanted to convey and then they went back and reworked the rest of the movie around that, but then kept the point of the story and the ending as it was. Being that they had built everything else up to make it more entertaining, the ending didn't really fit anymore. I definitely see why people were disappointed but I also see a level on which it does work. Surely though, you must agree that Anton was simply awesome and that huge gun cannon thing was absolutely crazy. They said that butchers use those air guns to kill steer and he[i] IS[/i] a butcher of sorts.
        
  The abrupt death of Llewellyn and the ending of the movie are very sad but that's real life. At the end, the bad guy should have been defeated but he wasn't. He's such a badass. Whether you think its karma or whatever that he got hit by that car, even if that was the case, karma was no match for him. He just got up and walked away. He was able to use money as his scapegoat, and his insanity kept him from panicking. He was an unstoppable force, more than man, especially more than an old man.  It's all about the corruption brought on in the world today by the power of money.

Many people won't find anything in it that they like, which is totally acceptable, but I loved it because it shows life for exactly what it is; confusing, helpless, violent and frustrating.  The acting is all great and the sound in this movie is amazing despite the lack of a soundtrack.  This is one of the few movies that manages to confuse and bewilder people when the title directly reflects what the movie is about. It was not very long before I watched 'No Country for Old Men' that I watched the other remarkable film of 2007, 'There Will Be Blood.' Back then I thought that Paul Thomas Anderson has delivered the Best Picture of the year with his oil epic, but after watching the Coen brothers chilling and violent adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's 2005 novel, I knew right away that here was a film destined to be even a greater film than any I've seen this past year.

It's not easy to watch 'No Country for Old Men.' The first time I saw it, I found myself dazed enough to not be able to stand-up immediately even after the whole end credits have finished. And yet, mixed with the feeling of shock is the profound sense of wonder and awe with what I have just witnessed on the screen. It took me another viewing to fully appreciate the meaning and intention of the film, and while the experience from watching the film is not one everybody will enjoy and understand, it certainly is one of the most moving and thought-provoking movies I have ever watched. This is the kind of movie that will make you think, the kind that stays with you even after a long time has passed since you've last watched it. On the literal level, it is a simple cat-and-mouse chase thriller movie, but from within its roots lie a very profound philosophical and penetrating analysis not only of the characters and the situations involved in the story, but also of the kind of world we are living in today and the more monstrous sides of it we often choose to ignore.

The story revolves around the chase between a guy named Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin,) who stumbles upon a stash of money in a drug deal gone wrong in the middle of the desert and a psychopathic but surprisingly "principled" assassin named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). The third party and the moral center of the story is the guy trying to find both the hunter and the hunted, Ed Tom Bell, the old sheriff of a peaceful, but increasingly becoming violent locality in West Texas.

The movie features the perfect mix thrill and excitement that would be expected out of a movie in this genre. The Coen brothers' direction of the particularly intense chase scenes between Chigurh and Moss are masterful, evoking emotions of suspense to the highest level and pushing the audience to the very edge of their seats. This is achieved by very careful editing and sound direction that perfectly recreates the tense atmosphere whenever a particular scene is being played out. Also remarkable is the photography (done by Roger Deakins) of vast scenes in the desert where even what the ordinary moviegoer would consider as "empty scenes", where no action is played out, tells a story in a visual manner, where even when there is no dialogue or action on screen, the sweeping images speak out for themselves.

'No Country for Old Men' is rich in such bravura kind of film-making. The particular camera move, position and choice of background and other trivial details such as time of day, cloud cover or positioning of the props and point-of-view perspective offer the best experience for the audience, and the most effective means of story-telling for the Coen brothers. Just watch the scenes of Tommy Lee Jones as the tormented old sheriff being burdened by the challenge of something that is greater a force than himself, something that he "does not understand," and you will realize what I mean. The environment and tone created by the filmmakers perfectly accentuates the performance of Jones and more importantly, the core messages of the film. This style is present throughout the film and one of the particular points that makes it more than just a chase movie.

I must say that I can't help but agree to most people when they say the Javier Bardem's Anton Chigurh is the most disturbing character (and yet mesmerizing) to grace the screen since Anthony Hopkins introduced us to Hannibal Lecter in 'Silence of the Lambs.' Chigurh effectively radiates evil and embodies violence in a very intelligent and forceful manner that touches the fear in all of us. Like Lecter, he personifies evil not in the conventional and simple sense, but in way that somehow presents to us the whole magnitude and complexity of its nature. In the dialogue he speaks, a kind of thinking revealed is one that is calculating and deeply philosophical but essentially ruthless and sinister.

The film's monumental achievement is in its ability to remarkably transport us into a world where the places, emotions, fears, anxieties, choices, morals and realities of life are strikingly brought to life and presented to us in a manner where we, after the whole experience, can reflect upon and look back with careful consideration. In the end, the moviegoer is left to marvel at the beauty (and madness) of it all. Here the theme of innocence lost as it is corrupted by evil and violence is explored in the most cinematic fashion, delivered perfectly with richness of emotion and the greatest impact possible. The violence and bleakness of it all is not there to simply evoke reaction or engage the audience, it is there to tell a story and impart an experience of great magnitude and intention, to which the Coen brothers have brilliantly succeeded. All at the same time the movie is a character study on the effects of evil and innocence lost, an exploration on the themes of fate and chance, an analysis of the freedom to choose and its consequences, a reflection on evil and good as forces of society and the investigation of basic human emotions such as hope, fear, love, violence and aspiration in the face of a variety of situations.

The Coen Brothers have been among the most interesting and influential filmakers of the past 20 years.  They have some misses along the way, but no one can excuse them of making boring films.  Heavily influenced by film noir, and with a great appreciation for dark humor, their most successful films have usually combined both.  Their latest effort, the Academy Award winner for best picture, noticably tones down the humor, and instead takes on a dark, philosphical tone.  It combines elements of perhaps their two best films, "Blood Simple" and "Fargo" creating a bleak vision of the future.   
 
[b]No Country For Old Men (2007) - 8.8/10[/b]
Director - Coen Brothers
Starring - Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, Kelly MacDonald, Woody Harrelson, Tess Harper, Barry Corbin.
 
Tommy Lee Jones stars Bell, an aging West Texas sheriff who longs for simpler times but instead watches as a violently changing society enchroaches on his sacred West Texas soil.  Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is a Vietnam Vet living in a trailer park with his wife Carla Jean (Kelley MacDonald).  One day while out on a hunt, Llewelyn makes a grim discovery.  Bodies, a bunch of them.  A drug deal gone bad.  He also discovers a briefcase of money and realizes it's his one chance at changing his and Carla Jean's life.  Only one problem, a ruthless killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) wants the money too and will do anything to get it back.  What follows is a suspenseful and brutal game of cat and mouse.  
 
The Coen Brothers pretty much did everything right with this film.  They took fascinating source material and came up with a brilliant adapted screenplay.  The casting is absolutely perfect.  Nobody could have played Sheriff Bell better than Tommy Lee Jones.  I'm sure many bigger named actors would have loved to work with the Coens and play Llewelyn, but once again perfect casting.  And the casting of Javier Bardem as the "evil outsider" was brilliant.  Quite simply he's one of the most memorable villians ever captured on film.  Even the supporting actors and cameos scream "West Texas".  Having lived there myself I felt I knew these people and that's a credit to the Coens for making these people seem so authentic.  As were the locations.  Filmed in West Texas and New Mexico, the locale seemed familar and authentic.  The cinematography fantastic.  Everything in sync.
 
There will be some who will argue the ending.  Without giving it away I'll just say it's an Anti-Hollywood ending that stays true to the theme of the film.  We may long for the past but there are no easy answers for the future.  
 
Is this the best Coen film yet?  Perhaps.  I think it's at least equal to "Fargo" and while it lacked that film's humor, I must say it's had more of a lingering impact.  So yes I guess it is the Coen's Brother's best film, at least for me!  Best picture of 2007?  Well I still need to see a few more, but right now this is the one to beat.

After watching "Juno" loose to this during the Oscar's I was determined to find out why so many people were talking about this movie. So, being the intellectual nerd that I am, I went out and read the book, which is utterly amazing, and have only just now watched the film. It tells the story of resourceful, yet seemingly challenged in all common sense, Llewelyn Moss who is out hunting mule deer in the Texas wilderness when he stumbles upon dead bodies, a truck full of heroin, and $2.4 million in cash. He takes the money back but then returns later that night, to give water to one of the dying mexicans he found at the scene, but is chased by a truckfull of people and there vicious dog. He escapes and begins a cat and mouse game with a psycopathic killer named Anton Chigurh who has been hired, by who we never actually discover, to get the money back. Meanwhile Sheriff Ed Tom Bell dedicates his last assignment to saving Moss from Chigurh and the rest of the Mexicans.

Although the film is rated for violence I would say that there were only two extrodinarily bloody parts, but what makes this film worthy of such a rating is the merely the creepy codes which Chigurh holds and his personality in gernral, but at the same time the movies triumphs are the tense yet beautiful scenes between the killer and his unknowing victims to be, as well as the washed out insite of Bell. All of the characters are somehow very real, Moss acting as the definition human, Bell being cynical yet caring, and Chigurh a mental inigma beyond most cerial killers. 

The movie itself is eerie, depressing, stays mostly with the book, which is refreshing, but, comparitively ends more happily than the book. Overall, I completely agree with the comparison made between both movies and would recommend everyone to see this.

A hunter finds a horde of dead bodies and a brief case with $2 million. Deciding to take the money and run he is soon pursued by the man who belongs to the money. This man is heartless and brutal, killing anyone who gets in his way with a weapon used to kill cattle. Effective when used at close range, pressurized air is shot out leaving a huge hole and no bullets behind. He is a sociopath who doesn't give up. Just as we get attached to the two characters and involved in the escalating battle between them, we are reminded of the title of the movie. The main character is an old-timer sheriff who can't keep up with the two men. He never finds out what happens to them and neither do we because he retires at the end of the movie. The most profound moment  is when he goes to visit his brother who lives alone and in a wheelchair. The brother refuses to let his sheriff brother feel pity for himself by telling a story of their uncle who was shot on his own porch by lawless men of the west not more than 70 years ago. Powerful but in a way unsatisfying. I got too attached to the two villain and want to know what happens. I like the old sheriff but its a bit as if he was reading a story and fell asleep so it just ended. Maybe that was the point but it lacked the delicious factor that I look for in a truly great movie.  Harrison Ford plays the right-hand man of a big city DA who had an affair with a woman in the office several years ago. Very worthy of raking up several BAFTAs and OSCARs, No Country For Old Men is a faithful novel to film adaptation which inevitably explores several themes: chance, free-will, fate and circumstance. I adore American Western settings, and this along with the theme of free-will already established a very understated yet unpredictable atmosphere to the film. The story being a hunter who is chased by a hitman armed with a captive bolt pistol in to retrive a Mexican gang's stolen cash and heroin with a Sheriff thrown into the mix, No Country for Old Men is the stuff Western's are made of, but there is a sense that the Coen brothers have taken a revisioned approach to the Western genre in this film. No Country for Old Men is certainly an absorbing film, expecially for those who are keen on raw drama. However, for those expecting lots of action, there will be a feeling of disappointment as the film relies mostly on understated cinematography, little dialogue and select moments of shoot-outs (some of which are cut out and left ambiguous) in order to create dramatic tension. Similar to There Will Be Blood, No Country for Old Men is like watching a literary masterpiece on screen, but unlike the latter, There Will Be Blood is completely original and more accessable to a wider audience due to the power-house acting rather than relying purely on dramatic tension. This is why I believe that There Will Be Blood was more worthy of the Best Film OSCAR than No Country for Old Men, but the latter is definitely still a masterpiece, and a great example of directing and cinematography.

For the first time in a long time I have agreed with the hype surrounding a movie. This one is superb. 

Josh Brolin stumbles upon the grim scene of a drug deal gone bad - making off with $2 million in the process. 

Javier Bardem, a psycho-killer for hire, is put on his trail to recover the money and punish those he finds with it. Meanwhile, Tommy Lee Jones is the local sheriff trying to piece together the grizzly murders that link the two men.

The atmospheric tension created by the Coen's here is outstanding. I can't remember the last film I saw that had such a formidable sense of forboding, a sense so tangible that you genuinely fear for some of the innocent characters in this film. 

This forboding is personified in the excellent Javier Bardem. His dodgy haircut and quiet demeanour do little to hide the bloodthirsty menace that lingers below the surface. All this man wants to do is kill - not for money or duty, but just for the act. He is the human equivalent of The Terminator. 

Josh Brolin, while not a lively character himself, is the closest thing we have to a hero in this film. He is not a cold-hearted killer, but he is a tough war veteran who matches Bardem in a game of wits that the audience watches on the edge of it's seat to see how it turns out. 

For me, however intentional this may have been by the Coen's, is where the film falls short of being perfect. the chase between these two men does end, but not in a way I was expecting. I leave it to the viewer to decide for themselves how they feel about it, as I would probably agree  that it is open to several interpretations. 

Despite the mixed feelings the ending may cause though, it is a fantastic film. It's almost timeless setting helps set it apart from it's 'New Hollywood' surroundings as it has something extremely 'classic' to it. This is one no film lover should miss.

Taut, spare, and intense, the Best Picture winner is the Coen Brothers' best film for five years at least, although maybe not even in their top five films ever.  That's more of a statement on the superior quality of their oeuvre than on the relative quality of this film, which is undeniably very high...

"No Country" seems at times like a loose remake of the Coens' striking debut "Blood Simple": the accents are the same, the bloody crime spree through dusty, empty landscapes is repeated, and there's a few sequences built on the masterful, skeletal structure of "Blood Simple"'s white-knuckle closing scene...

But "No Country" is a more thoughtful, mature, and even philosophical rumination on fate, aging, and moral decay, as well as a ballsy crime thriller.  Javier Bardem is often downright eerie, but a few fantastic scenes aside, he's mostly doing a standard-issue psycho-killer.  Tommy Lee Jones' mournful sheriff is certainly more interesting work from an actor who's consistently found vehicles for his talents lately, and Josh Brolin's doomed fugitive is revelatory in gradual doses, a Texas sunrise of a performance.  But this film is all about the Coens' impeccable orchestration of images and poignant deployment of words.  They're back at the peak of their powers after some brief wanderings in the wilderness, and what better time than that to give them their well-deserved Oscar?

I hate to disagree with my good friends on Flixster, but I really loved this movie. Tense, disturbing, upsetting, spartan and spare, with a cynical and vicious ending, it is a nearly perfect American Gothic film that has the courage to carry its story to its inevitable and awful climax. To me the end makes perfect sense, a horrific and brutal resolution to a film about the vagaries of fate and the existential nature of American violence.  With odd undertones around class and corporatism and with as evil a character to appear in film as any since Silence of the Lambs, the film has the nerve to say that in your own greed and individualism you may find that you cannot protect those that you love and that your stand, when taken, will end up hollow and meaningless. The tough man on his own cannot stop the forces that rise against him. The barbarity of his circumstance will, in fact, overwhelm him. 
In this great new era of rebirth in American film this is a standout, and though set in the 70's it speaks to the pulse of this era and reflects the banality of a time where the "principaled" are psychotic and the rest of us are just looking to get ahead or make a quick buck, no matter the result for others. You really don't have to do it.

[font=Tahoma][size=4][color=cyan]Wow. That's all I can say after watching this movie. I think that's all that needs to be said. This is everything that a movie geek like myself wants out of a movie. Interesting characters, a terrifying villian, some knock-your-socks-off violence, and tension tension tension. This movie is a masterpiece of tension. The plot involves a guy named Llewlyn Moss who stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad and being the clever guy he is, knows there must be a "last man standing" with the money. He retrieves the money and most of the rest of the movie involves this desperate man's attempt to escape the crazy criminals chasing him for the money.[/color][/size][/font]
[font=Tahoma][size=4][color=black][img]http://www.moviecritic.com.au/images/no-country-for-old-men-josh-brolin-1.jpg[/img][/color][/size][/font]
[font=Tahoma][size=4][color=cyan]One of said crazy criminals is one of the most frightening characters in the history of film. His name is Anton Chigurh and he's played by Javier Bardem. I've never been so scared of a character in a movie before. Every single scene that involves Chigurh and another person has me fearing for the other person. You really believe that this psycho will kill anyone for any reason, justified or not. The even more scary thing about him is that we don't know who he really is or where he came from. In a famous quote from the movie Tommy Lee Jones, who plays the sheriff trying to help Moss, refers to him as a ghost. So is this psychotic killer real or not? You decide.[/color][/size][/font]
[font=Tahoma][size=4][color=black][img]http://www.showcase.ca/BLOG/photos/films/images/15943/319x480.aspx[/img][/color][/size][/font]
[font=Tahoma][size=4][color=cyan]The acting in the movie is flawless. From Josh Brolin as Moss to Tommy Lee Jones as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell to, of course, Javier Bardem. One of the big factors that adds to the incredible tension of the film is the original score. There is none. There is no music in this movie. This was such a good decision because in most movies you will hear creepy music when the killer approaches, killing the suprise factor. In this movie, you will jump out of your seat at least once. The Coen Brothers have really gone to new heights with this movie. I liked Fargo and Blood Simple but I wasn't thinking about them for weeks after. That's how this movie affected me. Hell, it's been months since I've seen it for the first time and I'm still thinking about it! Something a lot of people have a problem with in this movie is the ending. I can understand to an extent what these people are saying because the ending is abrupt. If you haven't seen this movie yet, be prepared for that. However, I love the ending. I love movies that don't spoon feed you all the answers and make you think for yourself. The Coens love playing with the audience's minds and I'm into it. Also, this movie is based off the Cormac McCarthy book and supposedly the ending is exactly the same in the book (haven't read it myself). So I'm happy the Coens were faithful to the book. Recently a lot of trash has been released in theaters so seeing this was a breath of fresh air. It's nice to see a masterpiece of a movie once in a while and that is exactly what [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is.[/color][/size][/font]

When Tommy Leeâs diatribe ends the audience is introduced to the villain/main character, Anton Chigurh.  You quickly are introduced to his sadistic killing style as you watch him dispatch a Texas patrol man in the same manner a meet packer slaughters cattle. Shortly after coming face to face with Anton the audience stumbles on the tragic hero of the story, Leuellen Moss. No Country for Old Men is not your typical film. The charaters don't act in the way that we have been conditioned to expect from movies, and the story unfolds in a way that runs counter to typical movie patterns. And this, among manifold other reason, is why this movie is so bloody brilliant. Excessive amounts of ink have been spilt about the perfomances of the three main actors that to go on praising their virtues would be mawkish. The only thing I feel I can add them is that they define themselves by how little they talk, how talking as a whole is something one rarely seems to do in their Western Texas world. In a pop culture era previously defined by Wheadon/Sorkin style verbosity, this more than anything else stands out. I've heard that There will be Blood takes a similar approach to dialogue. A trend that I perosnally find very heartening, especially if it produces movies this good.

He appears after a drug deal gone awry and was hired to get back the money involved which winds up in the hands of hunter Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin).  Chaos ensues, people are systematically eliminated with Chirgurh unlikely weapon of choice.  During the ride there is some witty banter between the Sheriff looking for Chirgurh (Tommy Lee Jones) and his idiotic sidekick and there is a great scene at a diner between Tommy Lee Jones and Kelly Macdonald who plays Mrs. Moss, the wife of Llewelyn.  The only problem with the picture, if there is a problem, is the ending.  It ends rather abruptly with nothing being tied up.  Other than that, it is a fantastic picture and, possibly the best from the Coen brothers. When Llewellyn Moss discovers a bloody crime scene, a jeep's load worth of heroin and millions of dollars in cash, he decides to take the money and make a clean get-away. Meanwhile, Anton Chigurh, a psychopathic killer picks up Llewellyn's trail and begins a relentless, and merciless pursuit, to find Moss and take back what is his. Winner of 4 Academy awards including Best picture, Best director, Best adapted screenplay, and Best supporting actor, 'No Country for Old Men' was one of the most highly rated films of 2007. After witnessing the hype, I was anxious to see the motion-picture; but unfortunately, I feel my anticipation has somewhat lessened the impact of the film, and I'm left feeling slightly disappointed. However, there is still much to praise in this interesting thriller. The combined performances from Tommy Lee Jones, Javier Barden, Josh Brolin, Kelly Macdonald and Woody Harrleson are what really make the film so gripping. Each actor excels in their role, bringing a real sense of focus and direction to the narrative. I also admire the directional skills of the Cohen brothers. Their wide-shots of beautiful Texan landscapes and choice of close-ups during un-nerving action sequences create a very quiet, broody atmosphere. I also admire what the text is trying to say about the state of the world, and how 'there are no clean getaways'. My only true criticism is about the conclusion. I?m not one of those people who always has to have a set finale, and I understand that sometimes the openness and uncertainty of a conclusion is a films best feature, but with 'No Country For Old Men' I found the conclusion was a little to sudden and unexplained. A real slow-burner that requires a lot of patience, 'No Country For Old Men' is a tense, violent thriller that will leave a lasting impression.

Here is the true testament to a good book-turned-movie: I have not read the book upon which No Country For Old Men was based, but after seeing the film I would very much like to. And even though I have not seen many of its competitors, I can now wholly endorse this movie's Best Picture Oscar. All of this approval actually surprised me, since I don't often like movies that have the option of happy endings and either deny them or leave them ambiguous, as this film does. Nor do I often find myself liking action-dramas more for their drama than for their action. But this movie was, in a word, extraordinary. Every word, every shot, every character interaction, added something integral to the film's development and progression. The only detraction I could find was length, as the ending did seem to keep adding on scenes like Return of the King (though thankfully nowhere near as many).
The movie's soundtrack was particularly impressive, mostly because it did not have one. Where Quentin Tarantino will weave pop and rock songs into every element of his films, and George Lucas will orchestrally underscore every moment and then some--both successfully--the Coen brothers here chose to give their work only the sounds naturally heard in the towns and wilderness of West Texas. The effect was staggering, especially highlighting the skill of Bardem, as he had no fear-inducing music to supplement his creepy psychosis. It didn't matter: he didn't need any. I don't remember who else was nominated for Best Supporting Actor, but Bardem owned that award by the time he'd been onscreen for five minutes. 
I was also impressed with Tommy Lee Jones, whose milder-than-usual performance seemed a tempering rather than a fading-out, and with both Josh Brolin and Woody Harrelson; the latter for actually taking a mature movie role, the former for showing a slightly softer side and not playing a creepy stalkerish villain a la Planet Terror and American Gangster. And the tearful yet spunky innocence of Kelly Macdonald filled a small but important role as the film's compassionate female.
Bardem's character offers his potential victims a coin toss on two separate occasions. But for movie audiences, this film is anything but a toss-up. Like The Constant Gardener, it is not easy to watch, but it is worth it.

I love to trash films, it's always fun, but I just can't really seem to do it here. My only real nip-pick is with the outcome of Llewelyn Moss; well, not so much the outcome, but how it went down, I wanted a little more between him and Chigurh, but oh well, we can't have everything in life. Some people didn't seem to like the ending very much either: I loved the ending, perfect ending to this film I say! No Country is not quite as good as Fargo (arguably the Coen's finest work, few things are), but it is pretty damn close. ;)

[color=white]There is little about the film that i didn't know when i got the chance to see it, but that didn't take away from the enjoyment of seeing it. The first thing that really stood out to me was the way all of the characters had a "life's been long and tough" kind of feel to them. Their dialogue was brief but their attitudes spoke louder than their words ever could have. Through their slow step and hard edges they told us that this simple and plain setting could be as hard on life as it could be peaceful. For our characters times seemed to have been a little more peaceful, than the storm that was about to be unleashed on their pleasant lonliness, but not without their hardships. Enter our villian. It's true that a spoon full of sugar will help the medicine go down and for those who's medicine consisted of death by airgun our assassin Sugar made sure that they took it like a man. A very calculating opressor, Sugar was not the killer you'd expect. He killed without vengance, or greed, and regardless of his pay or employer. He seemed like a man without a soul, but still had a conscience to do the right thing, like keep his word. It just so happened that the word he had to keep was to kill you even though you had done nothing wrong to deserve it. There was no need to plead your case, because he couldn't feel mercy, he couldn't react to the pain of a hole in his leg or a bone sticking out of his arm, he couldn't feel anything except, the nagging voice in his head telling him to keep his word, and that voice often came from the flip of a coin. Still i couldn't help but thinking, in his final scene, that he had some remorse, some nagging urge to feel uneasy, which caused this very calculating machine to not calculate the fact that he was running a red light. I think Javier Bordem very much deserved the oscar that was presented to him for his role in this film as the most fresh villian i've seen on the screen in a long time. I also liked Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones, especially his monologue at the beginning of the movie, as the other actors in the film, but they were nothing close to the brilliance of Javier. The story... Well lets just say it was a cat and mouse chase with some twists but nothing that would catch you off guard, except... and this is a huge except, they never show you the final show down. There is no shoot out a the ok carroule... just a shot of the shot up carroule. There is no climax, there is no bad guy, good guy... lets finish this now scene. It just isn't there, and it works, brilliantly. One would say... well how'd it happen. I say that doesn't matter, what matters is, that the country that the old timers used to not carry guns in, doesn't exist any more because there is a deadening of the senses to right and wrong in our world... excecuted superbly by Mr. Sugar and the Coens. No Country for Old Men thematically addresses inhuman brutality and violence. In the films (senior) point of view, it is something scary and senseless. The audience, however, has an opposing and thrilling view: violence is a source of entertainment. Much of the fun and suspense comes from Anton Chigurh, one of the most cold-hearted killers ever to set foot on movies. He is played by the newly-minted Oscar-winner Javier Bardem. Equipped with a low calm voice and Frankenstein stance, the Spanish actor is absolutely formidable in the role. Chigurh seems to tower over the audience. Even a sliver of his shadow, just a hint of his presence could make you stop breathing.

The films harrowing tension is, of course, orchestrated by the Coen Brothers. They know how to punctuate with quick acts of carnage. And just as important, they proficiently prolonged spine-tingling sequences by playing the intense music of silence. Despite some excellent sections, the movie contains extraneous and languorous scenes. I admire the Coen Brothers. They have been established filmmakers for decades, often bringing a dark Americana humor to their own crafted stories. Its funny that Oscar finally rewards them (with Best Picture) when theyve adapted somebody elses work.

 So you got your main characters, a cowboy who just found 2 million dollars, and is running from a homicidal maniac.  A homicidal maniac that has probably the best weapon ever used in the history of motion-pictures, which was some kind of air-pressure gun, amazing.  And the sheriff of the town, Tommy Lee Jones.  Now, what I found interesting was the sheriff lives in a nice quiet town in the middle of absolutely nowhere.  Then this massive shootout of Mexicans happens, when a drug deal goes bad.  The sheriff finds this homicide spot, like CSI gone wild, and how does he act? He acts like this is something he sees every day, yup, thats a lot of dead bodies, lets move on.   The story itself is a cat and mouse game of trying to get the cowboy, who has the 2 million in a small suitcase.  I got into it, and was waiting for the huge climax, the part where the best shootout of American filmmaking was about to happen.  They completely didnt show it happen. There are times when I start to wonder if any truly good movies will be made anymore, considering the garbage that trickles out of Hollywood these days. It's a movie like this that gives me hope. The story is told magnificently by the Coen Brothers, who weave a web of tension like nothing I've seen in a movie in years. Basically, a retired man in 1980s Texas stumbles upon the remains of a drug sale gone wrong and finds a case containing two million dollars. He takes the money but is then tailed by this assassin that is out for the money. Armed with a type of pressure tank used to kill cattle, he calmly kills his way closer and closer to the money like some kind of disease. The story sounds simple enough but the direction and performances give it a depth that most movies dream about. The best character in movie is the sure-as-death assassin played by Javier Bardem. The guy is like the Terminator, even digging a bullet out of his own leg and slinging his compund fractured arm before walking away from a car accident (the bone was poking THROUGH THE SKIN). If that isn't a new kind of badass, I don't know what is. See this movie and see it now.

Fan's of the Coen brothers are going to like this film. I have been a fan since "Blood Simple" and I liked this film.

The plot is this: It's 1980. Llewelyn Moss (JOSH BROLIN) is Vietnam vet who lives in Texas. He goes hunting and stumbles across a massacre; a drug deal gone bad. The body count is high w/ one survivor asking for water. There's drugs in the back of a truck. Moss finds a briefcase containing $2 million. This tidy little sum will get him and his wife, Carla Jean (KELLY MacDONALD) a better life.

Moss makes the mistake of going back to help the only survivor. This is when the chase begins and Moss finds it harder to deal with the money (he can't get rid of it and he can't keep it). Moss escapes but he has hitman Anton Chigurh (JAVIER BARDEM) after him. The trail of violence is long and veteran lawman Ed Tom Bell (TOMMY LEE JONES) does not want to get involved. He's tired and he realizes the times and criminals have changed. It's no country for old men.

Moss tries to run from Chigurh. Bell tries to find Chigurh and Moss and bounty hunter Carson Wells (WOODY HARRELSON) joins the chase for the $2 million.

The movie works on many levels. The Coens use Cormac McCarthy's novel of the same name and they blend their own storytelling talent with McCarthy's and out comes a rather good film. Like "Fargo" the film has captivating characters, brutal violence, a plot that takes interesting turns and dark humor.

Themes I liked and which stood out in the film: chance, free-will, redemption, character of evil. Chigurh, the most evil character I have seen in a film for awhile , is the one who delivers the most theological questions and subject matter. Another thing I noticed about the film, very little if no mood music. You don't need music to tell you when to be scared or when an exciting moment is coming.

The ending may bother some folks but I found it challenging and it is one of the moments in the film about which I am still thinking. I may see this film again not only for the cinematography (which is good) but for the story.

He finds a case with 2 million dollars and takes it. Here begins a chase for the money from the pure evil hit man - Anton Chigur, played to perfection by Javier Bardem.  He is relentless and he leaves a bloody carnage in his wake as he kills his way across the state with his peculiar weapon - The pneumatic bolt gun.  The Coen Brothers capture each location brilliantly and every scene is stunning. The film uses little in the way of music and the quietness emphasises the sheer extent of their surroundings and adds to the tension wonderfully. Gripping and gritty - No Country For Old Men is a great film.

Days after seeing it, I am still haunted by No Country for Old Men. There is just something so effectual and uncompromising about it, that mere words will only begin to skim the surface of the cinematic excellence on display.

At its most simplistic, the film is a game of cat and mouse. The mouse here is Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a hunter who stumbles upon two million in cash after a drug deal gone wrong, and takes it thinking nothing of it. He tries to cover his tracks, but ends up letting the group looking for the money, figure out his identity. The cat is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a hit-man hired to find Moss and the money. But Chigurh is unconventional at best; he also happens to be bordering on mentally insane. And another man, a law man this time, Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), is on the trail of both men as they criss-cross around Texas.

Regaling from Oscar success, "No Country..." will be remembered for two reasons: a return to form by directorial siblings the Coen Brothers, and the uniquely memorable assassin played by Javier Bardem.  Epitomising the psychotic killer stereotype, Javier portrays a methodical, emotionless hit man that cannot be reasoned with.  Signature bowl cut, executions by compressed air gun and monotonic discourse all add up to elevate the character to cult status.  Equally on form are the rest of the cast including Tommy Lee Jones and Josh Brolin.  The abrupt open ending (being true to the novel) may not suit everyone, but this deliberately paced, brooding "chase movie" will please the majority.

Some people love this movie, and some hate it.  I'm in between.  

On the plus side, Javier-Bardem (sp) has to have delivered one of the best roles for a serial killing antagonist since Anthony Hopkins, and I applaud the Cohen brothers for not catering to the a-typical storyline of Hollywood movies where the good guy always wins.  Also, withholding music from the movie and not using it as a crutch to support the movie, but instead let the story stand on it's own two feet was a bold move that really paid off.   

However, the plot didn't exactly keep me on the edge of my seat the entire time either, and some of the performances were a bit overrated. I felt like I was watching Tommy Lee Jones in "The Hunted," with the Bardem and Brolin going at it ...and instead of Jones actually doing the chasing, he's off in some coffee shop, or relative's house, or office soliloquizing every chance he got about how old he was.  If that's all he was going to do, I would have preferred it if he just took Danny Glover's route to sum things up and move on.

Mind you, I'm not giving it bad marks for it being a slower movie (after all, anyone who loves Master and Commander as I do would definitely find this movie intriguing-and I do) but the relationships that this movie so heavily depends upon just doesn't draw me in as well as other movies, with the exception of BardemÃ¢ÂÂs role.

A worthy return to form for the Coens, who had strayed a little as of late into the comic wilderness with efforts like "The Ladykillers" and "Intolerable Cruelty".  This is a movie with a much darker soul, and none darker within it than Javier Bardem's vicious and methodical assassin on the trail of some missing drug cash.  You can easily see how Bardem walked off with last year's Oscar for this role, and that in a movie populated with some great character acting.  Josh Brolin is very good as the unwitting hunter who stumbles upon (and keeps) the cash, only to find Bardem and all kinds of related evil in quick pursuit.  And Tommy Lee Jones does a great job as the local sheriff trying to put it all together, but always coming up just a bit short.  The real stars here, however, are Joel and Ethan Coen, whose writing-directing tandem undoubtedly regained its former strength.  Disturbing, thoughtful and engaging, it's everything you would expect from a Coen film, Oscars and all.  Recommended.

For all of it's insanely high critical acclaim, I was a little disappointed with the movie. Maybe I've been corrupted by the typical Hollywood shoot em up action thriller, but this movie bored me. Not to say that there wasn't some great film making involved here, just that it seemed a little too flat to warrant all of the praise I've seen it receive. 
 
The plot revolves around a psychopathic man in search of a wayward case of drug money. Along the way, he randomly murders people in a cold blooded fashion that borders on disturbing. The cowboy who had found the money quickly learns of his pursuit and does his best to evade him.
 
Of course, it's a little more complex than that. Throw in a few cops and a nervous girlfriend, some trusting soon-to-be victims, and you get the idea. 
 
The director was clearly going for the "leave it open to the imagination" approach. Not every loose end is tied by the movies finish, and some key closure to certain parts of the story is not offered. Yeah this is a creative thing to do in some scripts, but I really believe it was overdone in this one. Most of the time if this is the case we usually just have to wait until the sequel to be satisfied. Clearly, however, it would be a insane reach to imagine a follow up film to this one since most of the main characters expire. But hey, I never thought I'd see a 4th Indiana Jones either. 
 
The main positive to the movie it's ability to keep you on your toes. The slow pace of the film makes it easy for the viewer to become anxious to the point where it's almost annoying. So in the "what will happen next" department, it far succeeds most of its genre. Still, once you have discovered what actually happens, I don't see how it could be anything short of a let down. That being true, the replay value is severely lacking. 
 
Yeah the villain was extremely dark and interesting, and yeah the 'hero' was brave and strong willed, but not in ways that I haven't seen in other thrillers. I have a belief that some critics like to give high marks to movies that intentionally throw in a lot of simple conversation just to make it seem realistic and down to Earth. Ok fine, but that alone is not enough to wow me into believing I've just watched a modern masterpiece.
 
It's not a total waste of time, and according to my peers I'm apparently missing the magic that made them love the film so much. If you enjoyed the conversational aspects of Kill Bill, and the bloody violence of The Departed, then you're already half way there to really liking this one. But for me, I never went any further than that. 
 
Rating: 5 out of 10

No Country for Old Men started out as a five star movie, but fell flat at the end.  The Coen bros had a great story, one of the coolest, AND ORIGINAL bad guys I've seen in a very long time and the movie kept me interested throughout... So, why give it 3 stars?  Because the movie didn't have a real ending!  It felt like they realized; "Uh-oh, we've reached 2 hours and 2 minutes!  We better just end it."  There seems to be a trend in Hollywood where, if a movie (even if it's good enough to make you not realize it's over 2 hours while you're watching it) should never EVER go over the 2 hour mark.  Sure there are films out there that are longer, some even 3 hours, but look at who made them.  Only the really big names, like Sergio Leone with Once Upon a Time in America, can get away with doing that.  So, if you want to see the best villain in a story that builds to a suspenseful climax, but doesn't deliver at the last minute, by all means see this movie.  But trust me, the movie is so good that you'll feel cheapened by how they ended the damn thing.

Impressive in certain respects, particularly the Coen brothers' mastery of direction and cinematography to evoke the themes of chance, destiny and man's choices subtextually. Even greater is the consistent theme of survival-of-the-fittest, whereupon characters interchangeably shift from predator to prey, hunting one another to evade an inevitable extinction. However, the picture is equally flawed as it is masterful; at no point do we see vulnerability in antagonist Chigurgh (indeed, villains of his nature are primarily driven by their innate weaknesses and overwhelming insecurities) nor do we particularly relate to protagonist Llewellyn Moss (should we sympathize for his senseless pursuit of a deed he long should've given up?) While it remains a faithful adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel, it is by no means, nor should it have won Best Picture.

As soon as where given Tommy Lee Jones naration of on going senseless crime we meet the devil in the making as he is taken into custody by a deputy who is unaware just how dangerous and lethal his suspect really is. In the middle of this ensuing chaos that starts with a drug deal gone sour in the middle of the Texan-Mexican Border a antelope hunter Lewellyn Moss (Played by a believable and likable JOSH BROLIN) His role here is the one audiences will have rooting for against impossible dangerous odds. Out in the desolate west is where many great films have taken place. The Coen brothers, Joel and Ethan, (winner of Best Director) are among the great American filmmakers. Their snarky noir to their screwball comedy have earned them prestige and respect and also a few Oscars. I've never cared for films that take place in the barren desert. They tend to be too formulaic. That's where you have the Coens take an overused setting and make it new and interesting. Their 2008 Academy Award winner for Best Picture, No Country for Old Men is a refreshing look out west. Josh Brolin (Grindhouse) plays a man who finds dead bodies in the desert, with a briefcase of two million dollars and a truck filled with heroin. He tries to escape with the money, but on his trail is a hitman with the world's worst haircut (Best Supporting Actor winner Javier Bardem). The Coens definitely produce, write, and direct the Thinking Man's film, due to he fact it's a bad idea to doze off through one of their films, otherwise, you might miss something very important. Many critics have said this films is a western horror movie, and in a way, they're right. You have your maniac, your refugee, your hero, and your ultra-violence. The violence seems brutal, from explosions to shots...in the head. Javier's hitman is one of the most original portrayals in film history. He's quick, slick, and keeps his cool, all with a very misfortunate hairstyle. Tommy Lee Jones (Academy Award nominee for In the Valley of Elah) is the good guy, trying to track down the killer and find who stole the money. The pursuit is heart racing, the emotionless face of the causes fear hitman as he walks closer to the door with his silenced gun. He's very eerie, and his raspy voice intensifies it. He is one of the most evil characters ever to appear on screen. He runs shivers up your spine. You may find that "Call it, friend-o." may be the most popular line of 2007. There's a little of he Coen's familiar humor hidden in the film, one liners and awkward moments. Joel and Ethan adapted the script from the novel by Cormac McCarthy. The great script and the wonderful storytelling is clear as day in this western thriller. The desolate wasteland where film takes place is haunting, as if you are alone and no one can help you. If you are trapped, laying in the sand covered in blood, and a man with a weird haircut calls you friend-o, you're dead meat. Joel and Ethan tell this story in a flawless style (and won an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay), and it is done it gorgeous detail. The ending has been causing controversy. Audiences have felt cheated. You are left with a cliff hanger, not as if it were to be made into a sequel, but just left on the edge of your seat, wanting more, but the film leaves you hanging. I did not care for the ending. I can not appreciate it. Other than that, No Country is a masterwork. A brutal, yet glorious film.

It is real and completely appropriate right down to the Sheriff who admits that he is being outmatched by the criminals.  The good don't always win, a condradiction of popular belief and an often uttered  easy saying used to convince oneself that good will one day arrive on the doorstep.  (We're all guilty of beleiving that - I beleive).  Not quite as Noir-ish as past Cohen Bros films, especially The Man Who Wasn't There, but similarly aluring.  A story about what is likely to happen as opposed to what the mass audience hope will happen.

I'm not normally a fan of Tommy Lee Jones but he really takes to this role. Coens move to Minnesota with Fargo and now down to Texas. The local dialects are a strong building point. One really gets a feeling of an inherent wild west timeline; the wild violent streak is still there but a certain sophistication has been achieved over time. Lee Jones has a sophisticated, philosophical non-chalant way of dealing with the crime that is a normal part of their life. Josh Brolin is mostly convincing but the Moss characters overall take on life is a bit blurred. Bardem is good; portraying a sharpish mind with no empathy and a crazed drive to achieve what he's set out to do; he's indifferent to the fact that this is chain of murders. Just hope he's not got himself stuck in a "bad guy roles" rut. Overall good movie, but balance between character building and violence could be better.

Undoubtedly, an unabashed and unflinching return to form for the maestros Coen, No Country For Old Men is possibly their most emotionally-effective, powerful film yet. A tale in the vein of some of the Coens' best work - one man makes a small, but important, decision (in this case, Llewelyn Moss' decision to take the $2 million from the drug deal gone awry) that snowballs into a series of events of cataclysmic proportions, leading to doom being spelled for nearly all the characters, No Country succeeds in that, once again, the Coens' use of the plot device is subtle and refreshing. 
The ace in the hole of this film is the actors, and, in particular, a Mr. Javier Bardem. Portraying the menacing, almost omnipresent Chigurh, Bardem endows the character with a kind of unnerving personality - for a character so utterly devoid of human empathy and so obviously a body of pure evil, you find yourself chuckling uneasily at his dialogue exchanges with characters, as his utter distaste for the quirks of humanity shine through (his response to hearing how the gas store owner came to own the gas store is laced with as much disdain as to be hilarious). Josh Brolin is a note perfect Coen brothers anti-hero, his Southern drawl and stony face perfect for the role of the disillusioned Llewelyn Moss, and Tommy Lee Jones is also fantastic as No Country's version of Marge Gunderson, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. His gaunt features and tired voice are perfect for this role, and as a conservative voice of reason who is too small to have any effect against Hurricane Chigurh, Jones endows the character with a quiet dignity and power. The other actors, especially Woody Harrelson, who gets some of the best one-liners in the movie as a sort-of comic relief, and Kelly MacDonald, whose plea with Chigurh for her life at the end is one of the most moving parts of the film, are also perfectly cast in their roles.   
The Coen brothers have crafted a masterpiece of 21st century cinema. Managing to turn on their head pre-established problems with their filmmaking, no man or woman can accuse this film of being emotionally lacking, and the sagging parts of the film are minimal.

No Country for Old Men is kind of a strange exercise in minimalism. Actors deliver their pithy lines with deadpan faces, music is used sparingly, and the plot is incidental, almost nonexistent. The only thing unrestrained in this film is its violence, most of which is dispensed with brutal efficiency by Chigurh, an emotionless, psychopathic killer played by Javier Bardem. He's the film's weirdest and most explosive ingredient, but he's only interesting until it becomes clear that there aren't actually any motives behind his actions. All the characters in this film are kind of like that: impassive, single-minded, and frustratingly insufficient in their characterization. Certain parts of No Country for Old Men works as a great thriller, with every burst of violence preceded by enormous moments of tension, but there are other parts, like the ambiguous, anti-climactic conclusion, that feels baffling and unsatisfying.

No Country For Old Men[/i] is the latest and most acclaimed offering from the Coen brothers and is also this year's best picture winner. Unfortunately, I don't think it's a movie for everyone. For a niched movie that I think appeals more to people who are passionate about film and filmmaking than the average movie goer looking for entertainment, it didn't end up boring me as I was afraid it would 20 minutes into the movie.
  
 Llewelyn Moss, a hunter, stumbles upon a mexican drug trade gone wrong along with a black satchel filled with 2 million dollars cash.  He takes the money and then becomes the prey when deadly assassin Anton Chigurh starts sniffing at his trail for the money. Trailing behind the two is a seasoned sheriff played by Tommy Lee Jones who hopes to make things right by finding Moss first and catching the killer.
  
 This movie wasn't for me in the end. On my own I was able to watch the entire movie without being bored or lost, but then having reached the end figuring what the movie is ultimately about is lost on me. From reading other reviews I understand the film a bit better, especially the unhappy ending and the significance of the sheriff along with the title of the story, and I can respect the film for that. In the end though, it isn't my cup of tea.

If you are reading this, by now, you probably know that âNo Country for Old Men,â directed by Joel & Ethan Coen, won the Academy Award for Best Picture 2007.  You may have even seen it already.  With so many well-written and glowing critical reviews, what more can I hope to add?  Still, I liked the movie, and so if you havenât yet put this one in your queue, hereâs why you should.

âNo Country for Old Menâ is the story of Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, played by Tommy Lee Jones.  Which is interesting, since he doesnât even appear until well over 30 minutes have elapsed of the filmâs two-hour running time.  Instead, the movie opens with Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a straight guy who stumbles upon a grisly scene in the desert of West Texas.  Itâs the aftermath of a drug deal gone bad.  That same grisly scene happens to contain a satchel stuffed with two million dollars, and Moss, deciding this must be the opportunity of a lifetime, takes the money, setting into motion a cat-and-mouse chase involving Sheriff Bell, who mostly just wants to see Moss get out of this mess alive, and criminal Anton Chigurh (Oscar-winner Javier Bardem), who wants that money, damn anyone who gets in his way.

Antonâs a peculiar fellow whoâs a bit like a killer cockroach.  Nothing stops this guy, not a car crash, an impacted bone fracture, nada.  He carries a kind of pressurized air gun (I looked it up on Wikipedia, itâs a captive bolt pistol) to dispatch of everything from door locks to inconvenient witnesses.  His single-mindedness is fascinating, and he has a code of ethics all his own.  âYou donât have to do this,â a character pleads with him at one point.  âAh, but I do,â he responds.  He made a promise to someone, you see, and the killing of an innocent person would fulfill that promise indirectly.  But instead of taking on the moral weight of deciding to kill an innocent, Chigurh asks his potential victims to call a coin toss for their life.  In doing so, heâs washing his hands of the matter.  Schluffing off the morality of his kills to fate or luck is just another way Chigurh manages to be a survivor in the dangerous world he inhabits.

And hereâs where Shefiff Bell (Jones) comes in.  Heâs come a long way from the days when the only trouble seen in his sparsely populated county might have been stolen cattle, or a drunk that started a bar fight, or maybe, just once a blue moon, a shooting.  âNo Country for Old Menâ is set in West Texas circa 1980, just as cross-border drug violence was beginning to get really, really nasty.  Thereâs no mafia code of honor here, just mass slaughter.  Bell, whoâs already on the cusp of retirement, sees this world and knows itâs not his anymore.  He realizes he canât keep up with this newer brand of criminal.  Bell is one of the âold menâ the filmâs title refers to.  Itâs his narration that opens, and then closes the film, in one of the boldest endings in recent memory that ultimately seals the picture as belonging to Bell, despite his limited presence in the story.

I loved the way this movie was put together.  The wide frame of the film is filled with the vast nothingness of the West Texas landscape in and around Marfa, where the movie was filmed.  The visuals are matched by the stark soundtrack â which is to say thereâs hardly any soundtrack to speak of, despite composer Carter Burwellâs name being listed in the credits.  Maybe there was some music, but I didnât notice any until the final credits rolled.  The movie is also edited in a more leisurely pace, befitting its Southwestern setting.

The DVD of âNo Country for Old Menâ includes three short featurettes that are a little better than the standard Electronic Press Kit (EPK) talking heads features that normally come on DVDs these days.  Thereâs a bit more serious discussion about the film and its themes rather than just glowing praise for everyone who worked on the film.

Speaking of the filmmakers... as for the Coen brothers, who took home the Best Directing prize at this yearâs Oscars, âNo Country for Old Menâ does seem to fit in with most of their oeuvre, with its look into the darker side of the human element, but unlike âFargo,â thereâs little humor to be found in âNo Country for Old Men.â  This is a deadly serious story, and also a deeply satisfying one.

This has to be, without a doubt, one of the best films of 2007. The Coen Brothers have again made their talent for film-making shine through this film. From the moment it starts to it's abrupt yet defining end, No Country For Old Men is a true masterpiece of a movie that should not be missed. I can say for a start that it wasn't quite what I had expected it to be. I knew little about the plot and tried to keep an open mind while walking into the cinema, which was probably the best thing to be doing. It surprised me, but in the best possible way. From the little I knew, I thought it would be perhaps more of a drama film. Instead, it came out to me as a very well done thriller. There was also more violence than I expected, and it wasn't just it being bloody, but everything seemed very sudden. I saw these things as compliments to the movie, for I felt that without them it wouldn't have been the multi-award winning, brilliant film that it is. Tommy Lee Jones was in the film for quite a bit less than I was expecting him to. Even so, his performance while on the screen was near perfection. Javier Bardem was... well, I can say that he 100% deserved that Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. He created a terrifying and fearless character, his performance in this film is sure to be remembered. Josh Brolin was also another stand-out performance, as was all of the acting. This is a must see movie that I strongly recommend anyone and everyone to see.

â~No Country for Old Menâ(TM) is based on a book of the same title by Cormac McCarthy, which, incidentally, is taken from the Yeats poem â~Sailing to Byzantiumâ(TM). Directed by the Coen brothers, whose oeuvre seems to be comedic thrillers, it is an improvement on the book, paring back a lot of the dialogue to reveal a tersely-plotted western thriller. Like many westerns, it is set in frontier land close to the United States-Mexico border, which has been influential on the look of the film. Almost everyone wears leather boots and a cowboy hat. The plot, though, is an inversion of a typical western: instead of a series of skirmishes leading to a final showdown, the showdown occurs before the movie starts, and the rest of the movie is the fallout. 

As a basic chase movie, it is highly successful. I donâ(TM)t think Iâ(TM)ve ever been so on edge in a non-horror movie. A large part of the credit for this goes to Javier Bardem, playing the menacing hitman Anton Chigurh. His performance is so compelling that afterwards Bardem had to make a string of romantic comedies to avoid being typecast as a bone-chilling psychopath. Josh Brolin is also fine as the cunning Llewellyn Moss, who thinks heâ(TM)s smart enough to make a clean getaway. The story is told from the alternating perspectives of Moss and Chigurh, creating tension as we watch Chigurh closing in and Moss barely escaping, wondering if heâ(TM)ll survive the next battle of wits. Particularly well-done is a scene in which Moss calls a desk clerk from his motel room. Anton has already dealt with the clerk, so the ominous sound of a ringing phone with no one to answer it informs both predator and prey that their nemesis is close at hand. The tension only builds from there. The Coen brothers manipulate the tone of the film masterfully, breaking up the tense thriller scenes with low-key comedic interludes, which arise organically from the filmâ(TM)s characters, situations, and dialogue. Kelly Macdonald is wonderful, especially given how little there is for the women in the film to do. The cinematography is also beautiful â" everything about NCFOM is well-crafted.

What deepens the film beyond being a competent thriller is a third plot strand involving one of the â~old menâ(TM) of the title, Tommy Lee Jones. As Sherriff Bell, he is reluctantly compelled to investigate into the swathe of violence left behind by Antonâ(TM)s hunt for Llewellyn. His amusingly slow-witted deputy (Garrett Dillahunt) counterpoints and underscores Bellâ(TM)s world-weariness. Who can stem the apparently rising tide of bloodshed in todayâ(TM)s world? McCarthyâ(TM)s work brilliantly portrays the pervasiveness of violence in the past (â~Blood Meridianâ(TM)), and the inevitability of violence in the future (â~The Roadâ(TM), which has also been made into a film). The ending of NCFOM is initially baffling. I understand Bellâ(TM)s monologue as a final statement on violence: most have given up trying to prevent it. But you have to keep on carrying the fire.

It starts typically enough, with bursts of violence, a central character who comes across as a bit of a moron (typical Coen fare),  an endlessly entertaining super-villain (Javier Bardem having the time of his life) and Tommy Lee Jones being Tommy Lee Jones, except for a thicker brawl.  (I had to go check some of his dialogue out from other sources afterwards, but that may have been just my hearing.)  Then things start happening: the bursts of violence begin to carry a heavy but never heavy-handed moral weight; Josh Brolin somehow becomes far less of a moron; Bardem adds gravitas to his flash; and Tommy Lee seems unwilling to turn into the character we are expecting.  And then the Coens' other favourite theme - fate, both as we plan it and as it actually develops - takes centre stage.

This is an adaptation of a reputedly very good novel, and what faults I could find with it are probably due to that.  Some narration comes across as both ponderous and incomplete; there is the occasional feeling of something missing, something the actors are not managing to entirely flesh out (despite uniformly impressive performances, particularly Kelly Macdonald in a role that could have been almost unnoticeable had she not been as strong in it) - Woody Harrelson, in particular, seems to have been sold short.  Around the second third of the film, the flash loses its spark, the funny aspects start to fall a little flat and a distinct whiff of disappointment threatens to grow too strong to be ignored.  This is when the film shifts gears and spectacularly recovers its ground, and more besides, by turning on its head and refusing to deliver what it had hinted it would.

"No Country For Old Men" is the kind of film that grows stronger in your memory as the days pass.  The presences of Peckinpah and Ford become less obtrusive, less a matter of homage than of heritage; the same for the use of violence, which in retrospect loses any pyrotechnical quality it may have had to acquire the resonance Scorsese has forgotten how to achieve.  And, fundamentally, Javier Bardem's character realigns in your mind: no longer a post-modern, vaguely ironic take on the Angel of Death, he becomes something far more human each time you revisit what he did and did not do in the end.  The same for Tommy Lee Jones: his weight to the whole can only be properly assessed in retrospect.  Without having read McCarthy's source novel, I cannot be sure that this is where the Coens make it their own (fate and its twists, again), but I have a feeling I am not far off the mark.

This may be the Coen Brothers' best film in years if not perhaps their best ever (it certainly deserves mention alongside Miller's Crossing and Blood Simple at the zenith of their work). In my honest opinion, this movie is easily better than their often lauded 1996 effort, Fargo (a movie that I thought was good but vastly overrated). The Coen's make a triumphant return to Texas, the state where they made their debut with the aforementioned Blood Simple. As with that film and with most of their work in general, the Coen brothers flawlessly combine violence, tension, drama and dark humor into a compelling, gritty noir-thriller (with flavors of a modern Western) about greed, deception and murder. One of the most noteworthy aspects of this film is the sparsity of cue music. Where most movies use music to elevate the levels of suspense and tension, this film shows that oftentimes the complete absence of music can achieve the same effect even more. There were several scenes that actually caused me to jump because the tension was so well-orchestrated. At just over two hours, the movie is well-paced and every time the proceedings threaten to lull us too much into our comfort zones, the Coen's jolt us back to reality usually with sudden bursts of action or similarly violent occurrences; best not get too comfortable for too long. And the Coen's prove that they can compose action set-pieces with the best of them. Their are several moments in this film that get the adrenaline pumping with amazing effectiveness. Arguably the best thing about this film, however, is the tremendous Oscar-winning performance turned in by Javier Bardem as the vicious, emotionless hitman, Anton Chigurh, one of the most compelling screen villains in recent memory. Here's a man who kills without compunction or remorse; the concept of mercy is one that is completely alien to him. Many have compared him to Hannibal Lecter and I believe that is entirely legitimate connection. Both are highly intelligent people and both are calculated in their often savage acts towards others. Without a doubt, most of No Country's best scenes revolve around Chigurh and a huge part of this is the way Bardem plays the role. Everyone else does a good job including Josh Brolin (who plays the protagonist), Kelly McDonald, who sports a flawless Texan accent and plays the protagonist's wife (I still remember her best as Ewan McGregor's underage girlfriend in Trainspotting), Woody Harrelson (as a rival bounty hunter) and Tommy Lee Jones  (as the world weary sheriff and, in many ways, the conscience of the film), but it's Bardem's work that dominates. Perhaps, the most controversial aspect of the film is the open-ended manner in which the Coen Brothers elect to conclude things. Enough loose ends are tied up but not everything is wrapped up in a neat and tidy package. This has infuriated many people but personally, I loved it. It was the perfect, unconventional ending to a very unconventional film, the cherry on top of a wonderfully dark but delicious parfait. I would love to see the Coen Brothers revisit these characters someday (perhaps if they can somehow option the rights from Cormac McCarthy, the author of the book on which this film is based). It worth noting that with this film and The Departed winning The Best Picture Oscar back-to-back, the tastes of the Academy have gravitated towards darker, grittier films. I personally love this trend because it proves to me that the members of the Academy are finally pulling their heads out of their asses and paying attention. Even if it didn't win anything, however, No Country for Old Men would still stand tall, not only as a monumental achievement for the Coen Brothers, but as one of the best- if not the best- films of 2007.
