  No Country for Old Men was the best film released in 2007. It was a haunting, disturbing, yet richly entertaining western\horror film filled with compelling performances from the entire cast. As they did in 1996 with "Fargo", the Cohen Bros. know how to take a serious film with dark subject matter, and really hit it out of the park making one hell of a movie. 
  
  Josh Brolin plays Llewelyn Moss, who is out hunting one day and stumbles upon a drug deal gone horribly wrong. Everyone is dead, or dying, and a truck filled with heroine and a case filled with $2 million is left behind. Naturally, he takes the case back home. Little does he know that the money belongs to Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a homicidal maniac who will stop at nothing to get his money back. 
  
  So ensues a game of cat and mouse between Llewelyn and Anton. Anton's pursuit for Llewlyn is a bloody and villianous one, for he removes anything and anyone that gets in his way. On Anton's case is Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who has been looking for Anton.
  
  The film will have you at the edge of your seat, with your heart pounding. There is not one false note or forced moment in "No Country for Old Men". Brolin really gives a great breakthrough role, but the film really belongs to Javier Bardem. He creates a menacing character, and one of the cinema's most menacing villians. Most of the time Bardem is on the screen he isn't speaking, but his mere presence sends chills up your spine. 
  
  Don't skip 2007's best picture.

[i][size=4]No Country For Old Men [/i]is Joel and Ethan Coens award winning 2007 film based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy, starring Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones and Javier Bardem. It concerns Llywellyn Moss (Brolin), who, while out hunting, discovers the aftermath of a drug deal gone awry. At the scene, he finds a MacGuffin of money, which he steals. Certain people are unhappy about this, however, and so begins the pursuit. After him is the brutal hitman, Anton (Bardem) and Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Jones) who has sworn to protect Llywellyn.

Neither Brolin nor Bardem are particularly well known actors, but they do their job here, brilliantly. Bardems character is creepy and his hairdo is awful. Despite this, he has a strangely hypnotic presence. The way he plays mind games with people before he does or doesnt kill them is bizarre, and creates considerable character depth- certainly deserving of his Best Supporting Actor Oscar. Brolins character is a tough, resourceful Texan, who it seems will do whatever it takes to evade his pursuers. Tommy Lee Jones does a fine job as the jaded lawman, saddened by his sense of helplessness to protect Llywellyn. Woody Harrelson- ever a good performer, makes a brief appearance as a slick bounty hunter.

From the first shot to the last, the cinematography in this picture is mind blowingly good. Quite how this lost the Best Cinematography Oscar to [i]There Will Be Blood[/i], I will never know. The Director of Photography, Roger Deakins deserves huge recognition for the brilliant job he did in making this visual masterpiece. It turns it into an extremely bleak film and conveys the expanse of the plains of Texas quite well. It feels strangely forlorn. The lack of any music throughout the picture also adds to the unhappy eeriness. The lack of morality in this film is strong.

I honestly enjoyed this film. The Coen brothers did an excellent job. Nevertheless, I preferred [i]There Will Be Blood[/i]. Whether that deserved the Best Picture Oscar more, I couldnt say. I wouldnt begrudge this film or its fine directors any awards, and they deserve all the praise they get. For me though, [i]TWBB[/i] was far less bleak and I enjoyed it more. I gave that an 8, but Im only giving [i]No Country[/i] a 7 out of 10. Despite only giving it a 7, it is still a must see movie. Usually, I operate a system whereby if I like a film, but wouldnt buy it on DVD, Id give it a 7. In this case though, Im prepared to buy this DVD even though I only gave it a 7. You really should see this film if you havent already. Rent it when it comes out on DVD, and then consider buying it. Id doubt if youll be disappointed.

Alright. Getting back to reviews at last, I'll try to tackle one of the biggest demons of 2007. First off, let me say, I know and recognize that I'm in the minority on this one. It's a widely adored film, for reasons I for one can't comprehend. Secondly, the Coens have made some films I enjoy, including Miller's Crossing and Fargo. However, I felt they threw away their style and substance for this film, simply to bow down and beg for Oscars. I honestly felt it was little more than a gun-chase B movie, lazily ripped of other films. How many times have we seen the "guy finds drug/stolen/ransom money, takes, gets chased by killer" storyline? Oh, and what about the Coen's apprenticing under Sam Raimi? Seems a bit suspicious to me considering Raimi directed "A Simple Plan. 
  
  To a large extent, the film felt false to me, from the man outrunning a truck sequence, to the cheesy "tension" of the 'coin-flip' scene. Some seem to feel the film was surprising, but I saw each and every moment coming. I constantly found myself thinking, 'what's the point?' One of my friend's once made the argument, "It's good because it's a film about nothing." What do I get from watching a film about nothing? Besides, that's been done many times before. To be even blunter, I feel the Coen's were just reveling in their own piss, as was proved for me by their behavior at the Oscars. It's a slasher flick for the pretentious, based largely around pointlessly brutal sequences. Then there's the pretentious title, which has very little to do with the actual plot. People would like to think so, but this film has no meaning at all, it favors the appearance of meaning over actual meaning. As for the acclaim surrounding Bardems performance as the hit man, I simply found myself thinking he been watching a bit too much of The Silence of the Lambs and Collateral.
 
   Ive been very bitter in this review, but to any friends who enjoy it, no disrespect, to each their own. To close, and reflect on the films of 2007, a quote from one of my former film professors: There Will Be Blood was infinitely superior to No Country.  It's like Spielberg vs. Kubrick; there's really no contest.

The Cormac McCarthy novel NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN is an ideal vehicle for the Coen brothers, who have used violence and emptiness laced with dark humor as an artistic aesthetic since the beginning of their careers--and although the setting and story are quite different it is very, very like FARGO in mood, style, and themes.

The story concerns Texan Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), who stumbles across the aftermath of a drug deal gone bad, takes the money, and runs. He is pursued by hit man Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem); both are pursued by sheriff Tom Ed Bell (Tommy Lee Jones.) Curiously, the film never allows any of the three men to meet; it instead follows their various paths toward and away from each other, paths that cross, diverge, and at times seem quite random.

Although the characters drive the story in the sense that they make the decisions they do because of who they are, the overall impression of the film is one of an initially calculated violence that becomes increasingly random as it progresses. There is no ultimate reason or deep meaning; just an open-ended emptiness of non-resolution and futility.

The cast is quite good, with Brolin, Bardem, and Jones perfectly cast and extremely believable in their roles; Kelly MacDonald, who plays the role of Llewelyn's wife, is particularly fine. The production values are also memorable. But like most Coen films, NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN seems to skate on the surface of its story rather than offer it to us in depth--the idea, one presumes, to allow us to impose our own ideas upon its very carefully crafted blankness. In this instance it works more often than not, but it is extremely noticeable when it doesn't, and the film often reads as self-consciously quirky as a result.

Jake  watched this a week before we did and said he thought it was good, but the ending was weird.  He was right.  But I'll get to that in a minute.

It was slow to get started with very little dialogue...which would have been okay, if there had been action.  But there wasn't.  It was a bizarre start to the movie, to say the least.  Once the characters got to talking, it got decidedly more interesting.  

Particularly Tommy Lee Jones' character...he stole the movie.  He had all the best lines and got to play a cool character to boot.  The only scene he was in that wasn't too entertaining was the final scene of the movie.  It just cuts off to a black screen.  It's almost like the movie makers just ran out of gas.  It was a strange way to end the movie for sure.

Javier Bardem played the purely evil for hire killer...and he did it well.  Cold, monotone...and almost robotic.  He wasn't over the top like you've come to expect with most action films.  I completely understand why he won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar this year.  As Aaron said, he provided us with a WTF moment every 5 minutes.

Josh Brolin was all scruffy looking, but still hot.  I laughed out loud a couple of times during his lines...usually while he was interacting with his not so smart wife.  It was really wrong, but I still thought it was funny as hell.

Both Aaron and I thought there were a few totally unrealistic moments in the movie that hurt its potential for credibility, but by and large, it was an interesting flick to watch.  This movie has a ton of violence in it, so if you're squeamish, skip it.  If not, watch on.

Whoa.  Where to begin.  I doubt there is a more spine shivering villan in modern film today than Javier Bardem as the killer Anton.  Cross his path and your fate is certain...almost.  He occasionally uses a coin toss to transfer the fate of his victim from his clutches to the cosmos, and those scenes are especially tense.  There's tons of blood in this fim about a drug deal gone bad in the west Texas barron lands,  and the stark uninviting landscape plays a role in the film also in a sort of "no where to run, no where to hide" element.  It's a hard place to live or just survive.  This is essentially a chase film.  Josh Brolin finds a massacre sight and eventually the drug money left behind.  Soon enough Bardem is on his trail and like a magician (with a remote receiver) he stalks Brolin day and night, killing anything that moves in his way - literally.   Tommy Lee Jones as the County sheriff knows the big wolf is indeed bad, and scrambles to find and help Brolin's who clearly did not know the evil he unleashed in the moment he decided to take the money.  Ultimately Jones and Bardem are headed for a facedown that never comes, though there is one scene that confused me when the sherriff returns to a crime scene.  We see Bardem hiding in the room in the dark laying in wait, but once the sheriff enters the room he does not pounce.  Thinking back perhaps the image of Bardem lying in wait is conjured up in the imagination of the sheriff, who is hesitant and anxious about entering the crime scene.  He knows the killer has returned to prior crime scenes, and he is admittedly scared.  This was the only time I had to rewind and watch again to make sure I understood.  The acting in this film is superlative.  I can't imagine any better actors for the roles and I believed each an every character, even Jones who seems to have played many Texas lawmen in his career.  I fell in love with Javier Bardem watching him at the Oscars, accepting the award, so I was curious to see how I'd respond to him as this insane character, and must admit he scared me.  Still - maybe he's just misunderstood!!!!!

"What's the most you've ever lost in a coin toss?" asked Anton Chigurh, in an odd Eastern European accent. The gas station owner is at a loss for words, and not quite sure of how to answer the tall man's query. This scene, in the Coen Brothers epic "No Country for Old Men" gives us as much insight as we are allowed into Chigurh's (oft ironically mispronounced Sugar) bizarre yet ordered psyche. He is the proverbial man in black, more of a driven angel of death than human being. His morality is defined by his concept of fate, hence his need for a coin toss; one that may violently end a life or preserve it. His weapons are his hands, a portable cow slaughtering stun-gun which he uses to get into locked doors with ease, and 12 gauge shotgun complete with a silencer attached to the barrel. Much about Chigurh remains a mystery, yet the unexplained questions about his motives, his ability to track his prey, or any kind of exploration into his history seems to lend to the ghostlike effect of his existence. Bardem's performance is so undeniably strong, that these questions have no need to be answered.
Josh Brolin plays Lewellyn Moss, a rugged out-of-work welder who happens upon a drug deal gone bad in the desolate West-Texas brush. After a little investigation, he finds the last man standing, although the man is actually dead and rotting against a lone tree. With him is a case of money, some $2 million dollars in small bills. Finally feeling that fate is smiling upon his life, he decides to take the money and run. Of course, every action triggers a consequence, and in this case, that consequence is the unstoppable Chigurh, who for reasons unknown, decides to track down Moss and claim the money for himself. 
In the middle of all of this mess is Sherriff Ed Tom Bell, played flawlessly by Tommy Lee Jones. His part is peppered throughout the film, as he tries to save Lewellyn and his demure wife from what he knows in his heart of hearts will be an inescapable death at the hands of Chigurh. 
This movie hearkens back to the early Coen Brothers movies Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing. It doesn't try to answer all of it's own questions. It doesn't apologize for the paths and motives it's central characters take. There is no right nor wrong in this world, only fate.
"No Coutry for Old Men" has chilling suspense some dry, dark humour and social layer, as well. Good actors and fine shooting make it an excellent thriller.

This has to be, without a doubt, one of the best films of 2007. The Coen Brothers have again made their talent for film-making shine through this film. From the moment it starts to it's abrupt yet defining end, No Country For Old Men is a true masterpiece of a movie that should not be missed. I can say for a start that it wasn't quite what I had expected it to be. I knew little about the plot and tried to keep an open mind while walking into the cinema, which was probably the best thing to be doing. It surprised me, but in the best possible way. From the little I knew, I thought it would be perhaps more of a drama film. Instead, it came out to me as a very well done thriller. There was also more violence than I expected, and it wasn't just it being bloody, but everything seemed very sudden. I saw these things as compliments to the movie, for I felt that without them it wouldn't have been the multi-award winning, brilliant film that it is. Tommy Lee Jones was in the film for quite a bit less than I was expecting him to. Even so, his performance while on the screen was near perfection. Javier Bardem was... well, I can say that he 100% deserved that Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. He created a terrifying and fearless character, his performance in this film is sure to be remembered. Josh Brolin was also another stand-out performance, as was all of the acting. This is a must see movie that I strongly recommend anyone and everyone to see.

Just like life, I guess. When you leave the cinema, youâll be asking those questions which, for Parisian waiters at least, are every day ones: are our actions dictated by Fate? Or, you might say as you munch on posh food, peut etre, life is meaningless and we are engaged in haphazard meanderings where each decision we make, every action isnât pre-ordained and we can be easily, randomly thwarted by chance, by accidents, byâ¦? So we have a bloody, tense, modern (set in the 1980s) âwesternâ; life and death struggles, gritty, visceral themes set in hideously modern buildings; trailers, motels â essentially fragile, ugly shoe boxes perched on the barren, unforgiving landscape of New Mexico, a terrain which will outlive the main characters no matter how muscular and brutal they are. The place names are familiar, El Paso, Rio Grande etc, they are the names of Western legend and movie mythology and while the struggles in this film are for life and death, and the bad guy, Chigur played with terrifying lack of humour by Bardem, is memorable and the perfect amalgam of every hitch-hiking, relentless, psychopath youâve ever seen on screen, youâre never in any doubt that this all means nothing. A conversation between Tommy Lee Jones, the sheriff and his retired from law-enforcement uncle outlines the philosophical heart of the film. His nephew talks about how things have changed, how the criminal has become almost untouchable and his uncle says simply, in that tobacco chewing way of westerns, Whatcha got ain't nothin new. This country's hard on people, you can't stop what's coming, it ain't all waiting on you. That's vanity. We cast ourselves as the heroes, the principal characters, it seems the Coens are saying, yet weâre not. In this blank view of human existence and purpose, thereâs a smattering of humour, plenty of desperate, painful violence and a relentless tour of the interiors of one Texan motel after another. In this film, everyone is on their own and vulnerable to sudden death. There are huge spaces between people physically and long moments of silence, no traffic, no other people â itâs a huge country. There is no perceptible soundtrack in the film yet the use of sound puts you right there in the protagonistsâ shoes so you can hear their breath, feel their reactions to an ominous footfall. Itâs extraordinarily tense and self-assured work. Special mention has to go to English cinematographer, Roger Deakins, who has found beauty somehow in the angular plains and ugly architecture. The three main protagonists are played with agonised intensity: Tommy Lee Jones cracking dark jokes and filled with blank wonder at the horror of the crimes heâs witnessed, his face a barely contained wrinkled mask of horror with only the eyes showing how heâs lost the heart and belief in what heâs doing. For this character, the good guys are too small, too weak to fight the modern evil; Josh Brolin is amazing; he looks like Nick Cave without the hair dye and his determination and virile fight against evil is both superhuman and human. He struggles against this Terminator style bad guy and has all our hopes pinned on his success. The actorâs struggles with mediocrity and his own personal demons before this role add poignancy to the experience. Hopefully this will be the beginning of a much deserved rise to the top for him. Javier Bardem won an Oscar for his part which, apparently, wasnât fleshed out in the novel where all we told is that Chigur has no sense of humour. Unlike the actor who, in his acceptance speech said, "Thank you to the Coens for being crazy enough to think I could do that, and [for putting] one of the most horrible haircuts in history on my head!" The exchange between Chigur and a hapless gas station proprietor will go down in cinema history as one of the most agonizing moments youâll witness â on a par with Joe Pesciâs âIn what way do I amuse you?â in Goodfellas. Chigur believes in fate and he has constructed his own fucked up rules and moral code about what has to be and what must happen. The man with all the power believes, ironically, that every action he takes is down to fate. It is a testament to the casting in this film that everyone, from the main characters to one-line speaking bit parters have such real personalities, so much history, such uniqueness that their deaths, if thatâs how theyâll end up, hurt you. These arenât the faceless victims of a serial killer, no; these are real people with real aspirations, real outlooks on life, coming up against a genuine monster and all we can do is cross our fingers for them. Whether or not youâll âenjoyâ this film is questionable. Itâs shockingly violent, unexpectedly visually beautiful, epic in theme but ultimately rather depressing. And it makes no sense â which is the point. Youâll be unsettled and haunted by it for days.I want to watch it again just to make sure, after all, what was all that stuff about the dreams at the endâ¦?

an excellent and thought provoking movie that is a world unto itself.  It doesn't tell a story as much as it reveals the characters to us through the circumstances of the plot.  Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem's character) interests me to no end.  It seems that many see him as just another crazed killer type character that kills because it brings him pleasure.  To me this is a misinterpretation of who this character actually is, and a misreading such as this takes a lot out of the film.  To me, the Chigurh character is an exercise in absolute adherence to an absolute set of principles.  He is a person who, unlike anyone who you will probably ever meet, has drawn for himself a plan of action which he applies to every situation he is thrust into unwaveringly.  He places his success in his various endeavors, and survival above all, and does not hesitate to kill anyone who even has the possibility of inconveniencing him in the future.  However, it appears to me that he adheres to this harsh course of action not because he believes himslf or his cause to be above others, but because the unfaltering nature of his behavior is the only tangible thing he has to hold onto in this world.  Although he accepts that he must hold himself up to this high standard of completely unchanging behavior regardless of situation, he seems at the same time to resent this.  hen he kills, he does so in the most humane way available to him using, when it is an option, a cattle gun used to kill steer painlessly before processing their meat.  He also, whenever possible, leaves the fate of people up to their calling of a coin-toss, perhaps in his mind putting their lives in the hands of fate, releasing him from his obligation to kill them, or even cleansing him of the guilt of killing them. Additionally, he doesn't kill people if they haven't seen him. 

-All in all, this movie was an excellent watch, a real "must see."  I do caution though that it should be watched with ones thinking cap on, lest some of the significance of this fine cinematic experience be missed.

Best Pictures, rarely, if ever, garner my attention.  They are more often than not trite, superfluous cash machines that do little more than pander to the masses.
      But No Country (like Crash) is different.  It's deep, bleak, and superbly written.  And stylish.  The cinematography here is unlike anything I've ever scene on the big screen.  Its brutal clarity and startling poignancy add as much to the movie as the Cohen's superb direction; maybe more.  It evokes a subtle noir that harkens back to Terrence Malick's  "Badlands" (a must see, by the way) and connects on every level.
     That said, I left the theater disappointed.  
     Unbelievable, I know, but true.  After emotionally investing 122 minutes in the event that unfolded on the screen, the ending left me cold.  Frigid, even.  
    Do not misconstrue my reaction.  I understood the ending, I just didn't like it.  Yes is was deep and yes it was pivotal and YES, it WAS philosophical, but after the cohesive screenplay we're subjected to for the first 115 minutes, the ending just seems...empty.  Maybe that's the point.  I have a feeling it played out on paper a little bit better.  Oh well.
       That scene where the sheriff is driving up to the motel though?
     Pure cinematic genius.  Worth two of those stars by itself.

The Coen brothers consistently write, direct, and produce excellent films and No Country for Old Men is no exception--indeed, it is one of their best.  The film opens with a monologue by Tommy Lee Jones (in one of his best performances) that generates an uneasiness that will only grow as the film develops and lingers long after it has ended.  There's good and there's evil (magnificently portrayed by Javier Bardem as the ultra-creepy villain) but the plot is a far cry from good vs. evil.  The film does not stray far from being an analysis of three strong character whose destinies cross despite their paths seldom intersecting.  From the opening monologue onward the film seems to be an exercise in comprehending human behavior, motivation, and moral boundaries.  The Kurgan-like villain is actually the most principled of the main characters.  The cinematography is excellent throughout.  I can this film earning more stars the more I watch it.

NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN

No Country For Old Men(Details here),is the latest release from the renowned Coen Brothers, who have created great films such as âFargoâ and âThe Big Lebowskiâ. This latest movie is based upon a novel, and promises to be a violent yet mildly surreal tale. 

A hunter played by Josh Brolin happens across two million dollars, on the plains of America, amongst a blood bath of Mexican violence. Soon after taking the money, he finds himself pursued by the psychotic Anton Chigurh(Javier Bardem). Not letting anything stand between himself and the money, Chigurh leaves a trail of death in his wake, as the hunter is pitted against the serial killer.

The performances here are quite dull, Tommy Lee Jonesâ sheriff character is his usual southern ârancher-esqueâ affair, as are all the other clichÃ©d characters populating the film. Javier Bardem however, does a solid enough job at getting across the bizarre nature of his character across, whilst facing several obstacles the movie presents.

With far too much emphasis on the quirky surreal concept, whilst dragging through the realistic yet horrific violence, we feel the film is confused as to what it wants to be. Humour generated from Anton Chigurh is amusing to begin with, until the idiosyncratic lines and action become a little too much, as the character fails to display anything above this single level, as with the rest of the protagonists who are just the simplest of fictional creations.

As the Coen Brotherâs ear for dialogue on this project seem to be dwindling, their direction still holds much sway and leaves a decent impression. Aside from the overuse of unnecessary static mid-shots, and the constant display of establishing shots, a solid amount of quality can be observed. Being one of the few films of recent years that used âshaky-camâ style to good effect in the right quantity, without overusing and loosing the importance of why the shot is used as much as what itâs shooting.

Overall, No Country For Old Men fails to live up the standard the Coen Brothers have set for themselves. Whilst the violence, often mindless, will please some of the more basic hedonist viewers, the intellectual calculation of previous works is subdued by an overexertion of the pointlessly quirky punctuated by basic stereotype characters. Brilliant use of sound, and good direction, however not much else to offer.

There is so much to write about this movie, its kinda hard where to start from. For people who consider movies like transformers and spiderman as some of the best movies shoudl stay away from this one as it requitres its viewers to pay constant attention to very fine details. This movie is build on characters and a very tight screenplay which keeps these characters gelled together.

These characters give insights to its viewers about various issues such as the love for the money and how this is slowly dehumanizing a capitalist society like US. One thing I particularly likes about this movie that it doesnt preach in any way, rather it has tried to portray its message through setting up the character of Josh Brolin who ends up in a position in which perhaps each of us would have done the same thing, and that is to fetch 1 million dollar which he found when a deal went bad between the drug dealers. notice how I used the word "fetch" and not "steal" since steal is usually constituted with a wrongdoing, but since its an illegal money, calling it as stealing is very subjective. From this point on, the movie builds on its message and viewer ends up asking the question to themsleves that of we would have been in the same situation as Josh brolin whether our action of ftching the money should be termed as wrong or immoral?

In terms of its climax, I am kinda 50/50 on this one, since I havent read the novel, i cant really reflect on how the climax was presented in the novel. Though personally I prolly would have had like to see the climax rather than leaving it to the viewers imagination.In terms of acting, all thre main characters turned in their finest performances to date. Though I have seen tommy lee jones in quite a few movies, I would love to see Javier Bardem and josh brolin. Javier Bardem's character is just unbelievable!His performance is so strong and when he looks into the eyes other characters, there is a sense of terror in his eyes and his facial expressions are such that they doesnt reflect his feelings or his actions. I cant recall a better villain thn this one. Overall,I would highly reccomend this movie for those who have the aptitude for understanding the complexity of the narrative and identifying and analyzing the subplot which is often lurking behind the characters and the plot.

[img]http://img177.imageshack.us/img177/9576/nocountry1ul7.jpg[/img]
 
 [b][i]No Country for Old Men[/i][/b]
 
 Director: Ethan Coen, Joel Coen
 Writers: Ethan Coen, Joel Coen,  Cormac McCarthy (novel)
 Release Date: November 21, 2007 (USA)
 
 [center][i]An aged man is but a paltry thing,
 A tattered coat upon a stick, unless
 Soul clap its hands and sing, and louder sing
 For every tatter in its mortal dress[/i]
 
 -W.B. Yeats, Sailing to Byzantium[/center]
 
 Times change.  Violence and greed are entwined with our current society, a far cry from a simpler time when one could feel relatively safe leaving his door unlocked when night fell.  Time changes nothing.  The sins of man are realized today as they have always been; they are interwoven into our species, only taking different forms as the years advance.
 
 Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), sheriff of a West Texas county in the 1980s, muses on those who came before him as [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] opens.  Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is a member of that county and leads a life that is anything but extravagant, spending time hunting and ending his days in a trailer with his wife Carla Jean.  The two men find their peace disrupted when another man, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), is found stalking the Texas landscape in search of a missing case containing a life-changing amount of money.
 
 As a native of Texas, Jones fits into his role like a pair of worn-in leather boots.  Jones has effortlessly displayed himself as a figure of authority, a lawman, in previous roles such as Marshal Samuel Gerard in [i]The Fugitive[/i], but his dry humor and philosophical wonderings as Bell offer more insight into the characters thoughts as opposed to simple, visual action.  It wasnt unexpected that Jones would fulfill a complex role laid out for him; what is surprising is how convincing Brolin portrays the part of Moss.  During the film I never connected Brolin to any of the characters Ive seen him play in previous years.  I accepted him immediately as Moss, a man who depends on himself to maintain his own fortune.  Shots of Moss set against the Texas brush and churning sky, fittingly free of any musical accompaniment, held me captivated.  Recalling Moss balancing his rifle on a dusty boot, I do not care to imagine who he would have been if Brolin had not been cast.
 
 Chigurh, questioningly referred to as Sugar by Moss, has been heralded by respectable movie critics as a villainous character who is as intriguing as he is deadly.  His appearance and seemingly whimsical methods of choosing death serve to alienate him from the world he inhabits.  He could be a man from Mars.  Wielding an unorthodox weapon that initially confuses rather than intimidates, Chigurh is indeed a sight to behold.  There is not a relaxed moment when he is onscreen, even if the hapless friendos he encounters (are they hapless?  perhaps that question requires a coin toss) have no idea of the danger they face when theyre in Chigurhs presence.  Bardem received an Academy Award for his role as the antagonist of [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], a decision thats difficult to disagree with.
 
 A sense of foreboding hovers over the first half of the movie, which moves forward at a determined pace and finds one man on the dangerous end of a cat and mouse game.  Think back to some of the more exciting moments between Tom Hanks and Jude Law in [i]Road to Perdition[/i] to get an idea of the razors edge being walked.  Moving forward, Im compelled to address the final and controversial scene of the film.  I don't mind an unexpected end, but I've never looked upon closing credits which such astonishment.  But, that's an issue that may be rectified upon second viewing or after some distance from the viewing - my chief critique lies with the pacing of the latter half of the film.  There are a couple of slow, philosophical moments that I was simply unprepared for, and this doesnt feel like the kind of film that should be wound down.  To make for a more even experience, the first of those moments (which I consider too much of a slowdown so late in the film) could have been placed earlier on to serve the same purpose.  With that being said, I have read that [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is a faithful adaptation of the novel by Cormac McCarthy, and if thats so, its difficult for me to argue on the side of changing the source material.  The best adaptations are those that are the most faithful, though watching the film before reading the book could prove disappointing in some aspects.
 
 I admit I was hesitant to review this film after only one viewing, feeling a need to ease some confusion with another trip to the theater.  But after discussing the film with others, and pondering on it myself, I feel more comfortable writing down my thoughts.  And I believe the people who appreciate [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] the most are those who enjoy continuing to think after the credits role and are prepared to search for meaning in the art.  If the Coen brothers are still an obscure reference to some moviegoers, it doesn't seem their destiny to remain that way.
 
 [b]Final Verdict: 90%[/b]

No Country For Old Men: 
***** (out of 5) 

Joel and Ethan Cohen created a modern western masterpiece in 2007 that stood out from the crowd thanks to its terrifying moments and nihilistic tone. Both Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones to excellent work in their respective roles, but its Javier Bardem's portray of the bizarre sociopath Anton Chigurh, that will be remembered years later as one of film's greatest villains. Despite being a western, the film feels closer than to a horror film. At times it even surpasses the scares in most horror movies, by enhancing the sounds and building the tension of every moment. The film is unnerving, as it deals with the themes of human greed, lack of hope, and the futility of human achievement. Apart from Fargo, no other Cohen brother's film has reached this level of artistry. It more than earned it's Oscar for Best Picture.  I've never read the book by Cormac McCarthy, but the adaptation is a breathtaking modern classic.

Subtle and profound, this film sucks you in with its seemingly simple cat-and-mouse plot only to lead you to much greater themes that come to take over the narrative of the film in the end, leaving the plot behind completely.  The Coen brothers managed to fit the perfect amount of action and suspense in the first half to allow you to invest your time and interest into the characters, only to see everything change wildly by the time the credits roll.  The ending alone will most likely leave you dumbfounded on your first viewing, but after you rewatch it, the pieces will start to come together to form a much larger epic picture.  It was also very refreshing that there is no music whatsoever in the film, and while this technique surely would not work for all films, it truly adds to No Country's dark and brooding severity.  Truly a masterpiece of filmmaking.

Where does one start on this movie?

This film was too close to reality for comfort.  The depiction of our world society having devolved to a point where fear, brutality, threats, death and murder are the tools of diplomacy was realism at best.  Anarchy, chaos, lawlessness all are the order (disorder) of the day.  It said to me, "anything can be resolved at the point of a suppressed shotgun."  While we live in a world that indeed suffers from greed, corruption, violence and mayhem, we do have a thread of contact with the days of yore when a sense of calm control kept the dogs of war at bay.  This war was one of right vs. wrong, good vs. evil.  The argument can be made that all war is defined the same, however, ideology, geography, politics etc are ingredients in what we commonly refer to as wars.  In this case there are no lines, political or geographic, no conflicts ideological in nature.  This war is fed only by greed and avarice.  The motivation is money and the love thereof...  the root of all evil personified.

The forces of law and order, seriously out gunned, manned and performed become jaded and unmotivated.  The desire to maintain the freedom of our society just becomes a cartoon-ish reminiscence.  One that no longer is reason enough to continue to strain against the river flow of evil pervading the fragmented crumbs of a weak and lost society.

There is as much violence and bloodshed in this movie as one can stand, probably more.  There are no heroes, just burned-out shells of men to who "serve and protect" was a way of life for decades and indeed, generations.  There are the shattered wrecks that were once lives, the hollow hulks of families and relationships.

This film is a warning of what will become of a Godless, guideless culture.  If the highest standard to which our humanity must aspire to is greed and the satisfaction of the desire for money and power, this movie shows us the inevitable result.

Is this our present reality?  To be sure, in some places, in some sub-cultures it is.  Do we have a chance to rectify this status of evil?  We do, rather God does.

The Coen brothers latest offering is a fantastic return to form and their best since the marvellously sureal The Big Lebowski in 1998. A dark and violent suspense drama set in Texas in 1980, No Country for Old Men tells the tale of a down on his luck Vietnam veteran (Josh Brolin) who discovers two million dollars in stolen drug money and goes on the run from a lethal hit man (Javier Bardem) who is determined to get it back. Following the trail of bodies they leave in their wake and attempting to piece together what is going on is a cop on the verge of retirement (Tommy Lee Jones), who is getting into a situation way over his head.

This film is really made by the scenes of tension that develop when Bardem's violently unhinged killer questions various local people about the whereabouts of his quarry and the sudden and brutal ways in which he dispatches all who stand in his way. Seemingly slow witted in countenance and possessing an almost comically lumbering gait, he can nevertheless turn intimidatingly menacing with just a few choice words; witness his putting the fear of god into a garage owner for what seemingly is his own amusement. As he pursues Brolin's considerably less dangerous protagonist he messily destroys his victims with contemptuous ease.

Brolin himself impresses as a man trying to make the best of his unexpected windfall and secure the safety of himself and his wife from his relentless pursuer (whom he encounters in a number of well executed and extremely tense action sequences). Courageous and self reliant in an extremely dangerous situation but smart enough to know when to cut and run his character is all to human in his motivations.

Tommy Lee Jones is his usual rugged self. His Texan sheriff is plain speaking and realistic but constantly one step behind both the hunter and his prey and, by the films close, all to aware that his is a role that will have little effect on the tragic outcome of the events unfolding. 
 
The films moves at a steady pace to a conclusion that may perplex some by it's unconventional resolution to the fate of one of it's three central characters. To me, however, it makes complete sense when one considers the major themes of the film; life is a series of arbitary events and even the most prepared can be hit by tradgedy from leftfield and events can overtake us all. In such a world all a person can do is keep a hold on what is theirs and hope for the best. The ending left me satisfied with the events of the film as a a whole and impressed me with it's originality. All in all a great movie that well diserved it's oscar success and another high point in The Coen brother's impressive resume.

A modern day Hitchcockian.  The Coens took Cormac McCarthys twisted novel of greed and brutal violence and turned it into the most suspenseful film of all time. The film is littered with subtle nuances of stories and dreams that intermingle and ultimately lead up to the amazing finale.  Although, most find the end to be a great let down I find that rather odd.  The other well received picture 'Fargo' also ends the exact same way that 'No Country' does.  Viewers must be aware that this film is a thinker, not a shoot 'em up brainless film.  If Alfred H. were alive today, this would've been the film he would have made.
On special note- I reference this film to Hitchcock, a well deserving individual indeed.  But the Coen's also make many nods to my second favorite director of all time, Mister Stanley Kubrick.  My guess is he would also adore this masterpiece.

It's hard to really find something to say about 'No Country for Old Men', the Coen brothers' remarkable return to form, that the Academy hasn't already said.  At the 2008 Oscars the film won best picture, achievement in directing, best supporting actor for Javier Bardem and best adapted screenplay.

Although Paul Thomas Anderson's 'There Will Be Blood' was considered by many to be the forerunner for best picture, I think that 'No Country' rightly won out.  Anderson's picture is certainly more ambitious and has a fantastic lead in Daniel Day-Lewis, but for sheer entertainment value, the Coen's ticked all the right boxes.  Anderson was also seen as an early favourite for the best director award, but as is often the case, best picture and achievement in directing was a double swoop.  

Bardem's performance, which was adjudged to be a supporting role when in fact Tommy Lee Jones or Josh Brolin could have easily replaced him in the same category, is certainly worthy of recognition.  5 minutes is all it takes for Anton Chigurh to establish himself as the malevolent force that drives the film - he is simply terrifying.  Bardem brilliantly fleshes out the role which is conspicuous by its lack of illustration in Cormac McCarthy's mesmerising source novel, the perfect narrative for a Coen's adaptation.

An enduring trend in the filmmaking of Joel and Ethan Coen seems to have been the theme of little people getting themselves into big trouble.  Think Tim Robbins as the foolish idealist who discovers that he has bitten off more than he can chew when he is appointed president of Hudsucker Industries, William H. Macy as the down and out car salesman who hires two mismatched henchmen to kidnap his wife in a crafty ransom scheme (what could possibly go wrong?!) or Jeff Daniels' immortal 'Dude' (or 'Duder', 'His royal Dudeness' etc.) who embroils himself in a plot that he could never fully understand.  Whatever Coen's film graces your screen you will find this trend in various incarnations.

'No Country' is no different in that respect.  Llewelyn Moss is a welder who lives in a trailer park in Texas.  His young wife Carla Jean, played by Kelly Macdonald who masterfully disguises her Scottish accent with a thick Texan drawl, works at Wal-mart.  When hunting one day near the Rio Grande, Moss stumbles upon a drug-deal gone wrong; the barren landscape captured so beautifully by long time Coen's collaborator Roger Deakins is punctuated with a scattering of machinegun peppered vehicles and sun-bloated bodies.  Moss locates the money and takes it, a decision which resonates throughout the whole film; such is the extent of the bloodshed that follows.  

The narrative is unconventional in many ways.  Rather than there being a protagonist as such (if one had to be chosen it would most probably be Moss) the film revolves around the ensemble of Moss, Chigurh and Sheriff Ed Tom Bell.  Moss leads the chase, his ultimate goal a better life for himself and his wife; he proudly tells her at one point "You are retired".  Chigurh hunts Moss, his goal to retrieve the money.  At points in the film you will question his motivations; it seems that he kills to give mere credence to the word 'death'.  Always a step behind is Ed Tom, who is aware of the situation with Moss and Chigurh but can never seem to come to terms with the unthinkable violence that is unfolding in his county.

In truth, each character subtely represents different things.  Ed Tom, as the aging sheriff, embodies the older generation who are so removed from the new trend of drug-runners that bring with them the aforementioned violence.  Moss embodies the working class.  A competent man and a Vietnam veteran, Moss is neither truly good nor truly bad.  We forgive him his decision because he is likeable and he appears to make it for the right reasons.  What Anton Chigurh represents is nothing short of death itself.  He is granted near omnipotence and omniscience by McCarthy.  You may have seen characters like him in other films, but often they come across as parodies of what they are supposed to represent.  It's not about how many bullets Chigurh can take before hitting the ground; it's more that he's always there.  His scenes are so overwhelmingly ominous that the tension is at points unbearable.

The result of this rich characterisation is a remarkably entertaining and involving story, and one which is told superbly.  One thing that I was struck by was the pace of the film.  Not only do the Coen's launch you into the story at a million miles an hour, they slow it down and speed it up expertly.  Fascinated as they are with the sheer simplicity of 'people doing things' every detail of every action is explored, whether it's the loading of a gun or the unscrewing of an air vent.  And just when you settle in to a rhythm they pull it from underneath you, replacing it with a frenzy of gunfire or an exploding car.  Even if you know what is coming the Coen's have a way of lulling you into an unguarded state of spectatorship, and that's exactly when they surprise you with something big.

This really is a must see film.  It stands head and shoulders above most other releases and marks a stunning return to the serious hard hitting style that saw the Coen's deliver classics like 'Blood Simple' and 'Millers Crossing'.  Yes, there's a lot of hype surrounding it - it's perhaps even in danger of being too lauded critically - but truthfully it is an absolute masterpiece of cinema.  

It is films like this that have established the Coen brothers as such a cinematic force and with their new offering - 'Burn After Reading' - resembling the lighter tone of their cult classic 'The Big Lebowski' it looks like they still have plenty to offer.

Few films could pull off being so barren on multiple levels without leaving you feeling simply empty or dissatisfied, but watching this movie, I was completely engrossed - I even caught myself holding my breath - both times I saw it, no less. Sporting this season's "sociopathic pageboy" hairdo, Javier Bardem is mesmerizing; you simply cannot get enough of looking at him every time he's on screen. Tommy Lee Jones's weary sheriff is a well-worn cliche, but one I felt oddly comforted by...he's kind of like the movie's broken moral compass - he can't help you navigate your way through all this horror, but you feel better having him around anyway. As for Josh Brolin as Llewellyn Moss, he's so disarmingly likeable as he plods, bull-headedly, towards his own doom that I found myself wondering why I haven't seen more of him in other films. Moss joins the Dude, Jerry Lundegaard, Barton Fink, and others on the list of Coen brothers's not-quite-Everyman characters whom you can't help but root for as they get themselves into a hot mess.

SYNOPSIS:
The film takes place in a small Texas border town in 1980. Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) has ruled the land for years without the use of a gun, but a new brand of reckless lawlessness has taken over his town. Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is an innocent Everyman with a devoted wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald), but when he stumbles across a drug deal gone deadly and finds two million dollars, he's determined to keep it for himself. After seeing a bold vigilante drama called [u]The Brave One, I am drawn to write about [u]No Country for Old Men which is a Western Crime Thriller with the Coen Brothers elements of dark humor, strong and/or scary characters, and many instances of graphic bloody violence. Best of the best selling novel by Cormac McCarthy of the same name and winner of the following Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Supporting Actor, Best Original Screenplay, and Best Director (in this case directors). Anyways, the story takes place in Texas, one of Cormac's favorite locales. We start the movie with a foreign looking, black-clad man who we come to know as Chigurh (a creepy and unsettling Javier Bardem with the agreed upon worst haircut in the history of cinema, move back Edward Scissorhands) and according to a wily Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson at his dramatic best) "he doesn't have a sense of humor." He is brought in to a police station for something, but we don't know why yet. Chigurh slips out of his seat that was chained to his cuffs and strangles the officer with his cuffs, blood spurting and Chigurh's wild eyes gleaming with madness.

After that, he takes the cop's car and trades it out with a local who gets a shot from a cattle gun in the head. We cut to LLewyn Moss (a blunt and bold Josh Brolin), a ordinary and everyman who stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad, with bloodied corpses littered around cars and crows picking at them. He finds the last living witness, a Mexican, and asks Moss for water right before he discovers heroin in the back of the pickup truck. Knowing a satchel of money is around, he searches in the scorching sun until he finds it in the form of $2 million dollars under a tree. Little does he know it has a radio transponder implanted inside, and Chigurh is on his tail. From the words of LLewyn Moss, he tells his wife Carla Jean (Kelly McDonald) that he found a "bag full of money." Keeping the secret from her, he knows their lives are in immediate danger and he promptly tells her before he gets water for the Mexican that "I'm about to do the stupidest I ever done." 

Returning to the site, he finds the man shot in the head and is discovered by Mexican gangsters who chase him across the landscape and let loose a vicious dog on him. Bruised and bloodied, Moss has to go on foot to whereever, since his truck was left behind. Chigurh gets the identification from his car and stops by his house to get his phone bills. Picking up on Moss's trail, Chigurh relentlessly pursues him from town to town and motel to motel to get what's rightfully his. Another man, named a soon-to be retired Sherriff Tom Bell (a intriguing and stern Tommy Lee Jones) is pursuing the both of them, aiming to put a stop to "what's coming." His deputy and him speak the two best lines of the movie (a lot better than [i]There Will Be Blood's "I DRANK YOUR MILKSHAKE!" "It's a mess, ain't it, Sherriff? "If it ain't, it'll do til the mess gets here." 

From here, the movie unleashes a vortex of graphic bloody violence between Moss, Chigurh, and Mexican hoodlums. Following the bloody trail closely is Bell, who is spellbound by its aftermaths. One way Chigurh contributes to the blood trail is by flipping a coin and wanting random people to call it, on terms of everything they have, meaning that they'll die if it's tails and live if it's heads. Creating a villian for the ages, Javier Bardem earned the 40 awards he garned in from more than 10 film festivals, and the Golden Globes and Academy Awards. Josh Brolin creates a solid working man with gravity and naturalness (he's from Texas and his friends were the source material for his character). The movie's violence is very graphic, from shooting to strangling and back to shooting with deep crimson blood. 

The Coen Brothers have fashioned Cormac's western thriller into a suspensful western/horror thriller with their dark and twisted humor and involving characters. Out of all the dark dramas last year (There Will Be Blood, Sweeney Todd, this one), this one was the standout. All in all, No Country for Old Men is The Coen Brothers' Best Picture Winner, and it deserves to be. Be ready for more Critiques and Opinions on Every Game and Movie I Can Get My Hands On!

There is a lot of talk regarding the Cohen brothers and their "return to form" with this movie, I do not personally feel that is the case, I have found plenty to enjoy in their recent efforts and could never truly name a Coen brothers movie that I have hated. Yes, I even liked The Ladykillers.

What No Country for Old Men actually represents is the Coen brothers returning to what they happen to do best, and it's a comeback for the ages.

Based on the novel by arguably one of the greatest American authors to have ever lived, this movie is one of the most faithful adaptations to a novel I have ever laid eyes on and when the source material is as good as Cormac McFuckingCarthy there is precious little reason to deviate and the Coens were smart enough to realize this. 

The movie begins in an understated but utterly unpredictable and sudden manner and it continues this formula of completely defying your expectations, especially concerning violence. The Coens, along with McCarthy found a way to present us with violence in an unexpected manner - it is subtle, as is much of the film, and they have managed to execute every act of violence somehow out of sync with our preconceptions. When we expect death, it comes sooner. When we don't expect death, it takes its time. They build the tension in a scene, as is the norm for a thriller but then they have found a way to catch you off guard.

The movie isn't as graphic as McCarthy's novel which was still like a children's book compared to his opus, The Blood Meridian (pray you never see a faithful adaptation of that movie, it will haunt you for life and make you crap your pants in horror, and then the crap in your pants will haunt you forever) but while the movie of No Country For Old Men does not revel in the violence, the Coens often decide to not show the violence in full and let us use our imaginations a little, make us think about what we have just seen. A real masterstroke, they stick close to the material but they use it to play to the strengths of the medium.

This (like the novel) is a movie with a lot on its mind, from the weary opening narration by Tommy Lee Jones' Sheriff Bell, this is a story about the supposed degradation of society and how the horrors of life and the monsters that walk among us are becoming too great. Bell laments on the differences between his time as Sheriff and when his grandfather and father were sheriffs. Has the world changed so much that there's no place for people like him, or has it always been this way and it's simply a world he has grown too old for? That is the crux of this movie and it's a thought provoking question on the state of the world, mankind's relationship with violence and the toll it takes on those who live through it - themes common for McCarthy's work and themes that fit the Coen brothers like it was tailor-made for them.

Josh Brolin plays Llewellyn Moss, a Vietnam veteran hunting antelope in the Texan wilderness. Tracking a wounded animal he comes across the grim aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong, corpses litter the land, blood and spent shells fill the spaces in between. He finds a survivor, bleeding to death in a bullet riddled car and he abandons him to continue searching the scene. He comes across another body a ways out, bled to death beneath the shade of a tree, a satchel full of money at his side. Moss takes the money and you would think that was his biggest mistake in the grand plan of his life but in actual fact it is what he does after he has stolen the money that sets his life spiraling out of control: His conscience speaks to him.

He decides to take water out to that survivor and help him out a little, he's in no position to do him any harm and he has the money now so what harm could it do? It is Moss' compassion that curses him, not his greed. If he had simply acted on his greed then he may have escaped without incident and life would be easy for him and his sweet and unassuming wife, Carla Jean, played by Trainspotting's Kelly Macdonald. This is a movie about choices and the consequences of those choices and how far reaching they can be. The movies general philosophy is that of fatalism, the idea that everything that happens must happen and could only happen that way. People are slaves to their fate and they cannot escape it.

The character that typifies this concept it is the chilling Anton Chigurh, played to Oscar worthy perfection by Javier Bardem. A mysterious assassin who is set loose on Moss' trail to track down the missing money and do whatever he feels is necessary to ensure that the job is completed. Chigurh is the first truly iconic depiction of cinematic evil to be seen since Anthony Hopkins waffled on about serving suggestions in Silence of the Lambs. I am hard pressed to find a figure who more perfectly represents Death itself than Chigurh; garbed in black, appearing almost supernaturally out of nowhere. He is a grim reaper, a cattle gun linked to a cannister of pressurized air is his scythe and he uses it to devastating effect.

Chigurh is an unstoppable force of nature, a tornado, and like a tornado he cannot be stopped and he will not listen to your pleas. Next time you see a tornado step in front of it and tell it about your family and friends and how you read to the blind. It won't listen to you, it's a tornado, all it wants to do is smash up your shit. It'll probably trash the place you read to the blind while it's out and about, because it doesn't care about the blind, either!

Chigurh believes strongly in fate, a concept more thoroughly explored in the novel and it is one of my few gripes about the movie that it cut out a weighty portion of dialogue in one of the final scenes which properly illustrates Chigurh's chilling philosophy, and also provides us with one of the cruelest moments in a story rife with them. That said the point is addressed well enough in the movie and it is this belief in destiny that makes Chigurh so steadfast in his ability to do his job. To affirm his beliefs he often uses a coin toss, if death was a certainty for the people he crosses then a coin toss would confirm this. It's a deranged ideology, but it fits him perfectly and only adds to his fearful presence. How can you bargain with a man who interprets a 50/50 act of chance to be a confirmation of destiny?

As I said, the movie has a lot on its mind and that is where the real meat of the movie's power comes from, but what else does it have going for it?

The performances are across the board brilliant, every actor delivering their career best. Josh Brolin brought his A game to the table with his portrayal of Llywellyn Moss, a game I do not believe has been seen until this film and in Ridley Scott's American Gangster. He has always been what is considered a great underrated actor but this was the year he truly becomes recognized for the talent he is capable of bringing. Moss is smart, sly and confident. Even when the odds are so greatly against him he manages to keep his head and stay a step ahead, even though he has no idea how long he can keep this up for, he continues to be secure in himself and brings a great deal of wit to his scenes. That is one thing that may be hard to believe in a movie of this grim nature, it has some very funny moments, they are often dark, dry and deeply cynical ventures into humour but they do work in cutting the tension, if only for a moment or two. This was also the case in McCarthy's novel, which is quite a rarity for his work but he can write snappy but believable dialogue with the best of them so the humour always hits you fast and always on target.

Tommy Lee Jones is a man who was born to read the words of Cormac McCarthy, he is a long time fan of the man's work and contributed a great deal to the movie, including helping devise Anton Chigurh's appearance for the movie and also convincing the Coen brothers to film the movie in Texas as well as Mexico because in McCarthy's novels the scenery is as important a character as the men and women reading his words. His opening narration is weary and tired, a loving retrospective on a time long gone and a sorry lament on a world going to Hell. He reads the dialogue to perfection, delivering note perfect delivery in every scene, many of which play across the underrated and underused Garreth Dillahunt who has proven with his exceptional work on HBO's Deadwood (among other things) that he can do just about anything. The exchanges between Jones and Dillahunt are often the funniest in the movie but also serve to shine a light on the cynicism that is ensnaring Jones' Sheriff Bell. This is Jones' finest performance in many years, his love and fealty to the source material brought out the best in him, I can only hope he gets to work on more McCarthy adaptations because he truly is perfect with the delivery of McCarthy's concise regional dialogue.

Javier Bardem is, as I said, a stand-out performance in a movie full of them. His performance is hard to read and impossible to predict, which is exactly how the character should be perceived. You watch Chigurh and you cannot conceive a man like that being born, growing through childhood and reaching this place in his life. You simply cannot. You watch him and you can only imagine he came into being fully formed, like a phantom figure marching in from a sandstorm on the horizon, a sign of the end times. This is the new yardstick for evil in cinema, by which all other scary men will be judged.

Kelly Macdonald's Carla Jean is one of the few lights of pure, sweet goodness in the darkness of this world. Her along with Tess Harper as Sheriff Bell's wife Loretta, are the women that hold up good men and can stay them from slipping into the chasm. Loretta keeps Ed Tom sane in the wake of the improbable cruelty surrounds him, gives him a reason to walk away and retain his humanity. Carla Jean gives Llewellyn a reason to fight, a reason to stay honest, or as honest as the world will allow him to be. Macdonald gives Carla Jean that gentle heart and natural sweetness that you could easily find yourself falling for, there's no bad in her, Macdonald also gives a brilliant Texan accent considering she has such a strong natural Scottish brogue. Your heart will go out to her as she suffers through these events that she played no part in orchestrating.

The movie is a masterclass of tension, it starts with a stark and shocking act of violence which sets the standard for the movie. The stakes are high, the wrong people are always one step behind, so close you can feel their breath prickle against the skin on the nape of your neck. Bullets hit close they graze your flesh and they ring in your ear. The whole film has you living on a knife edge, waiting to fall onto it completely. If the negative reviews have anything to say other than a particularly bland and inconsequential critique that it is "too bleak", they focus in on what happens towards the end of the film.

Now I will not go into specific details with this, but it won't be hard to fill in the gaps here, so you may want to avoid this portion. As the tension builds in the film there is a sudden, jarring break in the narrative and we skip ahead in time, a character we have followed for the entire film is suddenly dead. Killed off-screen, we can't even begin to really imagine what happened to them in this lost time but the detractors have struck out at this - feeling cheated - but this happens in McCarthy's novel and the Coens clearly understood the necessity of this in keeping the exact same execution. 

We, as an audience, have seen violent confrontations between protagonist and antagonist for most of our movie-going lives and there is a certain level of fantasy in how these confrontations are presented, in denying us that confrontation there is a disconnect for the audience. We are denied that morbid catharsis of seeing the violence, understanding the context, instead with this we see violence in a more realistic light - sudden and unexpected. It happens without us knowing and we are simply left to deal with the tragic aftermath. We can only use our imagination and try to understand what might have happened in this final moments but nothing seems to fit, nothing seems to make sense. Death doesn't make sense. 

It's a wonderful manipulation but I can wholly appreciate how some people would be angered by this if they were building themselves up for something that was never on the cards in the first place. There is no Hollywood showdown in the world of Cormac McCarthy. There is no satisfaction to be found, no justice or release. It is an unfair, cruel world utterly uninterested in the build of one's character, good or bad, there is someone or something out there that can destroy you and will if you are unlucky enough to meet it. This alone tells you a great deal about the nature of Anton Chigurh, you believe for a briefest of moments as the movie nears it's denouement that the universe has offered us a moment of karmic retribution, but that is not the case. Life is not always that convenient, sometimes the bad guy gets away with it and the good and the innocent must suffer for that.

I think what ultimately may throw people off with the way the story resolves for one character is that people up until that point believed they were watching the story of Llywellyn Moss and the stolen money, when in actual fact you are watching the story of Sheriff Ed Tom Bell and his dealings with the case of Llywellyn Moss and the stolen money.

This is a story about one man from a dying age, dealing with the horrors of a new age, one he does not understand and cannot understand but must, not just live in, but must actively fight against out of duty, and ultimately of the cost that fight has on his soul. This is why we witness this grim fate through Sheriff Bell's eyes and not in the moment with those who saw it happen because this is how Sheriff Bell is forced to meet that fate, as an outsider. One that cannot fully understand what has happened and truly does not want to understand it either. We share that feeling, the frustration and the confusion that follows a sudden and unexpected death. It's in this moment that we now share Sheriff Bell's perspective on the events, we are now with him and this is his story. It's always been his story. The transition is subtle, but as the film draws to its close it is clear this is the nature of the entire film, the clue is in the title from the very beginning but the way the plot is structured it is deceptive to the unassuming eye and perhaps that was the point.

Enough of the spoilers, back to the remaining praise I must lavish on this film.

The cinematography is gorgeous, it keeps things stark and very much as it should be, there is no tweaks or gloss added to the scenery and the location, so we are greeted with a montage of shots of the savage beauty of the Texan wilderness, perfectly matching the opening narration, and in the scenes where Moss discovers the aftermath of the massacre. It looks beautiful, and as if nothing was added to the photography of the scenes. When Moss returns to the scene at night the contrast in colour, with cold blues, only adds to the sense of dread running through the entire film. The scenes set in the cities and towns capture the mundaneness of every day living which helps make the sudden and shocking violence really stick with you.

The film runs largely without any music, only a low almost mechanical hum that permeates through key scenes, as well as music in the end credits but this absence of music works in its favour. It makes it less cinematic, less grand, and more unnerving and realistic. The movie works hard to taunt your nerves but makes it seem effortless, that is thanks to the Coens steady hand and keen eye matched with McCarthy's ability to paint a picture of a truly hopeless situation.

This movie is bleak, it is unforgiving but it is also has a sly wit and is filled with the best nerve shredding sequences the thriller genre has seen for some time. A thoughtful, at times chilling tale brought to life perfectly from a cast and creative team all working at the peak of their respective abilities.

"No Country for Old Men" is an adrenaline-packed Western that holds nothing back, especially when it comes to violence and blood.  The Coen brothers' screenplay creates a game of cat and mouse between a man who stumbles upon $2 million, a sheriff, and a hitman who kills without sympathy or remorse.  Javier Bardem is pure intensity and makes one of the most terrifying villains ever.  In addition to being big and scary, his emotionless use of a captive bolt pistol on anybody (particularly innocent people) that stand in his way makes him unpredictable and heartless.  It isn't often that an Oscar is given for a villainous role, but Bardem absolutely deserved it.  He is joined by Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones, Woody Harrelson, and Kelly Macdonald, who all turn in memorable performances.  While 2007 wasn't a very strong Oscar class, the quality of acting in this film definitely made it my number one for the year.  It is deserving of its Oscar wins for Best Picture, Director, and Screenplay, even if it likely wouldn't have won in more competitive years.  The script creates an atmospheric look at 1980's Texas and, while it moves slow at times, it tells an interesting story.  Everything is awesome about this film... except for its anticlimactic ending.  I know that many critics have defended it saying "But you have to read into the symbolism of his dreams" or "They ended it the same way as the novel," but if everybody walks out of the theater with disappointment, can it really be the right ending?  I'd definitely recommend "No Country for Old Men" as long as you aren't expecting anything lighthearted or calm.

Those who tell you that No Country for Old Men is a movie that tries too hard to be different are unfortunately misguided people. No Country for Old Men is a surprisingly entertaining movie and its plot is well expressed by the talented writers and directors Joel and Ethan Coen. The absence of any music throughout the movie just is different. And trust me when I tell you that without the music preparing you for a shot or a big bang, you will experience so much more while watching this life-changing masterpiece of a movie.
Another thing that captures your attention is the somewhat strange way of filming. The camera angles and lighting donât only tell the story set in the 1980s, but make you feel as if you are in the 1980s. 
And of course, the acting. One must mention the character of Tommy Lee Jones, who plays the sheriff of the little Southern American town where everything happens. That man is a hard-ass. He puts in a line and it makes the dialogue. He is afraid that eventually someone will come who is stronger than any sheriff will ever be. And that someone comes in the form of soulless Anton Chigurh, played by Javier Bardem, who definitely deserved that Oscar. I spent the entire movie and hours afterwards wondering how he managed to keep the same face expression for such a long time and how he managed to pull that haircut off. Another actor who has captured my attention is Josh Brolin, who plays the cowboy in the land of no cowboys. Llewelyn Moss (Brolin) encounters 2 million dollars in the middle of the desert and goes on the run with Chigurh (Bardem) following him and the sheriff following them both. This plot is not a tenth as regular as it might sound, and is supported by a fantastic ending that stays loyal to the novel the movieâs based on. 
I must admit though, not everyone will enjoy this film. If you are looking for a simple and easy shoot-out movie, you have come to the wrong place. If you are looking for something that will make you sit tight in your chair, grasping on to the handles and creating a million possibilities of an ending of your own, buy a ticket to this movie while it is still running at the cinemas.
So, on a finishing note, I thank the brothers Coen and hope for more movies like this one.

With literary and cinematic accolades under its buckle, "No Country for Old Men" is a fascinating renovation on the western genre. With westerns habitually, they are predisposed to scrutinize various circumstances that authenticate the protagonist?s sense of right and wrong. In this parable, it pioneers a character, Anton Chirguh, as an icon of the lack of ethics, that it simply twists everything out of proportion, shaking everything on its way. Both works, the book and the movie, are categorically not a convenient form of entertainment as they make their audiences work for it. And if they do, it?s cathartic.

Set in 1980?s Texas, a retired welder named Llewelyn Moss inadvertently stumbles upon a drug trade gone wrong. He finds a satchel full of bills, totaling to about 2 million dollars -- enough temptation for him to keep it. Trouble is, people who own the money wants it back fast, employing a hit man named Anton Chirguh, a character whose morality is close to zero and even uses virtue as an excuse to keep on his violent rampage. Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, an old timer and last on a generation of county sheriffs is on the case. With a labyrinthine con lined with unjustifiable violence, this shakes his notion of goodness to the very core.

Written by Cormac McCarthy, the novel definitely has this trademark fashion that may require a lot of effort to value. Each chapter starts with a stream of consciousness from Bell, nostalgic about his time as a Sheriff, when times and circumstances were comprehendible to him. The way that McCarthy writes for the rest of the novel is pretty similar to writing a script as he skimps on description and focuses on dialogue. He definitely has an amazing eye on tongue and this style instantly raises the sense of urgency the novel exudes even if some scenes span days between them.

With that, the Coen Brothers have easily loyally adapted the book to the screen. They were able to capture the essence of the novel within a 2 hour run time. Special kudos on the casting too as it is quite impossible to see other thespians hovering over these characters. Anton Chirguh is personified brilliantly by Javier Bardem, Oscar award and weird haircut in tow. With the first half of the film almost a carbon copy of the novella, the second half is where the Coens start to take liberty. They have reduced the Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) character and even almost immediately eliminated the female hitchhiker Moss met by subbing her with another motel customer seducing him with alcohol. Both decisions were pretty smart, as I could imagine how they could have easily slowed down the pacing of the movie. However, there were some ideas instantly detached from the film and I guess this will be left for the book readers to discover.

In the novel, a scene between Moss and the female hitchhiker becomes a standout. At a diner, both characters chatter about the past and how it eventually catches up. Moss laments about the illusion of starting over and its futility. This was a pretty poignant scene as it highlight?s Moss? regret and how he acknowledges that what he did can?t be undone. On the other hand, in the film, the conversation between Chirguh and Carla Jean seem to not loose its luster. The scene basically highlights Chirguh?s motivation for murder: to preserve his image as a character that doesn?t hesitate. 

"No Country for Old Men" is definitely an intriguing story of morality. It teases its audience of hopelessness by making the last sheriff of a long line of county sheriffs quit in the face of an Anton Chirguh. But then, it leaves the audience with a small glimmer of hope by reminding them that Chirguh is still indeed human and can expire, punctured by his own bone. Both works are very compelling and can exist without each other. At its surface, it seems like a celebration of violence however it gets richer with time and will further reveal what it?s really celebrating about.
