No Country For Old Men is a film that is carefully, meticulously constructed to linger, which it does. It's a film that, despite its cold, ominous eccentricity, is very down-to-earth, pessimistic, and wise. It's imagined so precisely that many details will not dawn on you till later, the appearance of a limping dog early in the film for instance. The film progresses naturally, untouched by any sort of convention, vogue or standards, and moves by way of its deep-rooted outlooks and views.

Visually, No Country For Old Men is of the highest cinematic order. The camera moves so deliberately and many images extract so many microcosms in life, a translucent reflection in a blown-out keyhole for example. Many shots rely more on a dooming presence in the out-of-focus background than in the unsuspecting foreground. Violence is portrayed on and offscreen as genuinely as this ungoverned yet restrained film possibly could. It's a standard-setting work of cinema, if that isn't shamelessly extreme in complement. It's so solid, you feel like you could go to Google Earth and rove around its settings finding no boundaries that divide the film set and the real external world. What I found to be outstanding, a strenuous thing to be in a film the sets the bar so high, is its use of sound, which very much opened my mind to the potential effects of the design of such in the movies. The film never uses music. Each scene is given seamless, faultless attention to ambient noises. In a hotel room, for instance, we hear that humming that we can never really locate. Also, there are at least two scenes where your heart is in your throat on account of the simple discerning of a transponder.

In his third appearance in an incredible movie in 2007, following Grindhouse and Amerian Gangster, Josh Brolin gives the best performance I've ever seen from him. He completely embodies a sort that is very relatable and likely to do some of the questionable things that he does in the story, a shrewd pragmatist that is resourceful and invariably stubborn, intractible, and changelessly intent. He speaks few words, he's dry as desert sand, and does not think for one second about the consequences or alternate outcomes of his dangerous choices in the film. Hindsight and deliberation don't exist in his fixed and steadfast world. The chase that ensues as he sees practical possibilities as practical inevitability written in stone in taking $2 million from the site of a gruesomely fated heroin deal is to him something he must staunchly work through with a stone face.

Javier Bardem, in the first film I have ever seen him in, is a presence to be reckoned with. He bears a knowing perception that telegraphs such a deeply dangerous villain. He's beyond the distance between audience and screen. He is so aware, precise, analytical, and thoughtful that he almost sees us peripherally. Pursuing the money that the narrowly engrossed Brolin has taken liberty of, he is what human beings have never faced or understood about fate. He has a mysterious philosophy that carries him serenely through a non-participating life of casual murder, perhaps that he somehow has reached an absolute certainty that there is no afterlife, that life is ultimately meaningless, and that his understanding of that existentialist conclusion admits him the privilege of controlling the fate of those he comes into contact with. How much of a match is Brolin against Bardem? The resourcefulness of the two men is transcendentally absorbingly suspenseful.

Serving as the film's actual hero is perhaps Tommy Lee Jones, who plays a creaky, weathered small town sheriff who avoids the federal investigation of the incidental heroin deal to protectively pursue Brolin. His manner puts off the audience, yes. All of us who have seen this film in theaters will agree. But the key to his philosophies, idiosyncracies, and pontifications are in how he also puts off other characters. Jones, an actor who is often very deterring in how glacial and inexcitable he can be, is really the only actor I can fully and seriously imagine playing the sheriff. The beauty in the film's dooming, melancholy realism begins and ends with him, as someone who has preoccupied doubts, conscious inquiries, and learned understanding that he does not communicate. When he talks, he's saying things that make sense to his views but never his actual views. To those who he shares the screen with, as well as to us, he's an old man whose mind wanders, as he humbly admits in one scene.

The three very incompatible key men never share a frame with one another, except for once very lucidly late in the film. How disconcerting, how painfully obstructing and displeasing. The devil is in the details, as they say. This movie seems to embody that cliche to the penultimate extent. The tagline for the movie is: There Are No Clean Getaways. After watching the film, that phrase is kind of haunting.

On the surface, it's a bloody story about a drug deal gone awry; a hunter that stumbles upon the aftermath of that scene (and all of the money left behind); a crazed psychopathic killer with a unique array of weaponry, and a Texas lawman who feels that he's lost his place in the world. If that's all you walk out of the film with, you missed the point entirely.

The devil is in the details.

There does seem to be some kind of binding thread that all humans are subjected to. We can make our own choices, but we are all subject to circumstance. Anton (the psychotic, heartless killer) collides with fate not through manifested retribution, but in the form of a car wreck. How generic is that? Exactly. We all live in the same world, and sometimes, no matter how well we plan for something, fate and circumstance fuck us over. Good and evil are only subjective.

In the beginning of the film, in the opening monologue, the Sheriff believes that the evil he can't comprehend is something that has just begun with the current generation. He idolizes the older generations and takes the bizarre and twisted crimes that happen around him as a sign of corroding values. But when he's talking to his uncle near the end of the film, he is made aware that the world has always been that cold and violent. This is a common perspective of old-timers. That the world was so great before. But when has it ever been so? Where is my generation's Adolf Hitler?

The average viewer will likely hate the ending. I don't. I think it's a perfect summation of everything the movie is about. The dialogue in the final scene is dry, laid back, and most people won't even listen to it, and then BAM! credits roll. That's when the complexity of the story hit me like a ton of bricks.

Now, back to Anton. He may be the best villain ever to be committed to celluloid. I mean that. This guy is so heartless -- he is the angel of death and all that is terrifying about the world. I have never loved to hate a fictional character so much. I can wholeheartedly say that I will never be able to do a coin toss again without thinking of his character.

My mum used to collect these crystals.  I don't really know why.  She was into tie-dye and other things hippyish as well.  One day she shattered one of them, sending streams of rainbows and flickering colours dancing across the walls and roof.  It was beautiful, but ultimately something broken.

So it is with No Country for Old Men. Llewelyn (Josh Brolin) stumbles across a gory crimescene, a truckload of heroin and a satchel full of hundred dollar bills.  Now a psychotic killer (Javier Bardem) and half of Mexico are trying to track him down as the local sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones) tries to stop a full-blown war from erupting.  

I'm having trouble describing the film in a legible way.  If I had to sum it up in one word, it would be "relentless".  If I had to sum it up as a haiku, I would be Japanese, so I won't.

The Coen brothers have gone out of their way to craft an environment that excretes eeriness... if that's how you spell it.  There's no music to set the mood, the desolation of the Texan frontier needs no soundtrack.  When I think on it, there's barely any dialogue throughout most of the movie, the images do nearly all the talking.  They aren't saying much, but they are projecting an air of turbulation, of foreseen fury.

Most people who have seen this movie and survived to talk of it will all mention the insane hitman played by Javier Bardem.  The character itself is menace incarnate, not because he kills and maims without thought, but because he lives by and fully believes in his personal philosophies that lead him to do so.  Add to this the manic calm portrayed by Javier and you have a new breed of bad-guy, the likes of which haven't been seen since the Silence of the Lambs.

I really, really enjoyed it and I know a majority of people who watched it enjoyed it as well, and this worries me.  I'm not the type that revels in blood and violence, and by criminy there's enough of both here at the highest calibre to start a party in certain circles.  But through all the gore, the animosity and death, there was something that touched a chord in me, something primeval, something familiar and that isn't something I wish to dwell on.

Bravo to the writers and director for unearthing a part of me I thought long buried.  I realy wish you hadn't.

As each character runs into their fate, you sink a little lower, until the stand with the same haunted eyes as Sheriff Bell does in the final scene. [font=Arial]After its release, I recall [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] earning a Best Picture award and a nearly flawless ranking on RT (95), and inspiring most of my friends to wander off into the realm of obsession. Needless to say, I had faith that it would be great. 
 
 And to be fair, it was.
 
 Still, I had a feeling that I was crazy when the movie was over. Somehow I had found my way into the minority of people (including other surprised critics) who didnt think this movie was an 11 out of 10. Allow me to explain.
 
 First, Ill get the good stuff out of the way. The movie revived the tradition of the Western in a way that I had never seen before. While Ive seen better strange-things-going-on-in-Texan-no-mans-land movies, this one had a very artistic twist to it. On a couple of dorkier notes, the cinematography and direction were superb. The simplistic cat-and-mouse plot of the movie made it easy to take in and enjoy. Furthermore, the sound tracking (or lack thereof) was a bold and excitingly creepy decision. That much I enjoyed.
 
 On the whole though, the movie was a little strange. There was little explanation for most major occurrences, the ending included. [img]http://moviesimdb.com/wp-content/uploads/2008/02/no_country_for_old_men_poster.jpg[/img]
 
 [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is an impeccably crafted film. It is also a masterpiece. Whatever personal reservations people over the notorious, yet faithfully adapted, ending, no one can argue with Coens' decision to artfully subvert genre expectations and just create an awesome film. 
 
 [img]http://nodesignstudio.com/inspiration/images/no_country_for_old_men.jpg[/img]
 
 At the surface, [i]NCFOM[/i] seems only like a perfect cat-and-mouse thiller. And it is -at the surface. The Coen bros. have understated the film's themes to the point where it almost difficult, at first, to notice the philosophical undertones regarding fate, chance, and violence. This is most most welcome since it opens up the film to multiple viewing, even on just a purely entertainment level. The use of a minimalist soundtrack (and I'm using that term generously because there really isn't one) is ingeniously because it avoids cheap scares and genuinely builds real, unbearable tension. Of course, it is also because the editing is so sharp and synchronized that the scenes perform as well as they do. Furthermore, the cinematography, provided by the great Roger Deakins, nicely showcases the haunting and barren lands of 1980s Texas.
 
 [img]http://manolomen.com/images/javier-bardem-in-no-country-for-old-men.jpg[/img]
 
 But at the front and center of this movie is an all-star, talented cast. Josh Brolin is funny and appealing as a desperate man who's in way over his head, as he tries to avoid a horrible fate that only seems to be coming ever so quickly. And the audience can do nothing but root for this honest, yet very logically flawed, man. Tommy Lee Jones is pitch erfect as the town's sheriff (he probably brought his own hat and boots to the set), but he is also, more importantly, the movie's conscience and moral message. But the movie's driving force in terms of acting is the psychotic, humorless, and scary Javier Bardem, who plays the mass-murdering Anton Chigurh effortlessly. His character is so remorseless, so haunting, it's also unsettling to find him very darkly funny-even though we know it's no laughing matter.
 
 [img]http://www.entertainment-movie-guide.com/images/No-Country-for-Old-Men_Tommy-Lee-Jones_Josh-Brolin_Javier-Bardem_9.jpg[/img]
 
Although, probably the Coens' most serious work to date, [i]NCFOM[/i] never skip a chance to provide some well-crafted humor as well, in order to ease the ever-building tension. And as for the ending, if the bros. had yielded to genre expectations by creating a contrived "final showdown" between characters, it would just be missing the more poignant point of this seemingly simple tale of a chase of fate. A masterpiece indeed.

I'll put my prejudice up first: this movie committed ever minor sin of film-making that irks me to no end.  I call them "minor sins" because they bother me and a small handful of other moviegoers, and while I acknowledge that, I find them shortcuts in filmmaking unbecoming of directors like the Coen brothers.  (Examples of these minor sins include trying to make me feel sympathetic to an anonymous dog and not establishing a setting until the movie is almost over) That being said, this movie's biggest fault was its inability to clue its audience in to what the hell was going on.  I am a very attentive viewer, and I was lost on more than one occasion.  "Suspenseful" is not another word for "not knowing what's happening."  Many of the characters' actions were unmotivated in the narrative, which doesn't speak of the actors but rather what was and was not included in the movie.  The movie meandered, and took way too long for the little bit of plot there actually was.  Woody Harrelson's character was a well-performed but extravagantly unnecessary feature... he added nothing to the plot but confusion.  This movies saving graces were the performances, as even the characters who I found poorly written were well performed; the cinematography, as I saw many of the Coens' ineffable touches in lighting and camera placement; and the few moments of true suspense that were sporadically sprinkled throughout this dry, dry, slow movie.  The ending was also misplaced.  A movie like this works best if the ending allows the audience to finally be told what has been happening for 2 hours; whether or not it is done in conventional ways is a completely separate matter.  Instead, we are given more questions and Tommy Lee Jones's synopses of a dream sequence.  This movie angers me not only because of the slip-shod filmmaking, but also because it had so much potential.  There is a really, really good movie in here somewhere, hiding.

I was hoping that the Coen brothers would return to form. What I got wasn't just a return to their past accomplishments; what I got may be their best film to date. From a technical perspective, it's hard to imagine there being a better film this year--it's rare to see anything this tightly edited, shot, written, and acted. There's not a wasted second of film, not a spare word to the story, and even the minimal (to the point of almost being absent) score only underscores the perfection of the film. The acting is uniformly superb; honestly, whether you're discussing Brolin (who's seriously having an amazing year), Bardem (one of the most chilling villains in recent memory), or Jones (who does something I'd almost forgotten he could do: act, instead of playing himself), you're talking Oscar-worthy work. The film captures McCarthy's tone perfectly, mixing violence and a world-weary outlook with the Coens' signature black humor, and the resulting film is a flat-out masterpiece. If you call yourself a film fan and don't see this, you don't deserve the label.

One word sums up my experience with this movie, disappointment. Going in, I really wanted to like this film. In addition to all of the awards and accolades that it received, the Coen brothers are among my favorite directors. I was especially surprised by the fact that the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay was awarded to this picture since, in my opinion, this was one of the main downfalls of the movie. Although I have not read the book on which this film is based, it seems that the best medium to tell this story would be the printed word. There were a lot of inner dialogues and descriptions that I felt I was missing out on. Instead, these moments were filled with long, drawn-out silences filled only with the character looking pensive and distraught. This only resulted in boredom for me. Another side effect of this flaw with the script was that I felt that I didn't sufficiently get to know the characters involved, and as a result, I didn't particularly care what ended up happening to them. The final problem I had with this film was the uneventful and non-linear story arc. There is never a sense of wondering or anticipation for what is coming next. I can understand that the filmmakers were trying to convey a sense of loneliness and desperation, and this would normally be fine with me, but the themes explored in this movie are ones that have been treaded and re-treaded several time before. In the end, I would have to say that this was not a pleasant viewing experience. The only saving grace was the astonishing cinematography depicting the bleak landscape of southern Texas and Mexico. Ironically, this was one of the few aspects of the film that was not recognized with awards.

Having not watched this movie, it makes it easier for me at least to start to consider what may be the non-summative whole that is this film.  The whole being the system that transcends the  parts. The audience, the culture, the current time/epoch,  The specific stories and myths that Americans embrace.  For me this movie provides a fascinating and mesmerizing take on America, most specifically WASP Americans and their confused place in the world.

Try asking the following.  What does it say about a people that would make such a movie, (culturally speaking not the Coen brothers specifically)?  Why would "a people" want to tell this story.  Meaning why would movie goers want to feel a part of this story?  Why invest one's time, one's head space to make room for these specific images in one's head?  Why? What does it say? 

I find it interesting that all the people being slaughtered down in the movie seem to be Red Necky Anglo-North Americans.  I find it even more interesting that the characters are so completely befuddled by Anton's modality.  

The scene in the gas station proves very interesting to me.  When Anton's character gets upset that the owner "married" into the property and business things get heated. 

I also find it interesting that Brolin's character stumbles upon the cash in the drug deal not unlike like the Europeans stumbled upon North and South America not too awful long ago.  

Contrast that with South American immigrants into now super-affluent North America.  It could be argued that "they" pretty much "lost" what perhaps could have been rightfully theirs.  But to get it back "they" have to illegally cross the border and work their asses off --  five dollars a day in Mexico or five an hour in North America?  Is it fair? Where's the justice, who wouldn't resort illiberal modalities for making a living under those circumstances?

It's the above unspoken nuances of the film that resonate powerfully with me and for me even more powerfully that a "culture" and that culture being our culture would tell this story in such a fashion.  Is this film is a metaphor for the ignorance of WASP America and it's place in the world?  I don't know but I find it interesting that Jone's Character is supposed to be retired and that retirement is supposed to bring closure to a lifes work and joy and relief yet it with Jone's charachter it only brings more questions and an unsettling lack of closure. 

For me it would not be fair to sum up this film to any singular thing.  However it could be possible that this film may provide a bigger insight into just who the viewers are than into just how scary Anton Chigurgh is.

A flawless film about good vs evil and one old man in the middle trying to make sense of the horror. The suspense is superior to that of any Hitchcock films and the lack of a soundtrack only strengthens the tension throughout the almost two hour running time. The cinematography is astounding though it lost the Oscar in that category to There Will Be Blood (respectively). The cinematographer really captured the unforgiving and barren look of the desert plains, even the county town areas feel deserted making it all a perfect hunting ground for the insane assassin Anton Chigurh. 

The performances given from every actor involved holds up. Javier Bardem is silently terrifying yet with a dark occasional sense of humor in what his best role yet, Josh Brolin is a believable anti hero using his skills from Nam to evade Chigurh (Javier Bardem) at every turn, Tommy Lee Jones is impressive as the sheriff trying to put the pieces together near the end of his days as sheriff of the county, Woody Harrelson plays his part surprisingly very well as the bounty hunter trying to get his case of money back before Anton gets to it first. Other notable performances come from Kelly Macdonald  as the innocent wife of Llewelyn Mosse (Josh Brolin) who hasn't got a clue of what's going on and Stephen Root as the man who hires bounty hunter Welles (Woody Harrelson).

Much criticism has been directed to the ending but in my opinion it sums up the meaning of the whole film perfectly if you listen closely and it's sure a lot better than an action popcorn flick ending. The pacing never lets up and the dialogue is some of the best ever in a film, the greatest lines are given mostly by Anton Chigurh. I recommend this to anyone who likes suspense, great dialogue, great memorable characters, modern westerns and films that make you think long after it's over.

This movie was well shot, but lacks the depth it needs to be great. It's extremely slow and has an ending that doesn't really fit.  I expected better. 
    
  NCFOM had a good feel to it and the art direction and cinematography was really well done, but that's what I have come to expect from a Coen brothers film. Stylistically this movie was amazing and that alone was able to keep my attention to the end.  its also the reason for the 5 and not a 3. 
   
  To me NCFOM seriously lacks depth and has little character development, which makes relating to any of the characters hard, on top of that it fails to really establish a leading role.  Tom "I just don't know what to make of that" Bell opens and closes the film completely unchanged in his bewilderment of the changing world around him.  I also can't be the only one tired of seeing Tommy Lee Jones in the same worn out law enforcement role, it really is distracting. 
   
  Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) the hunter turned hunted, was a resourceful lack luster hero (but hero doesn't seem like the right word).  His death was very odd, very sudden,  and is where the film completely lost focus. It was like the Coen's stopped trying and started scrambling for and ending.  
   
  Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem)  is a completely indiscriminate killer that is supposed to be complex yet simple and who also has an invincible quality to him.  In the last scene with Chigurh, a scene that doesn't really fit in with movie at all, the Coen's go out of their way to prove this invincibility.  Chigurh is a character who has many unbelievable quality's in movie where realism is one of the main points of critics praise.    
   
  NCFOM  was slow to a fault.  The suspense it had built for it self was ruined by the mind numbingly slow pace of the film and further destroyed by the lack of character development.  The ending was odd and seemed to drop off.  I couldn't help feeling like I was ripped off after watching NCFOM. This movie had so much potential, but wow did it disappoint.

There isn't a whole lot of good I can say about this movie.  The acting is decent, and Javier Bardem's performance isn't unworthy of an Academy Award.  There's a lot of suspense as the villain Anton Chigurh deals death to his unfortunate victims and tracks Llewelyn Moss.  The movie's Academy Award for Best Picture, however, is undeserved.  For the most part the movie crawls at a snail's pace, even during a nighttime firefight that's anything BUT pulse-pounding (though I guess it could be called realistic).  Everything feels like it's in slow motion - people move slowly, people talk slowly, people walk slowly.  That, plus the incomprehensible and nonsensical babbling that occupies a good 90 percent of the movie's dialogue (much of it from Tommy Lee Jones's annoyingly boring and garrulous character) and the dry, dusty, middle-of-nowhere settings of the movie make No Country for Old Men mind-numbingly monotonous.  And, not to spoil anything but this movie has a hugely anti-climactic and needlessly long ending.  I spent most of the second half of the movie wishing that it would end.

No Country for Old Men R 
Meditations on the inevitability of death and the unfathomable implacability of evil. Sounds like a barrel of fun, now doesn't it? Too often in cinema, we are treated to stories that are about beating the odds- characters who overcome circumstances that are seemingly insurmountable, felling adversaries that are next to unstoppable, and who walk away with nary a scratch to live happily ever after. It's strangely gratifying to see an exception made to this storytelling tradition: a film that acknowledges that there are harsh truths in life, not the least of which is the powerlessness of the individual will in the face of impending, certain doom. It's not a movie about beating death and the evil that causes it, but rather facing up to that unfeeling, unreasoning force, and seeing how different people deal with it and react to it. As is everything the Cohens have ever done, it is a fantastic character piece, even managing to spin some honest, realistic humor out of the different people involved and how they interact with each other (which this film desperately needed, given the weight of the material) while simultaneously crafting a seriously disturbing villain whose deranged actions are belied by his calm, relaxed (if exceptionally creepy) manner. The plot is fairly conventional: trailer-park resident Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon a botched drug deal while hunting on the plains of Texas, discovering a satchel that contains two million dollars in cash. Moss takes the money and goes on the run, but is relentlessly pursued by the Mexican drug-runners who were behind the deal and a psychopathic killer who uses a pressurized air canister as a weapon. Trailing behind both of them is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, a lawman in his autumn years who's seen a lot of misery and suffering in his time, but finds himself completely unprepared for the way the world has become. As Llewelyn Moss, Josh Brolin is a tough but likable kind of guy, a country boy with just a touch of smart-ass to him. Llewelyn is a capable man, certainly- he served two tours of duty in the Vietnam War, so he knows his way around a gun and basic tactical situations- but he's also just an ordinary guy caught in the middle of a situation he doesn't fully comprehend, trying to get away with significantly more than just his own skin; Brolin's performance gets us to root for Llewelyn, even though we know that, looking at things logically, he has no reasonable hope of getting through the coming ordeal in one piece. Another, lesser film might have vindicated that non-existent hope against the sheer inevitability of his predicament, like so many other thrillers have before it, so it really gets your attention when the Cohens allow his character arc to come to the most realistic conclusion possible. Hot on Llewelyn's trail is perhaps one of the most villainously evil characters in film history: Anton Chigurh, as played by Javier Bardem. Chigurh is something of a mystery, his introduction at the beginning of the film (his arrest for a crime that is never mentioned and his subsequent, violent escape) setting the tone for the character while never explaining who he is or where he came from; his allegiances are never really clear- if they aren't non-existent, that is (he tends to kill pretty much everyone, no matter who they're working for)- though his aims are crystal. What makes Chigurh so disturbingly evil isn't just the atrocities that he commits, but the laid back, detached air with which he commits them, and the total lack of empathy or conscience that he displays afterwards (a recurring motif is how he tries to make sure he never gets blood on his shoes, seemingly more out of concern for the shoes than anything, which is really subtly chilling). The film is really entirely hinged on this character, who (or rather what) he is and how others interact with him, and Bardem gives the character a perverse life that makes him both fascinating and terrifying to watch at the same time. Rounding out the principle cast is Tommy Lee Jones as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, a weathered country cop who's trying his best to get to Llewelyn before Chigurh does. Bell is even more of a cowboy than Llewelyn is (but then, almost every guy in the film wears a cowboy hat at least, with the notable exception of Chigurh), but he's basically from a bygone era, ill-equipped to deal with the kind of horrors that the world presents him with and ultimately ineffective against the crushing tide of darkness that he's sworn to battle. Jones gives a spectacular performance here as a man who's lost faith in his own calling, dispirited by everything that he's dealt with and forced to accept the inevitability of death- both his own and that of others. As usual, the Cohens fill out the supporting cast with a gaggle of brilliant character actors; the one who stands out most to me is Kelly Macdonald as Carla Jean Moss, Llewelyn's strangely childlike, innocently naive wife. The two of them- Llewelyn and Carla Jean- have a sassy, easygoing chemistry, and through their banter we see a truly loving relationship between the two. She has one wonderful scene right at the end of the movie that sort of sums up the film's whole theme- the collision of innocent people with incomprehensible evil- and she just pops as a nice Southern girl who's completely in the dark about what's going on. The script is tight and naturalistic, drawing you in with sudden, shocking violence and then investing you with sharp characterization and blazing dialogue (Roger Ebert and I agree that the scene in the Texaco station is absolutely masterful, and yet, ultimately, nothing actually happens in it. Can you imagine how hard it is to write something like that?); having never read the book, I can't honestly say how much of the film's impact stems from the work of the author, but I can say with certainty that the adapted script packs quite a punch. The shots are visually compelling, making use of the vast emptiness of the desert the contrast of light and dark brilliantly; the cinematography only emphasizes this, giving us a dusty yellow color palette that evokes thoughts of desolation and decay. The score- that is, what little score there is- is also naturalistic, forgoing melody in favor of simplicity and ambiance, working heavily with wooden percussion instruments and shakers. Many people claim that No Country for Old Men is the return of the Cohens to greatness. Truthfully, I couldn't say as much for myself, because I skipped out on most of their lamented recent works (though I did get an eyeful of the Ladykillers, and boy, do I wish I hadn't), but I will say that this is absolutely the Cohens in top form, reaching the brilliant heights of Fargo and then, dare I say, surpassing them easily. This is definitely the best film of 2007 (but it's not as if Spider-Man 3 was giving it a run for its money), and the best Cohen release I have ever seen (I'll always have a soft spot for Raising Arizona, though). A must-see.

4 stars: 10/10
 
The Coen Brothers seem to have utterly mastered every cinematic technique possible down to a "T". There are very few filmmakers today that understand what we, the audience, want and know how to correctly transfer that from writing onto film. In Europe, for instance, many film studies classes consider "Fargo" to be the perfect film, the perfect blending of genres, and it is now quite obvious to me why this is the case. 
 
"No Country for Old Men" flows well and never lets up the high tension that it creates very early. It boasts terrific performances by its three leads, most notably Javier Bardem, who plays a killer with unfocused motives, and holds you in its grasp while you can just sit back and watch one hell of a film that shows extreme cinematic superiority and textbook brilliance while still maintaining a feeling of originality.
 
I will not waste your time praising this great film that most avid film viewers will enjoy, but i will leave you rather with one extremely important form of advice for you going into viewing the movie: 
 
Do NOT go into this thinking it is an action thriller. It is merely a moral drama  shaded by an action thriller. Also, pay attention to every line of dialogue, because remember, since this is a Coen brothers movie EVERY line of dialogue and every scene is critical. Also, if you pay close attention, you will appreciate the beauty of the terrific ending instead of asking yourself "What the fuck?" and will end up not enjoying it.

A welcome return to form for the Coens, here adapting a Cormac McCarthy novella set in deepest, darkest West Texas. Javier Bardem, rightly winning an Oscar for his role, plays a real force of nature--a psychopath who will not stop until his task (ruled by a disturbing *amoral* code) is complete. Contrasting with him are Josh Brolin's good man who has made a choice that seals his fate as prey and Tommy Lee Jones' ageing sheriff, who makes choices but effects no real change. The film is also about the change in the United States from a feeling (however illusory) that all was in control to a land where chaos and chance prevail. The keepers of the old order no longer know what to do to prevent the coming debacle, and the only thing that stands in the psychopath's way is blind coincidence. A bleak portrait of hopes and dreams dashed: Brolin's dreams are built on a house of cards, Jones' hope is all he has now that his dreams show the walls closing in, and Bardem needs neither. Scary as all hell, relentless and heartstopping, it also makes you think long and hard.

Hopelessly dire in its style and tone, "No Country for Old Men" is the most entertainingly depressing film of the decade, and an A+ social commentary from the prolific Coen brothers. With its ambiguous and divisive ending about a discouraging dream had by the film's hero and moral centre (played with superb restraint by Tommy Lee Jones), the main theme of the film is about the futility of battling evil, and the desperation felt by those that take up the good fight anyway. Like the filmâs steely villain (an outstandingly creepy Javier Bardem), violence and chaos cannot be stopped. Delayed, wounded perhaps, but to try and vanquish it is a foolâs errand. It'll walk the earth âtil the end of time. Fun, huh? The Coens also dabble with themes of the randomness of the universe, what we can chalk up to fate and what we can control ourselves.
Ever the visual storytellers, the Coens use their DP of choice, Roger Deakins, to give the film a dark and foreboding atmosphere. The Coens themselves (under their longtime pseudonym Roderick Jaynes) cut the footage together as only they can, amping up the excitement so subtly that you barely notice. Equal praise must be given to sound designer Skip Lievsay, whose nuanced sound mix is one of the most effective of the decade.

No Country for Old Men had a great storyline, character development, acting, and cinematography, and still managed to disappoint me greatly with its crappy anticlimactic ending.

What is the purpose of suspense? I couldn't wait to see how the three main characters would interact when they inevitably met. But the Coens yank the rug out from under the audience by suddenly wiping out the protagonist 75% of the way through the movie. Why waste so much time building Llewelyn Moss'(Brolin's) character and emphasizing his resourcefulness if you're going to kill him off so abruptly with no explanation? There's easily an entire scene missing. Fine, I get it: the Mexicans found him. I don't need a happy ending, but at least reveal how his demise went down. I'm not even asking for a gory shootout sequence; just elaborate on what led up to it. Yes, there is an underlying commentary on fate and humanity, but this movie is also an action/crime thriller where multiple peripheral characters are strangled or blown away by a sociopathic killer. It seems disingenuous to skim over the main character's death. Moss never had a chance, and neither does the viewer.

As an exercise in genre stylistics No Country is exemplarily. That is more than enough reason to enjoy the film I suppose. In other words, I doubt the film really has anything that meaningful to say about evil, mortality, or violence: but then again the Coen Brothers have never been serious thinkers, as much as they have been masterful manipulators of style and film form. In that regard, the film ranks with The Big Lebowski and Barton Fink as one of their most expertly realized films.

It may sound glib to suggest that the film doesn't have anything really meaningful to say about evil, but that is an argument I would stand behind. Javier Bardem is brilliant as the psychotic killer in the film and gives one of 2007's  best performances. Yet, what is the purpose of his character? That he is thoroughly evil? He has no real psychological motivations, and practically comes across as a robot in his ability to repair himself. That said, every moment he is on screen is more enjoyable than about anything else I saw in 2007.

Tommy Lee Jones is also excellent as the weary sheriff, and it is through his character that, I suppose, the film tries to engage in a more serious reflection on mortality. Still, his observations come across as generically fatalistic and not very deep. He resigns more because the film has to end, and not because the film really has much to say about fatalism.

I thought that when I bought this on DVD, having not seen it, I wouldn't have any worries about it being bad. I would go as far as saying that this is the best film I have seen this year, so far. I didn't fully know what to expect, I didn't really know how the pace was set out and what really was going to happen. The pace starts off fairly slowly, we get a couple of pretty brutal kills at the beginning. It does keep quite slow for abit as we are introduced to the characters. You already have a good idea of what a psychopath Javier Bardem's character is like in the opening scenes, but we will get back to that later. Josh Brolin plays a hunter who stumbles across a drug deal gone wrong and finds a case with alot of money inside. This soon turns out to be a mistake as Bardems killer is soon on his trail. It then becomes an epic chase of cat and mouse as Brolin is on the run for his life. That may sound simple, but there is alot more to it. Tommy Lee Jones' character really adds the emotional depth to the story, he is the old man with no country. Most of these characters don't have a happy ending (one of which you have no idea what happens to them). Jones' shows his age but it doesn't effect his performance. He always gives raw, genuine performances in all his movies and this is no exception. I had only seen Josh Brolin in Planet Terror before this. He shows great talent, creating a very likeable character who you are always willing on. I look forward to seeing his performance in the upcoming W. But the real star of this picture is Javier Bardem. I think it would be fair to say I haven't seen him in anything much before. But this is one of the most chilling performances I have seen since Anthony Hopkins in Silence of the Lambs. His character, Anton Sugar, is like the Terminator. He seems to have no feeling, just kills for the sake of it at times as plows through not showing a glimpse of sympathy or anything what so ever. Even when he is fixing a gunshot wound, he doesn't wince, he just does what needs to be done. At the end, you are left gussing as to wether he has a deem of humanity or not. I think he possibly does, I'm going to go thourgh the last scenes fram by frame to see wether there is any indication to the truth! I started about talking about the pace at the beginning of the review, I would  describe as a rolling snowball. It starts slow but builds up and cranks up the tension so you are hanging on the edge of your seat. But then this snowball is suddenly abbliterized by a suddenly heat wave and it melts instantly. The ending is not really an ending. It doesn;t finish properly if that makes any sense. It is a bold move which doesn't really bother you but you crave more because of how good the rest of the movie is. It isn't a great big dramatic piece. This is a tense thriller which is an amazing piece of film making. Unusual, offbeat, and marvelous motion picture that climbs into the #2 slot behind only 'Raising Arizona' among the Coen brothers compendium. There is no soundtrack, which allows for the Coens' masterful use of natural sounds to create mood and heighten tension: unseen footsteps, the ticking of a homing device, labored breathing in the dark. Also present are typical elements like stunning cimematography (awe-inspiring Texas landscapes) and weirdo characters (a border guard with an attitude.)

Terrific cast with Oscar-winning contract killer Javier Bardem just another tower among a skyline of talent including TL Jones as a weary sherriff and Josh Brolin a man whose life changes drastically upon discovering a bagful of money. Ah yes, the old premise used a thousand times is given a new, sobering treatment that underscores the element of fate in our lives. Bardem's coin-flipping persona seems like an allegorical representation of Fate, inescapable and inevitable. We also see how law enforcement works at a constant disadvantage, after all the law can only react AFTER a crime is committed.

Unlike other films from Ethan and Joel Coen, No Country is a dark, disturbing portrayal of the choices one makes and their deadly consequences. It is based on the book by the same name, written by Cormac McCarthy (The Road is the most recent movie adaptation of his work). I haven't read the book, but the general consensus for those who have is that this is the novel on the screen and a crowning achievement. 

The story takes place in 1980 in the Texas hill country, when Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon a drug deal gone horribly wrong after a day of hunting. Everyone is dead, even the pet dogs of the drug runners. Moss finds a mountain of what looks to be cocaine and a satchel stuffed with hundreds of thousands of dollars. He helps himself to the satchel and to a couple of weapons. Circumstance and an instance of conscience leads to Moss being sighted by the criminals, barely escaping with his life, but it gets worse. A remorseless, unforgiving hitman is on his trail, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). What's worse is that Chigurh possesses the means to electronically track the satchel which contains a homing device, thus ensues a chase that leads from Texas to Mexico and then back to Texas, only to end on a major surprise. While Chigurh is tailing Moss, both are pursued by the sheriff of Moss' town, Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) and another hitman played by Woody Harrelson. The cinematography is wonderfully done and the period captured so well, it truly looks and feels like 1980, as if you're looking through a window into that period. That is a sign of pure talent on the part of a director or in this case, directors.  

This is a great story showcasing the rise in violence and lack of respect towards human life that is taking hold in the era. It is also a prelude to what the American-Mexican border would later and has become, which is a war zone. The running theme is how things continue to get worse as the old time sheriffs can do nothing but look on, as these drug runners from Mexico are more brutal than ever. Acting is second to none, from Brolin to Bardem, Harrelson to Jones, but the supporting characters and even extras are fantastic too. If you were to walk the streets of a small Texas town in 1980, this is as close to how people would be as possible. It's not stereotyped or over the top, but it's not under stated either. The Coen Brothers are not only great writers, they are spectacular directors.

One word sums up my experience with this movie, disappointment. Going in, I really wanted to like this film. In addition to all of the awards and accolades that it received, the Coen brothers are among my favorite directors. I was especially surprised by the fact that the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay was awarded to this picture since, in my opinion, this was one of the main downfalls of the movie. Although I have not read the book on which this film is based, it seems that the best medium to tell this story would be the printed word. There were a lot of inner dialogues and descriptions that I felt I was missing out on. Instead, these moments were filled with long, drawn-out silences filled only with the character looking pensive and distraught. This only resulted in boredom for me. Another side effect of this flaw with the script was that I felt that I didn't sufficiently get to know the characters involved, and as a result, I didn't particularly care what ended up happening to them. The final problem I had with this film was the uneventful and non-linear story arc. There is never a sense of wondering or anticipation for what is coming next. I can understand that the filmmakers were trying to convey a sense of loneliness and desperation, and this would normally be fine with me, but the themes explored in this movie are ones that have been treaded and re-treaded several time before. In the end, I would have to say that this was not a pleasant viewing experience. The only saving grace was the astonishing cinematography depicting the bleak landscape of southern Texas and Mexico. Ironically, this was one of the few aspects of the film that was not recognized with awards.

there are many ways in which to tell a story, and the Cohen Bros. always seem to take the road less traveled; No Country is no exception.
 
The narrative at the beginning actually tells you what the main theme is, but then what you're seeing on the screen seems like an entirely different movie until several seemingly innocuous scenes featuring Jones let that theme slowly seep back into your consciousness.
 
At the core there is a lawman, from a family of lawmen, who is witnessing an amoral evil he can't understand; to the point where it undermines his life and forces him to walk away from all that he is.  
 
But to make a movie solely about that crises of faith would have been a much different and much weaker film.  Instead, the Cohens surround this tale with a story of a hunt where the hunter becomes hunted and all the lines become blurred; the impetus, a drug deal gone bad and a force of nature who lives by a code that makes sense only to himself - a black hole that draws events to him and then deals with them in violent fashion - all against a stark and bleak backround of the dying old west; beautifully filmed in all its solitary glory.
 
The Cohens also take a poke at the seeming randomness of events that cause ripples through several lives.  That juxtaposition into the final scene of calm and veiled defeat is as jarring as the fade to black.  So many loose ends not tied up; and yet the story wasn't about that and the final scene pronounces the main charactor sentenced to a purgatory he has no choice but to accept.  Not many filmmakers would have made those choices, but once again the Cohens chose art over the easy way out.

A massive achievement by the Coen brothers.  Some will only take No Country for Old Men for its face value (which is considerable in and of itself)but to grasp the immense power that this film contains, one must examine closer.  Upon doing so, one discovers the layers upon layers of subtext that are mindblowing.  

The world is a dangerous place, and mankind must adapt and evolve to survive in it.  Thus the title, no country for old men comes forth.  Those who cannot adapt and understand the changes taking place are forced to sit back and wait until their time comes to leave.  This is represented wonderfully by Tommy Lee Jones, who gives an incredible performance here.

Ultimately, the film is large scale game of cat and mouse, and the younger players (Javier Bardem and Josh Brolin, both phenomenal) are left to conquer this new terrain.  

When man is pitted against something that he does not understand, he is either forced to adapt or to surrender and walk away.  This film shows what happens when both choices are made.  A thriller of the highest quality, No Country for Old Men goes for the throat, and kills.

Last years award winning film (splitting awards with There Will Be Blood) is directed by the coen brothers. A team which rarely ever make inadequate films, this is evident in their 'rotten tomatoes' profile. From Blood Simple to their latest 'Burn After Reading' Joel and Ethan know exactly what they want with a film and its most proven in their best film to date. People I talked to were put off by the Texas and country western aspect that was seen in the trailers and it seems that the genre is still struggling with popularity. However what has been made here is a loose but very finely acted and enjoyable thriller with old reliable 'Tommy Lee Jones' who comfortably provides a nice backbone to this otherwise dark and pretty violent thriller.The acting across the board is pretty impressive with Javier picking up many a 'best supporting actor' award upon its viewing by critics. The storyline seems pretty linear but with multiple characters you are never quite sure who your rooting for. The imagery is very 'western' from the opening black and white shots leading onto a sombre and very silent beginning. The only thing the film really lacks in my opinion is a decent musical score, simply because there isn't one. The film could really do with some accomnyment to convey the emotion some of the characters are feeling, and disappointedly this is never embarked upon by the directors. On the other hand with some great atmosphere and tension this film is stylish, quirky and a breath of fresh air amongst the usual poorly written thrillers.The ending is most frustrating with many fans trying to interpret the ambiguous ending where the 'final showdown' never happens. Personally I was a little disappointed but I can clearly see why it is so bewildering as it really provides a new twist explored the same year with Finchers very long and competent 'Zodiac', a thriller where the killer is never caught.A modern-day classic that rightfully deserves its reputation, and while it may seem slightly hit and miss in entertainment as a mainstream classic it fits snugly between the slight art house cinema and new popular culture thriller.

A well-paced, dialogue/action-mixed adapted screenplay from everyone's favorite filmmaking duo, this time around finally winning that Best Picture Oscar they've been going for the past couple decades.  Casting some actors they don't normally use, which is a change for them, the Coen brothers have three lead characters: Tommy Lee Jones as the aging but clever lawman in pursuit, Javier Bardem in an Oscar-winning turn as an almost inhuman murderous monster that stands up the hairs on your neck every time an innocent character shares a conversation with him, and Josh Brolin as a bored and self-conscious victim of Bardem's terrifying hunt.  Brolin, while hunting, stumbles upon some dead/dying Mexican cartel mobsters, a truckload of heroin, and a parcel of $2000000.  He takes the money and guns with him, but gets caught by some more cartel men, which ends with him shot in the shoulder.  One cartel mob hires Bardem to retrieve the money, regardless of how it turns out for Brolin.  Brolin, realizing this, sends his wife, Kelly Macdonald, away and runs away, staying in various motels and hitchhiking from place to place.  But the merciless killing machine of Bardem is close on his trail, and leaves a bloodbath behind him everywhere he goes.  Deciding wether to kill most of his victims based on a coin toss, Bardem's fear-striking nature and appearance makes him a classic movie villian, one of a dying breed.  Woody Harrelson makes a few appearances as an experienced enemy of Bardem's hired by the other cartel to find the money first.  At one point, Harrelson, on finding out that Brolin survived a firefight with Bardem, he comments "You saw?  And you're still alive?  Hmm...".  Garrett Dillahunt also appears a couple times as a young sheriff-in-training taken under Jones' wing.  After a few years of not hearing from them, the Coen bros return to a genre in which they are strongly talented in, and in which I hope to see them again soon, similar to 'Miller's Crossing'.  The dark cinematography and small cast give the film a purposeful sense of loneliness felt individualy by each character as well as us the audience.  Adapted from Cormac McCarthy's novel, the Coen brothers' 20th century western has an Oscar-worthy screenplay that provides many smart, dialogue-heavy lines that serve well individually and altogether like a brilliant screenplay does. My pick for the #1 film of 2007 is [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], directed by Joel and Ethan Coen. The Coen Brothers started off their careers in high fashion with [i]Blood Simple[/i] in 1984. They then produced a slate of films that most directors would kill to create. [i]Raising Arizona (1987), Miller's Crossing (1990), Barton Fink (1991), The Hudsucker Proxy (1994), Fargo (1996), The Big Lebowski (1998), O Brother, Where Art Thou (2000)[/i] and [i]The Man Who Wasn't There (2001)[/i]. They hit a little glitch, in my opinion, with [i]Intolerable Cruelty (2003)[/i] and [i]The Ladykillers (2004)[/i], but returned to form with this film.
 
[i]No Country[/i] is a deep and tangled psychological thriller whose message is far more layered and nuanced than the roots of its genre would indicate. I've not read the Cormac McCarthy novel upon which the movie is based. Perhaps, if I had, the movie would make a little more sense on first viewing. However, it's the eerie quality of the film that had me talking for hours after the final credits had rolled, and I have the sneaking suspicion that the Coen Brothers took the story and stamped their own unique mark upon it.
 
In many ways, [i]No Country[/i] borrows ideas from some of the Coen Brother's earlier works. The main story revolves around a crime gone wrong, a plot that the Coen Brothers have visited several times. In its thematic scope, [i]No Country[/i] is most like [i]Blood Simple[/i], with less humor driving the story line.
 
We follow Officer Ed Tom Bell (played by Tommy Lee Jones) who is investigating a crime and whose instincts are usually right, but are rarely timely. It seems he's always one step behind the action. This is also reminiscent of [i]Blood Simple[/i], and having a police officer in the role of narrator and central observer to the action (and acts in a smaller sense as our moral barometer) reminds me of [i]Fargo[/i]. Josh Brolin plays Llewellen Moss, a man who accidently embroils himself in all kinds of evil when he stumbles across a bag of money from a botched drug deal and decides to keep it. His nemesis is Anton, the uber-creepy contract killer sent to get the money back.
 
Javier Bardem is electrifying as Anton, and his character plays a similar role to the motorcycle killer in [i]Raising Arizona[/i], but with far less humor attached to the part. Anton seems less a man than a moving, soulless force of nature.
 
As the story unfolds, you slowly realize that Anton will not be stopped, and Llewellen is destined to meet him.
 
What makes [i]No Country[/i] stand out from other movies of its ilk is the subtext.  Officer Bell slowly recognizes that he no longer understands what his purpose is. I can't quite put my finger on it, but the movie tries to capture the feeling of what it would be like to wake up and suddenly realize that the world has moved on without you, that you are an anachronism in a once familiar landscape, and that the morals which guided you and guided those who fought against you no longer apply in this new world. This message isn't overt, but it's there, and it's haunting.
 
Anyway, I highly recommend [i]No Country for Old Men[/i], the best film of 2007.

No Country for Old Men is a simple story of a man (the protagonist), a true Texan cowboy type (Josh Brolin), who walks into a deserted area in West Texas where a drug deal near the Mexican border has gone bad leaving everyone dead except one man who kept asking for "agua, agua", and he discovers $2 million.  It is also a story about a sadistic, melancholic, ghost-like stalker of an antagonist who has a tracking devise on the suit case that has this $2 million.  It is also a story about a sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones), who is trying to uncover this mess before the cowboy and the antagonist rumble so to speak.

The cowboy's wife is played by Kelly McDonald, a real life Scottish woman who has an incredible ability to act as a Texan female.

The movie in many ways reminds me of Fargo.  There is violence, there's the cultural humor (poking fun at how people from a certain region behave, etc.), there's the darkness, great dialogue, and immense beauty in footage of barren scenery.

The Coen brothers have that down to an art form.  

To their credit, their casting was pretty close to perfect.  I liked all the main characters and their acting ability.  Javier Bardem rightly deserves the Oscar for best actor.  His energy was powerful.  Josh Brolin's acting was likeable, personable, and attracts the viewer in staying with the scenes.

Tommy Lee Jones acting wasn't half bad, but for some reason, I thought a few of his rambles (arias, so to speak) were superfluous and thus less convincing and more of a distraction such as the scene where he's talking with Llewelyn's wife and is rambling about some air gun killing cows.

I had a serious problem with the ending.  I mean come on Coen brothers!  You're filming in Texas.  There's clearly a cowboy, a sheriff, and a villain.  You have to have a final showdown in Western genre fashion.  That wasn't done.  Instead, they opted for the mysterious minimalist "preaching the movie title" sort of ending which I thought was too "alternative college radio station-esque."

I'm gonna dock this great movie 1 star because of the "artsy ending."

And besides, if our villain, Bardem is this amazingly intelligent killer, you'd think he'd be smart enough to drive intelligently, right???? I thought the ending was a flawed shortcut and too convenient.

A Coen brothers movie hardly contains groundbreaking script. Most of the time, the story is fairly straightforward - something slightly unusal gone more than slightly wrong. There is usually one main interesting character and a host of other minor, but intriguing characters. 'No Country...' is no different. A hunter comes across a drug-deal gone horribly wrong and finds a whole lot of money. He decides to keep the money, which leads to the inevitable pursuit by the ultimate bad-guy. The psychopathic killer on the trail of the hunter is a chilling character. He has a very clear, logical mind and not a shred of compassion, plus a liberal dosage of brutality. The pursuit leaves a trial of death in its wake.

The biggest asset of this fairly common story is its disturbing, ruthless, brutal antagonist, Anton Chigurh, who decides whether or not to kill perfectly innocent victims based on a coin toss, and asks the victim to call it. He is not completely devoid of principles, but does seems to possess a very twisted, sadistic turn of mind. The dry, barren & unforgiving landscape of the film perfectly complements this soulless, inhuman psychopath wandering around in it. The dialogue is minimal and the settings are bare, yet very apt and leave an impression on the viewer. The only problem is that there doesnt seem to be a point to the movie, besides the portrayal of this bad guy.

Young Americans
No Country for Old Men and Juno.
by Jimmy So

What country is the Coen brothers, or, more accurately, Cormac McCarthy, referring to? Adapted by Joel and Ethan Coen from McCarthys novel, No Country for Old Men is inhabited by plenty of old men. One such man opens the film: Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), his baritone accompanying a pre-dawn Texas landscape, musing about how times have changed. What exactly that change might include is served right up, in the form of Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). He kills four men, in memorable fashion, before we even see Bells face. Bardems haircut has suffered many a reviewers descriptions; I will add mine: It looks like He-Mans do. No matter how bad it makes Bardem look, you cant say it doesnt make him more unforgettable than he already is. Chigurh is a menacing, ghoulish killer laying waste to the country of No Country. Chigurh is the Master of the Universes alter-ego from hell, and hes been hired to retrieve some lost drug money.

Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam veteran played by Josh Brolin, is the man who came upon the money. In tandem with most good, honest American crime stories, No Country dictates that Moss is not smart, nor ruthless, enough to get away without being noticed. He is an average Joe, although in suggestively non-average-Joe fashion he didnt think twice about strolling onto the scene of a drug deal gone wrong, coolly surveying the aftermath of a carnage where symbolic imagery is sprinkled on the seta few corpses here, a dead pit bull there, a truck bed full of heroin, and a dying Mexican. He leaves the Mexican (and the heroin) and follows a blood trail to find a dead man under a tree with something that he couldnt take to the grave with himtwo million dollars.

So, what would you do with two million dollars? If, like Moss, you live a not-altogether pleasant life in a trailer with your wife, you would disappear to start anew somewhere, away from Texas. But this being a Cormac McCarthy book, the farthest that Moss goes is just across the Mexican border. For the McCarthy narrative, Texas has always been the ugly wife you cant leave, and Mexico the even-uglier affair that made you miss your spouse. For No Country, McCarthy added Chigurh, your wifes psycho brother who wont rest until hes blown your brains out.

Brolin is the only one of the films main actors who didnt have to take himself too seriously. Only Moss could decide anything on a whimsay, Alright, and resolve to go back to the crime scene with a jug of water for the dying Mexican. Only Brolin can afford to be a little lighter on the audience. Bell is the one-dimensional elder who has little left except his incorruptible, unchanging memories. And if Bardem played Chigurh with even a slight hint of gaiety, I get the feeling he would throw up his arms and bitterly laugh at his coiffure. His motifdeciding life and death on a coin tossis the very opposite of whimsical and fatalistic to the extreme. You've been putting it up your whole life, he says. You just didnt know it.

Moss is the easier-on-our-nerves guy, just the type whom we need to make a country out of No Country, the young man among the old men. Its fun seeing him run. He plays a capable mouse to Chigurhs cat, and the whole game is so thrillingly and expertly done by the Coens that youll dread a fate worse than death: a third act collapse. Why stop the game three-fourths of the way? Why not keep up the suspense until we reach a climatic hell-raising battle? Thats, after all, the essence of a good crime flick or a classic western. The answer is that, as theatrical the novel is, McCarthy didnt set out to write a screenplay. He wrote a book. And meandering monologues that wrap up books have been all the rage since Ulysses. Unfortunately, they dont work so well in movies. The Coens came close to delivering a rich and gripping movie for buffs who like their action flicks soaked in a mythological aesthetic. Too bad No Country is a book with what you could hardly call a finale and even less of a finish. We are only left to ponder: What might have been if the Coens had gotten their hands on Blood Meridian? How would they put that hair-raising, haunting ending on screen? Would, or could, any one? All eyes look to Mr. Tommy Lee Jones, who has bought the rights to adapt the book. We could only wait.


Juno is an ode to single mothersthats what hit me two-thirds of the way into the film, as Jennifer Garner, playing one-half of a well-to-do Gen-Y couple, the ones who get into The New York Times Vows page, looks so longingly at the bulging belly of the titled heroine that she seems to be able to see the very face of the son or daughter whom she wants so badly to raise. She and her husband, played by Jason Bateman, are adopting the yet-unborn baby accidentally begot by teenager Juno, played with spunk and delectable confidence by Ellen Page. That scene convinced me that Garner could be a very good actress, albeit a supporting oneshe is too pretty as a profound leading lady, but she is utterly convincing and subtly moving in this role, tapping into the deeper, more sentimental desires of the screenwriter, Diablo Cody, than are exhibited in the other cutesy characters of the film. Juno is a cheeky 16-year-old high school girl who is too smart to be a 16-year-old high school girlor at least thats what we thought, fooled by her quick-witted sarcastic remarks for everything. You shouldve gone to China, you know, cause I hear they give away babies like free iPods. Soon we find out that she needs some lessons on how to deal with the adult situations she finds herself insay, pregnancy. Her sarcasm is and has been what she hides behind. This being a light-hearted comedy where there is only one type of characteran independently charming human working for the good of the movieJuno, of course, learns to let down her guard, but not before delivering (besides an infant) dozens upon dozens of smart-ass lines like: Excuse me, I am a sacred vessel, alright? All youve got in your stomach is Taco Bell. Similar to 2006s Little Miss Sunshine, this is a movie for our times, a thoroughly contemporary pop flick that plays up our collective quirkiness. In the middle of that lies a strongly beating feminine heart and a long-overdue breakout performance, both likely to whisk by most viewers too busy laughing along with the jokes.

The most serious and critically lauded film to come out of the Coen brothers' oeuvre, it still has the haunted, vacant appeal of their earlier films. Based on the book by Cormac McCarthy, showing every slow, methodical, meaningful point so easily, and yet creating a distinguished, quiet air of thought. There is very little dialogue to this film, surprising since the Coens are most famous for chatty characters that rely their own quirky sensibilities. This is not to say that the Coens haven't used silence to show fear, dishonor, or even hatred at many points (most notably in "Barton Fink" and "Miller's Crossing") but instead of stifling and uncomfortable silences they're reflective at many junctures. Set in the desert and plains of Texas, there are many panoramic shots of the outlying surroundings of these places that oftentimes show the aloneness of the lead character, Llewelyn Moss, and his disconnect from help while he hides and fights against his predator. Moss is the prey in this cat and mouse chase, and what is so fundamentally interesting about his plight is that he oftentimes outwits the man who is following him. That person is Anton Chigurh, a contract killer who hunts down Moss, trapping him time and again and yet failing often. Though Anton is obviously going to win out against the irresponsible and slow Moss, Moss doesn't give up and ends up holding his own. Anton in turn is one of the most interesting and full bodied villains to be onscreen in some time. Though he operates on the same level as any other killer, the serial killer mentality of having rules and patterns towards his kills presents itself to the viewer in various ways, the most memorable being a coin toss to choose life or death. This is a multi-layered and large scale game of wits, and though not the traditional good versus bad narrative it does present unorthodox views of morality. Though Sheriff Bell does track Anton as well, he cannot chase down someone so malicious and without a sense of right and wrong. This is not an indication that evil has won, because the sheriff simply can't keep up thanks in part to his old age. Even Anton is not a clear villain because though he does kill indiscriminately he sometimes gives the option of redemption, and lets fate dictate many of his actions. He kills when he needs to, and oftentimes doesn't even want to thanks to his own code of cleanliness, reliance, and self-preservation. This film will blow you away with the complexity of the narrative and how interesting and poignant the plights of the characters truly are.

A flawless movie. Impossible to fault. The Coen brothers can make classic movies in their sleep. This one by all accounts shouldn't be as great as it is; the plot setup is familiar, the presentation is minimalist, the violence is pervasive, savage, and gory, and the (non)ending has the potential to infuriate even the film's biggest fans. It all works. The "familiar" plot setup is played for maximum terror and suspense. The minimalist presentation and slow pace allow for indescribable beauty to seep in; it's a thriller that plays like a tone poem. The violence? Truly disturbing, not in a fun way, but a way that makes us contemplate the world in which we live and how this kind of stuff can happen. And the infamous ending, one of the most controversial in movie history, is perfect; it reveals that the movie was actually about more than it appeared to be about, and on closer inspection, leaves the film feeling quietly haunting rather than viscerally rousing. Javier Bardem is shit-your-pants scary, Brolin is a badass, and Jones is his usual witty, likable self. I started my review with this and it's really all I can think to say... No Country for Old Men is a perfect movie.

This film is excellent.  The Coen Brothers strut their stuff once again and prove to us that they remain two of the greatest living film directors.

The Coens have had their share of great comedy (Raising Arizona, O Brother, Where Art Thou, and, most recently, Burn After Reading) and they have also had their share of thrills (Blood Simple, Fargo).  Here they create a bone-chilling thriller about drugs, the desert, and a psychotic serial killer.  With sparse dialogue, only used when absolutely necessary, No Country for Old Men keeps the viewer on the edge of his seat, always wondering in the silence what will happen next.  Allegedly, the film sticks to the plot of the original Cormac McCarthy novel of the same name like glue.  The plot follows three central characters: Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a retired welder who finds dead Mexicans, their truckload of heroin, and $2 million cash in the middle of the desert.  After he makes off with the money, a psychotic hitman named Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) follows him, killing everyone in his way.  Trying to protect Moss and solve the case is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones).  Bell is weary of his town as it grows more violent and more hostile.  He ponders his life, the choices he has made, and his fate throughout the film.

Bardem is brilliant in this film.  He creates the most chilling, psychotic character since Hannibal Lecter.  As he commits countless pointless murders, not an ounce of remorse or feeling is shown in his eyes, which are as desolate as the desert that surrounds him.  He makes this film.

Jones is also fantastic.  He is the philosophical character in the movie.  He asks questions of himself and of this world.  He discovers that fate and destiny are troubling subjects, but that they are always open-ended and that anyone can form his fate.

The Coen Brothers have never missed.  According to some, this is their best, and, although I haven't seen all of their films, I wouldn't doubt it, either.  It's great, and its well-developed characters are intriguing.  The ending, however, has taken some heat.  It is quite perplexing, and I admit I don't fully understand it, but I challenge all who say the ending is disappointing to give it a second chance.  It has meaning, and it makes sense.  If you're unhappy with it and don't understand it, try reading the book.

This is a great piece of film-making.  It is fulfilling from beginning to end.

I watched this film and absolutely loved it. Directed by Ethan and Joel Coen, the same guys who directed Raising Arizona, there's no similarity between the two, but I give both high marks. Where RA is funny and slapstick, NCOM is dark, spare and brutal. There is shocking violence in this film, but compared to other films currently out, it's not overboard. What violence there is, is perpetuated by the coldly psychotic Anton and is often undeserved, but so suited to his disturbing character that it seems right. The film takes place in 1980 in the desolate plains of West Texas and follows, Llewellyn (Josh Brolin), a good ol' boy and ex-Vietnam vet, who stumbles upon the bloody aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong. Looking around he finds a satchel, guarded by a dead guy, filled two million dollars and he takes it. Yet unbeknownst to Llewellyn the bag has a transponder in it, and the killer, Anton, has the tracking device and will stop at nothing to get it back. Behind them both is the small town's aging sheriff, Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who's struggling with his growing disillusionment in mankind and hoping to get to Llewellyn before the killer does. This film is one that will stay will me for a long, long time. The pristine editing, smart, unforgettable dialogue and gritty, realistic portrayals of these characters made this film, imo, truly one not to be missed.

An established piece of cinematic scenery, the Coen Brothers have been presenting their unique combination of Tarantino playfulness and Marx Brothers absurdity for more than a quarter of a century. From the experimental, hallucinatory wanderings of 'Barton Fink' and 'The Big Lebowski' to the sly parody of 'Oh Brother, Where Art Thou?', to the starkness and the strangeness of 'Fargo', the Coens have taken a delirious journey through the heart of American movies. Though last year's 'Burn After Reading' remains the latest does of Coen craziness, it's their picture before that, the one that finally saw them win gold for their particular brand of movies, that remains a monumental achievement.
Ever since 'Fargo' in 1996 everyone has wondered when the brothers would make another film on the darker side of black comedy. 'No Country For Old Men' is about as far away from their usual irreverent and zany antics as you could possibly hope for. Taking an already-classic American novel and breathing cinematic life into it, the Coens have turned out an extraordinary effort.
As noted from the title and the locations this movie is a modern Western, 'updated' to 1980, a time when the old Western playgrounds have been corrupted by newfangled drugs and gang warfare. Essentially though, the characters wouldn't seem out of place. Llewelyn is the retired soldier determined to keep his primal instincts alive. Sheriff Bell is the creaking old marshall who relentlessly pursues evil because it's the only reason he knows to exist. Carson Wells is the mediator with deals with the devil, exchanging the lesser of two evils to the increasingly caged in Moss, and of course Anton Chigurh is death made flesh, unstoppable, unreasonable, totally lacking in a sense of humour.
Since these archetypes can easily be pointed out it's testament to the incredible cast's skills they manage to make everything so fresh. The Coens themselves surely deserve praise for their fearlessness. Here is a film with no clean-cut hero, no specific development to observe, no triumph over evil, no assurance everything's settled, all played with the straightest of faces that only occasionally cracks into a smile. If anyone would make a film so convincing in its depiction of evil and not have any cloying technique to pander to the ADHD sufferers in the audience, the Coens can certainly be relied on.
Jones, Brolin et al are magnificent, giving warm, consummate and personalised performances. From Jones' pithy snipes at his assistant to Harrelson visibly breaking down when faced with his death, this is engrossing stuff, the kind of polished quality you thought died out in the 1970s. But if any turn is to stay in the mind it's Javier Bardem's monstrous Chigurh. Fully deserving his Best Supporting Actor Oscar, Chigurh is a disturbing mix between the Terminator's relentlessness and ruthlessness and Harry Powell from 'The Night of the Hunter's' strict commitment to a moral conduct; as Carson Wells says, 'He's a man who has 'principles'.'
With astonishing cinematography from the legendary Roger Deakins (who bagged yet another Oscar nom for his work on this), which imbues the visuals with a rich poetry that does away with pesky music, and with a Kubrickian attention to sound, etching out every tiny movement, this is a nervously charged, sweaty and adrenaline-inducing thriller, each one of its gorgeous frames filled with simmering detail. Whether you go for its crisply measured, slow-burning pace or the near pitch-perfect efforts of its wonderful cast, there's no doubt that from 2007 this certainly was the Best Picture.

It was needlessly puzzling and self-absorbed, and while there's nothing wrong with loose ends, ultimately this did not feel like a completed movie.

What did come together, however, did so very well. It was the fastest two-hour thinker I've ever seen. The violence wasn't nearly as bad as reported, which I thought was an appropriate decision. Bardem's villain was purely fascinating, a truly unique creation that stood out in its own right. Brolin was also good, as well as Jones; Harrelson makes me wonder how he still gets work.
