What is the point in doing good things when ultimately, evil will always triumph? At what point do we just give in, or is it better to die before we ever reach that point? This is one of the many provocative issues raised by the Coenâs masterpiece, perhaps their greatest film to date. Filmed from a totally amoral perspective, the film follows three central characters, each one-step further removed from the human condition, and is centred around a cat-and-mouse chase between an inhuman serial killer,  a cunningly resourceful hillbilly, and the jaded sheriff who is forever on their trail. The three characters, and the 1980s American setting, consistently reflect upon themselves, and us, the quirks and the futility of the human race. Playing like a cross between the Coens and David Cronenberg, and mixing strong philosophical themes with excellent action set pieces to an extent which puts the Dark Knight to shame, this existential take on The Terminator is a thoughtful, meditative, thrilling, and challenging piece of filmmaking at its very finest. 10/10

"No Country for Old Men," is a bleak, blood-rare crime drama that takes no prisoners, but it is a little too vague to be a Best Picture worthy masterpiece.  It is shamelessly faithful to the novel by Cormac McCarthy, and is really the perfect enactment of his focused but minimalistic style.  But film does not really lend itself to analysis as well as text does, and the film's ending, perfect for the thoughfulness of McCarthy's book, seems a little too sudden here, even if it is still comprehensible.  But the Coen Bros'. directing style is impeccable, and the cinematography is striking.  Javier Bardem plays psychotic hit man Anton Chigurh with enough understated menace to make Heath Ledger's Joker cower in a corner.  This film is a technical triumph, but won't win any more awards for being the most powerful feature ever to grace the screen.

This is a definitely a Cohens film. While it isn't as consciously quirky as some of their fare (Hudsucker Proxy / O Brother, Where Art Thou? / The Big Lebowski), it tramples all over the usual expectations and narrative structures you'd expect from a chase movie. In fact, it's almost directly lifted from the original book and it shows at certain key stages in the movie where major plot points get resolved in the blink of the eye. 

I reckon it's missing a certain something to raise it from a thought provoking and well made film into a true classic, but it still makes you sit up and think. Javier Bardem as the vengeful killer makes a chillingly perfect sociopath, although the Oscar for best supporting actor should have gone to his hair, which effortlessly steals the show. 

Possibly one of those 'Marmite' movies that, to mix food metaphors, won't be everybody's cup of tea, but I'd say give it go if you're after something affecting to go a bit deeper.

It battled "There Will Be Blood" in the same locations during shooting and at the Oscars, taking home 4 Oscars (Including Best Picture & Director) compared to P.T Anderson's 2. Comparing the two is difficult, both are top 10 of the year material in my book, but P.T Anderson's is a sprawling epic where one evil man can slowly turn the world into an evil place, The Coens' film concerns 3 men in an evil Godless world with no hope of changing it for the better: One purely evil, one good, and one caught in the middle of it all. 

After Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) discovers a bunch of twisted cars and dead bodies in the middle of a desert, he stumbles upon $2 million and promptly goes on the run, only to find later on that he's being chased by the world's most badass bounty hunter.

Anton Chigurh (Oscar winning performance by Javier Bardem, possibly the coolest guy not to have a driver's license) is pure evil lurking beneath a stone-faced facade (he uses an air gun ranchers use on their cattle which is kinda cool). He doesn't bellow, scream and shriek like Daniel Plainview or the Joker, he's more calm and unpredictable, far more unsettling because we never know what he's going to do next.

Tracking Anton & trying to keep the peace in this god-forsaken hell hole is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones who also narrated the story at the start, that's important later on), a world-weary guy who is close to retirement.

The 3 men almost meet each other many times, but one sequence in a motel where Anton first tracks down Llewelyn is incredibly tense, and when Ed is about to open a motel door with Anton hiding inside, your heart stops at the thought of what will happen next. Some of the death scenes are dealt with in an unusual manner: A car screeching out of a car park with screams coming from the inside of a shopping centre, even the shootout in the desert which set up the storyline is never explicitly revealed to the audience, the Coens trust us to decide how it all happened, it's probably their best directed film.

Speaking of those Oscars, Javier Bardem deserved his Oscar, but Josh Brolin gives a strong performance as the main character who doesn't get all of the screentime, Tommy Lee Jones makes you sympathise with the Sheriff effortlessly, a wonderful cameo from Woody Harrelson as a cowboy and former friend of Anton just adds to the film. The cinematography category was tough as hell that year: The upper class glow of Atonement, the dusty darkness of No Country, the out-of-focus to gloriously dreamy look of The Diving Bell and the poetic aura of Assassination of Jesse James all being pipped by There Will Be Blood. Anyone of those films would have been a worthy winner, but personally I think No Country would have deserved it slightly more.

The biggest talking point about the film is the ambiguous ending, which feels like the carpet's been pulled from right underneath you, even if you've been expecting an abrupt ending. But because this is not a conventional good vs evil story that has a happy ending, it does not warrant a conventional ending. There Will Be Blood's ending was designed to shock, No Country For Old Men's was designed to make you think about why the Coens ended it that way (it's the last words of the novel it was based on).

"Fargo" could be The Coen Brothers' masterpiece (I've always loved "Miller's Crossing" but that's another issue), but "No Country For Old Men" is a more serious darker story that aims at an evil ungodly world rather than a materialistic America, with one less woodchipper. The ending will disappoint people who want everything tied up in a nice little bow, but everything else about the film is of such high quality that a lack of a clear resolution only makes it better in my book. One of the Coen Brothers very best.

Non e' un Paese per Vecchi e' per vecchi. L'accezione non e' negativa, e' un film all'antica. Invita a rivalutare i lunghi racconti e i ricordi di chi in eta' avanzata ha modo di riflettere dopo averne viste tante, chiacchere liquidate come noiose da chi pensa di avere di meglio da fare ma che nascondono messaggi preziosi. Con questa introduzione potrei aver fuorviato il lettore sul genere del lungometraggio: e' un film d'azione con tutti gli ingredienti del caso: una valanga di soldi, droga, sangue e pallottole. I Coen riescono pero' a raccontare tutto con uno stile pacato sebbene ficcante: se Fargo era un dipinto di paesaggio rurale, NCforOM rappresenta un paesaggio desertico. I fratellini hanno il dono di immergere lo spettatore in certe atmosfere esprimendo quegli impalpabili elementi che davvero caratterizzano un luogo: il modo di fare della gente, i ritmi, odori e sapori. Non sono mai stato nel Texas ma ora potrei quasi dire il contrario.  In questo scenario si muovono i personaggi splendidamente caratterizzati di questa storia che dapprima racconta lo svolgersi degli eventi con regia egregia: gente ruvida che insegue ruoli e necessita' con pragmatica tenacia. La seconda parte del film e' quella che fa davvero la differenza: i protagonisti vengono messi faccia a faccia con loro stessi rivelando i piccoli messaggi che compongono elegantemente il significato di quest'opera. Il killer dotato di follia e profonda intelligenza, per cui uccidere o risparmiare una vittima ormai non fa alcuna differenza rifiuta dollari per mantenersi fedele a principi per lui piu' solidi ma si fa insegnare da un ragazzino che non tutto necessita di qualcosa in cambio. Lo stesso ragazzino poi contratta con l'amichetto smentendosi immediatamente. Lo spettatore assiste affascinato alle variabili incoerenze ed alle scelte di ogni personaggio alle prese con le proprie priorita' valoriali in un mondo che i Coen descrivono degenerato, attaccato al vil denaro (tema principe anche in Fargo) e dimentico di cosa e' realmente e genuinamente importante nella vita. Discorsi noiosi, prediche che potrebbe fare un padre, o un vecchio sceriffo di provincia, stanco di lottare per i propri ideali e di stupirsi di come non si finisca mai di stupirsi di come possa andare sempre peggio. Chissa' che un giorno non ci si svegli bruscamente da un sogno, anche noi vecchi per scoprire che il padre, o quello sceriffo, o il padre di quello sceriffo avevano ragione.

SOME SPOILERS AHEAD, READ AT YOUR OWN RISK! I think somewhere along the way, during the making of this film, something happened, and someone, or a few people involved in the making of this movie, made bad decisions. The film opens with a commentary on the world today, how it has become extremely violent and often senseless, compared with the time that your grandfather was a young man, where some lawmen hardly carried their guns on themselves. This brief commentary is voiced over scenery of the vast landscapes of Texas, which probably haven't changed much since your grandfather's time. Immediately after this, an extremely violent scene is shown, it is almost a perfect scene, I would have prolonged it by another 30 seconds or so, to make it even more realistic. But it's a major improvement over the 10 to 35 seconds stranglings we've seen in countless films before. Bardem is fascinating. Brolin is macho and gives a good performance, Harrelson spices things up. Unfortunately I can't say much for Jones, he gives a faint performance. Perhaps it was just as well that he didn't get a lot of screen time. There is some good suspense, but the pace of the film is a little slow sometimes, specially by two unnecessary scenes, (when Sheriff Bell talks to his wife, and when he talks to Ellis). Also there are some inconsistencies, I could even say botched scenes, two of them that comes to mind, when Bell enters the motel room, and the killer is hiding in that room, this scene is stopped halfway, then cuts into another unrelated scene. Also, it's unclear what happens to Moss (the hunter), there is one scene that suggest he died, but it's fleeting. And the ending could very well be the worse ending I've ever seen. It just closes abruptly without much of a conclusion, and goes to the credits. But even with this flagrant ending botch job, and the inconsistencies, and somewhat slow pace, the film has some good points, and is very realistic.

NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN (122 mins) DVD Dec 08

BARDEM KING OF JUNGLE IN CAT AND MOUSE GAME

Ok, let's begin by saying that this movie won the Oscar for Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Supporting Actor.  Now that's out of the way I'm free to say what I really think.

Javier Bardem gives a five star performance in a two star movie, hence the three stars.  He earns his Best Supporting Actor Oscar and is so riveting as a cold-blooded murderer, that I switched off whenever he wasn't on screen.

The story?  It's not even an interesting premise... Man finds money. Man goes on run from people who want it back... It's just all been done before.  It's a simple tale, simply told. So much so that it's a simpler version of A Simple Plan, (the superior 1998 Oscar nominated film with a much cleverer script and denouement.)

Don't get me wrong, No Country for Old Men starts strong with stunning panoramas of the Texan landscape and a voice over from local sherrif, Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones).  It's 1980 and local man Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is out hunting pronghorns when he stumbles on the aftermath of a bungled drug deal.  With men lying dead and a bag with $2 million, his choice is easy. He steals it.  And then we meet Bardem's bounty hunting monster, Anton Chigurh.  He's flipping a coin over killing a local, while calmly asking the man to call heads or tails.  However, from this highpoint of tension it unfortunately descends into chase-by-numbers, and only recovers during Bardem?s scenes.  There are other characters (eg, Woody Harrelson as another bounty hunter) but they're so inconsequential I won't mention them.

Apparently this is supposed to be a movie about how chance plays in your life, and that you never know what's coming.  Well, to me this felt like a cop out for unimaginative plot twists. 

Worse, with barely any character arc or development for all the major players, there was no sympathetic character with whom to identify.  How can the audience go on a journey, when there isn't one to go on?  No one grew. No one learned.  (Unless you count the sherrif whose big epiphany is to quit the force).  Oh no! I just ruined the astonishingly anti-climactic ending for you! 

If you want a great Coen brothers movie with a clever script and interesting ensemble of characters, try Fargo.  For in this cat and mouse movie, Bardem is the only king of the jungle, Brolin is Mighty Mouse, and Jones and Harrelson are simply neutered.

This is the Coen brother's masterpiece. "No Country for Old Men" is an extremely arresting and gripping shock-thriller that's surprisingly paired with art-house symbolism that rightfully makes this movie an extremely well-rounded and thoughtful movie.

On all levels, "No Country for Old Men" is outstanding. Cinematography is rightfully picture-perfect and marvelous. The cast all across the board are phenomenally superb. Javier Bardem -- easily surpasses the complexities and interest than Heath Ledger's Joker. YES I said it. And wow, the screenplay is extremely simplistic but richly innovative. And who could blame the direction? It's apparently obvious that there are disciplined and deft hands and minds that directed this masterpiece.

"No Country for Old Men" plays out much like a R-rated silent movie; viewers are expected to observe the settings and expect to make predictions on what the character's are thinking at the moment and seeing them played out afterwards. It's an incredibly immersive approach that truly sucks viewers in, whereas 95% of other movies nowadays must explain the character's actions through obviously blatant dialogue that is purposely placed there ONLY to fill in the audience's questions. It's truly unique and captivating to have such involvement with a film. For this alone, "No Country for Old Men" is a must watch.

Man, when the action racks up, its brimming with rich and dark tension that's extremely nerve-racking. It exudes tension. You're gonna be sitting there at the edge of your seat, frozen and waiting for the character's next move, all in the dark shadows of silence. This is something to behold: There's no music to be heard throughout the entire experience but yet the pacing is absolutely perfect. You're there at the scene of the crime. You won't look at thrillers the same way again. Easily one of the best scenes in cinema history is the gas station scene. 

As you can probably tell, "No Country for Old Men" is a dark, silent, and mesmerizing movie. "There are no clean getaways". After watching this movie, that's for sure -- I ain't gonna see movies the same way again. "No Country for Old Men" is a masterpiece.

No Country for Old Men is a modern day classic, but even so, it certainly is flawed. I'll start off with the good. The movie creates suspense and tension unlike anything else I've seen in recent memory. The best scene comes to mind with Josh Brolin sitting in his hotel room waiting. Ridiculous. The film also has extremely good acting. Tommy Lee Jones is perfect for a movie like this and he plays the role of a grizzled Sheriff extremely well. Javier Bardem has so many menacing looks in his face that you truly believe he is deranged. Josh Brolin rounds out the pack with some badass looks and badass style that just make his character feel like a god. The bad is the story. I understand how Moss falls into the money and Anton wants it back, but why is there so much dialog for a film that is about something simple. The movie tries to explore why Anton is so psychotic, but never reaches a conclusion or every really explains anything in the slightest. Bell also has nothing really important to add to the movie, regardless of how well Jones does act. There is some humor in the madness of Anton, though, so that sparks up a few dull spots. The action is also pretty tight with one shoot-out on a dark street coming to mind instantly. This is definitely a multi-layered movie, something that requires multiple viewings, but one cannot deny that the story is ultimately flawed. I still recommend this film wholeheartedly.

I watched this film and absolutely loved it. Directed by Ethan and Joel Coen, the same guys who directed Raising Arizona,  but where RA was funny and slapstick, NCOM is dark and brutal. 

Everything takes place in 1980s on the desolate plains of West Texas. The film  follows Llewellyn (Josh Brolin), a good old boy and ex-Vietnam vet, as he stumbles upon the bloody aftermath of a drug deal gone bad. Exploring the site he finds a satchel, guarded by a dead guy, filled with two million dollars and decides to take it. However, unknown to Llewellyn, the bag has a transponder in it and Anton the killer has the tracking device and will stop at nothing to get the money back.

Behind them both is the small town's aging sheriff, Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), who besides struggling with his growing disillusionment in mankind is hoping to get to Llewellyn before the killer does.  

Pristine editing along with unforgettable dialogue and gritty, realistic character portrayal made this film, imo, truly one not to be missed. A+

This movie gets 4.5 stars because:

1. A very interesting story with a lot of suspense and suitable violence. It's a rough-and-tumble plot with interesting complexity.

2. The gas station scene toward the beginning makes the movie worth watching by itself. It made me both laugh and cringe. The reasons for the laughter are obvious; the cringing came from watching the poor sad sack cashier quickly paint a chilling picture that deeply illustrates the vast wasteland of nothingness his life had become. It's as if he's already dead, he just doesn't know it yet, and letting him live was worse torture than anything Chigurh could have done to him. Full half-star for that.

3. Good acting all around. Chigurh is an anti-social, sociopathic prick who makes an excellent assassin stalking Moss, who appears to be a down-home yokel-type who likes hunting, but as we get to know him, we realize that he's got above-average intelligence which he focuses on his skills as both hunter and prey. Following them is Sheriff Bell, the kindly Sherlock Holmes of the Texas desert.

4. Visually stimulating. I really liked the wide-open scenery. The desert scenes were beautiful, and a lot of the shots of mundane cars (see below), buildings and everyday items are beautiful in their banality.

5. It's as if they rounded up the boxiest, ugliest cars from the 70's and 80's, like this late 70's Ford Granada: http://www.imcdb.org/vehicle_117259-Ford-Granada-1976.html?PHPSESSID=4f50d095fb93180f56504f83f244cfd2. It's so ugly, it's beautiful.

6. My only complaint is that the ending was a little confusing. I don't understand the significance of the last scene with Chigurh, and the Sheriff's dream discussion borders on 'foo-foo' or 'artsy'.

7. Fewer points for no nudity. Sure, it's mostly dudes, but would have hurt to have shown a little more of Mrs. Moss? Anyway, don't get me wrong, here. Kelly Mcdonald's acting was on par with everyone else's, and giving her more screen time could only have made the movie better.

After stumbling upon the aftermath of Mexican drug deal gone horribly awry, welder Llewelyn Moss thinks nothing of claiming the money involved in the intended exchange for himself. Soon enough, a sociopathic killer by the name of Anton Chigurh is hot on his trail, determined to both retrieve the small fortune in question and kill any and everyone that gets in his way. As this hunt continues, another is slowly getting underway as local sheriff Ed Tom Bell leads an investigation targeting Chigurh and (hopefully) his eventual capture. With Moss struggling to keep one step ahead of the deranged killer at all times, he must in turn employ all of the skills he's accrued throughout his life to do so, at least until Sheriff Bell completes the task at hand. This in mind, [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] is the Coen Brothers' superbly intense adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel of the same title.

Given the source material, it's safe to say that the Coens really had their work cut out for them with this one. Lucky for us, what the Coens have crafted is indeed a cinematic masterpiece, complete with a neverending supply of both mounting tension and, to some degree, a satisfying conclusion as a result of it all. The film's structural framework is mostly to blame here, always allowing us to share the feelings of dread that wash over Moss at various intervals due to its excellent pacing, despite the obvious lack of a musical score; this film doesn't need one, I assure you.

Even more impressive are the performances put forth by a majority of the cast, more specifically that of Javier Bardem in his chilling portrayal of Chigurh, earning himself a much-deserved Oscar in the end. Yeah, I know, it sounds redundant, but to be perfectly honest, I also thought the rest of the cast held their own just fine. Seeing as how all three central characters share very little screen time, I consider each of them responsible for keeping me thoroughly entertained whenever they make an appearance. Having said this, Brolin and Jones are just great in their respective roles, and even Stephen Root and Woody Harrelson provide ample entertainment, all thanks to the Coens' nearly flawless writing and directing we've come to associate them with.

In the end, it's hard to deny that [i]No Country[/i] is anything short of perfect. Oscars aside, the Coens never fail to impress, and this film is definitely no exception. Hell, I'll even admit that this review doesn't even come close to doing it justice; it's better to just see it for yourself, providing you somehow haven't already. With simply flawless performances, equally exceptional writing and directing, and even some above average cinematography, I feel it's safe to say that this film is very deserving of all of the praise it's received and then some.

It is neither one I would place in my hotspot "favorite films" simply because I took what I needed take from it, there and then. 

Its remarkable quality lies in the sheer literary breadth of one man's quest to re-capture his dollar. The Texas lonely ranger feel, is created through the lense the Coen's shot it through - a moody, eery feel throughout, the cat and mouse game winds up finally admonishing the guy who stole the cash and could only spend it on bought skirts off the back of men believing him to be a regular Joe. Justice? Maybe, and tartly achieved by a psychotic serial killer who is hunted down unsuccessfully by Harrelson and TLJ's "cannot be caught, cannot even be beaten by the brilliance of Brolin" suspect. 

Whilst you could be forgiven for your preoccupied brooding - there is a great deal of violence and graphic wounds - you would be silly to miss the sense of comedy and the timing in which TLJ employed with some cracking one liners. 

It is indeed a mess. And if it wasn't a mess, it was sure as hell a good build up to one. 

But then mess is what the Coen brothers do best. And whatever you do, try not to fathom a meaning - that would spoil all the fun.

Having squandered their talents on both Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers, the Coen Brothers mark a real return to form with No Country for Old Men. This faithful adaptation of Cormac McCarthyâs novel takes the existential darkness at the centre of his work and blends it with everything we love about the Coens: distinctive characters, surprising plot developments, black humour and striking visuals. It is easily their best film since Fargo, and an important piece of modern filmmaking.

As a Coen Brothers film, No Country for Old Men succeeds for two key reasons. The first is that disposes of all the overbearing quirkiness and kookiness which have lumbered their films (or at least their comedies) since The Big Lebowski. Watching The Ladykillers in particular, you get the impression that the Coens are more concerned with stuffing the screen full of irritatingly zany characters with outrageous personality traits than they are in constructing something more coherent and insightful.

Make no mistake, the characters in No Country are interesting and unique, but they are also a million miles from quirky. Listening to the dialogue, you never get the sense of the Coens being too clever to amuse themselves. The characters are distinctive, with their own voices and verbal tics, but save for a few fleeting moments you are never irritated by them. And unlike There Will Be Blood, where all the other characters were dwarfed by the almighty Daniel Day-Lewis, here there is balance to the cast, with all three leads firing on all cylinders.

The second key reason for the filmâs success is that it represents a return to the stripped-down form of Blood Simple. Like their debut, No Country takes a relatively simple event (the theft of a bag of money) and uses it as a springboard towards darker events and deeper analysis. The Coens have always been fascinated by individualsâ relationships with money, and most of their films centre around some sort of financial motivation: think of Paul Newman wanting control the company in The Hudsucker Proxy, or William H. Macy trying to use ransom money to pay off his debts in Fargo. The drug money in No Country is a similar device, although its existential implications are perhaps more complicated than in some of their other films.

The central theme of both the novel and the film is that the world has changed; there is a new kind of evil which has emerged seemingly out of nowhere, and none of the conventional methods of dealing with crime seem to have any effect on it. The fact that there is almost no soundtrack hints at the filmâs existential nature â the events which occur are very real, but hardwired into their reality are deep questions about meaning, purpose and reason.

The film is similar to The Dark Knight in the lack of any real back-story surrounding its villain; what we do know about them is conflicted, whether itâs the Jokerâs multiple stories surrounding the origin of his scars or the confused police reports surrounding Anton Chigurh. But whereas the Joker actually takes gleeful pleasure in the chaos he causes, and hence has some kind of twisted reason for doing what he does, Chigurh has no such reaction. He has the mechanical air of the Terminator in his pursuit of Llewellyn Moss, coupled with the sepulchral omnipresence of Death in The Seventh Seal and the other-worldliness of David Bowie in The Man Who Fell to Earth. He is cold and steadfast in his goal and methods, but is also willing to acknowledge the role of gamesmanship and chance.

Chance plays a huge part in No Country, and is bound up with the existential or nihilistic morality of the piece. The central conceit of the story is that the great horrors which unfold are not happening for any kind of reason; they arenât a punishment from God, the foreshadowing of any kind of apocalypse or a result of social decay. Everything surrounding the chase, the murders and the attempted escape to Mexico all occurs because Moss just happened to be in a certain place in a certain time. The Coens are showing us that great evil is all around us, all the time. There is no way to truly escape it: you just have to pray you made the right choice.

The now-famous coin toss scene is a great illustration of this. When Chigurh asks the dopey attendant to call the toss of a coin, he speaks about him standing to win everything. We know from previous scenes what Chigurh is capable of, and hence we know that the attendant stands to lose everything as well. Much of the sceneâs dialogue is Chigurh playing with the attendant: the first half of the scene is a classic Coens trope of unpicking unnecessary small talk in order to question peopleâs motivations. The comments about it being âjust a coinâ, and the coin having made a journey over 22 years to be to this point, are partially facetious, but the latter also hints at the element of chance. Both the coin and Chigurh just happened to have turned up here, and both are now the balance in which his life hangs.

For all our comparisons with The Dark Knight and other Coen works, the film which No County most closely resembles is The Hitcher. Javier Bardem is clearly drawing on Rutger Hauerâs performance in that film, especially in the interior scenes where he emerges from the shadows with murder on his mind. There is the same sense of great horror lurking in the landscape, that sense of unending pursuit by a force we cannot hope to rationalise. And like The Hitcher, No Country has a lot of scenes in motels, those most temporary oases which quickly become anything but calm. The scene where Moss and Chigurh are on opposite sides of the same wall, trying to claw at the bag of money in the air vents, is one of the biggest nerve-shredders in recent memory.

One sad consequence of this chance-based thesis is that the film has less character development than we might expect. The fact that Tommy Lee Jonesâ character is always one step behind the violent events means that he gets a little marginalised, and hence some of his comments about lawlessness and evil remain sadly unelaborated. Unlike a lot of Coens features, there isnât much to laugh at either: there is some black humour throughout, amid irritating bits of goofiness with Mossâ mother-in-law, but most of the time you find yourself wincing rather than laughing in the presence of all that blood.

On the other hand, the fact that there is so little reason for these events give the film a cyclical feel, which somehow seems to make more sense. The fact that Chigurh is involved in a car accident soon after killing Moss is both ironic and a continuation of chance; it didnât happen because he deserved it, it happened because he was there at the wrong time. Likewise Sheriff Bellâs speech about âcarrying the fireâ â a phrase also uttered in The Road â reflects the sense of perpetual despair in this world. Bellâs dream centres around the hope that the world will become a better place through dedication to what is right. The fact that he awakes soon after, and can barely remember the first dream involving money, shows that he is both despairing of reality and reluctant to admit his own failings.

Both as a standalone piece and as an adaptation, there can be little doubt that No Country for Old Men is a fine piece of work. It is a better film all round than There Will Be Blood, both in its characters and in the way its substance is channelled through them, and it is a more satisfying adaptation than The Road. There are several small problems with the finished product: some of the dialogue is difficult to understand, and there are little sections in which the sense of dread is compromised by concessions to obvious humour. But as a Western, and as a thesis on the nature of chance and evil, it deserves to be widely admired.

Days after seeing it, I am still haunted by No Country for Old Men. There is just something so effectual and uncompromising about it, that mere words will only begin to skim the surface of the cinematic excellence on display.

At its most simplistic, the film is a game of cat and mouse. The mouse here is Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a hunter who stumbles upon two million in cash after a drug deal gone wrong, and takes it thinking nothing of it. He tries to cover his tracks, but ends up letting the group looking for the money, figure out his identity. The cat is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a hit-man hired to find Moss and the money. But Chigurh is unconventional at best; he also happens to be bordering on mentally insane. And another man, a law man this time, Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), is on the trail of both men as they criss-cross around Texas.

Right up until its dÃ©nouement, the film is simply brilliant. Taut and thrilling, it blows right through the majority of its two hour runtime with ease. Even during moments of slowing down, the film stays right on track and never feels like it has run its course. It engages even when it appears that nothing is happening. The Coen Brothers truly crafted what appears at first glance to be a masterpiece, even if it is their first real shot at something that is not indelibly and inarguably their own. Even without reading Cormac McCarthy's novel, I know that the Coens have done it justice, even with their bitterly twisted and dark sense of humour scattered throughout the film.

But all of that comes to a standstill as the film concludes. The last twenty or so minutes feel like hours as the film wraps itself up, and it almost feels like these scenes belong to another movie entirely (one that borders on being pretentious and monotonous). I realize now that McCarthy's novel probably ends the same way, but it does not help provide closure to the fact that the movie is so break-neck paced right up until this happens. Its brilliance is shattered by what looks to be a series of tattered events thrown together to provide closure for all of the characters, alive or dead, and for its audience. It speaks volumes to the film's title, but it just does not feel satisfying compared to the rest of what we saw. Even with its enigmatic devices at play, I still cannot come to terms with how the film closes. It does haunt, and in a way, it may prove to be a significantly stronger ending as time rolls on. But as it stands now, it just feels weak.

What is also a bit of a surprise, and only seems to appear as the film concludes, is the music. It is not so obvious at first, but the majority of the film is audibly shown with just the sounds the characters make and no background music to speak of. This element is brilliantly used, as it helps intensify every situation and makes the film downright terrifying in some cases. It just helps truly make the film come together, and only helps establish the quick pacing even more so. It was definitely a surprise, and one that will probably help the lasting impact of the film become even stronger.

The lush and bloodsoaked visuals also help to define the film. Despite the film taking place mainly in deserted areas, or the desert itself, the camera manages to capture just the right essence of what the writing and acting is conveying. The isolation and the terror almost become characters themselves through these visuals, and are sure to be recognized as the award season rolls in.

The film's acting is also very well done. Brolin anchors the film and even when it is just the audience reacting to his attempts at saving his life, he manages to deliver the best performance of his career. He breathes life into Moss, and truly brings a sense of pathos to the character. We feel for him and his greedy mistake, and as he develops into a man unwilling to go down without a fight, he only manages to up the ante for himself countlessly. Jones, as the law man stuck on the fringe of every event, also does very well for himself. Most of his work is simply delivering dialogue, but it is delivered in such a fashionable sense that you feel like he is speaking to the bigger picture of things, and not just himself. I would have liked a bit more development in his character, but what little there is helps his performance greatly.

Supporting turns from Woody Harrelson and Kelly Macdonald are also done well, but are overshadowed by the main cast by both Brolin and Jones.

And even more of an overcast is Bardem as the ruthless Chigurh. He absolutely nails this character down to his very bones. If anyone is merely toying with the idea of seeing the film, it should be specifically for Bardem. His performance is calculating and plagued with petrifying silence. When he chooses to talk, his words sound like they are being given by the essence of evil. This is a man with a plan, but it is one that only belongs to him. His enigmatic presence is developed throughout the film, and never once does it feel particularly appropriate to understand where this menace comes from. Watching him on screen is a jolt to the heart, and will go down as one of the best performances of the decade. His terrible hair only helps to make his character that more scary and formidable.

No Country for Old Men is one of the best pictures of the year, even if it is flawed. Its brilliance and lasting impact with leave you haunted.

No Country for Old Men, the darkest, bleakest film yet by Joel and Ethan Coen, manages to be both an unsettling thriller and a statement of great concern for the future. As has always been the case with Joel and Ethan's work, the movie is cast to perfection. Javier Bardem's personification of psychotic evil fills the screen with an unflinching power -- it's as impossible for the audience to look away from him as it is for his victims to get away from him. Josh Brolin plays the Vietnam veteran who kick-starts the plot with a perfect mix of practicality, durability, and quiet desperation. You can believe he's seen enough horrible things during his years in the military that he's willing to go toe-to-toe with someone as malignantly evil as Bardem's remorseless killer. As Brolin's wife, Kelly MacDonald serves up a vivid, tragic character with very little screen time. Tommy Lee Jones centers the film as a Texas sheriff who notes early on that the old-timers never even wore a gun on the job. He longs for a time like that, and although he is a man not prone to emotional displays, his recognition of the horrors he sees registers in unmistakable ways.

The Coens build the tension like the masters that they are, often going minutes without any dialogue. What sets this film apart from their others is the refusal to let their comedic impulses temper the material. As always, they get chuckles out of the Texas patois, and there are characters on the fringe who stick in the memory because of their distinct speaking patterns. However none of the levity breaks from the remarkably serious intentions or tone. The one scene Kelly MacDonald shares with Bardem echoes the final confrontation between Frances McDormand and Peter Stormare in Fargo. But where that film offered some hope, some sense that there is an essential rightness in the world worth preserving, No Country is about the world we know coming to an end. Those expecting a pure genre film may be taken aback by the final act, especially since the first 100 minutes rank as an expert thriller. Consisting primarily of extended dialogue scenes, save for one last shocking act of violence, the closing passages of the film underline the themes that Jones' character lays out in the movie's opening voice-over. In Fargo, Margie grieved because she realized not everyone has the simple decency not to kill. No Country for Old Men is an expression of mourning for a world that seems to have lost any semblance of decency or order.

"It can't be reasoned with. It can't be bargained with. It doesn't feel pain or remorse, and it absolutely will NOT stop until you are dead". These are the words uttered by Michael Biehn's character in the original Terminator film when describing the utter futility of trying to outrun the title character. They could, however, also describe the pointlessness of attempting to escape Javier Bardem's Anton Chigurh; the flesh and blood but no less ruthless killing machine in No Country For Old Men.

With his Spanish accent, weird hairstyle, vacant stare and propensity for dispatching his victims using slaughterhouse equipment designed to kill cattle, Bardem is absolutely mesmerising as the cold-blooded killer. Whenever he is on screen, the tension is almost unbearable as nobody seems safe from his flippant disregard for life. That Bardem portrays such a terrifying character so well, only serves to highlight the performance of Josh Brolin, the object of Bardem's bloodlust. In what amounts to an elaborate chase movie, Brolin's Llewelyn Moss's desperate attempts to escape are riveting. Although a Vietnam veteran with well-developed street smarts, he is no match for the hitman on his tail.

Tommy Lee Jones once gain effortlessly play the craggy, world weary cop trying to make sense of the trail of bodies in Bardem's wake but as an actor he is in danger of retreading old ground. Since the success of his Oscar-winning turn in The Fugitive, producers have been keen to cast him in similar 'wise hunter' roles with his performances in US Marshalls, Double Jeopardy, The Hunted and In The Valley Of Elah providing ample evidence of his apparent reluctance to stretch himself.

Kelly MacDonald buries her Scottish accent under an authentic Southern drawl as Moss's waif-like wife who is drawn into Bardem's sights despite her seeming innocence. Woody Harrelson also briefly appears as a cocky fellow hitman whose arrogance you know won't serve him well when he comes up against Bardem's Chigurh.

No Country for Old Men adalah film crime thriller yang diadaptasi untuk layar lebar dan disutradari oleh Joel dan Ethan Coen. Diangkat dari novel karya Cormac McCarthy dengan judul yang sama.  No Country for Old Men berkisah tentang karakter manusia dalam menjalani pilihan jalan hidupnya.
Cerita dimulai ketika Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) yang sedang berburu di pedalaman Texas, menemukan mayat-mayat yang bergelimpangan diantara tumpukan obat bius serta tas berisi uang sebesar 2 juta dollar. Pilihan Moss yang memutuskan untuk mengambil tas berisi uang itu untuk dirinya sendiri, ternyata adalah pilihan yang salah, yang kemudian akan mengubah jalan hidupnya. Pilihan ini membawanya keserangkaian peristiwa yang mengenaskan. 
Berdasarkan alat pelacak yang berada didalam tas uang tersebut, seorang pembunuh bayaran psikopat yang sangat sadis dan dingin, Anton Chigurh (diperankan sangat menawan oleh Javier Bardem) melacak keberadaan Moss yang melarikan diri.
Pelarian Moss dan pengejaran Anton, mempertemukan mereka dalam drama kucing dan tikus yang sangat menegangkan ditengah kesunyian gurun Mexico. Sementara itu Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) yang menemukan mobil Moss di tempat kejadian, berusaha menemukan Moss dengan maksud untuk menyelamatkan nyawanya dari ancaman Anton. Bagaimana akhir kisah yang mencekam ini, akankah Sheriff Bell dapat menyelamatkan Moss dari kejaran Anton?
Sebenarnya cerita semacam ini sudah seringkali diangkat, seperti yang terakhir film Love Lies Bleeding. Tapi tema yang sederhana ini di tangan Coen bersaudara menjadi berbeda dan berkelas. Seperti film-filmnya terdahulu Fargo, O Brother, Where Art Thou?, Raising Arizona serta The Big Lebowski.
Dalam ajang Academy Award 2007, film  No Country for Old Men ini menyabet 4 penghargaan Oscar dari 8 yang dinominasikan, termasuk didalamnya sebagai Best Picture, Best Director (Joel dan Ethan Coen), Best Supporting Actor (Javier Bardem) serta Best Screenplay-adapted (Joel dan Ethan Coen).

Written and Directed by The Coen Brothers

Here stands a West Texas crime saga that stands up as the Coen Brothers' greatest accomplishment since they stormed filmdom with their debut Texas noir 'Blood Simple'. From the opening shots of the empty Texas landscapes, a drama unfolds in these barren fields when Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) comes accross the aftermath of a brutal shootout while out hunting. He discovers what inspired the shootout, a pick-up truck bed full of heroin. After carefully surveying the scene, Llewelyn sees a trail of blood and using his tracking skills follows it to the shade of a tree, where he finds the last man standing from the gun battle, only this hombre is sitting, and he's dead as a doornail. Here Llewelyn finds $2 million in a black satchel. He makes a choice to take the money and head home, without notifying anyone of the gruesome scene he came accross.

Llewelyn lives in a small town in Terrell County Texas, whose Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) and his deputy finally come accross the murder scene. Sheriff Bell is able to deduct what has happened at the scene, and upon discovering Llewelyn's truck, Bell knows that Llewelyn's life is going to be on the line if he's the one that ended up with the money.

Right from the opening the audience is introduced to the 'ultimate bad ass' Anton Chigurh, who makes a murderous escape from the local law enforcement. The camera follows Anton on his spree, as he slowly tracks the money, and sure enough Moss, brutally killing anyone that he comes across. His cold, complacent, and darkly humorous attitude is a telltale sign that killing is his profession, and he does his work well.

No Country For Old Men is thin on plot, but rich in subtext. It's about the difference, and the connection, of choice and chance, or as some would call it, fate. In one instance, Anton stops at a small roadside gas station, and through words alone, he plays a deadly game with the owner. The owner has lived in this town his whole life, and as is revealed in the conversation with Anton, he came to own the place by chance of marriage. The two men battle through conversation, and Anton makes his intentions clear, but being a man of certain principles, he makes it obvious that coin toss is the only thing that could save the man's life. As chance has it, the man lives.

To reveal any more about the plot would be a disservice to potential viewers. The rest of the film is part cat and mouse chase between Anton and Llewelyn, part philosophic questioning of the lives the characters involved lead. Sheriff Bell talks with various characters about how he came into the life of law enforcement, and he muses on how his life would have been different had his choices been not the ones he made.

Llewelyn's life also takes turns based on the life he has chosen since taking the money he found. He is forced to live an existence that, in afterthought, is not worth the money he's taken. Still, he accepts and lives with his choices, and makes further ones that will impact his and his wife's futures.

The Coen Brothers are modern masters, and in many sequences throughout the film, they display a Hitchcockian ability to create tense scenes where the viewer is completely aware of what has led these characters to these instances of chance and fate. In some cases, characters live purely because they are not essential players in the drama that unfolds at the behest of the stolen money. Anton makes it clear that obtaining the money is not his only goal. He lives a life of principal, and the final scenes of the movie reveal how he incorporates these principals into his life, and in the end, chance even takes its toll on Anton. He accepts this, as he understands that for every person that left with their life due to chance, could have also had it taken for the same reason. He experiences chance first hand in the final moments of the film, while Sheriff Bell's choices force him to accept what he has chosen, it is too late for chance to save him from his Earthly duties.

Woody Harrelson, Stephen Root, and a broad cast of bit characters also experience the wrath of their individual fates through either choice, or chance, and each of these characters is able to delineate the difference, some of them accepting their fate, others trying to change it. Even when their lives are spared, they are forced to live with the consequences of their actions, or on the other side of the coin, the benefits of their chance escapes.

Even after the stolen money is no longer a part of the drama, Anton sticks to what he knows, and the promises he has made, dire as they may be. These characters all face the internal struggle of their lives in the simplest of terms, from a coin toss, to a husband's wrong choices. A lot of important plot elements in this film are unseen to the viewer, although they are still readily apparent. The point is not seeing what happened, but knowing why the actions took place, and what choices or chances led to their ultimate fates.

Josh Brolin is a Texas good ole boy who knows what he has done, and he is willing to fight tooth and nail to justify his previous actions. Javier Bardem creates the first great screen villian of the 21st centure. Neither character ever recants, never regrets their choices or their paths in life. Llewelyn was aware of his actions when he performed them, as is Anton. The difference between the two men comes down to the choices they made on the type of lives they decided to live. The same goes for Sheriff Bell, who at the end of the film quietly resigns to accept the choices he made in life, reguardless of the fact that they were wrong or right at the time of the doing. This film isn't about what is show on screen, rather, it's about the inner turmoil created in each character by the actions that have happened. There is so much in between the lines of each scene, that second, third, and fourth viewings will be required, not because the viewer missed something, but because there is so much happening in each scene that each viewing will invoke a different reaction and thought pattern of the viewer every time they watch it.

This is as good a thriller as the Coen Brothers have ever made, I dare say it's their best film since Blood Simple, not only because the films are similar in tone, style, and setting, but because each film is a thought, a psychological study of the characters and setting the film is based on. Here is a timeless classic from the Brothers Coen, a fine return to form of moral ambiguity after many years spent on simpler, lighter films. If this doesn't make it onto every person's top 3 list for the year in movies, either they haven't seen it, or they watched a different film than I did today. Quite simply, this is what a masterpiece is made of, one of the few films I think is perfect in every way, shape and form. Must be seen to be believed.

With Tommy Lee Jones on the cover of the film's promotional poster assuming the identidy of a law enforcer once again, people may think No Country for Old Men is a blockbuster worthy material...that's not what you get with the film. The Coen's Brothers oscar winning feature is well adapted from Cormac Mccarthy's dark novel. Tommy Lee Jones gives a great perfomance as the incorruptible policeman in the town, and this is a huge boost for Josh Brolin taking the role of Lewelyn Moss, a Vietnam war veteran who stumbles upon up to 2 million dollars as the aftermath of a drug deal gone wrong. After taking the money, he unknowingly sets off a tripled action cat and mouse chase. Amongst the conflict is Carla Jean played by Kelly Macdonald who deserves credit to be able to stang alongside the powerful male perfomances in this dark film, as well as Woody Harelson as the type of character from the outside world that would provide the character who is doomed to die a chance to live, similar to that of the british agent in The Last King of Scotland or the fellow scholars in The Tragedy of Dr. Faustus. Aside from The Coen's achievements, the best thing of No Country for Old Men is the haunting perfomance of Javier Bardem. While he may seem to be only pulling the trigger and stand there without smiling, there are scenes that reflect his character's psychopathic personality while he kills in cold blood with his evil grin. Not only does Javier Bardem proves that he is versatile from previous films like Before Night Falls and The Sea Inside, he manages to maintain the character's brutality with his dark given cinematic presence and intensify the film as well as redefining the meaning of "relentless". From one landscape to the other, the Coen's large urban atmosphere given from their direction proves to be effective. The only minor drawback to this feature is the lack of music and paste by decision of Joel Coen, but overall, the film is the greatest thriller of the year alongside The Bourne Ultimatum and the most suspenseful adaptation in years.

#7 of the Decade: NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN
The Coen Brothers redeem themsleves after a few truly awful films (Intolerable Cruelty & The Ladykillers) with this incredible, highly violent and well written film about greed, undefeatable evil and unaviodable change.  Javier Bardem won a well deserved Oscar for his portryal of the film's force of evil.

Well stylized, sets the stage well, as well as the editor did a good job at extracting the best from each actor. The Coen brothers made the setting feel very isolated from higher law, they allowed evil to run free and rampant over the dry and dusty Texan country. They still managed to keep the continuity of the situation while having a very irregular chain of violent events take place. Javier Bardem plays the role of a psychopathic killer to a key. This film is filled with artistic subtleties that will likely go unnoticed by the masses in Hollywood demanding more formulated movies and uncomplicated themes that the audiences have become accustomed to, or more so become creatively numb to. No Country For Old Men stayed true to its concept and didn't give in to cinematic techniques that would make it more exciting and easier to swallow for the unsophisticated audiences. Unfortunately films have to pay for this dearly at the box office. Bizarre how films will make less money for producing a better piece of visual literature. My only complaint with this film regards its cinematography, although it still meets the criteria for a good film this film could have had more shots from the air of the Texas landscape but this was probably due to a lack of budgeting towards flying around in a helicopter with a camera all day.

It's a memorable character and it's probably what people will remember from the film 10 years from now. What also comes to mind is how street smart the main characters are and it helps make things more convincing. Although the parts with the sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones) were obviously important (to explain the title of the film for one), I thought they were slow and rather dull (although it's likely a conscious choice to show how it's "not a country for old men" anymore). The violent scenes were short, tense and felt realistic, sometimes skipped altogether. Like the Texas state where it takes place, the film felt desolate and gritty. I should mention that in several places, including the ending, the directors went for the unexpected and/or anticlimactic. I generally like surprises but overall the problem with anticlimax is that it leaves you unsatisfied.

So many great scenes and fantastic performances... such a horrible example of story-telling.  I am fine with slow pacing and minimal dialogue as long as the performances and visuals hold up. In most scenes that IS the case.  But string a bunch together and it bogs the story down.  
Just because a story and its characters are quirky and different, it doesn't mean it is good.  Tone, visuals and the intensity and emotions in each scene are top notch... but please... get to the freakin point... and while you're at it... have one.  I am not one that feels a movie has to spell everything out for you, but it seems certain 'films' are branded as a masterpiece due to some snobbish standard.  It's as if some people don't 'get it' but are afraid to admit it, so they declare the movie a work of art.  If it is obscure and open for interpretation it must be art. Put some crap on a bicycle seat, 'plant' the bicycle seat in a pot with some dry soil, stick it in a museum and now it is 'art'.  If it is up for interpretation it must be art, it must be great.  Look at the movie Adaptation for example, another 'artistic' clunker... tell a film snob you don't like it and they tell you you don't have the mental capacity to 'get it'.  What I 'get' is that original does not equal good.  

Anything can be interpreted as a metaphor for the human condition, life, death, capitalism, the loss of innocence etc etc.  Take the bicycle seat...  What does it say?  Well you could say that it represents our journey through childhood, our formative ('growth') years and how by the time we are adults we shit on our dreams, the journey is wasted, our innocence lost, our trek towards death begins as we fail to water the seeds of our life as we start a new quest for material possessions in our capitalist society.  Oh and I forgot to mention, the piece of crap on the seat is actually BULLSHIT.

Final thoughts on the movie... this is a rare example where the sum of the parts is actually greater than the whole.

No Country for Old Men is a complex, unsettling little movie with a star-making performance by Javier Bardem.  Its not complex in terms of plot though.  The films brilliance lies in its moral ambiguity, in its meditation on life and the role of chance in determining fate.  And there are a number of other, more subtle themes running through the story as well.

It opens with a haunting voiceover by Tommy Lee Jones.  Jones plays Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, a Texas lawman whos grown cynical and wary about the state of the world and the ways people have changed since he first put on the badge.  His voiceover beautifully sets the tone for the story to come.  

We then meet Anton Chigurh, a hitman whos being processed at some middle-of-nowhere west-Texas police station/jail.  The deputy who arrested Chigurh is talking on the phone to his boss, giving arrest details and describing some breathing-tank apparatus Chigurh carries that must be for emphysema or something.  Chigurh carries no ID and is somewhat of a ghost it seems.  As the deputy talks, Chigurh sits in the background, hands cuffed behind him.  The deputy is unaware as Chigurh expertly works his cuffed hands to the front of his body and coolly sneaks up from behind.  

As the deputy hangs up, Chigurh lowers the handcuff chain over his throat.  A violent, disturbing struggle ensues, with Chigurh murdering the deputy, stealing his car and using it to stop a random motorist on the highway.  Chigurh orders the motorist to step out of his car.  Hes carrying the apparatus the deputy had mistakenly believed a breathing device and tells the motorist to please stand still.  The motorist, confused and assuming Chigurh an agent of the law, sheepishly obeys.  Chigurh holds the tip of the apparatus to his head and another violent, albeit more merciful, cold-blooded murder ensues.

The movie then shifts to Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a Vietnam veteran who, while hunting close to home, stumbles on a failed drug deal.  Theres been an intense gun battle and the scene is littered with bodies, as well as several pounds of heroin.  Moss also discovers $2 million in drug money.  Unexpectedly, one of the drug dealers is still alive.  Hes been shot and is clearly dying; hes begging for a drink of aqua.  Moss tells him he has none and seemingly leaves the man to die, taking the money with him.  

He heads back to his trailer and hides the money but keeps thinking of the dying man.  Apparently, unable to deny his nagging conscious, he fills a gallon jug of water and even as he tells his wife (Kelly Macdonald) that hes about to go do something stupid, he returns to deliver the water.  The drug dealers dead though, shot yet again, and here I was reminded of the old proverb that no good deed goes unpunished.  Indeed, this good deed proves quite costly; the people whove finished off that last drug dealer--Chigurh among them--discover Moss, cutting him off from his truck and leading to an intense chase that ends Moss' escape.  Chigurh takes information from Moss truck to track him.  Moss, meanwhile, knowing that the dealers will be coming, returns home and puts his wife on a bus to her mothers.  He assures her everything will be okay and that shes officially retired from her job at Wal-mart.

An intense cat and mouse game between Moss and Chigurh ensues, involving several other players, including a former associate of Chigurhs and a Mexican hit squad hired by the same shady business man who hired Chigurh.  Moss is clearly in over his head and realizes this only little by little, fully understanding the lengths of Chigurhs depravity too late.  He manages to wound Chigurh in the course of the chase but its far from enough to stop him.

Chigurh is a full-fledged lunatic, but a controlled one.  Hes a machine of a man, a former Vietnam vet himself who has no qualms about killing his former partner (Woody Harrelson) and, ultimately, the man who hired him.  Chigurh kills without thought or remorse and Bardem plays him with beautiful nuance; hes cold, calculating and menacing.  At the same time, he displays a subtle, dark sense of humor that lends him an even greater air of menace and a touch of unpredictability.  Hes a man of his word as well; he lives by a code and if he promises to kill you or someone you love, say your prayers--unless of course, you can correctly guess heads or tails on a coin toss. 

I cant praise Bardem's performance enough--especially after seeing him in Vicky Christina Barcelona.  This is a powerful, unsettling transformation.  He goes from psychotic sociopathic killer to Don Juan-type lover with seeming ease.  No Country for Old Men is worth seeing for his performance alone.  But Bardem is by no means the only noteworthy performer here--only the best.  The entire cast is top notch.  Tommy Lee Jones is like a wise old grandfather, looking at the world through weary, haunted eyes, wondering if hes become the proverbial old timer whos lost touch with the job.  And Josh Brolin is terrific as the savvy Moss, an everyman who refuses to give up even after realizing hes in too deep.  Kelly Macdonald is very good as Moss wife, Carla Jean; she gets one of the films most interesting scenes near the end, as she too is forced to face Chigurhs wrath. 

Dont expect any happy endings here.  If you go for the typical wide-release Hollywood fair where boy gets girl, where bad guy gets his comeuppance and everyone lives happily ever after, this isnt a good choice.  No Country for Old Men is as disturbing as it is riveting; its contemplative and grim and an air of melancholy hangs over the entire production.  And yet, the notion that chance determines the courses of our lives as surely as any of the choices we make rings of truth.  Its got a sense of humor too, does this movie, but its very much gallows humor and we understand pretty quickly that Moss and his wife are headed for bad endings; yet were powerless to look away.  

Its not a feel-good experience, but if youre looking for a movie that will challenge you, that will resonate long after the end credits, that will stand up to multiple viewings, No Country for Old Men isnt a bad choice.

A masterpiece. Understated acting, amateur-like cinematography and a simple premise culminate with some of the finest dialogue ever written and most memorable moments ever created to create perhaps the best adaptation possible of Cormac McCarthy`s nearly unintelligible but beautiful work.

To say that "No Country" is a challenging movie is like referring to the 2008 Democratic primaries as simply competitive. The film purposefully lays the groundwork for "cat and mouse" style convention, and then deliberately pulls the rug out from under each of these standards. It was like watching a slight of hand magician who makes things disappear, but never bothers to finish the trick. Javier Bardem was absolutely brilliant as psychopathic assassin Anton Chigurh. I could watch the scene where he nonchalantly sweats an unsuspecting gas station attendant another 100 times and never grow tired of it. Unlike the novel's description of Chigurh as someone "without a sense of humor," I felt the exact opposite. He finds both irony and humor in everyone with whom he comes into contact. Wielding murder like a painter works a brush, he is quick to remind anyone who is lulled into a false sense of security from daily routine not to forget the fragility of life. He considers himself noble in a bizarre way, offering his "victims" an escape from the doldrums of their ordinary lives, by transforming them into some bizarre headline. Bardem exudes alpha male machismo in every scene-stealing frame of the movie. Tommy Lee Jones is also fantastic as an aging sheriff who, although not completely ineffectual, finds himself securely heading up the rear of this dynamic chase. At times, he even seems upstaged by his younger, law-enforcing protégé, adding greater definition to the movie's title. The Coens are masters at taking otherwise mundane landscapes, and breathing cinematic life into them, from a barren Texas prairie, to an unkempt trailer park. Composer John Williams was able to evoke portents of dread with two simple chords in "Jaws."  Similarly, the Coens manage to promote simple popped locks and alligator boots to the status of modern horror iconography. "No Country" forces us to abandon our assumptions of the suspense thriller, and like Tommy Lee Jones's spectator sheriff, just go along for the ride. As with the movies tagline, for both the characters and the audience, there are no clean getaways.

The Coen brothers are at it again, and anybody who is a fan of their films is sure to appreciate this masterpiece based off of Cormac McCarthy's award winning novel by the same name.  The plot of the film is basically a drug deal gone wrong and the consequences that ensue when innocent people get involved in someone else's business. The plot revolves around three characters: Ed Tom Bell (Jones), an aging sheriff as well as the narrator of the film, Llewelyn Moss (Brolin), a quiet working man with a lot of determination, and Anton Chigurh (Bardem), a cold, hearltess, and unpredictable murderer/assassin.  Chigurh, in my opinion, is the scariest and most intimidating villain in the history of film, and Bardem puts on a performance for the ages, establishing himself as one of the greatest Latin American actors alive.  In terms of theme, the film's moral is simply to show how pitiful and pathetic the protaganists, represented by Bell and Moss, are in the face of unrelenting and incomprehensible evil, represented by Chigurh.  While the ending may not be everyone's cup of tea, some may agree that it is basically a summation of the theme of the film, and a good one at that.  All three actors put on all-star performances, and when coupled with great writing, flawless directing, and some of the best cinematography, courtesy of Roger Deakins, the result is an Oscar-winning film.  I can't say enough about this masterpiece, but it can surely be said that No Country For Old Men deserves every award it received, if not more, and is the Coen brother's best film to date.

Here we have an everyday man stumbling upon stolen loot and a massacre scene in the desert. Sound familar? Yep it was an identical premise (and scene) to the plot for The Good The Bad and The Ugly. Only in the GB&U it was the "tip off" of where loot was hidden. Similar theme in It's a Mad Mad mad Mad World and Shallow Grave and many others.

Back to NCFOM and the man on the run with the loot who takes the law into his own hands also has too many cinematic historical similarities with too many other film characters to mention - but you could toss in the likes of D-Fens in Falling Down, Butch and Sundance, etc etc.

Enter the psycho who just kills everyone for the hell of it. Or as the bounty hunter Woody Harrelson says "he'll kill you for the inconvenience" Yep we've seen all these types before also - Arnie, Rambo, Mr Blonde from Resevoir Dogs, etc etc...

Then comes the straight Sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones) who doesn't use a gun if he can help it - yep we've seen this type before - see High Noon, Shane, etc etc. 

So the characters are fairly stereotypical and the plot not the freshest to ever grace the screens. But there is an added dimension, the psycho is in fact haunting the Sheriff and in fact will haunt him forever - this is fairly well done but it is pretty odd. Why? It would have been better and made more sense had the Psycho haunted the couple forever.

Cinematography is excellent, the direction pretty good but on the whole this is just a re-hash with style.

There were a few very stupid moments. Like Josh Brolin waiting for the psycho to come into his hotel room. Josh sits on the bed right in front of the door. Surely the sensible thing would have been to lie down behind the bed or move over to the side of the room to reduce the risk of being caught by the bulletfire. Also in another later scene, the way Josh Brolin entered Mexico pretending to Border Patrol he was a drunk was silly. Only outdone by him re-entering America with few clothes on having escaped from hospital. He tells the Border Patrol guard he's a vietnam vet but shows no ID yet he's gets the all clear to enter. Very silly.

Yet despite all the flaws this movie does work. It does create tensions and you do get caught up in the cat and mouse games. 

There are times when the dialogue is a bit slow and with no soundtrack sometimes it seems and age. Also the dialogue is sometimes difficult to follow because the accents are so thick.

All in all NCFOM is a bit overated but is certainly good cinema and the ending may leave some feeling cheated but at least it is different.

Avec cette adaptation par les freres Cohen d'une nouvelle de Cormac McCarthy, les amateurs de "Fargo" se retrouveront en terrain connu .  Les deux film partagent en effet de nombreux points communs : le traditionnel triangle de personnages (cette fois, le detenteur d'une valise pleine de billets poursuivi par un tueur poursuivi par un sherif), le cote atypique du tueur ou encore, les obsessions qui poussent chacun a aller jusqu'au bout (argent pour l'un, contrat pour l'autre).  Pourtant, "No Country for old men" n'est pas uniquement une simple variation sur le meme theme qui aurait abandonne les plaines enneigees du Minnesota pour le desert texan.  Pour commencer, l'humour y est nettement moins present et lorsqu'il survient, il repose davantage sur de discrets decalages que sur les cliches relatifs a la cambrousse americaine.  Ensuite, si, comme dans Fargo, le civil est avant tout en quete d'une avenir lumineux, le sherif y troque la sagesse populaire contre l'introspection desabusee.  Enfin, on ne saurait trip souligner la prestation de Javier Bardem : son personnage de tueur psychotique et incoherent domine assez nettement l'ensemble et s'impose comme l'un des meurtriers les plus flippants de ces dernieres annees (malgre sa coiffure absolument ridicule!).  Violent, pessimiste et beneficiant de toute la science du cadrage et de la mise en scene des Cohen, le film surprend principalement dans sa derniere partie, ou l'action s'efface au profit d'une reflexion metaphorique sur les motivations et les ambitions de chacun.  La fin reste ouverte, laissant libre cours au jugement personnel du spectateur.  Interessant...mais un peu destabilisant apres pas loin de deux heures d'une traque aussi rondement menee.

No County for Old Men depicts a very similar situation to Fargo, in which an otherwise ordinary citizen ends up at the centre of a bloodbath as a result of money and the escape that it promises. 

But there are some striking differences with Fargo. Here, it is greed for riches, not fear of bankruptcy, that is the driving force: and fleeing with a caseful of $100 bills produces a different experience to the desperate pursuit of money.

Our hero, played by Josh Brolin, is a likeable character with whom we can easily relate. Yet the relentless psychopathic Sugar, played by Bardem, has a stricter, albeit perverted, moral code, in which he adheres to the letter of his agreements, and even shows some compassion by allowing the possibility of escape with the toss of a coin.

In Fargo, the small-town sheriff is a young, shrewd, pregnant woman who succeeds in hunting down the vicious, yet stupid, baddies. No such luck for our sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones), who ultimately takes retirement with a large dose of melancholy.

As in Fargo, the Coen brothers explore, albeit in a harsher light, the futility and contradictions of the human condition. We should pay attention to the short, seemingly unimportant scenes, which are filled with meaning. 

For example, the boy who gives his shirt to the injured Sugar out of a noble sense of helping a fellow human being in distress, refuses to share his $100 gain with his friend, thereby bringing into question both his nobility, in particular, and, in general, the innocence of youth. This is the deeper meaning beyond the amusing dramatic irony of a well-intentioned boy assisting a cold-blooded killer.

Two things undermine the strength of this film. First, it was made after Fargo, so it doesn't seem as remarkable as the earlier film, which confirmed the genius of the Coen Brothers 11 years earlier. 

Second, Fargo was an interpretation of a true story, while No Country for Old Men is an adaptation of a novel. Announcing the film as a true story lends authority and credibility to the depiction of a bleak, depressing moment of unravelling insanity. A novel is a work of fiction, more akin - on the surface - to entertainment than didactic expression.

A select few movies deserve to be called great. Fewer still deserve to be called perfect. No Country For Old Men does. It is utterly flawless from the riveting performances by Tommy Lee Jones and the terrifying work from Javier Berdam to the Hitchcockian direction that stuns too many times to mention (for starters let's take the lack of a soundtrack or the nerve rattlingly paced shootout at the hotel). What Joel and Ethan Coen achieved through this adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel is the definitive statement on our society: this is no longer a country for old men or anyone with a sense of decency. The film powerfully makes the case that as a people we are progressively becoming more insane yet the argument isn't a stale "back in the days things were better" rant. What Sheriff Bell's uncle tells him at the end about the terrible incident eighty years prior strongly makes the case that men have always acted savagely and will continue to do so. And in a stark challenge to realist thinking, the monster they are dealing with is an unstoppable and inexplicable force. How do you reason with someone who doesn't want anything rational? (You can't). When Sheriff Bell wearily wonders if the villain isn't really just a ghost, it hardly feels far fetched or overwrought. In McCarthy's vision it's the truly noble (Sheriff Ed Tom Bell) and the thoroughly evil (Anton Chigurh) who survive. The middling opportunist (Llewelyn Moss) is swallowed whole (there's something distinctly Biblical about that). As good and serious minded as The Dark Knight was, it can hardly compare to the haunted existentialism of the Coen Brother's triumph.

No Country for old men is like a football game
 This is one of the only films I have seen in recent years that plays out in Professional Football quarters. It is not what I would call a 3 act play. It has 4 seperate quarters. I dissect this film this way because I was trying to wrap my brain around what is was I didn't like about the film. What was it that kept this film from A+ status and made it simply a "C" (in my book anyway)?

So I figured that this film had 4 quarters in it. The first quarter was somewhat intriguing where you have a guy, who we don't know anything about except he likes to shoot animals, who finds a whole bunch of dead Mexicans, a Mexican who is near death, and last but not least, a suitcase full of about $2,000,000.00 in cash. Obviously, he takes the money and goes home. Later we start to learn a little more about him. Then we are introduced to the crazy fuck who he stole the money from. Then things really start to get interesting. End of the 1st quarter the score is Pros 7, cons 3.

Quarter 2. Now we have met the so-called protagonist and the antagonist. Though they spend almost no screen time together, the two seem as if they know each other and they know what is between them. This quarter is also very intense. We have an aging/bouring sheriff played by an aging/bouring Tommy Lee Jones introduced and a rouge lawman, played with superb mannerism by Woody "White man can't jump" Harrelson. His screen time is not wasted though it is short lived. Tommy Lee Jones plays out his role as if he was told to channell his classic character Deputy Sam Gerard from "The Fugitive", only he seemed to not relate to the dead pan material and directing style of the Cohen brothers. The Spainard who plays the crazy fuck is also very good as is Josh "The Goonies" Brollin as the welder gone greedy gun totting get away man. The second quarter is close to film brilliance. The score is now Pros 21, Cons 3.

Then we get to half time. Somethings are explained about the crazy fuck and we realize, "Hey this guy is crazy". Or did we already know that. Third quarter starts. Woody is gone. Tommy Lee's character seems to have been forgotten about in the editing room, people are dying in order for Brollin's character maintain posession of the cash, and the Spainard is still crazy. Lots of people die in cool and unique ways. There are shootouts where lots of innocent people get shot, but Brollin still has posession of the cash. "Yey for him". At this point, as the third quarter starts to unwind, I thought to myself, "Ok, who am I rooting for here?" I guess I could be rooting for Brollin only I've seen dozens of ponds get shot over his obsession to keep his measely 2 mil. I could go for Tommy Lee but he's too old and slow and not very interesting. So I decided to cheer for Brollin's wife. Big mistake. (No spoiler intended). The score is now Pros 21, Cons 17.

So then came the dreadful fourth quarter.

This is where the movie went from "Fargo" status to "Intolerable Cruelty" status. It completely falls apart and what was once a gore fest that kept our attention, soon turned into a bore fest that kept me from enjoying one more second of the film. The consistency of the film came to a close and no more dead bodies were shown and no more answers were given. Instead we were stuck with our least likeable character, Tommy Lee's aging sheriff and his excuses for not doing his job good enough. For me, his final monologue where he tells his wife about his dream and how he can no longer be a lawman because he is not up to the task anymore was the excuse that the Cohen brothers must have told the editor when the final cut came out, "We couldn't match the film's first 3 quarters, so we didn't even try". So "No country for old men" is not even close to "fargo". I doubt the series siblings will ever match it. final Score Pros 21, Cons 31
