"Call it. You stand to win everything. Now call it." 

These commands usher forth from a man  who can not fully qualify as a human being. The bodies he leaves strewn behind, swollen by dust and flies, testify to his alien nature. The metallic gas canister and cattle prod by his side silence the ones his coin chooses. He is Death with a bad haircut. He is the bubonic plague in steel-tipped alligator boots. He is Anton Chigurh, the villain of Joel and Ethan Coen's "No Country For Old Men."

Near the end of Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight," a suspended Joker quips to his caped archenemy that "this is what happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object." In the world of Gotham, Batman is the immovable object who stands rigidly for justice, even when justice despises him. He is a superhero, a man who exists only in comic books. 

Anton Chigurh, though, is frighteningly real. An unstoppable force with no immovable object in his path. "No Country For Old Men" is a tale about violence and death and the destruction that fiends such as Chigurh reap on mankind. It is a story of men killing men killing men. And how a local sheriff dreams of the times before, when men were decent, and manners were natural, and life was sacred. Yes, sacred.

The sheriff is Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones). His dad was sheriff before him, like his granddad before him. They stood for tradition and unchanging values. Hmph, Bell scoffs, they had it easy. They don't know what it's like now.

Enter Llewelyn Moss, a man well-versed in the desert terrain he hunts from. He is a Vietnam veteran. Perhaps his experience with war gave him an idea of man's capability for evil. Perhaps he thought he had seen the worst. But Moss is about to find a force that transcends simple categorizations of good and evil. Chigurh will be that rude awakening. 

After Moss finds a briefcase full of money in the aftermath of a heroine war gone bad, he absconds with the cash and attempts to leave the desert town behind. His wife, Carla Jean Moss (Kelley Macdonald), finds out about her husband's plunder, but does not fully realize the gravity of the situation. He wants a better life for her and himself, and a trailer in west Texas just isn't cutting it. So they keep the money. 

But Moss makes a mistake. Out of good spirit, he returns to the desert. He brings water to a wounded Mexican that had begged of it, choking on his own blood, hours before. The man is now dead. Other men approach the site from above, confiscating Moss's truck and the information inside it. Now they know who he is. He is a marked man. Chigurh might be one of those silhouettes on the cliff. We can't know for sure. But, it is wrong to consider him part of the group. He is not a leader, nor is he a follower. He is just himself, and even that is overwhelming. 

The movie is one large chase. Chigurh chasing Moss, who has the money; Bell chasing Moss, who desperately needs protection whether he knows it or not; the easygoing bounty hunter Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) chasing Chigurh, a deadly prize that has so far eluded the self-assured Wells. Therefore, the film is all about motion and movement. Everyone is on the run. And when any one of them stops, tension takes root and unease pervades like a gaseous toxin. No one is at rest, even in the comfort of a motel room. There are scenes here where death is certain. It is irrevocable. Final. These moments are incredibly suspenseful. The conversations between killer and victim are made sickening by the fact that one will die in a matter of minutes and the other will walk out of the door. No blood on the boots.

This is the Coen Brothers' most violent film so far. They have said "No Country" is as far as they will ever go into the action genre. And that is a shame because they have constructed a masterwork here. From the opening strangle scene to Chigurh's sit-down with Carson Wells, we are witnessing unpredictable Coen territory. And it is all riveting. 

I have not read Cormac McCarthy's novel from which the film was inspired, but I have read some of his other novel, "The Road." And I can sense the McCarthy undertone here. The terse dialogue. The silence. The subtle deadliness of Chigurh. The fate of a human in the hands of a coin toss. And the ending scene where Bell describes a dream to his good-natured wife. His father, riding on past Bell through a mountain pass, carrying a horn. A horn of fire that shined like moonlight. That must be McCarthy at work. 

But this is a Coen film through and through. Shadows show the madness of Chigurh hiding behind a door. Moonlight is most of the light we ever see. Silence does not signal rest, but imminent violence. A light flickering, and dying. This could even be called a horror film. It certainly has more scary and suspenseful moments than most horror films these days. 

We also catch a glimpse of Hitchcock here. The shadow of Chigurh's boots on the other side of the door closely resemble the terrifying shadow of Lars Thorwald in "Rear Window." The camera angles from above a gas station also hark back to some of Hitchcock's movies. This is one team of great American filmmakers drawing on the influence of another classic American filmmaker. The admiration is there if you look close enough. 

I have not mentioned until now that Javier Bardem plays the cold Anton Chigurh, partly because the actor completely embodies this villain and becomes him. He gives such a powerful performance that it would not be unreasonable to question if Bardem was actually sane during the making of this movie. He is terrifying, he is incomprehensible, and he is not at all an actor. He is completely the monster of Anton Chigurh. 

Aside from all the suspense and blood and noise these pursuits generate, there are brief moments of reflection. Both involve Sheriff Bell, one with the sheriff of El Paso and the other with a retired lawman named Ellis. They speak on how the world has fallen. One man  says it's all a "dismal tide" what Bell's got on his hands. A tide of evil. And it's just a damn shame the way this country has gone. The other man, named Ellis, used to work with Bell's father back when he was a sheriff. He says the world's going to come down when it will and that it's "vanity" to think it waits on yourself. Quite nihilistic, quite Coen Brothers. 

The fact is that Bell lives in a country that is not his and never was his to own. He was born into it. But it is no country for old men, like Bell, like Ellis, like the El Paso sheriff. It is unforgiving land, and evil rears its ugly head in more ways for every new generation. Violence is king, and death a sick remedy. The flies will keep coming. The bodies will keep dropping. And the blood will keep flowing. It never dies, this tide. At least not in this country. Not in this life.

Ever since their dark debut "Blood Simple" in 1984, Joel & Ethan Coen have commanded an audience's attention. They followed that up with the wacky and kinetic comedy "Raising Arizona" in 1987, proving early on, that they were comfortable in any genre. That hasn't changed over the years but what it does do, is leave you with feelings of anticipation whenever they deliver another film. You just never know what light or dark delights they are going to deliver. This film is the darkest delight they have delivered so far.
 While hunting in the Texas desert, a young mid-west cowboy (Josh Brolin) comes across a botched drug deal and decides to snatch a satchel of cash. Unknowingly, there are bigger things at work here and his foolish decision attracts the attention of a relentless hitman (Javier Bardem) who has been sent to recover the money. As bodies begin to pile in their wake, a local Sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones) has the duty of hunting them down.
 To foreshorten the opening lines of this film and give an insight from the disillusioned protagonist Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, we are told  "... the crime you see now, it's hard to even take its measure. It's not that I'm afraid of it. I always knew you had to be willing to die to even do this job. But, I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand. A man would have to put his soul at hazard. He'd have to say, "O.K., I'll be part of this world."" Sheriff Bell is at a loss to explain human behaviour and the evil actions of people that he has pursued throughout his career in law enforcement. He is the weary heart and soul of this movie and a character that Tommy Lee Jones can do in his sleep. He serves as one part of three characters whose lives explosively intersect. The others include; Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) a foolish young man who doesn't quite grasp the enormity of his actions, which in turn, attract the attention of very  disturbed and dangerous killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) - who makes decisions on the flip of a coin and wields a hydrolic cattle gun as a weapon. Cleverly, the Coens have them sharing very little (if any) screen time and Jones' Sherrif always two steps behind the  aftermath of destructive events.
As always, the Coens are at the top of their game and have a good grasp on this adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel. They capture his recurrent themes; isolation, the passing of time and changing epoch's. In "The Road" McCarthy explored a post-apocalyptic change.  In this, it's the end of the western way of life and despite life-experienced characters, a lack of understanding in the reasons for it's happening. Throughout their films they have delivered consistent moments of suspense. Here though, they outdo themselves with regular scenes of unbearable tension (done without the use of music). The actors are all up to the task and despite Lee Jones and the Oscar winning Bardem receiving most of the plaudits, Brolin also delivers an absolutely solid, low-key performance. No Coen brothers review would be complete without mentioning the sublime talents of their regular cinematographer Roger Deakins. Yet again, his stark and beautiful camerawork compliments the barren landscapes that these characters roam. As always, his and the Coens' vision complete one another. One of the brothers' finest films and thoroughly deserving of its best picture and director(s) Oscar awards.
 If you're aware of the Coen brothers' canon (and most filmgoers are) then combine "Fargo" and "Blood Simple" and this is what you get... only better. A very gripping and powerful neo-western.

Having squandered their talents on both Intolerable Cruelty and The Ladykillers, the Coen Brothers mark a real return to form with No Country for Old Men. This faithful adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's novel takes the existential darkness at the centre of his work and blends it with everything we love about the Coens: distinctive characters, surprising plot developments, black humour and striking visuals. It is easily their best film since Fargo, and an important piece of modern filmmaking.

As a Coen Brothers film, No Country for Old Men succeeds for two key reasons. The first is that disposes of all the overbearing quirkiness and kookiness which have lumbered their films (or at least their comedies) since The Big Lebowski. Watching The Ladykillers in particular, you get the impression that the Coens are more concerned with stuffing the screen full of irritatingly zany characters with outrageous personality traits than they are in constructing something more coherent and insightful.

Make no mistake, the characters in No Country are interesting and unique, but they are also a million miles from quirky. Listening to the dialogue, you never get the sense of the Coens being too clever to amuse themselves. The characters are distinctive, with their own voices and verbal tics, but save for a few fleeting moments you are never irritated by them. And unlike There Will Be Blood, where all the other characters were dwarfed by the almighty Daniel Day-Lewis, here there is balance to the cast, with all three leads firing on all cylinders.

The second key reason for the film's success is that it represents a return to the stripped-down form of Blood Simple. Like their debut, No Country takes a relatively simple event (the theft of a bag of money) and uses it as a springboard towards darker events and deeper analysis. The Coens have always been fascinated by individuals' relationships with money, and most of their films centre around some sort of financial motivation: think of Paul Newman wanting control the company in The Hudsucker Proxy, or William H. Macy trying to use ransom money to pay off his debts in Fargo. The drug money in No Country is a similar device, although its existential implications are perhaps more complicated than in some of their other films.

The central theme of both the novel and the film is that the world has changed; there is a new kind of evil which has emerged seemingly out of nowhere, and none of the conventional methods of dealing with crime seem to have any effect on it. The fact that there is almost no soundtrack hints at the film's existential nature -- the events which occur are very real, but hardwired into their reality are deep questions about meaning, purpose and reason.

The film is similar to The Dark Knight in the lack of any real back-story surrounding its villain; what we do know about them is conflicted, whether it's the Joker's multiple stories surrounding the origin of his scars or the confused police reports surrounding Anton Chigurh. But whereas the Joker actually takes gleeful pleasure in the chaos he causes, and hence has some kind of twisted reason for doing what he does, Chigurh has no such reaction. He has the mechanical air of the Terminator in his pursuit of Llewellyn Moss, coupled with the sepulchral omnipresence of Death in The Seventh Seal and the other-worldliness of David Bowie in The Man Who Fell to Earth. He is cold and steadfast in his goal and methods, but is also willing to acknowledge the role of gamesmanship and chance.

Chance plays a huge part in No Country, and is bound up with the existential or nihilistic morality of the piece. The central conceit of the story is that the great horrors which unfold are not happening for any kind of reason; they aren't a punishment from God, the foreshadowing of any kind of apocalypse or a result of social decay. Everything surrounding the chase, the murders and the attempted escape to Mexico all occurs because Moss just happened to be in a certain place in a certain time. The Coens are showing us that great evil is all around us, all the time. There is no way to truly escape it: you just have to pray you made the right choice.

The now-famous coin toss scene is a great illustration of this. When Chigurh asks the dopey attendant to call the toss of a coin, he speaks about him standing to win everything. We know from previous scenes what Chigurh is capable of, and hence we know that the attendant stands to lose everything as well. Much of the scene's dialogue is Chigurh playing with the attendant: the first half of the scene is a classic Coens trope of unpicking unnecessary small talk in order to question people's motivations. The comments about it being "just a coin", and the coin having made a journey over 22 years to be to this point, are partially facetious, but the latter also hints at the element of chance. Both the coin and Chigurh just happened to have turned up here, and both are now the balance in which his life hangs.

For all our comparisons with The Dark Knight and other Coen works, the film which No County most closely resembles is The Hitcher. Javier Bardem is clearly drawing on Rutger Hauer's performance in that film, especially in the interior scenes where he emerges from the shadows with murder on his mind. There is the same sense of great horror lurking in the landscape, that sense of unending pursuit by a force we cannot hope to rationalise. And like The Hitcher, No Country has a lot of scenes in motels, those most temporary oases which quickly become anything but calm. The scene where Moss and Chigurh are on opposite sides of the same wall, trying to claw at the bag of money in the air vents, is one of the biggest nerve-shredders in recent memory.

One sad consequence of this chance-based thesis is that the film has less character development than we might expect. The fact that Tommy Lee Jones' character is always one step behind the violent events means that he gets a little marginalised, and hence some of his comments about lawlessness and evil remain sadly unelaborated. Unlike a lot of Coens features, there isn't much to laugh at either: there is some black humour throughout, amid irritating bits of goofiness with Moss' mother-in-law, but most of the time you find yourself wincing rather than laughing in the presence of all that blood.

On the other hand, the fact that there is so little reason for these events give the film a cyclical feel, which somehow seems to make more sense. The fact that Chigurh is involved in a car accident soon after killing Moss is both ironic and a continuation of chance; it didn't happen because he deserved it, it happened because he was there at the wrong time. Likewise Sheriff Bell's speech about "carrying the fire" -- a phrase also uttered in The Road -- reflects the sense of perpetual despair in this world. Bell's dream centres around the hope that the world will become a better place through dedication to what is right. The fact that he awakes soon after, and can barely remember the first dream involving money, shows that he is both despairing of reality and reluctant to admit his own failings.

Both as a standalone piece and as an adaptation, there can be little doubt that No Country for Old Men is a fine piece of work. It is a better film all round than There Will Be Blood, both in its characters and in the way its substance is channelled through them, and it is a more satisfying adaptation than The Road. There are several small problems with the finished product: some of the dialogue is difficult to understand, and there are little sections in which the sense of dread is compromised by concessions to obvious humour. But as a Western, and as a thesis on the nature of chance and evil, it deserves to be widely admired.

I can't remember the last time a movie's ending has left me at odds as much as this one did. NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN follows a deceptively simple narrative, but this being a Cohen brothers film, there is always something lurking under the surface-and hat something, as it turns out, is so strange and unusual that it would be wrong to spoil it in this review.

This is about as unconventional as a mainstream Hollywood movie can get, and the Cohen brothers manage to get away with a lot of tricks and unconventional tactics, thanks in large part to the compelling narrative and characters. Something you'll notice right away when watching this film is A. There is no soundtrack and B. There is very little dialogue. While this is unusual (not to mention in sharp contrast to some of the Cohen brothers' previous films), it fits in well with the story that is trying to be told, and I never found myself thinking "wow, I wish there was some music in this scene".

All in all, NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN is a daring experiment that ultimately succeeds. My only complaint is that the ending left me somewhat unsatisfied, but perhaps that might change upon a second viewing.

The suspense, western, drama No Country for Old Men is directed by the Coen brothers and stars Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, and Tommy Lee Jones. The film takes place in 1980 Texas.

	The film starts off with a man, Anton Chigurh (Bardem), being arrested. He is then brought to the police station and the officer who arrested him is on the phone. He is able to get his handcuffs under his legs and then brutally strangles the officer to death and frees himself, steals a police car, kills another person and steals their car. Then it cuts to Llewelyn Moss (Brolin) hunting deer. While checking to see if he hits one he notices an arranged of vehicles in a field. He goes over and sees that there has been a large gunfight and finds a lot of drugs in the back of one of the trucks. Soon he finds a satchel that contains two million dollars inside of it. The rest of the film is about how Moss tries to make it away with the money while being chased by Chigurh and while Chigurh is being chased by a local sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Jones). 

	The screenplay for this film was excellent. It was extremely suspenseful and all the main characters had great depth to them. Anton Chigurh will be a character like Travis Bickle from Taxi Driver that will be remembered for a very long time. Also I thought the ending was very deep, along with the rest of the film. Personally it is my favorite Coen brother film I have seen, but I still have to see a good amount of their films.

	The direction of this film was excellent and it well deserved the Oscar for it. To make a film this suspenseful without the use of music is extremely difficult and the Coens pull it off brilliantly. It is an edge of your seat film for the older generation, not just for the teens like most of the suspense films that come out these days. The Coens have proven yet again that they can get brilliant performances out of their actors. Truly an amazing job in the direction department.

	The acting for this film was as well brilliant. Josh Brolin played the lead and it truly brought him to now become one of the biggest actors in Hollywood. He was a stubborn Texas man that just wasn't going to quit and he was absolutely perfect. Javier Bardem delivered one of the greatest performances of the decade in his role and will go down in history for it. He deserved that Oscar so much that they shouldn't have even nominated anyone else in the category. Jones played his part fine, it just seems that he is a police officer in every movie and it is pretty annoying. This is an excellently acted film.

	Overall I give this film a 9/10, and I have no complaints with it winning the Best Picture Oscar, even though I like There Will be Blood more. I would recommend this one for anyone who likes great suspense films.

This Coen Brothers movie won the Oscar for Best Picture back in 2008, and for good reason too. The Coen Brothers always make excellent crime movies, and the book that they based this movie on was the perfect choice for them.

A sherif and an assasin have one thing in common: They're both looking for a man carrying two million dollars of drug money. The question is: How long can any of them continue with what they are doing until they realize thet they do not have control over their fate? The Coen Brothers love making films about fate vs. choice, and this crime drama emphasises this lesson the most. The main characters all have their own plan. One wants to be the hero sherif, one wants to retire with drug money, and the other is a complete nihilist that judges the fate of people's lives with a coin toss. But they are only human and their fates are a completely unknown, which makes this movie extremely thrilling.

"You Can't Stop What's Coming."

The first time I saw "No Country for Old Men", I'll admit that I didn't think much of it. My rating the first time I saw it was 7/10. But after a second viewing, I've seen it for the amazing, beautifully shot film that it is. It blends Western with Film Noir, and also Thriller, and it all serves to pack a fierce and relentless ride from beginning to end.

Based on the 2005 novel by Cormac McCarthy, and written by Joel and Ethan Coen in a screenplay that is verbatim to the novel. Set in 1980 somewhere in the desolate wilderness of West Texas, Vietnam Veteran Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), is out hunting one day when he comes across the wreckage of a drug deal gone wrong. He scavenges around it, picking himself out a nice sub-machine gun and finding a massive stash of heroin in the back of one of the trucks. Llewelyn is smart and wise to this unforgiving landscape, so he knows that there must be money somewhere. He follows a trail, and comes across a bag full of money. It's a very large find, and he takes it with him. During the night, he returns to the scene to check on a dying man he found in one of the trucks. He is chased by some Mexicans who are watching the site, and he leaves his truck there. A psychotic serial killer/hit-man is sent after him - Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem in a chilling performance). In the midst of all this is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones). Bell is about to retire, and he is dismayed and bewildered to what is happening here as Chigurh follows Moss, and Bell follows Chigurh's trail of murder and destruction; all while he tries to reach Moss before Chigurh does.

One of the things about this film that I didn't like first time around was it's slow pace. But now I realise that this is the key to what makes the violence that happens all the more shocking and random; and we feel like Sheriff Bell in a way as he can't comprehend what is driving these killings and why it isn't as easy as it used to be to find a reason and a culprit behind them.

The three main characters are portrayed by Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem and Tommy Lee Jones. Brolin was perfect as Moss, and he really strikes you as the kind of man who knows the terrain of the country and who is well able to look after himself; especially after two tours in 'Nam. Spanish actor Javier Bardem was a perfect choice to play Anton Chigurh. He is so creepy and evil that he changes the atmosphere every time he is a scene, and he sports what is one of the strangest weapons I've ever seen a killer use in a movie; a captive bolt pistol, that is used to kill cattle. He won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor; a very worthy winner, in my opinion. Tommy Lee Jones doesn't share as much screen time as the two afore mentioned actors, but his presence in the film is felt nonetheless and he was excellent. 

Jones also opens the film with very poignant narration that sets the atmosphere and gives us a nerve-wrecking sense of dread for what is about to come. He also closes the film, with dialog taking directly from the last page of McCarthy's novel. Many people don't like the ending, which is very abrupt, but I loved it, and would put it down any day as one of the best and most heart-stopping endings ever. The last line he speaks as the screen goes black will remain in my mind forever, and I felt that it was a very provocative line when put into regard everything that had happened in the movie. What's very interesting is that these three characters never once appear in a scene together; not even two of them at the same time. But when Moss and Chigurh do during a shoot-out they have, neither of them sees each other once. Symbolic that Chigurh is chasing a man who is like a ghost, and vice-versa, Moss is being chased by a man who is like a ghost.

Woody Harrelson ("The Thin Red Line") and Kelly Macdonald ("Trainspotting") provide two great supporting performances. I particularly enjoyed Harrelson's performance as Carson Wells; a Vietnam Veteran who is sent after Moss by a different party to offer protection from Chigurh in return for the money.

The cinematography is amazing, and there's beautifully shot scenes of the desert. This is all done by Roger Deakins, the cinematographer who shot some breathtaking scenes in the 2005 film "Jarhead". I'll give credit to the Coen brothers for remaining so faithful to the novel when they were adapting it. And after seeing "Miller's Crossing" and being very disappointed with it, this has put them back in my good books and I look forward to seeing more of their movies.

"No Country for Old Men" was a very deserving winner of Best Picture. It's a haunting, violent and symbolic film to the evil that we're all capable of, and to Sheriff Bell, who is the common law man trying to comprehend what makes these men do what they do. 

8.8/10 The Coen's Masterpiece

Like religion and philosophy, the best examples of the Western transcend generations-the current state of politics, mores, and, ironically, popular culture. Perhaps, this is why European cinema (and their longer-standing societies) has seen fit to adapt this inherently American genre to great effect (specifically, Sergio Leone). Though alternately thrilling and tinged with humor, No Country for Old Men, the Coen Brothers masterwork of genius, ultimately presents a bleak and telling landscape. 
 
In this R-rated Western thriller set in West Texas, a man on the run with a suitcase full of stolen drug money (Brolin) finds his getaway hampered by an aging lawman (Jones) and unscrupulous assassin (Javier Bardem). 
 
Every aspect of No Country for Old Men, an adaptation of Cormac McCarthys celebrated novel, rings of brilliance. Through sparse but wholly authentic dialogue, the script expertly captures McCarthys cold unpromising pastoral. Just as with the Coens Fargo (and Andrew Dominiks The Assassination of Jesse James just a few weeks ago), the deft hand of cinematographer Roger Deakins gives as much a starring performance as the principle actors. Neither Brolin, Jones, and Bardem stand apart from each other, simply because each of their unflinchingly honest portrayals are spot-on. It is the Coen Brothers best work, yes, but not just for the beautiful aesthetics that define this frank, humorous and adult Western. Just like a classic work of art hung on the wall of the Met, Prado, or Louvre, No Country for Old Mens perfectly played ending will encourage spirited discussion that will continue long after the popcorn has been digested. 

Bottom line: A modern classic.

This film is both inferior to and superior to Fargo, which will forever be the Coen Brothers' masterpiece.  It is inferior in the sense that it lacks the subtle, macabre humor of Fargo with its quirky characters and uproariously tainted scenes of mayhem; that peculiar Coen Brothers elan and atmosphere glimmers through occasionally, but this film is overwhelmingly oppressive and the atmosphere is morbidly opaque.  This arguable inferiority, however, bleeds into the film's alarming success.  Where Fargo was outrageous, No Country For Old Men is sly, brooding, wide-eyed.  Javier Bardem's performance as Anton Chigurh is horrifying; he, much like Louise Fletcher's Nurse Ratched in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, is an unblinking and totally formidable personification of pure, unadulterated iniquity.  Tommy Lee Jones (marvelous from beginning to end, but particularly brilliant in the contemplative finale), Josh Brolin (also exceedingly gifted), Kelly Macdonald, Stephen Root, Barry Corbin, and Woody Harrelson (shockingly great in only three scenes as the slick Carson Wells) are all beyond criticism. No Country For Old Men has great tension and suspence, with great performances by all the cast; the story gets quite confusing towards the end and the ending left my very unsatisfied.

The films plot (like most of the Coens films) revolves around money and graphic violence. The film starts with a stunning long shot of the empty texan desert. After that we see a man with strange bowl shaped hair due being arrested. We don't know why, he just is. After being taken to the nearest Police station he murders the police officer in cold blood and his face expression while he is killing this officer just says everything about this man, his name is Anton Chigurh. After that rather brillant opening where we see Anton's psychotic ways, we are introduced to Llewelyn, who finds this drg deal gone wrong and this is where he finds the bag of money. The money that this film revolves around. This is Anton's money and you don't fuck with Anton so, Anton is now on the the hunt for Llewelyn. And on the hunt for Anton is Cheriff Ed Tom Bell who is always 5 steps behind. It's basicly just a cat and mouse tale. The way in which the story progresses is through really tense scenes of action and there are many scenes with long stretches of no dialogue, which builds the tension up and makes the acts of violence seem that bit more graphic. I did feel however that the last 30 mins are poorly done and feel very rushed. When Llewelyn is finaly killed he was killed off by charcters of no importance to the story, making the conculison of his story very unsatisfing. Then it focuses more on the Cheriff and his bits of the film are very boring and he seems to be on the side lines for most of the time. The films first 1 and a half are some of the tense scenes I've ever seen but, towards the end, the film seems to want to finish so, the ending is very unsatisfing and can lead to lots of confusion.

The performances by the cast a very well done; Javier Bardem plays one of the most deraged, psycopaths in recent memory; killing in cold blood, with no emotion and his inteligence is staggering. Through out the film he gets wonded and when he gets wonded he tends to his injuries because, going to a hospital will get him arrested and when someone see's him he says to them "you didn't see me". Josh Brolin is also very good; not as good as Javier but, he does his job. Llewelyn's wife is played by scottish actress Kelly Macdonald, in her best performance to date and her most underrated; I thought she was very good and did a fantastic job. I really didn't like Tommy Lee Jones performance, he seems to always have the one expression on his face and it just seems that he is reading it off a card. The acting is still very good but, I thought Tommy Lee Jones was mis-casted, Javier Bardem did deserve his Oscar.

The film moves and a very tense pace and the cinematography really helps set up the desert waste-land of texas. The Coen Brothers direction is also fantastic; it's the way in which the handle the many scenes of no dialogue, the little details and the sound all build up the tension. The script writing is also tight. 

Overall No Country for Old Men is one of The Coen's best films but, like I said I hated the ending and after Llewelyn died the film seemed to drag on a little too much. Not Best Picture worthy IMO, There Will Be Blood should of won that year but, the film is still and tense thrill ride and was one of 2007 best films.

No Country for Old Men is a 2007 thriller film written and directed by the Coen Brothers. Starring Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem and Tommy Lee Jones, the film follows the three leads all on similar, yet different paths. Brolin plays Llewelyn Moss, someone who happened to find a large sum of money. Bardem plays Anton Chigurh, a hitman hired to recover the money, while Jones plays Sheriff Ed Tom, a man who always seems to be steps behind each of the first two characters.

The most prominently featured of the three characters is Llewelyn Moss. He gets the most amount of screen time, as well as the majority of the important moments. Originally shown to us as an "everyman" sort of character, we quickly realize that he is far more resourceful than the average person. Constantly on the run, getting shot, (and hit), as well as figuring out clever places to hide the money that he found, Llewelyn really is far smarter than he looks. This holds true with the man hunting him as well, as he constantly manages to find Llewelyn, as well as determine where people are with relative ease. The sheriff on the other hand, isn't quite that smart. He usually ends up being a couple steps behind Llewelyn, and at least one step behind Anton. An unsatisfying choice, as it means that the three never really get to meet up.

The fact that no real climax occurs is pretty the biggest problem I have with the film. Teased throughout the entire film is the potential encounter of all three men meeting one another. Sadly, this never actually happens, leaving a slight feeling of emptiness after the film ends. There is even a fairly big build up towards the end, but it just kind of fizzles out into nothingness. It almost seems like the Coen Brothers wanted to see if they could outdo the ending of the Sopranos. It's not quite as bad as that, but it still harms the overall quality of the film.

Apart from the ending, the film was really well made. The acting was very good, with each character playing their part nicely. Josh Brolin especially sold me on his character. Javier Bardem plays an emotionless killer, almost reminiscent of the very first terminator. I didn't like Tommy Lee Jones' character quite as much, but pinpointing why is a struggle. It might be due to the fact that his character never manages to figure out easy connections throughout the story, despite the fact that he is sometimes the one explaining them to the audience. Even though I didn't personally like the character, Jones' portrayal of him was just fine, as was the way the film was made.

One of the amazing things about the film was the way it was made. It was shot beautifully, acted well, and the dialogue was quite good. Some very subtle humor was added, and that didn't detract from the serious tone of the film. The dialogue felt real and alive. The dialogue helped bring the characters to life as well. The one problem I did have with it was that there were a couple scenes where it felt like it ran on too long. There were a few times where characters would continue talking about things that really didn't matter, and while it tried to flush out their character, it disconnected more than it immersed. These scenes didn't happen that often, but detracted slightly from what the film was trying to get across.

No Country for Old Men is a film worth watching, but don't be surprised if it lets you down near the end. An incredibly important story shift isn't even shown on screen, but instead off-camera. I'm sure that scene and the ending were made just to generate more discussion on the story than there would be otherwise, but I find it in poor taste. Looking past the ending though, the film is great. It's well acted, has great dialogue, and is shot wonderfully. Add in a better ending, and it is a superb film. As it is, it's very good, and still highly recommended.

No Country for Old Men, this was my first viewing of the Coen brothers. I am deeply impressed, and Fargo is now on my radar. This film uses suspense, a clever plot and extreme violence in one neat package. The films cast also is immaculate, no lead weakness, nor major weak brief characters. 
The plot follows Moss, on a hunting trip he finds a drug trade gone wrong, where everyone, except one almost dead person. He finds a suitcase with two million dollars, and a truckload of heroin. He takes the money, but greed he goes back for the drugs, when he gets there he is attacked. He escapes but they have his plates and know who he is, so he goes on the run, while all this is happening a Hitman or Psychopath (Javier Bardem) is hired to recover the money and kill him. Therefore, it becomes a chase, and Tommy Lee Jones plays the cop following them, but very lethargically.
The plot is very good, while I thought the beginning was slightly muddled and difficult to fully understand all details, it all comes clear as the film proceeds. The plot balance suspense very well and the chase have a non-cliché. The way things are done are really creative, and does not rely on past films. The ending also shows great complexity and challenges the modern day conventions.
The acting was superb, some of the best acting I have seen in this decade. Javier Bardem has been compared to Marlon Brando, while I cannot say that is true, he was fantastic. Although he was good in this film, I fell he needs a film where he can really define himself, like Vito Corleone. The rest of the cast as I said earlier are great. He plays the psycho excellently, and he just does not hold back in the people he kills, well except for the coin. 
Overall, we have a gem of the modern day films. I would not say masterpiece, for it was slightly muddled, and a bit too long. I would recommend to basically anyone who can handle a long film with heavy dialogue.

The very talented Coen brothers shine again in this exciting crime thriller, with three superb performances from the three main actors, Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin and most notably Javier Bardem who gives the best performance in the film as the emotionless hit man.

After Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon a drug deal gone wrong, a stash load of heroin and a healthy sum of $2million dollars, his life is in instant danger as he is being chased by a ruthless hit man Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem.) Anton Chigurh bears an uncanny resemblance to The Terminator.    

The acting is brilliant, Tommy Lee Jones, who is the moral heart of the film, his is usually reliable self as the Sheriff who has a pessimistic view of the state of America. Josh Brolin is great as a resourceful but poor hunter who stumbles upon the $2 million dollars, but it is performance of Javier Bardem that stands out. Bardem successfully portrays a  evil hit man with a devilish calmness while committing these crimes, his voice is always the same no matter the situation, and he walks, following Moss at the same pace, ever so calmly as though he does this every day(Which he most likely does.) He calmly bursts his way onto motel room, madness erupts for the briefest of moments, and then he is back to his calm, emotionless personality. This is terrifying as it is horrible to think that there could be people as merciless and cruel as this. 

The script is also brilliant, a highlight is a scene as a gas station, and each single line is delivered with utter perfection and conviction that you quite clearly know what is at stake in the coin toss. Credit goes to the Coen brothers for this quite magnificent script, but don't forget the performances of the actors involved who help the script reach its full potential.

Roger Deakins outstanding cinematography of the sparse, lifeless desert landscapes relate to the themes that are discussed within the film (and many other films produced by the Coen brothers) Nihilism being one of them the lifelessness of the desert sort of relates to the Sheriffs feelings about the current state of America. Fate is also discussed, with the coin tossing that stakes your life being an example. The permissiveness views of society are a concern of Sheriff Ed Tom Bell as well as the casual attitude towards drugs. Desperation also creeps in as the poor hunter as Moss risks everything to escape with the $2 million dollars. 

No Country for Old Men contains a mere 16 minutes of music (most of that is in the end credits) again the lack of a score increases the bleakness and the feelings of lifelessness of the film.

The film is also suspenseful and the levels of tension run high as Chigurh keeps on locating Moss in isolated motels, also the viewer is in constantly apprehensive to whenever Chigurh will kill the person he is with, and the audience is wondering if he will finally catch up and kill  Llewellyn Moss. The films levels of suspense will even the make the "master of tension" himself proud. The suspense creates a feeling of dread.

However the film had its flaws, the ending was not to my liking, and reading many other reviews many people feels the same way, and also, I really liked the film, but I don't love it, for me it never really lived up to the hype that it received, I'm not denying it's a good film, it's a great film, but for me there was a certain something missing. Other than that I thought it was a cracker. I personally prefer There Will Be Blood (which was released in the same year), the performance of Daniel Day Lewis is outstanding.

Winner of three Oscars (Best Picture, Best Director and Best supporting actor) and nominated for a further two more. Javier Bardem became the first ever Spanish actor to win an Oscar; he is also the first ever Spanish actor to be nominated for an Oscar for Best Actor, which Russell Crowe won.

A film i thought was overrated , until i actually saw it and boy do i have a lot to say about this film.

In rural Texas, welder and hunter Llewelyn Moss discovers the remains of several drug runners who have all killed each other in an exchange gone violently wrong. Rather than report the discovery to the police, Moss decides to simply take the two million dollars present for himself. This puts the psychopathic killer, Anton Chigurh, on his trail as he dispassionately murders nearly every rival, bystander and even employer in his pursuit of his quarry and the money. As Moss desperately attempts to keep one step ahead, the blood from this hunt begins to flow behind him with relentlessly growing intensity as Chigurh closes in. Meanwhile, the laconic Sherrif Ed Tom Bell blithely oversees the investigation even as he struggles to face the sheer enormity of the crimes he is attempting to thwart. 

For Starters , This film is jaw dropping. It amazes me how gritty and haunting the film actually is. It tells a dark story about a man who stumbles upon his own downfall. Josh Brolin potrays a man with not much to live for , and once he finds "the bag full of money" , events that lead him to a hideous fate begin to unravel itself.

Tommy Lee Jones gives a great emtional performance that really changes the way i look at him as an actor. He brings a lot of age and nostalgia to his performance. He clearly has some form of sadness before the events of the film take place , but you don't know what. But never the less , its moving and great to watch yet also tragic.

But The Highlight...Anton Chigurh. Simply a villian of excellence. He cannot be stopped until he gets what he needs. He's quick , quiet , fast and unstoppable. The Performance is unbelieveable and iconic. He shows no emotion when doing the evil things he does and that makes the character more chilling because you don't know what he is thinking. It makes you wonder what he thinks about during , before or after the killings. But never the less , one of the best villians in recent cinema history.

Overall , Coen Brother's best work and by far more than a classic film. Its A Film to be remembered for years to come.

I have have yet to see a film quite as awe-inspiring or as gripping as the Coen Brothers brilliant No Country For Old Men. A neo- noir western tinged with the veins of blackest comedy. Set against the backdrop of 1980's Texas, it centres around Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a welder and Vietnam veteran, who stumbles across a suitcase of $2 million. A chain of violence soon follows as hitman Anton Chigurgh (Javier Bardem) comes searching for the money, while Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) tries helplessly to stop it.

It is a beautiful film to behold, benefiting from the ever-magnificent camera work of auteur Roger Deakins, whose shots of sparse beauty lend the film a sense of tangibility and space. In fact, almost everything about the film is sparse; the music, the dialogue, even the story (to a certain extent). That is not to say that any of it is bad; the silence throughout most of the film, broken only occasionally by the eerie chimes of chinese bells, lends it, like the cinematography, a feeling of tangibility and, during the later stages, a feeling of intense terror.

The exchanges of dialogue are few and far between compared with most movies, but what seemingly little there is, is so air tight that it makes most movies compared with this seem rather second rate. This is, of course, largely thanks to the Cormac Mcarthy novel on which it is based (The Coen brothers were amazingly faithful to the source material, taking most of the dialogue from the book page-for-page). However, it is also due to the great all-round performances from the cast. Tommy Lee's cynical sheriff Ed Tom Bell muses about crime and punishment, and serves as philosophical centre of the film, while the conversations between him and his deputy sheriff Wendell (played by the underrated Garrett Dillahunt) make for some wonderfully deadpan moments. For instance, while viewing the scene of shoot-out, Wendell comments "It's a mess, ain't it, Sheriff?", Ed then replies "If it ain't, it'll do till the mess gets here." referring to the incompetence of the state police. Meanwhile the back and forth between Josh Brolin's Llewellyn and his wife (played by Kelly Macdonald, also underrated) sounds like typical chatter between a real couple:
"Where'd you get the pistol?" "At the gettin' place."

The real stand-out performance, however, is Javier Bardem's Anton Chigurgh. A terrifying, brooding presence whose menacing persona is only increased by his menacing haircut. In one particular scene which showcases his pure psychotic brilliance to its full, Anton walks into a petrol station to pay for gas. He then proceeds to challenge the proprietor to a game of heads or tails, after which the proprietor asks him what he's put forward to win, Chigurgh answers, "You've been putting it up your whole life you just didn't know it." As the conversation unfolds, you begin to realise that if the proprietor calls wrong, Chigurgh will kill him. It is a truly tense moment, one that really makes you hold your breath and when the proprietor's prediction is revealed to be right, you breathe a sigh of relief. Bardem was awarded an Oscar for his role here and it's certainly not hard to see why. His performance is both looming and blackly funny in the way that he seems so at odds with the way other people act and speak, often pointing out how pointless such phrases are, for instance "if that's the way you want to put it" or "you don't have to do this". It is truly mesmerizing to watch.

Another thing that is really wonderful about No Country is just, as touched upon above, how butt-clenchingly tense it is at times. Refering to a scene where Chigurgh is stalking a victim, as usual there is complete silence, save for the sound of ominous footsteps and the heavy breathing of the prey. The hunted man flicks off the safety catch of a shotgun which seems terrifying loud. Not to give too much away, but what happens after will shock you, no matter if you are expecting it or not.

This is just one example of the intense moments that play out during the film and a perfect example of subtle film making at its very best. It's one hell of a ride and by the time the credits have rolled, it will take up residence in your mind and stay there.

I'll be direct - this film had no redeeming qualities whatsoever. Imagine an episode of Looney Tunes played by real actors, with no uppity chase music, and you've arguably got the Coen Brothers' most lackluster production to (dis)grace the big screen. It is, effectively, nothing but a very drawn-out chase scene, executed by Bardem's chillingly murderous character. That's right, the first half of the movie is comprised of this guy running around shooting people down with some sort of modified oxygen tank. I'm not sure what the proponents of this film saw in such a drawn-out killing spree; perhaps it hearkened to ancient Greek drama or something. I've read a good many reviews making such inane comparisons, so nothing too out of the ordinary.

Movies, or any good story for that matter, are like sex - there's a setup, the action builds up and eventually climaxes, and there's a resolution in the end. Typically there is a plot involved in this process. Unfortunately, this film's structure features gratuitous chasing and killing throughout, with a slight dash of plot around the middle. It was something about drugs and money - you know, the cliche story elements directors go to when they're feeling uncreative - but mostly you get to see the main character run around the arid, desert setting like a chicken. 

To make things mildly more interesting (or, as I see it, to completely digress for the barely extant plot), they have Tommy Lee Jones act out the tired role of a grizzled old codger - a sheriff, no less - bemoaning and pitying himself as he recounts his glory days. Surely, the guy comes to be relevant to the main 'chase-and-murder' plot, but of course, only after more chasing. The main character and the sheriff character come to cross paths in a hospital (no, don't care much for symbolism, this isn't a literature class) when the sheriff imparts upon the main character a mission, of sorts. You see, I could go into detail about the plot, but I really don't care to. It's irrelevant, because it's unoriginal (nothing is original about drug money), and if you actually bother to sit through the chase and murder scenes (there's nothing else, not even a soundtrack or a setting change) then you are a sucker. That, or a literature teacher, who enjoys gleaning underdeveloped, unremarkable, and quotidian plots from works with a complete lack of literary style. An utter bore and a complete waste of time.

I decided to read Cormac McCarthys book before watching this movie adaptation, having been a big fan of his more recent novel The Road.  I loved the book and ended up uncertain if I wanted to watch the movie as I it was hard to imagine the Coen brothers being able to do it justice.  Overall though, I was impressed with their treatment of the story, both in following the text closely and in terms of playing out the author's intentions rather than undermining or erasing them.

Having said that, there are some real differences between the two which to me meant the film didn't quite deliver on the story in the way the book did.  Most of these differences probably came from a need to keep the running time down, but personally I would have been happy for the movie to be an hour longer and to follow more of the subplots of the book.  The most important of those differences for me:

â¢ In the book Carla Jean calls the coin toss incorrectly and Chigurh shoots her.  They have pretty much the same conversation in both versions, but in the Coens version she refuses to call the toss forcing Chigurh to see it is he, not the coin, deciding her fate.

â¢ The book explains why we meet Chigurh in jail, saying he permitted himself to be captured "to see if I could extricate myself by an act of will". Later Chigurh describes this as a vain, foolish act.  These facts are not in the movie.

â¢ The first hotel confrontation between Moss and Chigurh is altered in the movie; rather than punching out the lock and wounding Moss, Chigurh takes a key from the murdered receptionist and enters Moss' room, where a hiding Moss takes him captive at gunpoint, so they have a chance to see and know each other. Then Moss runs and the shootout begins.

â¢ In the book Chigurh delivers the recovered cash to a man he's never met before, and a conversation ensues.  In the film it is fairly unclear who Chigurh works for, which makes his character hard to understand.

â¢ Where the film last sees Moss alive heading off to have a beer with a lady who calls to him from poolside at her hotel, the book has a whole subplot between him and a young female hitchhiker, to whom he gives money and advice. He actually dies because he puts down his gun when the Mexicans following him take her hostage.  This was a big part of the development of the Moss character in the book, with it being clear that Moss was loyal to his wife and would not take advantage of the teenager even when propositioned, and afterwards the hanging question of what his wife would think when he was found dead in a motel with a teenage runaway.

Anyway, book versus film aside, this movie features some truly brilliant performances, and is an astounding achievement in storytelling and filmmaking.  Wonderful!

A wonderfully made genre spanning thriller, part western, part noir, part social critique, based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy, this violent tale demonstrates the Coens at the top of their game: the unflinching cinematography presenting the bleak landscape and gore with the same aplomb other films only present the beautiful, the script tight, with no spare dialogue, no unintentional actions. The film is brought to life by a chilling performance by Javier Bardem as the sociopathic assassin, Anton Chigurh whose own occasional brushes with humanity only make him more frightening, as well as an admirable, understated performance by Tommy Lee Jones as a good cop trying to make sense of the mess of the world, ultimately buckling under the pressure and retiring. Josh Brolin, Kelly Macdonald and Woody Harrelson all do admirable jobs in their own right, and Josh Brolin in particular as the semi-protagonist, captures the horror of his situation well, while at the same time remaining emotionally stagnant enough that his eventual fate can be viewed with a detached, secondary gaze.  The artistry here is palpable, it's impossible to watch this film without knowing how excellent it is, and yet at the same time, there is something immensely unsatisfying about it, as the film ultimately brings no real commentary, no satisfaction, and no conclusion to its stories, rendering it a wonderfully made but disjointed film that plays with social critique without following it up, that showcases performances without doing them complete justice, and ultimately leaves the viewer wishing, not for their time back, but for the time invested to have affected them more strongly. Granted, this is, due to the Coen's respect for source material, likely a problem pulled straight from the book, and so the fault is probably not even with the film so much as with the novel, and which would work better if the film were less fictionally bleak and more grounded in sheer realism as a commentary on the woes of reality, but does not work well, due to the weighty Western-Thriller-Noir tones pervading the story.  In the end, this issue leaves the film, while undeniably excellent, feel undermined in its own conviction, as it is ultimately empty and devoid of real insight.

No Country for Old Men is a 2007 crime thriller film adapted for the screen and directed by Joel and Ethan Coen. 
starring Tommy Lee Jones, Javier Bardem, and Josh Brolin. 

It tells the story of an ordinary man to whom chance delivers a fortune that is not his, and the ensuing cat-and-mouse drama, as three men crisscross each other's paths in the desert landscape of 1980 West Texas.

No Country for Old Men has been highly praised by critics.  The film was honored with numerous awards, garnering three British Academy of Film awards, two Golden Globes, and four Academy Awards for Best Picture, Best Director 
(Joel and Ethan Coen), Best Adapted Screenplay and 
Best Supporting Actor (Javier Bardem).

Well, as you can tell, I quite disagree with all the praise this movie has gotten, it's not that I hated the movie, cause I kinda did, but really it was more an expectations thing.

I was expecting so much more from it, instead of the crime thriller premise it promised, you get two-hours or a slow, dull, & utterly boring film.

The main character just stumbles onto alot of cash...the first half of the movie had hardly any talking, it's never explained how or what is going though his mind when he finds it. After finding it, he gets away, but for some reason decides to go back to the crime-scene...so the bad guys can get a good look at them.

Perhaps I will get it or enjoy it more after multiple viewings. Josh Brolin's acting was very bloated and gave nothing to his character, every once and awhile a quick action scene would raise your blood pressure, but that doesn't really qualify as a 'heart-stopping thriller' through out does it?

Javier Bardem's scenes were the only ones I heavily enjoyed, he had the right amount of creepy, mixed with the right amount of down right scary.

Was there even a score in this movie? again, a lot of it was silence, I kept turning up my headphones thinking my speaker died, then as previously mentioned all Brolin did was walk and stare at things, so nothing interesting in both video & audio.

I feel sorry for myself that I didn't enjoy it more, don't freak out, but after hearing about all it's praises...it really should have played out differently in my mind.

Overall 'No Country For Old Men' sadly disappointed me, despite Javier Bardem's role, it just wasn't dramatic or suspenseful enough.

This is, for me, a riveting and unsettling film experience in the best sense. The film was gritty, realistic, and generally intense. The Coen Brothers once again succeed in delivering a bleak and twisty thriller with a typically dark sense of humor. The story is straightforward yet very effective as we follow Llewelyn Moss, a Texas hunter on the run after obtaining money from the scene of a drug deal gone wrong. While the survivors of the drug deal are pursuing him, he must also deal with a psychotic and remorseless hit man named Anton Chigurh. Meanwhile, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell tries to make sense out of all the chaos. 

Josh Brolin is strong as Moss, showing his character's fear as well as his endurance. Javier Bardem is stellar as Anton by portraying him as a man who kills with no emotion whatsoever but shows an underlying complexity to the character. He definitely deserved to win Best Supporting Actor at the 2008 Academy Awards. Jones does very well playing a character he plays best, a deadpan authority figure. Kelly MacDonald is superb as Llewelyn's wife Carla Jean. She and Brolin have nice chemistry in their scenes together especially with their humorous banter. Woody Harrelson is witty as Carson Wells, the bounty hunter also on the hunt for the money but must compete with Chigurh. 

Overall, No Country for Old Men is my personal pick for the best movie of 2007. That is because the Coen Brothers have succeeded in generating suspense and complexity from a seemingly simple story. They do this with ominous cinematography, dark undertones, and by guiding and capturing flawless performances from their actors. In the world of darkly humorous and gory thrillers, I think that No Country is a masterclass.

*** This review may contain spoilers ***


If this doesn't end my year in the top two films of the year then we are in for one hell of an awesome year of movies.

The new film from two of the best filmmakers working today No Country For Old Men shows the talents of the Coen Brothers on top form. After a couple of disappointments (Intolerable Cruelty had flashes of Coen genius but felt more of a Coen imitation than the real thing; Ladykillers had the odd funny moment but was the blandest film the brothers ever made, and there's just no excusing Marlon Wayans!) they knock this violent western drama out of the park.

More in the vein of their superb early mostly-serious efforts Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing (my personal favourite of the Coen back catalogue) No Country For Old Men is a slow-moving, character-driven masterpiece about uncompromising and uncompromised characters. It is very violent and bloody and not always for the squeamish.

Shot through with moments of humour these come, as in life, from real situations and observations so don't be fooled into thinking this will be the serious film with goofy-characters Coens of Fargo. No Country For Old Men is a tough, gritty story.

The unrelenting pace may take its time but you are gripped every moment. This is a thriller that genuinely thrills.

Javier Bardem gives the best performance of his career. And, yes, I have seen The Sea Inside and he in superb in that but here he is simply extraordinary. It is a portrayal of unrelenting evil, of true derangement, of a human being with no shreds of humanity that ranks at the very top of studied film psychopaths. And I say film not movie because this is not a clichéd character. This is not a character whose lunacy you enjoy over popcorn. This is one of the most frightening performances ever committed to celluloid. I felt truly nervous of what was going to happen every time he walked on screen.

Josh Brolin essentially carries the bulk of the movie and he is excellent in a role that challenges him. I have never seen him perform to this level and if Bardem didn't steal the film you'd be talking about Brolin all the way home. As it is this gives him a showcase for his talents that should see him get a lot more attention.

Tommy Lee Jones is used sparingly but to great effect. Sounding more like Michael Parks than ever before his scenes pepper the movie with a wearied view on a world he doesn't really like or understand to great effect.

I did find Stephen Root a little distracting as i have never seen him in a serious role before and he just looks amusing but he is in very little.

Roger Deakins' cinematography is breathtaking as usual and the Coens' script is superbly crafted. There are moments, almost asides from the main plot, that would be superfluous in most scripts and excised in most studio films but which work perfectly in the overall context of the movie as only the Coens can achieve. One scene featuring Bardem in a gas station is up there with the best scenes i have ever seen on film.

I have not gone into the plot here because I saw this film having not read Cormac McCarthy novel and knowing little other than the basic log-line - a man out hunting comes upon a scene of dead bodies, guns, drugs and money on the Mexican border and comes to the attention of both those behind the scene and a local world-wearied sheriff - and i think that's the way to see this film.

Go in knowing as little as you can but knowing at least this: this is a serious, violent, slow-paced character piece from the Coens. This is not a Fargo. If you are squeamish don't see it. If you have a short-attention span don't see it. If you only love the Coens for their fantastic comedies like O Brother and Big Lebowski and the comedy/thriller Fargo don't see it. But if you want to see an intelligent, superbly acted, powerful, beautiful cinematic treat that will remind you of the true power of cinema see it, see it, see it. It's a masterpiece. Bravo Ethan and Joel.

I'm not really seeing the hype that much, and yet, to say that this isn't a rewarding thriller is almost as great a disservice to this film as its final act, because when it hits, it hits hard, not unlike its cinematography.

I don't even find the film's cinematography quite as impressive as many are saying it is, as Roger Deakins puts only so much flavor on and does little unique with the palette of this artistic thriller, but visual style is impressive, make no mistake, with moments in which Deakins haunts with his trademark emphasis on sparse lighting, complimenting a consistent rugged bleakness to the palette which compliments the grit of an environment that in turn compliments the grit of this film's subject matter. I don't feel that the subject matter presented here is as dramatically juicy as it ought to be if it stands a chance of conceptually being nearly as outstanding as the masses say, but as an intelligently extensive study on a classic story of cat-and-mouse narrative, and as a portrait on understanding your enemy and challenging your mortality as encroaches, - whether it be in the hands of fate or in another man's hand, guided by fate - it is not simply compelling, but so much harsher than anything that the Coens have ever faced. This is a very different project for the Coens, and as screenwriters, they fumble the ball in so many ways, yet generally adapt very well, with sparkling and often even thought-provoking dialogue, in addition to set piece molding that, despite often being too steady for its own good, immerses, while subtle characterization, despite often being too subtle for its own good, intrigues on the whole with characters who are, in a sense, both enigmatic and layered, and brought to life by equally subtly powerful portrayals. Working with much less fluffy material than the usual Coen cast, this film's roster of talents aren't allowed to really flesh out the charm which the Coens, as well-versed comedic filmmakers, work with best, but for this heavy dramatic twist, they spare no expense in showcasing notorious talents' gripping skills, and that particularly goes for the leads, with Tommy Lee Jones being as charismatic as ever, with some subtle emotional twists, in his portrayal of a wise sheriff coming to terms with a challenging case and his own age, while Josh Brolin proves to be subtly layered as a man on the run to defend his life which he may have to end up fighting for. Of course, just about everyone, including Brolin and Jones, is all but embarassingly outshined by Javier Bardem, whose impeccable nailing of a deafeningly quiet intensity leaves Bardem to transform into his Anton Chigurh character and, with only so much material to work with, project a sense of confidence, competence and instability so tight that you can't help but feel as though you're witnessing the birth of an iconic antagonist who ought to chill many to the bone whenever he hits the scene. Of course, Bardem's performance doesn't drive the penetrating kick of this intimate thriller single-handedly, as it's the performance by Joel and Ethan Coen, as directors, which defines this film, utilizing grizzly, if a little gratuitously disturbing violence and some traditional dramatic punch to punctuate a thoughtfulness that, upon finding material to draw upon, rather than draw out with cold atmospherics, kind of haunts, drawing you into a claustrophobic environment and allowing you to meditate upon dramatic and thematic depth, no matter how uneven. To me, the strengths are too subtle to really stand out, while the flaws prove to be great enough to seriously threaten the final product, but engagement value is never lost, even in the at least interestingly misguided final act, being sustained firmly and consistently enough by intelligent and inspired storytelling to make quite the compelling dramatic thriller.

In conclusion, exhaustingly draggy pacing is made all the more challenging by sometimes near-punishingly dry atmospherics, and some questionable developmental shortcomings, with focal inconsistencies, guide the final product to a startlingly flimsy final act that most reflects the film's being rather overrated, but not so overrated that rugged cinematography, intriguing subject matter, intelligent writing, effective acting - especially by Javier Bardem - and immersively thoughtful direction aren't able to guide "No Country for Old Men" to a generally rewarding state as a chilling and thought-provoking extreme dramatic turn for the Coen brothers.

Within the first 30 seconds of the movie, I had already fallen in love with it. This is one of the greatest movies I've ever seen. I mean it. It was just...phenomenal, in every way imaginable. The Coen brothers do it over and over and over...and over again. Every time they deliver, they deliver big. "No Country For Old Men" is one of the most intense, disturbing, beautiful, captivating, emotional movies I have seen, ever. It's a true representation of film making. 

The plot is simple. Josh Brolin finds some money from the aftermath of a drug shootout. Javier Bardem plays some sadistic psychopath. Once he learns about the money, it becomes a chase. That's the film. Tommy Lee Jones plays the sheriff who has to find out what the hell is going on. It's plot is simple, but every other component is so elaborate. 

This has to be some of the best acting I've seen. Jones is godly. That's all I have to say about that. He was wonderful. His voice overs, and live action sequences were all phenomenal. He was truly just a treat to watch. Javier Bardem was also fantastic. He gave you this disturbing feel, and he was truly scary. Besides being sadistic, he also just gave a brilliant performance. He was...phenomenal. Josh Brolin was pretty good as well. It's a finely tuned, extremely well put together cast. Every actor has this interesting chemistry with each other and that's why it works so well. It was superb. 

I fell in love with the cinematography right in the beginning. It was beautiful. The Coen brothers use the same cinematographer in all of their movies, and though I forgot his name, he's amazing. There are fantastic landscape shots, and the lighting textures during dark chasing scenes, as well as dolly shots during running or driving a car, are all brilliant. Shots focusing on one character close up are also brilliant. I really think this is the component that made the movie. It was beautiful. 

I loved how the film flowed. The Coen brothers could have gone in a direction with intense music, and dozens of shootouts. But that's not there style. What they did, was presented us with this calm tranquil atmosphere, that built up in intensity not for it's soundtrack, but because of the characters. This is a movie where you truly feel like your apart of what is going on. It's mind-boggling. 

Anyway like I said, though the story might seem simple, it's wonderful. Like I said, I loved Jones' narrations. That was another favorite aspect of mine. His voice overs put the film all together, and the last scene, though I won't give it away, teared me up because it was so wonderful. 

I've said it a million times in dozens of different reviews. The Coen brothers just know how to make a movie. They deliver every single time. These guys don't mess up. This film one best director and best picture, and it deserved it without a doubt. "No Country For Old Men" is an undisputed masterpeace, for it's beautiful presentation, it's wonderful acting, it's phenomenal craftsmanship, it's amazing story, and it's intense manifestation of perfection. See it.

This movie is a Nietzsche-esque macabre look at the dark side of humanity. Arguably, a social commentary about the loss of innocence in America. We start with a very compelling premise; a self reliant country boy finds a drug deal gone bad and makes off with a whole lot of cash. With a heavy dose of realism, a tangled web is told of several parties seeking the return of their cash, the country boy, and the sheriff. The unconventional plot structure leaves you guessing what the movie is truly about until a character "cleverly" reveals through a description of a dream he had, roll credits. The revelation of the movie's true plot is incredibly unsatisfying, landing with a tremendous thud. The message of the movie seems to be "shit happens, and one day your number will be up, too, sucka." In a word, I felt cheated by an intriguing premise that wound up making a proverbial flatuant in my face. The cinematography is great, but I disliked the negative tone. Just as I feel the film defies traditional plot structure, it also defies classificaiton. Western? No. Crime Drama? Nah. Horror? A little. Allegory? Now we are getting closer.  A movie that is self-aware and has to condescendingly tell me what it is about for me to make sense of it receives failing marks in my book.
