Days after seeing it, I am still haunted by No Country for Old Men. There is just something so effectual and uncompromising about it, that mere words will only begin to skim the surface of the cinematic excellence on display.

At its most simplistic, the film is a game of cat and mouse. The mouse here is Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a hunter who stumbles upon two million in cash after a drug deal gone wrong, and takes it thinking nothing of it. He tries to cover his tracks, but ends up letting the group looking for the money, figure out his identity. The cat is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a hit-man hired to find Moss and the money. But Chigurh is unconventional at best; he also happens to be bordering on mentally insane. And another man, a law man this time, Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), is on the trail of both men as they criss-cross around Texas.

Right up until its dénouement, the film is simply brilliant. Taut and thrilling, it blows right through the majority of its two hour runtime with ease. Even during moments of slowing down, the film stays right on track and never feels like it has run its course. It engages even when it appears that nothing is happening. The Coen Brothers truly crafted what appears at first glance to be a masterpiece, even if it is their first real shot at something that is not indelibly and inarguably their own. Even without reading Cormac McCarthy's novel, I know that the Coens have done it justice, even with their bitterly twisted and dark sense of humour scattered throughout the film.

But all of that comes to a standstill as the film concludes. The last twenty or so minutes feel like hours as the film wraps itself up, and it almost feels like these scenes belong to another movie entirely (one that borders on being pretentious and monotonous). I realize now that McCarthy's novel probably ends the same way, but it does not help provide closure to the fact that the movie is so break-neck paced right up until this happens. Its brilliance is shattered by what looks to be a series of tattered events thrown together to provide closure for all of the characters, alive or dead, and for its audience. It speaks volumes to the film's title, but it just does not feel satisfying compared to the rest of what we saw. Even with its enigmatic devices at play, I still cannot come to terms with how the film closes. It does haunt, and in a way, it may prove to be a significantly stronger ending as time rolls on. But as it stands now, it just feels weak.

What is also a bit of a surprise, and only seems to appear as the film concludes, is the music. It is not so obvious at first, but the majority of the film is audibly shown with just the sounds the characters make and no background music to speak of. This element is brilliantly used, as it helps intensify every situation and makes the film downright terrifying in some cases. It just helps truly make the film come together, and only helps establish the quick pacing even more so. It was definitely a surprise, and one that will probably help the lasting impact of the film become even stronger.

The lush and bloodsoaked visuals also help to define the film. Despite the film taking place mainly in deserted areas, or the desert itself, the camera manages to capture just the right essence of what the writing and acting is conveying. The isolation and the terror almost become characters themselves through these visuals, and are sure to be recognized as the award season rolls in.

The film's acting is also very well done. Brolin anchors the film and even when it is just the audience reacting to his attempts at saving his life, he manages to deliver the best performance of his career. He breathes life into Moss, and truly brings a sense of pathos to the character. We feel for him and his greedy mistake, and as he develops into a man unwilling to go down without a fight, he only manages to up the ante for himself countlessly. Jones, as the law man stuck on the fringe of every event, also does very well for himself. Most of his work is simply delivering dialogue, but it is delivered in such a fashionable sense that you feel like he is speaking to the bigger picture of things, and not just himself. I would have liked a bit more development in his character, but what little there is helps his performance greatly.

Supporting turns from Woody Harrelson and Kelly Macdonald are also done well, but are overshadowed by the main cast by both Brolin and Jones.

And even more of an overcast is Bardem as the ruthless Chigurh. He absolutely nails this character down to his very bones. If anyone is merely toying with the idea of seeing the film, it should be specifically for Bardem. His performance is calculating and plagued with petrifying silence. When he chooses to talk, his words sound like they are being given by the essence of evil. This is a man with a plan, but it is one that only belongs to him. His enigmatic presence is developed throughout the film, and never once does it feel particularly appropriate to understand where this menace comes from. Watching him on screen is a jolt to the heart, and will go down as one of the best performances of the decade. His terrible hair only helps to make his character that more scary and formidable.

No Country for Old Men is one of the best pictures of the year, even if it is flawed. Its brilliance and lasting impact with leave you haunted.

This movie is probably the Coens at the height of their moviemaking prowess, even though this isn't my favourite overall of their movies. That title still belongs to The Big Lebowski. However, I do think this is the best Coen drama, girded by exceptionally strong performances and a simple but enthralling premise. That guided by the Coen brothers' steady directing makes No Country For Old Men a definite must-see and a fitting entry into their collection. It's also very worthy of winning Best Picture and getting the Coens the directing Oscar that we all know they deserve. 

No Country For Old Men follows three storylines, centred around the three main actors, and the storylines all tie together. Llewelyn (Josh Brolin) finds over #2 million in cash as well as a stash of heroin and two dead bodies in an abandoned truck. He decides to keep the money and a cat-and-mouse chase ensues with Anton (Javier Bardem) the psychopath that is supposed to be tracking it down. Then, there's the subplot about the police tracking Anton down, including a city-slicker played by Woody Harrelson and a sheriff-deputy team played by Tommy Lee Jones and Garrett Dillahunt. 

The story is simple enough to follow, and it starts off a bit slowly but soon gets a hell of a lot better. The script...well, it's the Coens. The two directors have certainly earned their reputations as story and script men and they (as well as Pixar and Christopher Nolan. Plus, Duncan Jones to an extent, he seems to be emerging) have been the only people in Hollywood that can provide us with original ideas and stories nowadays. This is based off a novel by Cormac McCarthy, which the critics consensus says is darkly funny. I wouldn't know seeing as I haven't read the book, but I suppose one could call this movie darkly funny. This won Best Adapted Screenplay at the Oscars, and for good reason because it was terrific.

The movie rises even more on the strength of its perfectly capable actors. I generally like Tommy Lee Jones as an actor, and naturally he was awesome in Men in Black, but that's the last thing I had seen him in, so I didn't really remember his acting style. He was terrific in this movie and he played the role of gruff sheriff perfectly. I normally loathe Josh Brolin as an actor, and his performance is definitely not the strongest in the movie. However, no matter how much I loathe the man's acting, I can't deny that he definitely gave a good performance in this movie as Llewelyn, the man who found the money. The supporting performances are good too, like Garrett Dillahunt as the deputy and Kelly McDonald as Carla Jean, Llewelyn's wife.

However, why the movie is really worth seeing is Javier Bardem's performance as Anton, the main villain of the movie. Anton is one badass guy, and Javier's wonderful Oscar-winning performance has a lot to do with that. Anton is a cold, calculating serial killer that is tracking down the money found in the truck by Josh Brolin. I definitely found some similarities between his character and Arnold's character in Terminator. He almost seems immortal, like he can't die. Also, like Heath Ledger's Joker, we don't know anything about him, and the element of mystery adds to the creepiness of the character. We don't know anything about his background or whether he was born this way or had to go through some crazy turn of events. We just know that he's killing people for no apparent reason and he feels no remorse about it forever. He doesn't really smile at all so he doesn't really enjoy what he's doing. He just feels like he has to do it, and we have absolutely no idea why. Anton is probably one of my favourite villains of all time and a great performance for great actor Javier Bardem.

So I've praised it so much you're probably wondering why I gave it only an 80 and not a full perfect score? Well, it did lag in some parts, which is a problem that Coen movies (no matter how terrific they are) tend to have. The ending was terribly abrupt (as usual) but those were pretty much the only real problems with the movie, and those are problems that I have with all Coen movies. For those of you who may be interested, the film does contain some violence, and although it is somewhat severe, the violent scenes few and far between. However, this is generally a quiet movie so when violent things happen like gunshots or shots from Anton's fancy cow-executing gun, it is quite startling and took me by surprise quite a few times.

No Country For Old Men is a definite must-see crime thriller for anyone and everyone, especially fans of the genre and fans of the Coens. Featuring a simple but interesting story, strong performances, blacker-than-black comedy, a great screenplay, but some lag and a terrible ending. I am still rather unknowledgeable in the work of the Coens, and the next one I intend to watch (eventually) is Burn After Reading, their follow-up to this. How will Burn After Reading hold up? I have no idea, but this one certainly does. All in all, I really did like this one and if you are a fan of this type of movie, you will too.

A drug deal gone wrong, a pile of bodies, and two million dollars of missing cash; such are the things that many a gangster film, gritty cop movie, and shoot-em-up have been made from. And in the hands of Joel and Ethan Coen, it provides the perfect material for one hell of a modern day western.
	By the time hunter Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin) finds the money, he's already seen the bodies and the drugs.  He knows the stakes, and he knows that certain people will not rest until they recover that money. But how could he know that he'd be pursued by a man like Anton Chigurh. Chigurh (Javier Barden) is one of the deadliest, most merciless, and downright craziest men you could ever. If you present even the slightest inconvenience to him, he will look you in the eye, talk to you as calmly as if you were talking about the weather, and gun you down without a second thought. Sometimes he doesn't even need an excuse. He's the kind of person that bodies just seem to materialize wherever he goes, and if he's looking for you, you might as well already be in the ground.
Of course with all these people dying, it won't be long before the law get's involved. Enter Sherriff Ed Tom --- (Tommy Lee Jones). He's seen just about everything in his long years as county sheriff, and it doesn't take him long to figure out that Llewellyn is in way over his head. Now he's in a race to see if he can catch up with Llewellyn and the money before Chigurh can.
As you would expect from the Coen Brothers, No Country for old men is an intricate, compelling, and somewhat strange tale. Under their direction, what might be merely a simple chase movie takes on a higher level of complexity, as the characters try to outwit and stay one step ahead of each other. This movie also knows how to play its cards close to its chest. It withholds enough information to keep you guessing, but never so much that you become frustrated.
It should be noted that the Coens really have a way with dialogue. I haven't seen a script with this much restraint since The Magnificent Seven. There's not a single unnecessary word in the entire film. When the characters do speak, their words are full of wit and personality. For instance, when Ed Tom here's about the three men gunned down in a cheap motel room, he refers to it as 'natural causes.' "Natural for their line of work." 
Or take Chigurh's exchange with the convenience store clerk. On the surface, it doesn't seem to have any connection to the rest of the movie, or even to make sense, but looking deeper you realize there's a sinister subtext to every word, one that gives strong indication of just how screwed up it is inside Chigurh's head. And the final scene, which I will not reveal, is pure Coen. It's deep, inscrutable, and completely unexpected. It reminded me very much of Copula's The Conversation.
No Country for Old Men is a dark and violent film, with no interest in imparting morals or providing happy endings. It's not the kind of movie you want to pull off the shelf when you need an escape. But it is also a powerful and engaging film that you will not soon forget. Here the Coens have given audiences one of the most chilling pictures of evil in many years, along with their best movie since Fargo.

A satchel packed with two million dollars in cash. A pressurized canister used to punch holes in deadbolts and skulls. A West Texas stage of flatlands, small towns and old-fashioned, honest folk. These props, places and people, molded by the skillful hands of filmmakers Joel and Ethan Coen, float on the surface of a deeper melodrama that has played out since the beginning of time: the battle of good versus evil and the role of fate in shaping the fight. Based on the novel by Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men is unconventional and brilliant, earning four Academy Awards, including best picture, best director and best screenplay adaptation.

Set in the 1970s, the story focuses on three main characters, sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) Lewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin) and Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), who embody law, the average man and lawlessness, respectively. Moss hangs suspended somewhere between light and darkness. A twist of fate thrusts him into a fight against evil, even though he never consciously chose to participate in it. But fighting the surging force of evil is Bell's lifelong call of duty, and that of his father and his father's father - three generations of Texan sheriffs. For Bell, this call of duty is a haunting, elusive exercise. He can reconcile the threat of evil on a physical level and intellectual level, but not a spiritual level.

As the sheriff says in the narration that opens the film. "You can say it's my job to fight it but I don't know what it is anymore. More than that, I don't know what to do. A man would have to put his soul at hazard." This notion of testing one's soul against evil is frequently explored on film; but rarely as dramatically and disarmingly as in No Country for Old Men. The test is portrayed as glibly as the flip of a coin; temporally as a cat-and-mouse shootout; and as spiritually as Bell's pursuit of the other characters, the way he is haunted by the darkness of humanity and his acceptance that he can never shine a light on it.

After sheiff Bell's voiceover, the story gets rolling with Chigurh's brutal escape from a policeman. Flagging down a motorist and asking him to "hold still please", Chigurh murders the man at point blank range. This scene is immediately justaposed with Moss taking aim at a far away antelope through a rifle scope, muttering under his breath for the deer to "hold still". Moss squeezes the trigger, but the shot misses the head and neck and the antelope limps away. As Moss tracks it, he comes upon a wounded pitbull, a curious sight in the middle of the badlands. Moss quickly finds the dog's point of origin - a cluster of bullet-riddled pickup trucks, dead bodies and a colossal cargo of heroin. The area bristles with supreme danger.

One of the mexican men, though mortally wounded, is still alive in his truck. He begs Moss to give him water, but Moss has none. Still using his tracking skills, Moss soon finds the money from the drug-deal-gone-bad. He grabs the satchel of cash and two firearms from the crime scene, and returns to his wife, Carla Jean (Kelly Macdonald). The couple is in bed when Moss' conscience gets the best of him. He had left a dying man begging for water and now he can't sleep. In the hours before dawn, he fills a container with water and heads off to grant the man's final wish.

Back at the crime scene, Moss finds the man shot in the head. Looking up at the ridge where he parked his truck, Moss notices another truck parked adjacent to it. Note that all the action described thus far happens in the first few minutes of the film. The harrowing chase that follows and subsequent shoot-outs ar executed with a tremendous eye for detail by the Coen brothers. Chigurh and Mexican outlaws track Moss, and Bell brings up the rear, trying to make sense of the trail of bodies. The sheriff quickly recognizes the danger to both Moss. He appeals to Carla Jean to convince Moss that he needs help. But Bell is getting old. Will he be able to stop Chigurh, or will the mysterious, unblockable force of evil roll on, snuffing out the most innocent life in the story?

What makes No Country for Old Men so unconventional? Several factors, but the main reason is no final showdown in the classic sense. This lack of conventional resolution led to undue criticism from those who did not understand the story. Part of the film's appeal and genius lies in the way it dispenses with tying up the loose ends of conflict/resolution as deftly as it sets them up. The juxtaposition of Moss and Chigurh is fascinating. We watch them operate with comparable efficiency, both sustain injuries, both treat themselves. Both are motivated by the money. Both are skillful with firearms. We learn that Moss has served two tours in Vietnam. Chigurh's past is never revealed but, unlike Moss, he lacks any hint of remorse or conscience and he believes only in fate.

Characters as strong as these are not new to the Coen brothers. But in the Coens' earlier films like Fargo, the most brutal violence was often followed by a quirky levity that can't be described as comic relief. Even the most horrific acts, for example when a man is ground into tiny pieces, are minimized by farcical dialogue: "I guess that was your accomplice in the woodchipper." The sardonic humor, quirky facial expressions and odd, lifting accents are all legitimate devices that make Coen brothers films endearing and special to audiences. But those moments of levity are nowhere to be found in No Country. One can argue it is the first film from the Coens in which they despensed with the comic relief and made a movie that doesn't flinch from its own narrative flow or bend under its own weight.

In no way does this minimize the importance of the Coen's earlier body of work. As in Shakespeare's plays, comic relief makes the tragedy easier to take. And let's face it: part of the Coen brothers' gift is their sense of humor and timing. But to successfully tackle a story like No Country, they needed to dispense with humor for the most part, and I'm glad they did. Had they made this film in the 1990s, dialogue like that during the coin flip scene in the convenience store would have been peppered with humor. Instead, the Coens made sure the drama escalated with no hint of levity. The Coens simply execute. That is a great achievement for No Country because its real message is not traigc. It is merely an observation: evil can never be defeated, but when you're no longer gung-ho to face it and fight it, it's time to step aside.

West Texas, 1980.  Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) stumbles upon a drug deal gone bad and $2 million in cash. He decides to take the money. In doing so he discovers there are no clean getaways as the men responible for the deal come looking for their money, among them is contract killer Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) a merciless force of nature. As Llewelyn tries to make his getaway and as Chigurh's ruthless hunt causes even his employers concern Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) struggles to make sense of a world changing seemingly for the worst...

Mixing elements of the crime/western/noir genra's together the Coen Brothers film has rightly been called a masterpiece. "I got here the same way the coin did." Here lies the key insight into Anton Chigurh's character.  This just goes to show that he is not only an unstoppable force of death (mixed with an element of random chance) but the embodiment of fate: that the sequence of events prior led him there inexplicably.  Many themes are explored in this movie, and are all deserving of deep analysis.  But the ones most pertinent to me were the themes of fate and free will.  Llewelyn is a perfect example of free will: a person thrust into an unending spiral of fate and left fighting for his existence.  But since Chigurh embodies the implacable force of fate, he represents that death is an inevitability for Llewelyn. Anton doesn't understand our resistant nature towards death, just as we cannot understand his (fate's) inexorable nature. And as the parallel between Anton and fate is made, it becomes clear that the best deal fate is ever willing to grant on your life is a coin toss.  No matter how long you try to play, Tails is always sure to come up.

Brilliant black humor, incredibly suspenseful sequences, horrible hairdos, tragic characters, a completely unsatisfying ending ala The Godfather Part II that will make you analyze the Sheriff's dream for hours, etc.  You can interpret the Sheriff's dream in many ways, but I'm going to have to agree with Alan Noble's interpretation. In talking about Sheriff Bell's dream at the end of the film, Noble finds "a hope for redemption outside of mankind." By the film's end, he says, Bell seems to come to the conclusion that the evil that he has witness[ed] is unstoppable, and so he retires from his job as sheriff. This hopelessness concerning mankind's ability to confront evil leads Bell to comment to his uncle, "I always thought when I got older that God would sort of come into my life in some way. He didn't." Quotes like these have caused some critics to mistakenly label the film as nihilistic. The strikingly bleak cinematography, the lack of any music, the unrelenting violence, the absence of a show-down/confrontation between good and evil, and the sheriff's retirement all lead the viewer to conclude that humans are ultimately and unchangeably evil. But the Coens (like McCarthy) leave us with a glimmer of hope in the form of a dream Bell relates to his wife. Going beyond nihilism, No Country's final scene (if properly understood) gives viewers a hope for redemption outside of mankind. There are few filmmakers who do their job as good as the Coen Brothers.  There are even fewer, if any, writers who do their job as good as Cormac McCarthy.  With No Country For Old Men, these three men's talents are blended together to create one of the most outstanding crime films ever made.  It is a dark, horrifying, and thoughtful tale about a man who finds a case full of money, a ruthless hitman out to retrieve it, and an aging sheriff following the trail of blood and trying to understand why it's all so.
Josh Brolin stars as Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam veteran who goes hunting one day, only to come upon a drug deal gone wrong.  Dead men are littered all over the scene, and even a few dogs, but Llewelyn knows that with a deal like this there has to be money somewhere.  He's correct, and soon finds all 2.2 million dollars of it.  He's smart enough to know that taking it will be dangerous, but the temptation is too great.  He takes it home without incident, but soon his conscience gets the better of him and he goes back to the scene to bring some water to the lone survivor.  This mistake proves costly.
Llewelyn manages to escape from the Mexican drug dealers who had come to the scene themselves, but now he knows they're after him, and later discovers that the men behind the money have sent someone as well.  This man is Anton Chigurh.
Anton Chigurh is played by Javier Bardem, and this incredible, Oscar-winning performance will stand as iconic for years to come.  Chigurh is perhaps the most cold-blooded killer the silver screen has ever scene.  Truly a man without conscience, and as one character puts it, "He doesn't have a sense of humor."  Chigurh's one goal is to retrieve the money and kill Moss.  The second objective may have been contingient upon Moss' cooperation with any other man, but with Chigurh it is as essential as getting the money.  In McCarthy's book, there is a telling scene where a man asks Chigurh about his enemies, and he replies "I have none.  I don't permit such a thing."  This quality is on display in Bardem's portrayel from the outset, and is played out to perfection.
The third character we follow is Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, played by the always excellent Tommy Lee Jones.  This film takes place in 1980, just when the drug trade on the Texas/Mexico border was becoming increasingly violent, and Jones' portrayel of Bell's weariness of the fact is brilliant.  Bell doesn't shy away from his duty to serve and protect, but what he is up against in the drug dealers and in particular Chigurh is beyond his understanding, and it weighs on him throughout.
No Country For Old Men is an amazing story and film.  Its highly thought-provoking and perfectly acted.  It's no secret that it was the winner of the Best Picture Oscar, and even against such films as Juno and the incredible There Will Be Blood, it is a more than worthy recipient of the award.  I understand why much has been made of the abrupt ending by casual movie-goers, but this is perhaps where it helps one to be familiar with the work of Cormac McCarthy.  It may even help to view another film based on his work, The Road, which has similar themes that relate to the ending.
If you haven't seen this film and/or haven't read this book, I strongly urge you to do both, for both are masterworks of their kind and shouldn't be missed.

Joel and Ethan Coen's NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN [2007]: When it comes to the best picture winning films of the Academy Awards some films in hindsight do seem either dated, overtly sentimental or like the wrong choice in the face of the other nominees for the award. With the history of the best picture winners has been to a large extent seemed rather dogged some winners seems like the wrong choice but let's face it even The judges of the Academy Awards do make mistakes like everyone on the face of the planet. But when the Judges of The Academy Awards pick the perfect winners my god do they get it right, with the 2007 Best picture film NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN by the Coen Brothers is without a doubt one of the finest films the academy award judges in recent years crowned the best picture. NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN is one film that only comes around once or twice in every decade; it's an unquestionable masterpiece of epic power and above all incredibly bleak and tragic which makes it a truly gripping film featuring one hell of a performance by one Javier Bardem.


Based upon the novel by Pulitzer Prize winning author Cormac McCarthy, this is by far one of the Coen Bothers finest achievements to date since FARGO. Never has a modern Oscar winning film stunned me as much as this film has and in the fifth instalment of my seven day review marathon on RT dedicated to my exploration of the Coen Brothers work NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN is today's film I'm reviewing and just my rating alone spells out my feelings about this film. I loved it as much as I love that other 2007 classic THERE WILL BE BLOOD, so I just cut to the chase and jump right into reviewing this film.


Day Five NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN [2007]: with the movie adaptation of a novel by a Pulitzer Prize winning author a skilled hand by a renowned filmmaker is a must have. With the skilled story telling abilities of the Coen Brothers and the story telling skills of a Pulitzer Prize winning author was a match made in movie heaven in my view with this film.  NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN at its core comes across as brutal, viscous, cold, dark, and very unfair in a way just like everyday life. In this review expect me to go on about why I adore this films utter brilliance and why it deserved its Oscars. 


THE PLOTLINE


Set in the rugged landscapes of West Texas in the years of 1979 to 1980, hunter Llewellyn Moss (Josh Brolin) while out on a hunt in the vast and barren landscape comes across a truly dark sight. The remains of a drug deal gone wrong were men and pit bulls lye dead upon the ground, Llewelyn quickly establishes that there is something from the site; the money that was to be used in the deal is missing. Llewellyn finds it not far away under a shady tree next to a dead drug dealer and with no one around the cash strapped Llewellyn decides to take the loot with little thought of the consequences. 


Meanwhile else were in Texas a lone roaming soulless Psychopath called Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) is brutally killing anyone he feels like a lone highway patrolman and a middle aged man upon the side of the highway. Back out at the drug deal site a few of the dealers hire Anton to locate their loot (then Anton kills them for no real reason), so now Llewellyn must now flee his small town , send his wife to her mother's away from the possible danger that's now on the way after him in the form of the soulless Anton.

Llewellyn try's his best to run from Anton and after a brutal shoot out in a small town near the Mexican border Anton will not end the chase until he kills Llewelyn for his reason. Enter the local lawman of Llewellyn's home town Sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) who enters the chase across Texas to stop what is coming to Llewellyn, mainly Anton and the other drug lords who want to get their hands on him. But in an unforgettable, hash, dark and unsettling series of events leads to a climax that is just sudden and yet so original that burry's its way into the viewer's mind long after the end credits role.


THE ACTING, DIRECTION AND CINEMA-PHOTOGRAPHY


With the acting in this film only one performance instantly springs to mind Javier Bardem's jaw dropping performance Anton Chigurh. As one of the secondary characters describes Anton as "A Man without a sense of humour" those words alone sum up how terrifying this character is to view onscreen. Bardem's performance was awarded the best supporting actor Oscar for his performance as Anton and what can I say it's by far one of the best performances in a film that I have ever seen in a film and with that I don't think too much more should be added why I find this performance is amazing.


With the performances by Josh Brolin as Llewellyn and Tommy lee Jones as a Sheriff Bell, both of these performances are just as compelling as that terrifying performance by Bardem. With the performance by Tommy Lee Jones as the world weary Sheriff Bell pulls of the role extremely well. With the direction in this film the Coen's really hit their stride as directors with this film. In keeping with their style of quirky, bold and refreshing direction, NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN is by far the best film the brothers have been in the director's chair. Since the story is not of the Coen's imagination (due to it being a work of Author Cormac McCarthy) , how the  Coen's visually envision Cormac McCarthy's story upon the Silver Screen is that brilliant to say the least and also there is a good reason why it won the best picture Oscar. 

Another key element of this film is the cinema-photography and much like everything else in this film it's stunning. As a fan of visual rich films the compositions of that bleak, barren, harsh, dramatic and rugged West Texas landscape is just beautiful and yet at the same time fits the feel of the dark narrative to this film.



OVERALL THOUGHTS 


Overall I'm deeply impressed if not wowed, dazzled and moved by this film unrelenting power. For a best picture winning film NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN is by far one of the best films to have been crowned with that honour and also one of the darker films the Academy gave the award to. Unlike some winning films which are overly sentimental points, NO CONTRY is free from being anything that would give the audience viewer a new lease on life. In its cold hearted, unfair, brutal, disturbing dark and above all cynical nature NO CONTRY FOR OLD MEN is without a doubt pure cinematic art. So for this Coen bothers film I'm going to give this film the highest rating one could possibly give on this site which is of course 100% any other rating just wouldn't do.

"No Country for Old Men" is the Coen Brothers' first film to win the Best Picture Oscar. The premise is simple but wide-ranging; a Vietnam veteran (Josh Brolin) discovers a briefcase loaded with money at the scene of a drug deal gone badly wrong, triggering an unstoppable wave of violence as he is pursued by a psychopathic killer (Javier Bardem) who will assassinate anyone who gets in his way. The film is far more violent than earlier efforts by the Coens and is marked by long, mesmerising periods of no dialogue in which the action drives the story forwards. The cinematography is so very dark, so very textured, so very Coen, and it's a wonderful film to watch. The casting is spot on, especially in Bardem as Anton Chigurh, a spectacularly creepy character with an even creepier haircut and an arsenal of very peculiar weapons. Even his movements are unnerving. Tommy Lee Jones also does a good job as Ed Tom Bell, the Sheriff who is overseeing the weighty case, who surprisingly never seems out of place. 

The whole thing is a masterwork in atmospheric tension and while it may not be the filmmakers' best, it's certainly a very effective crime drama that refuses to let up until its shattering climax.

The darkest Coen brothers movie since their debut Blood Simple, and very downbeat fare overall, No Country For Old Men isn't for the faint of heart. It is however, an incredibly good film, stuffed to the brim with suspense and myster with a side order of fine performances and taut action sequences on top. Any Coen fan should check this out, as should film buffs and thrill seekers.

I'm going to come right out and say that I love dark films. They are just so depressing that it's actually hard not to appreciate it. And No Country for Old Men is one of the prime examples and a model for all dark films. This is a grim and depressing film. The film is just a basic plot, like most Coen Brothers movies. A man finds some money from a drug bust gone wrong and decides to go out on the lam with it. But with that one action, a spiral of misery and depression propels to a point where the film offers us no hope at the end. Of course the acting in this film is great, and Javier Bardem as Anton is one of the creepiest performances you will ever see. Everything he does and says leaves you terrified to the bone. The film is mostly about the complexity of the criminal mind and how they constantly grow worse and worse. The film is dark, the ending is depressing and there is no comic relief to be found anywhere. And surprisingly, I actually find that kind of refreshing. Too many people nowadays try to make up for dark films by throwing in unnecessary comic reliefs, or slapping on a bittersweet or happy ending to an otherwise dark film. Likewise, this film not only doesn't let up, it constantly gets more darker and more grittier the longer it goes on. Well-crafted from every aspect, including the acting, the directing, the writing, the pacing, even the lighting, this film is an experience unlike I've ever had, and likely one I'll never forget.

Prior to watching this film I had never seen anything by the Coen brothers. True Grit has always interested me but I have never got around to watching it. All I can say is that if the film making of True Grit is anything like that of No Country for Old Men then I can not wait to watch it. Old Men was a fantastic film with a great story, excellent performances and the films suspense was killing me throughout. 

The plot is as followed. It's Texas, 1980. Hunting in the desert, Llewellyn Moss comes across the wreckage of a drug deal gone wrong and takes the cash - without counting on the man sent after him, an implacable killer intent on recovering the loot.

Right from the off the film keeps you on edge as you are introduced to Bardem's character. Now this performance by Bardem is magnificent. Without a doubt the best performance in the entire film but that is not to say the other performances were poor. Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones give solid performances and the supporting cast were all outstanding. 

The narrative of the film is also very interesting. The fact that it will change between any of these three central characters whenever someone takes centre stage is interesting because it gives a feeling of nobody is safe. 

What was very interesting was the fact that the film kept my full attention and kept all the suspense without having any score in the film. I found this interesting as most films these days need a score to keep the flow going and for that, it instantly makes it a brilliant job of film making.

Whilst the ending of the film for me personally was a little underwhelming, I appreciate it in the sense that it leaves the fates of some to imagination and differs from the usual crescendo acts of most films. 

All in all I would recommend this film to anyone wishing to see a brilliant drama/thriller as it's one of the best pieces of film making of modern day. I now see why it swooped the Oscars a few years back.

The best part that I like about No Country for Old Men is that it works in the same way as Scorsese's Taxi Driver does; they are both character studies revolving around these three people in a pursuit of passion, and human morals. They have plenty of momentum to work with the characters and doesn't rush anything and going straight to the point. This sort of storytelling displays how great of an extent these characters would go to accomplish their main objectives. It even features a lot of the Coen's trademark moments of humor, but this is by no means a lightweight picture of comedy. The scene at the hotel in which Josh Brolin narrowly escapes is especially brilliant, and Brolin puts years of lesser films behind him with this terrific performance that holds the film together. Tommy Lee Jones is also exceptional in his best role in years, but the film realy does belong to Oscar winner Javier Bardem. He is, to quote the film, the ultimate badass but he's also chillingly believable and real. Barde creates one of the most vivid and unforgettable bad guys in movie history, a single-minded killing machine and he plays him almost like a human terminator.
The film is also a shining achievement in screenwriting as the Coens turn in one of their best scripts yet. It's almost the Texas equivalent of "Fargo". It's a joy listening to these smart characters spout their down-home way of talking, especially Jones. It's just one of the many reasons that "No Country For Old Men" is a one-of-a-kind picture. It reminded me of why I love the movies.

In the 2007 Best Picture Oscar race, it ultimately came down to two films: Paul Thomas Anderson's There Will Be Blood, and the Coen brothers' No Country for Old Men. And while Anderson's film deservedly won Best Actor for Daniel Day-Lewis' mesmerizing performance, it still falls before the sheer force of filmmaking that is No Country for Old Men. Not only is it possibly the best effort from the Coens' storied career, it may very well be the best film of the last decade. A dark, uncompromising film that is ultimately about morality and fate, No Country for Old Men bolsters all-time great direction and cinematography, a brilliant script by the brothers adapted from Cormac McCarthy's source material, and some of the most subtly excellent performances you will ever see, with one in particular standing out from the pack. The story of everyman veteran Llewelyn Moss and his cat-and-mouse game with violent hitman Anton Chigurh is a thrilling, occasionally terrifying, subtle, and ultimately poignant tale that also serves as a reflection of the perceived declining decency in this younger generation of Americans, as seen through the hardworking and decent older generation, represented through the eyes of aging county sheriff Ed Tom Bell. These three characters make up of the meat of the movie, and their performances serve them well. Tommy Lee Jones is perfectly cast as Bell, portraying the sheriff as decent, hardworking, and determined, but at the same time as reluctant and somewhat stoic. It's the kind of role almost written for Jones, and he absolutely nails it. Josh Brolin, a highly recurring actor these days, also does solid work as Moss, giving a strong portrayal of a ordinary man thrust into an extraordinary situation, and has to use ingenuity to elude his incredibly dangerous pursuer. And that's where the real heavyweight of the film comes in, as the 2007 Best Supporting Actor winner, Javier Bardem, portraying Chigurh. Bardem successfully executes one of the most frightening and complex screen performances in history, as his interpretation of Chigurh is the most frightening and dangerous screen villain since Hannibal Lecter. He's a distilled evil of the highest order, and his ultimate fate cements him as a human Terminator with an odd code of ethics, a psychopath who lives by his own rules. I could spend a whole 10-page paper analyzing Bardem's performance, but suffice it to say that it practically gives the Coen brothers their movie. The supporting cast also does a good job, with standouts being Woody Harrelson as a bounty hunter who previously crossed paths with Chigurh, and Kelly Macdonald as Moss' strong-willed wife. In all, No Country for Old Men is a film that must be seen to be understood, and you'd be an idiot to miss it. Years from now, it may be seen as the greatest effort the Coens ever put out, and maybe even as a cinematic benchmark.

I enjoy the storytelling abilities of the Coen brothers. This film is a nerve-wracking, ever-surprising and twisted story of three men circling around each other. The plot about the money case is just the setting that allows these three to hunt each other. I especially enjoyed the characters and the dialogue of the movie. Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) with his coin-tossing is perhaps a real world's equivalent to Scarface from the DC universe. They share the same faith in fate, though Chigurh is a lot calmer about it. The comparison is hard not to make, but it doesn't really bother the watcher even though he is always aware of the similatiry. The other enjoyable character was Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), who, while being just an unfortunate victim, still shows a surprising amount of backbone and even humour in the face an unstoppable threat. Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) was perhaps the weakest out of the trio, but he wasn't bad. He just didn't quite reach the teet-rattling horror that Chigurh and Moss managed with their game of cat-and-mouse. He felt unnecessary from time to time. And the reason why this movie doesn't deserve five stars is that I felt the ending was unsatisfying. It makes sort of sense now that I have had time to think about the themes of the movie, but when the film ended my first reaction was along the lines: Wait... that's it?! So, while the book may have ended similarly, I feel that the movie's ending should have been a bit different. How it should have been different? Hard to say. Once again the bit about the sheriff didn't quite reach me. Sure it was nice, but I just wanted to hear more about Chigurh, or not to hear anything about Bell.

"No Country For Old Men" was one of those movies that I was dying to see from the second that I saw the trailer back in early summer. Then I read the early reviews coming out of Cannes and I was totally psyched after that, and I couldn't wait for November to come around. The movie came out last weekend, November 9th, but I managed to see it this weekend due to its still limited, but significant expansion in theaters it had this week. The movie does not disappoint, but it did catch me off guard a little, and it ended up being something a little different than I expected.

Walking out of the film I could not help but discuss it with the person that I saw it with. It's ending is entirely unconventional and fairly uncommercial to be honest, but it certainly did spark conversation and thought. Did I like it? Not necessarily, but I'll get to that more later on. For now, I'd like to say, this was probably one of the best directed film's I have seen in a long time. The Coen Brothers absolutely mastered the art of suspense in this film and the action sequences are unbelievably unsettling because of how realistic they are. I don't know if I've ever seen this many character's killed off in a crime drama in such disturbing, realistic, unsettling manners as the character's in this film. It's a very violent film, and because it contains so much violence, it was incredibly important that the violent scenes throughout were handled with care and with proper attention. The action scenes in this film absolutely received the care and attention they deserved, no question about that. I was on the edge of my seat throughout most of the first 3/4's or so of the film and had they Brothers handled the end of the film a little differently, perhaps it could've been a pretty decent sized hit at the box office. The way it currently is, I don't think it can make more than 15 or so million just because of its inaccessibility with many regular viewers. That still has more to do with the writing than the direction so I'll get to that later once again. Otherwise this film's direction was pitch perfect.

The acting was no less impressive and was probably the most perfect thing about the movie. The best performance was no doubt from Javier Bardem who played "Anton Chigurh", in other words, the psychopathic bad guy. He is scary as hell throughout the film and his performance never ever goes out of character's, although the script does take him out of character at least once, but I'll once again, get to that later. I wouldn't be surprised seeing him not only with a nomination for "Best Supporting Actor" but with the Oscar in his hand come oscar night. He has to be seen to be believed. So far his performance and Tom Wilkinson's performance in "Michael Clayton" have to be the two stand out supporting performance's to come along this year. Josh Brolin is the main good guy through the majority of the film. He does a very good job, but his character is not nearly as interesting as Bardem's character is. Still, he deserves credit for his performance as well, but I don't expect that he'll get any oscar recognition. Then there's Tommy Lee Jones who did a very good job for the parts of the film he was in, and he definitely says some of the more interesting things in the movie. He's the only character that really talks a lot. The other two main character's are fairly manly and they tend to keep their mouth's shut, avoiding any really thought provoking character development on their character's while Jones's character tends to have a wandering mind, and he says some of the more profound things in the film. Woody Harrelson has a fairly small role, but he does a good job in the film as well. There was one casting decision that caught me off guard in a good way. Stephen Root who played "Milton" in "Office Space" and the dorky old "Gordon" in "DodgeBall" had a small part in this film that was entirely serious, and his voice was a regular old raspy southern one. It was interesting to see him in a non-comedic role, speaking his lines in a normal manly way.

Now for the script... The script is my only real issue with this film. Some parts of the script are fantastic. First off all that tension that the Coen's created with their great direction started in their screenplay that they adapted from the novel of the same name. There are some very interesting encounter's and conversation's from character to character through a lot of the film and much of the film is actually quite funny in typical Coen brothers fashion, which I honestly did not expect considering the fact that it looked to be an all out action-thriller from it's trailer. That was a nice touch as well. However here are some things I had a problem with.

(MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD!) The whole movie has people tracking things down. Now the whole first half of the film the main character is being tracked with a tracking device so that made sense, but then he tosses it out, and still, Harrelson's character finds him and says he did it in three hours. The main character was checked into a hospital in Mexico and Harrelson's character had no way of knowing this, and somehow he magically found the guy? Alright, fine. Then the script decides to avoid explaining how, and when the main character starts talking about how he can get away from Bardem's character Harrelson just says "You don't understand"... Alright, what doesn't he understand? Is there some weird connections that you're organization has to track people down? What? Well it basically just makes it look like these guys have super powers and they can find people with their laser vision or something. That was kind of annoying. Then there's the fact that the whole last quarter of the film the main character is dead. He is killed off screen by some regular old guys that the boss sent out to get the money that he had. Now what bugs me about that is the fact that the main character (Brolin's character) has been outsmarting and dodging those guys through the entire movie, and then a few of them run up and they all just shoot him to death nice and easy. When you see his body, he's not like off somewhere, like he ran and tried to get away. He's on the floor at the front of his motel room. He's also been dodging one of the smartest, most threatening bad guys to be in a film in year's and he was able to dodge getting killed by him... The slow ending following this death was bothersome and it honestly started to feel extremely slow and boring before the credits went up. The thing that really makes the movie unredeeming is the fact that Bardem's super bad character lives on after all this build up towards what looked to be his imminent death.... There is actually a scene where Bardem and Jones look as though they are about to face off, but Bardem runs out the window. This is totally out of character because througout every other scene in the film Bardem shoots firsts and does things like talking or running away later.

I gave the movie a few hours of thought before I came and wrote this review and after all this thought I decided that Bardem lives because he is the worst man can ever be, and that Jones lives because hes is the best man can ever be. Bardem kills without any real cause, and Jones can't even handle the sight of dead bodies anymore, he's tired of all of the bad thing's he's seen in his life, and he uses knowledge as his number one weapon, constantly spurting out facts through out the film's entirety. Both have to live on so that they can balance each other out. Good and evil...

Overall this movie was an expertly directed, extremely well acted film that had some flaws with it's script, but honestly, it had to much great things happening with it for any of that to matter. I really loved this movie, and I think I'll probably go see it again next week so that maybe I can understand it a little better than I did this first time around...

A faithful adaptation of the Cormac McCarthy book, written and directed by Joel and Ethan Coen, this modern Western thriller explores fate and circumstance in telling the story of a Vietnam vet (Josh Brolin), who absconds with two million dollars from a failed drug deal and is pursued by a psychopathic bounty hunter (Javier Bardem); while a disillusioned small town Texas sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones) is on the trail and tries to make sense of it all. Set in the desolate Texas landscape in 1980, this is a traditional Western with noirish overtones that suggests Peckinipah. Bardem, with a black bowl hair cut and monotone voice, is scarily menacing as the killer meant to represent Death. He uses a cattle stun gun against his victims and flips a coin to determine their fate. The Coen brothers do a superb job of building suspense with little action and there is great irony and humor too. Its also very violent without the snarky nihilism the Coen brothers are known for. Fantastic widescreen cinematography by Roger Deakins. Mildly overpraised, it won Oscars for Best Picture, Director (Joel and Ethan Coen), Supporting Actor (Javier Bardem), Adapted Screenplay (Joel and Ethan Coen). With Woody Harrelson, Kelly Macdonald, Garret Dillahunt.

This is the best film I've seen this year. "3:10 to Yuma" was very good, as was "American Gangster", but "No Country" is virtually flawless. It has a measured, deliberate pace that is neither boring or lacking depth. The three main characters seem to represent a larger contingent than themselves. The evil killer, who isn't random. He kills when it serves a purpose for him, or when he says he will. At times his victims get a fighting chance. There is the everyman, played by Josh Brolin. A simple, poor welder who stumbles upon the chance of a lifetime....being rich. He takes money that seems to have no owner. From that point on, he is on the run. The sheriff is a representative of things past. The old way. He doesn't care for the direction society is going, even at the simplest levels. He leaves the posturing and sense of excitement to others, the man just does his job.
The three men never really meet face to face in the film, but they are all tied together by money, death, obligation and duty. This isn't a stunning, over the top Hollywood film. It's subtle and steady. The ending may leave some scratching their heads and others in contemplating silence. If you enjoy Coen films such as Millers Crossing and Fargo, you'll probably like this one as well.      Freddy

With their own brand of subtle, dry humor and their matter-of-fact sensibilities for violence, the Coen Brothers have, in my opinion, come closer to the throne of Alfred Hitchcock than any directors in recent memory with "No Country For Old Men."  This movie oozed suspense and dramatic tension, and I'm shocked to hear someone say that they were bored at any time while watching it.  I was the opposite.  I was terrified.  Slow and quiet scenes in the film made me uncomfortable.  Impending moments of doom were as shocking as I expected them to be and the unexpected moments of chaos caused me to jump, cover my eyes, and even verbally respond while watching (which isn't something I tend to do).  And then there's Javier Bardem.  Boy...for once the person winning all of the awards DESERVES it!  I didn't sleep very well the night after I saw this.  I'm haunted by him.  A performance for the ages.  As for the rest of the film, it is a master class of filmmaking in two hours.  Being the film nut that I am, I found the frame compositions and camera work to be as exciting as the story itself.  And I love the fact that this movie can play to the common viewer as a standard thriller, when in fact it's so much more than that.  I saw it as a statement on the American desire to fix problems as fast as possible.  How do you find two million dollars like that and expect to get away with keeping it?  But at the same time, why wouldn't you take that chance?  Stellar acting, stellar direction, stellar everything.  Oh, and that open-ended finish...the one that's not satisfying?  One thought: SHOULD it be?

The Coen brothers create another incredible film based off of Cormac McCarthy's bestselling novel. Javier Bardem does a scary great job as Anton, the "no-sense-of-humor" killer of the film.  His emptyness in his facial expressions give the character a horror movie-like quality that, whenever he's onscreen, makes you tense and cringe.  The story is simple in text, but the Coen brothers put their filter through the book's plot, making it seem complicated. No Country for Old Men is an exceptional film from talented filmmakers and has a cast of excellent actors to bring a novel to life.  I personally haven't read the novel, but I am lead to believe the film is quite close to the book.  I liked the story, especially how it was an interesting spin on a familiar tale.  I know several people who didn't really understand the film thoroughly, but as I see it, you need to look at the story from the point of view of Sherriff Ed Tom Bell.  It is his story that we're watching and needs to be seen through his eyes.  The writing is sharp throughout, giving us many memorable lines and insight into the characters.  And speaking of the characters, this texas based story is populated with several interesting and capitvating people, but none will make as much of an impression on you as Anton Chigurh.  Portrayed by Javier Bardem, Chigurh is a methodical, and in his own way, an honourable hitman who is very good at his job.  I could go on, but suffice it to say, he is played perfectly by Bardem (who earned a supporting actor Oscar for this role) and is not someone you will soon forget.  The remainder of the cast is great in their roles, but Tommy Lee Jones also stood out for me as the world weary Sherriff Ed Tom Bell.  The directing and the cinematography were also exceptional, with the Cohens using the simplest of shots to tell the story, but they are as effective as they are simple, and when coupled with the fantastic cinematography, nearly every frame of the film is a work of art.  This is a very minimalist film, and with the near absense of music throughout the film, it gives the sudden smatterings of violence and gun fire more weight and added realism.  While this film does lean towards the slow side of the pace spectrum, the story and characters are intriguing enough that you should never get bored.  This is, however, a film that you need to pay attention to to get the most out of it.  And still having trouble working everything out?  Talk it out with others, you may find someone elses perspective helps with your understanding.  Just remember, there's a lot of metaphor here, but there is also gun fights and explosions.  Something for everyone.

No Country for Old Men is a vivid portrait of America, painted through drug smuggling, border hopping, homicide, a thankless criminal investigation, and a man on the run. The Coen brothers have presented a gripping tale of cat and mouse which is compelling from beginning to end. It moves effortlessly from beautiful shots of the Texas landscape, to gritty close-ups of the damage inflicted by weapons: a flawless mix of action and suspense, and a frightening look at the fallibility and naivete of the law. The atmosphere is complimented by the script, and by the captivating performance of Javier Bardem, who really steals the show. One of the Coens' most accomplished works, No Country For Old Men is a modern Wild-West tale which is as thrilling as it is insightful.

I hadn't seen this since it was in cinemas, and found that it's even better than I'd remembered. It's a very unusually-paced film, with a lot of long silences, seemingly-innocuous conversations and dangling plot threads that don't ultimately lead anywhere. In many instances that could make for some infuriating viewing, but in the Coen brothers' hands it all somehow comes together into a master tapestry. The word of the day is suspense, an emotion the brothers have excelled at in the past, and No Country is a glorious example of it at play. The film's three protagonists, retiring sheriff Bell (Tommy Lee Jones), stone-cold killer Chigurh (a terrifying, star-making turn for Javier Bardem) and land-living cowboy Moss (Josh Brolin), never actually meet face-to-face but the wake of ripples left in their dueling pursuits is enough to power several movies' worth of rich, intriguing material. Sweaty, intense action walks lockstep with outstanding characterization, top-notch dialog and a hearty dose of respect for the novel. Like many Coen classics, it gets better with each subsequent viewing.

[A/95] On its surface a kind of cat-and-mouse thriller that sees a strong man (played by Josh Brolin) seduced by mysterious ill-gotten money and forced to run for his life, this riveting Western crime tale broods with mythological themes in a suspenseful vortex of pursuit and escape, justice and pessimism, and the moral fight with a random universe.
 
At the heart of the tale seems to operate a straightforward juxtaposition of good and evil, here personified by Tommy Lee Jones' solid, down-to-earth, traditionalist Sheriff Bell with Javier Bardem's relentless and efficient force of murder (awesomely memorable). But, in this perspective, good doesn't so much combat evil as fumble in the dark of its wicked slipstream, chasing shadows, attempting to plumb the unaccountable malice while seeking to shield the occasional innocent from a harm that will inevitably strike.

And so Sheriff Bell spends much of the movie in a near befuddlement of moral anxiety and flat-footed fatigue, unable to address the surrounding madness in an age of decay, too slow and folksy (and decent) to apprehend physically or philosophically the irrational power of the psychopathic Anton Chigurh. What's more, the closer he gets to his quarry, as in the excellent moment when he returns to the scene of a murder, apparently trapping Chigurh in a room, the more he finds ghosts, his dim reflection, or the looming banality of his own shadow.

Appropriately, such a story offers little closure, but remains open to the eternal significance of human failings, where evil is elusive and the tough protectors are eventually worn down by time and memory. It rings with a disturbing dignity, at least as gripping as the chases, the sudden violence, and the startling sense of jeopardy.

Toying with the viewer's perception of moralities by exposing characters as double-sided, each stuck between their own nihilist and fatalist beliefs, No Country For Old Men is a western/noir/horror/drama/comedy film not to be taken lightly. Masquerading itself as a social commentary, it goes way beyond that by presenting us a diverse cast that is as dependent on the viewer's analysis as the familiar yet thin bonds playing with the very nature of causality that connect each character.
Delivering a poignant ending to what may just be one of the more ethically rich wastelands depicted by modern cinema, it is truly a film for the ages.

First and foremost, this was a brilliantly casted film. Brolin played a perfect anti-hero, Bardem was perfectly frightening while making you seriously question whether his character was really crazy or just enough not to care about anyone's life but his own. Also, I don't know how Tommy Lee Jones was coaxed into doing a half decent movie for once, but welcome back. 
One thing that was intriguing about No Country for Old Men was the fact that the Coen brothers pulled no punches about it. The story was entirely secondary to the underlying themes at hand. This was a very bold move in today's market of remaking every story 5 times because no one has any new ideas. The plot served instead as a catalyst for all of the different occurrences that coincided just because they coincided, according to Bardem's character. It wasn't until the end when he this philosophy is openly challenged that he becomes somewhat human, making for an interesting sort of personal climax for him. What makes the movie so affective is that we, as the audience, are constantly being reminded that things are always going to go wrong, things happen just because that's the way they are meant to be, and if something is coming, nothing is going to stop it. All the while we are hoping against all hope that it's untrue, and in the end our hopes are dashed brilliantly in every aspect involving the story. This is how tragedy is meant to look.

His words stir something inside that is imagined in many different ways.

The basic framework of the narrative (a game of cat and mouse) and its tone (often darkly comic) are trademarks of the Coen brand, but its the indistinct barriers formed around evil and morality that create a platform for audience discussion. Whats the meaning behind the coin toss scene? does Ed's dream penetrate the evil of the seemingly non-selective Anton Chigurh? we're left to rummage for these answers in the pieces placed in front of us. 

Only the brains behind the likes of Barton Fink and The Big Lebowski could comprehend the density of McCarthy's narrative. And by faithfully adapting it, the Coens have upheld the intentions of the writer, but most importantly, translated the power of the novel.

Out in the desolate west is where many great films have taken place. The Coen brothers, Joel and Ethan, (winner of Best Director) are among the great American filmmakers. Their snarky noir to their screwball comedy have earned them prestige and respect and also a few Oscars. I've never cared for films that take place in the barren desert. They tend to be too formulaic. That's where you have the Coens take an overused setting and make it new and interesting. Their 2008 Academy Award winner for Best Picture, No Country for Old Men is a refreshing look out west. Josh Brolin (Grindhouse) plays a man who finds dead bodies in the desert, with a briefcase of two million dollars and a truck filled with heroin. He tries to escape with the money, but on his trail is a hitman with the world's worst haircut (Best Supporting Actor winner Javier Bardem). The Coens definitely produce, write, and direct the Thinking Man's film, due to he fact it's a bad idea to doze off through one of their films, otherwise, you might miss something very important. Many critics have said this films is a western horror movie, and in a way, they're right. You have your maniac, your refugee, your hero, and your ultra-violence. The violence seems brutal, from explosions to shots...in the head. Javier's hitman is one of the most original portrayals in film history. He's quick, slick, and keeps his cool, all with a very misfortunate hairstyle. Tommy Lee Jones (Academy Award nominee for In the Valley of Elah) is the good guy, trying to track down the killer and find who stole the money. The pursuit is heart racing, the emotionless face of the causes fear hitman as he walks closer to the door with his silenced gun. He's very eerie, and his raspy voice intensifies it. He is one of the most evil characters ever to appear on screen. He runs shivers up your spine. You may find that "Call it, friend-o." may be the most popular line of 2007. There's a little of he Coen's familiar humor hidden in the film, one liners and awkward moments. Joel and Ethan adapted the script from the novel by Cormac McCarthy. The great script and the wonderful storytelling is clear as day in this western thriller. The desolate wasteland where film takes place is haunting, as if you are alone and no one can help you. If you are trapped, laying in the sand covered in blood, and a man with a weird haircut calls you friend-o, you're dead meat. Joel and Ethan tell this story in a flawless style (and won an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay), and it is done it gorgeous detail. The ending has been causing controversy. Audiences have felt cheated. You are left with a cliff hanger, not as if it were to be made into a sequel, but just left on the edge of your seat, wanting more, but the film leaves you hanging. I did not care for the ending. I can not appreciate it. Other than that, No Country is a masterwork. A brutal, yet glorious film.

After two slumps ('Intolerable Cruelty' and 'The Ladykillers'), the Coen Brothers seemed like they had dried up as storytellers. Those previous two movies exhibited none of the qualities that made their previous work such a joy to watch. Of course, as they are prone to doing, Joel and Ethan surprised everyone with their next film: an adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's haunting novel 'No Country for Old Men'. The Brothers' choice to adapt this book was inspired and the result of this perfect match of source material and filmmakers is nothing short of absolutely stunning.

'No Country for Old Men' is a violent, thrilling tale that showcases everything that has made the Coen Brothers masters of their trade. There are touches of 'Blood Simple' here and there, a bit of 'Fargo', even 'Raising Arizona' comes to mind. However, none of those films can possibly measure up to the all-encompassing power and beauty of 'No Country', the film that won the Coen Brothers their first directing Oscar and Best Picture of the year.

The acting is superb. The Coen Brothers have once again outdone themselves assembling a team of the finest actors the industry has to offer (their casting director deserves a raise). Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones are just fantastic, with Jones delivering one of his finest performances to date as a world-weary, aging sheriff. Woody Harrelson and Kelly Macdonald are here in top form as well, with Harrelson pulling off a really spectacular performance despite his short screen time. However, the real find here is, of course, Javier Bardem, as the terrifying beyond description killer Anton Chigurh. He earned an Oscar for his performance and it was more than deserved. His portrayal of this truly unsettling character is unforgettable and one of the greatest villains the screen has ever displayed.

The Coens are firing on all cylinders here as storytellers and visual artists. With every frame, they prove, once again, their mastery of the craft and it's nothing but exhilarating to behold. Roger Deakins finally gets another opportunity to demonstrate why he is one of the best cinematographers working in the business today, and it is, arguably, his best work yet. 

Thrilling, unsettling, and beautiful beyond all logic, 'No Country for Old Men' is the best movie the Coen Brothers have ever made and it deserves to go down as one of the finest films that cinema has to offer.

Et encore aujourd'hui, près de 11 ans plus tard, vous y voilà encore, recyclant éternellement cette même ambiance qui vous est propre et dont l'intérêt qu'on lui porte peine largement à s'épuiser.

Il est évident que [i]No Country for Old Men[/i] ne possède pas réellement de générique. Les derniers mots du shériff Bell s'enclenchent comme l'ombre du jugement dernier et les noms de ceux qui ont participés à cette folle aventure défilent. Et pourtant, pour moi, impossible de voir quoique ce soit d'autre que votre signature.

[i]No Country for Old Men[/i], c'est du Coen à l'état pur, et encore davantage. Encore en 2007, vos figures de styles métaphoriques bouleversent, elles bousculent le spectateur, l'interpellent sans relâche. En près de 120 minutes, vautré dans un sofa avec une demie-douzaine d'amis - Q20 étant absent -, les visages se sont progressivement métamorphosés au fur et à mesure que Javier Bardem donnait vie à l'essence créatrice de votre impitoyable scénario.

Stupéfaction. Effroi féminin. Élastique lubrifié. Toute la gamme d'émotion y est passé, et ç'aurait été une éruption de coeurs qui auraient défoncés collectivement nos poitrines si ce n'avait pas été de ces trente dernières minutes qui, bien que vitales, ont un peu contribués à affaiblir le rythme frénétique auparavant établi par le scénario et ses silences mortels immédiatement poursuivis par le brouhaha des balles qui sifflent. 

Votre bébé n'est en rien ascendant; c'est même plutôt le contraire. Et à mon avis, c'est ce qui le rend si spécial. Tout commence par une effusion de sang, de violence et d'inhumanité pour finalement se solver par un calme logique et transcendant. Tirer d'abord, réfléchir ensuite. Un vieux dicton américain à nouveau appliqué dans votre plus récente réalisation. 

Si j'avais toutefois quelque chose à vous reprocher, ce serait d'avoir caché quelques éléments de trop au spectateur, éléments qu'il m'a fallu éplucher sur Internet pendant plusieurs demie-heures avant de parvenir à saisir complètement. Ç'aurait pu me charmer s'il s'agissait de révélations spirituelles et symboliques, ou encore de ce genre de déclic qui vous procure une sensation incroyable quelques heures après le film parce que toutes les pièces du puzzle viennent de s'emboîter. Non, au contraire, les éléments manquants du scénario étaient vitaux à la compréhension, et cet illogisme a, malgré nous, imposé une barrière discrète entre le film et notre appréciation de ce dernier. Il ne faut pas prendre le spectateur pour un con en lui donnant l'intrigue tout cru dans le bec, dans la même mesure où il ne faut pas non plus surestimer l'auditoire. L'art d'être spectateur ne comprend pas nécessairement la fonction de devenir devin.

Sinon, images fracassantes, troublantes, mettant en relief les majestueux mais ô combien lancinants paysages du Texas et du Nouveau-Mexique. Effets spéciaux à couper le souffle soutenus par un Javier Bardem dans l'un des rôles les plus surprenants de sa carrière. ''Je ne fume pas, je déteste la violence et je déteste le sang.'' avait-il argué en refusant le rôle que vous lui aviez proposé. ''C'est justement pour ça qu'on te veut.'' avez-vous répliqué. 

Et franchement, ça mérite peut-être d'être la meilleure réplique du film.

Veuillez agréer de toute mon appréciation en tant que spectateur émerveillé.
Et, surtout, vivez pour l'éternité, jusqu'à ce que votre crâne soit défoncé.

Cordialement,
[i]Frank, respirant l'ère Coen[/i]

But the high point is the acting, and respectable stars Josh Brolin and Tommy Lee Jones are overshadowed by the magnificent Javier Bardem in No Country For Old Men and the brutality that he brings to the film and harnesses to overshadow any other form of intensity the film provides itself.
Javier Bardem gave a performance so fine that there isn't enough awards available to give him, so an Academy Award would be good to start off with. The simple fact is, Javier Bardem's performance is one so perfectly shocking with its brutality that as a character, Anton Chigurh will haunt me forever with fear, but as an actor, Javier Bardem is an actor whose career I would gleefully follow until his next Academy Award win and beyond, and any sane person who saw No Country For Old Men would agree with me. Javier Bardem's performance as Anton Chigurh was absolutely shockingly excellent, ripe with the talent to create an emotionless villain that isn't a hollow hulk, but rather a shocking moralistic villain which is never something I have so much as known to have existed. Javier Bardem is brutally incredible in No Country for Old Men.
Josh Brolin also makes a great lead as an ordinary man caught up in a game of cat and mouse and forced to suffer at the hands of hitmen, corruption and the violence of a western society which is no longer a country for old men. Josh Brolin delivers a fine lead role with insightful mind intensity to have the audience following him in terms of character insight as well as the physical perspective of watching a grown man run from a merciless killing machine with an oxygen tank and a shotgun. No Country For Old Men features one of Josh Brolin's finest.
Tommy Lee Jones did a great job providing a sense of nostalgia to the story as one of the titular old men, providing an empty side to the intense atmosphere as a sense of nihilism to the character of Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who still has the determination but lacks the power. Tommy Lee Jones' displays that his acting skills practically get better with age in No Country for Old Men.

Any fan of Woody Harrelson would enjoy his performance in No Country For Old Men, and then some.
 
In total, No Country For Old Men is a brutally shocking provocative tripper that displays the finest work of The Coen Brothers to date as well as Javier Bardem in a performance that is one of the greatest villainous performances in film history.

It has always been difficult for me to compare films to the stories or novels they are based on, but No Country for Old Men makes it easy.  This is one of the most faithful adaptations I have ever seen, often featuring sequences that are word-for-word identical to the book.  While I feel that Cormac McCarthy's violent tale is best told on paper, the film manages to be stellar in its own right, fueled by the talents of the Coen brothers.  The most appealing aspect of the film is Javier Bardem, who plays stone cold killer Anton Chigurh.  His performance is absolutely terrifying, while still managing to make the character completely believable.  That in itself makes it even scarier.  This isn't a guy with a hockey mask that seemingly won't die.  He's a strong, determined human being who is REALLY good at what he does.  Each character is unique, playing an important role in the plot, and the film does a good job exploring their values and afflictions, helping the viewer understand why they make the decisions they do.  While the film is extremely violent, don't expect noisy action sequences followed by an explosive confrontation.  The pace is slow and almost completely dialogue-driven, but that's what makes it a satisfyingly unique experience.
