Adapted from a Cormac McCarthy novel, fast becoming a Coen favourite, the brother directors take on a classic crime style story but add their own fantastical style.

Javier Bardem is almost perfect in the film, playing opposite the brilliant Brolin, whilst Tommy Lee Jones strange part in the story is carefully and gently crafted by an excellent performance from Jones.

But every component of the film is mastered to a particular thriller style, in a very Coen way. The normalities of any Coen piece are there, with the memorable storyline, complicated twists and turns and well above average cinematography. However the enticing poetic nature of the film is what makes it stand above the rest and pull you ever deeper into the character's lives, both normal and abnormal.

And what to say of the action sequences themselves? Superb, as well as never losing sight of the basic plot and using wonderful characterisation.

The plot itself is complicated and the end of the film, whilst panned by some, is actually devilishly clever and a fantastic ending. Its supposed ambiguity may frustrate some, although when you watch for a second time the majority of the ambiguity washes away.

The Coen's brother collection of films make it hard to point definitely to just one as their unchallenged masterpiece, but in the ranks of their greatest films, as well as some of the finest cinema to come out of America in years, 'No Country For Old Men' ranks at the top.

The directing in this film is unmatched by anyone in the past decade. The acting is superb, the tension makes you sweat and the pacing, though criticized by many, could not be any more amazing in my eyes. a perfect 5/5 in my eyes as this film is one of my all time favorites.

Evil comes in different shapes and forms - Along the way it tags with its deadliest counterpart "fear". As long as we have fear encapsulating us everything seems big and glorified. Any living being that conquers fear hits an impenetrable wall called "courage" eventually leading to absolute power. There are not many standing examples (alive or dead) for the analogy above bec
ause fear tramps and trumps almost all the time. When such a compelling feeling falls in to the lap of Coen Brothers through an enticing hand write from one of the most gripping authors, Cormac McCarthy, then the same fear runs amok with blood soaked feet. Outcome is no less gritty then "No Country for Old Men".

Plot:

Just when Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is having a bad hunting day in the wild desert lands of good'ol Texas, he comes across a blood bathed Mexican drug deal gone awry. Pretty soon he's packing a bag full of cash and is ready to whistle away for the rest of his life. He has no iota of an idea about the two monsters he has beckoned on to himself - one a tiny little tracking device sitting in his back and two a humanly monster of a hitman, Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), trying to track him down to the bones. Central portion of the story circles around this wildly gripping chase pulling along other commendable characters only when they are needed. What happens to Moss - What happens to Chigurh can only be answered after you feel enough of hot blood under your boots.

The movie starts off with an epic soliloquy of an introduction from Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones in one of his finest performances) about Wild West Texas, increased degree of violence and heinous crimes around the area.
"The crime you see now, it's hard to even take its measure. It's not that I'm afraid of it. I always knew you had to be willing to die to even do this job. But, I don't want to push my chips forward and go out and meet something I don't understand. A man would have to put his soul at hazard"
Cited above is one of the best quotes from the movie and that's what sets the pace to viewer expectations. Right from the word go the film has everything to do with being gritty, gory, insane, melancholic, violent and menacing.

Analysis:
Though we have the main characters Moss and Tom Bell - the movie is all about Chigurh (so nearly rhyming with Sugar but no hell of a sweetener). Javier Bardem as the cold blooded hitman is downright scary and wrought iron tough. He makes everyone fall in love with "BAD" and true movie lovers would want to see more of him as the movie culminates to a so called bizarre ending in the minds of many. But from a pure cinematic bliss, you don't want the character to end and Coen's deliver that in their unique style. All through the film Javier underplays his expressions to such ridiculous extent that at one point of time all you can visualize is violence. In a way it doesn't look like violence inflicted by a person but it transcends down to violence itself dancing in front of us.

Josh Brolin is effective as a huntsman and bizarrely caring husband at the same time. He's extremely natural in the scenes leading to fighting for his life and against his sugary foe - Chigurh. Tommy lee Jones as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell delivers one of the finest performances of his career. He is extremely empathetic over the course of film as he uncovers the truth of being "no match" to an evil. Kelly McDonald as Mrs. Moss draws in the sentimental quotient needed for the film. If there is one character that's absolutely wasted in the film then it's - Woody Harrelson as hired operative Carson Wells. He is introduced with so much of infused confidence and rigor but ends up dying cheaply like a bird shot.

Coming to the creators - Coen brothers never disappoint you with their eccentricity and thanks to the scripts and stories they choose - long live craziness. Just like all their movies, the film is filled with everything that can be evil and how it can outbeat things like good, law, order, faith etc. It's simply an outstanding mockery of everything a society or a community believes, in terms of their rules and operatives. There is no modus operandi but being zany.

Memorable scenes:

--> Chigurh unleashing his cylinder weapon for the first time
--> Chigurh shooting at a bird while driving over it just for the absolute psychotic pleasure of it - You cannot help but fall in love with this scene
--> Chigurh simply raising his foot from the floor and placing them over the bed as Carson's blood acts as an interruption to his phone call
--> Josh Brolin trying to escape from the vehicle hunting him and eventually killing the dog on his tail
--> Chigurh silently pulling the strings on a gas station owner showing his violent and not so negligible demonic side

The list just goes on as the whole movie is nothing but a culmination of 122 minutes of memorabilia. If there was no Joker then Chigurh would have been the best anti-hero Hollywood would've ever seen and we should thank Coen brothers down to their cheeks for giving us something so wonderful (on screen).

Once again, I have now seen every nominee in an Oscar category.  The 2007 Best Supporting Actor competition was generally considered not to be much of a race.  It was one of those categories where everyone knew who was going to win, just as everyone knew who was going to win Best Actor.  (The real horse race that evening was between the two movies for Best Picture, so far as I was concerned; this movie won.)  I don't dispute that Javier Bardem deserved the award, especially compared to the rest of his acting career.  However, I'm a little uncertain why it was considered such a total lock.  It was a fine performance, but it wasn't so high above the other four as all that.  I thought Tom Wilkinson's performance was extremely good, too, and Hal Holbrook is the kind of actor to have gotten it as a pity award.  Maybe they'd confused Bardem with his character and thought he'd go out and kill everyone who didn't vote for him?

One day, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) is out hunting when he comes across the remnants of a drug battle.  He's not interested in the drugs, but there is a case full of money.  He figures no one will ever know, so he takes it.  What he didn't know, what he couldn't have known, is that there is a radio tracker hidden in the money.  The men whose money it is want it back, and they hire Anton Chigurh (Bardem), pronounced roughly "sugar," to track him down.  Chigurh is cold, quiet, and fastidious.  His weapon of choice is a "cattle gun," a captive bolt gun.  It looks like a bullet hole, but there is no bullet.  And Chigurh does not stop.  He is pursuing Llewelyn, and there is no escape.  Meanwhile, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) is pursuing Chigurh.  He knows more about Llewelyn than Chigurh, and that's helping him on his trail, but either way, he's planning to retire.  The world is changing, and he can't change fast enough to keep up.

Really, I found Ed Tom Bell to be a more interesting character.  Yes, okay, he's a character that Tommy Lee Jones has played many times, but that's in part because he's just so good at it.  He's a surly old Texan.  Now, I think Real Tommy Lee Jones is better at keeping up with a rapidly changing world than Ed Tom Bell, but I could be wrong.  I've never met the man.  Either way, he projects a similar air of general decency.  He wants the right thing to happen.  He just can't understand a man of the single-minded brutality of Chigurh.  Hardly anyone in the story crosses Chigurh's path and lives.  Ed Tom wants to protect Carla Jean Moss (Kelly Macdonald), Llewelyn's wife, who didn't do anything and is still in the path of the storm.  Ed Tom's family has been in law enforcement for many years, and he regrets that he can't keep it up.  I don't think there's a fourth generation of Bells waiting in the wings to become sheriff, either, and that's a failing to a character like this.

Possibly the most interesting thing about the movie is that none of the three main characters ever share the screen.  Carla Jean meets and talks to all of them, but the others are never onscreen together.  There is a scene where Chigurh is going after Llewelyn, but the Coens filmed in such a way so that they're never in the same shot.  Each of the men is in his own separate world.  Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson, whose judge-killing father is referenced in the original Cormac McCarthy story) tries to bridge Chigurh and Llewelyn, but Chigurh has no interest.  In a way, he doesn't really interact with anyone, not completely.  He kills people.  He talks to people without killing them a time or two, even.  But he doesn't let them touch him.  There is a wall between him and the world that can never be breached.  I'm not even sure what's on the other side of it, if there is anything inside Anton Chigurh.

This is not a typical Coen movie.  They say that it is as close as they're ever going to get to an action movie.  (I can never remember which one is Ethan and which one is Joel, but the special features indicate that it just basically doesn't matter.)  The Coens dabble in various genres, but Coen films are their own genre.  This is a quieter Coen film than most; they tend to be talky, and this one isn't.  They trimmed dialogue from the original, though most of what is left is original.  They let the scenery speak for itself.  Their point is that Chigurh is as much a force of nature as the vast desert of West Texas.  Perhaps that's what I don't like about him.  Or rather, since you're not supposed to like him, what I don't find interesting about him.  He's a cipher, which is supposed to be a new and interesting form of violence.  However, I think it's just the same old violence, since there's only so much we can ever understand about most of the violence in the world.

A very stylish and well-made Western/chase movie. It's structurally interesting in that there are multiple chasers and multiple people being chased, and some characters are both chasing and chased. Yet none of the characters involved in the chasing ever meet onscreen, although a few shoot at each other once or twice. But they're never in the frame at the same time and never talk to each other except on the phone. The settings are a mix of sun-bright deserts and half-lit hotel rooms. A few critical scenes take place in or around cars and pickup trucks.

There is minimal dialogue, so the three key actors (Jones, Brolin, and Bardem) have to create their characters largely out of body language, gestures, and actions. They are all supremely effective, each displaying different facets of machismo. Brolin's character is the classic loner cowboy who thinks he's better at taking care of himself than he really is. Jones is a competent and courageous but tired, worn-out-by-life sheriff who no longer has the stomach for the brutality that men are capable of. And Bardem, finally, is the mysterious assassin who stalks the Texas landscape, clearly from somewhere else, hunting his prey with Terminator-like tenacity and total disregard for any collateral damage he may inflict along the way.

This is a violent film with a high body count, which begins in the first few minutes with a gruesome strangling scene. It is a dark story filled with tension as the prey just barely manage to stay one step ahead of their pursuers. It is a great example of cinematic art, but I have no idea what its message is. Marvel at the craft of it; be disturbed and haunted by its content.

''Whatcha got ain't nothin new. This country's hard on people, you can't stop what's coming, it ain't all waiting on you. That's vanity.'' Violence and mayhem ensue after a hunter, Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon some dead bodies, a stash of heroin and more than $2 million in cash near the Rio Grande. Nothing ever goes smoothly sometimes and before you know it he's on the run from a psychopathic cold killer. Josh Brolin: Llewelyn Moss. Javier Bardem: Anton Chigurh. Relentless in method, challenging in presentation, and unforgettable in execution; The Coen Brothers' adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's acclaimed novel borders upon pure genius in its characters and suspenseful build up, but sacrifices much of the clarity (though not the power) of its narration in the strict adherence to its source material. Boasting some of the finest performances of the year, the Coen's fantastically intricate thriller demands an astute mind and a perceptive eye to decipher the multi-layered parallels that lie in No Country for Old Men.
Having watched the two Oscar heavyweights No country for old men and There will be blood round about the same time period on the big screen, I can't help noticing the sharp contrast in audio style, while Blood came with background music so overwhelming that it threatens to take over foreground, Old men had only silence, natural sound and dialogue, with no music at all. There is no right or wrong: each style serves its particular purpose. Imagine the scene in Old men with Llewelyn Moss in the middle of the night in a sunken hollow strewn with a few abandoned vehicles and dead bodies. As the menacing headlight of an ominous looking vehicle at the top of a slope threatens to approach, any kind of music would do more harm than good to the blood-chilling atmosphere present. In their inimitable fashion, the Coen Brothers crafted this adopted story through a mesmerizing plot line that is ever elusive, giving you the slip every time you feel that you have got the hang of things. The plot line looks simple: a common young man who stumbles across two million dollars becomes the prey of a serial killer who is after the money (and his life), while a season sheriff comes after both in an almost standard cat-and-mouse story. But there are more than initially meets the eye. Moss the everyday man protagonist is not your ordinary reckless young man next door. Seasoned Vietnam veteran, he shows his stuff when chased by a ferocious killing bloodhound, hurriedly loading his pistol but never losing control, and firing it when the canine's deadly teeth is within three feet of his throat. He is undoubtedly the prey, but not one that rolls over and play dead. But this is really the hunter's show. Javier Bardem (The sea inside) whom has won every Best Supporting Actor in sight is good enough to give Daniel Day-Lewis a run for his money had he been put in the contest for Best Actor, to which he has every right. The most amazing thing is that while his physical appearance is at times even comical (mainly due to the ridiculous hair style), his mere presence is so chilling that it makes Jason Voorhees, Norman Bates and Hannibal Lector look like Disney villains. ''I always figured when I got older, God would sorta come inta my life somehow. And he didn't. I don't blame him. If I was him I would have the same opinion of me that he does.'' As the movie follows the standard cat-and-mouse crime thriller development, the audience may be so hung to the edge of their seats that they forget temporarily that this is indeed the Coen Brothers. The climatic showdown that they tricked you into expecting never presents itself. Everything seems to fall apart in the last third of the movie, or does it? For some people it may do, but these certain individuals lack sophistication in plain terms; Necessary train of thought or depth albeit an ability to see between the lines. Clearly No Country is going for it's source Novel and this Story is not a straight line but one of complication, one of poetic reflection. The ending to me was a marvel, like a newly born ray of sunshine upon ones face. The words reflecting deeper meaning and wisdom, that shamefully are wasted upon mainstream audiences. For those gracious enough to embrace the ending for what it is, will certainly come off all the better for it, not to mention inspiring and awe defining. The cat-and-mouse game ended almost as an afterthought, with none of the excitement the audience thought they had been promised. The focus has long since shifted to depiction of Bell, as one of the old men, in the title, one of disconnection and unparalleled from the main story yet ultimately part of it regardless. If you think back, most of the small roles (starting with the attendant of the now famous and memorable gas station scene at the start of the story) are old individuals. While the audience might have forgotten, the directors/screen writers have not. They haven't abandoned the concept, that this movie is trying to show why this desolate, seemingly endless horizon, Texas country is quite literally no country for old men. Added to this is the final touch, the accident; showing how karmic life and reality can be. There was so many great scenes in No Countrythat it is hard to cover it all in a single review. The tension, the sounds, the beats, the uses of silence all are definitely used to perfection. Had me jumping on numerous occasions in the cinema, and that part with Anton waiting for his pursuer after finding the transmitter was amazingly shocking. Without a doubt this film has you on the edge of your seat. The audience I saw this with didn't appreciate it. They didn't see the bigger picture, the gritty realism, the beautiful poetry of that ending, and if you see the words in that finale; allow them to sink in, then truly it will blow you away. Best film of 2007-2008 I've seen to date. The level of acting and vision is unsurpassed, and it will draw you in and stay with you. Definitely want to watch again and again, there's so much crammed in this. You will soak it up like a sponge. A masterpiece. Unrivaled entertainment; a haunting thriller and an unrivaled story adaptation. ''Yeah, I'm going to bring you something, alright. I decided to make you a special project of mine. You ain't going have to come looking for me at all.''

Okay so finally I am reviewing the last best picture form the 2000s to date. So without much more to be said, here's my review for No Country for Old Men.

Plot: The film starts with Llewelyn Moss hunting Pronghorn but while doing so, eventually comes across the aftermath of a drug deal that went bad and finds two million dollars in a satchel that he takes home. Eventually people find out about it and so a hitman named Anton Chigurh is hired to recover the money from Moss. But this also leads Sheriff Bell to investigate about this and try to find and protect Moss from getting killed.

In my opinion, this is a sort of film that you have to watch twice just to make sure you understand everything. I mean it may have been years when I saw it the first time and I had just saw it a second time, but it's a very slow paced film that you might not completely understand. When you can say that it is the Coen brothers at their best, you know you have something great on your hands.  'No Country for Old Men' is about a Texas man (played by Josh Brolin) who steps on an $2 million.  After that money too is Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem), a soulless psychopath who will do most anything to get what he wants.  Guiding Brolin is the local sheriff, played by Tommy Lee Jones.  The almost too real situation that this film tells provides enough suspense and thrills to keep viewers interested for two hours.  It certainly speaks to the skill of the Coen brothers when they can keep a film simple, yet nuanced.  The Coen brothers also bring out excellent performances in whoever they cast.  There are a lot of stellar actors in this film but the clear standout is Javier Bardem.  He is simply fantastic.  Every time he is on screen, the film peaks in suspense and intensity.  You just know that something bad is going to happen or someone is going to die.  Bardem has that ill-at-ease, yet calm creepiness that makes your hair stand on end.  This guy does not seem to feel any emotion and will make you twice about leaving your doors unlocked (however he has quite the fascinating mechanism to take care of those).  This is an excellent Coen brothers film that adds a lot to their already phenomenal repertoire and it was certainly deserving of winning the Best Picture Oscar.

True there is little character development, but there doesn't need to be; it's a chase plot between good and evil. Humans will inevitably side with the good character, especially when he's being shot at with a massive gun and I mean massive! So we don't really need to see his development over the course of the film. He is poor, he finds 2 million dollars, he takes the money and must pay the consequences. 

As for the character of Anton; the emotionless killer, all we know of him is that he was hired to track down the missing drug money and instead turns upon those who hired him and decides to go after the money for himself. When a character executes such an amount of random and senseless killing we need no more motive or background to feel satisfied about this character's actions, simply put he is evil. 

This film keeps you on the edge most of the time. As far as tense dramas/ thrillers go, it's one of the best I've seen in a long time. With brilliant direction and such an enigmatic character as Anton blasting people away you can't help but feel the heart begin beating a little bit faster.

"Adaptação do livro de Cormac McCarthy, obra dos Irmãos Coen entra na lista dos filmes mais supervalorizados da história do cinema."

Alguém acha uma maleta cheia de dinheiro e o verdadeiro dono dela vai em sua busca, em uma caçada de gato e rato. Este argumento, por si só, já é batido demais. Porém, os Irmãos Coen colocaram uma pitada de "os tempos mudaram" em sua narrativa, sob o ponto de vista de um velho (e incompetente) Xerife, para tentar fugir do clichê. Isso seria bem interessante se fosse melhor explorado, uma vez que só se evidencia no começo e no final da trama.


Para piorar, o desenvolvimento do filme é carregado de falhas. Chega a ser patético o fato do bandido Chigurh (Javier Bardem) encontrar Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), o portador da maleta, em qualquer lugar. No início, tal fato é justificável devido a maleta ter um localizador escondido, mas e depois que o mesmo é descoberto e retirado dela? Sem falar que estou até agora sem entender a parte em que Moss esconde a maleta no duto ventilação de um hotel e depois pega outro quarto, fazendo uma tremenda gambiarra para retirá-la. Lembrando que até essa cena ele não sabia da existência do localizador. Outra interrogação que ficou em minha cabeça foi: por que diabos uns assassinatos são mostrados e outros não? Se o objetivo foi o de tornar a trama mais complexa, não funcionou. E a maneira pela qual o veterano Xerife Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) é inserida na história, leva o espectador a questionar sua competência, chegando atrasado nas cenas dos crimes e sem falar que, em certo momento, ele vê os bandidos fugindo e prefere parar para ver o que aconteceu do que persegui-los.


Mas há também muitos pontos positivos na obra dos Coen. O mais destacável é a magistral atuação de Javier Bardem, que dá um tom assustador ao seu mitológico personagem, e faz muitos estragos apenas com um tubo de pressão para matar gado. A interpretação de Bardem e a caracterização de seu personagem faz o mesmo entrar na lista dos melhores vilões da história do cinema. O Oscar de melhor ator coadjuvante foi merecidissimo ao contrário dos outros 3 que o longa foi premiado. Falando em atuações, é sempre muito bom ter Tommy Lee Jones no elenco. Aqui, apesar de achar que o mesmo foi mal aproveitado, sua presença dá um charme a mais. Josh Brolin dá para o gasto, em uma atuação que não exige muito. O filme também contém alguns, digo alguns, diálogos interessantes e reflexivos. E quando existe o nome de Roger Deakins envolvido numa produção é certeza que temos uma fotografia magnífica e aqui, colabora para aumentar o tom sombrio e de suspense em algumas cenas. A mais memorável delas é a que Moss está em um hotel, percebe que Chigurh está lá, apaga a luz e fica com a arma apontada para a porta, observando os vultos do corredor pela soleira. Esses pontos salvam a produção do pior.


Quando o filme acaba (e por sinal o final é muito fraco), ficamos com a sensação de que "Onde Os Fracos Não tem Vez" poderia ter sido bem melhor. O rascunho é excelente, apesar da historinha clichê, mas contém furos gritantes de desenvolvimento. Existem detalhes no cinema que podem ser ignorados com facilidade e infelizmente isso não acontece aqui.
Talvez, o mais decepcionante foi ver este ganhar de "Sangue Negro" na disputa pelo Oscar de melhor filme. Definitivamente, a principal premiação de cinema do mundo não serve mais como referência de qualidade.

I'll admit that I was not impressed the first time seeing this movie. The second time around I was blown away by the dialogue and the tense atmosphere generated in this chilling cat and mouse Thriller. Javier Bardem is exceptional.

Most thrillers maybe entertaining but 'No Country For Old Men' invites its audiences right into the story, creating an incredibly tense, clever piece topped with black humour on the side.

The film follows, in essence, a bag full of two million dollars after it is taken by a Vietnam veteran, played by Josh Brolin in what must surely rank as his greatest role. He is tracked down by Anton Chigurh, a psychotic hired killer across Texas as the chain reaction escalates.

Adapted from a Cormac McCarthy novel, fast becoming a Coen favourite, the brother directors take on a classic crime style story but add their own fantastical style.

Javier Bardem is almost perfect in the film, playing opposite the brilliant Brolin, whilst Tommy Lee Jones strange part in the story is carefully and gently crafted by an excellent performance from Jones.

But every component of the film is mastered to a particular thriller style, in a very Coen way. The normalities of any Coen piece are there, with the memorable storyline, complicated twists and turns and well above average cinematography. However the enticing poetic nature of the film is what makes it stand above the rest and pull you ever deeper into the character's lives, both normal and abnormal.

And what to say of the action sequences themselves? Superb, as well as never losing sight of the basic plot and using wonderful characterisation.

The plot itself is complicated and the end of the film, whilst panned by some, is actually devilishly clever and a fantastic ending. Its supposed ambiguity may frustrate some, although when you watch for a second time the majority of the ambiguity washes away.

The Coen's brother collection of films make it hard to point definitely to just one as their unchallenged masterpiece, but in the ranks of their greatest films, as well as some of the finest cinema to come out of America in years, 'No Country For Old Men' ranks at the top.

I expect a film like 'No Country for Old Men' to be polarizing for some, especially if they're expecting a big finale with the good guy and the bad guy drawing their guns in the end to settle the score. 'No Country for Old Men' is a film that dabbles more in existentialism, despite all the crime that occurs. Basically, what I'm saying is that the film adapted from the novel is very unconventional not only for its genre, but also in its approach to storytelling. What the Coen brothers do best is combining altogether different elements and creating something with its own unique character. While there are subtle throwbacks to the old wild west, the story takes place in modern society where technology has advanced, society has advanced and unfortunately crime has too.

What are Anton Chigurh's true motives? Does he have a philosophical doctrine that we the audience are unaware of or are just unable to comprehend? What Anton does is create alot of questions that arise from his actions and his interactions with the other characters. To watch a character as odd as him is fascinating and I cannot give enough credit to Javier Bardem in portraying such a character that is so enigmatic and just his presence alone is able to evoke so much mystery. Even though Anton is very incomprehensive, it is all made up for by being able to be somehow captivated by him.

How every character deals with Anton is interesting, to say the least and as the film progresses, the feeling of despondency increases gradually. The lack of heroes is what gives this film its sense of hopelessness and that feeling of hopelessness is basically set in stone from the first few shots coupled with Tommy Lee Jone's epic voiceover narration in introducing the story. It is the perfect introduction to what we will witness in the story and what it all means for a sheriff like him in comprehending these events. As the events occur, we the audience reflect on these situations just as much as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell. Tommy Lee Jones' performance in this role is impressive and is injected with a great sense of humanity. I commend his portrayal as Bell, in that he is the character who carries the weight of the story.

The acting is a huge fragment in bringing this film to life, but what also does that is how the visuals are executed and it is definitely utilized to a great effect. From its majestic shots to its beautiful lighting and color tones, the Coen brothers set a mood that permeates the whole film. Its barren settings really add a feeling of desolation that is at the same time hypnotic and surreal. While the film can be suspenseful and its suspense is definitely executed perfectly, the film still somehow manages to maintain an air of mystique. The non-existence of a soundtrack really gives the film a feeling of loneliness, all the while adding an even greater sense of sterility to its already barren wasteland.

I can go on and on about the great acting, its memorable shots and its great script, but what makes 'No Country' a great film is that it manages to be truly idiosyncratic in its execution just like how the Coen Brothers' other great films are. Even if a film like this leaves me more questions than answers, if it still manages to captivate me to a point that I'm willing to return to it, then that shows that it doesn't matter if I don't have any answers to my questions. There are only a few films that are able to pull this off naturally and 'No Country for Old Men' is definitely one of those special films that can do just that.

The Coen brothers' No Country for Old Men is one of the best films they have ever made, and Cormac McCarthy's novel gives them the perfect setting for their stories of chaos in this seemingly normal world. The story involves 3 different men in search of the same thing, but for different reasons, which is a plot that resembles Leone's The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly. However, this is more of a western fable that deals with the moral decadence of society. Anton, Llewellyn, and Tom are the main characters searching for the money that was left behind at a drug deal gone bad. Anton is evil, he's played by Javier Bardem, who gives an amazing performance, Anton is searching for the money not so much because he's greedy, but because he thinks it belongs to him. And he will kill almost anyone who gets in the way of that, but he has what you can call principles, which really just means he kills only when it seems to have value for him. Llewellyn wants the money basically because he found it, and it's money, so he's not gonna give it up. And Tom is the only one searching for the money with honest reasons, he is the sheriff trying to put an end to Anton's blood trail, and the best way to end it is to get what is the cause of it. All these characters perfectly demonstrate where our ambitions have gone, how far our vanity has gone, and where our morals used to reside. This really is one of the most well written, directed, acted, and photographed of all the Coens' films. It is paced like a thriller, photographed like a western, and written like the Coens' brand of noir, which makes for a super entertaining film with much more depth than the average film. No Country for Old Men is a film that no one should miss, and every film buff should have multiple viewings of.

No Country For Old Men follows the same footsteps as the Coen Brothers previous just as dark and witty drama Fargo. But that is where the a likenesses stop because unlike Fargo, No Country For Old Men manages to thrill the audience on an even higher scale. It sees a small town sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) attempting to prevent the likely demise of a hunter Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) who stumbles upon a drug deal gone wrong and more than two million dollars in cash near the Rio Grande. Which happily leads to Javier Bardem. A ruthless, psychopathic hitman that wants Moss in the palms of his hands. So does this film seem simple enough to you. I mean, it is a cat and mouse chase film, that in small places reminds us of the Terminator but how simple this film may appear it certainly does one thing. It stands out from the crowd, with its exceptional writing and directing, this film is a flawless adaption of Cormac McCarthy's Novel. I don't think there is another screenwriter or director that can touch what the Coen Brothers have achieved here, however saying that we do have Quentin Tarantino for Pulp Fiction, but you get the picture. In No Country For Old Men, it is very much like a battle between Heaven and Hell, with one man caught in the middle. That man being Moss. With the four Oscars this film managed to achieve Javier held his Oscar up high with his supporting role as Anton Chigurh. Which maybe I wouldn't go as far to say it is deserved but it was certainly earned. 

To say that Chigurh isn't a character is faulty. It's like saying the film is beautiful except that, that and that. Just because Chigurh doesn't act with the same motivations of other movie killers, doesn't mean he isn't a character. As one great man said just because you are a character, doesn't mean you have character. Chigurh represents something more. You could even say he is the Hannibal Lector of the crowd with his random questions and subjects of conversations, not to mention his strong psychopathic nature. Chigurh is often referred by peers (not friends) as 'crazy', which is accurate but surly there is more to him than that, isn't there? He has a very easy mind but remains strong and firm against the moving world surrounding him. He clearly works solo and it doesn't feel that he works for anyone (Well I don't think he does anyway). He doesn't get angry when his life is in serious danger but more annoyed and frustrated when Moss' wife won't call heads or tails or when a receptionist won't tell him where Moss works. We see him toying and having fun with people, like the clerk at a gas station who married a wife who was into the gas station business. The interesting thing about this confrontation is you see that Chigurh isn't only just a killer, but he's not afraid to tell it like it is. 

I can genuinely say No Country For Old Men is one of my favourite films of this decade if not of all time and a clear Oscar grabber as its great writing, great acting and superb directing ensures that. However to fully appreciate this film it needs to be viewed several times but that's okay because it deserves to be seen more than once. Verdict: Films don't get much better and sophisticated as this and even though it is a cat and mouse chase film it certainly isn't predicable and has surprises around every corner. This film of course gets an A+.

I reckon Westerns deal mostly with physics. You got your forces and your stationary objects. Your forces are the good guys, and they have to move the objects, which are the bad guys, and then the movie's ended well. The question No Country for Old Men raises is, what if your object is equal to your force?

Javier Bardem supplies the object, a hitman who operates on a code that is always merciless and often sadistic, and is terrifying in the role. Josh Brolin is a cowboy that defies the object. If he can simply move it, he stands to profit immensely. If he can't, he loses everything. And so he'll do whatever it takes to move it. Woody Harrelson is a bounty hunter opposing the object. He moves it because that's his job. Kelly MacDonald is Brolin's wife, who refuses to play by the object's rules. If she doesn't accept it, maybe it doesn't exist. And Tommy Lee (playing a man instead of a cartoon, as he is so often cast in his age), well, he's the sheriff, who says this at the outset:

"There was this boy I sent to the 'lectric chair at Huntsville here awhile back. My arrest and my testimony. He killt a 14 year-old girl. Papers said it was a crime of passion but he told me there wasn't any passion to it.... Said that if they turned him out, he'd do it again. Said he knew he was going to hell: 'Be there in about fifteen minutes.' I don't know what to make of that. I surely don't."

What if your object is equal to your force? That question is No Country for Old Men.

I do generally enjoy the Coen brothers movies, but they're not always easy to watch. This one requires quite a bit of thought and reflection after it in order to figure out what you think happened and if it was good or not. This film is a tough one to digest. The trailer and the whole set up of the film makes it appear to be a western thriller with a villain chasing a hero, pursued by a supporting hero, and you expect the hero to come out on top with the help of the law-maker. But this is a Coen Bros movie. It doesn't work that way. Our villain isn't just a villain. He's a ghost, a phantom, a representation of evil. He doesn't conform to villain plots. Our hero thinks he is on top of things, but he does not understand exactly what he is doing. Our supporting hero is old and broken. Even our damsel in distress is no damsel, but distress is certainly at hand. 
If you like a film to build up plots and then have pay offs in a big, interlocking ending, then this film is not for you. Be prepared to question what it all means and be prepared for an ending that has no high points, no final showdown, no pay off. Just be prepared for a gritty, well written, well directed and brilliant but challenging film.

Movie Review: No Country for Old Men by Charles Firth

No Country for Old Men is not about drug dealing or cowboys or deserts or hit men. These are the trappings in which a grand story is set -- a story that deals with archetypes, questions of morality, meaning and destiny.

The Cohen brothers have created a cinematic masterpiece interpreting the same-named novel written by Cormac McCarthy, the Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award winning author. The brothers bring the story to film true-to-spirit, albeit with some editing for length and one noticeable character deviation which seems to be the result of their own philosophical prejudice (see Carla Jean's coin toss below).

In his book, McCarthy creates a paradoxical reality in which murderers are the only self-examined and morally consistent inhabitants. The seemingly innocent are doomed by virtue of their own philosophical and moral inconsistency.

In the book, and less so in the film, each chapter is prefaced with a narrative that, at first glance, appears to encapsulate the story's philosophical premise - that the world is going to hell in a hand basket. Yet in the end, this narrative amounts to nothing more than a kind of pervasive exasperation with the events that unfold and the world at large. The narrator, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell, defies the typical role of narrator. Narrators generally provide direction, context, even omniscience. But here, Sheriff Tom (Tommy Lee Jones) offers only bewilderment, expressed in between Texas colloquialisms that hint at a deep, yet unfulfilled, search for the truth.

McCarthy and the Cohens immediately throw us off the track, setting up a gruff cowboy, Llewellyn Moss, as the likely protagonist. Moss, as it turns out, is not our classic protagonist. He is simply a pawn, a failed man, doomed to suffer the consequence of his own moral corruption. He chooses to hoard manna over compassion for another human being -- even over the safety of his nubile and unquestioning wife Carla Jean (played to a "T" by Kelly Macdonald). But like the biblical manna, which also appeared in the desert, hoarding it again corrupts.

Moss is given more than one chance to redeem himself. When confronted by the film's guardian angel Carson Wells, complete with white hat and played with Texan precision by Woody Harrelson (think: a drawling Clarence from "It's a Wonderful Life"), he scoffs, insults and refuses what would appear to be divine intervention to save his doe-eyed Carla Jean. 

But the film is bounded by a universal law of justice, as doled out by our arch antagonist turned protagonist, Anton Chigurh. He is the character who continues to push the action forward. But is he the angel of death? Is he fate? No, it turns out he is simply a force of nature -- a probability become absolute certainty in the quantum-collapsed-wave now moment. Once you have seen Anton, there is no going back. And only those who violate Anton's internally consistent sense of justice need see him. 

Chigurh, or "Sugar" as Moss blasphemously refers to him, is the final curtain for those who cross him. And those who cross him always seem to underestimate him to the same degree that they under-examine their own lives. But seeing Chigurh is not a guaranteed ticket to the beyond. Some get a second chance by way of a coin toss, others are simply innocents passed over for another day. Yet others only have to run into Chigurh with their car to make the journey into the beyond.

What is it that McCormick is trying to tell us? A message that the Cohens so deftly bring to the silver screen... Is it Nihilism? Existentialism? Predestination? Or is he simply telling us that unless we examine our own lives and live with moral consistency we will never be able to make sense of the outer world? A world that appears to Sherrif Tom as full of ever escalating violence, corruption and chaos? 

What remains consistent throughout the story is Chiguhr's sense of justice and his sense of connection to what he believes is universal law. Everyone else is compromised. In the book we learn that Ed Tom abandoned his post and his men in WWII and is forever attempting to compensate for this primary moral failing. Llewellyn abandons a dying man and his wife when he could have saved both. 

Even Ed Tom's wife abandons the outside world by never reading the news or watching TV. Carla Jean abandons reality via blind, unexamined faith. In the film, she refuses Chigurh's offer of a coin toss. In the book she accepts, leaving her fate seemingly to fate. But the toss changes nothing. As Chigurh explains, he is there for a reason. He arrived, "the same way the coin did."

Chigurh reminds us, it is our decisions, made each day, one after another which bring us to this place we are in, in the present moment. And God help us if that place is sitting across from Anton Chigurh and his pressure-driven cattle gun -- just another dumb animal ready for the slaughter.

I'm kind of at a loss when it comes to this film. It is the story of a hunter who happens upon a drug deal gone wrong and finds a fortune in cash on the scene. Naturally no one will let that kind of money go, so he is pursued by a murderous psychopath. Javier Bardem is totally creepy, and can really make your skin crawl. There are moments where he says very little, but you can tell he is a moment from snapping and killing someone. It's great that he can make this clear without verbal threats, it adds a lot of intrigue to his portrayal. While this chase is going on between the assassin and his prey I was very entertained. No Country for Old Men is also beautifully shot. There are so few spoken lines in this movie that a lot of the storytelling falls on the cinematography, and I don't think they let you down. And as long as I'm praising the movie I should mention that I felt all the cast was solid, and did their best to keep up with Bardem who was constantly stealing the show.

Where I struggled with this film was the over-arching theme. It seemed to all center around a small-town sheriff played by Tommy Lee Jones. The problem is he is so isolated from the plot that he might as well be watching the film sitting next to me in the theater and commenting on it occasionally. I was more connected to the events of this film than he was! I get that the point wasn't to make an action movie or something, it was more about a world that had grown too dark and violent for the titular "old man," but he felt so insulated from the events because he kept showing up after the fact. As a result, I just wasn't impacted by the deeper story they were trying to tell. Now you can call me a typical, moronic, popcorn-eating movie-goer but in all honesty the hunt was the more engaging story of the film, and when they went for something bigger and more transcendent they lost me. Sadly, the resolution of the story we followed for more than half the film is not even shown on screen. The ending we're left with is devastatingly unsatisfying after they had me on the edge of my seat for so long. That being said it is still a perfectly constructed film. Everything works just right, I just happen to feel slightly let down by the story they chose to tell.

A Coen Brothers masterpiece, "No Country for Old Men" is a slow, plodding Americana film bolstered by powerhouse performances from it's three leads and a remarkable sense of gripping storytelling.

Poor hunter Llewelyn Moss stumbles upon the aftermath of a busted drug deal, finding dead bodies and a larger pile of cash. Deciding to take it for himself, he tells his wife to leave town and then heads immediately across the county line. The loss of the money attracts dangerous attention, however, as a hired hitman and the county sheriff begin pursuing Moss across the Texan landscape.

The three lead roles are played superbly by Tommy Lee Jones, Josh Brolin and Javier Bardem, with strong supporting roles also coming from Kelly Macdonald and Woody Harrelson. Bardem in particular was outstanding, leading to his Oscar for Supporting Actor.

Meanwhile, the film itself won a Best Picture award, and truly deserved it. A dark and slow film, it also finds time for some fairly black humour. It has all the Coen brothers hallmarks, and is slowly becoming recognized as a classic film. And it deserves that.

I can't put this any other way; "No Country for Old Men" is the best movie of all time. I watched it four times and each time saw something different, a new nuance that transformed the characters into metaphysical metaphors for good, evil and the commingling of the two into the banal. Of course, Bardem's Chigurh is a new definition of menace, social rejection and the arbitrary, a chaotic figure who makes his own rules with the same ruthless logic of a sudden bolt of lightning or an earthquake. The Jones and Brolin characters are both his prey and his embodiment; where does one end and the other begin? The final act will disappoint those filmgoers accustomed to the linear "justice" that exists only in American fantasies. But Jones' soliloquy frames his dreams with his reality. It's up to you to decide which is which.

The film flew by so fast because I was so invested in what was going on in a quite simple story that has many layers to it. The cinematography is absolutely beautiful and everything just looks very crisp and raw, it's beautiful to look at and once again Roger Deakins is ignored. Surprisingly, the film has a sense of humor, albeit a very dark sense of humor but it fit unbelievably well. It isn't perfect though, something happens about 30 minutes before the end that was quite questionable. While it didn't annoy me as I appreciated a smarter, more philosophical approach, I'm just surprised that it isn't in the critics consensus or that more critics haven't commented on it (but it wouldn't be a cinematic masterpiece, then, would it?). This ending that we got is probably more welcome than if it went the conventional action route, which probably would have gotten a mention in the critics consensus, it's just that some things that work in one type of media don't translate well to film, especially when you disregard a main character, who has had a massive scenario building up this whole time, right at the last minute. Credit to the Coens for sticking to the source all the way to the end but sometimes changes need to happen. After that part happened, it felt like someone else came in and did the last 30 minutes or they wanted to make the last 30 minutes completely different to the rest of the film, it's very strange as is the fade out transition right before the last 30 minutes. What would the overall experience have been like if, at that moment, it just faded to black and ended? Again, it didn't bother me, it's just something to comment on because I've seen very few people do so and it's strange, at least in terms of filmmaking, anyway, or maybe it's just me. But, hey, I haven't won 4 Oscars so what am I talking about, huh? 

Overall, it's a twisted, sordid affair that racks up the body count and is drenched in blood. It's great, but I don't think it's winner-of-4-Oscars great. I think the honor of Best Picture belongs to There Will Be Blood but here we are. However, with great attention to detail, assured direction by The Coen Brothers and a trio of powerful performances, how can you go wrong and what more could you ask for?

Review In A Nutshell:

Boy, how wrong I was about this film, claiming before that this was one of the Coen brothers' weaker films. It was almost a year ago since I have first viewed No Country For Old Men and since then I have learned so much about the directors and cinema as a whole, and through this growth I was able to gain a better appreciation of this film. I previously watched this at a time where it was late at night, expecting something great but nothing difficult; I found myself dozing off frequently during this film, finding it to be uneventful and lacking of drama. It is only now that I have watched this film at a time where I am more alert and a stage in my life where I could appreciate darker and more thought provoking films.

No Country For Old Men opens up with a Texas desert that feels empty and grim, supported by a narration that fleshes out the backdrops and its characters without becoming too specific, whilst listening we are treated to a visual introduction of the antagonist, committing a brutal and relentless murder that would then shape the silent menacing tone of the film. The film speaks about its themes of violence, greed and morality in such a way that looks slightly exaggerated but feels harrowingly honest. Its central protagonist, Llewelyn, stumbles upon a drug deal gone wrong and allowed him to struck gold, finding a suitcase full of cash, and decides to keep it for himself. This gave us a glimpse of what humanity has become, linking it to the aftermath of the Vietnam war with constant references on it spoken here and there, losing a sense of virtue and relying on their armoury to protect themselves from those that are greedier than their own; this idea of greed seems to be a recurring theme for the brothers with it being prominent in their earlier films including Fargo and The Big Lebowski. The film also explores upon the idea of morality, showing that goodness has slowly faded in the souls of the people, with only those that are passionately violent and strong-willed will survive, and this tragedy of the human soul is enriched upon the perspective of lawman Ed Tom Bell, who states at the start of the film this at the start of the film. The Coen brothers emphasise this through the minimisation of using extras to fill the environment, allowing it to create that sense of emptiness that connects effectively with the film's themes. It is only at the end, where Bell shares two dreams he had about his father where I felt lost, unable to make the connection with the film's themes due to its ambiguity.

The Coen brothers have shifted their playful quality into something that is much dire and serious, and I think the decision to do this allowed the film's themes and ideas to create more impact to the viewers; creating that sense of unpredictability that leaves viewers feel tense and fearful. What is more frightening is that the directors do not hold back in showing gruesome images, letting the camera be right there as it is happening. The film may follow three different characters, but each one is given a generous amount of time to be followed, with Javier Bardem's character as the deadly and arbitrary Anton Chigurh. In his travels, we see him encounter individuals, sometimes random, and for the bulk of it he tortures them psychologically, giving them a feeling of danger without actually showing it or making it plainly obvious, and it is through this foreplay that the audience could easily feel uneasy and when he does pounce and strike, it is then when we feel terror. The film however, does not over-exaggerate the character, especially when it comes to its physical appearance; there is something darkly comical about his notable and peculiar haircut and the usage of a high-pressure oxygen tank to murder his victims; practical but no doubt unorthodox. The rest of the central characters look and feel much more grounded but in saying they never at all came across as dull or generic.

In my initial experience with the film, I was bugged by the fact that it lacked musical score, as it allowed the more mundane moments feel more tedious than they already are. It is only now that I am able to appreciate the effect that this silence was able to create in regards to its story, ideas, characters, and atmosphere. It is this lack of sonic activity do we feel uneasy when watching threatening events unfold, aiding the feeling of unpredictability that no doubt runs throughout the film. No Country For Old Men never aimed to be a dramatic piece or a crime-driven film; it attempts to capture something real, something that we could see or feel in our own reality and future. The thought of it frightens me but I guess there is nothing much that we could do about it.

No Country For Old Men has taken its time to grow on me, but that was only because then I lacked the required awareness and understanding to appreciate something that is as dark and painfully honest as this. No Country For Old Men is an example of cinema at its finest.

Filming on the bleak, seemingly infinite deserts of Texas and New Mexico, the Coen brothers accomplished the impossible: the filming of a Cormac McCarthy novel. The movie opens with our protagonist, Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), stumbling upon the striking wreckage of a drug deal done gone awry, and finding a briefcase containing 2 million dollars. Attempting to make this money his own, Llewelyn takes the briefcase and unknowingly sets off an unstoppable chain of violence, as he is tracked down by the ruthless Anton Chigurh, played by Javier Bardem.

The performances in No Country for Old Men are spectacular, especially that of Bardem. Anton Chigurh embodies pure, brutal evil so convincingly, that at times it is hard to remember that Bardem is just acting.  The film offers amazing visuals and elements of a heart-pounding thriller, while also feeling like a character study of Moss and Chigurh. The film is also incredibly focused, with almost every sentence uttered by the characters feeling intriguing and important to the progression of the story.

One of the most interesting and effective tools used by the Coen brothers throughout the movie is the usage of silence. The film completely lacks any cinematic music or soundtrack, allowing the dead, yet piercing silence to take over some of the most suspenseful moments, making them more spine-tingling than any music ever could. 

Ultimately, No Country is an incredibly suspenseful, thought-provoking, and thrilling ride with incredible direction by Joel and Ethan Coen to bring the novel to life.

Joel and Ethan Coen have been making films since the mid 80´s and some of them had become beloved films or even consider classics, but by the mid 2000´s they were on the infamous list of "Great Directors that Had Never Win an Oscar" until they managed to free themselves from that curse with "No Country for Old Men".
Llewelyn Moss is a Vietnam veteran who comes across a drug deal gone wrong while he´s hunting in the middle of a Texas desert, he finds a case with 2 million dollars in it and decides to keep the money. Moss doesn't know that his naïve action makes him the primarily target of a psychotic hitman that will stop at nothing in order to reclaim the money. This series of events draws the attention of Sheriff Ed Tom Bell who will try to find Moss whereabouts before the psychotic hitman gets to him.
When you make an adaptation of a book/novel, there are two directions that you could go with: Modifying some segments of the source material in order to fulfill a 2-3hr runtime or you could try to make an adaptation as faithful to the source material as possible, the Coen brothers decided to take their adaptation of Cormac McCarthy´s novel into the second type of direction.  "No Country for Old Men" is an extremely well made film filled with greatness: The performances are solid with Javier Bardem stealing the film in a unforgettable performance as a creepy, calculating and bloodthirsty hitman; the story is extremely simple but is executed perfectly, a spot on pacing, memorable sequences, a surprising mixture of various genres (drama, action, thriller and even western), the Coen´s trademark black humor and over the top violence is here in little doses, Joel and Ethan´s directing is focused on the details, the narrative just throws you into this world and connects the lives of our three main characters in a credible way, a perfect amount of ambiguity, beautiful cinematography that perfectly creates a western style, a fantastic use of multiple themes, an impeccable use of dialog when it is absolutely needed, and the whole film feels not only as a feature movie but also like poetry as the conclusion comes closer. My only big problem with this film is the conclusion itself, it may be the same that the novel had and it concludes Moss quest of trying to literally outrun the devil in an appropriate way but it is also somewhat disappointing and lackluster for a film that had built up to its conclusion with such precision.
"No Country for Old Men" is an intense and unforgettable film that maybe the Coen´s finest work, but with the resume they have is extremely hard to pick, my runner-up film of 2007.

What's really intriguing about this film is that I couldn't figure out who the main character or main focus character was in the film. It was a mesh of 3 different lifestyles that were forced to come together. The plot follows the story of Llewelyn Moss who takes a bag full of money from a gang of drug dealers who've been massacred. Although things may seem good for Llewelyn now, he doesn't expect Anton to come after him to collect the money and will stop at nothing to get it. This film has outstanding acting from Josh Brolin, Tommy Lee Jones, and an especially dark Javier Bardem. The whole cast is memorable and fantastic choices because these actors played characters that seemed real and acted how real people would in the situation given. There's no demonstration of unnecessary action or gore to be found, everything that Anton does is totally effective in every way and NEEDS to be in this film. Every character has a different problem that they are trying to solve in their own lives besides the main one that they are involved in and it gives the characters depth. Ed wants to retire the police force, Llewelyn wants to help him and his wife with the money, and Anton wants to feel wealthy and dangerous in his own psychopathic way. What really reaches the standard for a great movie in my perspective is when I feel compassion for the characters and how they feel and how they create memorable scenes to show to other people. I got to the point in the very end of No Country For Old Men where I cared for Anton who was extremely intimidating and evil! This film is very much like Silence of the Lambs in the way where the characters have back and forths with the antagonist and it's just really compelling. Hannibal and Anton are two totally different characters but they both made super memorable characters. This film has so much to offer to an audience. It's dramatic, its suspenseful, it's thrill packed, it's whimsical at times, it's interesting, it's emotional, and above all super entertaining. No Country for Old Men tells the story of a redneck dude who finds a bag filled with two million from a botched drug exchange in the middle of a desert.  Tommy Lee Jones stars as a grizzled old sheriff who finds the crime scene sans cash and tries to piece together what went wrong.  

Meanwhile, hot on the trail of the cash, is Anton Chigurh, a sociopathic enforcer who uses a cattle gun for everything from a tool to kill, right down to a door key.  The story becomes a long-winded game of cat and mouse, with the redneck running to freedom, Jones in pursuit, and Chigurh relentlessly following behind.  

The film, from the Coen brothers, features their signature auteur styles; this time embodying the desolate nature of the desert and southern Americana.  It shows a world of crime that is not often explored, and explores the folly of man's greed.  The cinematography is great, the acting is top notch, and there's next to no music in the film, creating a beautiful ambiance that really sells the film.

Es ist das Fragende in seiner Stimme, die den ganzen Film beschreibt: No Country For Old Men ist vor allem ein Western über einen abgrundtief bösen Mann. Der Mann heisst Anton Chigurh (wie auch immer man das ausspricht, jedoch sieht bereits das Schriftbild furchteinflössend aus). Chigurh (Javier Bardem) ist ein grosser Mann mit herunter hängenden Schultern. Er hat strähnige schwarze Haare und ein diabolisches Grinsen. Mit einer Stuntgun für Rinder reist er durch Texas, um zu töten. Chigurh stellt einen Erzählstrang dar in einem Plot mit Twist. Ed Tom Bell, der Sheriff (Tommy Lee Jones) stellt einen weiteren dar und Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), ein armer Mann, der mit seiner Frau in einem Trailer lebt, einen dritten. Moss stösst eines Tages in der Wüste auf einen gescheiterten Drogen Deal. Die Fahrzeuge stehen im Kreis (wie im klassischen Western) - alle Beteiligten wurden erschossen, sogar der Hund. Das Ged aber fehlt. Moss findet es in der Brieftasche eines Toten. Moss nimmt nun die zwei Millionen Dollar an sich, Chigurh will sie ihm wegnehmen und der Sheriff versucht, Chigurh aufzuhalten beim Morden. Ausserdem treten auf: Moss kindliche Ehefrau Carla Jean (Kelly MacDonald), der grossspurige Jäger Carson Wells (Woody Harrelson) und der Geschäftsmann (Stephen Root), der wiederum Carson anheuert, das Geld zu finden. No Country For Old Men ist einer der besten Filme, den die Coen Brüder je machten. Er enthält Thriller Elemente und das Motiv der Jagd, vor allem aber ist es eine Charakterstudie. Wie reagieren Menschen, wenn sie auf das reine Böse treffen? Chigurh ist so abgründig, dass er manchmal sogar komisch wirkt und es keine Möglichkeit gibt, ihn zu begreifen. Carson gesteht ihm immerhin zu, er hätte Prinzipien. No Country For Old Men bietet phantastische Dialoge; man erinnere sich an den in der Tankstelle zwischen Chigurh und dem Tankwart: Fraglos hat Chigurh vor, den alten Mann zu töten und darum gehts in dem Wortspiel, dass er ihm anbietet. Und die zwei Millionen Dollar? Es scheint so, als wäre es einfacher, sie zu finden, denn zu behalten. Moss versteckt sich in schäbigen Hotel Zimmern, er flieht, doch Chigurh folgt ihm wie ein Schatten. No Contry For Old Men beschwört die Zeit, den Ort, die Charaktere sowie die moralischen Möglichkeiten des Handelns. No Country For Old Men handelt von der menschlichen Natur und vom Schicksal. Die Bilder von Roger Deakins und der Soundtrack von Carter Burwell vermitteln ein Gefühl von Schönheit, aber auch der Einsamkeit. Wie erbärmlich erscheinen menschliche Gefühle im Angesicht unerbittlichem Unrechts? Der Film zeigt viel Mitleid für seine erbarmungswürdigen Charaktere. Viele Szenen sind so perfekt konstruiert, dass sich ein regelrechter emotionaler Sog einstellt. No Country for Old Men is directed by the Joel and Ethan Coen and stars Josh Brolin as Llewelyn Moss, a hunter who stumbles upon two million in cash left from an apparent firefight. Moss is then on the run from a hitman (Javier Bardem) hired to take him down. Tommy Lee Jones plays Sheriff Bell, the sheriff of the country where this all takes place.

This movie was very captivating right off the bat. Javier Bardem delivered an Academy Award-winning performance, and it shows; his creepy villainous ways are captivating to watch. Tommy Lee Jones also delivers a solid turn as the only true "good guy" of the movie, despite the terrible acting of his partner. The Coen Brothers always deliver from a cinematic standpoint, and this movie is no exception. Also, the ending, while probably frustrating to most, really stood out as the strong point of the movie.

Unfortunately, this is just not an entertaining film. The dragging pace, absence of film score, and long periods of dialogue only made the movie feel longer than its two-hour run time. Josh Brolin's character is also one that is hard to cheer for. He is very cold and calculating for a non-criminal, making it hard to want him to escape from the hitman.

While I didn't love this movie (and don't understand how it won Best Picture), I appreciate enough about it to say it's worth watching if you have the patience. While Westerns aren't really my thing, No Country for Old Men is fine.

Final grade: B-

No Country for Old Men is directed by the Coen Brothers (Fargo, The Big Lebowski) and stars Javier Bardem as Anton Chigurh, a deadly and stalking killer hunting down Josh Brolin's character Llewelyn Moss who has stolen $2,000,000 in drug money.

The good? This is my favourite Coen Brothers film (so far), which isn't saying much as I haven't liked any of their picture's so far, keep in mind I've only seen a few. That is not a diversion from a recommendation however, No Country for Old Men is a successfully thrilling movie. Let's start with Javier Bardem, his performance is uncanny now in modern movie villainy and I fully understand why. His looming, eerie, intimidating presence caused major laps of full heart-in-chest moments by yours truly. A character delved with such mysterious creativity, who makes an oxygen tank of all things look like a AK-47 assault rifle. Josh Brolin acts well as Llewelyn Moss, you enjoy watching the predator, Anton, stalk his quick prey. No Country for Old Men may as well be silent, because the more intriguing and uncomfortable parts are set with no dialogue, just visual shock and skill. The Coen Brothers know how to set out a starting atmosphere in which nothing seems to be surviving, like a zombie apocalypse has just broken out. The key substance to the film is a bit iffy, but from what i could delve, it seems to try and push a hint that death is inescapable when living in a land of crime, drugs and money.

The bad? No Country for Old Men may be my favourite (so far) but it isn't an amazing movie. I found Tommy Lee Jone's character, Ed Tom Bell, to be unnecessary to the main man vs man survival situation. Adding no essence to what is otherwise a densely packed, realistically set thriller. In addition, the dialogue is droll for the most part. With the exception of Bardem's 'coin toss' exchange, a lot of scenes seemed to be set out just to falsely trick the audience into having some sort of relevance to anything that was happening. Oh, and please don't intrude Woody Harrelson into the movie halfway through, what a waste of a character and an actor. He seems to be a last minute icing on the cake to join two disjointed plots. Sad. Finally, the conclusion is left half-assed and stranded at it's peak of interest. Like they gave up or something.

All in all, I still recommend No Country for Old Men because it's moments of terror are worth watching just to feel your blood rushing through your skin, and an award worthy performance from Javier Bardem, seriously understandable praise of the highest order. Have your 'pee-breaks' whenever the movie switches to something you feel isn't fundamental, dangerous or putting you to sleep. You'll notice when it comes....Friendo.

Joel and Ethan Coen's direct a modern Western film for adults with their neo-noir Western thriller No Country for Old Men (2007). I am happy it won Best Picture at The Oscars as The Coen Brothers deliver a hard hitting serious film similar to their early neo-noir crime dramas Blood Simple and Miller's Crossing. The Coen Brothers find the beauty in the grisly with their strikingly quiet direction. They draw out each gunfight with skillful suspense and heavy atmosphere. 

Cormac McCarthy's story is fascinating and Joel and Ethan reinvent the wheel by taking a simple narrative and adding shadows and color with their warm direction. Every moment is tense as suspense builds into a hail of bullets and air blasts. No Country for Old Men is a cool Western that grips you from the brutal opening to the endless chase of a sociopath seeking out a man running away with 2 million dollars. I found myself practically holding my breath whenever Llewelyn encountered Anton.

Roger Deakins' iconic cinematography looks gorgeous and haunting with dark night and bright lights everywhere. His angles and framing for each gun barrel, man running, to locks getting blown out by air are breathtaking. I love Deakin's wide shot of Josh Brolin running over the sand dune away from the truck with blaring headlights at midnight. Joel and Ethan Coen's editing sharps cuts from ultra wide outdoors shots to indoor guns blasting with shocking efficiency. Their smart cuts and beguiling editing enthralled me for all 122 minutes of No Country for Old Men.

Joel and Ethan Coen's reflective writing and patience for the elderly feeling overwhelmed in a desolate wasteland with morality. Cormac McCarthy's nihilistic writing style is fully on display as Joel and Ethan adapt McCarthy's novel No Country for Old Men. McCarthy writes killers with no conscience, who wear down the police trying to capture them with their senseless killing. 

No Country for Old Men depicts the brutal realism of random people dying for no good reason and how depressing that looks. From a fearsome assassination, who relentlessly guns down all witnesses in his path, to a man desiring the wealth he's stumbled onto, to the sheriff out of his depth despite his years of experience. Tommy Lee Jones is amazing as Sheriff Ed Tom Bell with his shred observations and quick wit. Jones feels like he understands Bell's devastation at realizing old men cannot compete with the neverending hordes of evil that plague America with bloody crimes. Age and wisdom account for only so much when fighting against monsters.

Joel Coen's direction for his neo-noir Western No Country for Old Men (2007) is enthralling in every second. The Coen Brothers have achieved the remarkable in directing a fun and violent Western for contemporary audiences that does not feel old fashioned. Joel and Ethan Coen's writing is pithy and revealing, while the characters are unique types all their own. It is a slow burn like all Westerns, so you are going to have a good time watching No Country for Old Men.

I must mention the stellar acting from Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, and Tommy Lee Jones in particular. You will really feel like you have an understanding of who these men are at heart. They are memorable and complex characters that are a pleasure to watch perform. Josh Brolin is gripping with a nuanced lead role as welder and Vietnam veteran Llewelyn Moss, with his nervous face awaiting his pursuers with his sawed off shotgun. 

Whereas the impeccable performance from Javier Bardem is terrifying as he delivers one of the greatest villains in cinema as his stoic sociopath Anton Chigurh on the loose. His every moment feels intentional and compassionless. His cruel killings make No Country for Old Men a visceral experience. Woody Harrelson is excellent as Carson Wells, who seems smarter than he really is as you can never see your fate coming.

Tommy Lee Jones is entertaining as the hardened Sheriff Ed Tom Bell searching for these men. Garrett Dillahunt is funny as the stupid and simple minded deputy Wendell. Tess Harper is thoughtful and attentive as Ed Tom Bell's wife Loretta Bell. Barry Corbin gives a fantastic and poignant monologue about the pointlessness of fighting for justice in a cruel world with violent men. Stephen Root is fun as the tough businessman hired by the Cartel to hire Anton Chigurh and Carson Wells. Beth Grant's complaints as Carla Jean's elderly mother, who cannot stand the way things are is perfectly in line with No Country for Old Men's themes. Ana Reeder's cameo as the flirty girl by the pool is funny.

I adored seeing the ethereal Scottish actress Kelly Macdonald as her Southern drawl accent is flawless. I felt so bad for her innocent Carla Jean Moss. She's wonderful alongside Josh Brolin as they have realistic chemistry on screen. Her phenomenal natural acting makes for a delightful viewing until her sorrowful final scene with Javier Bardem. No Country for Old Men is certainly perfectly cast. You can even see a young Caleb Landry Jones before Get Out as the boy on his bike at the end astonished by Anton's bone.

Furthermore, I feel like in addition to No Country for Old Men's steady pace, the complete lack of music gives a sparse and empty feeling. Sound designers Skip Lievsay, Craig Berkey, Peter F. Kurland, and Greg Orloff hit you with each gunshot and gentle footstep. Alongside No Country for Old Men's steady pace, the subtle sound editing gives a sparse feeling. You are stunned with the minimalism of silence as you are witnessing quiet homicide with Anton's air gun over and over again. Carter Burwell is credited as composer, but only has a nice end credits song as the quiet in No Country for Old Men is very unsettling and builds atmosphere with an ever growing disquiet. There's no upfront score to be sure.

Mary Zophres came up with all these cool cowboy costumes alongside her fellow costume designers Lori DeLapp and Lisanne Scafine. Jean Ann Black's make-up gives everyone a natural, sweaty look, except for Javier Bardem in a ghastly wig that makes him all the more uncanny to gaze upon in horror. Jess Gonchor's production design and Nancy Haigh's set decoration ensures Texas, New Mexico, and Mexico look as impoverished and gritty as possible. John P. Goldsmith's art direction is lovely with dogs swimming down river to headlights shining through the darkest nights in No Country for Old Men.

Overall, No Country for Old Men is worth watching over and over again. It is the best neo-noir style neo-Western movie to come out in the 2,000's really. I would also recommend The Big Lebowski and Fargo from The Coen Brothers if you end up liking No Country for Old Men. For more modern Western movies, check out Hell or High Water, The Revenant, or Wind River.
